                        Dedication

To those men and women whose courage, determination and foresight has
contributed so much to the development of this great land of ours, we
respectfully dedicate this book.

Congratulations and Welcome
Pioneers and Friends

"It's '50 for Selby in '50". This is the slogan of the Selby Golden Jubilee
celebration. It is significant that Selby should be observing its fiftieth
anniversary at the midpoint of the twentieth century. During the first
fifty years of the century, tremendous strides have been made in science,
industry and agriculture. The United States has emerged from a minor power
at the beginning of the century to a position of world leadership in
government and economy. South Dakota has advanced from a prairie wilderness
to a well developed and stable farm prosperity. We can truly say on this
fiftieth anniversary that Walworth county and Selby have kept pace with
this development.

Selby is proud of its pioneers and friends who during the past fifty years
have contributed their industry, wealth and ability to the development of
this great agricultural area, and it is to their honor that this
celebration is dedicated. Many have been their joys and great have been
their accomplishments. They too have had numerous sorrows and bitter
disappointments. Such is the lot of the true pioneer. To those who remain,
Selby stands as a reward of the faith and confidence which they have
maintained during the past half century.

Fifty years are past, but with all the courage and vigor of our
predecessors, we who remain do on this occasion rededicate ourselves and
our posterity to continue for future generations the advancements which you
have begun. May your shining examples, as our pioneer forefathers, ever
serve as our inspiration.       A. M. HOVEN, Mayor, Selby.

Dear Friends:

     I have always been proud to call Selby "my home town". Its record of
growth and advancement is typical of the many similar communities
throughout our great State.

     The spirit of our pioneer parents who first settled this area has been
ever present as we of a later generation have sought to make it a bigger
and better city, and to have it assume its rightful place among the many
fine cities of comparable size in South Dakota.

     The Golden Jubilee Committee are to be congratulated for their
outstanding efforts in giving public recognition to this important
milestone in Selby's history.
                                        Sincerely,

                                        GEORGE T. MICKELSON, Governor.

        FOREWORD

           BY

Fritz Clement, Editor-in-Chief

Early in 1949 the Selby Commercial Club felt that it was fitting and proper
that Selby observe its Golden Anniversary in 1950 with a celebration
apropos to the occasion. In connection with this celebration it was decided
to publish a historical book and committees were set up to assume the
gigantic task of assembling material for such a publication.

In this book the committee in charge have tried to bring forth the
occurrences of the City of Selby from the time that it was founded in 1900
to the present day. Fifty years seem such a short time yet many things have
occurred during that period and the Jubilee committee has endeavored to
chronicle the happenings as accurately as possible. That we have made some
mistakes, we have no doubt, but we can truthfully say that we did the best
we knew how. The object of this book is to put into print biographies of
pioneers who have helped to develop this area; to give you histories of
Walworth county, the City of Selby and other surrounding communities;
histories of business institutions, organizations and other stories which
the committee felt would be of interest to the readers of this historical
volume. In this publication you have a permanent record of such happenings.

The source of information, in many instances, was meager, and the committee
members spent many hours searching out the facts. Many of the incidents
related in this book have been from mouth to ear and faulty memories made
the. going difficult at times. It is perhaps true that the book is not
complete and that some biographies have been omitted,--not because the
committee did not wish to include them, but because information necessary
to complete the biographies was not available. However, in this book, we
are sure that a true cross-section of the average pioneer has been obtained.

To select any one individual on which to heap praise for work done on this
book would be grossly unfair, for many of the committee members and other
volunteers spent hours upon hours compiling the data necessary to complete
a story. They have spent their time and effort with no hope for remuneration
other than a kind word or a friendly pat on the back for a "job well done."
Your editor-in-chief wishes to join with the entire committee in extending
deepest appreciation to those who wholeheartedly and with no thought of
reward, contributed so much to the publication of this book. To the
advertisers, who so generously bought space, we likewise wish to express
our thanks and appreciation. Without this whole-hearted cooperation from
all of you, this book could not have been undertaken. Again, we say "thank
you" and trust that you will not only enjoy this book but that you will be
with us when Selby celebrates its Golden Jubilee on June 22, 23 and 24,
1950. A committee has arranged a fine program for the three days.

                George H. Hoffman

Lieutenant Governor George H. Hoffman exerted a wide influence for the best
things in government and in civil and family life in the formative years of
Walworth county and South Dakota. He was deeply and sincerely impressed
with this then new country as a land of promise for the individual and was
just as sure that out on these prairies there would be created a bright new
star or stars in the constellation of states. He translated his faith into
works and was highly honored by his fellow citizens.

                George J. Schellenger

George J. Schellenger was one of the truly great educators of the early
days of South Dakota and Walworth county. He received fine technical
training and was actuated by a tireless ambition to see to it that the
children of the pioneers had the best possible schools. He served as
teacher, principal and superintendent of schools and became deputy state
superintendent, thus his influence assumed a state wide level. He returned
to his beloved Walworth county and literally his life was taken from him as
he labored at his chosen profession.

THE HISTORY OF SELBY

The City of Selby, as do so many of the towns located along a railroad,
owes its existence to a happenstance,--it hinged upon the decision of the
railroad officials and surveyors, as to where their new road, as it
gradually advanced westward, would locate. If, as was believed when the
town of Bangor was established as the county seat, the railroad had
extended its line from the Bowdle terminal straight west to the Missouri,
via Bangor, there probably would never have been a Selby.

By the middle of March 1900, Bangor's hopes were dashed to earth, and there
was no doubt that the road from Bowdle would angle northwestward and pass
about four miles north of Bangor. In May of that year, the NW 1/4 of Section
4-123-76 belonging to Adam Himrich and an adjoining 40 acres to the west,
owned by Isaac Smith, were definitely settled as the site for the new town
and were purchased by the Milwaukee Land company. In July the town had
been platted by the company and given the name of Selby. Just why it
received this name is not definitely known but it may have been named after
some railroad official.

        Adam Himrich, who once owned most of the land on which Selby is now
        situated. Still hale and hearty, he is shown with his woodworking
        hobby.

R. W. Reynolds was appointed townsite agent, with office set up in the
Farmers and Merchants bank at Bangor. The lot sale for the new town was
held at the Bangor courthouse on August 3, 1900, with prices ranging from
$200 for corner lots and $150 for inside business lots to $100 for corner
and $72 for inside residence lots. Bonus bids ranged from $5 to $130 for
choice. Sixty lots were sold, most of the buyers being Bangor residents,
with a few from Mound City, Bowdle and Gettysburg. A petition was
circulated almost immediately to submit to voters at the coming election
the question of moving the county seat to Selby, but Bangor's
disappointment in having been bypassed by the railroad was still too new to
accept the inevitable, and the question was defeated, lacking 164 votes of
winning.

Preparations for moving started at once, and on the day after the lot sale,
the J. J. Hoven & Co., located a small oil and tool shed on the back of
their lot in the new townsite. A few days later on August 7, the Auburn
hotel and barn were moved to lots 6, 7, and 8, block 13. On August 10, the
J. E. Hoefs residence and barn followed to lot 6, block 3. Basement
excavation was started for their store on lot 9. The J. J. Hoven & Co.
store, after several breakdowns enroute, arrived and located on lots 1 and
2 of block 7.

Then in rapid succession came the Flashman residence, J. J. Elfrink store
and barn, N. H. Kingman real estate office, the Reporter building, S. F.
Hoffman barber shop and bakery, the two blacksmith shops of B. W. Clark and
Lund and Drake, the Farmers and Merchants bank and the Walworth County
bank. The two banks started at the same time, a friendly rivalry as to
which would arrive first being witnessed by about 100 people. The time was
2- hours, 15 minutes, with the Farmers and Merchants bank winning by a
matter of seconds. Among the other first structures moved in were the Vail
and Kirkhoven building, the H. R. deMalignon and B. B. Potter residences,
the office building of Dr. A. Beil, physician, and Dr. Foster, veterinary,
the H. F. Ottman residence and barn, the A. F. Miles harness and shoe shop
from Mound City, the W. Vail, Fred Griffin, W. B. Burr and Mike Kirkhoven
residences.

        Mr. and Mrs. Siegel Hoffman, owners of Selby's first barber shop
        and bakery.

The first two trains, a work train and a mixed train, arrived in Selby on
August 17, 1900. A depot was built and equipped, and N. H. Kingman took
charge as the first depot agent. During the first three days of operation,
earnings were $2000. On November 1, the Milwaukee road decided to run a
regular tri-weekly mixed, passenger and freight train from Roscoe to Evarts
and return.

When several residents failed to get water on their lots, the railroad
company ordered in its well digging outfit which arrived September 7 to put
down an artesian well to supply the town with water. By the middle of
August hammers and saws were hard at it and several new buildings began
nearing completion. Among the new buildings were the Gross Bros. office and
implement building, a large addition to the Auburn hotel, the Guy Fletcher
barber shop, the Joseph Treanor drug store opposite the Auburn hotel, a
general store by J. H. Franks and John Dupper, the McCaull and Webster
elevator, the Victoria elevator, and the Amy, Kingman, and Taylor
residences. The A. S. Taylor and St. Croix lumber companies built office
buildings on their lots and by September 1, lumber stocks were. being
brought in. The St. Croix company was managed by Billy Mitchell, whose
family lived in rooms over the office.

The stock yards were built and Selby's first livestock shipment by rail, a
carload of hogs, was made by O. D. Buchecker August 24, and on September
22, Fenlon Brothers shipped out 11 carloads of cattle (286 head).  During
the latter part of August and the next three months, the town continued to
grow rapidly as more buildings were moved in--the majority from Bangor--
and others were built. Among those moved in were: George Clark livery and
stage barn, Woodman hall, Rudolph Cheskey building, M. E. parsonage.,
Stablein store building which had been purchased by D. B. Shaw & Son for a
furniture and undertaking business, the Melgaard drug store and Dr.
Gunderman building which was moved in two sections, the Bangor house which
started September 1 and because of difficulties did not arrive until late
December, W. R. Green bank building, Carscallen & Son harness shop, and the
residences of Dr. Beil, J. J. Hoven, Dr. Gunderman, H. P. Hankins and
George Clark.

New structures included: The P. V. Preszler general store north of the
Auburn hotel, the R. B. Wisch store building, a two-story business
structure owned by Wm. Flick and H. F. Ottman, the Isaac Smith hotel and
restaurant on the east side of main street, the Kashman and Bezankos
restaurant north of the Smith building, the Wm. Flick home, and a home
erected by Senator Varnum for his mother and sister. Geo. Clark and H. G.
Cartwright started dray lines, Campbell and Clark opened a meat market
November 1, Dr. Gibson, Bowdle dentist, opened an office in Selby, O. G.
Baker opened a shoe repair shop in the rear of Hoefs store, and Joe Nesbitt
opened a tin shop in the Hoven store.

Church services were held in the Woodman hall until the Methodist church
could be moved to Selby. The Ladies Aid Society held frequent chicken pie
suppers, the. proceeds being used to help pay the pastor's salary.

The Selby school building was completed and opened October 20 with Miss
Stella Douglas and Miss Varnum as teachers. Fred Griffin was appointed
postmaster and the office began operating December 17, 1900, in the front
part of the Record print shop building, located south of the Farmers &
Merchants bank. The mail was received by stage from Bowdle, and J. D.
Stewart was the assistant in the postoffice. The first dance in Selby was
held October 19 by the Woodman lodge in their hall. N. H. Kingman called
the first meeting of the John Manyan GAR post in Selby on November 3, 1900.
The first marriage was performed November 28, uniting Phil Lewis and Miss
Addie Wilson. The first death was that of Wm. Flick, who suffered a stroke
and died December 17.

By January 1, 1901, the town was well established and progressive although
only about five months old. Church services were being held regularly, the
Rev. James Davis of Bowdle, conducting Congregational services every two
weeks in the Woodman hall, Rev. Ingersoll of Selby held regular Methodist
services and Rev. Fr. Dahlman of Hillsview, held Catholic services every
two weeks. T. J. Thompson supplied and planted more than 300 trees in the
new town. Business additions early this year included the opening of a
blacksmith shop by Will Simon; E. C. Long, jeweler and gunsmith, moved in
with his house from Campbell county; H. R. de Malignon severed connections
with the Crown elevator and opened a machinery business, with a side line
of flour and feed, later purchasing the Parr coal and grain business; the
W. S. Schwartz tin shop moved into the Carscallen building and a bicycle
and hardware business added; R. W. Reynolds and Harry Baillet formed a
land, loan, insurance and law partnership; A. S. Taylor purchased the Phil
Lewis meat market and added a refrigeration plant, making it one of the
best in the state; Miss Esther Elfrink, doctor of osteopathy, opened a
practice; Dr. Eberhart, dentist, located a practice in the Auburn hotel.

Land seekers came in groups almost daily during the summer months. Selby
sponsored a baseball team, playing the first game on May 12, 1901, with
Java and winning 37-4. Main streets was plowed, graded and graveled and
sidewalks were built. Photo shops were located in town by C. W. Stoddard
and A. L. Artz. The Standard Oil company opened a tank station. A cemetery
association was formed and a cemetery located.

In July, a railroad well was sunk at the stockyards and water obtained at
53 feet. An artesian well was sunk and water and gas were struck at 1890
feet, with enough pressure to raise the water 50 feet and enough gas to
light all buildings on main street. The flow from the artesian well formed
the town's first skating rink. Selby had its first fire when a blaze broke
out in the Schwartz and Spork hardware store. about midnight December 20.
The Kirkhoven and Carscallen buildings burned but most of the contents were
saved.

In January of 1901, a meeting was held to consider the incorporation of the
town. Burr, Reynolds and deMalignon were appointed as a committee to take
further action. Late in July a proposal to incorporate passed by a vote of
45-2 and a few weeks later the following board of trustees were elected: A.
F. Miles, president, J. J. Hoven, Fred Griffin; other officers named were
C. E. Wilson, marshal; A. F. Stuck, assessor: Wm. Mitchell, clerk; H. R.
deMalignon, justice of peace; A. E. Birkholt, overseer of highways.

George Zeider moved in a home and A. F. Miles, P. E. Greenman, Tony
Birkholt, Dr. Foster, Joe Engel and Clarence Clark built new homes. The
first Memorial Day program in Selby was held May 30, 1901, with 500 people
in attendance.

The year 1902 brought the following changes: Consolidation of the Walworth
County and Farmers & Merchants banks on January 15; erection of a new
building south of the postoffice by Kirkhoven; Schwartz and Spork opened a
tinshop, hardware and harness store in the Gunderman store building; W. H.
Howe opened a law office in the Carscallen building and A. H. Smith opened
another in the Green building; Selby built a town hall and jail; official
railway mail service started in Selby on June 2; Selby held the biggest
July 4th celebration ever known in this section and a race track was built
for the occasion; Wilson and Kelly opened a livery feed and sales stable;
Baer and Wagner opened an implement business; Dr. R. W. Butturff, dentist,
located here; the St. James hotel, closed by Harry Van Horn in April 1901,
was reopened in July 1902 by Stevenson; Geo. G. Fredericks opened a jewelry
store and repair shop; Atty. Fred Tiffany of Mound City, moved to Selby and
became associated with the Reynolds office; the German Land & Investment
company opened an office with John Linden as manager; R. W. Reynolds
purchased a new car, one of the first in Selby; August Rettke purchased an
interest in the Simon blacksmith shop; B. B. Carscallen resigned as justice
of peace and was replaced by S. F. Hoffman.

        Once flourishing 60-barrel flour mill established in Selby in
        early days.

In 1903, the energetic little town attracted another industry,--a flour
mill, of 60-barrel capacity, opened by Lange and Schmeichel; August Schmidt
purchased the. Taylor home and meat market, the firm of J. J. Hoven &
company was dissolved, Mr. Hoven taking the Evarts holdings and Potter &
Burr, the Selby store; James Coffey and J. H. Holmes opened land offices,
a new chemical engine was used in fighting a fire at the Miles Harness
shop; the Walworth County bank erected a new building; a Selby Business
Men's League was formed with A. F. Miles as president, J. J. Elfrink, vice
president, B. A. Amy, treasurer, and A. H. Smith, secretary; Geo. Zeider
installed the first new light plant; W. E. Prann purchased the Swanson
building for a drug store; the first telephone system was installed during
the first week of June, with 45 patrons; the largest crowd ever gathered in
Walworth county attended an Old Settlers Day in Selby on June 19. The week
of July 11, a new $5000 school building was approved with the largest vote
ever cast at a school election in this area; Prof. G. J. Schellenger was
hired as principal of the school with Myrtle Potter and Bertha Burr,
teaching the intermediate and primary grades; a new baseball diamond was
made west of the lumber yard; an Episcopal mission was established; Michael
Wagner built a new home; W. S. Button opened a jewelry and repair shop in
the Prann drug store; contract was awarded for the construction of the new
Catholic church for $1750 to Ed Forte; $25,000 was spent on improvements in
Selby this year

A New Year's dance sponsored by the Episcopal Guild was held in the newly
completed schoolhouse to open the year 1904. School opened in the new
building the second week of January. George Flashman opened a Bowling alley
on the south side of the Gross Bros. Implement; the Mill company bought the
old Catholic church building and moved it to Main street to open a flour and
feed store; work started on the construction of the Episcopal church; a few
residents put in cement sidewalks; new homes were built by H. P. Gutz,
Fred Pressler and I. B. Niles.

In 1905 the Milwaukee Land company surveyors laid out an additional 10
acres north of the original plat of the fast growing Selby. New businesses
added were: The Mrs. James Kane millinery shop building on the corner next
to the meat market; the Selby creamery built near the mill, with J. A.
Chillquist as the first buttermaker; Dr. Gunderman erected a new building
south of his office for an undertaking and furniture business for A. F.
Miles. New homes were erected by Bill Simon and Martin Heen. The Selby band
was organized with H. R. deMalignon as leader. The Bert Smith barn with
horses and all contents burned September 30. The Selby Driving club
sponsored a carnival on June 27-28, with horse races and ball games. Dr.
Bergh, jeweler and optician, located in the Kane building. The first birth
officially reported under the new registration law was recorded at the
courthouse, a boy, on July 11 to Mr. and Mrs. Carl Abler. School opened
September 12 with Prof. Schellenger, Misses Flory, Farley and Burr as the
faculty and 84 scholars; an upright piano was purchased for the school.
Commissioner Birkholt graded Theodore street and hung three street lamps on
Main street. A well on the Reynolds lot was tubed, there being a plentiful
supply of soft water and a windmill and tower erected over it. O. G. Baker
opened a shoe repair shop in the Nusz building.

The year 1906 saw more business changes and additions, among them being a
new dray line started by the C. H. Baker family of Evarts; Dr. Myler,
dentist, located here; Chas. Dousman became the new attorney in the Kingman
investment office; John Ballensky opened a barber shop in the building
north of the Auburn hotel; a building was erected for the Farmers State
bank with H. P. Gutz as cashier, F. E. Gehrki as assistant cashier; A. E.
Byron, veterinarian, located in Selby; Geo. Raba opened a shoe repair shop
in the weekly reporter building; Otto Lincke bought the Gross Bros.
implement and H. C. Gross went into the Walworth County bank as cashier; L.
W. Maxwell erected an ice house and cold storage room in the rear of the
hotel; a well was bored on the Langhausen lot and a good supply of soft
water reached at 270 feet, Misses Paulson and Christenson opened the Palace
restaurant in the Berens building; Ernest Truesdale started a law practice,
A. F. Rounds opened a jewelry and repair shop. Selby's second city election
outcome was as follows: Board of trustees, B. B. Potter, A. F. Miles, Fred
Griffin; W. E. Prann, clerk; N. H. Kingman Sr., treasurer; H. R.
deMalignon, assessor; James Coffey, city justice; A. E. Birkholt,
commissioner of streets.

In 1907, Selby's volunteer fire department was organized and a new fire
alarm was installed over the engine house. Business changes included a new
elevator built by Montevideo Roller Mill company with Chas. Hoffman in
charge E. Moger opened a clothing store; John Schmeichel, who had bought
out Lange, sold the Roller Mill to Henry and John Nusz; Dudley Martin of
Aberdeen, opened a barber shop, the Preszler store closed out their stock
of merchandise; John Hoven bought the Cartwright dray line; W. B. Myler
purchased the Reynolds business interests; new homes were built by Dr.
Beil, H. A. Brockman and Frank Sawinsky. The first annual dance of the
Selby Fire department on New Year's Eve bid farewell to 1907.

1908 found Selby's citizens still making improvements. Cement sidewalks
were built on several blocks of main street and several residence streets;
feeling the need of a community hall, the Selby Development company was
formed to construct the Selby Opera House, Selby's second brick structure,
work starting on it in August; the Farmers State bank began excavation for
Selby's third brick building, to be erected by Contractor Webster when the
opera house is completed, laying of brick on this starting September 14.

On November 4, the proposal to move the county seat to Selby was approved
at the polls in the county, and after the official canvass of the vote by
the county commissioners on November 10, moving of the records began at
once and by evening, most of them were in Selby. On the following day, the
heavy moving was completed, making Selby officially the county seat. Moving
of the county seat, brought about the moving of more buildings into Selby.
Register of Deeds Emanuel Baer moved his Bangor residence to Selby, and was
the first county official to do so. More followed as rental property was
very scarce.

With the county seat definitely located here, Selby became one of the most
desirable residence towns.

The year 1909 saw Selby incorporated into a city. A special election was
called January 13, on the proposal of whether the town should become a
city, the vote being 57 for and 4 against, and Selby was therefore declared
a third class city. At a special election on February 13, officers were
named to serve on the city council until the regular city election could be
held in April. At this election, B. 13. Potter was named as Selby's first
mayor. Other officers were: Aldermen, Otto Doherr, M. W. Myler, Ward 1, W.
S. Schwartz Fred Griffin, Ward 2; A. F. Miles, August Schmidt, Ward 3; city
treasurer, N. H. Kingman; police justice, W. B. Myler; city justice, James
Coffey. At the first meeting of the new council on February 16, 1909, W. E.
Prann was appointed city auditor; A. C. Schmidt was named president, and W.
S. Schwartz, vice president. The first regular meeting was held on March 1,
and regular meetings thereafter on the first Monday of each month.

        B. B. Potter

On March 27, the grand opening of the new $12,000 Selby Opera House was
held. During this same week a special election was held on the question of
issuing $11,500 in bonds for a city waterworks system, with a vote of 34-4.
favoring the proposal. On April 4, new night service of a fast train to
Miles City, was started. On May 1, Selby's first rural mail route No. 1, was
started with C. O. Peterson as carrier, he being succeeded in the fall by
C. F. Hoffman. Business changes included a new barber shop opened by Chet
Peterson, a tailoring shop by Frank Pechek of Eureka, purchase of the Jay
Ervans dray line by Otto Steinhoff, a new meat market in the Berens
building by Turner and Gallon of Iowa.

On April 3, business men of the now thriving city called a meeting and
organized the first commercial club, naming the following officers: Fred
Griffin, president; A. A. Brown, secretary; G. C. Pierce, treasurer; W. S.
Schwartz, A. H. Smith, H. P. Gutz, W. E. Prann, A. Beil, James Coffey, O.
A. Alberts, W. B. Myler, directors. Meetings were held in the south room
of the opera house.

The first general city election was held April 21, with 90 votes cast and
the following elected: B. B. Potter, mayor; Aldermen. W. S. Schwartz, M. W.
Myler, Ward 1; Fred Griffin, H. P. Gutz, Ward 2; A. F. Miles, August
Schmidt, Ward 3; N. H. Kingman, treasurer; James Coffey, city justice;
appointed were: W. E. Prann, city auditor; T. P. Schwartz, chief of police,
at $40 per month.

At this time there was cause to amend Section 8 of Ordinance 1, to read as
follows: "Fast Riding and Driving: No person shall ride or drive any horse,
mule or ass in any public street, alley or ground in Selby at a reckless or
dangerous rate of speed; or operate any motor vehicle at a swifter rate of
speed than 10 miles per hour between crossings, 8 miles per hour at
crossings, and 6 miles per hour while turning corners. Nor shall any horse,
mule or ass, or motor vehicle be driven upon or across any sidewalk of said
city."

1910 brought a number of new developments in city affairs: T. B. Bowlus was
granted an exclusive lighting, heating and power franchise on April 4; at
the city election, there was no change in the officers, but a question as
to whether intoxicating liquors shall be sold in the city was approved, the
city council approved the building of an addition to the pump station to
house fire fighting equipment; additional bonds of $3500 were approved to
provide water for domestic use; in September the tax levy for the city was
set at 10 mills for general purposes and 8 mills to meet principal and
interest on bonds. Salaries of city officers were set as follows: Mayor,
$25 per year; aldermen, $15; city treasurer, $50; city auditor, $100. In
October T. P. Schwartz resigned as chief of police and John A. Schulte was
appointed.

New construction included the start of work on Selby's first cement block
building by John Berens, north of his business place; work started on
Selby's fourth brick building, 23x53 in size, by Dr. A. Beil for a hospital;
work also began on the new Methodist church; homes were built by E. G.
Powell, Dr. W. A. George and Jacob Baer. The telephone office was moved
from the Prann drug store to the south room of the opera house. In June
1910, water mains were laid for the city's air pressure system. In May,
Rural mail route No. 2 was established in Selby. Business changes included
opening of an ice cream and confectionery store by F. J. Prann, a general
store by J. H. Coates, opening of the newly completed John Berens garage,
V. V. Van Osdell bought the Big Onion restaurant from John Hagen.

On January 2, 1911 the city council passed an ordinance providing for the
appointment and salaries of a fire chief and assistants. T. P. Schwartz was
named as fire chief, with Charley Johnson and Charles Griffin, as
assistants. This year, the city also issued refunding bonds to cover the
city's indebtedness of $6,000 in order to get a lower rate of interest. On
March 6, water rates were set as follows: 60c per 1000 gallons; over 5000
gallons, 50c for each additional 1000 gallons; this rate was raised a few
months later to 80c and 60c. C. A. Potter replaced W. E. Prann as city
auditor. A curfew ordinance was passed to keep children under 16 off the
streets after 8 p.m., from September 1 to April 1, and after 9 p. m., from
April 1 to September 1.

Other interesting events were the dedication of the new Methodist church on
March 5, 1911; streets were leveled with a big road grader; contract was
let for the new courthouse and jail; B. P. Holter started a harness shop;
Edward Cords opened a loan and insurance office; J. P. Green erected a new
home; the Olympian and Columbian trains began service May 28.

At the annual city election of April 1911, W. B. Myler was elected as
Selby's second mayor; N. H. Kingman as treasurer; G. J. Schellenger, city
justice; F. J. Prann, police chief; Aldermen, C. Wagner, H. P. Gutz and
Henry Nusz.

        W. B. MYLER

1912 found the city council striving to add further improvements for the
welfare of the citizens of Selby. On January 6, an ordinance was passed to
the effect that all sidewalks henceforth must be constructed of cement,
brick or tile; funds were appropriated to purchase rubber outing clothing
and other fire fighting equipment for the firemen; on August 5,, an
amendment to Ordinance No. 3 was adopted prohibiting the erection of wooden
buildings or additions to buildings on Main street; a sanitary drinking
fountain was installed on the. Lincke corner; Main street was treated to a
regrading job and several hundred loads of gravel spread; hitching posts
were moved to side streets. Business changes include H. R. deMalignon
taking over the Miles furniture store; the Farmers Equity Union leasing the
Wagner grain house; and the purchase of the Selby Implement Co., by J.
Steil of Emmetsburg, Iowa. The commercial club was reorganized with H. P.
Gutz elected president; W. B. Myler, secretary; G. C. Pierce, treasurer,
and rented the basement of Dr. Beil's hospital as a meeting place. The new
courthouse and county jail were nearing completion. The April 16, 1912 city
election brought into office, three new aldermen: W. E. Prann Fred Griffin,
and Otto Lincke, and F. F. Haynes as city justice. The liquor question
carried by a vote of 77-27.

With 1913 came more events of interest in the history of Selby. Following
the destruction of the school house by fire in January, steps were taken at
once for the erection of a new school, which was ready for occupancy by
December 1 of this year. Selby had its first moving pictures this year,
with the Idle Hour theatre circuit of Aberdeen coming to Selby twice a
month. The first county fair was held on September 16, 17, and 18 and was a
big success. The Walworth county court house was completed and county
officials moved in on Monday, June 9. The old court house building was sold
for $235 to I. B. Niles who dismantled it. In July, another drinking
fountain was installed, this one on the Burr corner. In September sidewalks
were laid at the courthouse.

At the city election of 1913, G. M. Mickelson, H. P. Gutz and Henry Nusz
Jr., were named aldermen, H. R. deMalignon, assessor; G. C. Pierce, police
justice; W. B. Myler, re-elected, mayor; N. H. Kingman, treasurer; tax levy
was set at 10 mills. A number of new faces appeared in the business life of
the community: Jacob Repp of Akaska, took over the Stuck blacksmith shop;
Anna Larrabee opened a bakery and lunchroom in the building next to the
Wagner corner, Dr. Myler sold his dental practice to Dr. G. W. Vail; the
deMalignon furniture store was moved to the Gunderman building, better
known later as the Welton building; Frank Wall was appointed postmaster
with M. J. Hoven as deputy. Alderman G. M. Mickelson died while in office,
and W. S. Schwartz was appointed to fill the vacancy; N. H. Kingman
resigned as treasurer and G. C. Pierce was appointed in his place. Fire
damaged the Schwartz hardware store.

On January 16, 1914 the first Parent-Teachers meeting was held in Selby, and
this same month, the school with the aid of the Womans club, purchased a
piano for the high school room. In March 1914, a moving picture machine was
purchased by the opera house company, and shows were held every Saturday
night, with Albert Schmidt as operator. On June 27, the baseball club
purchased a grandstand from the Schultz Lumber company. Four of Selby's
present residents, made themselves better known locally this year when E.
H. Noteboom, was appointed county superintendent of schools upon
resignation of Guy Schellenger; Robert Abel was appointed manager of the
Victoria elevator; Leo Buchanan took charge of the Prann drug store; and
Albert Schmidt and Bob deMalignon took over the publication of the Walworth
County Record.

On April 6, 1914, just before the city election was held, W. B. Myler
handed in his resignation as mayor. At the regular election this month,
August C. Schmidt was elected mayor; G. C. Pierce, treasurer; Dudley
Martin, police justice; W. S. Schwartz, C. N. Burr, Otto Lincke, aldermen;
appointed were, H. R. deMalignon, assessor; J. A. Schulte, superintendent
of waterworks, chief of police and street commissioner, A. H. Smith, city
attorney; W. A. George, city health officer.

        August C. Schmidt

No changes were made in the city election in the spring of 1915. By October
of this year, Selby boasted of one of the best race tracks in the state.
The race horse sport had its beginning at Bangor and was moved to Selby
when the new town started, N. H. Kingman and Dr. Foster, both owning
purse.-winning horses. In 1915, a fine track was built at the fair grounds
under the supervision of Dr. A. E. Byron and N. H. Kingman Jr. Later Dr.
Byron was joined by others interested in raising race horses, notably the
late Eugene Overholser, and in recent years, O. L. DeSart.

In July 1916, a pair of cannon which had been donated to Capt. N. H.
Kingman from the Arsenal at Washington, D. C., were mounted at the
courthouse square. These were removed during World War II when the need for
scrap iron was so great that the county commissioners gave them to the
Legion post. In August of this year, Selby joined the Yellowstone Trail
association for the promotion of U. S. highway 12.

On November 6, 1916, Bird Wilcox of Ortley, S. D. was granted an electric
franchise which was to provide 24-hour service to the city and at a flat
rate of $50 per month to furnish lights on Selby streets with all-night
service. Five days later, three crews commenced work on Selby's first light
plant. One crew started on the construction of a building, the second
installed the street lights, including a row of ornamental steel standards
down the center of Main street. The third crew wired the buildings. Work
proceeded so rapidly that in one week a temporary building to house the
engines was completed.

On January 6, 1917, Selby used its first electric lights from the new
plant. The year also held other new developments for the city. Increased
demand for telephones necessitated installing a larger switchboard, and at
the same time, telephone poles were removed from Main street to the alleys.
Business changes this year included: The opening of a shoe repair business
by H. F. Hammer in the building north of the Berens restaurant; moving of
the Selby Mercantile store into the Elfrink building; reopening by John
Ballensky of the Dudley Martin barber shop in the basement of the First
National bank building, closed when Mr. Martin assumed his duties as county
sheriff; in May construction started on a garage north of the Smith & Brown
law office by Goodwin & Gruett; Selby's light plant, owned by Bird Wilcox,
was sold later in the year to the Mobridge Electrical Co., which was then
duly issued a franchise. In July work started on the new high tension line
to connect Selby with the new electrical plant at Mobridge. Juster Bros.
and Joseph Goldstone purchased the Campbell store, Gene and Royce
Overholser and R. E. Leach purchased the Schwartz hardware; Albert Schmidt
went into partnership with his father in the meat market; in October, work
started on a new garage at the south end of main street for N. K. Stablein
and Harry Mickelson; a contracting firm was formed by Hans Larson and the
Mitchell Bros.; many new cement sidewalks were constructed; Mrs. H.
Bergstrom and Miss Rose McIntosh each opened millinery shops.

The winter of 1917 was notable due to a heavy snow storm during the first
part of February, which halted all train service for four days, then after
three trains arrived in Selby, another two-day storm hit. It was necessary
to call men from Mobridge, Glenham, Selby and Java to help clear tracks in
the cuts in this area. A push plow with two engines, and the efforts of 300
men with shovels finally opened the. way for the trains.

At a city council meeting in March, J. A. Schulte resigned after serving as
marshal, waterworks and street superintendent for 7 years and Wm. Koch was
appointed at a salary of $79 per month. At this time Mayor A. C. Schmidt
and Alderman C. N. Burr also resigned. At the regular April election, Dr.
August Beil was elected mayor; J. E. Hoefs, city treasurer; Coleman Wagner,
H. P. Gutz and Henry Nusz Jr., aldermen, and G. C. Pierce as alderman to
fill the unexpired term of C. N. Burr; a tax of not to exceed 1 mill each
year was approved 52-5 for the purpose of raising funds to provide free
musical concerts to the public. A new recreation spot was created when a
tennis court was located south of the Selby hotel.

        Dr. August Biel

In January 1918, T. P. Schwartz, Selby's first fire chief, who had held the
position since January 1911, resigned and was replaced by the first
assistant chief, C. R. Johnson. At the city election all officers were
reelected with the exception of one new member, A. E. Byron, who became
alderman in Ward 3. In May, C. A. Potter, who had served as city auditor
for 7 years, resigned and A. C. Groth was appointed.

World War I began to force its influence upon the community in 1918. Wm.
Koch resigned his position to enlist in the Armed Forces; Robert Gruett and
Walter Goodwin were called and their Yellowstone garage was leased to Wm.
Drewein of Mobridge; O. S. Olson and John Ballensky took over the barber
shop when S. M. Johnson was called into the service; and W. G. Schmidt
arrived to replace Leo Buchanan at the drug store, so the latter could
answer his country's call.

War was not the only menace the country faced at this time, for in the fall
of 1918 came the terrible influenza epidemic. The mayor found it necessary
to issue a proclamation prohibiting all gatherings and parents were ordered
to keep all children under 18 at home and to allow no association with
others. The ban was in force for five weeks and was raised the latter part
of November. One of the closing features of the year was a fire in the
Schwartz Auto building which caused considerable damage. A forward step of
the year was the installation of street lights on side streets, and on the
depot platform and electric lights in the depot.

In the year 1919 Selby greeted the return of a number of the boys from the
Army, who resumed their places in the business life of the community. In
February Mr. Meyers, having purchased the Colburn and Moody estate, assumed
the controlling interest in the Walworth County bank and E. A. Walters
joined him as assistant. At this time Otto Doherr, severed his relations
with the bank, only to return 8 years later. The Selby commercial club was
revived again and engaged rooms under the First National bank for
headquarters, electing the following: E. A. Walters, president; R. L.
Overholser, secretary; Leo Buchanan, treasurer.

At the city election of 1919, August Schmidt was elected as alderman in
Ward 3, a position he had held in 1909; B. B. Potter was elected police
justice, and Frank Wall, city justice. A bond issue of $9000 was also
approved 134-39 for the purchase by the city of the Selby Opera House from
the Selby Development Co. A. H. Schmidt and Stewart Cook subsequently
leased the building for $500 a year. On July 1, a special election was
called to elect a new mayor to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Dr.
A. Beil. Eugene Overholser was elected the new mayor, a position he held
for 27 years. G. C. Pierce resigned as alderman and Otto Lincke was
appointed.

1919 also saw an extensive building program underway and numerous business
changes. Roy Hoefs had an auto warehouse constructed on the rear of the lot
occupied by the Schanzenbach cream station, to be used by Jake and John
Schanzenbach, who had secured the Dort auto agency; new homes were being
constructed by Eugene Overholser, Frank Wall, J. E. Hoefs, Walt Goodwin
and R. L. Overholser. Dr. W. A. George purchased the Beil hospital; C. E.
Boling bought the Jake Allerdings livery property and put in a tractor and
machine shop, with a repair and blacksmith shop in the rear; D. W. Welton
purchased the deMalignon furniture business and Leo Buchanan, the Prann
drug store; Chauncey Burr took over the Burr & Son store.

GENE OVERHOLSER

The year 1920 found the city taking steps to fill the need for a sewage
disposal system. The question of issuing $18,000 in bonds for construction
of a trunk sewer and sewage disposal plant was approved 106 to 22 at the
regular city election in April. The construction bid was let to the
Mobridge Plumbing and Heating Co., and work started in August. Ditch
digging operations for the sewer started in November but were halted in
December because of cold weather, but by then had progressed enough so that
many households could connect with the system if they wished. In April
1920, Selby streets were again regraded and graveled. Officers elected at
the regular city election were: Eugene Overholser, re-elected; W. M.
Goodwin, treasurer; J. C. Allerdings, Otto Lincke and A. E. Byron,
aldermen. Later in the year A. C. Groth, city auditor resigned, and N. D.
MacArthur was appointed to fill the vacancy; and Wm. Koch, who had returned
from Army service, was re-instated as chief of police, waterworks and
street superintendent at a salary of $125 per month. His position was
filled by Adam Himrich while he was gone.

Among the business changes which took place in 1920 were: A. H. Schmidt
assumed sole ownership of the Schmidt Market; W. B. Myler sold his interest
in the Myler and Cook real estate business to Robert Nusz; the Philip
Preszler pool hall managed by Jake Yost was sold to Brockel and Hauck; the
Modern Woodmen lodge leased the opera house at $70 per month from the city;
Chas. Hoffman resigned as mail carrier after serving 10 years, J. F.
Richardson being the new carrier; R. I. Rapkavitz opened a tailor shop;
Fred Shandorf replaced A. A. Brown in the Brown & Smith law office; W. R.
Hill assumed charge of the Boling garage; John J. Schanzenbach opened the
Central garage; Jos. Kalmer and Fred Rieger opened a cafe in the Selby
hotel.

1921 saw the letting of bids for a new high school building early in the
year and the completion of the building in November. On February 23, Jake
Yost rented the basement of the opera house from the city and after
concrete work and other improvements, he opened a bowling alley and
billiard hall. Work started on a sales pavilion on the fair grounds, and on
a county machine shop and warehouse. At an exciting city election, Leo
Buchanan, H. P. Gutz and Fred Shandorf were elected aldermen; B. B. Potter,
justice of the peace; and Frank Wall, police justice. O. J. Steinhoff was
appointed fire chief to succeed C. R. Johnson. In November an ice skating
rink was banked and flooded on the lots north of the Hoefs store.

In the 1922 city election, Mayor Overholser was re-elected, J. C.
Allerdings, Otto Lincke, A. C. Dobson and C. R. Johnson were elected
aldermen, the latter for a short term to fill a vacancy. W. M. Goodwin
resigned as city treasurer and was replaced by F. E. Gehrki. Business
changes included: Harry Mickelson became sole owner of the
Mickelson-Stablein garage; R. C. Swift opened an auto repair shop; Cook &
Nusz dissolved partnership; Mr. and Mrs. H. A. Taylor purchased the
Yellowstone cafe; Otto Steinhoff erected a large ice house; R. J. Gruett
installed Selby's first radio outfit in June, Harry Allerdings installing
the second on the following January. The city purchased 225 trees at a cost
of $117 to be planted as a start for a city park. Stewart Cook was
appointed city auditor in December of this year, a position he is still
holding. The postoffice was moved October 7, 1922 to the corner north of
the Burr store.

                1950 - SELBY COUNCIL OFFICERS

        Ed F. Perman, First Ward
        E. H. Noteboom, Second Ward
        Arnold Manke, Third Ward
        Stewart Cook, Auditor
        A. M. Hoven, Mayor
        Karl J. Kundert, Assessor
        F. J. Homeyer, Attorney
        Emanuel Baumann, Police
        Eugene Brenneise, Justice of the Peace
        Emil Kost, First Ward
        J. A. Vanderhoof, Second Ward
        Peter Kosters, Third Ward
        M. L. Baumgarten, Treasurer

In January 1923, Selby experienced its most costly fire when the Hill
Garage burned together with all contents including 10 automobiles. In
February, Mr. Hill and Geo. Schwarting took over the Mickelson garage. Two
other fires occurred in Selby in March of this year when the Hammer shoe
shop was destroyed and the Blacklidge home was gutted. The fire department
installed an electric siren fire alarm at a cost of $574.82, the city
paying half the cost. Only change in this year's election was D. W. Welton
becoming alderman. In cooperation with a movement started by the Selby
Womans club, the city council passed a resolution making it compulsory for
each grave at the cemetery to be marked. In August, management of the opera
house was taken over by the Mascot Theater Co., of Mobridge, with Geo.
Schwarting in charge.

The 1924 city election brought no change in the city offices. On May 1,
Adam Pressler of Hosmer, purchased the Overholser hardware. A daily bus
line was started by John Berens, operating between Mobridge and Pierre, via
Selby, and between Pierre and Linton, via Selby. Connections were made at
Linton with the Interstate Transportation Co., linking the North and South
Dakota capitol cities. The need for improvement of the cemetery street was
felt at this time, and on a set day, Selby's cooperative spirit was
demonstrated when a large number of residents turned out with teams, wagons
and shovels, completing in one day, a job which was expected to take
several days. Fire destroyed the Coleman Wagner elevator. Work started on
the Anton Allmendinger and Leslie Herring homes.

Early in 1925, August F. Hagen established a new modern hatchery in Selby,
an industry quite out of the ordinary in this part of the country. Other
business transactions were the purchase of the Walworth County Record by E.
H. Noteboom from Fred Griffin; the Burr store closed out its stock; A. E.
Kelly of Mitchell, leased the opera house; Wolff and Miller of Fredonia, N.
D., purchased the Hill garage, Henry Larson of Mound City bought the
Allerdings truck and other equipment of the Standard Oil Co.; the Taylors
sold the Yellowstone cafe to A. E. Kelly and Fred Dean; Fred Adolph's
tailor shop is moved from the Geo. Raba building to the Kingman office. A
special train is chartered by Selby business men to carry the band and fans
to the district tournament at McLaughlin, which Selby won, entitling the
Selby team to go to the state tournament. New homes were built by August
Hagen and Adam Pressler and the new Methodist parsonage went up. In
December, the city council purchased electric lighting equipment for its
first community Christmas tree.

One change occurred in the city officials in 1926 when H. G. Pipher
replaced Alderman J. C. Allerdings, who moved away. R. L. Overholser was
appointed assessor for the year. The Overholser brick business structure in
block 7 was started in June and completed early in the fall of the same
year, the Johnson barber shop occupying the north end, and a Golden Rule
store managed by Mr. and Mrs. H. W. Stoetzel in the south end. Walter
Goodwin and R. J. Gruett sold their garage to W. G. Chesky, Goodwin then
taking over the Standard Oil agency from Henry Larson. The John
Schillingstad family took over the management of the Selby hotel in
November. New homes were built this year by Frank Wall, west of the
schoolhouse, and twin bungalows by Mrs. Ella Christopherson and Joe
Maloney. In December Selby lost three buildings on Main street by fire,--the
Berens restaurant building, a small building adjoining it, and the Geo.
Raba building used by W. H. Hoffman for a cream station.

Several new businesses made their appearance in Selby in 1927: H. G. Pipher
opened a J. I. Case machinery business; a Texaco service station by Ervin
Kowalke and a Sterling Oil service station by Edward Mickelson were opened
on May 7. In June, Paul Bertha sold his interest in the Manke-Bertha garage
to Frank Taylor. The Golden Rule store sold out in July to J. C. Penney Co.
In August, Pat McNeely took over the opera house. G. T. Mickelson entered
the law firm of A. H. Smith. New homes built were those of Dr. Weiland and
Ervin Kowalke. In December, the county purchased its first rotary snow plow.

In February 1928, the J. C. Penney store discontinued its business in the
Overholser building and these quarters were rented by the Selby Mercantile
Co. In March, the city council appointed W. E. Hoffman as assessor, a
position he held for 19 years. Mrs. E. A. Walters was named to serve for
three years on the cemetery committee. The Congregational parsonage was
sold in March to Gottfried Wagner and work started on a new manse in May.
In the fall, W. G. Chesky began construction of a new brick and tile garage
building. Work also started on the new Dudley Martin home. This same fall,
Ed. F. Perman of Java, bought out the Lincke Implement Co.

During the first half or 1929, several business changes took place. In
January, H. A. Juster, after 15 successful years in the mercantile business
in Selby, sold out to Sam Raich of Ashley, N. D. In April George V. Head
purchased the Welton furniture business and Ed Hoven and Jake Nehlich
purchased the Jake Yost pool hall equipment. In July, a Piggly Wiggly store
opened, but closed its doors again on November 1. In June 11 men, including
Oscar Abel, Otto Fischer, Glen Bunday, Ed Mickelson, Frank Ross, Joe and
Kenneth Greene, Fred Goeman, John Schock, Sam and Bob Crawford purchased an
Eagle Rock airplane and constructed a 30x40 foot hangar, south of Selby.
The plane and hangar were destroyed in a fire on the night of September 2
of this same year. In June the city approved the purchase of a new fire
truck, which arrived in August, the city paying half the cost. In the April
1929 city election, Coleman Wagner, R. E. Hoefs and C. R. Johnson were
elected aldermen. There were no other changes in officers. The salary of
the mayor was set at $25 per year, aldermen $15 per year, and the city
auditor $20 per month. H. P. Gutz was named a director on the cemetery
committee.

 In February 1930, the city council approved the plotting of the Overholser
addition to the city. At this meeting Mrs. Pauline Clark was appointed as a
director on the cemetery committee. Walter Ress, who had taken over the
management of the opera house, installed the first vitaphone and Selby had
its first talking movies. In July, the city council approved $15,000 in
Refunding bonds. Transitions in business during this year were as follows:
Sterling Oil sold its interests to the Selby Equity; the Piggly Wiggly
store building was refitted for new quarters for the postoffice; A. C.
Avery purchased the equipment of the Yellowstone cafe, moving it to the
Selby Mercantile building, opening a bakery and cafe.

The year 1931 marked the end of the chapter for an institution which was
once the pride of the city,--the Selby Mill. The structure now owned by the
George C. Bagley Elevator Co., was dismantled, the machinery being sold to
a concern in Canada for $750. In March Robert Gruett took over the Avery
cafe business, the bakery being moved a few months later to the Burr
building. A WNAX service station was built at the corner of the junction of
highways 12 and 83. Fire damaged the Weiland dental office and Dr. Weiland
moved his practice to the basement of the First National bank building.
During this year, Selby merchants started a business promotion drive by
holding a Free Day once a month. One new name was added to the city council
as a result of the 1931 city election,--that of Adam Pressler as alderman.
Jacob Oswald built a home. In November Pete Thompson bought the J. P.
Wagner restaurant business.

No election was held in 1932, no opposing petitions being filed. Several
business places changed hands this year, among them being the Selby Bakery
which was sold by Avery to Adolph Oelrichs, and later in the year by
Oelrichs to Lloyd Sawinsky; Jake Nehlich took over the sole management of
the pool hall; A. D. Miles took over the Texaco service station and also
opened a funeral parlor; in December Gertrude Hoefs opened Milady's Shoppe.

In 1933, there was some building activity, Fred Adolph constructing a brick
building to be used as a cleaning and tailor shop. After it was completed
Leo Todd also opened a barber shop in this building. A new Catholic
parsonage was built. Gladys Gustafson purchased the Swanson beauty shop
equipment and opened for business in the Engebretson building. Dr. Gladys
Bratsberg, chiropractor, located in Selby. Robert Bauder purchased the
moving picture business from Walter Ress. Mrs. George Keiser and sons took
over the Thompson restaurant. Beer was legalized in South Dakota this year
and the city council approved several beer licenses. A. C. Beckman opened a
blacksmith shop in the Tom Engebretson building. In October H. L. Larson
was appointed as alderman to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of
Adam Pressler.

In the 1934 city election, Mayor Overholser and the following aldermen
were re-elected: H. G. Pipher, R. E. Hoefs and H. L. Larson. In May work
started on a new Phillips 66 bulk and service station by Emil Kost and
Henry Orth of Scotland. In July John Simon purchased the pool hall business
from Jake Nehlich. Several men's and ladies soft ball teams were organized
this year. In June A. C. Dobson was appointed alderman when H. P. Gutz
resigned, and later in the year when Mr. Dobson moved out of the ward, E.
H. Noteboom was appointed.

Early in 1935, Earl Payne opened a Gamble Store in the Franks building. As
was the case in a number of other years, no city election was necessary as
there was no opposition. In May Otto Fischer opened a liquor business in
the Thompson building where he was operating a restaurant.

In 1936 the city's sewer system was extended, improved and repaired under a
WPA setup. In February word was received that highway 12 would be rerouted,
proceeding due west from the Murray corner southeast of Java, to join
highway 83, 4 miles south of Selby, the combined highways proceeding north
to pass through the west end of Selby. In the April election, Mayor
Overholser was re-elected; Arnold Manke, R. E. Hoefs and Dudley Martin,
aldermen; police justice, Frank Wall. Voters also approved 75-41 the
question of establishing a free public library in Selby. On August 3, work
started on the construction of the overhead railway crossing bridge in the
southwest part of Selby. Later in the year a pump was purchased for the
fire truck, and the city also purchased ornamental lights to string at Main
street intersections during the Christmas season.

In January 1937, Ed F. Perman was named alderman to replace Dudley Martin,
who resigned to take up his duties as county Sheriff. Matilda Baumgarten
was appointed as city treasurer, a position she still fills at this time.
No election was held, there being no opposition. The DeLuxe cafe was sold
early in the year to Emil Hansen and Max Busch. A. C. Beckman purchased the
John Berens home and lots and the old Schanzenbach garage which he
remodeled and moved to his lots for his blacksmith business. In July of
this year, a livestock auction company was formed to hold weekly sales at
the fair grounds pavilion. Due to the change in the highway, the East River
Oil Co., purchased the Wm. Weigum property on the west side and moved their
station to the new location.

Major business changes in 1938 were the purchase of the Selby hotel by
Arend Lakeman, which left only one piece of business property in Selby
still under the same ownership as when the town started,--the Hoefs store
building. Walts Club sold out to Henry Neuharth of Mobridge, and the Selby
Equity purchased the Steinhoff dray line, which had been operating for
about 25 years. In December a WPA project was started to extend sewer lines
to the west end of the city.

In February 1939, A. D. Miles was appointed alderman in place of R. E.
Hoefs, who resigned. The city council approved the plotting of the County
Auditor's first addition to Selby. Nils Carlson purchased the Selby bakery
from Lloyd Sawinsky. Calvin Hamann of Eureka, purchased the Gamble store
stock from Earl Payne and moved from the Burr building to the south part of
the Overholser building. The Mickelson law office moved to the basement of
the First National bank building. Paige Keiser opened a dry cleaning
business in the Vail building. The Wolff service station was leased to
Oscar Byre.

With no opposition for any office, no election was held in 1940. Officers
serving now were: E. Overholser, mayor; Aldermen, Arnold Manke and A. D.
Miles, Ward 1; E. H. Noteboom and S. M. Johnson, Ward 2; H. L. Larson and
Ed F. Perman, Ward 3. Businesses changing hands this year were Lloyd
Sawinsky purchasing the stock of the Sam Raich store; Sam Raich buys the
Otto Fischer liquor store and Fischer, the Miles service station equipment.
In August A. D. Miles was employed by the city as night police. In this
same month, the Dakota Public Service Co., of Mobridge, was granted a
20-year electric franchise in a special election.

In January 1941, plans and specifications were pro. posed for the
remodeling of the city auditorium in the opera house. A. D. Miles presented
his resignation as alderman and A. M. Hoven was named in his place. In
October work started on the improvement and enlargement of the city
auditorium. Business news for 1941 shows Wm. Hoven bought the Selby Bakery
business; Adam Wahl became owner of the Texaco service station; Wilson
Wolff took over the Standard Oil business for Java and Selby; the Perman
Implement company moved their building from Java to Selby and started work
on a basement under the structure; in October a mattress factory was
started in the Burr building.

On Wednesday, March 25, 1942, just 34 years after the new opera house
building had been dedicated, ceremonies were held marking the opening of
the enlarged and improved auditorium in the structure. Late in the same
date, snow began to fall and later that night, the wind came up and there
began one of the longest lasting snowstorms in the history of the county,
the storm continuing for nearly five days, not clearing until the following
Monday afternoon. Power failed on Friday afternoon and was not restored
until Saturday evening, although the storm still continued. During the
emergency, candles, kerosene lamps and old fashioned stoves were pressed
into service. There was no motor or rail traffic from Wednesday evening
until Tuesday. Telephone and telegraph service was disrupted, short wave
telephone service being substituted. With World War II now underway, Mayor
Overholser, as chairman of the Municipal Defense council, appointed the
following as air raid wardens for the duration: A. M. Hoven, Dana F. Vail,
Herman Mecklenburg, Leo Buchanan, E. H. Noteboom, J. W. Hoven, Robert Abel,
H. L. Larson, Ed F. Perman, Clarence Bucklin and Albert Moos.

1943 was a period which saw many residence properties in Selby changing
hands. A few business changes also took place, two landmarks passing out of
existence: the Burr building which was purchased and dismantled by August
Lutz and sons, and the Welton furniture store building which was purchased
by Frank Gosch Jr., and moved to his farm where part of it was used for a
blacksmith shop and the remainder dismantled. Another business place, the
former Yellowstone cafe building owned by Franks brothers, was partially
dismantled late in the year. About this time, the Elfrink building on the
corner south of the Franks building, was also dismantled. In March, the
wellsite easement was renewed with Emanuel Himrich at $125, payable on
March 1 of each year. In June, Wm. Unker was appointed alderman to replace
H. L. Larson, who moved from the city. In September Emil Kost was named as
alderman in place of Dana Vail, who was called to serve in the Army. It was
also decided by the city council to cooperate with the Selby School
district in purchasing 4 acres of land, north of and adjacent to the city
park in Outlot B.

With the second World War well under way, 1944 was rather a quiet year as
far as expansion and business progress was concerned. Rationing and
scarcity of many items limited business activity. However, one of Selby's
largest and finest buildings, the Rabenberg Implement structure, was built
this year. Another change was the purchase of the former Lincke Implement
building, vacated by Perman Implement, by A. C. Beckman, who remodeled it
and opened a hardware store. The Walworth County bank building was
purchased by Robert Bauder and converted into a home. In June, the Selby
Record suspended publication due to labor shortages.

In 1945, several more business changes took place. In April, F. Clement of
Java, purchased the Selby Record from E. H. Noteboom and commenced
publishing the paper in May, after an 11-month suspension. In May, another
landmark, the Clark livery stable was sold to John Thies, who dismantled
it. In April Robert Bauder leased the opera house. In June, a long-felt
need was fulfilled when new and modern rest rooms were completed in the
Milwaukee depot. In July, the Schmidt Meat Market was sold to Lester
Simons. In August, C. L. Helm of Java, purchased the late Jacob Helm's
share in the Selby Livestock Sales Co. In September, Mayor Overholser died
suddenly. In October, Leo Walz of Ipswich, opened a Red Owl Agency store in
the former Hoefs store building, and Elmer Swanson opened the Texaco
station, which had been closed for some time. In November, work was started
on the North Central Propane Co-op plant, south of the railroad tracks. In
November, 1945, C. A. Potter, cashier of the First National bank, passed
away suddenly and Max Gutz, assistant cashier since 1930, assumed his
duties. This same month, F. J. Homeyer became a partner in law of George T.
Mickelson. In December, Geo. W. Paul of Milbank, purchased the Rexall drug
store from R. L. Overholser, taking possession January 1.

In January, 1946, Art Chesky opened a shoe repair shop in the front of the
former Smith law building, now owned by W. A. Eckart. Other business
changes included the purchase of the Overholser building by Adam Pressler,
the Simons Meat Market by Hettich Brothers of Roscoe, sale of the Lakeman
hotel to R. C. Hepper of Java, who sold it a month later to Wallace Young of
Hastings, Nebr. In March, the city council began laying the groundwork for
an extensive street improvement project and eventual hard-surfacing of
some of the streets. New water mains were to be laid and a new lighting
system installed on Main street. Albert M. Hoven became mayor of Selby in
April, Ed F. Perman and A. C. Beckman being new aldermen in place of Wm.
Unker and A. M. Hoven. No election was held as there were no opposing
petitions for the vacancies. In April, the opera house theatre was equipped
with new RCA equipment, the first in South Dakota. Work also started on the
Rabenberg airport, 1-1/2 miles south of Selby. In May the DeLuxe cafe was
sold by the Kronwalds' to H. L. Larson and Jack Vyse. Selby's first
pre-fabricated house was built this year by Jake Rabenberg. In September,
work started on the new Perman Implement building on the lots north of the
Hoefs store building. In November, George T. Mickelson was elected Governor
of South Dakota. Late in the fall, the Java Herald building was moved from
Java to the corner formerly occupied by the Elfrink building, and equipment
from the Selby Record office was moved into it. The grandstand at the fair
grounds was sold this year to the Mobridge rodeo association.

        A. M. HOVEN

More business changes took place in the year of 1947. The Sam Raich bar was
sold to Milo Swift; the West mattress factory located in the Raich
building, south of the bar; E. B. Brenneise purchased the Adolph building
and opened a dry cleaning and tailoring establishment; Alert Beckman took
over the management of the Texaco service station from Wm. Ackerman; the
Red Owl Agency store was purchased by Bernel Manke; Perman Implement moved
into their new building; Paul Smith opened a locker plant in the former
Perman Implement building. In April, the Delzer family purchased the Deluxe
cafe; in June the first poles for the new Cam-Wal REA co-op arrived; in
July J. S. Hopkins opened an implement business and Ernest Flemmer
purchased the Red & White grocery stock of the Pressler store and moved it
to the Smith Locker plant building; the Pressler store became exclusively a
ready-to-wear store; Wm. Knecht opened a cream station in the former
Jederberg building; the Midget recreation parlor was opened by Henry
Weiszhaar in the building south of Swift's Bar; Claus Kuehl opened an
implement shop in the building formerly occupied by the Byre blacksmith
shop.

Alferd Moos was appointed as city assessor and night police for the months
of July, August and September. S. M. Johnson resigned as alderman and Dr.
J. A. Vanderhoof was appointed in his place.

With the end of the war, restrictions were lifted and Selby's amateur radio
operators once more became active. Selby has three radio "hams" at this
time, who have federal permits to operate on short wave. They are David
Hoven, Arnold Manke and F. Clement.

In October, 1947, a petition was filed for the purpose of issuing revenue
bonds for the improvement and repair of the city water system, in the
amount of $70,000 at 3-1/2% interest for 20 years. Late in the year farmers
and the local fire department cooperated in a drive for funds for the
purchase of a new and completely equipped community fire truck which will
be on call at all times to fight fires in town or in the rural areas. In
September, a sign was erected on the double highway passing through the
west end of town, the sign designating Selby as Governor Mickelson's home
town.

The year 1948 saw the continuation of the expansion of Selby's business and
residence sections which had started the year before. Construction started
on a new and modern service station for the Selby Equity; J. S. Hopkins
remodeled and repaired the old postoffice building for his implement
business; Arnold Manke started construction of a modern brick structure as
a showroom adjoining his garage; a large warehouse was put up north of the
new Perman Implement building; Art Chesky started work on a cement block
structure in front of his home for a shoe repair shop; Bud Swift purchased
the Schmidt Meat Market building and after remodeling and redecorating it,
moved his bar into it; the Rural Electric company opened an office and
warehouse in the Hoef's garage building; Wm. Hennig Jr., purchased the
Beckman hardware; in October work was started on a new brick and tile
structure to house Hettich Bros. Meat Market; in November, Ernest Drown
purchased the L & H store from Lloyd Sawinsky; Henry Weiszhaar moved his
recreation parlor to the Raich building vacated by Swift's Bar; in
December, Ed Schanzenbach and Herbert Wolff purchased the Phillips 66
station; La Verna Baer purchased the Classic beauty salon.

In August work started on the city's $70,000 waterworks improvement project
and in November work was completed including the construction of a water
tower with a 50,000-gallon capacity, located north of the schoolhouse.
Emanuel Baumann was hired to assist W. C. Miller with police duties and
maintenance of streets and waterworks.

In the residence sections of Selby four basement homes were built, 16 new
homes went up and about 25 homes were moved in and remodeled, during the
years of 1947 and 1948. As a result of this extensive expansion, several
outlots were replatted into lots, streets and alleys.

Early in the year 1949 Selby began to make plans for the observance of its
Golden Jubilee in 1950. In March the Executive committee announced that the
dates had been set as June 22, 23 and 24, and sponsored a slogan contest
with prizes being awarded as follows: 1st, Arlo Kuehl. Selby, with "It's 50
for Selby in '50"; 2nd, Ardith Baumann, Selby, with "Fifty Years Old, and
Good as Gold!; 3rd, Edna Mecklenburg, Marshall, Minn., with "Selby Is
the Town to Cheer, 1950 Is the Year"- 4th, Mrs. Lorraine Holscher, Bowdle.
with "Selby's Olden Days Have Fled, Now Her Golden Day's Ahead"; and 5th,
Ellen McCoy, McLaughlin, with "Jubilee Hit! Selby's It!"

In the spring of 1949, ground was broken for the new $250,000 Berens hotel
erected by Joe Berens, the largest and finest building in Selby. In the
city election held April 19, Emil Kost and Arnold Manke were re-elected as
aldermen; Emanuel Baumann was appointed city marshal and waterworks
superintendent, with W. C. Miller as deputy. The city council having
accepted the bid of Glader Bros. for construction of a new white way street
lighting system on Main street, construction started May 18 on the project,
which was a big improvement. In June federal approval was received on a
street-oiling project, and in a special election on September 6, Selby's
voters approved the issuance of $30,000 paving bonds to help finance the
$80,000 project for the blacktopping of approximately 14 blocks of city
streets. The vote was 298-31. In October work started on the project, which
is scheduled for completion in the spring of 1950.

        ARLO KUEHL
    Winner First Prize
  Jubilee Slogan Contest

Business changes in 1949 included the purchase of the S. M. Johnson barber
shop by Herbert Aman of Mound City; opening of the new Hettich store
building in February; Leo Kuehl purchased the opera house theatre equipment
from Bob Bauder, who had operated it for 16 years; the city sold the old
jail building which is to be converted into a residence; Paul Smith
purchased the Red and White grocery and meat market from Ernest Flemmer;
Carrol Peterhoff opened a lunchroom on highways 12 and 83; Wilbert Hettich
opened the Minute lunch room, which was purchased several months later by
Ed Schaffer; construction began in the fall on a new theatre being built by
Ernest Flemmer and to be known as the Star theatre.

With fifty years of progress behind it, the City of Selby now looks
forward- to the second half of the century with its promise of continued
growth in view of the vast Missouri river development project which is just
beginning in South Dakota. This project is expected to bring about a new
period of industrial expansion and the resultant growth and prosperity will
be shared by nearly every community in the state. Selby, located
strategically as it is on the main line of the Milwaukee railroad, and on
the double highways U.S. 12 and 83, faces a bright future.
