THE HISTORY OF WALWORTH COUNTY

The history of a nation, a state, a county, city or village is written in
its people. Not its boundaries of earth and water, its soil and trees and
rocks but the blood and tears, the laughter and joy of the men and women who
make it their own. So for Walworth county the first re corded history is
that of the Arikara Indians who called it home--a peaceful agricultural
Indian tribe who built permanent dirt lodges, farmed the land and finally
made their last stand in fortified villages in the territory late called
Walworth. The first record of white men in Walworth county were no doubt
the Verendrye brothers, sons of Pierre Verendrye. Seeking the Western Sea
they must have made their camp ten sleeps from the Mandans within the
confines of this area. Later Lewis and Clark camped with the Rees, as they
were commonly known, leaving the record that they were friendly and
hospitable. The nomadic and warlike Sioux Indians fleeing before the
Chippewas from Minnesota, and with a predatory eye on the rich hunting
grounds of the Rees, beset these peaceful people with the guns of the white
man, against which the bows and arrows of the Ree were of little avail.
Associating the fire stick of the white man with the Sioux engendered a
hatred of the whites in the Ree Nation. Driven into a war of aggression and
attrition they made reprisals on the whites, ruthlessly destroying lone
trappers, hunters, and settlers, earning the name of treachery.

        Early Day Walworth County Residence

In June, 1823, General Wm. Ashley with a stock of merchandise, and a large
company of hunters, trappers, and river men, journeyed up the Missouri,
bound by boat for the head waters, where he and Major Andrew Henry had
established a post the year before.  Safely reaching the Ree village at the
mouth of Grand river near the present Ashley Island, he stopped to trade
with the Rees, who received the company in a friendly manner. Without
warning in the early morning before daylight the Rees made a desperate
attack on the sleeping company, killing twelve men and wounding eleven, one
mortally. Ashley got the men into the boats and across the river but they
were so disorganized that they refused to proceed further, threatening
desertion if he persisted in his orders. Determining to send a messenger to
Major Henry on the Yellowstone, he asked for volunteers, the only response
being made by a boy of 18, Jedediah Smith. Before setting out on his
dangerous mission the boy quietly knelt among the dead and dying and
offered a prayer, a prayer of such eloquence and power that the whole
company of hardbitten frontiersmen, hunters and river men felt for those
few moments the strength of Faith. In that solemn act the first recorded
Christian service was held in South Dakota, in Walworth county on the east
bank of the Missouri river be- low the present town of Mobridge. Jedediah
Smith accomplished his mission, reached Henry on the Yellowstone, returned
down the river to St. Louis and was back at the Ree village to lead a
command in the fight in August. Four thousand miles in sixty-six days with
no means of travel more rapid than Indian pony or canoe. Improbable as this
achievement appears, it is substantiated by military records.

As the sun, bursting from a bank of clouds, depicts in sharp light and
shade, objects in bold relief, so the deeds of man or group shine out from
time to time on the pages of history for good or evil. So the feat of eleven
young Teton Indian boys stands out in the chronicle of Walworth county
history. Learning of the outbreak of the Santee Sioux in Minnesota and the
massacre at Shetak Lake, the Teton tribe at Ft. Pierre, despite the urging
of some of the older chiefs, decided to take a neutral position. But some
of the young men of the Tetons organized a "Young mens association" to
render the whites active assistance. These boys led by Martin Charger were
eleven in number, the others, Kills and Comes; Four Bear; Mad Bear; Pretty
Bear; Sitting Bear; Swift Bird; One Rib; Strikes Fire; Red Dog and Charging
Dog. These boys were the object of ridicule, even open hostility from the
rest of the Tetons, and were known as the "Crazy Band" or "Fool Soldiers",
because they had sworn on oath to help the whites at all costs to
themselves. In early November, 1862, Major Chas. E. Galpin and his Indian
wife who were coming down the river with a party of miners, having moored
their boat at the mouth of Beaver creek were set upon by hostile Indians.
Due to quick thinking on the part of Mrs. Galpin who seized a hatchet and
cut the mooring line, they escaped down the river. Before they were out of
hearing distance, however, a white woman ran down the bank and shouted that
there were white captives in the Indian camp. Major Galpin reported this at
Ft. Pierre. Immediately Martin Charger and his band determined a rescue.
They gathered up their furs and robes, trading them at Primeau's store for
a large supply of food, and that day crossed to the east shore of the
Missouri and camped at Okobojo. The next day they went as far as the Little
Cheyenne and the next day camped at the mouth of Swan creek near LeBeau
with a band of friendly Yanktonais. Here they were joined in their missions
by two young Yanktonais--Dont Know How and Fast Walker.

        The homestead of Mr. and Mrs. T. G. Olson (deceased), a typical
        pioneer sod house in Walworth county.

The next day they found that White Lodge, sometimes known as Grizzly Bear,
the Santee chief who held the whites captive, had moved his camp down the
river to a stand of fine timber opposite the mouth of Grand river. There
they found that the captives were two white women and six children--Mrs.
Julia A. Wright and her five children, Mrs. Wm. J. Daly and one daughter.
The young Tetons and Yanktonais made a feast, invited the Santees and
immediately began negotiations for the release to them of the captives.
White Lodge became very angry and threatening, denying the right of the
Tetons to interfere in his affairs. The boys, however, were persistent
offering to trade their horses and other property and after much parleying,
bullying and jockeying with threats of bringing their own people, the
Tetons, and soldiers to destroy White Lodge and his band, they succeeded in
buying all the captives save Mrs. Daly, an attractive young woman, whom
White Lodge claimed as wife. The two sons of White Lodge, Black Hawk and
his brother, forcibly removed Mrs. Daly from White Lodge's tepee, trading
her for the one remaining horse. The weather was severe, it was the 19th of
November, snow had started to fall and the captives were turned over to the
band literally naked. Of their own property only their own blankets, a
teepee and two guns remained.

Wrapping the captives in their own blankets the band retreated down the
river pursued by White. Lodge and a few of his warriors. At dusk they were
forced to stop and pitch the teepee, the captives were placed inside and
the boys marched all night around the teepee to guard the captives and to
keep from freezing. Nightfall and the increasing storm, while causing them
untold suffering, still no doubt, saved them from White Lodge and his
warriors. This campsite was on almost the exact spot where Jedediah Smith
had offered his prayer for the dying in 1823. In the morning they started
on, reaching the camp of the Yanktonais on Swan creek. There they traded
with the Yanktonais, giving their remaining guns for a horse, an old cart
and a supply of food to last them until Pierre was reached. Mrs. Daly had
been shot in the foot so rode the horse, the children were packed into the
cart. Mrs. Wright was strong and able to walk but had no shoes. Martin
Charger took the moccasins from his own feet and gave them to her, the
remainder of the party divided into squads who assisted the pony by pushing
the cart.

Traveling as swiftly as possible without making camp at all they traveled
down the river, fearing at any time to be overtaken by White Lodge and
menaced by timber wolves. They were entirely unarmed, their food and
clothing scanty. In this way they reached Ft Pierre in two days where they
crossed the freezing river with great difficulty and were received kindly
by their own people and the trader. Chas. E. Primeau, the Indian trader,
dressed the captives as well as he could from his rough stock, and after a
short rest they were taken to Ft. Randall by Louis LaPlant and Frederick
Dupree; from there they were returned to Minnesota. Probably there is not
in history a parallel case to this act of gallant heroism and humanity
performed by untutored young Indians. Considering that they undertook this
mission realizing with what savagery the Santees might act in case of
failure; knowing the Indian code of no mercy to the enemy, these boys
traveled one hundred miles in bitter winter weather and at the risk of
torture and death delivered two women and six children of an alien race,
bringing them to safety through terrible personal suffering and hardship.

In 1881 Peter Couchman became friendly with Mad Bear and through him
learned the history of the "Crazy Band". Couchman bent every effort to have
these Indians recognized and honored. At the first official Old Settlers
picnic at Bangor in 1900 the survivors of the band were guests of honor.
They were Charger, Four Bear, Swift Bird, Mad Bear, Pretty Bear and Strikes
Fire.

In 1869 certain tribes of the Sioux Nation signed a treaty with the
government ceding a definite land district, which included Walworth county,
for settlement. Though the survey was not made until some time later,
settlers came as squatters, afterward filing on the land as homesteads or
other claims. The county was given the name of "Walworth" after Walworth
county, Wisconsin.

In 1875 Antoine LeBeau, hunter, trapper and trader, made the perilous
journey up the river and at the mouth of Swan creek established an Indian
trading post. Almost simultaneously Alec Landreau came down from the north,
stopped briefly at Swan creek and then settled on the west side of the
Missouri, though much later, in 1903, he made his home in Evarts.

The first of the squatters to enter Walworth county was John McLean, who
first stopped at Swan creek, later went to LaGrace in Campbell county and
then to Oak creek. The first to locate permanently was Jerry Brown near the
present town of Glenham, in the early seventies. Then came Tom Carter, who
lived at LeBeau until his death in 1888. He in turn was followed by Dave
Curler, Proper Perrault, "Old Tex" (who was never known by any other name)
all on Swan creek, and B. J. Olson, Lewis Larson, Martinus Olson and Simon
Olson at Reigstad. First white woman in the county was Mrs. August
Siebrecht, who came with her husband, their son, Swan being the first
white child born within the county boundaries. August Siebrecht "proved up"
the first land, the east half of the SW 1/4 and the west half of the. SE 1/4
of section 8-121-78 on February 25, 1883. This was a preemption as was also
that "proved up" by Wm. D. Ryan March 3, 1883. The first homestead was
proved up by Peter Johnson March 19, 1883. The first deed of record is from
Jesse L. Snipes to M. H. Montgomery which on the 19th day of May, 1883,
conveyed an original one-half interest in three quarters for one dollar.

The survey of the county began May 12, 1882, and was completed October 21,
1884. The township lines were surveyed by John N. Miller and C. M. C.
Swoon. The first town platted was LeBeau, the surveying and platting of
which was completed by Ebbaning Chilcott May 11, 1883. This town was
increased shortly after by additions which made an aggregate of 6,000 lots
in the city of LeBeau which prospered wonderfully for several years.

The first county seat was Scranton which was later added to and called
South LeBeau. The first meeting of the commissioners who were appointed by
Gov. Ordway was held at the home of Antoine LeBeau April 3, 1883. They were
Frank Kennedy and Oliver Shannon, Sr. May 12 Charles Wilkins presented his
commission and was also sworn in. On this date Frank Kennedy was chosen
chairman and Oliver Shannon Jr., was appointed register of deeds. May 24,
the commissioners appointed J. W. Zink, county treasurer, and on June 15,
made the following appointments: Fred J. Bowman, probate judge; Peter
Couchman, sheriff; and Andrew A. Johnson, justice of the peace. June 21,
the board appointed Lewis C. Bordwell, assessor; W. B. Burr and R. M.
Fairburn, justices of the peace; J. M. Paul, superintendent of schools; C.
J. Sturgeon, coroner; and Joe Ludlam, surveyor. At this meeting the county
seat was located at Scranton or South LeBeau and the license for sale of
liquors set at $200.00. The first warrant was issued to Richards and
Hollenbeck for stationery, $21.50. September 3, Wm. M. Evans was appointed
justice of the peace which completes the first set of officers including
Robert Bingham, clerk, who had previously been appointed by the Governor.
The first election on November 2, 1884, added W. B. Burr as states
attorney, the duties of that office having been performed previously by the
district attorney at Pierre.

        A group of early day county officials about 1908. Standing, left to
        right, A. H. Smith, state's attorney; G. T. Baumgarten, treasurer;
        seated, left to right, Tom Bowlus, auditor; G. J. Schellenger,
        county superintendent of schools, E. G. Powell, clerk of courts;
        Emanuel Baer, register of deeds; W. B. Burr, county judge.

The first newspaper under the title "The LeBeau Leader" was established at
LeBeau by Wallace Brown, immediately followed by "The Pioneer" published at
Scranton by Fred Bowman.

The first school districts were Scranton and LeBeau organized
simultaneously by action of the commissioners in 1883, Scranton being No. 1
and LeBeau No. 2. Charles Wilkins was the first teacher with a salary of
$30 per month. The first school building was erected at LeBeau at a cost of
$1,800.

By decision of the voters, November, 1884, the county seat was removed to
Bangor, nearly the geographical center of the county.

The period of growth in South Dakota from 1877 until 1885 has been called
the "Dakota Boom". The population during those years increased five-fold,
of this increase Walworth county received a fair share. Promoters there
were, and adventurers, but also a large class of honest but inexperienced
persons, clerks, factory hands and mechanics--veterans of the civil war,
both Federal and Confederate, and a flood of immigrants from northern
Europe--Scandinavians, Germans, Russians, English, Irish and Poles. In the
northern part of the county in Blue Blanket and Hiddenwood there was a
preponderance of Scandinavians; around Java, Akaska, Lowry and the old town
of Theodore, the Germans and Russians settled. Essentially these people
came to establish farm homes, attracted by the free government land. Even
those who knew how to farm in the eastern states and the old countries,
found that similar methods would not work on the Dakota prairies. The
successful method of working our soil had to be learned by sore experience.
Many, disheartened and disappointed in their high hopes of building homes
and accumulating riches, returned from whence they came, but many stayed,
facing and enduring the hardships and finally reaping the reward so dearly
won. Many flourishing farms today attest the stern determination of the
families who learned to know this land, a land that so generously repaid
those who loved and nurtured it. Small towns and villages sprang up, almost
overnight: Flora on the Joe Anderson farm on the river; Brisco on the
Carscallen claim, Theodore on the George Erbe land, a real town surveyed
and platted; Tislo at Rev. Skartvetts; Scranton, first county seat, so soon
to be absorbed by the bustling town of LeBeau and rechristened South
LeBeau; Evarts, famous and infamous; Bangor, so long and disputatiously the
county seat; Pontis, the little town that flourished during the construction
of the trans-Missouri bridge; Blue Blanket, on the Howell homestead. Gone
with the blizzards and burning suns of yesterday.

Not so bad as the rest of the state, the year 1889 for Walworth county was
dry, and the year following crops were also light. During the summer and
early fall of 1890 great uneasiness arose concerning the Indians. A
religious craze had broken out among them fostered by a Paiute named Wovoka
from Nevada who, claiming he was the Indian Messiah or Christ, instituted
"Ghost Dances" among the Indians and declared he would restore their lands,
hunting and all their dead warriors, if they followed his teachings. To his
credit let it be said that he advised them not to molest the whites nor tell
lies. Short Bull, a Sioux chief, interpreted this differently; designating
himself as the Messiah, he advised the Sioux to leave the reservations,
join in the dances which the Indian agents were vainly trying to quell. His
advice was an all-out rebellion against the whites. In this he was
enthusiastically abetted by the young Hunkapapas. It was rumored that
Sitting Bull had deliberately broken the Peace Pipe. Sitting Bull,
deservedly or not, was a name of terror. Memories of the Black Hills war,
the Red Cloud war, the Minnesota massacres, were too recent to have been
forgotten. Uneasiness grew along the river and throughout the county
despite the fact that Mad Bear, one of the "Fool Soldier" band, lived
across the river from the Nesbitt boys, and daily sent runners to them and
to Peter Couchman saying that there was no danger.

One night in the fall of 1890 a self-appointed Paul Revere rode from the
north to south of Walworth county--his terrifying cry, "Rouse and flee for
the Indians are coming!" was to create a panic that lasted for a week.
People hastily gathered their families and as many belongings as they could
take and fled to such places of protection as were available. Mound City
was swamped as were Bangor, Bowdle and the Olson store at Brisco. People
slept on store counters, saloon bars and in churches. At the Howell
homestead on the stage line, fifty people gathered and stayed for two days,
until word came from Mad Bear's camp that the Indian scare was baseless.
One family with six children tucked into the back of a spring wagon,
galloped their horses toward Bangor unaware that one child had rolled from
the back of the wagon. Two young men in a light buggy had picked up the
screaming child almost immediately and reached the family before the
frantic parents had more than turned their team to return in search of
their offspring. The family were the Kirklands and the lost child, Joe,
grew up to be a well-known ranchman and sheepman in the west river country.

Charles Ottman, an enterprising young homesteader in the northwest corner
of Walworth, had that fall acquired a sorghum machine, sorghum cane being a
new venture for crops in Walworth. Hitching his team to the machine,
Charlie started out, picking up his betrothed who lived on the adjoining
homestead, an attractive young lady named Julia Molstertiegen. Afterward
their young neighbors made merry with a poem of fifteen stanzas, every one
of which ended with "Fleeing the massacre who can be seen, but Charlie and
Julia and the sorghum machine!".

However humorous some of the incidents may seem, the terror and panic were
real. People returned to their homes very slowly. On December 15 Sitting
Bull, resisting arrest, was killed in his camp on Grand river and the
Messiah war was ended.

Following the two years of drouth in Walworth county came good crop years.
Bangor, the principal town and county seat, thrived, adding to its
population and businesses. The Walworth County Record, a consolidation of
the old "Rustler" and "Central Dakotan", edited by Fred Griffin, became the
official newspaper of the county. A stage ran daily between Bangor and the
end of the Milwaukee road at Bowdle, proprietor, George Clark. Drs. A. Beil
and H. R. Gunderman administered to the health of the community; W. R.
Green, attorney, upheld the law; J. Hoven and company, A. W. Vail, followed
by J. J. Elfrink, supplied the drygoods and groceries; they were soon
joined by J. E. Hoefs; Nesbitt Brothers, tinners and roofers; the Croix
Lumber company furnished needs for building new homes, the Auburn house, L.
W. Maxwell, proprietor, extended hospitality to the traveler; the N. H.
Kingman Investment and Real Estate company, and O. D. Buchecker were busy
locating new homeseekers.

A keen interest developed in Walworth county concerning the admission of
South Dakota as a state. Peter Couchman was chosen as delegate to Sioux
Falls to sign the constitutional amendment. First in 1885 and again in 1889
when the state was finally a reality. In 1891, Geo. H. Hoffman of Bangor,
was named lieutenant governor of the state, serving until 1893.

The economic panic and depression that hit the whole country from 1893
through '96 had its effect on Walworth county as farm prices dropped
disastrously. Beef was 4 cents per pound; pork, 5 cents; eggs, 5 cents a
dozen, and butter, 10 cents per pound. The barter system still prevailed,
however. Farmers came to town to "trade". Corn reached such a low that
farmers refused to sell, and used their excess for fuel. Land values took a
slight drop. Money, always tight in a frontier community, became virtually
non-existent. 1897 brought a brighter outlook to Walworth county as well as
the rest of the country. The war with Spain touched off by the destruction
of the Battleship "Maine" in the spring of 1898, created a better farm
market.

Three young men of Walworth county enlisted: Dick Kirkhoven of Blue
Blanket, Charles Green and C. Lindholm, both of Bangor. All of these young
men returned to Bangor with honorable discharges and citations, having been
attached to the South Dakota regiment in the Philippines of whom Gen.
MacArthur said, "The record of the South Dakota regiment in the Philippines
has no equal in military history, so far as I know."

The ladies of Bangor organized a chapter of the Women's Relief Corps. This
organization had a membership of twenty-five to thirty women with Mrs. N.
H. Kingman as chairman. Like the Red Cross workers of the First World war
later, they made dressings and rolled bandages, made up kits and packages
for the soldiers. Most of the meetings were held at the home of Mrs.
Kingman. Other workers in this organization were Mesdames Burr, Potter,
Clark, Elfrink, Gunderman, Beil, Vail, Howell, de Malignon, and the Misses
Anna Shaw, Anna Nesbitt, S. Douglas, Louise Treanor, Bertha Burr, and Maria
Nesbitt. Miss Maria Nesbitt, who had been a Civil war nurse read a letter
from an associate of Civil war days, Clara Barton, president of the
American Red Cross, which she founded in 1881. Miss Barton at the time was
personally supervising field work with the Army Relief Corps overseas at
the age of 78.

A song "Blue Manila Bay" composed by a Walworth county girl, Nora Robinson
Winkley, daughter of W. P. Winkley, gained nationwide popularity in the
year 1899.

In 1898-1899, the Milwaukee road was wooed by both the coal interests for
the lignite mines in North Dakota and the huge cattle interests in South
Dakota for an extension of its line from Bowdle; the North Dakota interests
promoting a proposed route through Eureka and on to Bismarck; the cattle
industry plugging for an extension to the Missouri river to serve the
shipping from the huge west river territory. The cattle interests won, and
in February, 1900, the survey was begun for a railroad line from Bowdle to
the river. In that year Walworth county entered into a period of growth
that continued for many years. Work on the line was pushed rapidly to
accommodate the fall shipping. Four towns were platted on the right of way.
Selby on the Himrich claim, Java on the McDowell claim, Glenham on Mrs.
Lowry's homestead, and Evarts on the Peter Couchman land.

Bangor, the county seat, was bypassed four miles to the north, and its
rival town on the railroad held its sale of town lots on August 3, 1900,
with the thermometer registering 120 degrees, probably the hottest day ever
registered in Walworth county, but the coldest day for Bangor for the lots
in Selby were bid in to a great extent by Bangor business men and the
handwriting was plain on the wall. October 24, townsite lot sales were held
for Java and Glenham with James Corson, agent for Java, John Lowry for
Glenham. The brash, new little town of Evarts had a growing population and
several business places operating, before the sale of town lots with T. F.
Orr as agent.

Frank Finch was the first station agent in Walworth at Evarts, with N. H.
Kingman Jr., at Selby a close second. The first train rolled over the
tracks into Walworth county on July 20, 1900, about 15 years after the
railroad had been extended from Ipswich to Bowdle.

July 10, 1900, Auditor G. L. Baumgarten made a detailed sworn statement of
the assets of the county, the same being $39,979.31, the liabilities
$36,663.13. The total assessment rolls of Walworth showed a valuation of
$1,487,366.00. The average price of a quarter of land rose from $900.00 in
1898, to $2,000.00 in 1900. The area of the county was 745 square miles and
the population in 1900 was 3,839.

In 1883 there was one teacher in one school at LeBeau by 1885 there were
twelve teachers. In 1890 seven more school districts were established and
by 1900 the register at the summer institute at Bangor listed seventy-eight
teachers' names.

During the week of July 28 Walworth county met and defeated its first
strike, that of the construction crew on the railroad grade. A new crew was
rushed from St. Paul and work on the grade barely interrupted.

John Lockhart was appointed first game warden in August, 1900. He named ten
deputies.

Early in the summer of 1900 the long struggle for the county seat of
Walworth county was ushered in by a petition signed by the necessary
two-thirds of the voters to remove the courthouse to the railroad. Bangor
fought back with everything she had. The issue literally divided the county
into two hostile camps. Selby, backed by the press, the railroad, the
northern half of the county and the undeniable advantage of location on the
railroad, never-the-less lost at the November elections and the courthouse
remained at Bangor.

From 1901 to 1909, the huge cattle interests contributed a large share of
the wealth of the county directly or indirectly. Gradually the farmers were
turning to stock and horses, hogs, and dairy produce for a source of
income. Better farm machinery became available to more farmers. Farm work
horses commanded good prices and were in great demand. The blacksmith shop
and the livery barn were important businesses in every town, large or
small.

Rangy Texas and grade cattle were being improved by crossing with Hereford,
Shorthorn, Black Angus, and Galloway stock. Ridgeway and Johnson shipped in
good Hereford grade cattle from Minnesota with several good thoroughbred
herd bulls. O. D. Buchecker tried to promote Galloways with but little
success as that breed never became very popular in the county. P. J.
Thorstenson established shorthorns in the county, and Gene Overholser and
Frank Boehmer improved their horses with some of the best imported strains.
Some notice was given the German coach horses brought in by Mr. Buchecker
though the Percheron was the most popular draft animal. Adam Himrich
advertised Percherons. While most farmers concentrated on work horses, a
few ranchers also raised running horses and trotting horses. Outstanding
horses in this class were owned by Gene Overholser, N. H. Kingman, Dean &
Boehmer, O. D. Buchecker, and the Foster ranch. R. E. Mudge and John Lowry
tried a venture in sheep but though the sheep made money, both sold their
ewes and returned to cattle. A few sheep were raised on farms, but ranches
given to sheep raising exclusively were not popular. Most farmers raised a
few hogs. Imported thoroughbred brood sows and boars made a great success,
as hogs at the time brought better prices than cattle, were a cash crop
more readily matured, and were comparatively easy to raise. Bertil Olson's
Duroc Jerseys were the pride of the county as well as of Mr. Olson himself.
When it was proposed to plot the new town at the Missouri river bridge on
Mr. Olson's land "Duroc" was the name chosen. Subsequently the site of
"Flora" on the Anderson homestead was also a tentative choice, but the town
was finally platted on the flat above the river bottom and named "Mobridge"
from the address labeling each piece of equipment and material sent for the
construction of the bridge, Mo-Bridge, a contraction of Missouri river
bridge. To date it is the only town of that name on any map.

For several years the breeding and sale of horses ran far ahead of cattle.
A serious threat to the welfare of that endeavor was the spread of
glanders, dreaded horse disease, from an infected herd, the Rousseau horses
across the Missouri. State Veterinarian, Dr. J. W. Elliot, for years fought
without much success for the destruction of all glandered animals. In 1901
he was ably seconded by a young man from Walworth county, Dr. J. P. Foster,
graduate of the Ontario Veterinary surgeon and dental college. In February
of that year Dr. Joe Foster, as he was known, received his commission as
state veterinarian from the governor.

Despite threats, undesirable comments, and downright libelous stories in
the press of the state, Dr. Foster pursued his investigations of the
spreading disease of glanders in the interest of farmers and stockmen.
Destruction and burial of the infected animals was the only means of
stamping out this dread disease. Dr. Foster worked untiringly to bring it
under control. An incident at the time made Dr. Foster something of a hero
in the eyes of the whole country. Called to the ranch of a well known west
river stockman, Chas. Johnson, where anthrax was suspected, he found 20
cattle dead and also a small pustule on the wrist of Mr. Johnson's son, a
boy of 15. Correctly diagnosing the condition as anthrax, Dr. Foster having
driven his team all the previous night, immediately rushed the boy to a
doctor in Pierre where quick surgery saved the boy's life. The grateful
father and his friends did much to further Dr. Foster's intrepid fight for
health on the ranges. Recognition came for his service to the county and
state at large. Two papers made apologies for the earlier stories. In
addition to his public duties, Dr. Foster was for years a practicing
veterinarian in Selby and vicinity.

In 1901, the post office at Blue Blanket was discontinued. This was the
first post office established in the northern half of the county, in effect
before the county was organized.

In October 1901, Walworth county mourned with the rest of the country in
the tragic death of President Wm. McKinley. On the same day, occurred the
death of one of Walworth county's young educators, Wm. McKinnon.

The question of water was a crucial one in that early day. Shallow wells
were prone to run out and the ever increasing population of the small towns
rejoiced when an artesian well was successfully brought in. The railroad
company, promising a well at Selby, was disappointed in several attempts
and finally at 1890 feet, Norbeck & Nickolson brought in a well of good flow
with the added advantage of natural gas,--enough to light the town with a
small outlay for equipment. The Walworth County Record of November 23, 1901
says: "According to the result of lighting from the well at Pierre, Selby
may well be furnished with light at small expense. While there may be a
dirninuation of the supply through the years, possibly some farmer or
mechanic may discover some cheap means of illumination which will enable
the people of Selby to dispense with a gas plant."

        Commet-McGlenn straw-burning threshing outfit operated in Walworth
        county about 1895.

In 1903, real estate men headed by R. W. Reynolds and N. H. Kingman, backed
by the Milwaukee Land Company and Milwaukee road, advertised extensively,
creating a land boom in Blue Blanket valley. Testimonials of the
advantages for farming and stock raising were signed by many of the
successful farmers of the region and printed in the Walworth County Record.
Among them were James Meagher who came to the county in 1884, P. J.
Thorstenson in ]886, John Himrich in 1894, Wm. Kelly in 1888, Henry
Sawinsky in 1885, Edwin Jurgerson in 1883, W. J. Breidenbach in 1888,
Modeste Marin in 1883. Without exception, these able farmers came to this
county with little capital or none at all. At the time of writing, each had
a well-stocked farm with good buildings and machinery. To a man, they
advocated a more diversified and better farming program with an application
of business methods to farming.

        Early day sod-breaking outfit operated by Henry, Mark and
        Bill Potter.

As the farming methods improved, so did the yield and quality of the grain
harvested. In 1903, Lange and Schmeichel erected a sixty-barrel capacity
flour mill on land donated by the Milwaukee Land company south of the
Milwaukee tracks in Selby and the railroad company extended a side track to
the mill. Walworth county's prime No. 1 hard wheat made excellent flour and
before fall, the mill was a going concern.

Early in 1904 the county seat fight became a lively issue, with Java
entering the ring as an aspirant. At the meeting of the county
commissioners early in the year, Selby was found to have the most names on
the petitions and Java was out of the running as a site for the court
house. Despite the very active campaign put on by the Selby faction, the
election was lost by 39 votes. Immediately Selby instituted contest
proceedings against Bangor, which resulted in an order from the circuit
court virtually giving the decision to Selby. The contest action served on
the county officials was not answered and the following week, judgment by
default taken by Selby. The records were moved to Selby and the court house
in Bangor torn down. Said the Selby contingent, in excuse, "The court house
was a dangerous structure, could not be moved and should have been
condemned long before." "Vandalism!" cried the Bangor faction and took
steps to regain the county seat. Bitterly, the contest raged; the county
officials, most of them with homes in or near Bangor, were in an
uncomfortable position. After much recrimination in the press of the
county, several contradictory court orders, much litigation and delays that
carried the fight well into 1906, the supreme court handed down a decision
in favor of Bangor and the county records were returned. In the meantime,
however, the county officials had sought homes in Selby some like Philip
Spiry, county treasurer, moving their houses to Selby. When the decision of
the court re turned the county seat to Bangor, Mr. Spiry drove the four
miles to Bangor daily from his home in Selby for the remainder of the term.
Bangor at that time was a veritable ghost town,--the population in 1905,
numbering 19 and the buildings not more than a half dozen.

        Missouri River Bridge near Mobridge under construction.

        Alexander M. McKinnon as a School Boy
        Mr. McKinnon attended the first school ever held in Walworth county,
        at LeBeau, and so far as is known is the only surviving person who
        attended or had any part in organizing or conduction this school.
        It was taught by J. W. Blair, later a prominent citizen of Bangor,
        Herried and Mobridge, and was held in a cabin.

        Mrs. J. B. Johanson, mother of Mrs John A. Chillquist and
        grandmother of Mrs. Clark Brown of Selby, spinning a wool yarn, a
        common household task of pioneer county women.

During this period, Evarts on the river was shipping thousands of cattle
weekly and enjoying a wonderful prosperity with hopes of a bridge to cross
the river at that point and an extension of the Milwaukee road west. Troop
A, 1st South Dakota cavalry was mustered in at Evarts with 40 men, with
Gene Overholser as captain and R. W. Reynolds as lieutenant in charge of
the Selby contingent. This was a part of the state militia under Adj.
General Conklin. With the drastic cut in the 1905 budget, the state militia
was forced to reduce to one regiment. Troop A of Walworth county was one of
the four cavalry troops retained.

Five regular baseball teams, from Blue Blanket township, Evarts, Selby,
Java and Glenham, besides some pick up teams scattered over the county gave
the baseball fans at least a game every Sunday all summer. Every holiday
celebration was highlighted by baseball and a tournament was arranged for
the season's end. True, the umpires were an unhappy lot and many teams
won by default when the opposing team having taken umbrage at the umpire's
decision, stalked off the field in a huff. Horse racing, too, was popular
and a driving club had a large membership.

Late winter of 1905 and the spring of 1906 brought more rumors of railroad
crossings of the Missouri by several different roads. A survey at the mouth
of Swan creek, near the deserted townsite of LeBeau, stirred speculation
pertaining to the renewal of that town whose only remaining building was
the old school house. Surveys at Evarts with a report of good shale bottom
in the river boosted the prospects of a rosy future. A proposed extension
of the M. & St. L. seemed certain at the same time agitation for the
opening of the Cheyenne reservation across the Missouri was renewed.
Surveys were made by the Milwaukee road at the mouths of Oak creek near
Evarts and the B. J. Olson land on the Missouri opposite Grand river, the
latter site being selected.

The M. & St. L. commenced grading operations on a line to run from
Watertown to the location on Swan creek known as LeBeau, two miles distant
from the former townsite. At the same time plans went ahead for the
plotting of a town on the river near the bridge site. The Walworth County
Record states "It appears that 'Duroc' is not to be the designation of the
new town on the river but that the name 'Grandby' has been selected
instead." A small settlement of railroad workers, construction men and
engineers, sprang up on the river bank near the bridge construction and was
called "Pontis". On July 21, 1906 from the Record: "Another guess, and this
will be the last. The new town is to be named Mobridge and is located on
the northeast quarter of section 30-124-79, four miles east of the Grand
Crossing bridge over the Missouri". The work on the grade and bridge were
pushed to the utmost and on September 28 at five in the afternoon the first
train crossed the new bridge to the west side of the Missouri. The opening
sale of town lots took place on October 3, 1906, the sale conducted by C.
A. Padley, agent of the Milwaukee Land company. A special train was sent
out from Aberdeen for the occasion which was in the nature of a
celebration, with the Hon. John Lind, ex-governor of Minnesota, and Gen. S.
E. Olson delivering addresses. The Allerison-Murphy company served
luncheon. The sale realized about $18,000 for the townsite company.

In 1906, advertisements appeared for the Riverside Nursery and Fruit Farm,
proprietors, F. M. Thomas & Sons, Glenham. Telephone lines were extended
through Glenham to the river. Land values increased to $3500-$4000 per
quarter. Old style steam threshing machines were being replaced by new
models operated by gasoline-powered engines.

Mobridge, on the river, grew quickly into a thriving bustling little town.
The Milwaukee road installed a round house, with sixteen stalls. The large
railroad pay roll and the advantage of the west river trade territory
created an opening for many new business ventures. In early 1908, A. H.
Smith presented to the county commissioners a petition signed by J. J.
Klein, F. M. Goodman and sixty others, asking that proper steps be taken to
incorporate the town of Mobridge. The town was well on the way to
prosperity.

LeBeau, on its third venture as a town, was having a wonderful season of
growth and economic welfare. On the other hand, Evarts was fading out of
the picture, abandoned by the Milwaukee and shorn of its cattle shipping
wealth, the business men of its heyday removed to other towns. The once
colorful little village sank back into the obscurity from whence it sprang,
the ancient Medicine Tree and Rock a lonely sentinel on the hillside
keeping watch over the ghosts of shattered dreams.

In 1908, F. M. Thomas of the Riverside Nursery & Fruit Farm, was elected
Walworth County Horticultural director by the State Horticultural Society.
Mr. Thomas put on a campaign of tree planting in Walworth county with the
sincere cooperation of leading business men and farmers.

By 1908, the automobile had come to stay. Real estate men especially were
quick to grasp the advantage of the motor car and of real estate men,
Walworth county had a goodly share. Farmers were more conservative about
accepting the tractor for farm work; horses still were the acknowledged
answer to that problem.  Early in 1908 Selby again roused to do battle for
the county seat. Restraint, however, was the keynote of the campaign.
Chastened by the memory of the 1904-05 fiasco with its subsequent
embarrassments, a petition openly stated the facts and was signed by
virtually every voter in the county. The election was quiet and uneventful.
The victory was unmarked by any celebration, other than quiet satisfaction.

        Threshing scene on the Heinrich Nusz farm at the turn of the
        century. This engine is said to have been the first gasoline engine
        ever used in this section for furnishing farm power. It was what
        was known as a portable engine, that is it was mounted on wheels
        but was pulled from place to place by horses. These machines were
        used for many years before the engines that moved about on their
        own power, known as tractors, were perfected.

In 1909, the opening of the Cheyenne reservations land became an
accomplished fact. Land seekers poured into the new towns on the Milwaukee
and into LeBeau on the M. & St. L. Excursions were run by both roads. In
that year, LeBeau started another nose dive into obscurity. Business from
the huge interests of the west river cattle industry, whose open range in
the west river was now curtailed, was the life blood of the town. In
addition, the Matador, owned by Murdo McKensie, had a personal grievance.
Dode McKensie, son of the owner, was shot and killed in Phil Dufrann's
saloon, by Bud Stevens, bartender, in December 1909. In March 1910, Bud
Stevens was acquitted after a trial at Selby, despite the battery of legal
talent hired by the Matador and the sympathy of public opinion for the
McKensies. The Matador pulled their business out of LeBeau, followed by
most of the big outfits. A couple of disastrous fires, clearly of
incendiary origin, finished the town.

Between 1910 and 1914, many changes took place in the county. Real help
came to the farmers through institutes set up over the county, conducted by
men from North and South Dakota agricultural schools. Better methods of
stock raising and agriculture raised the farm income. Dairy and poultry
schools were added to these sessions. In the towns, as well as on the
farms, an extensive building program was carried on to house new
businesses and improve farm living conditions. In 1910 the first movie
theater was built in Walworth county by Ross Stacey at Mobridge. It was
called the Mascot, a real theater with a regular projection room. This
served Mobridge and the surrounding territory until the New Mascot was
built in 1921. In 1912, the Milwaukee Hospital association built the
Milwaukee railroad hospital, a three story building, fully equipped, with
Dr. G. H. Twining, district surgeon for the Milwaukee, in charge. For
several years, a nurse s training school was operated in connection with
the hospital. This hospital at Mobridge offered Walworth and vicinity
hospital and surgical facilities for the first time. The nearest hospital
with an adequate surgery and staff had heretofore been no closer than
Aberdeen.

The outbreak of the war in Europe caused scarcely a ripple in the summer of
1914. Walworth county crops were fair; business in the towns was good.
Selby, Mobridge, Java and Glenham were all making a steady growth. The
Milwaukee road with two branch lines running out of Mobridge increased its
office personnel at that division point. Automobiles were becoming very
common. Several dealers were selling the Maxwell, the Hudson, Reo,
Chevrolet, Buick and Ford.  Road improvements were one of the main projects
of the county. The section of Yellowstone Trail running through the county
was in excellent condition for the highways of that time. 1916 found 50,000
autos registered in the state; Walworth county residents added materially
to this number. Livery stables were on the way out and garages appeared in
every town.

The Mexican border incidents created the alarm and excitement in Walworth
county that the European war failed to rouse. Young men joined the Lemmon
militia enroute to Camp Hageman, and proceeded from there to the Mexican
border.

On August 17, 1916, the fourth annual Walworth county fair opened at Selby.
The largest crowd ever assembled in the county attended the fair on the
second day of its three-day run. This was, by far, the most ambitious
undertaking of the county and especially the town of Selby to date. Horse
and auto racing, a carnival company, livestock, hog, poultry and vegetable
exhibits combined with the varied exhibits in the women's building made the
fair an exciting, as well as satisfactory affair. An outstanding feature of
practical benefit was the gas tractor exhibition put on by two firms: The
Selby Implement company with the Heiden gas tractor and Krieg & Son of
Gettysburg with the Common Sense gas tractor. To E. H. Noteboom, fair
secretary, went a lot of credit for making this fair such an unqualified
success.

In 1916, for the first time in the history of the county the name of a
woman appeared on the ballot: that of Miss Nellie Lyons, democratic
candidate for superintendent of schools. While Miss Lyons was defeated, she
rolled up a nice minority vote. Perhaps the 19th amendment was even then
peering over the shoulders of the voters.

At the end of 1916 the statement of W. E. Hoffman, county auditor, listed
the assets of Walworth county as $282,126.04; the liabilities $280,160.00.

Though the government's severing of diplomatic relations with Germany in
1916 caused little feeling, late in the year a note of uneasiness crept
into the picture and by early 1917, a suspicion grew that we might be
embroiled in the war with Germany. When in April 1917, the President
declared a state of war with Germany, a wave of suspicion swept Walworth
county, in most cases entirely unjustified, against our citizens of German
birth and origin. This hysteria, fostered by a few fanatics, envisioned a
spy or saboteur behind every bush, and led to some of the serio-comic
sentimentalism sweeping the country. This fervor of ill-judged and
misplaced patriotism resulted in all sorts of rigid laws and orders for the
display and recognition of the American flag, the wearing of patriotic
buttons, banning of German speech and German newspapers. German measles and
German fried potatoes became Liberty measles and American fries! Not in
itself, dangerous, this state of mind fostered antagonism against some of
our best citizenry,--the German-Russian settlers,--who had helped to build
Walworth county to its present prosperity.

In the ensuing months, the lists of names growing on the honor rolls,
displayed so proudly, contained quite as many names of German origin as
those of other nationalities. In the Liberty bond drives, our
German-American neighbors set a shining mark. The war years of 1917-18 saw
Red Cross chapters established at Mobridge, Selby, Java and Akaska.
Walworth county residents gave generously of their time, effort and money;
and more important, there was scarcely a family that didn't have a son,
brother, husband or father in the armed services. On the river near
Mobridge, Camp Pontis was established. Recruits were sent to this camp, had
their initial training, were transferred to other camps in the United
States and thence to the European battle front. In the meantime, the slogan
"Business as usual" was the keynote of Walworth county's activity as well
as the rest of the country. With the shortage of food, a critical
danger,--Walworth county farmers made an all out endeavor. Home gardens and
home canning and conserving of vital food was the order of the day. In
Mobridge a newspaper war created four newspapers at the same time,--two
dailies and two weeklies: The Mobridge News and Mobridge News Tribune,
daily and weekly publications, edited by Lulu Wolf Barth, with Guy De Shon
as business manager; the old Bulletin, and the Dakota Democrat with Edward
McBride, former editor of the Bulletin, in charge. The dailies flourished
but a very short time.

By 1917 all towns in Walworth county had electric lights. Mr. Griffin's old
prediction of "a cheap means of illumination" had materialized.

Drawings for the Selective Service draft held in July, drew the names of 70
young men of Walworth county. The first ten (numbers of the drawing being
the order they were registered in the county) were: No. 2 Peter Arbach,
Hoven; No. 10 Pierce Anderson, Mobridge; No. 15 K. Akatsuka, Mobridge; No.
18 John Artin, Mobridge; No. 43 Pearl Alvin Brown, Glenham; No. 46 Ted
Brown, Mobridge; No. 75 Will Brazel, Mobridge; No. 107 Walter R. Crawford,
Lowry; No. 117 James Church, Mobridge; No. 126 Albert Christopherson,
Mobridge. Some of these men were exempt.

In the years 1917-18, the Milwaukee road changed its personnel to include
women in every possible position, even engine wipers, car clerks and
checkers. Walworth county went over the top in the first Liberty Loan drive.
Co. L Militia of Aberdeen guarded the railroad bridge. Foreign buyers
during 1916-17 bought up horses and mules for war work. In December 1917
the government took over the railroads, increasing the pay of the lower
class salaries and wages which increased the pay roll at Mobridge by 10%.

During the war years and the immediate post war period, livestock, dairy
and poultry prices went to a new high; so did small grains, corn and wild
hay. 1918 and 1919 were drouth years in the county.

        Aerial view of the Geo. Vojta farm, southwest of Selby, which
        placed first in a Walworth farm improvement contest in 1949.

In February 1919 the S. D. Legislature enacted a law creating a Hydro
Electric Commission, appropriated $50,000 for its use, and defined its
authorities and uses. The commission employed the engineering firm of Mead
and Seastone of Madison, Wisconsin, who made a report on findings
concerning a dam for the purpose of creating hydro electric power. This
survey covered all of the Missouri river in South Dakota and a report was
made April 10, 1920 which was later checked by The Fargo Engineering
company whose report coincided in every detail with that of Mead &
Seastone. The main facts of the report summarized as follows:

1. That physical conditions are favorable to the safe development of
hydro-electric power plants at various sites of the Missouri river in South
Dakota.

2. That the best site for immediate development is about four miles above
the city of Mobridge (Ashley island) where a plant may safely be
constructed with a 30-foot head at less cost than at any other point on the
Missouri river in South Dakota.

The report amplified its findings in a resume of the tremendous benefit to
the state of the use of this natural power; to Walworth county its value
was inestimable. An estimated cost of the project in 1920 was $8,716,983.

A great deal of activity over the northern part of the state, delegations
to Pierre meetings, and plans for irrigation and flood control brought
hopes of a realization of the dam at this point. The measure was defeated at
the polls, however, and interest in the project lay dormant for a number of
years.

Two years of drouth and grasshopper infestation were followed by a banner
crop year in 1920. The national Farm Bureau was established in Walworth
county. Most of the boys who had been in the service had returned home.
High prices still prevailed, but wages were dropping. The Milwaukee
railroad's personnel was reduced severely. Unemployment began to present a
problem.

Two progressive farmers added silos to their farm buildings: J. C. Schlepp,
and Arend Lakeman; making four for the county, the other two being in
operation on the farm of Garret Noble and on the Gutz and Myler farm.
Walworth county boys and girls joined pig clubs, a forerunner of the 4-H
clubs. Even in Walworth county, the importation of foreign farm products
pouring into the country was felt; cattle prices declined in the years of
1921-22-23 as did those of hogs, sheep, and dairy products. 1924 opened a
period of better prospects for farmers and business men. The wagon bridge
over the Missouri linking Walworth and Corson counties was finished in 1g24
and formally opened for traffic in November. This brought increased west
river business to the river town. Capt. Jacobson's ferry, so many years the
means of conveyance for all transriver travel, except trains, tied up on
the river bank--its heyday past.

        This farm is the former Buchecker, place, one of the best known
        farms in Walworth county. The buildings were erected in 1898 and at
        that time the place consisted of 1440 acres, mostly grass. It is
        now owned by Henry Seyer and is still one of the very best improved
        and most fertile farms in a wide area. It now consists of 640
        acres, all but 40 acres tillable, and has been improved by the use
        of modern soil conservation and tillage methods.

Between 1924 and 1929, this county, together with the rest of the nation
enjoyed an era of almost hectic prosperity. Credit was unlimited. Farmers
bought machinery on time; tractors, combines, cars, trucks, implement and
car dealers did a tremendous business. The war time slump seemed over. The
crash of October 1929 hit with the unexpected violence of an earthquake. The
midwest, including Walworth county, were slow to enter the depression
suffered during the next four or five years. The situation of this region
was never as desperate as in the more crowded centers. No human being
starved in this county, although some livestock did. Added to the downfall
of real estate values, and farm prices, came years of drouth and dust
storms. In the west river territory, huge barren areas of land left by the
farming boom of the war years, literally dried up and blew away.

A region of light snowfall, denuded of the natural grass which held the
soil, beset by drouth and high winds, the air was constantly filled with
fine silt, the top soil from thousands of acres. Selby went democratic for
the first time in its history in the fall of 1930, and in Walworth county,
the democratic ticket carried. A valiant struggle was made by banks and
business. Delinquent tax lists lengthened. There was very little money in
the country.

Continued drouth, hot winds, dust storms and grasshoppers plagued the
farmers of the county and the people in general. A few exceptional farmers
weathered this period in good shape, but the majority, were hard pressed.
Gloomy predictions came from the rest of the country. "South Dakota was
becoming a desert. It would take 20 years for the buffalo grass to come
back to the prairies". True, the conditions were bad, but the spirit of the
people was fine. Walworth county invoked the pioneer fortitude of its first
settlers.

Government relief agencies, a farm relief program, eased the serious
unemployment and the more critical farm problems. Rainfall in the spring of
1935 revived hope for a good crop year; not a bumper crop, for the yield in
staples in 1935 was well below the "prosperous" years, but so far above, in
volume and value the years of 1931-32-33-34 as to make the farmer more
prosperous than ever in the uncertain '20's.

The year of 1935 saw many changes in the county. The Hickory Stick, a
schoolmen's organization, was formed. Old age assistance became one of the
major issues. The Ashley Island dam project of Mobridge had a rebirth of
interest and was backed by every citizen of Walworth county. Julius Skaug
of Mobridge, whose unflagging efforts had kept this project alive, headed
the new activity. Citizens committees in every town of Walworth county made
plans to advance the project. Money was raised in all these towns for the
expense of furthering this proposed dam site. The relief program changed to
work relief. The shelter belt program was inaugurated. The. county planning
board organized. With farm prices still below parity, the AAA programs were
continued. The dam at Hiddenwood lake was completed, as was the dam for
Lake Evarts. R. I. Hall, popular Walworth county game warden, worked
over-time stocking both Hiddenwood and Lake Evarts with thousands of
fingerling bullheads; later came crappies and bass. Swan creek, above the
Akaska dam was stocked with bass to supplement the bullheads planted
earlier. Legal liquor came back to Walworth county. Six counties including
Walworth, formed a road association to promote the blacktopping of U. S.
highways 83, 12 and 212.

In the 30's, Walworth county became politically conscious,--not a few, but
the whole rank and file of the citizenry. For the first time in history,
Walworth county as a whole became aware of the two major parties. Young
Democrat clubs sprang up, quickly seconded by the Young Republicans. A
women's republican organization became very active. In fact, women for the
first time became active in both major parties. A semi-arid condition still
prevailed although the rainfall far surpassed the previous years. The rain
that fell came at the right time and crops were fair. In addition, the
situation in Europe gripped the attention of the people.

Gone was the inertia and inattention of 1914-17, every person in Walworth
county watched the rape of Europe with vital and at times personal
interest. The world had grown smaller. Communication and transportation had
changed a localized conflict to a world affair. In 1939, a decided raise
was noted in real estate tax collections and again in 1940.

On February 2, 1940, the first meeting of the Walworth County Livestock
Improvement association was held in Selby with Chas. Cheskey of Selby
elected president. Jake Rabenberg, farming the largest acreage in Walworth
county in 1940, tried out on his land several new type machines for water
and soil conservation under the direction of the county agent, James
Hopkins. Rainfall in 1940 brought back the green grass and wild flowers to
the prairie, as well as visions of a bumper crop for the farmers.

Selective service was set up under the conscription bill (federal); a draft
board was recommended for Walworth county to act after the registration of
all young men from the ages of 21-35. All were given the privilege of
enlisting by volunteering before their number was called in the draft.
There were 759 names listed.

        Aerial view of the W. J. Sawinsky farm south of Selby.

Lloyd Sieck was the first volunteer from Walworth county in the selective
service to be accepted for active service. Sadly enough, Sgt. Sieck was the
first Selby boy to give his life from wounds suffered in action in World
War II.

The agricultural year of 1940 ended with twice the crop returns of 1939.
The following spring, rainfall brought hopes of a banner crop and business
year for the county. The M. & St. L. railroad line from Conde to Akaska was
abandoned, cutting out the Walworth area including the town of Lowry.

Ground school training for 28 students was completed at the CAA flight
training school sponsored by the Mobridge Junior Chamber of Commerce, with
actual flight instruction scheduled within the month of February 1941 by
Instructor Clyde Ice of Spearfish.

An extensive tree planting program was continued at Lake Evarts,
Hiddenwood, and the lake at Molstad dam finished in the late 30's. In
1939-40-41 about 40,000 trees were planted around Lake Evarts alone.

Another CAA flight training school opened in July. In the meantime, young
men from Walworth were being called for the selective service, a number of
them, both volunteers and draftees, being sent to induction headquarters at
Ft. Snelling every month.

Harvest in 1941 was the best in 9 years. Wm. Klein, auditor of Walworth
county, announced the assets of the county as $632,855.48. Liabilities
$403,008.67. Surplus $229,846.81.

A dam for power and irrigation on the Missouri river was again highlighted
in Walworth county news. Encouraged by reports from the Bureau of
Reclamation and the army engineers, Ashley island was again submitted to a
Senate subcommittee, together with other dam sites at Gavins Point, Big
Bend and Fort Randall.

Welding classes and radio operator schools were held in the county in the
summer of 1941. The hard surfacing of highway No. 12 "The Yellowstone
Trail" was finished in Walworth county in 1941. Just in time, for September
brought 4.05 inches of rainfall, the heaviest precipitation in 14 years.

In response to the "More Food for Defense" campaign, farmers and 4-H clubs
in Walworth showed a substantial increase in dairy and poultry products,
sheep, hogs and cattle. At the Northern Show of Progress held at Mobridge
and the Achievement Days at Selby, 4-H clubs, both boys and girls,
presented a gratifying display of stock raising, homemaking and gardening.

Willingly enough, Walworth county prepared for defense,--subscribed to the
largest peace-time quota of the Red Cross. Measures were taken to collect
waste paper, scrap aluminum, conservation of food and vital materials were
subjects for editorials in the county papers. Public men made speeches
about the "Defense of Preparedness". On the afternoon of December 7, the
average Walworth county citizen would have conversed fluently on the
subject to the accompaniment of the usual Sunday afternoon radio programs.
Perhaps at the moment, someone was saying "The Axis doesn't want trouble
with us, we are too strong!" and then, the sudden silence on the radio, the
unbelievable, "We interrupt this broadcast to bring you a news flash,--the
Japs, at dawn this morning, attacked Pearl Harbor. No details are as yet
available." "They wouldn't dare!" was the first stunned reaction and then,
"It's a hoax, remember the men of Mars!" As the broadcasts went on, "Where
is Pearl Harbor?--It's in Alaska, no, that's Dutch Harbor--lower
California,--the Philippines--Pearl Harbor in the Hawaiian Islands! Why
that's where"--to so many homes in Walworth county and vicinity came the
heart-wrenching knowledge that their boys were in the danger zone. The
first garbled reports of casualties, and then the relief of the first
cables and wires. "I am OK.--We are safe,--don't worry."--Following those,
the days, weeks, and months of the siege of the Philippines. The
Philippines, where in 1898, our boys had won such signal honor. By some odd
repetition, the majority of the soldiers, sailors, marines and air force
men from this territory were again in active strife in this same arena.
There was no flag waving, no brass bands met the trains, very few songs made
a new appearance. The old songs of 1917-18 were dusted off and heard over
the radio. We were not entirely unprepared and in grim earnestness, the
men, women, and even the children of Walworth county settled down to cover
the skeleton of defense with the flesh and blood of honest endeavor.

        P. J. Thorstenson farm in Blue Blanket Valley.

Scores and scores of those unfit for, or exempt from, active service went
into war work. Farmers carried on an all-out program of production that
doubled any previous output. Even nature smiled on the war years; crops
were enormous. Cattle, hogs, sheep, poultry, and dairy products doubled and
tripled as did the price of these commodities. Every one put in vegetable
gardens. The county divided into areas which took in every town; instituted
a drive for the mobilization of woman power. This in turn led to
concentration on those twin problems, food and transportation. The canning
and preserving of food became the major home industry. Walworth county,
center of a huge territory, whose consumption of canned food per capita
topped any other in the nation for the war years, canned its own food. Not
only canned its own food but used home grown food products, releasing
hundreds of tons of space in transportation. There was virtually no black
marketing of food. In addition, never were families better fed. The same as
in the country at large, the point rationing system and ration books
presented a few problems. The long distances of travel in this open country
made the gasoline shortage acutely felt. Lack of new cars and trucks was
another headache, as was tire and tube rationing. New electrical equipment
and tools were scarce, nearly nonexistent. With such a high percentage of
the young and middle-aged men in the service or war work, the labor
shortage became desperate. Retired railroad men, doctors, clerical workers,
farmers, a great majority of them rolled up their sleeves and got back on
the job. Women were at work in all jobs possible. Many schools closed for
lack of teachers. Economically those years showed an amazing profit. War
bond issue quotas were always
oversubscribed.

Tons of usable scrap iron, aluminum, paper, rubber and used fat were
collected, as were "Bundles for Britain" and tons of clothing for other
devastated countries. Packages went out in every mail to boys in the
service.-- overseas packages as true to specifications of measurement
and weight as a Red Cross dressing. Through the Red Cross other packages
were sent to prisoners in German and Japanese prison camps. It was
difficult for the soldiers home on furloughs to believe that the home folks
couldn't just step out and buy limitless quantities of cigarettes, coffee,
T-Bone steaks, nylon hose.

A Walworth county girl served during the war as buyer for the Navy at a
base in Seattle. Odd requisitions came in at times; none more so than the
one from Army nurses in Alaska: "72 pairs of nylon hose or 51 gauge rayons,
size etc",--a note clipped to the requisition at the Base Commander's desk,
where the mail was first opened, read, "If you can find these, Bette, my
wife would be interested!" Added to this was a notation from every desk
enroute between the commander's and the buyer's --"Me, too!"

On May 8, 1945, the end of the war with Germany was proclaimed. Called V-E
Day, it was an occasion for joy. But the Japanese war still raged on. With
the cessation of hostilities in Europe, redoubled effort and interest was
centered on the Pacific theatre,--that war so peculiarly our own. Ample
rainfall after a somewhat dry spring pushed crops and gardens and another
banner year for farmers seemed likely. Restrictions were eased, too. More
vital products were released.

In the summer of 1945, the Bureau of Reclamation and the army engineers
ironing out some of their differences, in a series of articles published in
the county papers, proposed four power plants generated by water controlled
by dams on the Missouri, but completely ignored the site at Ashley island.
An allocation of $3,200,000 was announced for the development of Missouri
river resources in eight departments.

Selective service draft calls showed a definite reduction, and the
discharge of 70 World War II vets was recorded.

On August 14, at 6:00 P.M. (CWT), President Truman announced that the
Japanese war was ended, ending a vigil that had been kept since Friday,
when the Japs indicated that they would accept the Potsdam terms with a
proviso. The world went wild with joy.

Bells rang and whistles sounded. People screamed and sang, wept and prayed.
Very few people slept that night as the celebration swung into high gear.

The years immediately following the war brought many necessary adjustments
to the county. A Hunter's League was formed to protect and conserve local
game. Ray E. Travis of Mobridge, was elected president, A. L. Stoddard,
Selby, vice president; L. O. Lay, Selby, secretary-treasurer. Immediate
plans were made for improvement and extension of highways. The site at Oahe
near Pierre was selected for the power dam on the Missouri.

At the end of 1945, all rationing except for sugar was ended. A G. I. Bill
was proposed for the aid of discharged veterans of World War II. George T.
Mickelson, young attorney from Selby, expressed his willingness to run for
governor. Mr. Mickelson was attorney general at the time; had served
several terms as representative, one as speaker of the house. He was chosen
almost unanimously in the primaries and again in the general election.
Strikes in 1946 slowed down businesses. Reconversion of many war plants was
curtailed. Machinery, electrical equipment, tools, car, trucks, and many
needed articles remained scarce. Farmers continued to prosper. Farm prices
remained high. Payments for 1947 conservation would total nearly $70,000 in
the county, AAA Chairman W. J. Sawinsky announced. REA lines were staked
out early in 1948; one substation to be located in Walworth at Selby.

The county game warden, Albert Schmidt, with Dalton Logue, chief game
warden, Pierre, game technician; Reuel Janson of Mobridge, and Lewis Smith,
game warden of Ipswich, working 11 traps set up in congested areas over the
county, transferred pheasants to depleted areas in the state. 1110 birds
were transferred in two weeks of operation. The final count was 2072.

The Northwestern Bell Telephone company announced that 72% of all farms in
this area had telephones in 1948. This compared favorably with 42% in farm
homes in the nation as a whole.

At the spot where the new spillway was being constructed, Lake Molstad dam
gave way March 23, 1948 and nearly all the water washed out of the lake in
a few hours. Huge chunks of ice and dead fish swept across the highway
between Mobridge and Glenham. The destruction of Lake Evarts in 1942 and
Molstad, ruined hopes of fishing spots for this area.

In the years of 1946 47-48 two aerial hunting teams, W. D. Kelley, pilot,
with Pat DeSart, gunner, and Ray Knott, pilot, with Carl Erck, gunner,
materially depleted the coyote population in this area. Many business and
professional men in Walworth county as well as farmers, owned and operated
their own planes in 1948.

George T. Mickelson was re-elected Governor of South Dakota in November
1948. Republican candidates won in Walworth county with one exception.
Harold S. Freeman, Walworth county man, was elected state superintendent of
public instruction.

        Aerial view of the Jake Rabenberg farm west of Selby.

The years 1948-49 saw many new building projects throughout the county,--a
swimming pool for Mobridge, a modern hotel for Selby, new homes and places
of business in all the towns of the county, new farm buildings. Farm
products and prices suffered a slight decline in 1949. A storm on January
2, 1949 ushered in a month of the worst winter weather ever recorded in the
county, bringing to mind the terrible winter of 1880-81. Blizzards and
subzero temperatures continued for the whole month of January and into
February. Deep snow buried feed,--fuel and food grew short in farm homes
and even in inland towns. County snow equipment proved entirely inadequate.
Railroads were blocked. January of 1950 brought the same conditions with
even more snow. Old timers in the territory told how in 1880-81 settlers
along the river and from the LeBeau trading post, traveling on crude
homemade snow shoes and skis, brought fuel and wild game on hand sleds to
the snowbound and destitute prairie settlers. In 1949-50 skis had a great
deal to do with errands of mercy to isolated homes,--though now the skis
were on planes. Food and fuel, medical supplies, feed for cattle, parts for
machinery were carried in this manner. Doctors were flown in to patients,
patients were flown out to hospitals; many a trip was a race with a stork.
History was repeating itself with different equipment.

When the emergency arose in 1949, a number of these private operators
volunteered to help. Among them Pat DeSart, Al Weishaar, Norman Dayton of
Mobridge, Burdette Thompson of Timber Lake. In 1950, W. D. Kelly with David
Hoven of Selby, in an agreement with the Red Cross for emergency, made
daily surveys of the area. From January 2 to February 8, 1950,
approximately 10 emergency missions had been completed by the Kelly Hoven
team.

In the 67 years since its inception, Walworth county has passed through
many phases of good times and bad. Its sons and daughters have gone to make
good records for themselves in the outside world. Sons of the pioneers of
these prairies have penetrated deeply into the mysteries of the soil. Our
first agriculturists, the Rees, plowed the land with the shoulder bone of a
buffalo, a few acres here and there. Today, modern science tills thousands
of acres with a machine that closely resembles that simple early tool.

From the day when a few earnest settlers instituted the first school board
in the county, our scholastic record has been high. Many able, professional
men came to us and established an enviable record of service to our county.
Of the. medical men, Dr. Edwards, the first doctor in the county located in
1883 at Theodore, long-forgotten village near Spring lake. In early 1900,
Dr. Wm. George came first to Evarts and later to Selby. For nearly half a
century his name has meant help for the sick in Selby and vicinity.

Other doctors there were in numbers, among them, Dr. A. Beil of Selby, and
H. R. Gunderman of Bangor and Selby, who gave for a time their able and
selfless devotion to our ills. Of the Walworth county-born doctors, two
have returned to practice and to make the county their home. Dr. A. W.
Spiry, son of one of the earliest pioneers, Philip Spiry of Bangor and
Java. Dr. Spiry was graduated from Creighton in 1930, finished his senior
internship at St. Mary's hospital, Salt Lake City, Utah, and in August of
1932 returned to locate at Mobridge, where he has practiced continuously
with the exception of a period in 1942 spent as a surgeon in the army with
the rank of Captain.

Dr. John Lowe, son of Dr. C. E. Lowe of Mobridge, graduated in 1937 from
the Illinois college of Medicine, finished his internship in the Research
and Educational hospital of the University of Illinois and in July 1948,
returned to practice medicine as an associate of his father in Mobridge.

Pioneer attorneys in Walworth county, W. B. Burr, county judge,
representative in the state legislature, states attorney for the county;
and C. F. Clement, states attorney and publisher of the Java Herald; A. A.
Brown, attorney; R. W. Reynolds, attorney and real estate man in the early
days. Of the native-born sons of Walworth who made the law their vocation,
two returned to practice in the county: Arend Lakeman, graduated in 1937
from the South Dakota Law school of the University at Vermillion, and after
practicing for a short time in Java and Selby, moved to Mobridge in 1942
and is our present states attorney.

The present Governor of South Dakota, Geo. T. Mickelson, son of Walworth
pioneers, graduated in 1927 from the law school of the University of South
Dakota, practiced law in Selby, filled the office of states attorney for
Walworth county, served several terms as representative, one as speaker of
the house, was elected attorney general, which office he filled with
exceptional ability. With a vote unequaled by that for any public office in
the state he was elected governor in 1946 and again in 1948. His record as
governor, over a period as trying as any in history, has amply repaid the
confidence of the men and women who chose him so enthusiastically for the
head of our state.

Musical talent in Walworth has been of an exceptionally high caliber, both
vocal and instrumental. Our educators have been leaders in the state.
Many of the thriving business houses carry the same names, proudly borne
for almost fifty years, handed down from father to son. This same order
prevails on many prosperous farms. Walworth county has prospered slowly but
well. The numbers of the cattle compare favorably with the days of the
cattle barons. The quality of the breed far outstrips them. County assets
have raised from a few thousand dollars to very nearly a million. The
energy, thrift, kindliness of the early settlers has endured; that was, and
is a quality and an asset of our people that does not change.

        One of the beautiful modern homes of Walworth county. Built in 1949
        by Ralph Burnette, Selby farmer. It is stone-coated with native
        limestone shipped from Seligmann, Mo., near the Arkansas state line
        and his former home.

        WALWORTH COUNTY COMMISSIONERS Left to right: J. F. Hand, John
        Lemler, A. Rye, Emil Wagner, F. E. Bauer.

THE HISTORY OF LEBEAU

The chronicle of LeBeau presents three separate faces--the Frenchman,
Antoine LeBeau, trader and trapper, made the dangerous journey up the
Mississippi and Missouri rivers in 1875 locating an Indian trading post at
the mouth of Swan creek. There he built a log and mud house, married an
Indian girl and reared a family of boys and girls. Descendants of his name
are still to be found in that section.

LeBeau's trading post was also port of call for the river boats that plied
their trade up and down the Missouri river in Dakota territory.

In 1883 when the County of Walworth was organized, LeBeau experienced a few
years of wonderful prosperity. Though the county seat was located at the
Scranton post office, the meetings were held in the home of Antoine LeBeau.
Scranton became South LeBeau and in the spring of 1883 Captain Strong and
an associate named Pudor bought 160 acres from Antoine, platted a new town
to the north and named it for the former owner.

        Early scene of LeBeau.

By autumn 200 persons lived in LeBeau, the second. By November it boasted
60 buildings--3 hotels, 6 stores, 3 lumber yards and a bank. A newspaper
was published--The Leader, edited by Wallace C. Brown. Additions were made
until 6,000 lots were platted into the town.

Scranton made a valiant struggle for a separate existence establishing a
separate school district and a rival weekly edited by Fred Bowman.
Gradually LeBeau absorbed the business, heavy river traffic was augmented
by stage lines from Pierre, Blunt, Bismarck and twice daily stage service
from Aberdeen. Advertisements couched in superlative terms appeared in
newspapers over the signature of C. C. Pudor of Winona, Minnesota, and I.
H. Hauser of Aberdeen. A sample from the Aberdeen Republican of May 10.
1883: "LeBeau is destined to be the metropolis of Central Dakota. Across
the river in the Moreau valley lie millions of acres of fertile wheat
lands, timber and grazing lands. Swan lake is a never failing source of
pure water enough for a city of 100,000. It is the logical crossing of the
Missouri for railroad extensions to both the coast and the rich Black Hills
territory."

Why this small frontier town faded out of the picture no one knows--over a
period of years buildings were torn down or moved away. The people drifted
to other towns. Finally only the school house remained to mark the site. To
the north the young hustling, roistering town of Evarts drew the business
of the cattle industry. The stage lines centered around Bangor, the county
