seat, and river traffic was virtually abandoned for the more efficient
railroad service.

        Indians encamped near New LeBeau.

In 1907 the Milwaukee and St. Louis railroad built an extension to a point
two miles below the old townsite and a new LeBeau arose to fulfill in part
the glowing promises made by Pudor and Hauser. The abandonment of Evarts on
the Milwaukee road, together with the fact that the west river territory
offered obstructions to the north, threw the bulk of the huge cattle trade
into the new town.

From Evarts came Lou Davidson to promote the Dakota State Bank as president
with Sam Overby, vice president and W. L. Merrick, cashier. Directors were
L. T. Davidson, W. L. Merrick, Jessie Knight, Sam Overby, and J. H. Holmes.
Wm. Jay erected a building which housed a hardware store, E. J. Zimmer with
his son Bill came. as carpenters and contractors, Harry Van Campen came
with his bride to establish a pharmacy, two young doctors, C. L. Olson and
F. H. Creamer, formed a partnership to practice medicine. Edward McBride
established the LeBeau Phoenix, a weekly newspaper, in 1907. Mr. McBride, a
man of vision whose subsequent career was both colorful and full of service
to his town, state and country, did not choose the name of his paper at ran.
dom. The name "Phoenix" recalls the mythical bird that rose ever stronger
from the ashes of its past.

From the west river cattle industry the town of LeBeau derived much of its
economic prosperity. Especially from the Matador whose "spread" lay in
thousands of acres of succulent grass land directly opposite the town
across the Missouri. Thousands of dollars were spent yearly by the foremen
in supplies for the home buildings as well as for the camps located at
intervals over the spread. The advent of the cowboys into town after weeks
or months on the range with their accrued pay checks brought other dollars
to be spent riotously in a few days fun.

So stimulated, the town attained a population of 500, boasted two churches,
a school, a town hall, a railroad round house, bakery, millinery store,
drug store, meat market, pool halls and many saloons. The town took great
pride in its band and baseball team. Those were prosperous days for LeBeau
in 1907-08-09.

However in 1909 the Cheyenne and Standing Rock reservations were opened to
homesteaders and as the ranges were fenced the knell of the great cattle
companies sounded. Of those, the Matador spread was the largest, and so
too, the owner of the Matador, old Murdo Mackenzie, topped in stature most
other men. Murdo Mackensie, six feet six with beetling brows and a scotch
burr on his tongue unsoftened by the Texas drawl of most of his "boys". His
foreman and right hand man, dignified soft-spoken James Burr was, like
Mackenzie, a native of Scotland, both were graduates of the university of
Edinburgh.

David G. Mackenzie, or "Dode", as he was popularly known, inherited his
father's rugged physique but not his Scotch reserve. Handsome, generous to
a fault, turbulent and roistering when drinking, his friends deny that even
at his worst "Dode" ever sought a man's life. Strangely enough "Dode" had
not been drinking when bullets from a .45 ended his life in Phil Dufran's
saloon one morning in December, 1909. A .45 held in the hand of a
frightened nondescript little man, squint-eyed and bandy-legged, "Bud"
Stevens, barman in the saloon. Evidence immediately following the shooting
and at the preliminary hearing before Justice H. R. deMalignon 16 days
later was both contradictory and confusing. Bud Stevens entered a plea of
self defense. When the case came to trial before Judge J. H. Bottum in
Selby on March 22, 1910, the battery of attorneys facing Bud Stevens across
the council table was impressive. Associated with Smith, Brown and Van
Slyke were Howard B. Case of Watertown, and his partner Henderson, also an
attorney from Colorado Springs. Seasoned veterans of the law backed by the
money and prestige of the Mackensies, as well as strong public sentiment
against Stevens, small wonder that against this formidable array the two
young attorneys engaged by Phil Dufran in behalf of Bud Stevens presented a
forlorn hope for the defense. Young Harkin of Aberdeen, not too experienced
or well known, and young Pat Morrison of Mobridge, pleading his first
criminal case. Bud Stevens told his story. Whatever the sentiment against
him and however justified, Bud Stevens evidently believed that he was
defending his life when he shot and killed "Dode" Mackenzie. The evidence
presented by Morrison and Harkin proved it. "Murder or self defense?"
screamed the headlines. "Self defense" said the jury, and acquitted Bud
Stevens. In spite of the acquittal and the passage of years, opinion of the
case in the minds of those concerned remains unchanged. "Cold-blooded
murder," insists Bob Horn, resident of LeBeau at the time, later sheriff of
Walworth county.

The late Dr. C. L. Olson, then practicing in LeBeau, and the first man to
reach "Dode" after he was shot always declared that "Dode" had both hands
empty clasped to his chest and that the gun fell out of his coat afterward.
"A clear case of self defense." Morrison still maintains. Both Morrison and
Harkin have rolled up a brilliant score of victories in the criminal
courts, particularly in the field of defense.

LeBeau resented the acquittal with action--Bud Stevens left town suddenly,
by request.

Conjecture, gossip, speculation were rife. Why did "Dode", with his
knowledge of firearms, load a .45 with .38 cartridges if he was serious,
and not, as his friends insisted, "putting on act?"--did someone promote the
"act"--if so, who? At the same time did some one play upon the credulity of
Bud Stevens, telling him that "Dode" was "gunning" for him, needling him
into alarm and watchfulness ? Or was the web of "Dode's" life span cut
suddenly by the shears of the Fates when a practical joke backfired?

Whatever the answer, the results of the killing, direct and indirect, to
LeBeau were disastrous. That same fall a fire wiped out nearly the whole
town. That it was of incendiary origin there was no doubt as the fire hoses
were deliberately cut in many places and traces of an inflammable chemical
was found between the walls of buildings.

Murdo Mackenzie pulled the Matador interests out of LeBeau leaving serious
gaps in the town's economic structure. Another fire a year later finished
the town entirely.

Today LeBeau is a memory. The little brick building that stood a lone
sentinel on the site for so long is gone. The old cellar holes are mere
dents on the prairie--nature has healed the scars with grass.

THE HISTORY OF JAVA

The City of Java came into existence in 1900 soon after the Milwaukee
railroad was extended from Bowdle to Evarts. Up until 1903 it consisted
mainly of a few scattered buildings, but its growth was steady and the
population increased to 150 in October of that year. In this year of 1950,
back over fifty golden years, an interesting history of the development
from the village to the present City of Java can be traced.

Much can be written about this interesting little city but time nor space
does not permit. Your writer will attempt to point out some of the
highlights.

It was not long after the town had started that its townsfolk decided that
it should be incorporated from a village into a town, accordingly in 1903 a
mass meeting was called for the purpose of making this decision. As a
result of this meeting a special election was held on October 19, 1903 in
the W. P. Winkley store to decide upon this matter. The vote cast stood 45
for and 2 against. Another election, for the purpose of electing a Board of
Trustees was held on November 23, 1903 with the following elected to serve
on the first town board: David Blinderman, first ward; W. F. Ewald, second
ward; John Hofmeyer, third ward- Jacob Schafer, marshal; W. F. Dyer,
treasurer; Fred Krause, justice of the peace; Joseph Bosch, overseer of the
highways; Christ Huether, town clerk; and Martin Gehrki, assessor.

The board held its first meeting in the Hofmeyer store four days after the
election. At this meeting Carl F. Clement, father of Fritz Clement, present
publisher of the Java Herald and the Selby Record, was engaged as city
attorney at a salary of $30.00 a month.

Progress in the development of the little town was rapid in the next few
years. In 1904, the first municipal building was erected. This was a jail
and was built by Jacob Fiechtner at a contract price of $239.00. It was
first erected on a lot just west of the new municipal building but later
was moved on a lot just back of the old city hall on Main street. Later it
was sold to Adam Lorenz and was converted into a dwelling house and shoe
repair shop. Some years afterward, it was sold to Henry Boschee who moved
it to his farm.

During the years 1904 to 1906, many improvements were made in the new town.
Wooden sidewalks were built and streets were laid out, a town hall and a
water reservoir were constructed, a well was dug and a windmill was put up,
a fire engine and some hose was purchased. These were paid by city warrants
as the town was not yet bonded. In 1906, however, the citizens of the town
voted a $2,000 bond issue to take up the warrant indebtedness created by
these necessary improvements. Thus in five years from the time the town was
started, Java had provided for graded streets, sidewalks, a municipal
building and fire protection.

In 1903, the school district built a $3,500 school building, and to this
another wing was added in 1907, when a two-year high school course was
introduced.

The population of the town continued to increase steadily during the years
from 1906 to 1915 although no other changes took place in the development
of the town. In the years of 1908 and 1909, the Milwaukee railroad changed
their right-of-way, moving the main line to its present location one-half
mile north of the city, and built a spur into the town. This was a serious
blow to the little city, although the spur served its purpose to some
extent. Railroad officials had asked the city to move its town further
north but were turned down by Java citizens who deemed the move unwise.

        Municipal building in Java.

The year 1915 saw another improvement that marked an epoch in the history
of Java, when the wooden sidewalks on Main street were torn up and replaced
with cement walks. At the same time many residents of the town improved
their home property by building cement walks in place of the old wooden
ones. In the fall of that same year, the town hall was remodeled and the
jail was moved to a lot just back of the municipal building, the work being
done by George Berreth. A tower was also constructed that year for a bell,
which was used for fire alarm and curfew.

In the spring of 1916, a petition was circulated among the qualified voters
of the town to call a special election for the purpose of determining if
the town should issue bonds in the amount of $8,000 for the construction of
a municipal electric light plant. This election was held on June 4 of that
year and resulted in 48 votes in favor and 32 against the venture. Contract
bids for the project were opened in July with A. F. Kaufman of Appleton,
Minnesota, being the successful bidder for the amount of S4,730 for the
plant, with Gunder Johnson getting the building contract for $875. By the
latter part of September of that year, the new building was completed, the
plant installed and current turned on.

In the fall of 1918 one of the biggest booms in the history of the town
took place and it was during this year and the year following that most of
the beautiful residences on Helm street, those north of the railroad track
and the former Wm. Kunz residence on Yonder street were built. Several
other new and modern homes were built during the ten years following and
during this time the population of the town increased rapidly.

In the spring of 1921, the Java Independent School district voted bonds in
the amount of $50,000 for the construction of the present fine, fireproof
school building, the old structure being unsafe as well as inadequate to
house the increased enrollment of students. In the summer of 1921 many of
the streets in the town were resurfaced and graveled. That fall, the town
was incorporated into a city and the present aldermanic form of government
adopted with C. F. Clement being elected as the first mayor.

Late in the summer of 1923, because of dissatisfaction with the inadequate
electric service, citizens requested 24-hour electric light and power
service, so that fall the city council purchased a new 50 h.p. engine to
help take care of the increased demand.

In the following year, the fire fighting apparatus was improved with
additional hose and two chemical engines. In 1925 the streets were given a
heavy coat of gravel. That summer, the old engine at the electric light
plant being inadequate for further local use, a new 60 h.p. Diesel type "Y"
Fairbanks-Morse engine and a new generator was installed, and the building
was correspondingly enlarged to properly house the new equipment.

In the spring of 1936 an intensive street program was launched with a new
street opened from Chicago street north across the tracks to connect with
the county high. way north of the city. That fall saw the start of the
construction of a skeleton water system and installation of hydrants at
strategic points in the city for more adequate fire protection.

Following this project steps were taken to have the system enlarged for
private and commercial use, and as a result construction on the PWA project
for the improvement of the system began in May, 1939 and was completed
early in July that year. With the completion of this fine new waterworks
system, another outstanding milestone of progress of the city was passed.

In December 1939 another improvement was added in the form of a truck which
was purchased by the city and converted into fire fighting equipment by
members of the Java Volunteer Fire Department.

In June 1940 plans for a new municipal building were approved and Roland
Wilcken, architect, was instructed to draw up plans and specifications. The
project was under WPA and work started in late fall and continued
throughout the winter, the building being completed in 1941. The structure
is approximately 74 by 50 feet in size and is built of reinforced concrete.

About this time the city realized that a more adequate light and power
system was needed and after several attempts were made to convert from d.c.
to a.c. current by installation of new equipment and lines, the matter was
finally brought to a head in 1946 when an election was held and it was
decided to sell the present plant to Montana-Dakota Utilities and approve a
20-year franchise. The election carried and Montana-Dakota built a complete
new transmission line in Java.

It was also during 1946 that Main street was filled in and later covered
with new coats of gravel. Other streets in the city were also improved. In
April 1946 the old city hall was sold to M. Moore of Leola, who later resold
the building to a group of Java men who turned the building over to the
LaVerne Bauer American Legion Post.

Although back in April 1944 the city authorized a survey to be made for a
sewer disposal plant it was not until 1947 when a start was made on this
important project. The city was bonded and revenue bonds were issued and
construction on the system was started in 1948. This project gave Java an
up-to-date sewer disposal plant, an improvement long needed.

In 1947 too, came the creation of a park board and that portion of property
lying west of the school house was converted into a city park.

Java, like Selby, is celebrating its Fiftieth Anniversary this year. A
committee, headed by Mayor A. C. Schlepp as chairman, are making extensive
plans for a two-day celebration on June 14 and 15, 1950.

THE HISTORY OF EVARTS

During the period from the late 1870's through the 1890's the cattle barons
of the southwest--Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona--hard-pressed by periods
of drouth and encroaching landseekers turned over north and west to the
promise of the western grasslands. Over the old buffalo trails came the
roar and rumble of trail-driven cattle, vast herds from the L-7 in 1876,
were joined later by the Matador, Turkey Track, Sword & Dagger, Hat Ranch
and J & A together with many smaller outfits.

        Pontoon Bridge near Evarts in early days.

Late in the 1890's owners and representatives of the cattle companies
negotiated with officials of the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul railroad to
establish a shipping point on the Missouri river for a more direct route to
the cattle markets than that furnished by the M & St. L., Milwaukee's rival
line. Coinciding with the railroad's own desire to push their line west, a
survey was made from Bowdle to the river and early in 1900 crews lay the
track to the new town. H. B. Erling and Harry Hunter, president and general
agent of the Milwaukee road, on a tour of inspection of the proposed
townsite, overtaken by a sleet and rain storm and ensuing darkness, were
welcomed at the Gene Overholser ranch adjoining the townsite. Grateful for
shelter and charmed by the young Overholsers, Mr. Erling declared that the
new town would be named in honor of Mrs. Overholser, whose maiden name was
Everts. "Evarts" was the spelling as Mr. Erling jotted it down in his
notebook and that spelling remained.

Quickly the town mushroomed into growth and for a few years became one of
the largest cattle shipping points in the world. R. E. Mudge had the first
store, located on his ranch at the southern edge of the town. Soon Ross
Peterson opened a general store in the town as did "Whitlock and Johnson",
later to become "Dean and Whitlock". A. V. Decker and his crew began
construction of new buildings and a cement plant was started, operated by
W. H. Nesbitt.

On July 20, 1900, the first engine, No. 671 with Engineer Slater at the
throttle and in charge of Conductor Ed Stephenson rolled into Evarts over
the new tracks. For two years ferries shuttled back and forth across the
river carrying cattle to be loaded for market. As soon as buildings were
available the Evarts State Bank with J. W. Harris as president and the
State Journal edited by R. Kellogg were established. Soon a hotel was
erected, its genial host, J. O'Mally. A commercial club was organized with
Col. T. G. Orr, president; F. A. Finch, secretary; and J. W. Harris,
treasurer. Saloons and gambling houses did a huge business, for the
transient population of the town was large,--hundreds of young cowboys from
the ranges, cattle buyers, stockmen, promoters. The people of Evarts
enjoyed a satisfying period of prosperity and hopes were high. The young
town was envisioned as a New Chicago, plans were made for packing and meat
processing plants.

In 1901 Evarts organized Co. L, Second South Dakota Infantry of the
National Guard, under the temporary command of Col. T. G. Orr. On April 27,
they were mustered in, a ceremony honored by the presence of Governor
Herreid and Adjutant General Conklin.

In that year huge corrals were built on either side of the river by the
Milwaukee road to facilitate the transfer of cattle to the shipping point
at Evarts. Coinciding with this, a tract of land was granted by the Indians
of the Cheyenne reservation 6 miles wide for the accommodation of herds from
the west river territory. This strip of land ran from the river to the
Standing Rock reservation to the north.

        Gene Overholser Ranch near Evarts.

In 1902-03-04 the little town gathered impetus for the metropolis so
certainly predicted. Engineers came and went, surveying and building hopes
for an extension west across the river either to the Black Hills or to the
coast.

In 1903 the railroad built a pontoon bridge joining the huge corrals on the
east and west banks of the Missouri, easing the labor of transportation of
the herds of cattle.

The colorful history of the town of Evarts has its inception and its record
in the cattle industry, not the least of which is the presence of crowds of
young cow boys who made the town their headquarters for recreation. They
came swarming into town on Saturday night, riding their horses on a dead
lope down Main street, guns blazing. Many of them were transients but some
came to stay. James Nichols of the Matador, who was made brand inspector
and served in that capacity through the years that Evarts remained. Mr.
Nichols also established an ice business in Evarts and built the first
entirely fire-proof cement block building in the town. Cal Smith, another
Matador boy, settled in Evarts with his family. Lou Aherns of the Turkey
Track, Phil DuFran, Percy Page, Dick Holmes as well as many others made
this their home.

The Evarts commercial club, a very active organization, promoted the advent
to the town of new businesses and projects. Lodges were organized--the Odd
Fellow, Rebecca, Modern Woodman. The latter contributed a dramatic club to
the social life of the small town. Its cast enjoyed quite a small local
fame in the surrounding towns where their plays were shown to generous and
appreciative audiences.

In 1904 on an excursion of the Milwaukee road, a reporter from the Chicago
Herald came to town. Seeking local color for a feature story he registered
at the Golden West hotel, unfortunately on a Saturday night. The cowboys
advent into the town was all that any local colorseeker could wish. In
addition an argument arose between a couple of the boys and their
leavetaking in the early morning hours from the Golden West was so colorful
that the genial host was forced to take action and the two boys wound up in
the justice chambers which happened to be back of Bickerts butcher shop.
"Tex" Richards' plea was a plaintively drawled protest "that, if that
hombre hadn't a been under the bed the bullets couldn't no wise have come
so close to him". In any event a lurid account of the reporter's sojourn in
the town of Evarts appeared in the due course of time as a feature story in
the Herald, much to the indignation of the good people of Evarts who
resented hotly the name of being the toughest little town on earth--with
seven saloons, six brothels, several gambling houses, population of gun
men, thugs and cut throats, and one church. They readily admitted the seven
saloons but insisted truthfully that the one church administered to the
spiritual needs of the whole community regardless of color, age, creed or
condition of servitude. Sunday morning probably found numbers of cowboys, a
few gamblers and what-not in the congregation. One young minister of that
church became so well liked and respected, so well known that from the Rio
Grande to the North Dakota border he was known as "The Sky Pilot" and no
one bothered to remember his name, which was Howard. He left Evarts to
become a missionary in India and still lives there.

In 1905 the E. J. Zimmer family moved to Evarts. Mr. Zimmer, a contractor
and carpenter, was also an able musician. He and his son "Bill" organized
and directed the Evarts band and orchestra. Musical programs enjoyed by the
town included the voices of Mrs. Gene Overholser, Mrs. J. W. Harris, Mrs.
Wm. Nesbitt, the Wrigley sisters, Eliza and Ethel, the cowboy songs and
minstrels rendered by Albert (Pete) Frazier accompanied by his own guitar,
mandolin or banjo, Miss Lucille Peck, accomplished pianist, and Harry
McLaughlin with violin solos. A program was an almost weekly event, the
musical numbers varied with dramatic and humorous readings by Miss Myrtle
Potter of Selby (a teacher at Evarts), Mrs. Frank Finch, Mrs. Ross
Petersen, Eugene Overholser, Eb Mudge and Bill O'Connor.

Wm. McKinnon was the first school teacher in Evarts with a student body of
approximately 20 pupils covering 8 grades. He was followed by Professor
Day, Miss Annie Nesbitt, Miss Lou Schellenger and Guy Schellenger, Miss
Myrtle Potter and Mrs. J. R. Howell.

In 1905 the certain hope of an extension from Evarts west of the river to
the coast drew more business men to locate in Evarts. Surveyers and
engineers sought for a site for the bridge over the Missouri.

J. S. Smithberger erected a two-story building that housed the telephone
company, the drug store and the Evarts State Journal, which Mr. Smithberger
took over as editor. Jas. Wrigley came from Mellette with his family taking
over the lumber yard and coal business. An important figure in the economic
life of the town was Dan Johns, the waterman. Wells had been found
impractical being entire alkaline or the water so hard as to be unfit for
use. Every family had water barrels which were filled at regular intervals
by Mr. Johns with river water from a large wooden tank drawn by horses. In
the early years Mr. Johns also operated the ferry, the "Pearl".

Huge dipping tanks were built just south of the loading chutes at the "Y".
There every Sunday hundreds of cattle were run through the tanks from a
sloping chute on one side where they slid unwillingly into the horrible
mixture which was the dip for the cure or prevention of ticks, lice and
scab. Alert cowboys stationed on either side of the tanks, armed with long
iron hooks, restrained the crowding cattle or urged on the laggers. A
dangerous job and never a dipping day that one or more of the luckless boys
were not catapulted into the tanks.

Crowds from Evarts augmented by spectators from Glenham, Selby and Java
made these dipping days a gala event. Shouts from the cowboys, the clash of
hoofs and horns of the frightened cattle together with their muffled
bawling as they struggled and fought their way through the nauseous liquid
dip, a mixture of sulphur and nicotine and creosote from which rose an odor
like nothing so much as the essence of thousands of rotten eggs.

In 1906 the future of Evarts suffered a crushing blow with the report of
the railroad engineers to the effect that no feasible site for a bridge to
span the Missouri could be found at that point. To the north at the mouth
of the Grand river, shale rock suitable for the pilings had been found and
to that point were shipped the supplies and crews to begin the construction.

In the ensuing year the exodus from Evarts began, principally to the new
town of Mobridge, LeBeau or Selby. By 1908 only one building of concrete
block stood on the townsite of Evarts. Gaping cellar holes and a few broken
wooden sidewalks remained. Even those disappeared leaving Evarts not even a
ghost town, only a memory in the minds and hearts of those who dreamed of
the Young Chicago--gateway to the West.

THE HISTORY OF GLENHAM

The town of Glenham had its beginning October 24, 1900, when town lots went
on sale through John W. Lowry. The town was platted on part of the homestead
of Mrs. Lowry, the former Carrie Carscallen. Among the first stores to be
located here were those of G. B. Thomas, Anderson Bros., and D. B. Shaw and
Son, the latter having moved their store building from Bangor to Glenham.
The erection of the depot began May 25, 1901. Surveyors also arrived at
that time to survey the country to the west, preliminary to extending the
railroad. They set the elevation of Glenham at 1679 feet above sea level.

        Glenham in 1907.

Glenham was incorporated July 1, 1907. W. M. Thurston, F. A. Shaw, and G.
G. Anderson composed the first board of trustees, with Chas. E. Keller as
clerk. The first ordinance they passed was one regulating the driving and
riding of horses on the streets of the town, and setting the speed limit at
eight miles an hour within the corporation. J. W. Thurston was the first
town marshal.

A. M. McKinnon was the first justice of the peace, and one of the first
cases tried before him was that of "The State of South Dakota vs. Theodore
Taylor", who was charged with shooting with the intent to kill, having shot
Gus Nelson early in the morning of July 10, 1907, in front of the Ed
Sheppard saloon. Gus Nelson died the following day, and A. H. Smith,
attorney for the state, moved to dismiss these charges, as now, Taylor
should be charged with murder. The defendant, personally, and by his
attorney, waived examination July 17, 1907, and was committed to the county
sheriff, J. J. Hoven, without bail. W. B. Burr appeared as council for the
defendant. Sheriff Hoven placed Taylor in the Brown county jail to await
trial, but he, with several other prisoners escaped from the jail, and
nothing more was ever heard of him.

With the breaking up of Evarts in 1908, many buildings from there were
moved to Glenham. Among them were the Presbyterian church, schoolhouse, the
Carpenter house, now owned and occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Chas. Prasek; the
Mike Costello building, occupied by Mr. and Mrs. H. H. High; the Lawien
house, now occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Schaible; and the McKinnon house,
now owned and occupied by Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Schlomer. The Shaw house, now
owned and occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Richard Schlomer, was built in Old
LeBeau in 1884, and moved to Bangor, and, later to Glenham. It is one of
the oldest frame buildings in Walworth county. C. A. Kuehn and George
Lehnert were the carpenters who remodeled and made these buildings ready
for occupancy, after being moved.

The first school in Glenham was a one-room structure of wood, located on a
site west of main street. It was bought by A. L. Price, moved to a location
east of main street, and remodeled for a dwelling house. It is referred to
now as the Elverson house, since A. G. Elverson bought it and lived there a
number of years, until he and Mrs. Elverson died. The second school was the
four-room building, moved from Evarts, which had been built there in 1904.
Carpenter work was completed on it January 3, 1909, and it was then ready
for occupancy. Three teachers were employed. In 1914, another teacher was
employed and the first four year high school course was introduced. The
first class to complete this course was graduated May 23, 1918, with E. C.
Woodburn, then of Aberdeen, delivering the commencement address. Helen and
Susie Vail were the graduates. E. O. Ronning was then superintendent. The
present school, a spacious brick building, was completed in 1927, and was
ready for occupancy at the opening of school that fall. Seven teachers were
now employed. There was some vacant room at first, but, with the addition
of athletics, music, dramatics and other extra curricular activities, the
entire building is used.

The first lumber yard was built by the Lamb Lumber company, but they
discontinued operating it in 1904 and sold it to P. G. Anderson, who, in
turn, sold it to James Wrigley in 1905. A. M. McKinnon came up from Evarts
to act as manager and remained in that capacity for five years.

The Glenham State Bank was started in a new building west of main street in
1906, by J. W. Harris and Pete Jali. Charles W. Conyne was the first
cashier. Ownership and personnel of the bank changed several times, but it
remained in operation until March 14, 1930, when it was closed. M. J. Van
Orman was the last cashier of the bank. Since 1930 the town has been
without a bank.

George W. Leise was the first postmaster of Glenham, and the post office
was housed in the depot for some time, until a post office was built. His
successor was A. M. McKinnon who remained in that position until he was
retired by the post office department March 31, 1940. Mrs. Hattie Van Orman
was appointed acting postmaster, April 1, 1940, and remained until the
appointment of the present postmaster, George Lehnert, February 1, 1941.
Two hardware stores were started in 1906, one by Allen and Frank Thurston,
and one by C. L. Lawien. The Thurston hardware was destroyed by fire in
1907. The Lawien hardware has changed hands several times, but still
remains in operation. The present proprietor, Chas. W. Schlomer, has
enlarged the building and increased the stock to meet the modern demands in
hardware.

Livery barns, started by Harve Thurston and Ezekial Harris, in the early
days of Glenham, did a thriving business, but were outmoded with the coming
of automobiles. Frank Kotterman and S. W. Thomas were the first draymen, in
those days of horse-drawn vehicles.

Saloons were started by Charlie Anderson and E. C. Sheppard. Later, one of
them was owned by Otto and Fred Goebel. Both of them went out with the
coming of prohibition.

There were two elevators in the early days of the town, the Crown, managed
by Chas. E. Keller, and the Bagley, managed by Lou Stabelfeldt. The Crown
later became the Columbia, with H. E. Blood as manager. Still later it was
bought by a co-operative organization who changed the name to the Glenham
Equity Exchange. Managers succeeding Mr. Blood were Fred Goebel, Lloyd
Engebretson and the present manager, Ora Hoffman. In 1947, the Equity
people bought the Bagley elevator, then managed by A. W. Callen, so there
is just one elevator, with a bulk gas and oil station in connection.

In the beginning days of the town, George W. Leise and James Stewart bought
a weekly newspaper in Evarts, known as the Evarts State Journal, and moved
it to Glenham in 1908. They changed the name of it to "The Glenham State
Journal". A few years later they sold their interests in the paper to James
N. Kain, who edited it for two years. With his moving to Minnesota, the
Glenham State Journal went out of existence and Glenham was without a paper.

James N. Kain was also the first rural mail carrier out of Glenham. When he
resigned to move away, he was succeeded by George Lehnert, who held the
position nearly seven years. When he resigned to devote his time to
farming. Albert L. Brown, the present carrier, was appointed October 25,
1920.

The first hotel in Glenham was kept by Mrs. G. B. Thomas, in her home,
which was the house now owned and occupied by Mr. and Mrs. A. M. McKinnon.
It was then located back of the G. B. Thomas store, on the west side of
main street, but was later moved to the northeast part of town, where it
now stands. In 1906, Mrs. Elizabeth Elliot built a larger hotel on the east
side of main street, which she operated until 1910, when she sold it to Mr.
and Mrs. H. E. Blood. They remodeled and enlarged it to accommodate the
growing trade, and Mrs. Blood continued to operate it until 1940, the year
following Mr. Blood's death. It has been purchased by the board of
education and is used as a school dormitory.

The Presbyterian church, moved up from Evarts, became the first permanent
church for the town, and at one time it had a large membership and
attendance. In 1921, the German Lutherans built a basement church, in which
they held services for about five years, until the present edifice of St.
Jacobi church was completed.

The town installed the electric light and power system and had homes and
business places wired in the fall of 1917. The wires were energized
February 7, 1918, and the old gasoline system, previously used, was
discarded.

During the time Glenham was at its best, it boasted of two butcher shops, a
doctor, a drug store, hardware store, two restaurants, hotel, bank, ice
cream parlor, two saloons, pool hall, two livery barns, two blacksmith
shops, mill, two elevators, lumber yard, and printing office.

A disastrous fire, of unknown origin, burned six buildings on the west side
of main street, June 25, 1925. The buildings lost at this time were the
post office, I. O. O. F. hall, C. C. Schlomer store, Equity Cash store,
pool hall, and Gullickson cafe. The same year saw the erection of new
fireproof buildings to replace those which had been destroyed. Some years
later the Equity Cash store. and the C. C. Schlomer store went out of
business, and have changed hands several times. At present Adolph Sulzle is
operating a grocery store in the C. C. Schlomer building and Mr. and Mrs.
Olaf Johnson have a grocery store in the former Equity building. A grocery
store, operated for several years by A. G. Elverson, was operated by George
and Elizabeth Elverson for twelve years after his death, until the Elverson
estate was closed. The pioneer store buildings changed hands many times,
until they became old and were torn down. The last to go was the Thomas
building, which served as an implement building, operated by G. E. Brorby
for about twenty years, until he terminated his business, January 1, 1946.
The barber shop, operated by B. J. Davison, was bought and remodeled for a
dwelling house, and is now occupied by Adam Mitzel, who operates an
off-sale liquor store in the building which was formerly the L. H. Frankie
pool hall. The I. O. O. F. hall was bought by Albert Hanson and used for an
auto repair shop, and later, remodeled for an on-sale liquor store. The
large, modern garage, which was erected on the east side of main street in
1925, by J. S. Salzsiedler and Frank Vojta, known as the Glenham Auto
company, is still operated by Mr. Salzsiedler. These men dissolved
partnership and Mr. Vojta bought the Thurston livery barn, used many years
by G. E. Brorby as an implement warehouse, and remodeled it for a garage
and auto repair shop.

The Glenham mill, which had been built by the Glenham Milling company in
1910, and did a thriving business over a period of years, under the
management of C. J. Hanstrom, was destroyed by fire early in the morning of
November 23, 1936, and was never rebuilt. A fire, also burned the lumber
yard, which was replaced by the Central Lumber company, with S. A. Hagerty
as the last manager. They sold this building to the Mobridge Commission
company and it was moved to Mobridge, since which time the town has been
without a lumber yard.

W. F. Matz has remained the longest as agent for the C. M. & St. P.
railroad and was retired by them in August, 1940. Since then Fred A. Mosser
has acted in that capacity, making his home in an apartment in the depot.

The latest additions to the town include the spacious, modern garage,
erected by Frank Vojta, in 1947, on the site of the old Thurston livery
barn, which he tore down to make room for the new structure, and two cement
block buildings, filling the space between the Hanson liquor store and the
Sulzle store. The one was built by Albert Allmendinger, while he operated a
grocery store in the Elverson building, and is now occupied by the Sulzle
family as a home. The other was built by Albert Hanson, and is occupied by
him and his family as a home.

Among the pioneers of Glenham were: Mr. and Mrs. Geo. B. Thomas, Mr. and
Mrs. G. G. Anderson, K. G. Anderson, Mr. and Mrs. D. B. Shaw, Fred Shaw,
Mae Shaw (now Mrs. W. F. Matz), Anna Shaw, who became Mrs. Tom Vellam, Mr.
and Mrs. A. L. Lindel, Mrs. John Thurston Sr., and sons, Will, John, Harve,
Allen and Frank Thurston, Mr. and Mrs. Chas. E. Keller, Tom Vellam, Mr. and
Mrs. A. W. Vail, Mr. and Mrs. Charlie Anderson, Mr. and Mrs. Lou
Stablefeldt, Mrs. Elizabeth Elliot, Mr. and Mrs. O. L. Cline, Mr. and Mrs.
J. N. Kain, A. G. Elverson, George W. Leise, Ezekial Harris, Frank
Kotterman, C. A. Kuehn, George Lehnert, A. M. McKinnon, Mr. and Mrs. Ole
Tronson, Pete Jali, E. C. Sheppard, Chas. W. Conyne, S. W. Thomas and Joe
Bunney.

FAMILY BIOGRAPHIES

HANSON FAMILY

About the year 1880 Hans H. Hanson and family consisting of two sons, Sam
and John (or C. J. as he signed himself, his name being Charles John) and
one daughter, Esther, moved from Iowa to South Dakota where they became a
part of a fairly new settlement west of Bowdle, the nearest town to the new
settlers. Later Selby became the community center.

In 1889 John married Helene Halvorsen who had recently come over from
Norway. The daughter, Esther, married Guttrom Braaten the same year and
they too settled in the same vicinity, later moving to North Dakota. Esther
is the mother of six boys and two girls. Esther still survives her husband
and lives with her children in North Dakota.

John and his wife, their children, and his brother (Sam), who remained
single for a number of years, were farmers and became active friends and
neighbors and a part of the community affairs.

In 1901 John with his family moved to Alberta, Canada. where they became a
part of another new and growing community many of whom were migrants from
the Selby, South Dakota, community.

        MR. SAM HANSON

John and Helene lived in Alberta for 40 years. Their youngest son was born
in Alberta. Thus they had four daughters and three sons. Grandma Hanson
died in South Dakota. Grandpa Hanson accompanied his son, John, to Alberta
where he lived the remainder of his life.  Sam later married and became the
father of three girls. He also moved to Alberta where he died. His widow
died recently, in this year of 1950, in Leeds, North Dakota, where her
children at present are all living.

John died in 1943. Helene survived him six years. Their children, 21
grandchildren, and 15 great grandchildren, survive them.

Sam Hanson took a very prominent part in locating homesteaders near Selby
in the early days.

MR. W. R. GREEN

William Ringgold Green, known to old timers in Walworth and Edmunds
counties as "Billy" Green, was born at Howellsville, Delaware county,
Pennsylvania, June 10, 1852. He moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in September
of 1883 and in November came to South Dakota, settling in Edmunds county.
In the fall of 1885, he came to Bangor and opened the Walworth County State
Bank, the first bank in the county, and was the sole owner of the
institution. The next year he opened the People's State Bank at Bowdle,
conducting both banks until 1889 when he sold the bank at Bowdle and
centered his interests in Bangor, also engaging in the abstracting
business. That year he was also admitted to practice law in all courts and
set up in the practice of this profession at Bangor.

        MR. W. R. GREEN

On December 10, 1896, he was united in marriage with Della Palmer whose
parents were homesteaders in Blue Blanket township and who lived on a
number of places in the vicinity of where Selby now stands, among them the
places now occupied by Max Hoven and W. J. Sawinsky. They had four
children. In the year 1907 they sold out their interests in Walworth county
and moved to Sioux Falls, where he purchased the S and S Packing plant
property and other real estate. He passed away in Sioux Falls in December,
1922.

"Billy" Green is remembered as a real booster and promoter who believed in
the future of this country and who invested his time, energy, and money in
successful enterprises and did much to get the commercial machinery of the
new country into motion.

MR. EDWARD B. GREEN

Edward Baker Green was born at Media, Delaware county, Pennsylvania,
December 16, 1861. He was a direct descendant of General Nathaniel Green
who was considered as being second only to George Washington among the
commanders of the Revolutionary armies in the War for Independence, and of
Benjamin West, also famous in that period of our country's history. He
received high school training and some higher education in the schools of
Pennsylvania and taught school in the Keystone State before coming west. In
the year 1887 he came to Bangor to work in the first bank in Walworth
county the Walworth County State Bank, which was started by his cousin, W.
R. Green, and to help in the abstracting business which W. R. Green also
owned. The latter had come to Bangor in 1885 and was an important person in
the early affairs of that city.

In 1890 he was united in marriage with Marie Lindholm of Bowdle, he being
then employed in the People's Bank of Bowdle, also the property of W. R.
Green at that time. She bore him four children and was taken from him in
1906, leaving him with the family to raise. In the year 1900 he took a
homestead near Evarts and in the year 1906 filed on 80 acres southwest of
Akaska in the Kubier neighborhood. He was engaged meantime in the banking
and real estate business at Bowdle and Evarts but, when he filed on the
land near Akaska, the family made their home on it for a number of years.
Mr. Green and his eldest son, Marion, taught school in the southern part of
the county. The M. & St. L. railroad built down the Swan Creek valley in
1906-1907 and hopes were high, people flocked there for land, and it was
thought that there was a grand future for that particular section. In 1913
the Green family moved to Sioux Falls and he called that his home but came
back to Walworth to teach school for many years afterward. His aged mother
came from Pennsylvania and spent her last days with him. The last few years
of his life were spent at Baltic, in the home of his daughter, and were
passed as he chose them to be, in hunting and fishing.

Ed Green was ever interested in the better things of life, was a student
and writer, was interested in dramatics and art and the children he taught
received plenty of training in those subjects. He was public-spirited and
gave freely of his time to public enterprises. He could put on an
entertainment on his own most any time and any of his schools could furnish
an exhibit of busy work, art work, and penmanship on short notice at any
time. Politically he was a staunch democrat; he was much interested in
history, particularly in the early history of Walworth and Edmunds
counties. If the material he had gathered were available now it would be an
easy matter for anyone to compile a history of Walworth county.

He related to his children that in the first days of Bangor he left the
bank to go to dinner one day in a blizzard, desiring to cross the street.
After somewhat of a struggle with the elements, he found that he had circled
the bank and was again at the front door. His struggle to keep a home for
his four children, and maintain and educate them, after the death of his
wife, must have been a hard one. But he was rewarded by living to see each
of the four reach maturity and attain success in life. He passed away in
1945.

The eldest of his children, Marion L. Green, was born at Bowdle and got his
education there and in Minnesota. He taught school in Walworth county and
was cashier of the LeBeau Bank for some time. When the family went to Sioux
Falls, he became an employee of the Morrell plant and has been with them
for more than 35 years, being head of the truck hog buying department. He
had a son in the service in the late war.

Helen, the only daughter in the family, was one of Walworth county's
successful teachers for a number of years, in LeBeau, Lowry and Glenn
districts. She is married to George Bidne and resides at Baltic, South
Dakota.

Francis Green has been a successful electrical contractor in Sioux Falls
for many years, is prominent in the city, and has been a candidate for
mayor.

Dr. George Green graduated from the medical department of the University of
South Dakota and Rush Medical college. He served in the army in World War
II and is a Major. He resides near Washington, D. C., and was president of
the South Dakota Society there last year.

DOCTOR WILLIAM A. GEORGE

One of the best known and most beloved residents of the Selby community is
Doctor Wm. A. George. Born in Garden City, Minnesota, January 16, 1874, he
came to South Dakota with his parents in 1885 and settled in Beadle county.
The next year they moved near Gettysburg in Potter county. He attended
State College at Brookings and received his medical training in the College
of Physicians and Surgeons of the University of Illinois at Chicago,
graduating in the spring of 1905.

Money in those days was not too plentiful for the young student and he
worked his way through college, getting jobs after classes during the
school terms. Part of the vacations were spent working on the ranch for
Frank Boehmer near Evarts and LeBeau.

Immediately after graduating from medical school he started practice in
Evarts. On September 5, 1905, at Sioux Falls, he was united in marriage to
Julia Sevesind of Gettysburg. Mrs. George was born at Caledonia, Minnesota,
January 29, 1876. In 1884 she came with her parents to a homestead six
miles east of Gettysburg where her childhood was spent. This home was far
from a railroad and in the midst of primitive surroundings. The buildings
were of sod which saved them more than once when great prairie fires swept
the country.

She received her schooling in the country schools there and finished the
two-year high school course at Gettysburg in 1893, having the highest
standing of any member of the class, and receiving as a reward, a free trip
to the World's Fair at Chicago, given by the county superintendent of
schools. Later she attended Madison State Normal school and Northwestern
University at Evanston, Illinois, where she specialized in elocution and
prepared herself to teach English and History. She taught these three
subjects in the college at Ames, Iowa, and also at Pawnee City, Nebraska.

The new home was started in Evarts, and on December 25, 1907, their only
son, William Allen, was born. They lived in Evarts until 1908 when the
doctor moved his family and practice to Selby.

Dr. George is one of those pioneer country doctors whose general practice
included working frequently under difficulties and with limited facilities
on hand. It often meant driving many miles out into the country over bad
roads or no roads at all--in early years with horses and later with a car,
in all kinds of weather, to minister to the sick. It meant triumph when a
difficult case was brought through safely in spite of all odds against the
doctor and the patient--and it meant heartbreak when even his best efforts
were of no avail. It meant hard work and sacrifice and long hours with no
thought of self.

The doctor could probably relate many a poignant and dramatic story of his
experiences during his many years of service in Walworth county. One of
these stories concerns the time when he was first married, and not
possessing too many riches, had only one suit--that in which he was
married. He was called to the bedside of an Indian woman to deliver a baby.
She lived on the other side of the river which he crossed with great
difficulty. Then to top it off her bed was on the ground and he had to get
down on his knees to perform his duties. His wedding suit was ruined; but
the Indians named him "Iron Horse" for his bravery and skill in crossing
the river.

He tells of the first operation he ever performed, operating on a man who
didn't know that "Doc" was doing the work, and who bragged about the
wonderful job a well-known doctor had done for him. It was years before the
secret came out. Dr. George has no idea of how many babies he brought into
the world, but it must have been many hundreds. At one time while making a
trip with a team and buggy and crossing a frozen creek to reach his
destination, the ice gave way, and both horses and buggy were lost in the
icy current. The doctor and the driver he had along with him barely escaped
with their lives.

After the Dr. Georges had moved to Selby a baby girl, Elizabeth, was
adopted and added to the family. Mrs. George, from the time she moved into
the community, was very active in nearly all the enterprises for the
betterment of the community. She was one of the organizers of the Selby
Woman's club, she was an active member of the Eastern Star and was a Past
Matron of Hope Chapter in Selby. She affiliated with the Methodist church
in Selby and helped with the Sunday school. She directed nearly all of the
plays put on by the school, community or organization during her life in
Selby. There were few who did not benefit through contact with her in those
25 years. As wife, mother, homemaker, friend, and neighbor she had few
equals--and her sudden passing on June 16, 1933, from an attack of apoplexy
while attending an Eastern Star picnic at Lake Hiddenwood, was a terrible
shock to her husband, children, and friends. She was buried in the cemetery
where her parents and the parents of her husband rest.

For many years Dr. George operated his own hospital in Selby. He had as
many as three or four nurses employed at one time. The hospital building
was purchased from a former Selby doctor, Dr. Beil, who had the building
put up for his own practice. Some years after his wife's passing Dr. George
moved with his children from his private home into an apartment in his
hospital building. Still later he closed the hospital, and although he
keeps several rooms for an office, and for examinations and emergency
cases, he takes his patients to the Mobridge hospital.

On February 12, 1942, his son, Allen, was married to Miss Vivian Wild, who
operated a beauty shop in the basement apartment of the hospital building,
and kept house for the doctor and his son. His adopted daughter Elizabeth,
married Jake Schlepp of Java, where they live. They have a family of four
children: John, William, Julia, and Helen.

On December 2, 1946, Allen lost his life in a hunting accident, which was
another severe blow to the doctor. Allen left his widow with two small
children, Thomas twenty months, and Kathryn, six months.

On January 16, 1949, the people of the surrounding communities and of Selby
decided to honor Dr. George on his seventy-fifth birthday for his years of
faithful and untiring service as their doctor. Plans were made for an
afternoon program and party. A lovely birthday cake was prepared especially
for the event, and a beautiful leather chair and foot stool were purchased.
However; a raging blizzard on the 16th made the party impossible --but the
chair and cake were delivered to him and many of his friends telegraphed,
phoned, and called on him in spite of the weather.

It was decided later to have a "Doctor George Day" on June 23, 1949, at
which time a capacity crowd from all the surrounding communities gathered
in the city auditorium to honor him. A program was given after which a
lunch was served. Names of those present were recorded in a guest book and
presented to him.

In June, 1949, his son's widow married again and she, with her children and
husband, Arnold Chesky, who is associated with his father in a local
garage, live in the basement of the hospital building where she keeps house
for her family and the doctor.

Doctor George is a member of the Eastern Star and Masonic Lodges in Selby.
He has served for thirty-two years as county physician and still serves in
that capacity. He is still a very active man and is one of the few
remaining doctors who continue to go out on calls when sickness prevails.
Even this winter some of his trips were made in blizzards where people came
to meet him, breaking the roads through drifts of snow so he could reach
his patient and minister aid.

MR. FRANK E. GEHRKI

Frank E. Gehrki arrived in Selby, South Dakota
February 14, 1902 from Hillsview, South Dakota, having accepted a position
in the J. J. Hoven & Co. department store in Selby. He held this position
until September 1, 1902. From then until the fall of 1906 he was the Selby
Agent (grain buyer) for the Victoria Elevator company of Minneapolis. After
that for a short period of time he was assistant cashier in the Farmers
State Bank in Selby. On May 1, 1907 he accepted the position of assistant
cashier of the Akaska State Bank in Akaska, South Dakota; later on becoming
cashier of said bank, which position he held until January 1, 1909 when the
bank was sold to K. J. Kundert. Mr. Gehrki then returned to Selby and
engaged in the real estate business.

        MR. AND MRS. FRANK E. GEHRKI

On January 5, 1910 at Elk Point, South Dakota, he was united in marriage to
Miss Agnes L. Ward. Miss Ward had been the stenographer and bookkeeper at
the Walworth County State Bank from April, 1902 until the summer of 1908.

After their marriage, Mr. and Mrs. Gehrki started their new home in Selby.
In the spring of 1910 Mr. Gehrki entered politics as a candidate for the
register of deeds. He was elected and served two terms. Later he served two
terms each in the offices of county treasurer and county auditor. On March
1, 1923 he was appointed highway superintendent of Walworth county, holding
this position until March 1935. From May until July of 1935 he served as
Walworth County shelterbelt supervisor (Government work). He planted trees
on more than one hundred farms.

On September 1, 1935 he was appointed state maintenance superintendent with
the South Dakota state. highway department in District 4A. This included
the counties of Potter, Sully, Hughes, Corson, Dewey, Ziebach, and
Armstrong. He held this position until April 1937.

From September 1937 until April 30, 1942 he held various foremanships on
Federal Relief projects, such as: Water works, sewer, street graveling,
county highway construction and county road graveling.

On or about September 1, 1942 he was appointed by the board of
commissioners of Walworth county as county real estate agent, which
position he held nearly two years. During his term as highway superintendent
in the spring of 1926 the earthen dam at Lake Hiddenwood was constructed.

Mr. Gehrki was city treasurer of Selby for a number of years. About January
1, 1946 he sold his residence in Selby, and in June of that year moved to
Sioux City, Iowa.

Mr. and Mrs. Gehrki raised a family of four daughters: Margaret, is the
wife of Dr. John Vanderhoof, the local dentist and is the mother of five
children, John Micheal, Mary Margaret, Paul Francis, Patrick Ross, and Ann
Louise; Louise is Sister Barbara Ann, and is a teacher of English and
Dramatics in the Saint Mary's high school at Bismarck, North Dakota; Mary
Jane lives in St. Louis, Missouri, is the wife of Dr. G. J. Niedermeyer,
and they have one son, George Joseph, Jr.; Barbara Ann is a student at the
university at St. Louis, Missouri, majoring in Sociology.

MR. CHRISTIAN FLEMMER

Christian Flemmer was born in Gluecksthal, Russia on October 16, 1859, to
Rosina (Klein) Flemmer and Christian Flemmer, Sr.

Christian Flemmer attended grade school in Gluecksthal, and remained with
his parents until his marriage on November 15, 1883, to Rosina Eichelberg,
daughter of Fredrieka (Ritzer) Eichelberg and John Eichelberg, whom he had
met as a child while attending Sunday school. They remained in Russia 6
years, during which time many of their friends and neighbors had been
leaving Russia for a new land. Reports of America were so encouraging that
Mr. and Mrs. Flemmer and their two children, Christine (who died at the age
of 12 years) and son, John, who was then a baby of ten months, and a group
of five other families started for the new land, to establish a home and
independence.

        GRANDPA AND GRANDMA FLEMMER

The trip to America took them twenty-nine days, during which time they
encountered a severe storm, lasting over forty hours,--no one being
permitted on deck or to sleep during this time. They landed at Ellis Island
October 3, 1889, immediately going to McPherson county.

Mr. Flemmer's pioneer story varies a bit from that of the majority of early
settlers in the fact he did not immediately homestead, but worked on farms
as a farm laborer until 1892. At this time Mr. and Mrs. Flemmer with their
family moved to Walworth county, where they moved upon a homestead, four
miles northeast of Selby, living in a sod house with home made furniture.
Here they began their farming career much as did hundreds of others,
breaking a few acres of sod and sowing their seed by hand, from then on
their farming experience was probably little different from that of the
majority of other new settlers.

As better equipment was acquired, the labor was made easier and the results
more satisfactory, even though the prices of farm products were exceedingly
low during many of the first years. They remained on this homestead until
1908 at which time they bought a farm three miles east of Selby. This was
their home until 1912, when they moved on a farm one-half mile east of
Selby, living here seven years and then chose to move ten miles south of
Selby, which was the family home until March 1927, at which time Mr. and
Mrs. Flemmer retired and moved into Selby to enjoy good health and take
life a bit easier. They attended the German Lutheran church every Sunday
until ill health made it impossible.

The Flemmers never had a desire to return to their native land in spite of
disappointments, scares, blizzards and hardships suffered. They fully
appreciated their freedom and independence of the new land,--America.

To this happy, well satisfied couple. nine children were born: Christine,
deceased; John; Lydia (Mrs. Frank Peterhoff); and Christ, living on farms
near Selby; Carl of Omaha, Nebraska; Jacob of Canistota, South Dakota;
Harold, deceased; Margaret (Mrs. L. W. Heppersett) of Red Granite,
Wisconsin; and Arthur of Seattle, Washington.

Mr. Flemmer became seriously ill in January 1947 and passed away at his
home in Selby August 5, 1947. Mrs. Flemmer is handicapped by the loss of
her eyesight and is making her home with her eldest son, John and family
part time. and with a daughter, Mrs. Frank Peterhoff and family.

MR. GEORGE C. ERNST

George C. Ernst was born at Centralia, Iowa, April 23, 1876. At the age of
18 years he came to Hoven, South Dakota where he worked in the harvest
field, returning to Centralia that fall where he entered the seminary,
enrolling for a business course.

After the death of his father he went to St. Louis where he worked in a
grocery store for three months, returning to Hoven in the fall of 1896,
this being the severest winter South Dakota ever knew. He worked for his
room and board for his uncle, Chris Genteman. Mr. Ernst, being a firm
believer in the future of South Dakota, proved his sincerity by paying down
$25.00 on an earnest money contract for a raw quarter section of land in
the Hoven territory. He broke 40 acres and put it into flax, the sale of
which flax paid for the land, which was $600.

In the winter of '97 and '98 Mr. Ernst worked in a general store at
Lebanon, South Dakota. In April of '98 he went to Edmonton, Canada with
five cars of emigrant goods, returning in the fall. Edmonton was a small
city at that time of about 3000 population and no railroad. At the time Mr.
Ernst was in Edmonton he could have purchased a quarter of land upon which
Edmonton is now built for $25.00 per acre, but with his heart in South
Dakota he thought best to keep his interest there. so passed up the
opportunity. Edmonton now has a population of one hundred thousand.
Returning to Hoven he went to work for Hoven, Potter and Burr freighting
goods from Bowdle to Bangor. When the railroad extended west in 1900 the
company decided to move their building to the new townsite which was called
Selby. The building was 40x80, and a complete stock of general merchandise
was left intact. It took 74 horses to move the building and six weeks time,
and the. store was doing business the entire time. Mr. Ernst continued to
work for Hoven, Potter and Burr for two years in their new location at
Selby.

During Mr. Ernst's employment in Selby he became acquainted with a very
fine young lady by the name of Stella Douglas, who is remembered by Selby
citizens as one of their first school teachers. In 1902 Mr. Ernst and Miss
Douglas were married, and moved to Aberdeen South Dakota, where Mr. Ernst
continued to clerk in a store. In 1905 he purchased and operated his own
grocery store until 1907 when he sold his store and bought a farm 5 miles
southwest of Aberdeen where he still resides. They became the parents of
one son, Ray Ernst, who is now affiliated with his father in their farming
operations. The Ernst farm, which at the time of purchase. was but
unimproved land, is now a very modern farmstead and a lovely home, and is
known as the Ernst and Son Lakeview Farm.

In 1917 a loan association was organized, known as the Pioneer National
Farm Loan association and now known as the Brown County National Farm Loan
association, an association affiliated with the Federal Land Bank of Omaha.
George became a borrower and a member of this association, and was elected
president of the Board, which office he has held since with exception of a
few years when from time to time he took leave of absence to attend to
other affairs. Last year Mr. Ernst was appointed by Mr. Van Horne,
president of the Federal Land Bank of Omaha to meet with delegates of other
states at Washington, D. C., to formulate plans for the future agricultural
policies to be presented to the 81st Congress.

In 1923 Murphy of the Minneapolis Tribune selected two delegates from each
state., Montana, North and South Dakota and Minnesota to meet with the
Agricultural Committee of the House and Senate for the purpose of borrowing
fifty million dollars as a loan on hard spring wheat which was the
beginning of stabilization of prices for farmers. George Ernst was one of
these delegates. In 1930 he became interested in politics and ran on the
democratic ticket for a chair in the state senate. He was elected and
served in the '31, '33 and '35 session. He was again elected to serve in
'41 and '43 sessions. And then again he ran on the ticket and was elected
to serve in the '49 session. Mr. Ernst was one of the fact finding
committee appointed by Governor Mickelson on October 3, 1949 for the
purpose of making an on the ground study of the Arizona and Nebraska public
power distribution systems, as they may relate to South Dakota's problems
in obtaining its fair share of Missouri river power.

TOM ENGEBRETSON: CORN KING

In commemorating its 50th Anniversary, Selby and Walworth county are justly
proud of the accomplishments of Tom Engebretson, the Corn King,--one of its
most illustrious sons. Engebretson is a pioneer not only in the literal
sense, but also a pioneer in the most difficult of all horticultural
endeavors, that of selective corn breeding. Tom was born in Oslo, Norway,
on January 8, 1881, and immigrated to America with his parents, Helge
Engebretson and Haldes Engebretson, in 1884. They lived in Lincoln county,
South Dakota, for a short time and then the family settled in southern
Campbell county in 1885, where young Tom grew to manhood. He purchased his
own farm about six miles northwest of Selby where he now resides, in 1902,
and has lived there continuously since that date, except for a span of nine
years, 1922 1931, when he leased the farm and lived in Selby, still,
however, retaining an interest in his corn breeding. Tom enjoyed all of the
hardships and joys which were the lot of other early pioneers in this
section, and were we to limit his story to such matters, his life would not
vary much from others which are so beautifully related in this book, but
this young Norwegian was intensely interested in progressive farming, and
particularly in improving the quality, strain and type of corn adapted to
the late springs, minimum rainfall and early frosts which confront the
farmer in this area.

        MR. TOM ENGEBRETSON

In 1905, Tom took a short course at St. Paul, where he learned the
rudiments of grafting, pollination and cross-pollination of grains and
corn. With this fundamental training, he spent much time experimenting on
his own initiative, and also observing methods employed by others, and
profiting much from discussions with prominent horticulturists. During his
early years, he wasn't too successful, but he was learning. In 1926 he
started raising his now famous Engebretson's Silver King Corn. His first
sample was purchased at a crop show at Pierre in 1925, and he started
crossing this with a sample of white dent corn which he purchased east of
Aberdeen. Progress was slow and the advances made would have caused a man
lacking the patience of Tom Engebretson to give up in utter dismay in a
very short time, but not so with Engebretson. He had faith in the soil of
this section of the state. He had faith in his own ability and he was
confident that corn could be raised in this "small grain belt" which would
compete favorably with corn grown anywhere in the nation. As he progressed
with his corn breeding, he started entering samples of his corn in
competition with other corns in the International Livestock and Grain Shows
held annually at the Union Stock Yards in Chicago. A repetition of the
awards won well exemplifies the progress and success which Tom Engebretson
had as a corn breeder. In 1927, he won his first award, a No. 4 Junior
Rating for Region One, which included South Dakota. In 1928, he won a No. 4
award in white dent corn. In 1931, he. won a No. 9 award, and then followed
the dry years and World War II, and Tom ceased entering his corn in
international competition but nevertheless kept constantly working on
improving the quality of his corn, and developing the long, well-filled ears
with deep kernels, which have made it famous. In 1946, he again entered
international competition and won a No. 3 award. He achieved his climax in
1947 when the Engebretson's Silver King Corn won a No. 1 rating at the
International Show at Chicago. During all of these years, Tom also entered
his corn in local shows and won five sweepstakes awards at the Northern
Corn Show at Mobridge and three first place awards at the Northern Show of
Progress at Mobridge. He won eleven first prizes at the South Dakota State
Fair, four district championships at the South Dakota Crop Show at Brookings,
and a reserve championship in 1946, a grand championship in 1947, and
a reserve championship at the State Crop Show at Brookings in 1948. Tom has
been active in the leading corn shows throughout the country and for a
number of years served as vice president of the Northern Corn Show at
Mobridge.

        Prize Winning Corn by Tom Engebretson.

The highlight of Engebretson's career came in February, 1948, when more
than one hundred twenty five friends, neighbors and relatives gathered at
Selby and honored him with a Recognition banquet. At this time, Tom was
presented with a plaque which he won at the State Crop Show in Brookings
the previous year, and a first prize ribbon which he had won at the
International Livestock and Grain Show at Chicago in 1947. The featured
speaker was U. J. Norgaard, extension agronomist from the State College
at Brookings. He paid a fitting tribute to Engebretson and in referring to
Engebretson's Silver King, he predicted: "This corn, which year in and year
out gives good yields in central South Dakota, will undoubtedly become one
of the basic corns from which a hybrid for the area will some day be
developed. Silver King is one of the best yielding corns grown in central
South Dakota, and is recognized by farmers as being outstanding.
Engebretson ranks with the greatest corn growers South Dakota has produced."

After these statements and the making of the awards the heart of Tom
Engebretson, who had led a life of simplicity, hard work and Christian
endeavor, was overcome and his only words were a humble "Thank you." To
those who know Tom, those two words were more than ample because his life
has been, not of words, but of contribution to the welfare of his fellow
man and to generations yet unborn, his "Silver King Corn" will ever serve
as a monument to the memory of Tom Engebretson.

MR. AND MRS. HANS L. ENGEBRETSON

Hans L. Engebretson was born in Elverud, Norway on September 17, 1866 and
his wife, Anna K. Savold was born near Ossian, Iowa, on October 19, 1868,
at which place they were married March 31, 1889. About a year later,
wishing to establish a home for themselves, they came to Walworth county,
South Dakota. They brought with them, horses, cows, machinery, household
goods and enough feed for the first summer. They settled about two and
one-half miles west of old Bangor, having bought a relinquishment from E.
T. Hinds for $300.00, covering the northwest quarter of section 25,
township 123, range 77. Here he built a good house and farm buildings and
began his farming operations.

        MR. AND MRS. HANS ENGEBRETSON

The first year, only a small crop of feed was raised as all land had to be
broken. He continued to turn more sod into cultivated land each year and to
improve his property. As was true of all pioneers, he had to haul wood a
long distance for fuel. Bowdle was the nearest railroad town so all grain
had to be hauled the twenty five miles to market. Coming home from Bowdle on
one trip, he was caught in a prairie fire which burned the wagon and all
supplies he was bringing home and he was only able to save the horses.

Crops were good and poor intermittently and winters were very severe. On
May 24, 1896, at about six o'clock in the evening, after a beautiful bright
day, a cloud in the sky which formed into a cyclone, wiped out everything
they owned. All of the buildings and personal possessions were destroyed
and they were left with only the clothing they were wearing. They had been
invited to the George M. Mickelson home about five miles distant for a
Sunday dinner and in the afternoon they went to a meeting at the school
house and then to the home of Ole Savold, brother of Mrs. Engebretson, who
lived about two miles from their home. From there they were able to watch
the destruction of their home.

Having faith in the country and a determination to succeed, they started
over again and erected new buildings about a quarter mile south of the old
place and lived there until 1906, when they sold it and built a new home on
the southwest quarter of section 26, township 123, range 77, where they
resided until 1920 when they moved to Sioux Falls. In 1926, they returned to
the farm in Walworth county and lived there until 1939, when, on account of
poor health, they went to be near their children.

During the forty three years they lived in Hilde town- ship, Mr.
Engebretson served as road supervisor, school district treasurer and as
county commissioner. Both Mr. and Mrs. Engebretson were members of the
Norwegian church and were active in the organization of a Sunday school in
their community. Mr. Engebretson was among the first members of the Woodman
Lodge and helped to build the Woodman hall at Bangor.

Six children were born to them, four boys and two girls; two boys died in
infancy; the living children are two sons, Lloyd and Earl; and two
daughters, Mrs. Verne Kingsbury and Mrs. Wesley Herrman, all of whom reside
in South Dakota.

Mr. Engebretson now lives at Lead, South Dakota, and at the age of
eighty-two years is still very active and interested in the news of the
county and the people he knows. Mrs. Engebretson passed away March 31, 1941,
at Philip, South Dakota.

J. J. ELFRINK FAMILY

My grandparents were born in Germany. Grandfather Elfrink was a bridge
builder in Holland before coming to the United States. He located on a farm
near Barrington, Illinois, thirty miles from Chicago. I was born at
Barrington on September 28, 1881, and moved to Bangor, South Dakota, with
my parents at the age of three. My father, J. J. Elfrink, started out for
himself at the age of seventeen learning the blacksmith trade. He worked
for two years for $50.00 and board a year. At the end of two years he had
saved $52.00--then started in business for himself. His parents had a few
sheep and a spinning wheel, and my grandmother often spun and made my
father's clothing. After about ten years, father sold his business and came
to South Dakota with $5,000, my mother and three children. He bought 320
acres of land in Grant county, 160 acres in Kings bury county, a house and
lot in Watertown, and then took a homestead and a tree-claim sixteen miles
west of Bowdle. At that time Ipswich was the nearest railroad town but the
rails were soon laid to Bowdle. Oxen were used for farming at first, then
father bought two horses from Barney Bole and one from Ritter. Father filed
on the land in 1883 or 1884. In 1888 Clara and I had scarlet fever. I had a
relapse and was sick for about a year.

        MR. AND MRS. JACOB ELFRINK

During that time my father took a horse and buggy and ran it all the. way
to Bowdle to see a doctor. He took a team of spotted broncs and ran them
all the way back, and they were ready to run away after making the sixteen
mile trip. Once when we lived on the farm, my brother, Walter, went to
Bangor without money to get a sack of flour. The stores gave no credit.
Then he dug winter onions, peddled them out and thus got the money for the
flour. We farmed about eight years and then father was elected county
commissioner. My brother, Walter, did most of the work in the office and he
was only sixteen. Father and mother rented a store building in Bangor and
were successful selling general merchandise. Later they bought a store
building in LeBeau with five rooms upstairs, and lean to with three rooms
downstairs. They moved the granary from the farm adding it to the length of
the store building. It was later moved to Selby where the family continued
in the general merchandise business until 1912. There were five children in
the family. Walter and Esther were osteopathic doctors. Walter passed away
in 1929, and Esther in 1919. Evelyn married Walter Smith, had three sons
and passed away in 1941. Clara married Guy Schellenger, has two sons and
lives near Eugene, Oregon. Father passed away in 1916 and mother in 1918. I
was a traveling salesman during 1906 and 1907, traveling in Idaho, Utah,
Oregon and Washington, and then was in the store at Selby for four years.
On January 29, 1908, I was married to Olive Young of Athol. She was
teaching in Selby when we met, and I thought right away that she was the
girl I had been looking for. Olive's parents had a farm near Athol. During
January and February, 1912, I was again a traveling salesman, but this time
in Canada. That spring we moved to the Loan Walters' place and farmed. We
sold out that fall and moved to Brentford, and farmed there until the fall
of 1918, when we moved back to the Elfrink farm six miles southeast of
Selby. Soon after we were married I joined the Masons and both of us joined
the Eastern Star. I served on the school board for several years at Selby.
In 1937 we moved to Glad Valley, South Dakota, where we have a general
merchandise store. We have two children, Clifford and Marian. Clifford has a
general store at Isabel, and Marian lives on a farm near Melvin, Iowa. (By
Paul Elfrink.)

MR. STEVE RABA

Steve Raba was born near Budapest, Hungary, where he grew up and received a
good Hungarian education.

Mrs. Raba died in 1887 leaving her husband with seven small children to
care for. Mr. Raba kept his home for a couple of years. Finding it hard to
make a living for his family, because of Hungary's overcrowded population,
Mr. Raba decided to come to the new land which everyone was hearing so much
about.

He left his five youngest children with their grandfather, and they were
later taken by an aunt, due to their grandfather's death. Steve. Raba and
his oldest daughter, Julia, started for the United States. Landing in 1890
they came directly to this part of the country through the influence of
friends. He homesteaded on land in Walworth county and made plans to
prepare a home for his family.

In 1893 with what money Mr. Raba had saved and with what he borrowed from
Emory Bruckner, he sent for his four remaining children, Agnes, age 13;
Andrew, 11; John, 9; and Rosie, 7 years of age; Mike having come over
before with a friend.

Mr. Raba lived on his farm southeast of Selby until 1909 when he sold it to
his son, John.

In 1910 Steve Raba moved to Canada, where he died some years later at the
age of 86.

MR. JOHN RABA

John Raba came to Selby from Budapest, Hungary, where he was born on
November 23, 1883. At the age of four years his mother passed away. For the
next two years the home was kept intact, but in 1890 the home was broken up
when his father and oldest sister, Julia, came to the United States to
prove up land. John and his two brothers, Mike and Andrew, and two sisters,
Agnes and Rosie, were left with a grandfather.

The children waited anxiously for the time when they could again join their
