father in their new home. They had heard such very fine things about
America--that the streams and creeks were flowing with milk and bread could
be picked from trees. These stories were hard to believe, but they wished
to see for themselves. In 1893 the time had come and they sailed for the
United States. When John reached the age of 15 he started working out.
Sometime later he met Julia Bertha, and on April 22, 1907, they were
happily married and went to live on a farm one and one half miles southwest
of Lowry. It was here their first child, Mary, was born.

In 1909 John bought and moved to his father's farm. On March 23, 1910,
while Strand, a neighbor, was burning in preparation for spring work, the
fire got away in the wind and burned John's house and barn. They were able
to salvage nothing from these two buildings. Mr. Strand paid five hundred
fifty dollars for the damage. However, Mr. and Mrs. Raba will never forget
the many kind and generous neighbors and friends who helped them by giving
clothing, money and other items.

Mr. and Mrs. Raba made their home with Mrs. Raba's folks, the Steve
Berthas', from this time until June when John bought a house from Fred
Shandorf and moved it on his farm. In July they started building a new barn,
so as to be ready for the coming winter.

To this couple ten children were born: Mary, Mrs. Joe Lemler, Selby;
Johnny, Selby; Charles, Selby, who served in an Army Medical division in
World War II; Emma Stangl, Selby; Benjamin, deceased; Sylvester, who
served in the Army Air Corps and who was reported missing in the Pacific
area; Clara, Mrs. Edgar Holzworth, Gettysburg, South Dakota; August and
Joseph, Selby; and Julia Ann, Mrs. Henry Scherer, Jr., Selby.

Mr. and Mrs. John Raba retired from farm life and moved into Selby in 1944,
selling their farm to their son, Johnny, and the four unmarried sons are
living there at the present time.

OLSON--ELLEFSON

Eli Ellefson lived on the south half of section 27, township 124, range 77
from before the time South Dakota was admitted to the union until her
death, January 19, 1941. The story of her experiences is another portion of
the history of the area.

Her husband-to-be, Johannes Olson, came with his brothers, Olaus and Jacob,
to Michigan about 1883. Later they went to a Scandinavian settlement in
Kansas and from there came to Walworth county in 1885 and with Hans
Ellefson filed on homesteads and proceeded to build homes.

In August, 1886, Eli Saettemsli, Gunhild Ellefson, Mrs. Olaus Olson (Ildri)
and sons, Ole and Olaf, and Mrs. Hans Ellefson (Martha) and daughters,
Martha and Dena came from Norway to Ipswich, South Dakota, to meet their
husbands and future husbands.

The relationship in the group is interesting to trace. Gunhild Ellefson
was Hans Ellefson's sister and became Mrs. Jacob Olson; Mrs. Hans Ellefson,
affectionately known as "old" Aunt Martha from the time she was forty years
old, was a sister of the Olson brothers; Eli Saettemsli became Mrs.
Johannes Olson. Like many of the other Norse immigrant girls Eli brought
her spinning wheel when she came. Her small chest and big trunk were
painted the same brilliant blue as the spinning wheel. The original paint
remains on the wheel to this day, a precious family possession. Hundreds of
yards of yarn for socks and sweaters came from work on that spinning wheel.


        MR. AND MRS. JOHN OLSON
        Mrs. Olson is the late Mrs. John Ellefson. Children in picture:
        Upper left, Oscar; upper right, Edward; lower left, Martin; lower
        right, Carl. Martha and Johnny not shown

Ipswich was the end of the railroad at that time. The men came with teams
of oxen and wagons, and the trip from their homesteads five miles northwest
of Selby took three days. Homes were already prepared for all of them--sod
houses with lumber shanties on the Jacob and Johannes Olson houses. The
main room was large and partly a dugout which made it cozy in the prairie
winter The lumber shanty, about 12 by 14 feet, was too cold for winter
living. The walls of this room were of ceiling board. A second sod room was
added later which had fine fir flooring and wall to wall carpeting. The
plaster walls had pink kalsomine, and there was a pink spread on the bed
which provided part of the seating when the ladies aid was entertained.
The room was large enough so a frame could be set up for occasional
quilting bees. The barns on the places were made of sod also, with rough
lumber doors.

In 1892 John Ellefson, brother of Hans Ellefson and Gunhild Olson came to
homestead two and one half miles north of the Johannes Olson place. He had
been working on the railroad at Lincoln, Nebraska, with his brother Ole.
Later he was to become a part of the Olson family.

In 1897 Johannes Olson sought medical attention at Bowdle. After a few
weeks it became evident his condition was serious so he was taken to St.
Paul where he passed away on May 10, 1897. The youngest child was but three
months old. This was John E., who now lives in Harding county. The older
children were Edward, now at Camp Crook, South Dakota, Oscar, at Northwood,
Iowa; Martin, who was killed in a mine accident at Butte Montana, in 1927;
Carl, at Victoria, Vancouver Island B. C.; and Martha Backer, at Selby.

In 1899 the lightning of a prairie storm struck near a spring by an old
well at the east end of the farm. As farm animals were precious, it was a
tremendous loss when it was found that three young horses were killed and
another one died later.

In 1900 the widow, Eli Olson, married John Ellefson. Three sons were born:
Edgar, who died in infancy; Edgar T., who lives at Missoula, Montana; and
Ingwald W., who is at Great Falls, Montana. John had fallen from a tree
when he was a young man in Norway, and this injury resulted in a leg-bone
disease after he was married. It was necessary to have the leg amputated
when he was older. In 1922 he passed away.

In 1907 the present frame house was completed on the place, and the family
moved into it in the spring. A Syrian peddler sold brocade cloths to most
every farm family in his journeyings that year, and one with the date
"1907" still commemorates the move.

These sturdy pioneers have passed. Their farm northwest of Selby was for
many years one of the best improved in the locality and the farm was always
well kept up and today is still one of the good farms in the section.

MR. HENRY RICHARD DE MALIGNON

Henry deMalignon was born February 19, 1860, in the city of New York. His
father, a typical Frenchman, was a member of the royal house of France. His
mother was an English woman.

At the age of fifteen he started learning the manufacturing of pianos with
the Chickering Piano company of New York and while he trained had the
chance to make his spending money by acting as an usher at Chickering Hall
where he had the opportunity of hearing music and seeing operas not to be
excelled at that time. He devoted his time to the study of music and while
not an outstanding musician he knew and loved good music.

On March 27, 1884, he married Marie Hofmeyer, the daughter of a maker of
fine jewelry, and in 1886, with a son, Harry, came to the territory of
Dakota and filed on a homestead north of Selby on the Campbell county line.
On December 12, 1887, at the town of Bowdle, Frank, the second son, was
born and then on September 30, 1889, Arthur and on October g, 1891, Robert
were born on the homestead. In 1893 the deMalignons purchased Lots 16 and
17, Block 14 in Bangor from H. B. and Hattie M. Foster. A dwelling was
purchased in the town of Scranton, near Lebeau, and moved to these lots.
Afterwards it was again moved to Selby together with the rest of the town
of Bangor.

Mr. deMalignon served as county auditor of Walworth county from 18g3 to
1898 in Bangor. At Selby he ran the elevator and bought grain for the Crown
Elevator company for several years and then went into the grain and farm
machine business for himself. He also operated a furniture sales and repair
business until the end of the First World War when he sold out and moved to
Plana, South Dakota, where he conducted a grocery business until he died in
1922. He is buried in Aberdeen. Mrs. deMalignon made her home with her son,
Frank, in Minneapolis, since that time, until October, 1949, when she
passed away. He was very active in the Maccabees and Modern Woodmen in
Selby, also the Masonic Lodge. Mrs. deMalignon was secretary for the Yeoman
Lodge for many years and very active in Red Cross work during World War I.
Both were members of the Episcopal church in Selby.

Harry deMalignon, oldest son, served his country in the First World War,
attaining the rank of captain. He now resides in Santa Ana, California.

Frank's military service began with the South Dakota National Guards, and
in 1916 he was called into the federal service for Mexican Border duty
which lasted ten months with service at San Benito, Texas. Thirty days
after being mustered out he was recalled for World War I duty, serving
about twenty-two months. He spent one year in France, with direct contact
with the enemy at two different times. He was gassed at Mountdidier Front on
May 3, 1918, and received a slight shell wound at Soissions on July 18, the
same year. He was discharged to the reserve corps at New York (Statute of
Liberty) on January 3, 1919. On August 28, 1917, Frank married Francisca
Anderson of Atwater, Minnesota. To this union one son was born in 1920.
Frank has made his home in Minneapolis ever since his discharge from Army
service.

Arthur deMalignon married Ida Schmidt of Selby, and during their early
married life lived in Selby. Arthur, known as "Bob", worked at the
printers' trade in Selby. In 1919 this couple moved to Aberdeen where Bob
has continued his profession and home up to the present. They have one son.

Robert deMalignon, known to all as "Bert", chose the undertaking and
funeral business. He married Emily Rossiter of Ipswich, and now lives at
Bowdle, South Dakota, where he conducts a very fine business of his
profession. They have a son and a daughter.

OLAF AND MARTHE EKREM AND FAMILY

Olaf Elias T. Ekrem was born April 14, 1873, at Sovden, Sondmore, Norway.
He came to America at the age of 19 years and settled at Selby, Walworth
county, South Dakota, in 1892. Two brothers, Peter and Rasmus Thorstenson,
had preceded him in coming to this country.  His common school education,
plus an additional year, had been completed before leaving Norway. After
arriving here he spent his first winter ('92 and '93) at Augsburg Seminary
in Minneapolis, Minnesota, where his brother, John Ekrem, was also a
student.

After leaving school he found work at various places in Minnesota and South
Dakota for a short time before homesteading two and one-half miles
northwest of Selby. Here he first built a sod house, which he replaced with
a three-room house he had purchased and moved to the present site. As the
year went on the home was added on to until it reached the size it is at
present.

Bowdle was the nearest town in those early days and the only way to get
there was to walk or ride or drive the horses. It was to this place that
Olaf had to go for his mail and supplies.

The slough east of the present buildings was filled with water, as at
present. This attracted him to file on this particular land. The early
settlers would stop here for water while driving their cattle overland, as
there were no wells at that time.

There was an abundance of rocks which had to be cleared off before much
successful farming could be done. When after a few years the water dried up
for a time he found that there were many rocks even in the slough bed. As
Selby was being built, Olaf helped to excavate many of the basements, also
to haul rock from his land for many of the foundations.

After having dug a well which yielded an abundance of good water, he hauled
drinking water to many of the Selby residents.

MR. AND MRS. OLAF EKREM AND DAUGHTER PAULINE

In 1910 he was married to Pauline Seljeseth. To this union was born one
daughter, Pauline Marguerite. On the tenth day following her daughter's
birth Mrs. Ekrem passed away. It was through the efforts of kind neighbors,
relatives and friends that it was possible for Olaf to keep his child and
to raise her. Much credit is due to Mrs. John Smith, a neighbor, who kept
her for a year. Mrs. Buchanan provided the baptismal dress which was used
at Pauline's christening.

I, Marthe Karine Hafnor, was born July 1, 1880, in Hole, Ringerike, Norway.
In 1888 I immigrated to the United States with my parents, who settled in
Brown county, sixteen miles southeast of Aberdeen.

In 1900 I graduated from the Lutheran Normal School at Madison, Minnesota.
I taught school for ten years in all. It was in 1905 that I came out to
teach Parochial school in Walworth and Campbell counties and first met
Olaf. We were married in 1913. To this union were born Palma, Orville and
Hazel.

We were among the first in the community to have an automobile and to put
electric lights and appliances into our home. We have been members and
workers in the Bethany Lutheran congregation.

Prior to the consolidation of the Hiddenwood-Bangor townships, Olaf acted
as clerk of the Hiddenwood School district.

There were many good years which we experienced in our work of farming and
the raising of cattle, but there were also those years which taxed every
inch of strength, ingenuity and faith that we were able to gather. Such
were the years of the grasshoppers, drought and the dust storms of the
years 1934 to 1938.

Perhaps one of the most unpleasant thoughts we have of those years is when
Olaf used to drive east of Aberdeen each week with a hay rack behind his
car hoping to get a load of hay to feed to his cattle in order that he
might save them. The hay turned out to be mostly thistle but it was the
best he could find.

We feel that it was these trying years which aggravated his failing health,
causing his death on November 12, 1937. He was buried at the Bethany
cemetery.

He felt grateful that he had been able to save his home and property during
those years of financial stress so that his family would be well cared for
after his death.

SHORT BIOGRAPHICAL ACCOUNTS OF OUR CHILDREN

Pauline Marguerite Ekrem

Was born July 13, 1911, at Selby, South Dakota. She attended grade school
and four years of high school at Selby, graduating in 1929. The following
fall she attended St. Olaf College at Northfield, Minnesota, receiving her
13. A. Degree in 1933 from that institution. One summer term was spent at
the University of Minnesota and another at the American University,
Washington, D. C. She taught in the high schools at Selby, South Dakota;
Moose Lake, Minnesota; and Robbinsdale, Minnesota. She accepted an
assignment with the American Red Cross in December of 1943 and reported for
duty January 1 at Camp McCoy, Wisconsin. Other assignments since that time
have been at Chanute Field, Illinois; U. S. Naval Hospital, Great Lakes,
Illinois; Percy Jones General Hospital, Battle Creek, Michigan; Station
Hospital, Fort Lawton, Washington; and Sopporo, Japan, where she is located
at the present time.

Palma Theresse Ekrem

Was born March 30, 1915, at Selby, South Dakota. She attended grade school
and high school there, graduating in 1934. She then attended a beauticians'
school in Minneapolis, Minnesota, and went to Watertown, South Dakota,
where she worked for several years. In April, 1939, she was married to
Norman Slater of Watertown. During the war he went overseas to the South
Pacific as an officer. He is still in service, being stationed now at Camp
Stoneman. They have one son, Donald, and two daughters, Martha Louise and
Dorothy Jean. Their home address now is 2456) Upland Drive, Concord,
California.

Orville K. L. Ekrem

Was born January 13, 1917, at Selby, South Dakota. He too attended grade
and high school there, having graduated in 1937. Since his father's death
he has remained on the farm working the land, raising cattle and keeping
the home place up. In addition to this he has rented and purchased more
land to farm.

On December 31, 1946, he was married to Miss Minnie Bender of Mobridge,
South Dakota.

Hazel Melvina Ekrem

Was born November 12, 1921, at Selby, South Dakota. She attended grade and
high school at Selby, graduating in 1938. She attended the Mankato Business
College at Mankato, Minnesota, and from there went to Washington, D. C.,
where she was employed by the U. S. War Department as a secretary for
several years. From there she went to California, where she held a similar
position for some time.

Later she lived in Minneapolis where she was employed in the Insurance
Division of the Veterans Administration at Fort Snelling, and is now
holding a government position in Tokyo, Japan.

                By (MRS.) MARTHE EKREM.

MR. AND MRS. OLE DYBVIK

One of the prominent pioneer couples of Walworth county who would have
celebrated their golden wedding anniversary this year was the late Mr.
Dybvik and his wife, Ida.

Ole Dybvik, a well-known and familiar figure around Selby for almost 40
years, was born in Sondmor, Norway, on September 24, 1874. Tragedy struck
early in his life when, at the tender age of four, both his parents passed
away within a few hours of one another and he was left an orphan. For some
years he lived with foster parents, but in his early teens he struck out
for himself by joining an English fishing fleet that fished for cod off the
banks of Lofoten Islands. When 18 years of age he made his first trip to
America, but returned to Norway within two years and again spent many years
living the hardy and fearless life of the sea.

        MR. AND MRS. O. DYBVIK

In 1900 he married Ida Seljeseth, a childhood schoolmate, and the same year
they migrated to America, homesteading five miles west of Selby.

Ida Seljeseth, born April 22, 1873, was the eldest of seven daughters of
Johan and Anna Seljeseth who later also migrated to America and for several
years lived near the Dybvik homestead. They were a venerable old couple,
loved and respected by all who knew them.

Ida Seljeseth attended teachers' training school at Volden, Norway, and for
five years she taught school at Narvik, Norway, in the land of the midnight
sun.

These two young people started out with very little as measured in world
goods. At first they lived in a sod house and suffered privation the same
as the other pioneers of that day, but by hard work, thrift, and
perseverance they steadily improved and added to the homestead until it
became one of the fine farms of the county.

Mr. and Mrs. Dybvik were among the founders of the Bethany Lutheran church.
They were active members of their church and sought to live up to the
teachings of the Master.

They gave their children fine religious and educational advantages. Seven
children were born to them. Three sons passed away in infancy and one
daughter, Esther, passed away at the age of 19 while a student at Oak Grove
Seminary, Fargo, North Dakota.

Elmer, Amy, and Paul survive. They were all educated in the schools of
Walworth county. Elmer attended Northern Normal and Industrial school at
Aberdeen for a time. For several years he operated his father's farm and is
now employed by the Milwaukee road.

Amy attended Northern State Teachers college at Aberdeen and Black Hills
Teachers college, Spearfish, South Dakota. She taught school for several
years prior to her marriage to Ray Raab of Yelm, Washington, where they now
reside. One son, Jimmy, was born to them.

Paul, after completing high school, attended Augsburg college in
Minneapolis. He married Bebe Steiger. They have one daughter, Sylvia Ann.
At present they live in Tacoma, Washington.

In 1925 Mr. Dybvik, accompanied by his brother-in-law, Sigvald Veien, made
a trip to Norway to visit the land of their birth. They spent a wonderful
summer together re-visiting the scenes of their childhood and becoming
re-acquainted with their old friends and relatives.

Mr. Dybvik was always interested in school, church, community and county
affairs. At different times he served on various committees and boards. At
one time he was a member of the school board. For some time he served as
assessor. From 1934 to 1938, during the worst of the depression and
probably the most trying years in the history of the county, he served as
county commissioner for the Selby district.

Mr. Dybvik was well-read and always an interesting conversationalist. He
was considered an honest upright citizen, a good neighbor, and a provident
parent. On May 3, 1939, after a lingering illness, he passed away at his
farm home west of town.

Mrs. Dybvik is a sweet, refined, little lady, deeply religious, liked and
admired by all who make her acquaintance. Since her husband's death, she
has spent most of her time with her son and daughter on the west coast.

MR. AND MRS. RALPH DROWN

After a winter spent in bed with sciatic rheumatism, Ralph Orson Drown was
advised by his doctor to leave New York state and seek his fortune in a
drier climate. After spending a year with his uncle, Jack Crawford, in
Wilson, Kansas, his health had improved so much that he went to New Mexico
for a while to work as a day laborer on the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe
railroad. His cousin was the section boss. The wages were $1.40 a day, with
$5.00 taken out of each week's check for board. While helping out at a
sister's home in Valley Springs, South Dakota, his stepbrothers, Nate and
Henry Sunderland, wrote him of open government land adjoining theirs in
Walworth county. At twenty-four years of age he filed on the northwest
quarter of 9-127-77 as a preemption, and on the southwest quarter of
4-123-77 as a tree claim. The proving up of these claims was more of a joke
than anything else. They had to swear they had a stoned up well and a house
on the preempted land, so Mr. Drown built a rough frame shack in which he
spent several nights but cooked no meals. He worked for Nate and Henry so
boarded with them. He also dug a well and stoned it up, although there
never was a drop of water in it. For the tree claim they went to the river
and brought home a bundle of tree cuttings and stuck them around here and
there in the plowing. They would have been astonished if any had grown.
Henry and Nate had quite a flock of hens and there was practically no
market for eggs so there were eggs in all the dishes and kettles and pans.
Henry. (the cook) served five eggs each per meal for weeks until they got
them all eaten. Mr. Drown had built his claim shack but only had roof
boards on and no shingles. One night it started to rain and as he was
getting wet he grabbed a blanket and started across the prairie to Nate's
dugout a half a mile away. It was dark and he headed in the right direction
and started out. After walking for some time he looked up and saw a
building which to his great surprise turned out to be his own shack. He had
been walking in a circle. The old timers say this was a common experience
on the prairie--the vastness of the land had a sameness unbroken by any
landmarks. Leaving his claim he returned to Minnehaha county where he
worked with Jewett Brothers in Sioux Falls. He was later transferred to
their new wholesale grocery house at Sheldon, Iowa, where he worked as
shipping clerk for 15 years. It was during this period that he met and wed
Miss Pearl Vanderbeck. When Jewetts closed their Sheldon branch house they
offered him a job in their Sioux Falls and Aberdeen houses, but Mr. and
Mrs. Drown decided to go to Selby to farm. They moved to Selby with their
three children, Mildred, Hazel and Claude, to improve their farm. During
this time two more children, a son, Ernest, and a daughter, Laura, were
born.

        MR. AND MRS. RALPH DROWN AND FAMILY
        Standing, left to right--Mrs. Tom Potter (Mildred), Ernest, Mrs.
        Lloyd Sawinsky (Hazel). Seated, left to right--Mrs. Hugh Crawford
        (Laura), Mr. Drown, Mrs. Drown, and Claude Drown.

Mr. Drown was one of the organizers of the Equity Union of Selby. He was
the first secretary-treasurer of that organization. He was on the school
board of the Hilde school district for a number of years. They farmed for
six years and then returned to Sheldon where Mr. Drown went into
partnership in the furniture store with his father-in law, who was failing
in health. They continued in this business during World War I, and then
came back to South Dakota where they have lived ever since. Mrs. Drown owns
the Home Studio in Selby which she has operated for ]7 years. She is a
member of the Methodist church, was one of the organizers of the Jolly
club, is a member of the W. S. C. Society of the church, the Selby Woman's
club, and a Past Matron of Hope Chapter No. 73, O. E. S., Selby, who in
1949 presented Mrs. Drown with a gavel in honor of her 52nd year as a
member of that order.

Mr. Drown has a very interesting hobby of collecting crossword puzzle words
and their definitions. He is an excellent penman, using the print script
and has several volumes filled with these crossword puzzle words, and their
definitions. So, although this couple find their work lighter than in the
early years on the farm, yet their days are filled with interesting and
useful duties.

Mr. and Mrs. Drown celebrated their Golden Wedding anniversary in 1947,
with all their children home. At the present time Mr. and Mrs. Drown live
in Selby. Their daughter Mildred (Mrs. Tom Potter) lives on a farm near
Sheldon, Iowa. Hazel (Mrs. Lloyd Sawinsky) lives in Onida, South Dakota,
where her husband operates the theater. Claude lives in Sheridan, Wyoming.
He is manager of the Mutual Life of New York Insurance company in Wyoming.
Ernest owns and operates the C & E Store (general merchandise and
groceries) in Selby, South Dakota. Laura (Mrs. Hugh Crawford) lives on a
ranch south of Selby. Mr. and Mrs. Drown have 15 grandchildren and three
great grandchildren. The family went through good years and bad in South
Dakota, and endured many hardships of that time. One source of danger they
encountered with the rest of their neighbors were the frequent prairie
fires which often threatened life and home of the early settler.

Mr. Drown relates the following incident: "One of those years, Henry
started out with the oxen and wagon with a quarter of beef lying on some
hay in the wagon. He had been smoking a pipe and had put the pipe in his
overcoat pocket and threw the coat back on the hay. The pipe set the coat
and hay afire, and to save the wagon he threw the hay out on the prairie and
started a fire that came near burning their straw, barns and their granary.
Their granary was full of wheat and they had some wheat piled up outside
against it and covered with straw. The fire, in spite of them, got right
into the edge of the straw that covered the wheat, and Henry laid down on
the ground and rolled in the fire and saved their granary and wheat but got
his whiskers pretty badly singed. They fought the fire for the rest of the
day which traveled with a southeast wind clear up Blue Blanket lake. That
night Nate became uneasy and got up and the wind had changed to the
northwest and the fire was coming back and they had all they could do to
save their buildings again. It burned at least to Bangor or thereabouts.
There wasn't enough grass left on my half section to make a hen's nest."

MR. AND MRS. A. C. DOBSON

Alma C. Dobson and wife, Jennie Newcom Dobson, both were born and reared
near Deloit, Crawford county, Iowa. After finishing the village school,
both attended Denison Normal and Business college in Denison, the county
seat of Crawford county, both teaching rural schools to earn money to
finish their college courses, she taking normal, he commercial work.

He graduated in 1892 and was chosen to give the oration for the commercial
department. He attended summer school in Sac City and taught school in Sac
county, Iowa. Later he was head bookkeeper and overseer on the Cook ranch
north of Odebolt in Sac county, Iowa. Then he became cashier in his uncle's
bank in Deloit, Iowa, but was not satisfied with indoor work so came to
Charles Mix county, South Dakota. by team and buggy, in the fall of 1900,
where he and W. B. Myler spent the winter baling hay for the ranchers and
Indians in that part of the state. J. H. Holmes, a former instructor in the
Denison college, at the time these two young men were in attendance there,
had come to Armour, South Dakota, for his health and cordially welcomed the
"boys" into his home. Later Mr. Holmes and family came to Selby and engaged
in the real estate business. Through his influence, Mr. Dobson came by team
and buggy to Selby in October, 1903.

        MR. ALMA C. DOBSON

Mr. Holmes and family were domiciled in the property of the late Attorney
A. H. Smith, on North Main street in Selby, but moved to Aberdeen that
fall. Through Mr. Holmes, Mr. Dobson rented the Nance farm, east of Selby,
now occupied by Max Hoven. Here Mr. Dobson established bachelor quarters
and put up some hay for next year's use.

In December he returned to Deloit, Iowa, by train to marry Miss Jennie
Newcom, who had in the meantime been teaching in the states of Iowa,
Washington and Minnesota, most of the time receiving $28.00 or $30.00 per
month for her services. They were married in the beautiful farm home of the
bride's parents, Mr. and Mrs. James T. Newcom, near Deloit, on February 3,
1904.

After the parents and relatives of both had given them such items as a few
pieces of furniture, a team of ponies, and so on, it necessitated
chartering an emigrant car. Yes, and the bride had saved enough from her
"big salary," while teaching, to buy a bedroom suite complete except for
the mattress, but a mattress was not considered necessary as one of the
mothers had put in a new straw tick to be filled later with Dakota straw.
The groom came out with the emigrant car. The bride arrived two weeks later
on March 1 in the worst blizzard of the winter. Mr. and Mrs. James Coffey
had Mr. and Mrs. Dobson up for dinner. Mr. Coffey was in the real estate
business. Soon after dinner Mr. and Mrs. Dobson started for "home." The
storm was so severe they could only occasionally glimpse their team. Those
two miles seemed long ones. They had many experiences, some laughable, some
otherwise. Mrs. Dobson put eggs under two setting hens and hatched 25 baby
chicks. They had at that time never heard of buying baby chicks. These were
the pride of her heart. She knew chicks sometimes had lice, also knew her
mother put something on-them to kill the lice. Maybe it was kerosene, maybe
lard. So she put both on to be sure and did such a good job at it that
those little chicks shriveled up until they looked like cracklings.
Twenty-four of them died. The one that survived committed suicide by
drowning in a pail of water. That was her first experience at chicken
raising.

Mr. and Mrs. Nance, owners of the farm, decided to farm the place next
year. Mr. and Mrs. Dobson moved onto the Charlie Reistad farm, adjoining
the Fremont Stewart farm, eleven miles southwest of Selby. They rented that
farm six years. While living there, their little 6-months-old son died of
pneumonia. They took the little body back to Deloit, Iowa, for burial.

In December, 1907, they bought a piece of raw prairie land, all of section
30, in township 123, range 77, and in February, 1911, built a granary on
the place and moved into it until the crop was in, when they planned to
build a house. June came. The crop was in but there had been no rain and no
seed had come up. The building job was postponed until it did rain, which
was not until September. The building fund had to be kept to buy next
year's seed and horse feed. They rented a quarter of hayland two miles from
home. By taking their dinners and water for the horses with them in the
morning and mowing with two mowers all day they could cut two loads of hay,
which was loaded onto two wagons and taken home with them each evening.
Flax came up and blossomed after the September rain. It was left to mature
until snow came October 18. Next day they went out to cut what flax was
above the snow. The flax bolls contained nothing but frozen water blisters
but it would make some feed for the four milk cows they had kept when
forced to sell the rest of the herd in September, due to lack of feed.
There was no cash crop and cash was what was needed to pay interest and
taxes. Mrs. Dobson suggested they hire a neighbor boy to take her place in
header box Saturday and she would go to Selby to see the county
superintendent about getting a teacher's certificate. As she had been out
of school work for eight years, it was with fear and trembling that she
appeared before County Superintendent Guy Schellenger. He said she would
have to write the entire examination the next Thursday and Friday,
including South Dakota history, which she had never studied. She borrowed
the book and returned home. She said that was once she improved the time
while driving with horse and buggy that twelve miles through the snow, for
she read South Dakota history all the way home.

Invited Sunday dinner guests prevented further study until Monday. Then
came three days to cram for exams. She passed and school began at the
Powell school about November 1, with eighteen enrolled from the families of
Zabels', Slaughters', Stewarts', Erps' and Larsons'. There were seven in
the 8th grade. She recalls that she taught for $30.00 per month to pay 10%
interest on a farm mortgage. Note the difference in teacher's wages and
interest rate then and now.

Next year wheat went two bushels per acre. No grade. By repeated fannings,
Mr. Dobson got enough that was sufficiently filled so it would grow, for
his next years' seed. Crops slowly improved but not until they had lived in
the granary seven years, did the crops warrant an investment in a house.

Mrs. Dobson continued teaching until 1915, E. H. Noteboom being county
superintendent at that time. The later years of school were taught in what
was known as the Mickelson school with children enrolled from Lemkes',
Seeleys' and the two Tucker families.  In the spring of 1918 they rented
their farm to Mr. and Mrs. Art Zabel. In September 1918, Mr. Dobson bought
the northwest quarter of section 29, township 123, range 77, from Roy
Dearinger of Reasoner, Iowa. This provided a good well for his five
quarters of land.  In the fall of 1919 they moved to Selby when Mr. Dobson
bought the Selby lumber yard of O. W. Schultz. This business he continued
to own and operate for fourteen years; then sold it to the Central Lumber
company in October 1933.

Throughout Mr. Dobson's long career as a farmer and business man, he was
active in a quiet way, in all civic and public affairs, willingly and
untiringly working for the betterment of the community at all times. He was
county assessor one term, served for many years on the city council of
Selby, was a member of the cemetery association, the Walworth County Fair
association, the Lake Hiddenwood project, and served in countless other
capacities for many years, doing good for the community and its people,
supporting all charities and good works of whatever nature.

Mr. and Mrs. Dobson were members of the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ
of Latter Day Saints, that has its headquarters in Independence, Missouri.
There being no church of that denomination here, they always gave loyal
support to local religious works, Mrs. Dobson having taught a young
people's class in the Methodist Sunday school continuously for many years.

After Mr. Dobson retired from business, they traveled quite extensively but
were always glad to get back to Selby. He often remarked that he had never
seen a place where he would rather live or make a financial start in life
than right here in Walworth county, South Dakota. Although he experienced
the same disappointments due to drouth, grasshoppers and low prices that
others had to meet, he never lost faith in this area.

Mr. Dobson was born November 26, 1871, and passed away August 2, 1941, of
encephalitis, the dreaded sleeping sickness, of which so little is known.

Mrs. Dobson still resides in Selby.

THE HELGE LUND SR. FAMILY

Helge Lund Sr., was born in Voss, Norway on December 7, 1831 and his wife,
Inga Bolstad Lund, was born on November 10, 1831.

In 1859 Mr. and Mrs. Lund and two sons, Helge Jr., and John left their
native land in search of a new home in America. It took nine weeks for them
to cross the ocean, in a large sailing vessel, which landed at Quebec,
Canada. From here they came down into the United States, settling in Dane
county, Wisconsin. Here they lived for seven years, then they moved to Iowa
in the vicinity of Osage and Estherville. This was their home until 1884
when they came to Dakota.

The family now consisted of eleven children: Helge Jr.; John; Martin; Ole;
Anna; the twins, Andrew and Mary; Ida; Herman; Adolph; and Eddie. One son
and daughter, Ivar and Anna, passed away in infancy. Two of the boys had
come to Dakota the previous year, 1883, and homesteaded on land near the
present site of Selby. Helge Jr., on the SW Quarter, Section 31-124-76. He
made final proof on September 19, 1890. This land is now part of the
present Adolph Thorstenson farm. Ole homesteaded on the NW Quarter Section
3-123-76. This was filed December 10, 1889, the grant being issued by
President Benjamin Harrison. This land is a short distance east of Selby
and is now owned by Albert Schmidt. The slaughter house is located on it.

The trip from Estherville in Emmett county, Iowa took two weeks. They
crossed southern Minnesota through Pipestone. Albert Thompson and Charlie
Anderson came with them, Albert stopping off in Day county. They saw no
other emigrants on the way except a few living in shacks near Bowdle. As
Bowdle was the last place at which they could get water before reaching the
river, they filled everything and watered the stock well before continuing
on the way toward the Missouri river. When they got within seven or eight
miles of the river, the cattle seemed to smell the water and made a
bee-line for it. They were so thirsty they plunged into the
water,--however, none of them were lost.

Mr. Lund purchased land, including a house, from an elderly German "Squaw
Man", as they were called when married to an Indian woman. He farmed the
land which was located on the river bank and was called bottom land. This
land was in Campbell county, north of the present site of Mobridge. The
Lunds got their mail at Campbell post office operated by Skinners. Later
their post office was at Grand Crossing.

The Lunds endured the many hardships, privations, and perils of the early
Dakota pioneers including the blizzard-of 1888 and the Indian Scare of
1890. On this latter occasion Mr. Lund sent his wife and the younger
children down to his son, Helge Jr's., place near what is now the present
site of Selby, he, himself, remaining to protect the home.

Years later Mr. Lund filed on a tree claim in Campbell county about
fourteen miles east of the Missouri river. Mr. Lund donated an acre of land
on which the "Lund schoolhouse" was built. A new building has been erected
on this same land since, but is still known as the "Lund school."

Mr. and Mrs. Lund celebrated their Golden Wedding on June 16, 1906 at their
farm home, at which time all of their children and most of their families
gathered for a reunion. Mr. and Mrs. Lund continued living on their
Campbell county farm until Mrs. Lund passed away on August 18, 1911. For
several years previous to this, their married son, Adolph and his family
resided with them and farmed the land. After Adolph and family moved to
Hettinger, North Dakota, another married son, Andrew and his family came
from Benedict, North Dakota to make their home on the Lund farm.

After his wife's passing, Mr. Lund continued living with his son, Andrew
and family for a time, then visited with his daughters, Mrs. Anna Dahl of
Aberdeen, and Mrs. Ida Slate in Platte, then going on to McLaughlin, to be
with his son Martin and family, where he became ill and passed away on July
11, 1912.

Mr. and Mrs. Lund and family were charter members of Norway Lutheran church
in Campbell county. They reared their family with religion and education as
important factors in their lives. In the early days church meetings were
held in private homes, and when there was an occasional visit by a
minister, people came from far and near for services. Some brought their
small children to be baptized, some traveling by team and wagon, some on
horseback, and the nearer neighbors would walk.

Helge Jr., received most of his education in Iowa. He was a diligent
scholar; it has been said that even in grade school, he often equaled his
teachers in his studies. Helge attended Carlton College at Northfield,
Minnesota one year. He was one of the first teachers in Walworth county. He
boarded at home while teaching at various schools around there. He loved to
read and study Shakespeare. On April 6, 1892 Helge Jr., was united in
marriage to Miss Belle Gjefle of Campbell county. They moved to Bangor,
where Mr. Lund was register of deeds and county auditor while Bangor was
the county seat in the early '90's. While living in Bangor, he and his
brother, Martin, were associated with J. J. Hoven in a farm machinery
business. This firm was dissolved in February 1896. It had been known as
the firm of Lund Bros. and Company of Bowdle and Bangor.

In 1896 he and his brother, Andrew and their two families moved to North
Dakota, spending the first winter at Washburn, then moving on north of Cole
Harbor in McLean county, where they filed on land and ranched for a number
of years. At first their nearest neighbor was a bachelor living seven miles
from them. The two families lived in a sod "duplex," later Andrew built a
frame house about a mile north of the sod home. Here he and his family
resided until returning to South Dakota in 1909.

        MR. AND MRS. HELGE LUND, SR.

In 1907 Helge Jr., and his family moved to Red Deer, Canada where he farmed
until his passing away. His wife followed him a few years later in death.
They had a family of eleven children.

Inga Mathilda (Hilda) now Mrs. Ingeval Espeland of Campbell county, who
lives on a farm. Their farm home and all its contents was burned to the
ground on January 17, 1947, the cause of the fire being unknown. They have
since built their farm up again. They have six children: Gladys, Mrs.
Palmer Anderson, with two children; Ellen, a nurse in Alhambra, California;
Dorothy, a nurse in Los Angeles; Joyce, taking nurse's training in
Minneapolis; Earl and Marvin at home.

Herbert, Alfred (married), Otto, and John Thomas at home in Alhambra,
Canada. Lottie, Herbert's twin sister, passed away in 1918.

Sophia, Mrs. Bert Bonham, lives in Saskatoon, Canada. They have three
children; Isabelle, David, and John.

Olga, Mrs. Fenske, passed away in 1945. Her husband is a minister and he
and his family reside in Canada.

Marie, Mrs. Wilson, lives in Murryville, Canada.

Nina and Christine are twins. Nina is cashier in a large bank in Vancouver,
British Columbia. Christine is a nurse. She served in World War II in
England, Italy, and France. She had the pleasure of being present at a tea
given for a group of nurses by the Duke and Duchess of Kent, just a few
days previous to the Duke's tragic death in a plane crash. Christine is at
present a nurse and missionary in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

John Lund received his education in the common schools of Iowa and also
attended the Lutheran college at Decorah, Iowa. He was graduated from this
institution in 1884 and then taught school for three years, one year in
Nebraska, one near Aberdeen, and one in Campbell county where he filed on a
claim. After this he went to Aberdeen and commenced the study of law. He
moved to Webster and was admitted to the South Dakota Bar in the spring of
1888. In 1894 he was elected states attorney of Day county and was
reelected in 1896. He was elected county judge in 1900 and held this office
until 1908. He resumed private law practice until 1920, when he was again
elected county judge. He was reelected every two years after that until his
death, serving as county judge for about 22 years. He was a member of the
Masonic lodge. In 1884 he married Beathe Bakke Anderson of Decorah, Iowa,
who passed away in May 1929. Judge Lund was president of the Day County Bar
association at the time of his death, June 5, 1934.

Martin Lund came with his parents and family to this section of Dakota in
1884. He proved upon a homestead, preemption, and a tree claim. For a
while he was associated with his brother, Helge Jr., and J. J. Hoven in a
farm machinery business. Later he moved to Bowdle where he went into the
store business, losing everything in a disastrous fire. From there they
went to Kenmare, North Dakota; then to Glenham, South Dakota where the
family resided for several years. While here Mr. Lund was employed in a
general store. In 1911, Martin and family moved to McLaughlin, South Dakota
where he and his brother-in-law, O. J. Dahl successfully conducted a
mercantile business for many years. Martin was married in 1895 to Miss Lena
Ellingson at Bowdle. Five children were born to them: Harold, the oldest
grandson in the Lund Sr., family, saw service in World War I, is an
attorney at Brookings, is married and has two daughters, Lolita and Shirley
Beth; Herman is a doctor and lives at Walla Walla, Washington, is married
and has three children, Lona, Charles, and Kathryn; Marie Mrs. Everette
Kline has two children, Rose Marie and Robert; Lola, Mrs. Harold
Balsinger, has one daughter, Charlotte; Roberta, Mrs. Wahlstrom, has two
daughters, Harriet and Arlene. Martin Lund passed away at McLaughlin on
March 17, 1930 and was laid to rest at the Norway church cemetery in
Campbell county beside his parents, sister, brothers, and a host of
friends. Mrs. Lund now resides with her daughters in San Diego, California.

Ole Lund operated a blacksmith shop in Bangor for a time. He became a
master blacksmith and owned and operated a shop in Bottineau, North Dakota
for a number of years. Included in his works he constructed a very nice
church steeple. He passed away in 1920 at the home of his brother. Andrew
with whom he had been making his home. He was laid to rest in the cemetery
at the Norway church.

Anna Lund, Mrs. O. J. Dahl, came to Dakota with her parents when a young
girl. Her girlhood was spent on the small farm on the banks of the Missouri
river. She remembers many events of the pioneer days, and often speaks of
the day of the blizzard of '88. She and her brother, Martin had attended a
dance at Skinners', coming home a little before nine in the morning. They
had been in the house about half an hour when they looked out and the snow
stood just like a wall outside the house. After growing up she spent
several years in Seattle, Washington. Here she was married on March 2, 1898
to Ole J. Dahl. They lived in Seattle for a year after their marriage, then
moved to Aberdeen, South Dakota. Mr. Dahl was a master bricklayer and
assisted in erecting many of the fine brick buildings in and around
Aberdeen. He also helped build the Masonic temple and the high school
building at Mobridge. Later the Dahls moved to McLaughlin where they
operated a store in partnership with Mrs. Dahl's brother, Martin. This
establishment was known as Lund & Dahl. After leaving here they lived for a
time in Colome. Mr. Dahl passed away suddenly while they visited the John
Lund home in Webster. The Dahls have two children: Rolf, a dentist in
Chicago; and Naomi, Mrs. Fred Scallin, of Mitchell, whose husband operates
the Scallin drug store in that city. Mrs. Anna Dahl is now eighty-two years
old and lives with her daughter.

Andrew and Mary Lund were twins born February 28, 1870 and came with their
parents when they were fourteen years old from Estherville, Iowa. Andrew
told that much of the trip he spent on foot following the cattle, and he
often stated what a welcome sight the Missouri was after the long trek from
the last watering place at Bowdle. Mary passed away March 25, 1895. She
taught school near Mound City for several years. She was laid to rest in
the Norway church cemetery.

On April 27, 1894 Andrew was united in marriage to Miss Emma Olson. The
young couple operated a restaurant in Bowdle for a time. After that for a
while they lived on the Ole Rorgo farm down near the river. Then they went
with the Helge Lund Jr., family to Washburn, North Dakota where the first
winter was spent. The next spring they continued to Cole Harbor in McLean
county where they made their home on a ranch. Helge Jr., and Andrew and
their families were the first settlers in that locality, and they located
the later newcomers who came to seek land. They were also the witnesses
when the settlers went to Minot to make final proof on their land. In 1909
Andrew Lund with his family returned to South Dakota to take over the farm
of his elderly parents. They continued to live on the home place after the
death of his parents for about 25 years. Then they moved to Glenham where
Mr. Lund passed away August 28, 1941. Mrs. Andrew Lund makes her home at
the Mascot apartments in Mobridge. The Andrew Lund family consisted of ten
children: Ida May, Mrs. P. A. Brown of Selby, whose husband is a World War
I veteran and a rural mail carrier out of Selby, and they have two sons,
Raymond Dean and Harlyn Francis; Anna, Mrs. W. J. Booker, a rancher's wife
at Toston, Montana, has three children, Mitzi, married and a technician
at a hospital in Cut Bank, Montana, Billy and Keith; Clarence, who made his
home in Montana for a number of years working at various places and passed
away suddenly on September 6, 1945; Agnes, Mrs. A. L. Brown of Glenham,
whose husband "Bert" is a rural mail carrier out of Glenham, and they have
four children, Berniece, Mrs. Ted Schweigert, of McLaughlin, who has a son,
Douglas Lee, and Lyman, Charles, and Laurel Jean at home; Ina, Mrs. Joe
Marinchek, whose husband operates the Rustic Inn at Mobridge, and they have
one son, Roy; George, married and farms near Glenham, and they have three
children, Aldene, Gerald, and Jackie, all at home, and who suffered a
disastrous fire on February 16, 1950 which destroyed their lovely farm home
and all contents; Blanche, born in McLean county, North Dakota in 1909, and
passed away May 23, 1930 in a Mobridge hospital; Hazel, passed away in
infancy; Marlowe and Marshall, twins; Marlowe is married and has two
daughters, Marlys Ann and Frances Marie, and resides on a farm near
Glenham; Marshall is married and lives in Selby where he is employed by the
REA, has two daughters, Marsha Beth and Charlene Kay. Marshall is a veteran
of World War II and saw 4-1/2 years of service in the Pacific Theatre as a
radio technician and Communications Chief on the following islands:
Hawaiian, Marshall, Gilbert, Makin, Guam, and Iwo Jima.

Ida Lund, Mrs. C. F. Slate came to Dakota with her parents while she was a
small girl, and she, too could relate many interesting early day
experiences. On February 16, 1895 she was united in marriage to C. F.
Slate, a druggist of Bowdle. They lived in Bowdle for about eight years,
operating a drug store there. Then they moved to Platte, where they
continued in the drug store business. Mr. and Mrs. Slate had three
children: Florence, Mrs. H. Anderson of Los Angeles, California, who has two
sons; Hazel, Mrs. Wm. Quinlan, she and her husband are associated with her
father in the drug store, Hazel also spent several years teaching in
Alaska; Charles, who passed away as the result of a tragic accident during
his high school years. The Slates celebrated their Golden Wedding in 1945.
Mrs. Slate passed away two years ago.

Herman Lund passed away in 1898 at the age of twenty-four. He was
freighting for the George L. Robinson store at Cole Harbor, North Dakota.
It being cold and icy he was chilled and started to walk while driving two
teams of horses. He slipped on the ice and the wagon wheel passed over his
leg breaking it. Two days later his brother Andrew went to search for him.
He was found badly frozen. His father came at once and he was taken to a
Bismarck hospital where he died as a result of the accident.

Adolph Lund was born in Iowa and came with his parents to Dakota when a
small lad. He grew to manhood on his father's farm on the Missouri river
and the homestead in Campbell county. He married Clara Olson. They lived
with his parents for a time. Later they moved on a farm near Hettinger,
North Dakota. To them were born five children: Hazel, Mrs. Smith of
Seattle, Washington, who has two children, Alfa and Alice in Yakima,
Washington; John who passed away when a young lad; Edward, who saw service
in World War II, being stationed in Bermuda, and after his return attended
college in Denver, Colorado. Adolph Lund served many years as a railroad
employee. He now makes his home in Yakima, Washington. He visits relatives
and friends in South Dakota almost every year.

Eddie Lund, the youngest member of the Lund family, spent most of his life
on farms and ranches. He now resides in Forsyth, Montana.

The Lund bible, which is ninety years old, was given to Ina Lund Marinchek
by her father, Andrew Lund. Needless to say this family heirloom is a
priceless possession of hers. It may also be noted here that of the Helge
Lund, Sr., family of grandchildren, Andrew Lund's daughter, Ida May Esther
(Mrs. P. A. Brown of Selby) is the oldest and her twin brothers, Marshall
and Marlowe, are the youngest.

FRED A. THEILEN FAMILY

Fred A. Theilen was born in Oldenburg, Germany and came to the United
States when a young boy. An older brother had come to America sometime
before. Upon arrival in the United States he boarded a train for Illinois.
When the train arrived at the town where he was to get off, the conductor
failed to call him and as Fred was unable to speak or understand the English
language he stayed on the train. A few miles out of town the conductor
realized his mistake. The train was stopped and the lonely immigrant boy
got off the train and trudged into the dark night to his destination in the
new world.

Fred Theilen was a miller by trade as his father was before him. Upon his
arrival in Illinois he worked in mills and on a farm. He was married to
Marie Memmen, a native of Illinois, and they set up housekeeping in a small
town in central Illinois. Mr. Theilen owned and operated an old fashioned
flour mill run by wind for a few years and then converted the mill to steam
power. He also farmed to some extent.

In 1908 the Theilen family moved to South Dakota. They moved on a farm
which they had purchased and which was known as the "Preacher Brown" farm.
This farm was located a half mile west of the old town of Bangor. In 1919
they sold this farm and in 1920 moved on a farm they had purchased and
which was located one half mile east of the old Bangor townsite. This farm
was known as the. "Kingman" farm and was rather a historical place as far
as Walworth county was concerned. It is said the first newspaper published
on the prairie was printed in the Kingman house.

In 1932 Mrs. Theilen passed away and in 1939 Mr. Theilen passed away. The
two daughters continued to live on the farm until 1943 when they moved to a
home they had purchased in Selby and where Helen passed away shortly after
moving to Selby. The farm was later sold.

Mr. Theilen, from the time he moved to South Dakota, had a deep abiding
faith in the future of the state and even during the drouth, black
blizzards and grasshoppers of the 1930's he never completely lost faith in
South Dakota. During the early years when he lived here prospective land
buyers were often taken to the Theilen farm and the virtues of South Dakota
were extolled.

Little incidents in those days created great excitement for the children.
In the spring and fall of the year quite a large encampment of Indians came
from across the river and camped on the outskirts of Bangor for a short
time. This was always a great source of interest.

Those were pleasant days in the hot, dry summer when "Old Dick and Flora"
were hitched to the buggy and the family drove to the river to pick buffalo
berries, grapes and plums.

Mr. Theilen farmed extensively and was keenly interested in the feeding and
the promotion of better livestock. He took pride in his herd of roan
shorthorn cattle. For one so interested in South Dakota it is to be
regretted that he never lived to see the bumper crops of the 1940's.

During the years the family resided here they cheerfully accepted their
share of the hard work and hard times. Mr. and Mrs. Theilen were always
willing to do all they could for the promotion of education and to promote
the best things for their community.

Mrs. Theilen was interested in painting and music but her duties as a
housewife on the farm rarely permitted her to indulge in this pastime. Mrs.
Theilen and Helen were members of the Jolly Club, of which Mrs. Theilen was
a charter member. Helen, who loved music and who had had considerable
training in playing the piano, cheerfully shared her music at gatherings
whenever asked and it was possible for her to do so. She gave music lessons
and at the time of her death was librarian in the Selby library. Never very
strong her happy disposition and cheery smile will long be remembered.

At the present time, Inez, the only surviving member of the family, resides
in Selby and is the present Walworth county superintendent of schools.

WILLIAM GEORGE CHESKY

William George Chesky was born near Danzig, Germany January 21, 1867, the
son of Christian and Albertina Chesky. When he was about six weeks old the
family came to America in search of a new home. They settled in Berlin,
Wisconsin. Here his early boyhood was spent. He attended the American
grammar and German schools of Berlin and was confirmed in the German
Lutheran church of that city. When he was about 14 years old William
decided he could take his place among men in the world. He quit school and
worked in the pinery near Warsaw, Wisconsin.

In the early spring of 1883 he, his eldest sister's husband, John
Weisenthal, and a young man by the name of Powers also of Berlin, decided
they would come to Dakota to see if the opportunities were as great as they
sounded. Their original plan was to go to Day county. They stopped in
Aberdeen, which was at that time the end of the railroad. There they met
and got to talking to several other men,--Elliott and Smalley. These men
were going west of Aberdeen. They convinced the Wisconsin boys to go along,
declaring that some day there would be some "Chicagos" built along the
Missouri river. Each outfit had their own equipment. William and John
bought a team of mules, a wagon, a walking plow, their tent, and
provisions. Ipswich and Roscoe and Bowdle at that time were not railroad
towns, merely wide spots in the road,--mostly groups of tents. After they
left Bowdle there were no homes until they reached LeBeau, located on the
banks of the Missouri river a few miles north of the site now known as
"LeBeau."

Elliott had been out there the summer before and had left his tent pitched
to serve as a landmark on his return. Using a compass and a glass and
climbing the highest hills in their course, the group sighted the tent.
Although it had blown down it was still fastened to the stakes. This
location is slightly west of the present Chesky Brothers farm. They reached
this place and camped for the night. The next day they started for the
river. There were no roads to follow. They only knew there was a river west
somewhere. They wandered on, got lost in a gully, and finally climbed a
high hill and were able to see the great "Muddy." However, it looked too
far away and they returned to camp before darkness would set in. The next
day they decided to go straight to LeBeau. As before, there was no road,
but Elliott knew the way as he had been there the summer before. They found
the lively, little cattle town without trouble. There was a saloon, store,
hotel, lumber yard and so on. Wallace & Smith were running the store; Gus
Siebrecht the hotel, and Foster the lumberyard. They stayed in LeBeau a day
or two, then decided to return to their camp and see about some land. At
that time there were only two townships surveyed in Walworth county, Brown
and Scranton,--the rest were surveyed that summer. They decided to squat on
the Land they chose. Going to the corner of Brown township they measured
with a rag on a wagon wheel. When the government men surveyed it later they
found they had gotten within a small number of rods with their wagon wheel
measure. Elliott already had his land picked out. Smalley settled in Brown
township. Powers chose the SW Quarter of Section 6. Weisenthal, NW 1/4,
Section 6 and Chesky the SE 1/4, Section 6. They discovered two other men
in this part of the country,--E. R. Brown and his son, Zellie who were
living on the SE 1/4 Section 1. These were the only other people they found
in that part of the country. William and John built a little shack to live
in with lumber they brought from LeBeau. This is still a granary on the
Chas. E. Cheskey farm. They then decided to build a sod barn for the mules.
John having been a sailor and William only a town boy, both were new at
this. They laid the pieces of sod lengthwise one upon the other. The walls
were erected and a manger put in. They put the mules inside one night
before the roof was on. The next morning they found the walls had fallen in
on the mules. Luckily the walls weren't high enough or the mules would have
been buried. They profited by their mistake and rebuilt the barn, this time
laying the sod crosswise which kept it from caving in. They also broke up
about ten acres of land with a walking plow, and with the use of an axe
seeded it to squaw corn. The season was late but they were told that the
crop would mature. They then went back to LeBeau and hauled lumber from the
river to Foster's lumber yard. In July they returned to look at their corn
crop--and found E. R. Brown's cow had wandered over and eaten it off. Brown
and his son. Powers, and Brownell lived together where their land joined.
Today a few trees still mark the spot--and it is still known as "Brown's
Corners." During the summer of '83 Powers made a trip to Aberdeen and
brought back the August Voy family with him. They settled in Brown township
on what is now the Elmer Randall Jr., home. C. O. Peterson came out and
lived with them that winter.

After they discovered the fate of their corn crop, John and William went to
Aberdeen where John took a contract to haul lumber for the railroad which
was being built between Aberdeen and Ipswich. William helped him with this
work. That fall William's father, Christian Chesky came out and filed on
the land which William had picked out, but had been too young to file on
himself. The rest of the county was being surveyed at this time and the men
could have got jobs at this had they wished. However they decided to return
to Wisconsin to their families. That winter William again worked in the
pinery near Warsaw. It was that winter he had his first experience hunting
deer with the men at camp.

        MR. WM. GEO. CHESKY

In the spring of '84 Christian Chesky brought his family out to Walworth
county. The family now included Adeline, Henry, Rudolph, William, Mary,
Anna, Emma, and Charles, the latter a mere tot several years old. Henry
remained in Wisconsin where he was employed. Adeline came out with her
husband. The other six children accompanied their parents.

The railroad now extended as far as Ipswich and they came that far by
train. From there the trip was made with the wagon and team which had been
shipped from Wisconsin. They lived in the little house which William and
John had built the summer before, and planted a little crop with the
implements they had. The older boys, Rudolph and William then looked for
work. William went back to Ipswich and worked on the section for awhile,
then on to Milbank where he worked for a farmer for three months, returning
home for the winter. During the years when the crop failed here at home the
elder boys worked elsewhere and helped the family at home. For two seasons
William took a team and went up into North Dakota. He worked on the
Dalrymple farm near Castleton. This was known as the biggest wheat farm in
the United States. The farm was about 20 miles square. During harvest the
grain was handled with binders. There were 100 horse teams and 100 mule
teams at work here. The work was hard, but the food was good for both man
and beast. The men were required to take excellent care of their team which
always came through harvest in better shape than they went in. There wasn't
much opportunity to spend money, and William would collect his wages and
buy groceries for the folks at home. He said his mother once remarked, "You
were just like a Santa Claus to us when you came home."

The trading was done at LeBeau or Bowdle and on one of his trips to LeBeau
after supplies William met Sitting Bull, the famous South Dakota Indian
chief. He happened to be in the Wallace & Smith store when the Indian came
in, accompanied by several squaws. Wallace introduced him to those present.
William said the Indian merely shook hands and said "How" when introduced.

When the county seat was moved from Scranton to Bangor, William was hired
by the county to haul the records to Bangor. Scranton was located about
where the Boehmer ranch is today, and was at that time only a handful of
buildings. He made the trip down alone with a team and wagon, but Mr.
Shannon, one of the county officials, returned with him. They stayed at the
Chesky home that night and finished the trip to Bangor the next day.

At the time of the Indian Scare. William was returning from the river with
a load of wood. He was met by Willis Brown, son of Rev. Samuel Brown, who
told him to hurry as it was reported the Indians were on the warpath,
having crossed the river up north at the little town of LaGrace and would
be down in several hours. William reached home and found his mother and
younger children frightened, packed, and waiting for him to take them to
Bowdle. He was hungry and insisted on having supper. They didn't want to
stop. Before the question was settled Mr. Powers, who lived in Bowdle,
drove into the yard. He had come out after a load of wheat. The wheat had
been stolen and he was returning with an empty wagon. A deal was made with
him to take Mrs. Chesky and the children to Bowdle. Mr. Chesky took his
team and drove over to Rev. Brown's to see if they wanted to leave, as he
knew they had no team. The Browns, however, decided to stay, and Mr. Chesky
stayed with them. William turned the remaining stock loose, took his saddle
horse and rode into Bangor to see what was going on. Rigs were coming into
town every few minutes--most of them on their way to Bowdle or further east
where they would be safe. Everyone had heard rumors, but no one had heard
anything definite. Some families going through town had guns and ammunition.
They were asked to leave them in Bangor so those remaining behind would
have something to use against the Indians if they should come. There were
only two shotguns and a few revolvers in town. However, the owners refused,
being afraid the Indians might circle ahead of them and shut them off. A
little child had died in one of the neighbors homes. The parents were so
frightened they left the corpse in the house when they went away. One
family loaded all their dishes in the wagon without packing them. They were
broken when they reached Bowdle. The Indians didn't come but the
government, to quiet the people, sent out arms and ammunition and a sort of
militia was formed. William was a member of this. They were drilled by
Captain Kingman, an ex-soldier, and Gus Siebrecht, a soldier from Germany.
This militia was never called for active duty and was later disbanded.

Speaking of the blizzard of 1888 William says he remembers that the night
seemed very long. The family waited for daylight to come. They finally got
up and found the windows covered with snow. They opened the door--and the
doorway was piled full of snow. They had to tunnel their way to the barn.
William says his mother remarked how easy it was to obtain water by merely
reaching from the door or window. The pioneer was very lucky who had an
adequate supply of water in those days--most of them had to haul it several
miles.

In 1889 William made a trip to Chicago in search of work. The city was
preparing for the World's Fair which was to be held there the following
year. However, the city didn't appeal to him and he returned home. For
three years he clerked in a general store in Bowdle for I. H. Cobb.
Everything was handled here,--groceries, clothing, harness, hardware, even
caskets.

In 1894 he went to California to look up his older brother, Henry, whom he
hadn't seen since leaving Wisconsin in '83. The brother was located and
William worked on a hay press, baling hay that summer. He says this was the
hardest manual labor he had ever done in his life, but he gained weight all
the season. That winter he spent with a Danish companion in the mountains
where they had taken a contract to cut wood. Enough supplies were sent with
them to last the winter. In the spring he came down to Gernville,
California and worked in a sawmill running a planer. It was at this time he
decided that although he was getting good wages, there was no future for
him in such work, as one sick spell could eat away all his savings. He
decided to come back to South Dakota, get a walking plow if necessary and
start out for himself. He felt California was alright for someone with
money or a trade, but South Dakota was the ideal place for a young man with
limited capital to start out. That is what he did,--bringing his bride
along with him. Mrs. Chesky was the former Gertrude Formschlag of
Penngrove, California. She was born March 2, 1877 of German parents. She
had attended the grammar school near her home. The two met while William
was employed the summer before by Mrs. Chesky's mother on her farm. They
were married October 19, 1896. On their arrival in Walworth county they
lived with his folks the first winter. William bought and filed on a
relinquishment of Albert Brown, another son of E. R. Brown, NW 1/4 12-77.
That winter he had a home built and the next spring they moved into it.
This was about a half mile north of the present Chesky Brothers farm. Later
William bought SW 1/4 Section 12 from his brother, Rudolph, for $1100, next
he bought the NE 1/4 for $4000 and lastly the SE 1/4 was purchased from
John Schanzenbach for $6900. This land is today the farm home of two of his
sons, George and Ben. He also purchased a half section of pasture land
several miles south of the home. This was, and still is, used as a summer
pasture for stock.

William also remembers the county seat fight between Bangor and Selby.
After the Selby people had taken the records to Selby the case was taken to
court. The fight lasted several years. The supreme court in Washington
decided the county seat belonged in Bangor. William was a county
commissioner at that time. He was appointed to see that the records were
moved back to Bangor from where they had been taken. A new building had
been erected in Bangor and rented to the county as a court house. With the
help of other Bangor men the records were loaded and taken back. However,
the safe was too heavy. The Selby drayline wanted fifty dollars to move it.
William thought this was too much to pay and he put in a call to Bangor
about this. O. S. Crawford from Lowry happened to be in Bangor and he
offered to haul it for ten dollars. He was hired and the job was done. The
reason the Bangor people were so anxious to keep the county seat there was
that surveys were then being run north and south for a possible railroad
site. If this went through Bangor being in the center of the county would
be the ideal county seat spot. However the railroad didn't mature and later
the county seat was moved to Selby by popular vote of the people.

William is a charter member of the Selby Equity Union exchange. He was a
member of the first board of directors, and still holds stock in the
company. He served as clerk of the Brown School district No. 10 for over
thirty years, and treasurer of the Selby Independent School district for
over ten years. He joined the Masonic lodge in Bowdle and later transferred
to Selby. In 1947 he was awarded a fifty-year membership medal and the
local lodge made him an honorary member.

In 1926 he decided to leave the farm and move to Selby. He sold part of the
property and leaving his son George, in charge he purchased the Yellowstone
Garage building, stock and equipment from Walter Goodwin and Robert Gruett.
He secured the agency for the Ford car, truck and tractor from the Ford
Motor company. The new business was called Chesky Auto company and remains
so at the present together with a Standard Oil company filling station in
connection which he operates with two sons and a daughter.

Mr. and Mrs. Chesky raised a family of ten children: George, Albertina,
William Jr., Gertrude, Esther, Mabel, Arthur, Ben, Robert, and Arnold Jack.
George, and Ben, who is married, live on the home farm; Albertina (Mrs.
Alfine Johnson) resides on a farm southwest of Selby; William Jr., and
Arnold Jack (married), and Gertrude are associated with their father in the
garage; Esther (Mrs. Jess Mills) of Washington passed away in 1943; Mabel,
(Mrs. Wm. R. Roberts) of Cambridge, Nebraska; Arthur, a World War II
veteran, is married and owns and operates the Selby Shoe Shop; Robert (1st
Lt.), a pilot in the Air Corps, is missing in the CBI theater since July
1945.

Mr. and Mrs. Chesky are still very active. He is manager of the garage
business, and Mrs. Chesky is busy keeping house for her family which now
includes eleven grandchildren and three great grandchildren. One six-year
old granddaughter makes her home with her grandparents.

Perhaps the most vivid lesson Mr. Chesky passed on to his children,--gained
through his years of experience is the fact that, "In union there is
strength."

MR. RUDOLPH CARL CHESKY

Rudolph Carl Chesky was born March 21, 1864 near Danzig, Germany. He was
the second son of Christian and Albertina Chesky. He came to America with
his parents in the spring of 1867, settling in Berlin, Wisconsin where his
father was engaged in the marble-cutting business. Rudolph attended the
German and American schools of Berlin and came to South Dakota in the
spring of 1884 with his parents and their family. They settled on the land
where the present Charles E. Cheskey family now reside. Later Rudolph filed
on the SW 1/4 of Section 12--this land he afterwards sold to his brother,
William.

        MR. AND MRS. RUDOLPH C. CHESKY

For the first several years out here the older boys Rudolph and William
assisted their father on the home farm. After the home work was finished on
the small farm the boys sought work elsewhere to enlarge the family budget.
Rudolph spent one year in Washington state working for a lumber company. He
related afterwards that the snow got to be twenty feet deep out there that
winter.

Rudolph was a very active man and possessed unusual physical strength. In
his young manhood he was noted for this quality and it is said he could
lift a hundred pound sack of sugar with his teeth. He enjoyed music and was
a member of the Bangor band.

In 1896 he was elected sheriff of Walworth county on the democratic ticket,
serving for one term. Many and interesting are the experiences he
encountered as sheriff in those pioneer days. Lacking a regular jail he
often kept his prisoners, handcuffed or otherwise, depending upon the type
of prisoner, at the family home overnight before taking them to the nearest
jail next day.

During the county seat fight between Bangor and Selby, Rudolph represented
Bangor in the court.

He operated a general store in Bangor for a number of years. October 5,
1904 he was united in marriage to Miss Lavina Taylor, born 1883 in
Richmond, Canada. She was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Jabe Taylor who came
to Walworth county in 1903. Mrs. Chesky assisted her husband in the store.
Three daughters were born to them: Helen, Eunice, and Doris.

In 1909 because of failing health he sold his store and the family moved to
Taylor Falls, Minnesota. The next year they moved to Centuria, Wisconsin
where they operated the Maple Grove Truck and Dairying farm. In 1914 and
1915, as his health did not improve as they had hoped, he and his family
spent traveling in California, Washington, and Oregon. In 1916 they sold
their farm and moved into Centuria, Wisconsin. Here they lived until 1919
when Mr. Chesky passed away.

After his passing his wife and children continued to live in Centuria until
1922 when they moved to St. Paul, where Mrs. Chesky secured work. She held
positions as a clerk, dressmaker, operated a millinery store, and a wedding
veil shop. She is now employed as an Oriental rug reweaver. She still
possesses land which her husband owned in Walworth county which is located
south of the Chas. E. Cheskey farm.

Helen, the eldest daughter attended Hamline University, and the University
of Minnesota where she graduated with a Bachelor of Science degree. She is
now the wife of John Wallgren of St. Paul. Her husband is employed by the
Chandler Wilbert Burial Vault company. They have four children: Ronald, 19,
Barbara Jean, 17, Nancy Elaine, 13, Carol Evelyn, 10.

Eunice is living with her mother in St. Paul. She attended Wilson high
school of St. Paul and at present is employed by Griggs, Cooper & company.

Doris, the youngest child, passed away in 1912 while the family was living
near Centuria.

MR. CHRISTIAN HENRY CHESKY

Christian Henry Chesky was born Octoer 25, 1818, near Danzig, Germany. His
wife, Albertina Priske Chesky, was born January 28, 1839. In March, 1867,
they and their family of four children, the youngest of whom was less than
two months old, started for America in search of a new home. The trip on
board a ship took thirteen weeks. The family settled in Berlin, Wisconsin,
where Mr. Chesky worked as a marble cutter until the fall of 1883. The
family now consisted of eight children: Adeline, Christian Henry, Rudolph,
William, Mary, Anna, Emma, and Charles.

In the late fall of 1883 Mr. Chesky came to Walworth county, South Dakota,
where one son had preceded him that spring. He filed on section 6, township
122, range 76. He returned to Wisconsin that winter and in the spring of
1884 brought his family, with the exception of his eldest son, Henry, who
was employed in Milwaukee, to the new home, Mr. Chesky and one son coming
ahead to prepare the way. Mrs. Chesky and the other children followed. They
came as far as Ipswich by train. There they were met by Mr. Chesky. The
balance of the trip was made by wagon.

        MR. AND MRS. CHRISTIAN CHESKY

The family endured the droughts and severe winters of the early years, the
blizzard of 1888 and the Indian scare. Mrs. Chesky was a wonderful wife and
mother and encouraged her children to get an education, and kept her
family, even under those adverse conditions, as close to the church as she
could.

Mrs. Chesky passed away April 10, 1896, and her husband followed her a few
years later. Both were buried in the little Bangor cemetery south of the
present site of Selby.

Of their children, Adeline (Mrs. John M. Weisenthal), Christian Henry,
Rudolph, Anna (Mrs. E. R. Ingalls), and Emma have passed away. Wm. G., and
Chas. E., still reside at Selby, and Mary (Mrs. Willis G. Brown) at
Amarillo, Texas.

MR. CHARLES E. CHESKEY
