It was in April, 1883, that Christian Henry Chesky, his wife and family
came to the Dakota territory from Berlin, Wisconsin, "Squatting" on what
was later determined to be SE 1/4 section 6-122-76. This account is being
written about Charles E. Cheskey, the youngest member of that pioneer
family.

Charles was born in Berlin, Wisconsin, on April 11, 1881, and was a mere
two years old when brought here by his parents. He received his elementary
education in the first rural school established in Walworth county, that
school being located on their own land. Walter Winn was his first teacher.
He continued his high school education at the Bangor high school. Upon
graduating from high school, he worked on his father's farm for a couple of
years. During this time he was a member of the Bangor band and the Bangor
baseball team, both groups playing for numerous community gatherings. He
entered Curtis business college in Minneapolis, Minnesota, where he
completed a general business course. After returning home from college, he
was employed in the county auditor's office in Bangor, which office was held
by George W. Ryan. He continued working in that office after the records
were stolen and the court house moved to Selby. Then, for a brief period of
time, Charles assisted his brother, Rudolph, in his general store located
in Bangor. It was at this time that Charles and his school and college
chum, Glenn Clark, enlisted in the State Guard at Selby, being made members
of the infantry. Later they were transferred to Troop "A" of the cavalry
where they served until receiving their discharges. They were mustered out
at Evarts. After this, he worked in his brother's store at intervals and,
having rented the farm, engaged in a business of buying and selling
livestock. It was while operating this business that he realized the
advantages of raising purebred Herefords and in 1906, he started in the
Registered Hereford business with two females and one sire. He continued
raising registered livestock, holding sales, buying and mixing better blood
lines and increasing his herd until its number grew to approximately 750
head, the most he ever had at any one time. It was because he won so many
blue ribbons on his livestock entries at county fairs that he eventually
named his place "Blue Ribbon Stock Farm". It is widely known by that name
today.

On March 16, 1911, Charles was married to Gertrude E. Peterson, only
daughter of Mr. and Mrs. C. O. Peterson, another pioneer family. To this
couple were born the following children:

LaRue, presently located in Bishop, California, where he operates the
Inyo-Mono Propane Gas business; married to Eva Dion; they have one
daughter. Wayne, associated with his father on the farm and in the
Registered Hereford business; married Maxine Schlepp; they have a family of
four. Vivienne, married to J. E. Cravens, who is associated with Whalen
Drug company; they reside in Bellflower, California, and have two sons.
Dorothy, married to Elmer R. Jett, who is employed by the Rural
Electrification association; they make their home in Selby and have a
family. Arlo, deceased. Florence, deceased. Gloria, married to Melvin
Delzer. They operate the DeLuxe Cafe in Selby. Cameron, presently enrolled
at the University of South Dakota at Vermillion.

Charles has been very active in community affairs and extremely interested
in the progress of the county. He has served at various times on the rural
school board in Surrey district, the Walworth County Fair board, the
Walworth County Telephone board, the election board, etc. He is a member of
the Selby Lodge A F & A M, having joined in January, 1926. He was one of
the first automobile owners in Walworth county, purchasing a white Buick
touring in the summer of 1907.

Despite drouth, blizzards and depressions he has continued through the
years to farm and raise Registered Herefords, striving constantly to
improve the livestock in his herd and, through sales and individual buyers,
the other cattle in Walworth county, South Dakota, and neighboring states
as well.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN CARLSON

Jennie Bassett was born in Wisconsin, April 11, 1856. When she was a child,
her parents moved to the Rochester, Minnesota, area, which was then
frontier country where the Indians were still making trouble for the white
people. Her parents would take the children and hide in the woods when
warned of danger.

About the year 1882, Jennie, her sister, Dell, and a younger brother had
pushed west as far as Aberdeen, where the girls were teaching school. They
decided they would like to own some land so hitched an ox and a horse to a
covered wagon and started west. They stopped in what was later known as
Bangor township in Walworth county. Both girls filed on homesteads and
proceeded to build a house to live in. The brother broke up the ground and
the girls carried the sod, laying one on top of the other for the walls.
They had brought some boards with them from Aberdeen which they used for
the shed roof, covering them with sod and had what they thought was a cozy
sod shanty. The first night they occupied their new home, a rain began
which lasted all night and soaked up the sod. The roof caved in on them and
they had to spend the next few days in the covered wagon until they could
rebuild a "soddy". They spent the summer on their land but when fall came
returned to Aberdeen to work and lodged in a rooming house.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHN CARLSON

A young Swede named John Carlson, who had been a sailor all his life, was
staying at this same hotel, working in a livery stable. He had crossed the
ocean many times and could tell many interesting tales of the sea. He could
not speak English so Jennie Bassett undertook to teach him,--she spent the
remainder of her life at it because she married him on December 25, 1887,
in Aberdeen.

John became a citizen and filed on a tree claim south of Aberdeen. The soil
was poor and sandy so they decided to move back to Walworth county on Mrs.
Carlson's homestead. At this time they had two children, Mae and Paul, and
had acquired some horses and cattle and household goods. Before Mrs.
Carlson was married she had made proof on her homestead and had built a
one-room frame house on it, doing most of the work herself. This was added
to as they prospered and was their living room as long as the family lived
there. The first water was hauled from a pond about a quarter of a mile
south of the house and strained to remove the pollywogs. Several shallow
wells were dug later, all of which went dry after a season or two. They
finally were able to get a good well about one-half mile southwest of the
buildings, which lasted as long as the family lived there.

As there was no doctor near, Mrs. Carlson helped her neighbors in times of
sickness and assisted in bringing many of the babies of the neighborhood
into the world. The Carlson family served in three wars and were good
American citizens. Mrs. Carlson's brother served in the Civil War, her son,
Ray, in World War I, and her grandson, Harlan Hoyt, was killed in action in
World War II, on July 15, 1945. Both John Carlson and Jennie Carlson lived
long and useful lives. They are both now deceased and left surviving them
their four children, Ray and Paul of Bothell, Washington; Hazel
Gildmeister, of Portland, Oregon, and Gladys Hoyt of Stevensville, Montana.

MR. HARRY A. CAMPBELL

Harry A. Campbell was the son of Walter J. and Jennie Campbell, being born
at Manilla, Iowa, on April 5, 1884, where he spent his boyhood days and
graduated from the Manilla high school. After completing a business course
at Dennison, Iowa, he moved with his parents to Bowdle, South Dakota in
1901 where he and his father were engaged in the mercantile business for
several years.

In 1907 he filed on a claim at Lemmon, South Dakota. After proving up on
his land in 1909, he sold it and with his father purchased the Wolff
general store in Selby. The following year they purchased a general store
at Glenham, his father moving there while Harry remained at Selby. Both
stores were operated under the name of "Campbell and Campbell".

MR. HARRY A. CAMPBELL

On December 7, 1910, Harry was united in marriage to Ethelind E. Brown of
Kimball. Minnesota, and two daughters, Ione Campbell Trowbridge, now of
Washington, D. C., and Iris Campbell Leffler, now of Sioux Falls, South
Dakota, came to gladden their home.

In 1915, due to failing health, "Campbell and Campbell" sold their business
to Juster Brothers and Harry became manager of the Selby Equity Union with
elevators at Selby and Sitka, the position he held until the time of his
death 13 years later.

Harry believed in the betterment of his home, business, community and the
slogan "The biggest little town in South Dakota" and worked hard to make
Selby just that. He firmly believed in "doing unto others as he would have
others do unto him".

He was an active member of the Selby Fire department, Commercial club,
Isaak Walton League, Selby Lodge No. 133 A.F.&A.M., Hope Chapter No. 73
O.E.S., and numbered his friends by the people he knew.

He worked with untiring effort and loyalty for his community to make it
better for living until he was suddenly snatched from his earthly duties on
September 23, 1928.

RALPH BURNETTE

Ralph Burnette is not what we could call a pioneer of Walworth county but
one of our progressive farmers who has helped to show what Walworth county
farm land with a will can do.

Ralph Burnette was born at Stanton, (in 1909 the name of Stanton was
changed to Greenland) Northwest Arkansas, on September 28, 1898, to
Lillian, nee Laney Burnette and George Burnette.

His education consisted of the first eight grades.

At the age of eleven years Ralph started working after school and in his
spare time in a nursery of plant life. At the age of sixteen years he left
home to start out on his own, going to Texas in 1915, where he worked for
three years. In May, 1918, being young and adventuresome, and wishing to
see more country he decided to go to Oklahoma, spending a matter of a few
months there before moving on to Nashville, Tennessee. Mr. Burnette worked
in a DuPont Engineering plant, helping to make gun powder, at Nashville.

Kansas is the next state Ralph decided to look over, and while there worked
in the oil fields for three years. His next stop was a return trip to
Oklahoma for six months, then to Iowa.

He had become acquainted with Boyne Swift, who had been to Walworth county,
South Dakota, and Boyne persuaded Ralph to return to Walworth county and try
his hand at harvest and threshing work in South Dakota. Liking this type of
work and possibly a bit tired of being on the move, the spring of 1926,
with his worldly possessions, a model A coupe and shirt wealth, finds Ralph
and Boyne Swift renting what was known as the Gress farm, northwest of
Sitka, and starting to farm for himself. Here he remained for two years.
The spring of 1929 Mr. Burnette farmed southeast of Selby on the Gordon
farm. In the spring of 1932 Ralph rented one-half section of land southwest
of Selby near his present farm.

On June 14, 1932, Ella Kindt of Glenham, became his bride. Mrs. Burnette is
a Walworth county girl, was formerly a Selby girl, having been born on the
N. H. Kingman farm, south of Selby, and later moving with her parents north
of Glenham. It was here Mr. Burnette made her acquaintance.

In 1940 the Burnettes bought three quarters of land and in 1946 purchased
another three quarters (this includes the present farm and buildings). Mr.
and Mrs. Burnette own a total of 1440 acres of land at the present time. To
them six children were born, all of whom are still at home. Donna Rae, a
senior in the Selby high school; Myrtis, a junior of Selby high; Jimmy,
Barbara, Dale, in the grades of their rural district; and Paul, 4.

Upon several occasions Mr. Burnette returned to his native state; in 1927
for a visit with relatives; in 1928 when he was called home by the death of
his mother; and in 1949 returned with his family for a visit.

MR. JAMES BYRNE

James Byrne was born February 10, 1839, at Wicklow, Ireland, and married
Margaret Fleming, who was born in County Carey, Ireland, in May of 1847.

In 1883, at the age of 44, Mr. Byrne and family came to Walworth county, to
file on land, raise cattle and farm. They came in an emigrant car to
Ipswich, the end of the railroad, and then drove out to old LeBeau. They
brought some household goods, farming equipment, horses, cattle and feed.
The James Byrne family settled on the land where Claus Kuehl now resides,
and broke a little land for wheat, and bought a frame house at Scranton to
live in. They built a sod barn and the water was hauled from Swan creek.
Later a well was dug and water was struck at 160 feet. The early winters
were almost all on the severe side, summers not quite so dry or hot.
Breaking the sod seemed to absorb what moisture that did come, faster than
the old days when it was all pasture and hay land.

        MR. JAMES BYRNE

The three sons, James, Thomas and John, remained in Walworth county on the
homestead during the last up rising of the Sioux, and waited for the coming
of Chief Sitting Bull. There was much excitement, and later also more fun.

Mr. Byrne was always interested in community affairs, and especially in the
establishment of the county seat, first at Scranton and later at Bangor,
then later the coming of the railroad to Evarts, and the moving of the
county seat to Selby.

James Byrne and his wife, Margaret, had a family of seven children. Only
three of the boys came to South Dakota with their father and remained here.
The oldest of these sons, James Jr., married Jennie Smith at Madison,
Wisconsin. They came to Dakota and resided on James Sr.'s homestead, where
their family was all born. Edward, the oldest son, is at Mobridge with the
Wist Produce company. The oldest girl, Margaret, passed away at the age of
10 years. The next two daughters, Alma and Norma, are now living in
Mobridge--Alma is Mrs. Webster Nichols; Norma, Mrs. R. B. Ivey. Dick, the
second boy, is at Miller, South Dakota, in the insurance business. The
other daughters are all married and have moved out of Dakota, except Mrs.
A. Klocker who resides at Hoven, South Dakota. James and his wife Jennie,
have both passed away and are laid to rest in the Selby cemetery.

Thomas, the second son of James Sr., married Katherine Smith at Aberdeen,
South Dakota. They resided on Thomas' homestead where they raised wheat,
flax, and in later years, corn. His wife, Katherine, homesteaded on Swan
creek, west of the present town of Akaska. Their family were all born here
in Walworth county. Mrs. E. G. Sweet, the eldest, resides in Minneapolis,
Minnesota. Bernice, the second daughter, resides in Selby. She married
William Unker, now sheriff of Walworth county. Of their five sons, John and
Robert are still in Dakota farming, but have moved farther west for more
room in Corson county. Thomas Jr. (Bill) and Gene are in Hastings,
Nebraska, both on the road for the Nash-Finch wholesale company. Donald is
also in Hastings with the Reder wholesale meat company. Of all their girls
only one is on a farm, Catherine (Mrs. George Ehrenberg), Andover, South
Dakota. The other daughters are all in California, married and happy, but
love to return to Walworth county as often as possible to visit. All the
children grew up to womanhood and manhood in Walworth county.

Thomas Byrne and wife, Catherine, went to California in 1943, where Thomas
passed away on November 22, 1946. Mrs. Byrne maintained her home at Ukialo,
California, and divides her time between visiting different groups of her
children.

John, the third son, who came to Walworth county in early days, was married
to Lettie R. Riley of Mound City. For a time they resided on John's
homestead, later they lived in Mobridge for a number of years, while John
was on the police force there. Now both John and his wife are deceased.
Their son, Arlington, lives in Portland, Oregon, and James, the youngest
son, is in the insurance business at Devils Lake, North Dakota.

JUDGE WILLIAM HAMILTON BURNS

William Hamilton Burns was born October 24, 1848, in Hamilton, Ontario. His
parents, Patrick and Elizabeth Burns were born in Ireland. About 1850 they
moved to the young and growing city of Chicago where Patrick Burns started
a ship-building industry. Elizabeth Burns died about 1854, and the family
was broken up among relatives and boarding schools.

When the Civil War started Patrick Burns and his oldest son, Thomas,
enlisted. Patrick was killed at Shiloh. William was at this time in a
boarding school in Fulton, Illinois. In the spring of 1865, when he was not
yet seventeen, he and several others ran away from school and enlisted. No
data is available on the name of the Illinois regiment in which he served.
He was in Sherman's Army all that last summer of the war and he saw far more
blood and horror than a sixteen year old boy was prepared to encounter. In
later years he was very unwilling to talk about his experiences in the war.
He agreed with his commanding general that "War is Hell."

        JUDGE AND MRS. WM. H. BURNS

In 1867, William Burns graduated from the Law department of the old
University of Chicago. He considered Chicago his home, but he lived there
only occasionally. He disliked the climate. He liked the mountain country
and at different times lived in Colorado and Montana. He was for a time in
the regular army under General Crooks. When gold was discovered in the Black
Hills and the mining towns sprang up, he conducted wagon trains through the
Indian country, hauling freight from Chamberlain on the Missouri river to
the Hills. The Indians were hostile and the wagons sometimes had to fight
their way through.

About 1885, he settled in LeBeau, but it is not known whether he practiced
law there or not. He had a wide acquaintance among the early settlers, the
Indians, and half-breed families along the river.

The town of Bangor up on the prairie had been made the county seat and he
established a law office there. He was elected county attorney. All the
rest of his life he was either county attorney or county judge and was
known as "Judge Burns". He was an ardent republican and always took a keen
interest in politics. In a Roman Catholic family, he was the only
protestant and the only republican. On September 12, 1893, he married Mary
Alice Brown. She was the daughter of the Rev. and Mrs. Samuel F. Brown. She
was born in Brooklyn, Pennsylvania, July 22, 1866. She came with the
others of the family to Bangor, Dakota territory, at the time when that
place became the county seat of Walworth county, November, 1884, and the
county organization was established by popular election. Her father had
been a Methodist pastor for many years in Pennsylvania. He was pastor of
the Methodist church in Aberdeen for a year before coming west to Walworth
county. He took up land bordering on what was later the site of Bangor. The
Rev. Brown founded Methodist churches among the settlers, not only in
Walworth county but in Campbell and Potter counties. He drove many miles in
horse and buggy days in all kinds of Dakota weather and was known to his
scattered flock as "Father Brown."

Mr. and Mrs. Burns had two daughters: Dorothy and Ellen. Judge Burns died
in Bangor on April 6, 1906, and was buried in the cemetery near Bangor.

Judge Burns was a very studious man, a constant reader, and had a large law
library as well as an unusual private library for the time and place. In
spite of his roving, frontier life he had never acquired the typical vices
and never drank or gambled. He joined the Bangor Methodist church after his
marriage and for the rest of his life was a faithful member.

While living in Bangor Mrs. Burns was for several years village postmaster.
She was active in the social and religious life of the village and was an
accomplished musician. In 1907, Mrs. Burns and her daughters moved to Selby
where her parents were then living. For several years she worked in the
office of E. G. Powell, register of deeds. In 1912 she moved with her
daughters to Hamilton, New York, a college town where her daughters
received advanced education. Later she moved to Franklin, Indiana, where
she died at the age of 71. Services were held from funeral parlors in that
city on April 8, 1938, in charge of a Methodist minister, and the body
taken to Hamilton, New York, for interment.

The older daughter, Dorothy, after attending Denison University for two
years, married William Gear Spencer, Associate Professor of Latin at
Colgate University, in 1916. Dr. Spencer was later president of Hillsdale
College, Hillsdale, Michigan, and president of Franklin College, Franklin,
Indiana, for fifteen years. He is now retired as President Emeritus
following an automobile accident and consequent ill health. They have six
children, five sons and a daughter. Three of the sons were in the Army
during the late war, two of them overseas. The five sons are all married
and there are four grandchildren. Just now Dr. and Mrs. Spencer are living
in the home of their son, the Rev. Mr. John Spencer. He is pastor of the
Baptist church in Alexandria, Ohio.

Ellen, the younger daughter, graduated from Denison University in Ohio in
1921. She taught high school English in Ft. Wayne, Indiana, and Norwood,
Ohio, until 1943 when she became a lieutenant in the WAC and served as a
recruiting officer for two and a half years. Since leaving the army, she
has been on the faculty of Western Michigan college at Kalamazoo. She is
the wife of Harold W. Collins and lives in Moscow, Ohio.

REVEREND SAMUEL FRANKLIN BROWN

Rev. Samuel Franklin Brown was born in 1825 in northern Pennsylvania where
sprung the headwaters of the beautiful and mighty Susquehanna river. There
he came to youth and young manhood, and engaged with others of his region
in felling the trees, shaping them into rafts, and floating them on the
crests of the spring freshets down to Chesapeake Bay, where they were sold
and exchanged for merchandise. They returned home afoot, carrying back such
supplies as they could. It was in this enterprise that he competed with his
mates in tests of strength to see who could life the most, and suffered a
rupture of the heart which changed the direction of his life to service in
the ministry.

REV. AND MRS. SAMUEL FRANKLIN BROWN

He learned the carpenter trade and cabinet making while studying for the
ministry, and for a time followed this line of work. He gained his
education at the Towanda Seminary, Towanda, Pennsylvania, and later was
superintendent of that advanced school, which today would rank of high
school grade, but was then considered a college preparatory school.

Mr. Brown was married to Miss Elizabeth Ely, of a prominent pioneer family,
in the community near his home. His wife, passing on, left him with six
children. Later he married Mrs. Marvin Ely, a widow of his first wife's
brother, who was killed during the Civil War. To these children were added
those born by his second marriage, making a total family of twelve
children, of whom Mrs. Brown assumed the care assisted by her sister, Miss
Emma Luce, who remained with the family.

Given his admission to the ministry of the Methodist church, Mr. Brown was
assigned from time to time to various pastorates, the rule of the church
then limiting its pastors to one year in a place, with a rigid three-year
limitation possible by request of the local official board.

Then followed a call by the bishop in 1884 for a volunteer as a missionary
to the almost unknown region called Dakota territory. None of the younger
men volunteering, Mr. Brown offered himself, but three times was refused
because of his age and as too valuable to go into a virgin region where he
could reach few people with his message. Finally, still lacking a
volunteer, he was accepted and assigned to this duty, at a salary of
$200.00 per year, in a large wild field having as yet no county government,
no transportation facilities. The only supplies available being at two
Missouri river trading posts (Evarts and LeBeau) fifteen to thirty miles
away. So, at fifty-nine years of age, having to finance the moving of his
large family himself, from a very scanty store, he had to leave three of
them behind to earn their own rail fares to a point (Aberdeen) ninety miles
from the bare, unplowed, prairie spot he chose for his home site, from a
map as yet unsurveyed into acreage and having no county organization. Harsh
winter was at hand. He was permitted to serve the church at Aberdeen,
Dakota, until spring, when he and the family gathered on the claim a united
group, and by amazing faith and unremitting toil, built shelter of a sort,
broke the tough prairie sod, and (also of a sort) planted five acres to
corn and a small grove of young trees. The change from the comfortable
financial means supplied him in the east to the tough rigors of a new
country with plenty reduced to barest necessities, and the daily recurring
pangs of broken personal relationships, were endured with steady faith and
strength by the father; but to the mother they were tragedy unspeakable,
endured and outlived in devotion to her children.

Rev. Brown's field comprised two large counties and three appointments. His
home location, one fifteen miles away, and another one thirty miles away.
These required him to start a day or two ahead and come home after Sunday.
For fifteen years he never missed an appointment but once, this trip being
driven in a hot wind which scorched all vegetation and drove people to their
cellars. He traveled winter and summer, forty below and one hundred fifteen
above zero, riding in a two-wheel racing surrey affording no protection but
what he could wrap about him. This in spite of his heart injury from which
he never had recovered. Later he built a small, comfortable frame home, a
barn for his accumulated oxen, cows, etc. He did all the work himself in
his intervals between preaching, marrying, visiting the sick, burying the
dead, and planting and gathering his scant crops, in which he was aided by
his sons as they grew able. Then, as the family one day sat at dinner, they
heard the roar of flames and saw cinders falling on the dinner table. The
fire consumed the home utterly in a few minutes, and the father, who had in
the house a few hundred dollars hidden, was cut off trying to save the
money, broke out through a window, and was so seriously burned that for
two months he was confined to his bed. But, indomitable still, the first
day he was able to walk he paced off the ground for the new house he had
drawn plans for when confined, and later he started and applied his
knowledge of building to the house.

So great and so strong an attachment to him among his congregations had
grown during the years, that as soon as his loss and personal plight became
known, his loving friends came driving in, bringing every kind of needful
thing, from lumber, hardware, paint, to clothing and house furnishings,
some from as far as a hundred miles away, until the value of their gifts
exceeded the material loss. But some things could not be restored; among
them the old family Bible in which he had entered the record of his family
covering several generations. For this reason much that would enrich this
short account of his life is not available now.

Mr. Brown lived to the age of seventy-nine, passing away in 1904 in his
home at Selby, South Dakota, near which place his body lies in the small
Bangor cemetery which he platted as a service to his community when no
other burial place was available in that section.

MR. FRANK MORRISON BROWN

Frank Morrison Brown was born on November 19, 1881, at Newton, Iowa. He was
one of seven children born to James and Sarah Brown.

He grew to young manhood at Newton attending common school and one year of
business college. At the age of 26 he decided to look for greater
opportunities and in the spring of 1907, together with his brothers, Ed,
Eben and Bert, moved to Selby and on March 9 they settled on a farm ten and
a half miles west of Selby, known as the Ole Hilde Farm. The brothers
farmed here until 1909 when they purchased the land two and a half miles
south of Selby, building their home. and improving the land.

        MR. AND MRS. FRANK M. BROWN

He was married on February 8, 1911, to Madge Stewart, who was born and
raised in Walworth county and the youngest daughter of Frank Stewart. Three
children were born to them: Mrs. Marjorie Marxen, Mrs. Emma Nestell, both
of Eugene, Oregon; and Ivan Brown of Phoenix, Arizona.

The spring of 1911 Mr. Brown and his brothers dissolved partnership. Frank
continued to live on the home place, farming and raising registered cattle.

He was a member of the Methodist church, joined the Masonic Lodge on
February 8, 1916. and later became a member of the Shrine and Eastern Star.
He was always interested in his home. and schools and was one of the
outstanding leaders of the community. He served on the board of directors
for the Selby Equity Union for 15 years, and the Equity Union Creamery of
Aberdeen for 19 years. Among other organizations he was affiliated with
were Equity Auditing association, Walworth County Farm Loan association,
Walworth County Telephone company, Walworth County Farm bureau, Walworth
County Fair board and Northwestern Grain association of Minneapolis,
Minnesota. He left Selby in the fall of 1935 due to poor health and moved
to Eugene, Oregon.

MR. ARTHUR A. BROWN

Arthur Adney Brown, or as he was more commonly known, A. A. Brown or "Red"
Brown, pioneer lawyer of Selby and Walworth county, was born at Storm Lake,
Iowa, in 1880. He graduated from Storm Lake high school in 1898, following
which he attended Buena Vista college at Storm Lake for two years before
taking a law course at the University of Iowa at Iowa City. After a year
spent in the law office of F. F. Faville at Storm Lake, later a judge of
the Supreme Court of Iowa. Mr. Brown began the practice of law at Pomeroy,
Iowa. He came to Selby about 1908, shortly after the courthouse was moved
from Bangor to Selby. Brown maintained his practice at Selby for about ten
years, being associated with Albert H. Smith, under the firm name of Brown
and Smith. About 1918, he moved to Missoula, Montana, where he practiced
his profession for about one and a half years and then again returned to
Walworth county and opened a law office at Mobridge, which practice he
conducted until the time of his death on April 26, 1933. A. A. Brown was
city attorney for a number of years at Selby and later at Mobridge. He also
served as state's attorney of Walworth county for several years.

In 1909, Brown was united in marriage to Miss Eunice Watters at Holstein,
Iowa. Mrs. Brown is still living; and resides at Maquoketa, Iowa. The
Browns had four children, the three oldest being born at Selby, and the
youngest, William, being born at Missoula, Montana. Eunice Brown, the
oldest daughter, is now a surgical nurse at Maquoketa; Arthur Brown is an
athletic coach at Riddle, Oregon; Louise Brown is an English teacher at
Prescott, Arizona, and William Brown is engaged in business at Maquoketa.
Their first home at Selby was in the apartment above the Dettman building
which then had an ice cream parlor on the first floor. In 1909 they
purchased the home now occupied by the John W. Hoven family, which the
Browns later sold to John Schell.

        MR. AND MRS. ARTHUR A. BROWN

A. A. Brown was prominent in business and civic enterprises while residing
at Selby. For many years he was a director of the First National Bank at
Selby and the Brown family held stock in this bank until 1945.

Mr. Brown built up an enviable reputation as a legal practitioner in
northern South Dakota. The high esteem which he enjoyed among his brother
lawyers is best exemplified by the following resolution which was adopted
at the first regular term of court in Walworth county following his death
and a copy of which forms a part of the permanent records on file in the
court house: "Whereas, since the last term of this court it has pleased the
Supreme Law Giver to call to his final reward, one of the members of the
Bar of this county and an officer of this court;

"Therefore, BE IT RESOLVED by the members of the Bar of Walworth county and
by the officers and judges of this court at a regular, adjourned term
thereof held at Selby, Walworth county, South Dakota, this 14th day of
November, 1g33, that in the death of Arthur A. Brown, we feel that the bar
and the citizenship of this county and state have lost a valuable and
esteemed brother and an upright citizen, and that we, as members of the bar
have lost an able, fearless and conscientious member of this bar. We honor
him as a sincere and honest friend, as a lawyer of tact, ability,
aggressiveness and perseverance, but withal, human and honorable and
courteous and fair in all his business and professional relationships. We
honor him further as a citizen able to meet and influence people in all
walks of life, and as a devoted husband and father who with his family was
ever efficient in the upbuilding of the community in which he lived. To know
him well was to honor, love and respect him."

In comment to the editor concerning the early pioneer days at Selby, Mrs.
A. A. Brown recalled that their first years at Selby were "hot, dusty, dry
and windy;" particularly their first year when the grain never came up and
the crops were a total failure. She vividly recalled the constant fear of
prairie fires, and one particular occasion when the dust was blowing so
that one could hardly see across the street and Mr. Brown rushed home with
the news that a train had started a bad fire west of town. He said
excitedly that every one was rushing to fight the fire and demanded a broom
"quick". Mrs. Brown handed him the kitchen broom and excited as he was, he
said "No, I don't want the good broom; I want the scrub broom." An hour
or so later he dashed in again and demanded that Mrs. Brown get everything
packed and ready to leave on the afternoon train because it looked as if
there was little chance of saving the town. Mrs. Brown then recalled that
while everyone was so excited and too scared to reason, a Mr. Franks calmly
hitched a team of horses to a plow and began to plow across the west side
of town. This enabled the fire fighters to stop the fire and Mr. Franks was
given credit for saving the town. That evening after the fire, the air
cleared and Mrs. Brown remembers it as "one of the most beautiful nights in
her memory."

MR. T. B. BOWLUS

Thomas B. Bowlus was born March 3, 1851, at Freemont, Ohio, and died in
1935. Mrs. Bowlus (Melcena) was born January 2, 1863, at Napoleon, Ohio,
and died in 1931. They resided on a farm in Henry county, Ohio, before they
came west in the spring of 1886, to file on land. The end of the railroad
at that time was Ipswich, South Dakota, and they hauled their belongings by
wagon from there to Walworth county, about eighty miles, where Mr. Bowlus
filed on a preemption and later on a tree claim, about eight miles
northeast of Selby. Here they engaged in mixed farming, during good years
and bad for about twenty-four years. Later the Bowluses moved to Bangor,
then the county seat of Walworth county, and then to Selby while he served
as county treasurer.

        MR. AND MRS. T. B. BOWLUS

During the heavy snows in the early years, several neighbors with a shovel
apiece, would start for town and if they met another wagon or bobsled, the
one who had the lightest load would have to unload and go around and then
reload again. This operation sometimes required a lot of shoveling before
they were back on the road again. Deep snow banks required many steps to
get to the top of them and often there would be no daylight in the home in
the morning until the snow was shoveled away from the windows.

The Bowlus home was kept warm by a strawburner. Grass grew tall then, and
the straw burner made of sheet iron, was packed tightly with straw or hay
and then turned upside down over the fire box in the range. It would burn
for hours and give a great deal of heat.

During the later years, the Bowluses spent their winters in Florida and
California and then came north for the summer and fall. They also lived in
Salem, Oregon, for about five years.

Mr. and Mrs. Bowlus were blessed with three daughters: Hattie May Bowlus
Swartzwelder, Cleveland, Ohio (deceased); Anna Grace Bowlus Carrel and Lulu
Edna Bowlus Mork of Lemmon, South Dakota.

MR. FRANK J. BOEHMER

Frank J. Boehmer, pioneer cattle king of Walworth county, was born February
22, 1863, in Pacwaukee, Wisconsin. Here his young boyhood was spent and
here he received the first four years of his schooling.

When still a lad in his teens he determined to go west to Dakota where
several of the family were already located. His first destination was
Forest City, Dakota, where his sister and her husband, J. G. Read, operated
a trading post. Then for some time he drove freight wagons from Blunt to
the Cheyenne Agency. In 1883 he homesteaded in Potter county west of the
present site of Gettysburg. In the later '80's he left his homestead and
came to Scranton, a little river town and one time county seat of Walworth
county, which was located near where the buildings of the Boehmer ranch now
stand. Here he operated a trading post store, roadhouse (hotel), and stage
barn. Business was good. The hotel and stage barn were needed as there were
daily stages from Pierre, Bismarck, and Aberdeen, besides the other
transient and local patrons. His store customers consisted of the white
people of this section, also the Indians, many of whom came from across the
river in row boats, bringing buffalo hides stock (usually cattle), and even
some of their handiwork to trade for store supplies.

It was while in this capacity that Mr. Boehmer became interested in and saw
the possibilities of the cattle business. Having by this time accumulated a
start for a herd of his own he decided to make that his life work. He,
therefore, sold out his store stock and closed the hotel. He moved the
store building, adding it to the stage barn giving more barn room for his
stock. About this time his mother, having been left a widow in Wisconsin,
came out and kept house for him.

He continued ranching and building up his herd. He had a business
connection with J. F. Witlock regarding the pasture lands, which extended
as far south as Cheyenne creek. At one time his herd numbered from 1000 to
1500 head and the pasture land from ten to twelve thousand acres. In 1897
Frank Boehmer was married to Miss Cora Dean of Forrest City. Miss Dean was
born in LaPorte, Indiana, in 1871, and had come to South Dakota, locating
at Forrest City. The first several years after their marriage were spent on
the ranch. Mr. Boehmer purchased a home in Evarts, another river town north
of LeBeau. The years 190S and 1906 were spent here. In 1907 Mr. Boehmer
moved his family back to the ranch where they lived until 1913. Mr. and Mrs.
Boehmer had a family of five children: Dean, George Claude (passed away in
babyhood while the family was living in Evarts), Nellie, and Elizabeth. The
children at tended the school in New LeBeau. In 1913 Mr. Boehmer purchased
a home in Fulton, South Dakota, where the family resided for the next four
years, the children at tending grade and high school here. The summers were
spent on the ranch at LeBeau. During this time in 1915 Mr. Boehmer suffered
a cerebral hemorrhage, which resulted in his death. Mr. Boehmer was a
member of the Masonic lodge in Gettysburg. He and his wife were very close
friends of Dr. W. A. George and family of Selby. He was well known by most
of the pioneers of Walworth county and was always a booster for his local
town. In the early years the town sponsored several annual celebrations or
Old Settlers picnics. Special excursion trains were run for these
occasions, bringing crowds of people from the east. The celebration would
usually last several days, the Indians as well as the white people taking
part. It was put on in truly western style with riding and roping as the
main events topped off with a dance in the evening. On one of these
occasions Mr. Boehmer donated a beef to the Indians with the understanding
that they barbecue and eat it in their native manner. This they did,
exhibiting their tribal dances and rituals. This was a thrilling sight for
the easterners who witnessed it, and even the local people never forgot the
spectacle.

After her husband's death Mrs. Boehmer and her family continued operating
the ranch. George passed away during the winter of 1919-1920, a victim of
the flu. Up to this time the old roadhouse or hotel had been their dwelling
house, and it continued as such until 1932 when they moved into the present
building. Mrs. Boehmer passed away in 1939. She was a member of the Order
of Eastern Star at Gettysburg.

The three remaining children are: Nellie, Mrs. L. R. Houck, who lives near
Gettysburg, where her husband operates the Triple U Hereford ranch, and
they have a family of two sons and two daughters; Elizabeth, Mrs. F. H.
Wolvington, who lives at Belle Fourche where her husband is an implement
dealer, and they have two children, a son and daughter; Dean, who owns and
operates the home ranch, employing a family who reside there with him.
There has been hired help on the ranch ever since it was started. One of
these deserves mention: Charlie Francisco, who, coming from Michigan in
1883, homesteaded south of Hoven for awhile then worked in and around
LeBeau for several years. Still later he was employed on the ranch by Frank
Boehmer and has continued with the family ever since. However, he has spent
part of the last several years in Selby. A broken hip sustained in a fall
last summer incapacitated him, and he is still recuperating from the
effects of the injury.

Dean, besides managing the home ranch, has outside business interests in
public affairs among which is the REA of this part of the country, serving
as president of the Board of Directors of the Cam-Wal Electric
Co-operative, Inc., located in Selby.

Anyone traveling that way today and topping the rise east of the ranch is
impressed by the natural beauty of the scene before him. The ranch
buildings nestled in the little valley, surrounded on the north and east by
hills, on the west by the wooded banks of the Missouri, and on the south by
the flat meadow lands.

So today the ranch at LeBeau still stands in its beautiful picturesque
setting, one of the ever diminishing symbols of the pioneer life of Dakota.

JOHN BIBELHEIMER

John Bibelheimer was born in Odessa, Russia, on July 22, 1875. When still
quite young he came to America with his parents, who settled in South
Dakota. Here he grew to manhood and graduated from the South Dakota State
Teachers' college at Madison and attended the Baptist college at Sioux
Falls.

Mr. Bibelheimer was active in public life. He was elected from his district
to the state legislature and he also served as deputy state auditor. During
the building of the state capitol building at Pierre he served as secretary
to the industrial commission. In 1902 he was elected to the office of
superintendent of schools of Walworth county. On October 15, 1908, he was
united in marriage to Sadie L. Millett.

        MR. JOHN BIBELHEIMER

In March, 1911, Mr. Bibelheimer accepted a position as manager of the
Kingman Investment company of Selby which he held until April 1, 1913, at
which time he accepted the managership of the Selby Equity Union, serving
until March 17, 1917.

In 1918 he and his wife moved to Washburn, North Dakota, where he took over
the elevator which belonged to his brother-in-law. This he operated for a
number of years. When it was closed he was appointed superintendent of
highways for McLean county, North Dakota, a position he held at the time of
his death in 1939.

Mr. and Mrs. Bibelheimer, having no children of their own, adopted a
daughter, now Mrs. Chas. White of Williamsburg, Kentucky.

Mr. and Mrs. Bibelheimer were deeply religious people all of their lives
and he was a leading figure in the affairs of the Methodist church. They
were both influential workers in the Asbury Camp Meeting association, which
they helped to organize. Mr. Bibelheimer had held an office in the
association for twelve years just prior to his sudden death May 6, 1939.

GEORGE LOUIS BAUMGARTEN

A pioneer's story is a drama as vital as life itself. In back of every cold
statistical fact lies a story of hardship and warmth, faith and courage.
The stage is a vast grassy plain where a prairie owl watches with solemn
eyes a covered wagon laboriously making its way out of the east. The
lilting notes of a meadowlark greet its arrival while from afar a coyote
makes careful investigation. Where the wagon stops a small crude home
evolves and in time forms part of a pleasant community. Thus is the life of
a pioneer interwoven in its development! George Louis Baumgarten was born
at Columbus, Wisconsin, July 15, 1858, the eldest of six children. Later
with his parents he took up residence at Tomah, Wisconsin, where he
received his elementary education and attended high school. He entered
business college at Hamlin, Minnesota, after which he returned to his home
to assist with farming operations.

On March 31, 1885, Mr. Baumgarten and Emily Hoffmann were united in
marriage at Tomah. Emily Hoffmann and her mother had followed sisters and
brothers to America from Germany when Emily was thirteen years old. She
often mentioned her joy in the new land and gave a lifetime of love and
loyalty to her adopted country.

        MR. AND MRS. GEORGE LOUIS BAUMGARTEN

After their marriage, Mr. Baumgarten left immediately for the Dakota
territory, where he had previously filed on a claim near Kelly, South
Dakota. Kelly was abandoned when the railroad came to the present site of
Bowdle, two miles southeast.

In a few weeks Mr. Baumgarten had erected a home for his bride. She soon
followed her husband and came to enter a life far different to that she had
known.

But what at first appeared to be an endless expanse of grassy land, quickly
developed into a friendly community, with all of the challenge for endeavor
which goes into pioneer living. Other young men with their brides came to
start life on the rich prairie land. Their methods of living would be
considered very inconvenient today, yet out of their dependence on each
other grew deep and lasting friendships.

Life was ever a constant struggle and challenge. It took drive and purpose
to combat drought and blizzard, hail and prairie fire. A blizzard on the
prairies with few landmarks was a serious business. With a raging blizzard
at its full height of ferocity, men going to their barns would tie clothes
lines around their waists and the other end on the door knob. Thus would
the young wife feel secure in the thought of her husband's safe return.
Miles of drouth-stricken grassy land made wonderful fuel for prairie fires.
Billows of smoke clouding the horizon came as a signal for men and women to
take sacks and pails of water to fight in saving all they were striving
for. Sometimes the fight was lost, which was the event when a prairie fire
took the barn and granary on Mr. Baumgarten's farm.

The drama of pioneer life would be incomplete with out an Indian scare.
Many residents of those early days will no doubt remember the exodus of the
countryside to the nearest town that fearsome night.

The Baumgartens awoke as usual, but to a very quiet world. They noticed
that no men were working in the fields, no travelers along the busy country
roads. Could they have made a mistake on their calendar and might this be
Sunday? With a feeling of apprehension they took up their daily tasks and
the day wore on. Finally a neighbor stopped to inquire why they were not in
Bowdle! That was the first they heard of the Indian scare--somehow they had
not been warned. Mrs. Baumgarten, with two small girls clinging to her
skirts, went weeping, in search of her husband. It was nearing evening and
Mr. Baumgarten thought over the situation and decided that if the Indians
were really on the war path, a flaming horizon would herald their approach,
giving time to make a safe departure. Very soon everyone was returning
home and peace and quiet were restored.

Yet life was not all serious struggle. A warm community spirit prevailed.
In time the little white schoolhouse just over the hill, became a realty
and the center of community interest. Here religious and social gatherings
took place. People. must look to themselves for social entertainment and
literary societies came into being. Everyone took part in contributing
entertainment, which is by far a richer experience than being a mere
listener. Many a cold winter evening found a cheerful group of old and
young gathered for a few hours of social pleasure. Later bob sleds would
take each one merrily along snowy trails to his door. As the years passed,
across the prairie miles sounded the peals of the bell in a country church
on Sunday mornings. This was known as the Baer church.

Then there were the colorful Fourth of July celebrations! In spite of poor
roads and crude methods of travel, people paused in their busy days and
traveled to the nearest town for the big celebration. For days before.
children would anxiously scan the skies--and, oh thrill of thrills, when
the great day dawned bright and clear! Mother had probably been busy since
dawn preparing and packing a hearty lunch. Finally all was ready for the
gala occasion, little girls in stiffly starched white dresses, little boys
self conscious in new straw hats and big bow ties ! The few who were more
fortunate, packed themselves and their families into a surrey "with a
fringe on the top," others brought out the family democrat, but many
climbed into the lumber wagon, children; lunch and all, and away they went,
following friends and neighbors all along the way!

What a spectacular array of styles! Women came forth in elaborate silks and
satins, picture hats and lacy parasols. Will Aurand, the college son of a
leading merchant, took part in a bicycle race, dressed in the sport style of
the day--trousers turned up to the knees. This garb was most shocking to
the aesthetic sensibilities of some of the ladies present.

Entertainment was varied. Races and band concerts, ball games and bowery
dances were enjoyed. There was always a bowery built of fresh fragrant
lumber and cool green branches, brought miraculously from somewhere. At one
end was a raised platform draped with red, white and blue bunting. Here the
serious side of the day was stressed through a patriotic speech given by
some leading citizen. But perhaps the most enjoyable hours were those spent
in pleasant communion of friend with friend, who in the busy life of a
pioneer, had time to pause for a bit of fellowship.

There were also ways of combining business with pleasure and many were the
camping trips down along the old Missouri, in search of wild fruits.
Neighbors would plan to spend at least one night and after a delightful
outing would return home lavishly rewarded with nature's gifts. Thus would
delicious preserves and jellies further the winter's stock of supplies.

Spring Lake was also the scene of many pleasant occasions. When the Old
Settlers' Picnic became an established custom, they would gather here for a
day of pleasure and festivities.

The busy years extended into 1898 and Mr. Baumgarten with his family, moved
to Bangor where he was to serve as county auditor of Walworth county for two
terms. Situated on the pleasant countryside, lay the small inland town of
Bangor. People came from the east looking for the fulfillment of dreams, be
it fortune or adventure. Doctors and lawyers, ministers and teachers,
merchants and businessmen, had come by train as far as Bowdle and then by
stage, here to take up residence in an environment quite different from
that they had left. On arriving at Bowdle, one lady from New York City
pleaded with her husband not to go on, but take the return train back. She
protested all of the way on the stage and declared that she would never,
never stay. However, she remained to offer her musical talent in serving two
generations.

The development of Bangor was to be rudely blocked. The railroad, playing
so large a part in the drama of the rise and fall of towns, extended four
miles further north, and so drew, like a magnet, a large part of Bangor to
become Selby.

In 1903, Mr. Baumgarten returned to his farm, where he was to remain for
four years. In 1907, he was again elected to the office of county auditor
and during this period the courthouse was moved to Selby.

In 1911, Mr. Baumgarten took the position as manager of the Bowdle Flour
Mill, where he resided four years. In 1919 he returned to Selby to serve in
the county offices for eight years, first as county treasurer and later as
county auditor, retiring from public life in 1927. He had been suffering
from ill health and on November 3 passed away at his home in Selby. Mrs.
Baumgarten still lives at Selby with her daughter, Matilda.

There were five children: Matilda, who is now serving a term as county
auditor; Edith, married and living at Stoughton, Wisconsin; Elsie, married
and living at Mobridge; Fern, teaching at Wenatchee, Washington; and one
son, George, who met an untimely death at the age of eighteen years.

Mr. Baumgarten was spared the ordeal of seeing the country in which he had
so much faith, pass through the recent years of drouth and depression. Yet,
like many pioneers who have built on the knowledge of past experience, he
might have looked to the future with fresh hope and courage!

MR. AND MRS. JOHANNES BAUDER

Johannes Bauder was born at Grossliebenthal, South Russia, March 31, 1834.
In the year 1855 he was united in marriage with Elizabeth Koenig who was a
native of the same village. Seven children were born to them, all of whom
have passed away but one daughter, Mrs. Elizabeth Max, who resides at
Scotland, South Dakota, and is now 94 years of age. The wife and mother was
taken from the family by death in 1872.

        THE JOHANNES BAUDER FAMILY
        Mr. and Mrs. Bauder are the center figures. Mrs. Max, of Scotland,
        now 94 years of age, is at Mr. Bauder's left. The first in the
        upper row and to the left is Carl, late of Selby; William, of
        Selby, is the third from the left, and the tallest in the top row
        is Henry, formerly of Bowdle. Emanuel, now deceased, is third from
        the right in the lowest row, and third from the left in the same
        row is Mrs. Jacob F. Wolf of Java. The others are unknown to
        Walworth county people.

In the year 1873 he was married a second time to Barbara Bauder and soon
after their marriage they came to America where he filed on 480 acres of
land, a home stead, tree claim and pre-emption about 20 miles north of
Yankton, in Bon Homme county. The land was broken up and the farming done
mostly with ox team power. Though the country proved to be good, the
seasons were often bad. Yankton was then the jumping off place-that is, the
end of the railroad. The 22 miles from the home to the little city was
farther away by ox team than the other side of the world is now by
airplane. Soon after they settled, the railroad built north to Scotland and
they were only two and a half miles from the station of Estherville.

Lured by the promise of the fertile prairies of the Blue Blanket valley,
they sold their land in Bon Homme county and, in the year 1900, he bought
640 acres of land of Henry Ehret, southeast of Selby. The family moved on
it the next September. This land remained the family home until 1915.

Mr. Bauder passed away June 16, 1915. Mrs. Bauder continued to make her
home on the farm with her son, Emanuel, until his death in 1923. She spent
the last year of her life in Selby in the home of her daughter-in-law, Mrs.
Emanuel Bauder, and passed away on March 25, 1924. Eleven children were
born to the second marriage. Those surviving at the time this is written
are: Henry of Salem, Oregon; Lydia, Mrs. Jacob F. Wolf, of Java; and
William of Selby; the others having passed away at different times.

This large pioneer family must have left its impression on the community in
which they lived in Bon Homme county, and they certainly have in the Selby
community in Walworth county. Those who chose to farm were good farmers,
the land always being well tilled and the farmsteads well kept. The young
people have been active in all of the affairs of the community and all have
always stood for the best things in life.

At the present time, Henry is retired after a long and successful business
career at Bowdle. William has retired but is serving as janitor in the
Selby school, and Mrs. Wolf and her husband are living a retired life at
Java. Their children all are active in business life or on farms.

MR. EMANUEL BAER

Emanuel Baer was born in South Russia on December 28, 1880. He was the son
of John and Margaretha Baer. Their were 13 children in the family. Living
now are Mary, Mrs. Henry Schreter of Java; and Reinholdt, who lives at
Lewiston, Idaho.

The family emigrated to America in 1893 at the same time, and for the same
reason many other families left--to escape the military rule of Russia. The
Baer family came to Freeman, South Dakota, and then to Walworth county
where he filed on land now owned by the John Schnaible family. When Emanuel
was 13 years of age he herded sheep in the vicinity of Hoven for the
fabulous salary of $8.00 a month. He received a part of his education in
Russia, and acquired what schooling he could in the schools in the
neighborhood of his father's homestead. He clerked for H. A. Mason in his
store at Bowdle; later Emanual worked for Bauer and Stoller in their store
at Java, and for John Hofmeyer, also of Java.

        MR. AND MRS. EMANUEL BAER

At this time, July 25, 1905, he was united in marriage to Mary Schnaible of
Java. Mary was one of a farm family of six, all of whom had to help with
the farming. Many were the days that Mary, as a young girl, had to work out
in the fields, walking behind a plow.

He and his wife endured the same hardships, had the same joys and possessed
the courage to have faith in the future of the city of Selby which was
manifest among all the early settlers. His faith in the future of this
section was well founded as he was engaged in extensive real estate
business.

At the time of his marriage his salary was raised from $50.00 to $60.00 a
month. This salary enabled him to save enough money to purchase a house and
furniture in Java. In 1906 he was elected to the office of register of
deeds of Walworth county and took his office at Bangor, South Dakota. This
raised his salary to $100.00 a month, of which $50.00 was saved. Due to an
acute housing shortage the young married couple were forced to take
quarters in the old post office building in Bangor. He was re-elected in
1908. While serving as register of deeds at Bangor the courthouse was moved
to Selby, so the family home, with furniture, Emanuel, his wife, two
daughters, and two cats were moved into Selby, Tony Birkholt doing that
efficient job with horses. After his second term he moved to Java and
engaged in the real estate and insurance business for four years. Then he
was re elected to return to the office of register of deeds. After another
four years he sought and was elected to the office of clerk of courts, and
Emanuel continued to serve in that office up to his death in 1925.

In 1917 the N. H. Kingman house was purchased, and the family settled as
permanent residents of Selby. In the same year, by paying $42.00 an acre,
another quarter of land was added to his holdings. The renter received the
first year's flax crop for the breaking of the quarter.

He was a member of the American Lutheran church and served as trustee and
treasurer of his church. He was a member of the Commercial club, belonged
to the Golf club, was a member of the Java band, and sang in a men's
quartet.

To this union were born seven children, two of whom passed away in infancy.
The children are: Clara, Mrs. Alfred Bastian of Mobridge; Erna, Mrs. Edward
Zabel of Selby; Leander of Aberdeen; Herbert and Emanuel of Selby. The
three sons served in World War II, Leander and Herbert in the Army, and
Emanuel in the Navy. At present, Leander is an agent for a private grain
commission company of Minneapolis with headquarters in Aberdeen; Herbert is
the manager of the Baer Recreation parlor, and Emanuel is a student at the
University of Nebraska.

While in the courthouse Emanual Baer was the advisor and friend of all who
came to him, and was particularly beloved and helpful to the German-speaking
people of the county.

MR. LARS ANDERSON

My childhood home, a cherished spot in my lifelong memory, is nestled in
the foothills on the banks of Swan creek near the spot where Grandfather,
Lars Anderson, ended his long trek from native Norway. He found this place
to be that which he sought in that magic "Freeland America."

This pleasant picturesque valley, which today constitutes an abundant
source of livelihood to many people, from practically all northern European
countries, is a far cry from the trackless, neighborless, homeless sea of
lush grass found here by Grandfather Lars in 1885. Today's thrifty,
well-painted, rural-electrified, windmill bespecked farmsteads, the rolling
hillsides generously sprinkled with the white faces of well bred cattle,
and the verdant little fields of grain and tame hay of all kinds, is indeed
a transformation wrought by God's abundant blessings and the toil of
progressive immigrants who, like Lars, came to this country for a new
opportunity. All of this would have been a wild stretch of the imagination
indeed in the early spring of 1885, when Lars in his own mind had come to
the end of the long trail which led back to Christiania, Norway. Here he
stopped to permanently establish a home for his wife, Kari and five sons.
Today's three homey church-spired villages of the valley were yet to be
founded. Surely he could not have envisioned that the fruit of his toil,
and that of subsequent comers, would some 65 years later produce the
hard-surfaced highways giving foot to fleet automobiles, modern homes
boasting of electricity, running water and all modern facilities, which was
unknown even to the richest in his day. Horror might have stricken his
heart to see today's skies cut by four-motored planes winging their way up
and down the valley on transcontinental flights.

        MR. AND MRS. LARS ANDERSON

Lars Anderson was one of the very first settlers in the Swan creek area. He
was born near Christiania, Norway, in March, 1843. He claimed his Norwegian
bride, Miss Kari Kalstad in 1865. This progressive, ambitious young couple
felt that the "Old Country" held little opportunity for them. They
subscribed to the great bulwark of all countries, the middle class. The
country was crowded. The people were many. Opportunities were few. All over
central and northern Europe young people so situated were being spiritually
drawn to that magic new country which was so anxious to provide room and
opportunity that it gave free land to those who would come and people it.
After much consideration, Lars and Kari decided to forever break their home
ties, pool and borrow, in any way scrape together the needed kronen for the
cheapest fare to New York. The necessary preparations were made. The few
and simple belongings were gathered into nondescript luggage, and the long,
trying, distasteful journey began. The family then included the two eldest
sons, Martin and Antone. Several months later they landed in New York and
were caught up in that mass of immigrant humanity which flowed ever
westward.

Lars and Kari's first attempt at a home in the New World occurred at Coon
Valley, near LaCrosse, Wisconsin. This attempt was unsuccessful. They, like
most immigrants of that day, did not know the language, were entirely
unaccustomed to the unethical business methods of many "sharpies" who
preyed upon the few remaining pennies of "ignorant immigrants." Lars
attempted to buy some property and despite extreme thrift and willing sweat
of the brow, the odds were too great, and he lost his small investment. By
this time the family had grown from the two Norwegian-born sons, Martin and
Antone, to three additional sons, the twin boys of Charlie and Louie and
the youngest of the family, Otto.

Discouragement overtook the family as responsibilities increased and
opportunities decreased. Much the same situation seemed to prevail as in
the country of their birth. Hence, another decision to move, pushing farther
west, deeper into the unpeopled wilderness of South Dakota. This decision,
in the spring of 1885, ultimately brought the Lars Anderson family to
Ipswich, the end of the Milwaukee railroad. There the immigrant family
composed of the father and mother and five sons, together with little in
worldly possessions embarked from the train, and finally procured an ox
team and rough cart, in which the family again pushed westward beyond
towns, railroads, fences and people. After more than a week of jolting over
the prairie, marked only by occasional herds of antelope, an acceptable
site was found near the present village of Lowry. Even this leg of the
journey which was a mere patch on the total length, was trying in itself.
Hotel accommodations were provided on the ground with scanty bedding. At
night the oxen were tethered to graze while the family slept. Otto, the
youngest, was then three years of age.

As is ever the case, the first order of business upon arrival was to
establish a home for the family. There was an abundance of building
material,--native sod. Implements of any kind were completely lacking. The
sod was cut by hand and walls were raised by the same means until after
days of hard labor a crude sod shanty was erected. Here at last was the new
home in a spacious wilderness several thousands of miles from the homeland
and the ties of preceding generations. While the sod shanty provided a
crude home and a fair protection from the weather, the thatched roof leaked
generously in the driving South Dakota rains. Bedding, even for the summer,
was scanty. There was no furniture. The only available meat supply was wild
antelope, one of which would be taken as needed. An old hand-loaded musket
was Lars' sporting rifle. The necessary steps were taken to file on a
quarter of land, as a homestead, and an additional quarter for a tree
claim. The little town of Lowry is now situated on Lars' tree claim. Land
adjoining these claims on all sides was regarded as free range. In
subsequent summers additional earnings were made through taking in herd
cattle from as far south as Lebanon, and north to Selby.

Even to start in this land of potential plenty required some capital, all
of which was now gone. Lars' first earnings were procured by walking more
than 70 miles to the Mellette Ashton area to work in harvest fields at the
stupendous rate of 30c per day, plus board. From such toil, sacrifice and
confidence in the future, plus extreme thrift, came the first necessary
cash to procure a few cattle, a saddle horse, necessary provisions for the
winter, and such household necessities as could be procured at Ipswich, the
nearest shopping point. Opportunity for education of the boys was
practically nil. Every available effort of every member of the family had
to be pooled to insure livelihood for all. The five barefooted boys herded
cattle over an area many miles in diameter. There were no fences, no
neighbors, no confines. The cattle had to be kept only in herds and in
known areas, and where they could be immediately accounted for. Range was
limited only by access to water. As the cattle were herded farther and
farther afield, the twins, Charlie and Louie, would spend weeks on end with
cattle, protected only by a crude herd shanty away from the rest of the
family.

Much could be written with interest and authenticity about the early life,
sacrifices and privation of these early pioneer builders. However, this
amateur biographer is reluctant to make such an attempt since these days
have been so ably embellished by such authentic South Dakota pioneer novels
as "Giants in the Earth," "A Prayer for Tomorrow," "Turkey Red," and a host
of others. The experiences related in those authentic novels parallel to a
large degree the experiences of most of the early pioneers. Today's
generation stands in deep gratitude to those writers who have crystallized
those experiences into novels.

Swan lake, which is the source of the placid little Swan creek, was even in
1885, when Lars first came to this valley, a full, welcome body of water
which enhanced the rolling prairie. At that time, however, the cause of the
lake, a beaver dam, was much more plainly visible than today. Thanks to the
work of beavers, the valley is enriched throughout the entire season by a
slow disgorging of the lake's contents rather than allowing the stream to
be only a spring torrent, as it undoubtedly was prior to the days of the
beaver dam.

Swan creek valley has been dear to the hearts of four generations of Lars'
descendants. While some of the clan has scattered widely, most have
remained. They have, like Lars, made this pleasant valley their permanent
homes, and are contributing to the worthwhileness of the community. More
great grandchildren will take up homes in the Swan creek area, and
undoubtedly a host of descendants will scatter far and wide, but all with a
pleasant memory, and a thankfulness for a wise choice on the part of Lars
and Kari in 1885. Grandmother Kari's toil was ended in August, 1914, while
Grandfather Lars lived on until 1922.

Martin, the eldest of the sons, who was joined in marriage to Eva Mauch,
was born in 1868 and passed on in 1942. To this union were born Edwin,
Caroline, Raymond and Norman.

The next son, Antone, who was born in 1871 passed on in 1915. To his
marriage with Ethel Swisher were born three sons, Orville, Howard and
Bernard.

The twins, Charlie and Louis were born in 1879. Both are living. Charlie
was united in marriage to Amy Hinckley. They still reside on the banks of
Swan creek. In the Charlie Anderson family, there were three children:
Dana, Louis and Floris. Louie, the other twin, who never married, resides
at Selby.

Otto Anderson, born in 1882, was married to Nettie Smith. In this family
also there were three children: Myrtle, Clarence and Elizabeth. Otto passed
on in 1939.

So runs the story of the life and progeny of one of Walworth county's very
first settlers. He saw the opportunity to progress in a new, untried land,
and at the expense of forever turning his back to all family and friendship
ties of generations in his native Norway, he came to "the blessed land of
room-enough" to build a new home for himself and his descendants. We, who
today are his progeny and enjoy the fruit of the sacrifices and toil of
those early days of privation, can only be grateful for his foresight and
effort, and say with one acclaim, "Our gratitude to you father, grandfather,
and great-grandfather, Lars. Yours was a good choice."
                Compiled by Clarence O. Anderson.
                Written by Louis R. Anderson.

WALTER BUCKLIN

Walter Bucklin was born February 28, 1851, in Henry county, Ohio. His wife,
Florence Olive Van Tassell, was born June 12, 1853, in Wood county, Ohio.
They were married June 14, 1874, and remained on a small farm in Ohio until
1884 when they seemed to hear the west calling. So they, with their five
small children, Mary, Harriet, Maud, Allen, and Belle came west to South
Dakota. They came by train as far as Ipswich which was then the end of the
railroad, and continued their westward journey with team and wagon. They
homesteaded in Walworth county where they made their new home.

When the railroad reached Bowdle, they were happy as they could now make
the trip for groceries in one day by getting up early and starting. When
hauling grain, two days were needed for the trip.

One day when Mr. Bucklin arrived home from Bowdle he told his family he had
seen something that day that he had never seen before and no one else had
ever seen it either. Of course the children were very curious. He told them
he had seen the first train pull into Walworth county.

Four of their children, Art, Bessie, Clarence, and Ray were born in South
Dakota.

Mary Bucklin Hutchins passed away leaving one small son, Bert, now of
Vallejo, California, who lived with his grandparents for about ten years
when his father married again.

Harriet Bucklin married Guy Hopper in 1908 at Selby. They with their three
children moved to Washington. Mr. Hopper passed away in November, 1g48. Two
of the children, Ray and Genevieve Hopper Rankin, live at Kelso,
Washington, near their mother. Aurilla Hopper Martin lives at 29 Palms,
California.

Allen Bucklin has been living in Oso, Washington, since 1934.

Maud Bucklin and June Franks were married in Bangor, South Dakota in 1896.
Nine children came to bless their home: Tom and family live in Chehalis,
Washington; Ada and family at Selby, South Dakota; Olive and family at
Hettinger, North Dakota; Edward and family at Glencross, South Dakota;
Florence and family at Caro, Michigan; Nellie and husband at Walford, North
Dakota; Minnie and family at Monrovia, California. Clarence died in 1924.
Albert was lost in battle in Italy in 1944. June Franks died in March, 1924.

Belle Bucklin was married to Albert Cummings in Soptember, 1935, at
Arlington, Washington.

Art Bucklin married Mable Coull at Selby, South Dakota, December, 1913.
They have four children: Mrs. Luella Moos, Mrs. Agnes Chesky, and Dorothy
of Selby, and George of Minden, Louisiana.

        WALTER BUCKLIN FAMILY
        Pictured, top row--Art, Allen, Belle, Clarence. Bottom row--Bessie,
        Harriet, Walter Bucklin, Mrs. Walter Bucklin, Maud. (The youngest
        son Ray was not present when this picture was taken.)

Bess Bucklin married Charley Pooler in June, 1914, at Selby, South Dakota.
They with their three children moved to Washington in 1934. Evelyn Pooler
Baker and family live at Arlington. Walter lives at Arlington. Ivan and
family live at Everett, Washington. Bess passed away in December, 1938.

Clarence married Bertha Marxen at Selby, South Dakota, in February, 1929.
They have three sons, Dwane of Glencoe, Minnesota; Raymond and Blaine of
Selby.

Ray married Verna Lincke in Selby in 1924. They moved to California in
1929. They have one son, Melvin, of Baldwin Park, California.

MR. O. S. CRAWFORD

O. S. Crawford was born in 1870 in Volney, Allamekee county, Iowa. Alice
Irene Christler, his wife, was born in 1869 at Meridan, Illinois. She came
from hardy Pennsylvania Dutch stock, while Mr. Crawford was of Scotch Irish
origin. Seven of their twelve children were born in Iowa and Mr. Crawford
found it very hard to prosper and expand in thickly settled Iowa. In 1899 he
came to Walworth county and purchased the Kingman ranch, eight miles south
of Bangor, the nearest town at that time. He returned to Iowa and in the
spring of 1900 moved his family out. They brought 200 head of heifers with
them, arriving in Gettysburg and driving the stock across the prairie to
the ranch. The following winter 140 head of the heifers perished in a
severe blizzard. The remaining herd gradually increased and by taking in
herd cattle the financial position of the family was greatly improved.

        MR. O. S. CRAWFORD

In 1907 when the Minneapolis & St. Louis railroad was built through the
ranch, Mr. Crawford started a livestock shipping business as a side line to
ranching. This was continued until 1935. In 1920 the Jackson ranch was
purchased and at various times other land was added until the original
ranch has grown to a good many acres with four sets of buildings. In 1940
he decided to retire and turn the ranch over to younger hands. At present it
is managed by three sons. Mr. Crawford was educated in the common schools
of Iowa. He had no formal education or training but through the years has
learned much from experience. He was always interested in community
progress and was president of the Farmer's Elevator in Lowry and
instrumental in organizing the Walworth County Fair association. He served
on the registration board of World War I, and the Selective Service board
of World War II. He also held county offices, serving as county assessor
from 1921 to 1924, and county commissioner from his district from 1925 to
1936.

DAVE JONES FAMILY

On July 4, 1883, Dave Jones and wife, Sarah, three sons and two daughters,
landed in New York city, from Bala, North Wales, to seek a new home in
America. Their first experience in the new land was losing all their money
when they were victims of a pickpocket on the train from New York City to
Chicago.

The family settled in Wisconsin for one year. In April, 1884, the father
and son, Evan, came to Walworth county, filing on land in what is now
Spring Valley township, the father on the northwest quarter of section
18-123 75, Evan on the northeast quarter of section 13-123-76, which was
Evan's home until he died in January, 1934.

Mr. Jones and son, Evan, built a house and made preparation for the rest of
the family to join them later. The mother, Dave, Ted, and Sally came in
September, 1884. Margaret stayed in Wisconsin until 1885. One daughter,
Jane, stayed in Wales and her family still lives there. It is hard to
picture in terms of today what this new country must have seemed like to
this family from the hills and valleys of Wales.

Their nearest railroad town was Ipswich, fifty miles away, where they
hauled their grain and brought supplies enough to last all winter, the trip
taking several days. It was several years before the railroad came to
Bowdle.

Farm life in this country was new to them and what they knew of farming. It
was a different adventure than they were used to in Wales. But they stayed
and adopted the pioneer life with the rest of the early settlers of the
country.

GRANDPA JONES

The father, mother, Sally, and Evan died and are buried in the Selby
cemetery. Ted and his family settled in Denver, Colorado, and he has since
passed away. Dave and his family live at Fawcett, Alberta, Canada. Margaret
married Bradley Stowell in the fall of 1890.

Bradley Stowell's family came from Vermont to Sauk Rapids, Minnesota, where
he was born July 17, 1859. There were three brothers and two sisters in the
family.

His early life was spent in Minnesota. In the year 1884, he too, set out to
join the landseekers of the west. Settling in Walworth county, he
homesteaded on land in section 15-123-76, three and one-half miles
southeast of Selby. This was the family home for several years, the family
later living on farms near Java and Selby until retiring in the early
1930's.

Their home was blessed with nine children, three sons and six daughters,
Edward and Esther passing away in their early teens. Mr. Stowell died
February 22, 1936 and Ethel (Mrs. W. R. Crawford) in April, 1936. Norma
(Mrs. Elmer Swift) and family live south of Selby; Nellie Swift is with her
family in Seattle, Washington; Margaret and Sadie live with their mother in
Mobridge. Harry and wife live in Mobridge, and Lee and wife and family live
on the Jones homestead southeast of Selby where they have built their home.

As we look back, many happy days have been their fortune. Sorrow, grief,
sickness and hard luck have broken in now and then, but they were always
able to share a good turn with their neighbors who needed help.

We close another chapter of history about ancestors through whose tireless
