efforts, countless sacrifices and faith, a blessed heritage is ours in this
fair land of America.

MR. AND MRS. HENRY SEYER, SR.

Henry Seyer, Sr., was born at Fehmern in Holstein, Germany, on March 23,
1874, coming to America at the age of 15 years to Avoca, Iowa. His father
was a shoemaker and from their home they could see across the Baltic sea to
the Island of Laaland, a part of Denmark. It took him a week to find work
after arriving at Avoca and his first job was on a farm near Shelby. He
recalls that he worked eleven months for $50.00.

On March 3, 1896, he was united in marriage with Agnes Blunk, also born in
Holstein on November 30, 1878. She came with her parents to America and
Minden, Iowa, at the age of 12 years.

The young couple started life together on rented farms in the vicinity
where they had lived and were quite successful. However, Iowa land was
becoming high priced and rents were high and it seemed to them that there
were greater opportunities for them and their family on the cheaper lands
in Dakota. Many of their friends and neighbors thought the same and in the
year 1908 Seyers came to Walworth county, moving on the farm six miles
south of Selby, then known as the Abe Taylor farm, which Mr. Seyer had
purchased from Otto Lincke, who moved to Selby to engage in the farm
implement business.

In the year 1919 they sold this farm and moved to the Gordon farm in Spring
Valley township where they resided until 1925 when he purchased the place
known as the Buchecker farm, four miles south of Java, from Mrs. Anna
Noteboom, which has since been the family home. Mrs. Seyer passed away
February 23, 1944. The first farm purchased eventually came back to them and
is now occupied by the youngest son, Walter.

        MR. AND MRS. HENRY SEYER AND FAMILY
        Standing, left to right, upper row--Walter, Henry, Jr., Fred C.,
        Dora, Henry Seyer, Sr., sitting left; Mrs. Agnes Seyer, sitting
        right, Ella Seyer, standing between those seated.

Five children came to bless their home. Fred C. married Bertha Gosch of
Glenham, and they have four children. They own the farm known in early days
as the Ritter place adjacent to the Strand farm, south of the West Spring
Valley school. They have greatly improved the place and by purchasing
additional land have one of the fine farms of that community. Henry, Jr.,
operates the home farm where he and his father reside. Dora was one of
Walworth county's school teachers for a number of years and is now married
to K. N. Salmen, who is foreman at Golden's Chevrolet garage, Golden,
Colorado, where they reside. They have one daughter. Walter resides, as
before stated, on the first farm purchased south of Selby. He married
Mildred Rishel and they have two sons, Kenneth and Marvin. Walter is a
member of the board of education of the Selby Consolidated school and Fred
has been chairman of the Spring Valley district school board for many
years. Ella, a graduate of South Dakota State college, Brookings, South
Dakota, has taught school, successfully, for many years in the high school
at Redfield, South Dakota, and also in Iowa and Michigan.

Henry Seyer, Sr., has long been rated as one of Walworth county's
prominent farmers and stock raisers. His farm and the farms of his sons are
well improved and well kept. The Seyer families and their farms are a credit
to the community.

ANDREW A. HILDE FAMILY

More than seventy years ago Norway demanded every able bodied young man who
reached the age of 21 to serve in the army for two years.

This irked the most ambitious of them and was the greatest motive in
stimulating the immigration of these young Norsemen to our shores.

Among these thousands who came to the United States in those years were the
family of Andrew A. Hilde.

The oldest of the family was Ole A., who had borrowed money from an uncle
who had come some years before and had served in the United States Army
during the Civil War.

Ole A. took passage from Guldsvig, Hollengdahl, Norway, in the early summer
of 1878. Weeks of rough and stormy weather hampered the progress of the
small craft, but when he finally beheld the Statue of Liberty, stretching
toward him, her hand of welcome and torch of hope, he vowed, "I'll work and
work and save and save every penny to bring my father, mother, sister, and
four brothers to the United States!"

Two months later he reached Rose Creek, Minnesota, where he made his home
with an uncle and cousins. He worked through harvest and threshing, earning
his first money--a fabulous sum--$1.00 a day and board. Yes, he would soon
possess the coveted amount that he needed.

The next to arrive in two years was Brother Hans, who in turn helped to
earn passage for the rest, who all had arrived by 1880.

In 1881, they set out for South Dakota,--here each of the brothers filed on
a homestead, tree claim and preemption. This area, when organized later,
became Hilde township in Walworth county.

Ole, after proving up his homestead, traded it for one in Brown township,
where he resided until moving to Fort Ransom, North Dakota? in the summer
of 1902. When he retired, he moved to Fargo.

Constant labor that only pioneers can understand, breaking the rich prairie
soil with a horse-drawn breaking plow, hauling wood from the Missouri river
bottom for fuel, digging by hand, wells to provide water, erecting their
simple buildings of wood or logs, then hauling their grain over thirty
miles to Bowdle to market, kept them employed from early dawn till late
into the night throughout the years.

On February 4, 1887, Ole A. married Minnie Tostrud of Cashton, Wisconsin,
who had also come to take a homestead. She accompanied her sister and
brother-in-law, Charles Reistad, who also filed on land in the same
vicinity. They all came from Cashton, Wisconsin.

To Ole A. and Minnie Hilde were born seven children, Tillie R. Hilde, who
has operated the Capital Commercial college for several years in Bismarck,
North Dakota; Leonora, Ruby and Hazel, who live in Fargo, North Dakota, and
are all business women; Albin and Vernal, who operate farms near Lisbon,
North Dakota; William passed away two years ago and is buried at Lisbon, as
are his parents, Minnie, who died in September, 1911, and Ole, who passed
on in April, 1927.

Hans Hilde married Sarah Hall of Westby, Wisconsin. To them was born a
daughter, Rhoda, who is now Mrs. Clifford Schroeder of Lyle, Minnesota.
This is where Hans moved upon leaving South Dakota more than forty years
ago. He passed on in June, 1932; his wife in 1946.

Steiner Hilde married Gertrude Larson of Blue Blanket in 1890. To them were
born ten children. In 1896 he and his family moved to Camrose, Alberta,
Canada, where again he experienced pioneering. Several children still
reside in Canada, two in California, one in Florida. Rev. Selmer Hilde is
the Lutheran pastor at Michigan, North Dakota. Steiner passed on in 1943.
His widow resides on the homestead with two of the children.

Roy Hilde married Amanda Reistad and in 1900 moved to Oakes, North Dakota,
and to them were born five children. Three reside in Minneapolis, Dolly
passed away in 1947, Kyle is employed in Fargo, Roy died in 1938 and is
buried at Oakes. His widow resides in Fargo.

The youngest in the group of men, Andrew, resided for a time in Hilde
township, but bent on seeking new fields he moved to Reedstown, Wisconsin,
where he married and is the father of two daughters, both of whom live near
Viroqua, Wisconsin. To this town Andrew moved after his wife passed away
and here he still resides.

Rose Hilde for several years ran a dressmaking shop in the Old Dumont Hotel
in Bowdle. She moved to Cashton, Wisconsin, upon her marriage to Charles
Tostrud of that place. They later moved to Minneapolis where they resided
until their death in the late thirties. They had one daughter, Miss Melise,
who makes her home in Minneapolis.

The sterling qualities of these Vikings, instilled by their hardy, thrifty
ancestors of the Norse Country, imbued them with the brawn and fortitude to
face the vicissitudes of this prairie land, hardships a-plenty came with
years of drouth, hot winds, hard winters. But, there were always promising
springtimes, when all nature smiled, and rich black furrows laid bare to
the sun and the rain, looked promising; so hope each year flourished in
each successive heart. When harvest was bountiful, it spurred them on and
on! They faced Indian scares, prairie fires and blizzards as just another
exciting adventure.

As the years passed and they retired in comfort, memories of life's
experiences in the Dakotas remained sweet and they loved the land
throughout their years.

MR. JULIUS E. HOEFS

Julius E. Hoefs was born in Wangeritz, Germany, April 20, 1857 and came to
America with two of his older sisters at the age of 15 years. His brother,
William had immigrated to America before and had settled at Watertown,
Wisconsin and Julius made his home with him. He worked and went to school
as best he could. Wages at that time were well paid for at $15.00 a month
and the work was often quite difficult for him as he was small for his age.

He came of good parents, fairly well established and strong believers in a
good education but the lure of America was stronger. At the age of 26 in
the spring of 1883 he came to Watertown, South Dakota and worked for a
while, having decided to try his chance of life in the west. Here he met
Henry Ehret and J. J. Elfrink and the three of them hired a team and came
out to seek a location for homesteads. They selected land about 3 miles
east of Bangor.

He filed on the southwest quarter of 23-123-76 in 1884 and his tree claim
is now owned by Guy Schuh. His brother, William, filed on a tree claim on
the northwest quarter of 24-123-76 and Julius planted the trees on both
quarters from stock shipped from Wisconsin.

        MR. AND MRS. JULIUS E. HOEFS

On June 21, 1885 he was married to Emma Zirbel at Big Stone City, South
Dakota and they came to Walworth county to build their future home. Emma
Zirbel was born in Roman, Germany, January 16, 1862. She came to America
with her parents at the age of 10 and settled near Watertown, Wisconsin. It
was here she met and became engaged to Julius before he left for Dakota
territory.

At the time of settling in Walworth county they had four horses, four cows,
two chickens, a wagon, a plow and $90.00 in cash. He had built a one room
claim shack before he was married.

They farmed until 1898 and then moved to Bangor and entered the mercantile
business with J. J. Elfrink. They dissolved partnership and moved to Selby
in August 1900 and built the store which they operated for 43 years and
which now houses the Red Owl Agency store. Both Julius and Emma Hoefs are
members of the Methodist church. He gave much time and financial support to
the Methodist church and Sunday school and found great happiness in working
and doing for the church and its organizations. He was a member of the
first school board in Bangor, was district road supervisor and district
assessor. He was also a member of the school board in Selby and served as
city treasurer for a number of years. He helped form a stockade at Bangor
during the Indian Scare and experienced the blizzard of '88, the terrific
hail storm of '85 and the severe droughts of 1911 and 1934.

Ipswich was the nearest railroad town when he came and they hauled all
their grain there and brought supplies back. He plowed with oxen. They had
no fences, and used picket pins and ropes. They pulled water out of their
well with a bucket. Eggs were 3c a dozen, butter was 10c a pound, hogs were
raised only for their own use as there was no sale for them. Wheat was 45c a
bushel delivered at Ipswich.

Julius and Emma Hoefs have two children. Their daughter, Mrs. May Magers
lives in Selby, their son, Roy now runs the Tourist Cabins in Mobridge. They
have two grandchildren and two great grandchildren. Mr. Hoefs died some
years ago but Mrs. Hoefs still resides in Selby.

Mr. Hoefs thought that life was well worth living, that mankind had a
definite purpose and destiny and was vitally interested in all things that
made for community betterment and he gave his support and financial aid
willingly to those ends.

MR. SEVERIN M. JOHNSON

Severin M. Johnson, known to his friends as "Steve" came to Selby in 1915
and barbered for Irvin Dudley in the shop known as the Sig Hoffman Shop.

Steve was born and raised on a farm near Round Lake, Minnesota. After his
father's death he operated the farm for his mother but deciding against
farming as a lifetime profession, he went to Minneapolis and took a
barber's course.

He read of the opportunities offered a little further west so answered a
newspaper ad that resulted in his coming to Selby. In 1916 he purchased
this barber business, moving his shop to the present Dettman building.

        MR. SEVERIN M. JOHNSON

In May 1918 he was inducted into the Army of World War I and was discharged
in February 1919, being stationed at Fort Lewis, Washington, all during his
service period. He rented his shop during his absence but resumed business
in Selby on completion of his military service, never regretting his move
to South Dakota.

In 1925 he moved his shop to the newly constructed Overholser building and
continued in business there until his retirement in 1949. This same year he
married a local girl, Delphia Buchanan and they have resided continuously
in Selby.

Steve has always been an ardent baseball and basketball fan. In 1927, '28
and '29 he managed a junior baseball team and again in 1949 with more time
to spare, he organized and managed a junior junior baseball team.

He has been and still is an active member of the American Legion and the
Masonic lodges from the Blue Lodge to the Shrine, served approximately
thirty years on the city fire department and was a member of the city
council for several years.

The Johnsons have no children but "Steve" believes that good clean
recreation for young people is one of the greatest assets a town can boast
of and has done all in his power to promote good sportsmanship in his
community.

MR. GEORGE H. HOFFMAN

George H. Hoffman was born in Adams county, Pennsylvania, on January 21,
1838. He came with his parents to DeKalb county, Indiana in 1844, where he
was reared to manhood on the pioneer homestead. His education was secured
principally at home under the direction of his honored father. He thus
conned his lessons by the light of the tallow candle and the blaze of
hickory bark from the great fireplace, after the days work on the farm was
done. He also attended common schools and Kells Academy, near Hunterstown,
Allen county, Indiana, so that he laid substantial foundations for the
broad fund of knowledge which he had in the practical school of experience
and active association with men and affairs. Mr. Hoffman initiated his
independent career as a farmer and carpenter in 1859, and continued to
follow these occupations.

On the 27th day of September, 1860 Mr. Hoffman was united in marriage to
Miss Sarah J. Crouse, who was born in Dayton, Ohio, in the year of 1841.
They were both Free Methodists.

In 1864, he enlisted in Company A, Thirteenth Indiana Volunteer Infantry,
which became a part of the Third Brigade, Second Division, Tenth Army
Corps, the division being commanded by General Ames, while the Corps was
commanded for a time by General Benjamin F. Butler and later by General
Terry. Mr. Hoffman was an active participant in the engagement at Chapins
Bluff, near Richmond, Virginia, and in the campaign which thereafter
extended through and including the engagements at Deep Bottom, Dutch Gap
Canal and Bermuda Hundred, and later was with the expedition which operated
against Fort Fisher, and Newbern, North Carolina. He took an active part in
the battle at Fort Fisher and Fort Caswell being evacuated upon the fall of
Fort Fisher and assisted in the capture of Fort Anderson, and Fort
Sugarloaf, Willmington, South Carolina; Mount Olive, Bentonville, Goldsboro
and Raleigh, being stationed in the last mentioned city at the time of
surrender of Johnstons Army. He was mustered out of the service at
Goldsboro, North Carolina, on September 5, 1865, and received his honorable
discharge, in the city of Indianapolis, Indiana about two weeks later.

After the close of his faithful and valiant service as a soldier of the
Republic Mr. Hoffman returned to DeKalb county, Indiana, where he effected
the purchase of the old homestead farm upon which his father had originally
located and upon which he himself had been reared to manhood. Four years
later he disposed of the farm and moved to Auburn, Indiana where he engaged
in the handling of agriculture implements, building up an excellent
business and continuing operations in the line for a period of seven years.

        MR. AND MRS. GEORGE H. HOFFMAN

In September, 1883 he came to what is now the state of South Dakota, and
with his two oldest sons, William and Siegel, took up government land in
Walworth county, and here they improved a valuable estate. When South
Dakota was admitted to the Union in 1889, Mr. Hoffman was nominated by the
republicans of the thirty-sixth senatorial district, composed of the
counties of Walworth and Campbell, to represent the district in the upper
house of the first general assembly of the new commonwealth. He was
victorious at the polls and proved a valuable and popular member of the
legislature, whose work was exacting, onerous and important in the
formative period, when much was to be accomplished and planned for the
well-being of the state. At the state republican convention held in
Mitchell in 1890, Mr. Hoffman was made nominee of his party for the office
of lieutenant governor, being elected to this office and serving one term.
In 1892 he was a candidate for governor and in the state convention of his
party, at Madison, received the second highest vote of the convention on
the ballot, being beaten by one vote for the governorship. Mr. Hoffman cast
his first presidential vote for Abraham Lincoln, in 1860 and had ever since
given an unfaltering allegiance to the republican party. He was a member of
the Grand Army of the Republic, also a charter member of John Mangan Post
No. 150, and its first commander.

He was appointed by the governor to serve on the board of the Soldiers Home
at Hot Springs.

During all his political and business career he was always interested in
farming and ranching with his sons. Without a railroad close by they went
through a lot of hardships in marketing their products, which in the
earlier years, was all by ox team, their closest town being Bowdle, and
they also did some of their hauling to and from Gettysburg, South Dakota.
In the early days he operated an implement shop at Bangor, and also a
newspaper called the Rising Sun, the first issue being printed August 8,
1901. In the spring of 1903, he sold the paper to George P. Vick and Carl
F. Clement of Java, who rechristened it the Java Herald, the first issue of
which appeared September 10, 1903. After selling the Bangor paper he went
to Lowry and started an implement business. On January 23, 1908 he started
the Lowry Dispatch, and in 1910 sold ii to Stanley Thomas, then retiring
from business activities.

There were eleven children born to Mr. and Mrs. Hoffman, five of them still
living: Ed and Ben Hoffman and (Mabel), Mrs. Henry Moos, all of Selby;
(Laura), Mrs. C. T. Smithers of Albany, California; (Jessie), Mrs. Denslay
Carman of Glenham.

Mrs. Hoffman died in 1910, and Mr. Hoffman in 1922. Two sons preceded them
in death, George and John. Will died in a Bismarck hospital, interment was
made in the Bangor cemetery. Siegel and Charles died in California and were
laid to rest there. Clara, Mrs. Clarence Clark, died at her daughter's home
in Hayti and was laid to rest by the side of her husband in the Selby
cemetery.

B. P. HOLTER AND FAMILY

B. P. Holter came to Selby in 1908 and went to work in the Schwartz
Hardware and Harness shop as a harness maker and shoe repair man. In the
summer of 1909 he went to Sherburn, Minnesota and returned with his family
consisting of his wife and five daughters, Marie, Agnes, Dorothea, Emma and
Besse. He worked for the Schwartz Hardware until about 1911, when he rented
the building now occupied by Rose E. McIntosh's store, and started up in
business for himself. From a small beginning his business of harness and
shoe repairing grew to be a large and profitable business. He carried a
full line of harness goods, men's footwear and also sold gasoline and oil.

In 1917 he purchased the building he was occupying from the Hamm Brewing
Co. and the family moved up stairs where they resided until the death of
Mrs. Holter in 1933. Mr. Holter was industrious and a very good workman and
managed his business successfully until his death in 1922.

Mr. Holter was born in Norway in 1860 and at the age of 19 came to America
and settled in Faribault county in southern Minnesota. He was married to
Anna Hagen who was also a native of Norway. The home was established in
Delavan, Minnesota, where they lived until 1900, and then they moved to
Sherburn where he ran a harness shop until the time when they moved to South
Dakota. Mr. Holter made a trip to Norway, his native land in the spring of
1921. It is significant to note in the comments which he made on his trip
that his most frequent remark was of the thrill he received when he caught
his first glimpse of the Statue of Liberty on entering New York harbor and
how glad he was to set foot on American soil again.

The daughters all attended Selby high school and later taught school.
Marie, who is now Mrs. George Fritz of Morristown, South Dakota taught
school in the Selby public schools for several years. Besse also taught in
Selby and is now a home demonstration agent in Deuel county and lives at
Clear Lake, South Dakota. Agnes was married to Paul Dettman and has served
as county treasurer of Walworth county for two terms. She is serving as
deputy treasurer at this time under Rose Schmidt, the present treasurer.
Dorothea was married to George Smith, now deceased, and still lives on the
Smith farm, just west of Selby. Emma was married to James Hicks of
Hettinger, North Dakota and lives on a farm near that city.

        MR. AND MRS. B. P. HOLTER AND THREE DAUGHTERS,
        JOSEPHINE, MARIE AND AGNES

Thus the Holter family, residents of Selby in the earlier years, played
their part in the affairs and up building of the Selby community.

MAJOR JAMES R. HOWELL

James Robinson Howell was born in Goshen, Indiana, June 7, 1844, a son of
pioneers of Indiana of Welsh and Scotch-Irish descent. He was educated in
the public schools of Goshen and Marsh Military academy, which he left at
the outbreak of the Civil War to enlist in the army. He joined a company of
cavalry in Goshen, which was immediately attached to a regiment of Indiana
Volunteers. This regiment was engaged in some of the heaviest battles of
what was called in the Civil War "The West"--and suffered tremendous losses
in men and officers. Due to that fact and also to his military training
young James Howell received rapid promotion. At the end of the war in 1865,
though barely twenty-one he held the rank of Major. He remained in the army
until 1881-82 and during that period received a colonelcy,--he was known
later and throughout his life as Major Howell. After the Civil War in 1866
he was sent to Fort Laramie in Wyoming where he established a government
telegraph station--those were the days of the pony express, the stage
coach, and also a period of trouble with the Oglala Sioux. There rose at
that time differences of opinion in regard to management of the Indians,
between the military and the Civil Indian department. The Indian department
no doubt held the view that the Indians would be more amenable to authority
vested in the civil rather than the military,--an idea that soon proved
erroneous. Small bands of roaming young Oglalas harried the settlers,
attacked the wagon trains, cut telegraph wires and burned poles. Some of
the incidents were merely petty and irritating, others were tragic. Excerpts
from Major Howell's diary of that period read, June 18, (no year): "Scouts
brought in Mrs. Lewis and children, Lewis and son, John killed in
field--Mrs. Lewis scalped--Scouts report Indians routed without
difficulty.--No doubt small band.--it is feared Mrs. Lewis will not
survive." August 5: "Wires cut again or torn down--no signs of Indians this
morning.--will send out scouts."-Sept. 11: "Martens (evidently stage
driver) wounded in jaw--not serious--passengers badly shaken up and
frightened--no Indians sighted--."

In 1868 Major Howell was transferred to New Orleans, Louisiana, in charge
of Army ordnance and supplies. In 1869 in South Dartmouth, Massachusetts,
he married Eleanor Frances Smith born August 17, 1845 in South Dartmouth.
She was of New England pre-revolutionary stock of English and Holland-Dutch
descent.

Major Howell took his bride by boat to New Orleans and they established
their home there during a period most difficult for any northerner, that of
the reconstruction of the south following the Civil War. Never-the-less the
Howells spent many happy years in that city. There eight of their ten
children were born. They adopted three children, the son and two daughters
of close friends, orphaned by the yellow fever epidemic: Edward, Alice and
Kathryn Hanlon.

Major Howell sent his own family out of the city during the epidemic so
that they escaped the scourge that so often wiped out entire families. He
himself contracted the fever in a light form so that he recovered but his
health was seriously affected.

Eventually the doctors advised that if he was to regain his health at all
he must try a drier climate and higher altitude. Hearing glowing accounts
of the climate and beautiful country of southern Oregon, Major Howell
decided to make the long trip out to Oregon, to inspect the country.
Resigning from the Army with regret, he accepted a last commission,--to
establish a government telegraph station at LeBeau in Dakota territory.
Traveling by boat up the Mississippi and Missouri rivers he landed at
LeBeau in the late spring of 1881. The severity of the winter and deep
snows of 1880-81 had created a belated spring. Buffalo grass, lush and
green, starred with countless wild flowers, covered the rolling prairie
surface, a dozen shades of green marked draws, ravines and river bottom
where choke cherry, wild plum, cottonwood, ash, boxelder and buffalo brush
grew in profusion. Major Howell wrote to his wife: "This country is strange
but most interesting. The plains are covered with grass like a mat, waist
deep in the draws and along the river bottom. There are many wild flowers
and birds. Quantities of game along the river bottom, deer and birds."--And
again: "Drove with Peter Couchman north to territories known as Blue
Blanket and Hidden Wood (Indian names). Government land for living is open
in this locality. They tell me that this soil is ideal for the growth of
many crops, especially wheat. Peter and I carried our canteens and
provender. Peter shot two birds, he calls 'chickens'. Very much like our
Indiana grouse. Like true campaigners we rolled them in mud and roasted
them in the coals of a campfire. Do not wrinkle your nose at me, my dear,
they were delicious! In fact I find my appetite so improved that I am
gaining weight. I feel amazingly well, the cough has disappeared entirely.
I shall never be such a man of substance as Peter, he must weigh over three
hundred pounds. We must present a remarkable appearance. Your fears of the
Indians are entirely ungrounded. They are very friendly. They have buffalo
skins cured into robes which they sell for from 50 cents to a dollar. They
have, I must confess, a peculiar odor but are very warm. These early
September days are warm, but the nights are chilly. I like this country,
my dear, I think that you would find it very similar to your native New
England. But I hope to rejoin you soon and we can then discuss this matter
more satisfactorily."

Major Howell returned to his family in New Orleans by the last boat down
the river in the fall of 1881.

His wife, delighted and amazed at his almost miraculous return to health
declared: "Any country that could do that for you, is the place for us to
live." The Oregon project was abandoned. Early as the boats ran in the
spring of 1882, Major Howell returned to Dakota territory to file on land
in the Blue Blanket area. Filing with him in a section were Peter Couchman,
a Mr. Sproul and Mr. Parker. They built their first house, a shell of four
rooms, on the exact center of the section, so that each lived on his own
quarter. In the meantime to Mrs. Howell was left the arduous task of
selling their property in New Orleans, packing and buying supplies for
their residence in Dakota territory. Major Howell wrote to his wife: "Pack
and ship only the essentials, our living quarters must Or a necessity be
very limited." Mrs. Howell's idea of essentials of that time must have
created a great deal of amusement among the early settlers of Dakota. They
included a grand piano and an organ, mahogany clothes presses from each
bedroom and a huge and wonderful contraption made of iron and called a
"sitzbath." Two emigrant cars were crammed to overflowing with furniture
and supplies, for the idea of river travel was abandoned for the more
convenient and faster railroad.

The family at that time consisted of Major and Mrs. Howell, their children:
Eleanor, Lucy, Charles, Alice, Annie, Golda and Josie, and their adopted
children, Edward, Alice and Katie. Also included were Major Howell's great
Aunt Mrs. Davis, Mrs. Howell's sister, Miss Lou Smith, and in addition two
elderly colored women, one a nurse of all the Howell children and the other
a cook, ex-slaves whose own "white folks" had perished during a yellow
fever epidemic and who had with the characteristic devotion of their race
attached themselves to the Howell's. Unfortunately they were utterly
terrified in the new and alien country and Major and Mrs. Howell found
employment for them among friends in New Orleans and sent them home the
first fall of their stay in Dakota territory.

Major Howell, after spending the winter in New Orleans and Goshen, Indiana,
returned to Dakota in the spring of 1884 and the family followed by railroad
in May. Ipswich was at that time the end of the Milwaukee line. From there
the family came over land by wagon and buggy to Blue Blanket, where their
furniture and supplies had been freighted the previous month.

Mrs. Howell must have been a woman of indomitable will and courage. Leaving
a home of fifteen rooms not including servants quarters in New Orleans, in
Dakota territory she found a house of four completed rooms with four rooms
in the second story under construction. A dugout most inadequately housed
the furniture the house could not hold. The precious "sitzbath" sat out in
a slough and remained there.

        MAJOR AND MRS. JAMES R. HOWELL

The first fall the problem of a school arose. Mrs. Howell and her sister,
Lou Smith, both graduates of Mount Holyoke college in Massachusetts,
organized a school for their own children and invited any neighbors who
wished to send their children.

The land immediately surrounding the Howells' was settled mainly by
Scandinavians. Many of the children walked miles to attend school in the
Howell home. Due to the fact that the Howell ladies spoke no Norwegian and
most of the children spoke no English, amusing incidents arose. The same
fall, Blue Blanket post office was established in the Howell home. A church
service was held every Sunday at the Howells'. It made no difference what
the denomination, any minister was welcomed. Neighbors came from far and
near. Some times in the event that the minister was delayed due to weather
conditions or other reasons, Mrs. Howell held a lay service by reading
chapters from the Bible and prayer book. The fact that the people attending
the services spoke different languages had no bearing on the sincerity of
the services or perhaps intensified their solemnity. The years 1884 85 were
boom years. Many settlers came to Blue Blanket and the surrounding country.
A roster of those early names reads like a cross section of the melting pot
that is America: Larson, Thorstensen, Olson, Odland, Hoveland, Lee,
Tisdall, Clark, Mudge, Newell, Orr, Nesbitt, Couchman, deMalignon, Sawinsky,
Hanrahan, McCaslin, Schellinger, Elfrink, Webb, Brown, Murray, Kirkhoven,
Kingman, Burr, Foster, Grady, Peck, Hoven, Marin, Schmidt, Griffin,
Stewart, Jacobson, Buchanan, McCoy, Craft. Those were all names known in
the '80's and there were many others. Those are only names gathered at
random not for any reason except to stress the different nationalities
represented.

During those prosperous years of 1884-'85 friendships were instituted which
the hardships of the years of 1886-'87 cemented firmly. Through these years
Major and Mrs. Howell moved serenely on with the joys and sorrows of their
friends and the community. The irrepressible young Howells organized a glee
club and literary society. True Welshmen from Aunt Adeline of 80-odd to
baby Josie, they all sang. Aunt Adeline's voice was still clear and true.
The girls had glorious voices.

The huge supply of drugs and medical supplies brought by Mrs. Howell was an
asset during those years. Doctors were at a distance. Rough surgery was
often performed in the Howell kitchen, bones set, a crushed foot amputated.
Major Howell himself pulled countless aching teeth with a set of dentists
forceps sent by a friend in Indiana. In response to letters from Mrs.
Howell to friends in the east and south, many barrels and boxes came filled
with clothing, and supplies. Finally 1890 and good crops again, but in the
fall a great uneasiness grew in this section due to reports that the
Indians were making war medicine and dancing the war dance. Sitting Bull
and the Hunkpapa Sioux were fomenting trouble. On a midnight in November
hoofbeats pounded on the frozen ground, fists beat at the door and a hoarse
voice cried, "Go to Bowdle the Indians are uprising. The Indians are
coming!" The four adult members of the family, white-faced took grave
consultation, "What do you think my dear?" Major Howell's unfailing query to
his wife in any crisis. "I think," said Mrs. Howell sturdily, "that the
Nesbitt boys on the river, would have been here to let us know if anything
of the sort were true, they are friendly with Mad Bear, and his camp is
across the river from them". In both their minds rose the vision of their
one team and spring wagon for conveyance. Twelve children and four adults,
one an aged woman. The bitter November weather. All through the rest of
that night and the following day panic stricken settlers streamed by or
stopped at the Howell homestead to be reassured and remain. Fifty or more
people were gathered at the Howell home the following day and night. But
before nightfall of that day, young Bill Nesbitt rode up from the river
with the comforting word that the Indians were not on the war path. Direct
from Mad Bear's camp came the assurance in Maggie Mad Bear's flowery, if
faulty English, that the majority of the Hunkpapas wished friendship and
peace with the white people, that only Sitting Bull and his mad young men
were responsible for the war dances. Unfortunately that word could not
reach many of the panic stricken settlers. The midnight rider had done his
work only too well. During that week they gathered in Bowdle, on foot with
bundles on their backs, in every means of conveyance available. Stores,
churches, saloons, homes, were filled with frantic settlers. On the other
hand some settlers in inaccessible sections never even knew there was a
panic, and continued the even tenor of their lives without a qualm. Some
left their homes never to return.

Major Howell served as justice of the peace for many years. Disagreements
were settled, citizenship papers soberly explained, homesteads proved under
his friendly guidance. Many of the problems brought to him were outside his
jurisdiction. He was deeply interested in young people, organizing the
first public school in the district, helping to organize the county and
working earnestly to promote statehood for young South Dakota. Though not
particularly active in politics he was a life long republican, serving
several terms as senator at Pierre. He was a member of the Episcopal
church, a Mason, a charter member of the Masonic lodge at Selby and one of
its first masters. He was a member of the G.A.R.

Two children, James Chester and George McCoy were born to the Howells
after they came to Blue Blanket. One daughter, Mary died in infancy and
during the epidemic of typhoid in 1895 they lost their youngest daughter,
Josie. Four sons and seven daughters including their adopted children grew
to young manhood and womanhood in Blue Blanket.

Major Howell's great aunt, Mrs. Davis, who made her home with them, lived
to be 98 years old. Of some interest is the fact that according to the
records she filed on a homestead in 1894, being at that time 94 years of
age as she was born in the year 1800. She had a most excellent memory
recalling vividly the war of 1812 in which her father and older brothers
fought. She always referred to her husband as "Mr. Davis," and was a little
shocked that Mrs. Howell boldly called her husband "Jim." Mr. Davis was an
uncle of Jefferson Davis, president of the Southern Confederacy,--dismissed
with a sniff by Aunt Adeline as, "That scamp Jefferson!" She pioneered in
three states, New York, Indiana and South Dakota, and lived to see her
country involved in four wars, in each of which sons of her family fought.

In 1905 Major and Mrs. Howell and daughters moved to a ranch in McLean
county, North Dakota where they joined Charles Howell who had been
operating the ranch for a year. There Mrs. Howell died in 1911. Mr. Howell
died in 1917 shortly after the outbreak of the first World War. He and Mrs.
Howell are buried at McClusky, North

EDWARD C. INGALLS FAMILY

Edward C. Ingalls was born in Vermont, December 19, 1843. He was a Civil
War veteran. After the war he came to Minnesota where he settled in
Faribault county.

In December 1879 he was married to Emmie Louisa Stockman (she was born in
Wisconsin). They lived on a farm and raised a family of five children:
Edward R., born January 19, 1881; Clare Vern born January 27, 1883, passed
away several years ago; Bessie Marion born June 3, 1885, married to N. B.
Smith and lives at Lodge pole, South Dakota; Earl S., born April 25, 1887,
passed away a few years ago; Zane E., born 1889, passed away many years ago.

In 1900 they heard of the wonderful opportunities in South Dakota and
decided to move out here. They came and bought the present Ted Tisdall
farm. Their life in South Dakota was short however as Mrs. Ingalls passed
away in 1902 of a heart ailment. Mr. Ingalls sold the farm and returned to
Minnesota where he resided until his death several years ago.

The eldest son, Edward R. Ingalls, better known as "Ned" is the only
remaining one of the family left in South Dakota, and this has been his
home since 1900.

        MR. AND MRS. N. R. INGALLS

He had attended the country schools in Faribault county and in Elmore,
Minnesota. He was baptized in the Presbyterian church. His boyhood was
spent in Minnesota where he learned to love swimming, fishing, and hunting.
The year previous to moving with his parents to South Dakota he had spent
on the west coast, where he worked part of the time on a fishing vessel.

When he came out with his parents in 1900 he bought a relinquishment and
filed on a homestead, the quarter west of the present Jake Tisdall farm.

On December 10, 1902 he was married to Anna, the third daughter of Mr. and
Mrs. Christian Chesky. She was born December 24, 187S at Berlin, Wisconsin.
In the spring of 1884 when she was eight years old, she came with her
parents to Walworth county to settle on the land her father had filed on
the fall before. The journey from Wisconsin, the new home on the prairie
the strangeness and wildness of this new land was all very exciting to the
little girl. Even the small children of those early pioneer families had
many duties such as gathering fuel, dropping seeds, stripping feathers,
helping to make candles, etc. Anna did her share of such things. Also it
was her lot to sleep with her grandmother in her small claim shack on the
land which she Mrs. Priske, the grandmother, was filing. One night during a
wind storm the roof of the filing shack was blown completely off. Anna and
her grandmother awoke to see the sky overhead.

Anna didn't care for sewing or patchwork, but she did love to read. Many a
scolding did she get for reading the newspaper that was pinned on the wall
behind the kitchen table, while she was doing dishes. Anything she could
get to read she read. Good books were always one of her prized possessions.

After Anna finished what education she could get in Walworth county she
attended Dakota Wesleyan college at Mitchell. Upon the completion of her
work in that institution, she began her teaching career in Walworth county.
Teaching in those days was no easy task. There were few books, little
equipment, and the buildings were very poor. The pupils were of almost any
age. Sometimes a teacher found herself with a pupil older than herself. In
those days the school terms were only several months in the spring and
several in the fall. She had many exciting and even frightening
experiences. Her teaching career lasted practically throughout her life as
she taught many years--even after her family was partly grown. She taught
in the rural schools of Walworth county and also in the city school in
Selby. When she wasn't teaching she was always helping someone with their
studies. Someone once said a real teacher is some one who can tell a child
something over and over again--and then over and over again without losing
patience. Anna was a natural born teacher, one of the finest the county has
had. She was one who not only taught blindly from books, but always
combined good common sense with her teaching. She also did considerable
work with oil paints and won many blue ribbons at county fairs.

After their marriage in 1902 Mr. and Mrs. Ingalls spent the first winter on
his father's farm. The next spring Ned traded his homestead in on a ranch
near Lowry--the present Clarence Anderson home. They lived there for many
years and encountered many of the hardships of those times. The only mode
of travel was, of course, with horses, and the closest railroad was Selby.

In 1911 they moved to Selby where Ned was a cattle buyer for a number of
years. In 1918 they moved on a farm near Selby where they lived until 1939
when they again moved into Selby. While living in town Mrs. Ingalls was
active in many organizations, always ready and willing to help in any way
she could. She was a charter member of the Selby Woman's club, and its
president in 1914. She was a member of the Order of the Eastern Star
serving as Worthy Matron in 1939 and as secretary in i943 44. She was a
member of the Library board. She attended the Methodist church and helped
with the Sunday school work for many years. Her ability to understand
people made her a wonderful mother and wife, and a wonderful friend to many.

Mr. and Mrs. Ingalls had a family of five children and have eleven
grandchildren. Donald, born April 18, 1904, is married and lives at Palmer,
Alaska. He has three sons. He taught school in Walworth county and other
counties in South Dakota as well as in Alaska. He is now employed by the
highway department at Palmer.

Ruth, born February 1906 and died in 1911.

Emma, born December 24, 1908. She is married to Kenneth Henderson and lives
near Lodgepole, South Dakota. They have two sons and two daughters. Emma
taught school in Perkins county prior to her marriage.

Lois, born May 28, 1910. She married Bernel Manke and they operate the Red
Owl Agency in Selby. They have three daughters and one son. Lois taught in
the rural schools of Walworth and Campbell counties prior to her marriage.

Howard Ingalls born October 14, 1912. He is married and is in the Air
Transport business between San Francisco and Siam. He lives in California.
He was in the Air Transport Command during World War II.

On January 27, 1945, after an illness of a few months, Mrs. Ingalls passed
away, and the Selby community lost another of its early pioneers as well as
one of its most honored, beloved, and useful citizens.

Mr. Ingalls is residing in Selby at the present time.

MR. AND MRS. OLIVER JOHNSON

Selby's Golden Jubilee book would not be complete without the name of
Oliver Johnson, who was one of the earliest citizens of the Blue Blanket
district. Oliver Johnson was born in La Crosse, Wisconsin, August 31, 1861.
His father was killed in the Civil War. In 1866 his mother married Johannes
Tisdall, and the family moved to Iowa where he grew to manhood with his
half brothers and sisters. On May 22, 1884 he married Amelia Belle Potter
at Atlantic, Iowa. This was indeed a union of pioneer stock. She had been
born in Indiana, March 30, 1870, and had come with her family to Cass
county, Iowa in 1880.

MR. AND MRS. OLIVER JOHNSON

The United States government that year, 1884, was putting on an intensive
campaign to get Dakota territory, which had been organized as a territory
in 1861, settled. This opportunity appealed to Oliver Johnson, so, leaving
his bride of a few months with his mother, he set off for Dakota. With him
were his two cousins, Sam Sampson and Sam Hanson. Arriving at the end of
the Milwaukee railroad at Ipswich, Dakota he had no way of going further
west whither he was bound. Ever alert to possibilities he recognized the
need of transportation facilities. He hustled around and by a little work
and keen trading got possession of a team of horses and a lumber wagon.
Immediately he set himself up in business. Boards across the front part of
the wagon made seats for passengers, while the back part carried the
supplies. He has often told the tale, that he drove the first team of horses
and wagon into Walworth county. He spent that summer and fall locating
emigrants on homesteads, and hauling supplies and freight from the railroad.

The country fascinated him. As he drove about he saw the possibilities, so
in that year, 1884, he filed on a tree claim and a preemption in Campbell
county, and a little later took up a homestead in Walworth county. In time
he sold the preemption and bought a half section in Walworth county, buying
also, the intervening quarter of land between the tree claim and the
homestead from a Mr. Fulsom. His land holdings now consisted of a section
of land in Walworth county joining the original tree claim.

With a little nest egg accumulated in the summer and fall of 1884, he
returned to Iowa. He took with him glowing reports of wonderful Sunny
Dakota and the great future in store for anyone willing to take the chance.
In the spring of 1885, he returned to Dakota bringing not only his wife and
baby son, John, born March 13, 1885, but also his stepfather, whom he had
enticed to go back with him. Later Mr. Tisdall took up land near Selby. He
brought out from Iowa many useful supplies, consisting of seed grain,
cattle, chickens, a few pigs and household effects bought with the money
earned in the territory.

Oliver Johnson had built a one room shack on his land and it was here he
brought his little family, 65 miles from the nearest railroad. One could
listen to him for hours telling of the almost unbelievable hardships
endured in those early years. There were continued rumors of Indian
uprisings west of the river, so he kept his shotgun hanging on nails on the
side wall by their bunk beds. He said that the Indians that crossed the
river were usually friendly to the homesteaders. He often laughed at his
precaution, for a few times they found traces of Indians who had slept on
the floor near the stove, but had come in so quietly they did not hear them
and who had left before they awoke. One morning he awoke at daybreak to see
an Indian buck and his two squaws slipping out the door. Only in 1890 at
the last unrest stirred up by Sitting Bull, chief of the Sioux tribe, did
they make arrangements to leave. His little family now consisted of wife
and four boys, John, Will, Clarence and George. He kept a wagon loaded with
supplies ready to leave at a moment's notice, so if the Scouts sent word
that the Indians had crossed the river, off they would go to Ipswich.
Before this happened word came through that Sitting Bull had been killed by
native police while resisting arrest. So all became serene again.

Not only was there the constant menace of Indians, but the hard winters
brought their difficulties. One time they were out of flour and it was
impossible to get through the snow to Ipswich to get some. The ever
resourceful pioneer wife went to the wheat bin and ground the wheat in the
coffee grinder, so they had whole wheat biscuits until it was possible to
take that long trek for needed supplies. Mrs. Johnson was not only
resourceful in cooking, but also kept her growing family in clothes, buying
denim by the bolt, and using her own patterns she made overalls and shirts.
She knitted sweaters, socks mittens and caps. Six boys came to them before
the arrival of the first little girl, Mary Jane, born March 18,1896. In
fact the family ran to boys for the complete family consisted of ten boys
and only four girls. Mrs. Johnson not only cared for her own family, but
found time to help usher into the world little ones of her friends and
neighbors and often made long trips to care for the sick and injured. She
set many broken bones with a skill that would have done credit to an expert
surgeon.

Oliver Johnson took a keen interest in school and municipal affairs. He was
among those who moved the courthouse from Bangor to Selby. He helped
organize the Blue Blanket School district and served as school clerk for 16
years. He served as county road commissioner for a couple of terms. He was
one of the instigators in building the little Blue Blanket Lutheran church,
now known as the Bethany Lutheran church. In fact there was no public
improvement but what Oliver Johnson took a prominent part. He contracted
for and built a half mile of the Milwaukee railroad grade beyond the dam
east of Sitka.

Oliver Johnson was the hub of the wheel of the Johnson family. Because of
his large family of boys to do the farming he was able to branch out to
other activities. He had one of the first horse power threshing machines
used in the county. It was a gala day when he brought home the first steam
engine outfit. Not only did he plow his own land, but he did contract work
around the community, breaking up new land and threshing grain. He also had
a well digging outfit. All of the boys were natural mechanics and were
thrilled when their father chose them to go about with the various outfits.
He had his own blacksmith shop on the farm and kept all the plow shares
sharpened and made necessary repairs on the machinery while the boys did
the work.

Pioneering was in Oliver Johnson's blood, so as Walworth county became, as
he used to say "too thickly populated," he looked for new horizons to
conquer. Glowing reports came from Saskatchewan, Canada. In the fall of
1910 he sold out in Walworth county. In 1911, leaving the two older boys,
John, who now resides on a farm near Mobridge, and Bill of Mound City, in
South Dakota, with five carloads of stock, farm equipment and household
goods, Oliver Johnson and family set out for Ogema, Saskatchewan, Canada.
Again in that northern country history repeated itself. He organized the
Albert Springs school district and was serving his fourth year on the rural
municipal council of Bengough, Saskatchewan, when a bad cold developed into
pleurisy. He took his final trip into the Unknown, February 18, 1920. His
body lies in the Blue Blanket church yard in the state of South Dakota, for
it was there where he had lived the greater part of his life.

Mrs. Johnson passed away February 4, 1945, in Ogema, Sask., Canada, where
her body rests. She left four daughters: Mrs. Will Taylor; Mrs. Kenneth
McCrea; Mrs. Ed Thompson; Mrs. Howard Thompson, and seven sons: John and
Will of South Dakota; Clarence of Oregon; George of Michigan; Alford, Dewey
and Joe of Ogema, Sask. Three sons preceded her, Jess in 1907; Albert in
1910 and Harry of Bengough, Saskatchewan in 1943. She left 63 grandchildren
and 41 great grandchildren.

Oliver Johnson was one of Nature's noblemen. Everyone who came to his home
was given such a hearty welcome that anyone who met him once, retained an
indelible memory of him that time could not erase. He was a large man
physically, weighing around 230 pounds, but he had a larger heart. His
early struggles and hardships mellowed him. He had a touch of quaint humor
and philosophy that had profited much by his experiences in life. Mrs.
Johnson bore up as bravely as he, and it was gratifying to see that he
appreciated this to the fullest extent and gave her full credit as a true
helpmate through thick and thin. It was characteristic of them both, that
in spite of all they had gone through they had not soured on life, but were
still full of good cheer and enthusiasm for their work. Such is a little
glimpse of the life history of two staunch pioneers of Walworth county.

MR. HANS LIDWIG LARSON

Hans Lidwig Larson was born at Oslo, Norway, March 19, 1887, to Gurene (nee
Himle) Larson and Hans Larson Sr. His early life was spent at Oslo. He
attended the common grade school of Norway and completed the eighth grade
in the United States.

        MR. HANS LIDWIG LARSON

When Hans was fifteen years old, on a Friday morning, September 12, 1902,
in company with an uncle, Bent Hendrickson, he climbed aboard a small ship
which took them to Hull, England on their way to the United States. In
having to cross England they encountered a storm, causing them to miss
their next ship. Due to this misfortune they had to remain in England three
days before another passenger ship left Liverpool. The next ship was one of
the large up-to-date ships of the time and the voyage to America took
approximately eight days, the ship landing at Boston, Massachusetts. From
Boston they immediately went to Dodgeville, Wisconsin, where Hans found it
necessary to find work in order to repay his uncle for his fare to the new
land. This Hans found on a farm. He remained in Wisconsin for two years.
The next four years were spent in Sibley, Iowa, and Worthington, Minnesota.
In 191)8 Hans and a friend started for Montana, stopping off at Selby to
visit a cousin, Lidwig Orbick, who was a carpenter. His cousin wanted him
to stay here and work with him, which he did. This was the beginning of the
carpenter profession for Hans. The next two years Hans and his cousin
continued to do carpenter work. In the fall of 1910 carpenter work
slackened up and Mr. Larson accepted a job as bartender for John Berens.

On September 20, 1911 Mr. Larson and Emma Neumiller were married.

Emma Neumiller was born April 13, 1894, to Mary (Munch) Neumiller and
Phillip Neumiller.

Mr. Larson became acquainted with Mrs. Larson while she was employed at the
Buchanan hotel, where Mr. Larson was rooming.

To this union three children were born: Gertrude, Mrs. Jack Vyse of
Seattle, Washington; Clarence of Vallejo, California; and George, who met
an untimely death.

Mr. Larson continued to work for John Berens until 1914 and then for George
Schaick (who leased the Berens Saloon) until 1919, when the state of South
Dakota was voted dry. Mr. Larson then returned to the carpenter work,
joining with the Mitchell boys.

In 1918 Mr. and Mrs. Larson bought property in the west side of Selby
which they still own.

Hans became manager of the Central Lumber company in 1922 where he remained
until 1925, again returning to his previous profession, where he worked
until the fall of 1942. It was at this time Mr. and Mrs. Larson moved to
the west coast. Here they remained for nearly four years, when they
returned to Selby. In 1946 Mr. and Mrs. Larson purchased and ran the DeLuxe
cafe, with the help of Mr. and Mrs. Jack Vyse, until 1947.

Mr. Larson has been active in civic affairs, being a member of the city
council for eight years, a fireman since 1910, a member of the Masonic
Lodge, where he was Master in 1929 and held the office of secretary from
1934 to 1941. Mr. Larson is a member and officeholder of the Modern Woodmen
of America.

In 1948 Mr. Larson built a fine new home in Selby where he and Mrs. Larson
reside.

MR. AREND LAKEMAN

Arend Lakeman, one of Walworth county's early pioneer settlers, was born in
Holland, November 22, 1816, the youngest of 13 children. At the age of
seven, he came to the United States with his parents and 8 brothers, three
sisters having passed away in Holland and one sister being married, did not
come. The family settled on a farm near Loup City, Nebraska.

Six years later the family moved to Walworth county, South Dakota, to join
a Holland colony which was settling in this part of the county. The father,
Dirk Lakeman Sr., homesteaded the land next west of the quarter section
where the town of Java is now located. The mother passed away in Nebraska.
The other brothers, after a few years, settled elsewhere. Arend and his
father continued to farm this land until the spring of 1900, when he formed
a partnership with his father and H. J. Cook and built a hardware store in
Java, later enlarging the store and putting in dry goods, groceries,
dishes, crockery and furniture.

On New Year's eve, 1903, he was united in marriage with Kittie E. Hall.
Three children were born to this union: the oldest daughter, Niesjie,
preceded her father in death April 22, 1913; the other two are, Emma K.
(Mrs. Ed F. Perman) of Selby, and Arend E., of Mobridge, states attorney of
Walworth county.

MR. AND MRS. AREND LAKEMAN

After a few years the father, Dirk Lakeman Sr., wishing to retire, sold his
interest in the store to his son, Arend, and H. J. Cook. A few years later
Arend, wishing to start a dairy farm, sold his interest in the store to Mr.
Cook. He bought a farm one and a half miles northeast of Java known as the
Consolver farm, and started in the dairy business raising purebred
registered Holstein cattle and operating a milk route into Java. (Milk then
sold for five cents per quart delivered at your door.) While still on the
farm, he and J. C. Schlepp decided to open a movie theater in Java. The
pictures were not talkies then. After a year or two, he bought J. C.
Schlepp's interest in the theater and operated the movie business alone,
later selling it to Fred Dufloth.

In March, 1925, he sold the farm to Jacob Helm and the family moved to
Java, purchasing the building which was formerly the Jesser mercantile
store, and opening the Java Cafe. They operated the cafe until October 14,
1937, when he and Mrs. Lakeman moved to Bassett, Nebraska, opening a cafe
there. The children, both having married, did not go. The next year in
March, 1938, they purchased the Selby Hotel in Selby from Mrs. Mary Artz,
and moved to Selby, changing the name of the hotel to the "Lakeman Hotel &
Cafe," putting in the first commercial ice cream freezer in Selby. They
operated the hotel and cafe until he passed away on September 24 1942. Mrs.
Lakeman closed the cafe, operating the hotel until February 13, 1946, when
she sold the business to Robert Hepper, who in turn sold to Wallace and Mary
Young, the present owners and operators. It is now known as the Marywall
Hotel.

MR. HENRY F. KUEHL

Henry F. Kuehl was born November 25, 1898, in Rock county, Minnesota, near
Everly, Iowa, and came with his parents to Campbell county in 1905. They
began farming on land southwest of Mound City, and later purchased a farm
in the same community, which farm they improved and made into one of the
fine farm homes of Campbell county where they raised a large family. Henry
left the parental home in 1918 and worked as a hired hand for farmers in
the vicinity of Selby in Walworth county, and liking the community
southwest of town, made up his mind to make his home there. On January 30,
1924, he was united in marriage with Clara Rossow of Mound City. They lived
on rented farms for a number of years and in 1942, Henry purchased what was
long known as the Schulte farm, southwest of Selby, from Mrs. Rossow's
parents, who had purchased it from the Schultes when they left the
community and moved to Hoven.

Mrs. Kuehl is a native of Campbell county, having been born on the Rossow
farm south of Mound City, on April 23, 1898. Her parents, Mr. and Mrs. John
Rossow, came to Campbell county many years ago, being among the early
settlers of that area. They raised a large family and three of their sons
now own fine farms in the old home community. The Kuehl's have improved
their farm and home from year to year by repairing the buildings, planting
trees and more recently have completed a new and modern farm home. They
have two sons, Norman, who married Viola Mauch and is now residing on the
farm known as the John Lapp place, which his father purchased a year ago,
and Marlo, who is at home assisting with the farm work.

MR. CLAUS KUEHL

Claus Kuehl, son of Anna and Claus Kuehl, Sr., was born November 13, 1907,
in a sod house two miles west and two miles south of Mound City, South
Dakota. In 1909 his folks sold or traded this farm for another two miles
west and four and one-half miles south of Mound City. Here Claus grew to
young manhood, attending grade school in their rural district. In September
of 1922 he was fortunate enough to be able to attend Dr. Martin Luther
college, at New Ulm, Minnesota. In the fall of 1923 Claus returned to
college, but in April, 1924, he was called home because of his father's
illness. Due to the fact the older boys had started out on their own it was
up to Claus to help his mother shoulder the responsibility of providing for
his younger brothers and sisters. Claus took over the management and work
of the farm for his folks. The father, never recovering to a great extent,
died in 1927.

In 1929 Claus started pitching ball for Selby, most of his Sundays through
the next six years being spent on the mound.

        MR. CLAUS KUEHL

In 1931 Miss Hazel Schmidt of Herreid, South Dakota, became his bride. In
the spring of 1933 Mr. and Mrs. Kuehl moved to Walworth county. Here they
remained through the dry and discouraging years until October, 1937, when
they sold out and moved to the west coast. Here Claus took a course in
diesel engineering and also metal work. In 1938 Mr. and Mrs. Kuehl, with
their small son, Claus Cameron, born October 2, 1935, and baby daughter,
Gertrude Ann, born February 2, 1938, chose to return to Selby, renting the
land known as the Jim Byrne farm. Two years later he bought this 480-acre
farm and since has bought land close by this farm, until now he owns and
farms a thousand acres, a fair sized farm. The Kuehl's have built and
placed many improvements on their farm until now it is one of Walworth
county's up to-date modern farms.

In 1947 Mr. Kuehl obtained the Minneapols-Moline machinery business in
Selby. Due to the help shortage he sold this interest to Melvin Stulken,
who took possession in December, 1948, and operates the M. & M. agency at
this time.

MR. CARL KUEHL

Carl Kuehl was born in a sod house two miles west and two miles south of
Mound City, South Dakota, to Anna and Claus Kuehl, Sr.

In 1909 the family moved to another farm two and one half miles further
south. Here Carl Kuehl attended a country school and on completing the
grades, attended Dr. Martin Luther college, at New Ulm, Minnesota.

Mr. Kuehl came from a large family of nine boys and three girls: Reinhart
of Missouri; Henry and John of Selby; August of Illinois; Ernest of Pueblo,
Colorado; Carl and Claus of Selby; Elsie of Gaylord, Minnesota, with whom
the mother resides; Anna of Brockway, Montana; Bill of Bismarck, North
Dakota; Erna of Palo Alto, California, and Herman, who died at the age of 5.

In 1923 Carl left home to start out on his own. He worked out two years and
while doing so met Mary Wandmacher of Herreid, South Dakota, who was born
at Holta, Providence, Germany.

        MR. AND MRS. CARL KUEHL

In June, 1925, they were married and came to Walworth county to live,
renting the farm known as the Hilde farm. On June 2, 1933, a night storm
completely demolished the barn and they lost all of their chickens. The
storm blew the windows out of their home, and the family found it necessary
to leave their home during the storm. They tried to get to the home of
their neighbor, George Vojta, a mile and a quarter away, by truck, only to
find part of a building had blown across the road. Mr. and Mrs. Kuehl then
decided their only alternative was to walk and carry their two small
daughters. In leaving the yard as the storm raged on, Mrs. Kuehl was quite
seriously hurt by running into the clothline wire which had been placed in
their path by the storm. After great difficulty they finally made it to
George Vojta's, where they spent the rest of the night. The next morning
Mr. Vojta took them back to their wrecked home, where windows were replaced
and the home made livable again. In the days to come things were again
replaced and repaired. The lumber that could be salvaged was used to
rebuild another barn.

After having rented this place for twenty years or until 1945 Mr. Kuehl was
able to buy this farm. Since then the Kuehls have made a great many
improvements and have added a large cement block double garage and machine
shop.

Mr. and Mrs. Carl Kuehl are the parents of two daughters: Helen, Mrs. Alton
Sulzle of Akaska, and Lorraine, Mrs. Alvin Kulm of Aberdeen.

MR. AND MRS. GEORGE KEISER

George Keiser was born of German parentage on April 2, 1878, at Roanoke,
Illinois, the son of a Civil War veteran who fought under Stonewall
Jackson. On December 18, 1897, he was married to a German French girl named
Tillie LeConte. They farmed in Jones county, Illinois, for some years and
then decided to come west along with his sister and husband, Mr. and Mrs.
Abe Switzer, arriving in Selby on March 4, 1905, and settling on the Lon
Walters farm, southeast of Selby. They later moved to the Doctor Gunderman
farm, southwest of Selby. After farming there three years, they moved with
their family to the Cartright house in Selby until their present home could
be built. George, having had training in the carpenter and mason trade,
took up this work at Selby and his handiwork can be found in many homes in
and around the Selby community.

        MR. AND MRS. GEO. KEISER

Mr. and Mrs. Keiser have five children, namely, Deedie (Mrs. Emil R.
Gruett) of Sioux City, Iowa; Frank, of Northwestern Public Service,
Aberdeen, South Dakota; Freda (Mrs. Woodmancy), a cafe owner at Peoria,
Illinois; Howard, who is with the Campbell Soup company at Sacramento,
California, and Paige, of the Vallejo Lumber company, Vallejo, California.

They have six grandchildren and two great grandchildren. They celebrated
their fifty-second wedding anniversary on December 18, 1949.

THE B. B. POTTER FAMILY

Benjamin B. Potter, pioneer of Walworth county, was born in Clarion county,
Pennsylvania, on April 26, 1846. While still a small boy, his parents moved
to Freeport, Illinois, and then a few years later to northeastern Iowa,
where he spent his boyhood and received his early education. Still lacking
a few months of attaining his 18th birthday, he enlisted in the Union Army
as a member of Company F, Ninth Iowa Volunteer Infantry, on February 27,
1864. He saw active service, part of which was with General Sherman on his
famous march to the sea. Potter was wounded in action, spent considerable
time in a government hospital and on July 18, 1865, was honorably
discharged at Louisviile, Kentucky, returning to his Iowa home where for
about the next 20 years he engaged in school teaching, farming and pharmacy.

The pioneer lure was strong in Potter and he came to Walworth county in
1883 to look over the land. He was immediately fascinated with the
beautiful country southwest of present day Selby and in 1884 made homestead
entry upon the SW 1/4 of 91-22-76, in what is now known as Surrey township.
He became a permanent resident of Walworth county in 1885 and during the
spring of that year helped assess the county, tramping over a large portion
of it on foot. During the fall of 1885 he served as a delegate to the First
Constitutional convention at Sioux Falls, at the conclusion of which he
continued to LeMars, Iowa, where he talked his future wife, Lulu Derby,
into returning to Dakota with him. At Aberdeen, he purchased a
relinquishment on the SE 1/4 of 9-122-76 for his wife for $75.00 and they
continued to Ipswich where the Potters were married in the fall of 1885.
The Potters remained on the farm until 1894 when Mr. Potter was elected
county treasurer and served two terms. The Potters retained ownership of
this farm until 1930 when, after Mr. Potter's death, it was sold to Alex
Bruckner, the present owner. Mrs. Potter died in the spring of 1925.

Following his service as a county official, Potter opened a general
merchandise store at Bangor in partner ship with W. B. Burr and John J.
Hoven. In 1900, shortly after the beginning of Selby, the store was moved
to the present location of the Berens Hotel at Selby. John J. Hoven
terminated his business association with the firm shortly after moving to
Selby but the Potter and Burr store continued until 1917 when Potter sold
his interest. Mr. Potter continued to be active in the civic, political and
social life of Selby until his death on March 6, 1930. He served as mayor
of Selby and was still acting as justice of the peace when he died.

Potter was a charter member and also the last survivor of John Mangan post,
Grand Army of the Republic, and a charter member of the Selby chapter of
the Eastern Star. He spent more than fifty years as an active Mason.
Selby's Memorial Day observances for years were the function of B. B.
Potter. Practically alone, he arranged the programs for proper observance
of the day. The Selby Union cemetery was another favorite diversion. He
spent much time and work in beautifying the cemetery by planting trees,
flowers and shrubs.

        MR. AND MRS. BENJAMIN B. POTTER

Shortly prior to his death, B. B. Potter wrote a long letter of his
experiences to Steve Rule of Shullsberg, Wisconsin, an attorney, and
comrade of his 1884 pioneer days. The letter was published following Mr.
Potter's death. We quote excerpts from this letter so characteristic of
homesteading days: "The winter of 1885 and 1886, I spent in Iowa, getting
my outfit together to farm with, which consisted of four medium sized mares
and harness, three cows, two wagons, one mower, hay rake and hay rack. * * *
John Sawinsky met me in Ipswich with a team and wagon. We hauled everything
out in three loads including some coal (as I had not got the folks used to
gathering buffalo chips yet, though they did later) and lumber to build a
barn 14x20 with shed roof. * * * The following winter was one long to be
remembered, '86 and '87. I built a sod barn that fall 24x40, made 27 trips
to the river for wood and poles to cover the barn. * * * Well, it commenced
to snow the 22nd day of November and never let up until we had about three
feet. My barn stood on an east slope. It drifted under so I had to put a
fence around on the tops of the drifts and the horses and cattle would
slide down into the barn like a boy sliding down hill. * * * Our first boy
(C. A. Potter) was born on Christmas Day. Well, Steve, I promised my Maker
many times that winter while standing at the window looking out and seeing
nothing but snow sliding--one day from NW to SE and the next day from SE to
NW--you could not even see a weed sticking up through the snow. It never
thawed a bit until the last day of February and the first day of March. As
I was going to say, I promised my Maker many times that if He would take
care of us until spring, I would get out. Feed got so scarce that a man
offered me 11 good cows for my organ that I paid $75.00 for. * * * But
spring came and the snow commenced to melt and as the snow softened our
feelings for South Dakota softened too and we stayed. * * * The first
school house on the prairie was built on the SE corner of the SE 1/4
6-122-76, on the Chesky land, fall of 1885. * * * I had intended to name
the township Lena after the first child born in the township, and the first
child away from the river,--that was the little girl born to Brownells at
Browns' Corners but they (the English) had a meeting while I was away and
named it Surrey from Surrey in England. When our girl * * * was old enough
to go to school, I set stakes with white rags tied on them from the house
* * * to the school house. There is where she started to school and had to
walk two miles. * * * 1887 was a fair year. I had a well put down and
fenced a pasture. I raised 700 bushels of wheat. 1888 was a good year. I
raised 1100 bushels of wheat. Got $1.11 a bushel. 1889--2 bushels per acre.
1890--4 bushels per acre. 1891--a fair crop but no price for anything. Sold
a fine pair of 4 year-old steers with yoke for $45.00; a pair of young
horses for $100.00. I ran in '92 for county treasurer but got beat by the
combined forces of the Democrats and Populists. '92 was a fine year but
prices were lower. '93 a fine year, '94 was a good year. '95 we had a
bumper crop. I had wheat that went 32 bushels per acre. All these years I
kept raising horses and cattle. The spring of '95 I sold a bunch of ten
heifers, nine 2-year-olds and one 3-year-old, all good grades, for $111.
Horses were better, sold a pair for $225.* * * Went into business (at
Bangor). The R. R. came out in 1900 and the town of Selby was started. We
moved the store building to Selby on trucks. The building was 50x60. Had 72
horses pulling and pushing it. * * * I guess I never mentioned the Indian
scare. Well, Steve, that and the blizzard of January 12, 1888, will never
be forgotten by the old timers. Nobody knows how the scare started. Myself
and Lieutenant Governor Hoffman called up the governor. He assured us that
he could find no cause for the excitement. When I got home, I found
everybody on the go. I expected to find my wife ready to fly with the rest
of them but she was perfectly cool and laughed about it. * * * That night
you could hear wagons going on the run all over. Well, we went to bed.
About midnight someone rapped on the door. It was one of Smith's boys. * * *
He was out of breath and scared. He could not talk but he finally told us
700 Indians had crossed the river and they were killing and burning
everything in their road. * * * What caused the most excitement in our
country, a young fellow from Bowdle had a sister teaching in the west part
of the county. He left Bowdle (while I was there) for her. I told him not
to make any fuss but just go quietly but he went through the country
shouting 'The Indians are coming!' You remember George Schellenger. Of
course you do, as he was from your part of the country. There was a lot of
old wagons and farm machinery around his place in Bangor and he pulled it
in a circle so as to make a hollow square to use as a fortification, and
the place went for years as Fort Schellenger. A family by the name of
Reeds, who lived about a mile west of our land, left a dead child in the
house. * * * Well, the next day I went up town and found all excitement.
While there the Ottmans drove in town headed for Bristol, three men and two
women. They had three good rifles. We tried to prevail on them to let the
old gentleman take the women to Bowdle. They would not do it. We wanted
them to leave their guns. No. They wanted to get the women to town, then
they would come back, but we never saw them until things had quieted down.
Well, that afternoon we sent three fellows on horseback to the river to
investigate. They found white children and Indians playing together. This
was in November and to make things worse, the country was full of hunters
shooting geese and they sometimes kept shooting nights. * * * The blizzard
of January 12, 1888, was something long to be remembered. * * * It came too
early in the day in this county to do much damage. People had not turned
out their stock yet. My wife's brother went out to do chores. A little
later I went out to milk. I got a glimpse of him going from the granary to
the barn. I yelled to him to come in. He had hard work to get to the house.
We did not get out again until about sundown. The thermometer stood at 18
degrees above zero and at sundown 18 degrees below. There was something
peculiar about the storm. It did not seem to make any difference which way
you went, it would strike you in the face and take your breath. We had a
barrel half full of ice standing about six feet from the east window and
the air was so thick you could not see it. * * *"

Clarence A. Potter, son of B. B. Potter, was born December 25, 1886, on the
old homestead. He attended the schools at Bangor and later took an advance
course at Brookings, following which he returned to Selby and began working
in the First National Bank of Selby as office boy, gradually advancing to
the position of cashier, completing almost forty years of service with the
bank at the time of his death on November 14, 1945. "Cap" Potter was active
in city and county life, holding the offices of Commercial club president
and Republican county chairman for many years. He was married to Clara
Lueck at Ripon, Wisconsin, on May 10, 1911, and Mrs. Potter still lives at
Selby. A daughter, Shirley Carney, and grandson, are now living at Lincoln,
Nebraska, where Mr. Carney is attending the University of Nebraska.

Claude Potter, second son of B. B. Potter, was born on the family farm in
Walworth county on December 4, 1890, and is presently living at Great
Falls, Montana, where he is employed by the Monarch Lumber company.

Myrtle Hess, a daughter of B. B. Potter by adoption, lives at Aberdeen,
South Dakota.

THE HANRAHAN FAMILY

The forefathers of the Hanrahan family were natives of Garry Green county,
Limerick, Ireland. Mr. and Mrs. Roger Hanrahan Sr., grew up in that
community, migrating to America with their respective families, she being
Elizabeth O'Connor. They were married at Rochester, Minnesota, and in the
early eighties moved to Ordway, South Dakota. Six of their seven children,
Joe, Pat, Roger, Mary, Kate and Elizabeth were born in Minnesota, the
youngest, John, being born at Ordway. In the year 1883, the family moved to
Walworth county settling on what was long known as the Hanrahan ranch,
later known as the Coffey ranch and still owned in part by Mrs. Clara
Coffey of Selby. The old postoffice of Smalley was located on the Smalley
homestead a short distance north of the ranch and when that settler left
the country, the postoffice was moved to the Hanrahan place and Mrs.
Hanrahan was postmistress for many years. Several members of the family
took homesteads and by this means and by purchase and rental, a large
acreage of land was acquired.

The father passed away in 1896 and the mother and children continued to
operate the ranch until her death in 1905, four of her children passing
away before her, namely, Mary, Kate, Lizzie and Joe, in turn. Of the seven
children only two married. Pat married Etta Basford who remarried after his
death in 1915 and is now Mrs. Etta Sundeen of Des Moines, Iowa. John
married Tillie Byers and they had two children, Roger and Helen. Roger
