passed away in 1939 and Helen married Eddie McCafferty and they now live in
Mobridge. They have two boys. John Hanrahan passed away in 1936 and Mrs.
Hanrahan is now a resident of Selby.

The father of Roger Hanrahan was Joe Hanrahan who also came to America and
to Walworth county, died here and is buried in the Bangor cemetery. He had
five children, Jack, Matt, Anne, Joe and Roger. Of these children, Jack and
Matt are best remembered as they resided southwest of Selby until
comparatively late years. Jack departed this life in 1929 and Matt in 1937.
One of the most beautiful monuments in the Selby cemetery marks the last
resting place of these two men. Jack homesteaded near Groton and never sold
his land; Matt homesteaded the SE 1/4 of 32-123-77, and he too kept his
land. Their father, Joe, homesteaded the NW 1/4 of 33-123-77, cornering
with Matt's land and lived with his sons until death.

They inherited his homestead and never sold any of their claims, making
their home on the land southwest of Selby practically until their deaths.
Anne married Hugh Donahue and he proved up on the quarter next north of
Matt's homestead. She never lived on the land but ran a millinery store at
Groton. They had no children. Joe married Deborah Van Riper, a half sister
of the late Mrs. G. H. Mickelson of Selby. Roger was a mounted policeman in
Ireland and also played in a bagpipe band before coming to America as
outlined in the first paragraph of this sketch. Mrs. Tillie Hanrahan has
what is left of his bagpipes. The mother of this group lost her life in a
runaway accident.

Of this large Hanrahan family group, who had so much to do with the affairs
of the early days in the section southwest of Selby, only one remains in
the Selby vicinity, Mrs. Tillie Hanrahan, who owns the land at Groton and
Selby, acquired by Matt and Jack. Her daughter, Mrs. Helen McCafferty of
Mobridge, is the only remaining blood relative of the group, she being the
granddaughter of Roger Hanrahan and a great granddaughter of Joe Hanrahan,
the original patriarch of the family in Dakota. It became the lot of Mrs.
Tillie Hanrahan to lose her husband, John, after a long illness, to be
charged with the care of the aged bachelor brothers during the last years
of their lives and through long illnesses, and to lose her only son, Roger,
after many months of suffering. Faithfully and tenderly did this noble woman
nurse and care for all. She is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. E. Byers,
who came to Walworth county and the community southwest of Selby in 1904
from Minnesota.

The Hanrahan ranch, when at its best, ran up to five hundred head of high
grade Hereford cattle, the herd improved always by the purchase of purebred
sires and a large herd of horses also headed by the best of Percheron
sires. The men were good stockmen and the ranch business added much to the
commerce of the county in the early days.

Older residents tell many stories about the almost boundless hospitality of
the occupants of the Hanrahan ranch. Neighbors and strangers were welcomed
alike, the latch string was always out to the wayfarer. Also the large
family group were almost a social center themselves and the home became a
meeting place for quite a large community. The bachelors, Matt and Jack,
were of the same disposition, friends to everyone, kind and hospitable
always and much loved by all who knew them.

MR. JACOB REPP

Jacob Repp was born in South Russia on February 2, 1868. His parents died
when he was nine years old and he grew up in the family of an older brother
with whom, and from whom, he learned the blacksmithing trade. In 1894, he
was united in marriage with Emilie Schamey who grew up in the same village.
Ten children were born to them.

In 1899 the family immigrated to America, settling on a farm south of
Roscoe, remaining three years, when they moved to Evarts where he took up
his trade of blacksmithing. When the Milwaukee crossed the Missouri river
and Evarts was moved away, he chose to go to Akaska rather than to the new
town of Mobridge. After five years at Akaska, he moved his shop and home to
Selby and followed his trade here practically until his death on February
1, 1939. The shop was located on a lot in the northeast corner of the Tony
Birkholt property. The blacksmithing outfit was sold to Anton Weisgram of
Bowdle, and a deal was made whereby Mr. Birkholt dismantled the building
and received a deed to the plot of ground as pay for his work. The lumber
was used by the purchaser at Bowdle. The Repp residence is the house
probably better known now as the Den Otter house owned and occupied by Mr.
and Mrs. Willie Bauer at present.

        JACOB REPP AT WORK IN HIS SHOP IN SELBY

Jacob Repp was a skilled workman, much interested in his trade and always
anxious to do his work well. He was a kind and provident husband and father.

Mrs. Repp passed away six months after her husband's death, and the family
was scattered, the only one of the family now living in the community being
Mrs. Elmer Swanson. The others are: Hugo Repp of Alexandria, South Dakota,
who is in the service station business; George Repp of Scranton, North
Dakota, on a farm; Edwin Repp of Minneapolis in the window and door
weather-stripping business; Mrs. Clara Smith, residing in Pennsylvania; and
Mrs. Hilda Kuhns, whose husband is employed in Aberdeen. Mrs. Ella
Schanzenbach resided in Selby until her death in 1943 and the three other
children of the family passed away in infancy or early youth.

JUDGE WALTER B. BURR

Walter Bissell Burr was born May 15, 1850, at Middletown, Indiana, one of
ten children of Chauncey H. and Jane (Williams) Burr. His parents were
natives of New York state who had moved to Indiana about the year 1828. The
family is of English descent but has been represented in America since 1631
when Benjamin Burr settled in Hartford. Connecticut. His descendants are
widely scattered over the country, Judge Burr being of the eighth
generation in descent.

Judge Burr received his education in the schools of Henry county, Indiana,
and in the year 1871 removed to Stockton, Missouri, where he was admitted
to the bar in 1874. He was successful in the practice of law and served
three terms of two years each as prosecuting attorney for Cedar county.

        JUDGE WALTER B. BURR

In April, 1883, he came to Theodore, near Swan lake in Walworth county,
soon afterward locating on a homestead just south of Bangor. He set up in
the practice of law in Bangor and served as state's attorney and as county
judge in one office or the other almost continuously over a period of
approximately thirty-five years. He was appointed justice of the peace by
the first county board of commissioners to meet in the county in 1883. With
his law practice and civic activities he was also a partner in the
merchandising firm of J. J. Hoven and company; at Bangor, which business
removed to Selby in 1900 and was operated for many years under the firm
name of Potter and Burr. In the course of time, both Mr. Burr and Mr.
Potter dropped out of the firm and it was taken over by Judge Burr's son,
Chauncey.

With the exception of Knights Templar, Judge Burr belonged to all of the
Masonic bodies that existed in South Dakota and became Grand Master of
South Dakota Masons in 1919 and was honored with the 33rd degree.

On March 31, 1879, he was united in marriage with Miss Lizzie Nippert and
to them were born three children: Bertha L., who died March 6, 1924, in
Long Beach, California; Chauncey N., who was married in 1908 to Miss Rose
Personius at Selby and now resides at Rosemead, California; and Ethel, who
died in infancy.

Mrs. Burr was prominent in the early days of Walworth county in the Bangor
and Selby communities, teaching school for many years and carrying on in all
of the worthwhile enterprises of the pioneer wives and mothers. She passed
away suddenly in 1921 while on the way to California by automobile.

Bertha Burr was a successful and well known teacher in Walworth county
schools for many years before the family removed to California. Chauncey
Burr was one of the younger of the pioneers of Selby who helped build a
flourishing little city out on the prairie in a remarkably short time.

The Burr family were prominently identified through their residences in
Bangor and Selby in all worthwhile undertakings of the new communities. The
Judge was prominent in politics as a republican and had a part in all of
the political affairs of the county until he left, and was quite
influential in state affairs.

MR. AND MRS. GEORGE FLASHMAN

George Flashman purchased the Bangor News in the year 1885, changing the
name to the Weekly Reporter, publishing it until the year 1901 when he sold
it to George H. Hoffman who changed the name to the Rising Sun. Mr. Hoffman
later sold the plant to George P. Vick and Carl F. Clement who moved it to
Java and started the Java Herald which has served the people of that
community to the present day. Flashman worked on the Bowdle Pioneer for
awhile after selling out.

Mrs. Flashman was Emma Smithers. This family came to Walworth county
directly from England and homesteaded on land east of old Bangor and
southeast of where Selby now stands. They knew nothing of farming, so it
was quite an experience for them to settle in the new country and on the
new land. They were a large family and the home was a popular gathering
place for the young people for miles around. Mrs. Flashman now resides in
Alameda, California, and the two children also live there.

MR. HENRY CARMAN

Henry Carman was born in Canada on July 11, 1824. At about twelve years of
age, he moved with his parents to near Rockford, Illinois, where he spent
the balance of his boyhood days. In the year 1846 he took a squatters claim
in Iowa near what is now Strawberry Point, and was one of those who named
that town. In the fall of 1847 he caught the "gold fever" and sold his
claim for $800 and started for the gold fields of California by the
southern route. After going through a siege of yellow fever, he took the
Fremont trail, reaching the gold coast in the spring of 1849, barefoot and
without money. As soon as he was able he went into the mines where he made
money quite easily for a while. After eight years he returned to Illinois
to visit his parents and became acquainted with Miss Alice Holcom and in
January, 1857, they were married and soon afterwards moved to Floyd county,
Iowa, where they lived for about thirty years. Mr. and Mrs. Carman were
blessed with eight children: Roman; Marcellus, who lives in Hillsboro,
Oregon; Silas; Alice Belle; Sada, who was Mrs. Frank Skinner; Nella May,
who was Mrs. George Skinner; Denslay, whose widow is Mrs. Jessie Carman and
who lives six miles north and five miles west of Selby at the present time;
and Charles.

        MR. AND MRS. HENRY CARMAN

In the spring of 1886, Mr. and Mrs. Carman followed their three eldest sons
to Walworth county, South Dakota, where he homesteaded the NW 1/4 of
section 6-124-77. They lived in Walworth county until they built a new
frame house just across the road from the claim in Campbell county and here
they resided until the time of his death, which occurred in 1905. Charles
Carman took over the farm and resided on it and continued to improve it
until his death in 1936. A short time afterward, the Charles Carman family
moved to Seattle, Washington, where they now reside. However, they still
own the farm and maintain it in such a manner that it is a credit to the
community.

Henry Carman and wife were truly pioneers of four states. In Illinois in
the 1840's, which at that time was a long distance to the west, in the
western half of Iowa which was almost a wilderness in 1846, and the Fremont
trail and California were rough and wild in '49 and starting in Walworth
county in 1886 was surely pioneering.

MRS. NAN VELEY

Mrs. J. C. Veley was one of Walworth county's pioneer school teachers, her
career starting in the state of Indiana and covering a period of forty
years in the profession. She was born at Butler, Indiana, on November 22,
1844, and was reared, received her education, taught school and was married
in that locality. In 1891 she came to Walworth county to make her home with
her daughter, Mrs. W. E. Hoffman. Mrs. Hoffman passed away the next year
and Mrs. Veley kept house for her son-in-law until he married again, his
second wife, the late Sada Hoffman, being a cousin of his former wife and a
niece of Mrs. Veley.

          MRS. NAN VELEY

Her work in Walworth county was in the Surrey, Bangor, Spring Valley and
other districts and continued until the year 1911 when she retired and made
her home with the Hoffmans until her death which occurred in 1923 at the
age of 79 years.

Many residents of Walworth county during the first decade of the century
received their early educational training from her. She was a kindly woman,
highly respected by all who knew her and is remembered as one of their
"best" teachers by those who were privileged to attend the schools she
taught or to know her as the "teacher" outside of school.

MR. CONRAD MILLER

Conrad Miller, son of Louisa nee Zeller Miller and Christ Miller, was born
September 27, 1888, at Coglack, Rumania.

He came to the United States at the age of fourteen years, with his parents
and brother, Christ. Coming west to the end of the railroad, which was at
Eureka, they went by wagon to Mound City where they stayed with a sister,
Mrs. Fred Steiger and husband from December 15, 1902, until spring when
they rented and moved on to the John Franks farm, three miles north of
Selby. Here the family remained for two years, before moving to the Colman
Wagner farm (known as the Henry Scherer farm now). In 1906 the family sold
out and moved to Texas.

        MR. AND MRS. CONRAD MILLER

On August 30, 1909, Conrad Miller was married to Rosie Diegel at Archer
City, Texas. Mrs. Miller was born at Eureka, South Dakota, January 20, 1892.

Mr. and Mrs. Miller remained in Texas until the fall of 1910, when they
came to Tolstoy, South Dakota, where they spent part of that winter. On
February 28, 1911, they moved to Harding county; here they filed on a
160-acre homestead. Harding county didn't have much in store for the
Millers, but severe hardships. A young married couple just starting out,
they had seven miles to walk to the closest country store. A hail storm
took their crops for four straight years. During this time they picked
bones in the summer and sold them for $12.00 a ton. With this money they
bought the winter supply of flour.

Having become a bit discouraged with Harding county, they sold their
homestead in the fall of 1914, for $600 and returned to Selby. Here they
rented what is now the Art Zabel farm from Lewis Hime.

In the spring of 1918, when having overcome the hardships, difficulties and
drawbacks encountered a few years previous, Mr. Miller bought the
Breidenbach homestead of 320 acres, which was their home until 1943. During
this time Mr. Miller served for a number of years on the rural school board
of his district. He also served on the Congregational church board and as a
Sunday School teacher.

Mr. and Mrs. Miller were the parents of eight children: Fred of Selby;
Robert of Longview, Washington; Louise, Mrs. A. R. Josephs of Elizabeth,
New Jersey; Reinhold (Sam) of Barnard, South Dakota; Ida, Mrs. R. J. Nelson
of Rosalia, Washington; Herman and Ruth, deceased; and Elmer of Selby.

In 1942 Mr. Miller met with a serious accident, becoming entangled in a
power takeoff which forced him to quit farming.

In the spring of 1943 Mr. and Mrs. Miller bought a home and moved into
Selby. Since then he has been doing odd jobs and carpenter work in and
around Selby.

MR. CHRIST MILLER

One of the men to see Selby in its earlier years was Christ Miller, who was
born in Coglack, Rumania, on December 25, 1884, to Louisa nee Zeller,
Miller and Christ Miller Sr. At the age of six years he started school, his
father being his first teacher, he having been a public school teacher in
Rumania. The custom in Rumania was to study in German from the ages of 6 to
8 years, then change to the study in the Rumanian language from 8 to 12
years, going back to German one half day each week. Christ remained at home
and helped with the work. At the age of 19, in the year 1902, Christ came
with his father, mother and brother, Conrad, to the United States. His
father had been influenced by three daughters who had immigrated to this
country earlier: Mrs. Fred Steiger of Glenham, Mrs. Gold of Kansas, and
Christina, now deceased. The trip from Rumania to the United States took
eleven days. Upon docking, the family traveled by train to Eureka, South
Dakota and were met there by Mrs. Fred Steiger with whom they stayed until
spring. The first year it was necessary for Christ to find a job to help
buy equipment for the farm and this he found in the section of Herreid. The
summer of the second year he worked out but spent the winter months at
home. One fall Christ worked on a threshing machine and drew fifty cents of
his wages and when his work was completed, he returned home with eighty
dollars to turn over to his father.

In 1905, the family moved to the Coleman Wagner farm southwest of Selby and
in 1906 they sold out their farm equipment and moved to Texas. There Christ
found the lady of his choice, Pauline Allmendinger, who was born in Russia
and with her family immigrated to America, settling in Texas six months
before their marriage, which occurred in Holiday, Texas, where they farmed
one year. In the fall of 1910, they sold out and returned to Tolstoy, South
Dakota, where Mr. Miller's parents had preceded them, spending part of the
winter in their home. In February, 1911, the Christ and Conrad Miller
families moved to Harding county and filed on homesteads three miles apart,
25 miles south of Buffalo, which was their nearest town. For the next four
years they had hard sledding as they were unable to even grow feed because
of drouth and hail storms. They hauled feed in from North Dakota at times.
In 1914 they moved back to this area and rented a farm 12 miles west of
Selby (now owned by George Schaffer) where they farmed for three years
before buying their present farm. To Mr. and Mrs. Christ Miller seven
children were born: Bertha, Mrs. Carl Bronneman of Harrold, South Dakota;
Emma, Mrs. Robert Allmendinger of Miami, Arizona; Robert, who is the
Congregational minister at Scotts Bluff, Nebraska; Jake of Glenham;
Pauline, Mrs. Dick Lanam of Glenham; Rosie, Mrs. Robert Jones of
Bellflower, California; and Irene of Yankton, South Dakota.

        MR. AND MRS. CHRIST MILLER

On July 27, 1937, this family lost their beloved wife and mother. On
September 3, 1939, Mr. Miller was married a second time to Hannah Fucs of
Avon, South Dakota, who was born at Springer, Germany, and came to the
United States in June of 1922.

In the fall of 1939 Mr. Miller rented his farm to Reynold Idler and moved
to Avon, South Dakota, where they worked on a dairy and in a service
station for three years. To this marriage, one daughter, Charleen, was
born. In March, 1943, the family moved back to the farm southwest of Selby
where they live at the present time.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN W. BLAIR

John W. Blair was born in Pennsylvania in the year 1853 and came to
Walworth county in 1883 from Iowa where he had migrated from his native
state. He came to LeBeau by way of Pierre and in the year 1884, opened the
first school in Walworth county, having been issued the first teacher's
certificate in the county by J. M. Paul who was the first county
superintendent of schools. The school was held in a log cabin belonging to
August Siebrecht, who was clerk of the newly organized Scranton school
district No. 1, Walworth county. Incidentally, this was the first school
north of Pierre. The president of the board was a Mr. Williams and Mr.
Blair was the treasurer. He later engaged in the drug business in LeBeau,
moving to Bangor when that town was started and then to Mound City, Eureka
and Herreid in turn, after most of Bangor moved to Selby, remaining in
business in Herreid until his retirement. He died at Mobridge in 1936.

In the year 1893, John Blair was united in marriage with Kittie Hughes at
Britton. Miss Hughes was a popular school teacher of the Bangor community.
To them were born three children, all of whom have left South Dakota.

Mr. and Mrs. Blair were well known, highly respected and much loved
citizens of the Bangor community for many years, and up to the time of his
death at the ripe old age of eighty-three years, he continued his interest
in civic affairs and did his bit for civic betterment.

THE OVERHOLSER FAMILY

In writing concerning this family, it is the son of the father who occupies
the pioneer distinction. Eugene Overholser, son of Samuel L. Overholser and
Eva L. Overholser was born at Rock Branch, Iowa, on December 4, 1870. He
received a grade school education at Rock Branch and attended high school
at nearby Correctionville, Iowa. When but 19 years of age, young Gene
arrived in Walworth county and immediately with his father, bought and
filed on virgin land adjoining the Missouri river, south of present-day
Glenham. Always a lover of horses and animals, Gene soon started a ranch
with a few horses and several head of cattle. Ranching was a lonesome
business so Gene returned to Correctionville, Iowa, and, on December 12,
1892, was married to Olive Everts, with whom he became acquainted while
attending high school at Correctionville. The young couple returned to
their Dakota ranch after their marriage and resided there continuously
until 1918, when they moved to Selby.

Pioneer Evarts, now a ghost town of Walworth county, was located on the
Overholser ranch. The village was named after Olive Everts Overholser, who
was its first postmistress, and was platted and subdivided into lots and
blocks and during the early 1900's enjoyed great fame as a cattle town.
Until the railroad bridge was completed at Mobridge, the railroad ended at
Evarts, and cattle from the vast range west of the Missouri were forded to
Evarts for shipping to eastern packing plants. A pontoon bridge at this
point permitted pedestrians and vehicles to cross the river. It was always
hoped that the railroad would build its bridge opposite Evarts but
treacherous footing made impractical the construction of a bridge at this
point. The railroad engineers found a firmer footing near the Grand river
crossing and the bridge was constructed at that point. This was the death
knell of Evarts. Once a thriving cattle town, in a few short years,
practically all business establishments and dwelling houses were moved to
nearby Glenham, Selby, or the new town of Mobridge, and the townsite of
Evarts again became ranching terrain.

Soon after arriving at Selby, Gene Overholser and a younger brother, Royce,
entered into the hardware business in partnership with R. H. Leach of
Glenham. The partners operated stores at Glenham and Selby until 1923, when
the Overholsers purchased the interest of Leach and continued the business
until 1924, when they sold their store to Adam Pressler, present Selby
hardware merchant. Shortly afterwards, brother Royce built the fine brick
and tile structure immediately north of the First National Bank building
and used a portion of it as a drug store. This building is now owned by
Adam Pressler and houses the Pressler Ready to-Wear store, the Paul drug
store and the Aman barber shop. Gene became associated with Royce in the
drug business in 1937 and continued this association until his death on
September 8, 1945.

        MR. AND MRS. GENE OVERHOLSER

Gene was intensely interested in horses and particularly in raising
thoroughbred pacers and trotters for harness racing. In this hobby he was
associated with Dr. A. E. Byron and the Overholser Byron horses were rated
among the best in this field and for many years won major racing honors at
fairs and celebrations in South Dakota, adjoining states and in Canada.
During all of these years, Gene was interested in farming and banking. He
owned considerable farm land which he leased on a crop share basis and from
1923 to the time of his death was a stock holder and director of the First
National Bank of Selby.

From 1907 to 1909 he served as state senator from Walworth and Edmunds
counties and was Walworth county's state representative from 1925 to 1933.
He was elected mayor of Selby in 1919 and held that office for 26
consecutive years until his death. While living on the ranch, he was clerk
of the Kennedy school district from 1899 to 1903 and treasurer of said
district from 1908 to 1918. From 1925 to 1930 he served as a member of the
board of education of the Selby Consolidated school district. In addition
to these various offices, Gene was an active member of the Selby Commercial
club during the entire term of his residence in Selby.

Gene Overholser became a master Mason on April 11, 1903, and for many years
was a member of the Royal Arch at Selby and the Knights Templar and the
Yelduz Shrine at Aberdeen. He was a past master of the Masonic lodge and
past high priest in the Royal Arch. He became a member of the Order of the
Eastern Star on August 7, 1909, and was worthy patron of the Selby chapter
for six years. On December 12, 1942, Mr. and Mrs. Gene Overholser
celebrated their fiftieth wedding anniversary.

Olive Overholser was born in Iowa on July 17, 1869, where she grew to
womanhood attending high school at Correctionville. She taught school in
that vicinity for several years prior to her marriage to Gene Overholser.
Mrs. Overholser was a charter member of the Hope chapter of the Order of
the Eastern Star at Selby, being initiated on February 4, 1904. She was
worthy matron in 1920 and 1921, and secretary from 1925 to 1943. She was an
active member of the Methodist church and Women's club at Selby. Olive
Overholser died at Selby on October 20, 1945.

Samuel L. Overholser and Eva L. Overholser, the parents of Eugene and Royce
Overholser, were born and reared in Lancaster county, Pennsylvania, and
were married there on January 22, 1870. Shortly after their marriage, the
senior Overholsers moved to northwestern Iowa and settled on a homestead
near Sioux City, Iowa. They moved to Aberdeen, South Dakota, in 1898, and
then to the Overholser ranch at Evarts in 1907. They disposed of their
ranch holdings in 1919 and moved to Watertown, South Dakota, where they
resided until their respective deaths, Mr. Overholser in 1923 and Mrs.
Overholser in 1937.

Royce L. Overholser was born at Correctionville, Iowa, on May 22, 1882,
where he attended grade and high school. He graduated from Highland Park
college at Des Moines, Iowa, with a degree in pharmacy in 1904. In 1907, he
entered the drug business for himself at Andover, South Dakota, and
operated a drug store at that place until 1915, when he sold out and
purchased a drug store at Canova, South Dakota. Royce was in the drug
business at Canova until 1917 when he sold the business and moved to Selby.
From 1919 to 1924, he was in the hardware business at Selby and Glenham.
From 1926 to January 1, 1946, Royce operated the Rexall drug store at
Selby, selling to George W. Paul, the present owner at Selby, in the fall
of 1945.

Royce became an active Mason in 1907, and is presently a member of the
Royal Arch at Selby, and the Knights Templar and Yelduz Shrine at Aberdeen.
He is also a member of the Order of the Eastern Star. Royce is still living
at Selby and is presently a director and officer of the First National Bank
of Selby, and is also serving as state representative from Walworth county
for the term from 1949 to 1951.

Royce was married to Eda Werness on June 15, 1915, at Minot, North Dakota.
Eda was born at Red Wing, Minnesota, on January 21, 1886, and attended
grade and high school in that vicinity. She graduated from St. Joseph's
School of Nursing at St. Paul, and prior to her marriage, worked at her
profession in St. Paul. Eda has been active in Eastern Star work at Selby,
and in the Selby Woman's club and the Methodist church. She and Royce are
now living a comfortable retired life in their fine home at Selby.

DOCTOR AND MRS. AUGUST BEIL

Dr. August Beil was born at Ehrenbreitstein, Coblenz, Germany, March 27.
1863, where he grew to manhood and later turned to the sea, visiting many
parts and ports of the world. He came to America in 1886, locating in New
York City where he took up the study of medicine. When he graduated in 1896
he came to Bangor, practicing his profession there until Selby started when
he moved to this city and practiced until his death in 1919, during the
influenza epidemic. His obituary in the Walworth County Record states that
he died of acute Bright's disease, that early in the flu epidemic he was
himself stricken with a severe attack, but refused to take proper care of
himself, insisting on caring for the other sick people, and that he thereby
hastened the onset of the disease that took his life.

        DR. AND MRS. AUGUST BEIL

Dr. Beil was an energetic and public spirited citizen as well as a devoted
and beloved physician. At the time of his death, he was serving his second
term as mayor of the city. He gave much time to Masonry being a member of
all of the Masonic bodies in Selby, also of the Woodmen, Maccabees and
Yeoman orders.

Mrs. Marie Beil was also born in Germany and came to America and New York
City in her young womanhood. She was well educated in the old country, was a
graduate musician and was fluent in the German and French languages. She
served as a governess for nine years for the Isador Straus family in New
York City. She and Dr. Beil were married in Minneapolis and she came to
Bangor with him as his bride in 1896. She immediately took a keen interest
in local affairs, was probably the first music teacher in the county,
driving to Bowdle regularly to give lessons in that city. After the
doctor's death, she sold what property they had, spent a season in
California and then went to Barcelona, Spain, to join her brother who was a
wealthy wine merchant engaged in the importing and exporting business.
During the Civil War in Spain they were forced to flee for their lives by
airplane and abandon the properties but were glad to get away even though
they were left penniless. They returned to their native Wiesbaden in
Germany where she passed away. In accordance with her wishes, her body was
cremated after her death and the ashes disposed of on the graves of her
parents, that the dust of her body might be mingled with that of theirs
throughout eternity.

Dr. Beil built the Selby Hospital in 1910-11 and for many years it served
the community very well. At the time it was constructed, hospitals were few
and far between and it was a very well-known institution--in fact was
considered one of the city's land marks. Dr. George purchased the hospital
from Mrs. Beil after the doctor's death.

MR. AND MRS. ELBRIDGE G. POWELL

Elbridge G. Powell was born March 7, 1861, at Viroqua, Wisconsin. He
received his education in the common schools of Viroqua, Viroqua academy
and the LaCrosse business college. At the age of twenty-seven years,
attracted by the great open spaces of South Dakota, he filed on the
northeast quarter of section 29, in township 123, range 77, in Walworth
county, which is located six miles west of old Bangor.

He was married to Flora Eva Meacham on June 23, 1888, who was born at
Neillsville, Wisconsin, on February 15, 1866. Mrs. Powell had filed on two
adjoining quarter sections, thus forming the Powell place, which remained
Mr. Powell's chief interest and hobby during his whole lifetime, and which
interest is being continued by his son, Harold E. Powell.

After a few years of farming Mr. Powell was elected as clerk of courts and
they then moved to Bangor, where Mrs. Powell taught in the Bangor school.
During his term as clerk of courts, Mr. Powell became interested in
abstract work and shortly acquired the controlling interest in the Walworth
County Abstract company which he continued to operate until the time of his
death.

Two children were born to them: Irma E., having been born on April 20,
1889, and now residing at Mountain Lakes, New Jersey, and Harold E., born
July 17, 1900, a real Golden Jubilee baby and product of Selby, who now
resides at Passaic, New Jersey.

The year 1900 was the high spot of life to the Powells,--a new baby and a
new town. Again their house was moved and this time to Selby. During the
county seat struggle, Mr. Powell commuted daily, via horse and buggy, or
sleigh, as weather conditions demanded, to Bangor to carry on his work as
clerk of courts and with the abstract company. He was a member of the Selby
Lodge A. F. & A. M., and Mrs. Powell became a charter member of Hope
chapter of the Order of the Eastern Star.

With the removal of the county seat to Selby and the building of the new
court house, Mr. Powell enjoyed his work there until he passed away
suddenly on July 25 1937. Since the death of Mr. Powell, Mrs. Powell has
made her home with her daughter, Irma E. Hibbard and now lives in Mountain
Lakes, New Jersey. The son Harold E., attended the public schools and was
graduated from the Selby high school. He was a veteran of World War I and
attended the Rapid City School of Mines and since the year 1926 has been
employed by the Bell Telephone laboratories in New York City.

MR. AND MRS. J. E. BYERS

J. E. Byers was born at Dixon, Illinois, in 1862, and when a small boy came
to Black Hawk county, Iowa, near Waterloo, the crossing of the Mississippi
river being made in rowboats. Crossing the "Father of Waters" in this
manner was quite an achievement when it is considered that all of their
belongings had to be either carried across in the boat, rafted or floated.
They homesteaded at Washburn, a village near Waterloo. Mrs. Byers was born
at Lanesboro, Minnesota, and her parents were natives of Dublin, Ireland.
Mr. and Mrs. Byers were married at Orange City, Iowa, their families both
having moved to the vicinity of Sheldon, Iowa. They began housekeeping on a
farm near Sheldon, then moved to the vicinity of George, later to Cedar
Falls, Iowa and Jasper, Minnesota. At Jasper, a sister of Mr. Byers was a
member of the faculty of Iowa State Teacher's college and the daughter,
Tillie, now Mrs. Hanrahan of Selby, began her education by attending the
college demonstration school.

In 1904, Mr. Byers came to Walworth county and purchased part of the land
now owned by George W. Turner, through Charles Smith and Charley Lennan. He
also bought a quarter section from Mr. Lennan upon which he moved a house
from old Evarts. This house was the one which Frank Gosch Jr., dismantled
when he built his present new home on his farm southwest of Selby.

In the spring of 1906, Mr. Byers came from Minnesota with nine head of
horses and started breaking up and cropping his land, the family following
him later. In later years, he operated a huge Reeves steam breaking outfit,
pulling fourteen plows, and farmed on a large scale. In 1912, Mr. Byers was
hired as the first manager of the newly organized Selby Equity Union
Exchange and the family came to Selby. After leaving the Equity management,
they moved to Trail City where he bought a large ranch southeast of Trail
City near the Moreau river and entered the cattle, horse and mule business
on an extensive scale, at one time owning 100 head of mules. He was active
in civic affairs in Dewey county, serving as county commissioner, township
clerk and on the local school board. He later sold the ranch and live stock
and moved to Trail City where Mrs. Byers passed away in 1924 at the age of
62 and Mr. Byers passed away at Aberdeen in 1940 at the age of 78.

They had seven children: Hattie, now Mrs. Harold Stewart of Morristown;
Anna, now Mrs. Rufus Vining of Aberdeen; Lela, now Mrs. Vincent Bousle of
Cutbank, Montana; Will, of Edgemont, South Dakota; John of Helena, Montana;
and Tillie, now Mrs. John Hanrahan of Selby; and Nellie, who died at the
age of 17.

The Byers family had an important part in transforming the area southeast
of Glenham and southwest of Selby into farms and ranches. They found it
unbroken prairie and left it a community of good homes. With them from
Minnesota came Ed and Rufus Vining, Mrs. Ed Vining being a sister of Mrs.
Byers and Mrs. Rufus Vining was a daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Byers. Ed Vining
homesteaded a quarter section which is now a part of the Turner holdings.
The house he built was moved to the Jerry Brown farm northwest of Glenham
and is now the home of Mr. and Mrs. Ted Molstad. Mrs. Vining died in 1919
and is buried in the Selby cemetery and Mr. Vining went to Bemidji,
Minnesota. Rufus Vining homesteaded the land occupied for many years by
Othiol Turner, south of Glenham, and he and his wife moved to Aberdeen many
years ago. Both are prominent in the Townsend organization and have
traveled extensively.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN RABENBERG

John Rabenberg was born in German Friesland in the year 1855 and as a young
man, helped to build the great Kiel ship canal connecting the Baltic sea
with the North sea, a part of Prince Bismarck's far reaching plans for a
greater Germany, working with pick, spade and shovel and wheeling the dirt
out with wheelbarrows. He also served two years in the German army. At the
age of 21 he came to America, being desirous to escape the militarism in
his native land, which he and many other young men felt reduced them to the
status of cannon fodder in time of war. He came to Hastings, Nebraska, and
worked on farms for wages as low as four dollars per month. In 1876 western
Nebraska was still new country and living there was almost pioneering. He
became acquainted with a young Englishman and together they debated the
advantages of free land in Dakota, finally deciding to make the move.
Traveling by ox team, they came as far as Douglas county, South Dakota,
during the first season, coming on to Aberdeen, then the end of the
railroad the next year. From Aberdeen they came out to LaGrace, six miles
northwest of where Pollock now stands, then north to old Winona in Emmons
county, North Dakota. He took a homestead directly east of there and about
forty miles from Eureka. At that time these towns along the Missouri were
served by steamboats plying between St. Louis and the forts and towns on the
upper Missouri river. In the early days of Eureka, they sometimes made the
trip to town on snow shoes, having been taught to make and use these useful
appliances by their Norwegian neighbors, who had them in the old country.

He was united in marriage with Dorothea Laemmle in 1893. In 1896 they moved
to Herreid, in 1906 to the place now owned by their son, John, north of
Glenham, and in 1918 to the farm in Walworth county, northeast of Glenham.
Mrs. Rabenberg was born in South Russia and came to America with her
parents and family to the community of Eureka. Her brothers, Christ and
William Laemmle were residents of the Java community for many years before
they passed away. They became the parents of ten children, one son, Christ,
died while serving in the armed forces of World War I; the others are: John,
Henry, Jake, Anna, William, Martha, Carl, Herman, and Edward. Mr. Rabenberg
passed away in 1945 and Mrs. Rabenberg now resides in Selby, having
purchased a home here. The farm was sold to James Anderson, a neighbor, who
now resides on it.

The Rabenberg group represents the hardiest of pioneering stock and what
they have, they have attained the hard way, by work and frugality. Their
contribution to the economy and society of every community in which they
have resided has been and is, progressive and fruitful.

MR. AND MRS. JAKE RABENBERG

Jake Rabenberg, son of Mr. and Mrs. John Rabenberg, was born in South
Dakota, near Herreid, moving to a farm north of Glenham in the year 1906,
and growing to manhood in the Glenham community. He attended rural school
and worked on the farm with other members of the family group. In the year
1924 he was united in marriage with Johanna Schlomer at Glenham and they
began housekeeping on the N. Brink section of land six miles northeast of
Glenham. Mrs. Rabenberg is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Cody Schlomer and
was born at Bowdle but grew up in the Glenham community and received her
education in the Glenham schools.

Jake built the buildings on the Brink land, being the farm now occupied by
Mr. and Mrs. Jake Miller, and branched out, becoming one of the pioneers in
the use of internal combustion engines for farm power. He early saw the
possibilities of farming larger areas of land so as to make economical use
of big power units and modern farm equipment. In 1929 he purchased the
first large crawler type of tractor and tried it out on his farm and with
the use of this machine he was able to get into the fields much earlier
than his neighbors in the spring. In 1934 he purchased the Central Park
farm, long owned and operated by W. H. Mickelson, who then moved to
Michigan. Jake then extended his holdings and farming operations from year
to year. He was always a keen student of the art and science of agriculture
and lost no opportunities to learn more about the growing of farm crops and
was never averse to experimenting with new ideas and new machines. The rod
weeder, the furrow drill, and the basin tiller were among the new machines
tried out on the Rabenberg farm. He constructed the first header barge ever
used here and made the first trial of the modern idea of summer fallowing
land in the year 1925.

His keen interest in the best types of machinery drew him into the farm
machinery business in a small way at first and in l939 he went into it as a
business rather than as a sideline to his farming. Jake started his
business in Selby with the John Deere line and later the Minneapolis-Moline
and Oliver contracts. His first location was the building now used for
storage just north across from the Marywall Hotel.

In 1944 he began the construction of a new brick and tile, all modern
implement house in Selby, measuring 70 x 70 feet, which really marked the
beginning of a building program that is making Selby into a new city. He
purchased eight lots of abandoned property, cleared off the weeds and
rubbish and turned them into one of the finest business properties of the
city. He employs seven men and in addition to a complete line of farm
machinery and equipment, operates a modern machine shop, servicing tractors
and other machines and has the contract for the sale of Hudson automobiles.
His business territory extends from Onida to Linton and far into the west
river area.

Mr. Rabenberg has also made a start in providing the Selby community with
an airport, having provided a landing field and hangar two miles south of
town primarily for his own private use, but which field is open for
community and transient use at any time. It is probably the beginning of
what will at some future time be a well patronized airport for Selby. He
also sells "Cessna" airplanes and owns and operates the only airplane in
the community.

The Rabenberg residence remains on the Central Park farm which has been
entirely rebuilt since he purchased it. The house is new and modern and the
owners hospitable. There is a large grain elevator and other commodious
buildings which make it one of the finest farmsteads of the county.

The Rabenbergs started with nothing except brain and brawn and in the short
period of twenty-five years have not only attained the leading position in
finance and business in Selby but have shown what can be done in such a
manner that their success has had a marked effect on the agriculture and
business of the city and community. During the years of Jake's huge farming
operations he was widely known as "The Wheat King from Walworth County" and
many of his neighbors were lulled to sleep at night with the hum of Jake's
machines in their ears, as his were the first round the clock farming
operations in the county.

LARS LARSON FAMILY

Lars and Hanna Larson came to Walworth county on August 22, 1887, from
Denver, Colorado, where they met and married. They came to Bowdle, South
Dakota, which was the end of the Milwaukee railroad at that time. From
Bowdle, they came by ox yoke and lumber wagon owned and driven by Peter J.
Thorstenson, brother of Mrs. Larson. They lived in a small stone house on
the Peter Thorstenson homestead the first few months until they got their
own sod house built on their homestead just two miles north and two miles
west of where Selby South Dakota, now stands. This farm with additional land
added to it by Lars Larson was owned by the Larson family until early in
the year of 1949 when it was sold to John Miller, J. B. Stiegelmeier, and
Milton Schauer.

Lars Larson, like all early pioneers, started tilling the soil of the new
homestead with a yoke of oxen, for the reason they were cheaper to buy than
horses and would do a good day's work without hay or grain--and you could
just turn them loose and let them feed on the prairie. A two-room sod house
was the first home which the writer can well remember. This was our home
for ten years, until the spring of 1897, when Mr. Larson with help of
neighbors built a new home of native brick, composed of clay, straw, water
and wooden moulds dried in the sun. This house was later sided with lap
wood siding which added to the appearance and protection of our home. This
dwelling is still being used.

        MR. AND MRS. LARS LARSON AND FAMILY
        Top row, left to right--Martin L. and Richard T. Second row Mrs.
        Larson. Lars Larson, the infant Linnie and Marie E.

There were many hardships in those days that people of this day and age
will never realize,--very short crops and no work to be had. Lars Larson
and Peter Thorstenson walked from their homesteads to some fifty miles east
of Aberdeen, South Dakota, to do threshing work at 50 cents per day,
leaving the women folks at home to care for the children and stock. They
told of the long days they had to work. They would be in the fields before
daylight waiting until it was light enough to work and worked after dark as
long as they could see.

The winters in those days were really tough--so much snow that it was
impossible to drive oxen or horses and the men would go on skis or
snowshoes to the little inland town of Bangor, then located about five
miles south of where Selby, South Dakota, now stands, to get (mainly) a
50-pound sack of flour and a few badly needed groceries, carrying all home
on their backs.

Coal and oil stoves or furnaces were not used in those days and the
pioneers would have to haul wood early in the fall from the Missouri river,
a distance of twenty-five miles or so. Twisted hay was also used for fuel
when the wood would run short and also corn cobs, which were very few, not
to forget the buffalo or cow chips which were used to quite an extent for
fuel.

Ten children were born to the Lars Larson family, all at the farm home
without a doctor. Only some good neighbor lady (Grandma Tisdall) would come
to the home to take care of the babies until Mrs. Larson was able to do it
herself. The children are as follows (oldest to youngest): Martin L.
Larson, Richard T. Larson both of Mobridge, South Dakota; Marie (Larson)
Johnson, deceased; August I,. Larson of Glenwood, Minnesota; Louis H.
Larson of Mobridge; Regina (Larson) Williams of Mobridge; John A. Larson of
Rapid City South Dakota, Edwin R. Larson of Redwood Falls, Minnesota;
Theodore Larson, deceased; Helmer O. Larson of Albuquerque, New Mexico.

In the fall of October, 1907, Lars Larson attended the first town lot sale
held at Mobridge, which was then a new town of less than a half-dozen
buildings, and purchased lots 3 and 4, block 6, of the original plat of
Mobridge, where Larsons' Furniture and Perron's Toggery are now located.
Lars Larson built the front part of the present Larson Furniture store in
February, 1908 shipped in the first carload of furniture sometime in March
that same spring and continued in the furniture and undertaking business
until late summer of 1916 when his health failed him. After seeing doctors
in Minneapolis and Rochester, Minnesota, Lars Larson passed away on
November 7, 1916.

After Lars Larson's passing, Martin L. Larson and August L. Larson bought
the furniture and undertaking business from their mother and have continued
ever since. From this little furniture store, the younger brothers have
branched out to three other larger stores--John A. Larson at Rapid City,
South Dakota; August L. Larson and son, Marvin, at Glenwood, Minnesota; and
Edwin R. Larson and son, Edwin Jr., at Redwood Falls, Minnesota.

Mother Hanna Larson still lives and occupies the apartment built for the
Larson family in 1908.

Lars Larson was active in civic affairs and, while living on the farm, was
on township and school boards for years. He also organized and started the
first Sunday school in the Blue Blanket school house and was a charter
member of the Bethany Lutheran church, helping build the structure. After
moving to Mobridge, Lars Larson acted on the city board as alderman for his
ward for two terms and was also a charter member of the Trinity Lutheran
church and one of its first founders. Lars Larson and daughter, Marie,
organized and started the first Sunday school in the Trinity Lutheran
church of Mobridge and he was always active in the betterment of the
community in which he lived.

Marie E. Larson served as county treasurer of Walworth county for four
years, and Louis H. Larson served as register of deeds of Walworth county
for four years.

MR. AND MRS. OLE P. LEE

Among the early settlers of Blue Blanket township were Mr. and Mrs. Ole P.
Lee.

Both were born in Norway and immigrated to this country in the early
eighties, coming to Blue Blanket township in 1886.

His brother, Hans O. Lee, and family also came in 1886.

Other pioneer neighbors were the Soren Petersons', the O. G. Bakers' and
the J. B. Webbs'.

They were members of the first Lutheran congregation and charter members of
Bethany Lutheran church near Selby. They had a family of three sons and four
daughters.

After the death of his wife November 24, 1919, Mr. Lee retired from active
farming but continued to live on the homestead until his death July 1, 1947.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN W. LOWRY

John W. Lowry was born in Indiana, Pennsylvania April 10, 1860. There he
grew to manhood, receiving his education in the excellent schools of
Indiana and the state seminary at Pittsburgh. At the age of 23 he, decided
to try his fortune in the west.

After a few months of looking over different locations he bought a ticket
to Ipswich, Dakota territory, at that time the western terminal of the
Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul railroad, though the survey-was made into
Bowdle. Traveling overland with a team and buggy young John finally stopped
at the Kennedy ranch in Walworth county. He filed on section 29, township
124, range 78. He accepted the job as foreman for the Kennedy ranch,
holding that position until Kennedy Bros. sold out in 1889. In the meantime
his sister, Miss Nannie Lowry came out and filed on adjoining land. John
built a frame house to replace the old claim "soddy", a large house, for a
claim shack, and in the early days many dances, basket socials and social
meetings were held there. John and Miss Nannie were splendid host and
hostess. As the surrounding country settled slowly but steadily John
Lowry's home became the nucleus for a small village called Brisco. In 1892
an attractive young lady named Carrie Carscallen filed on a quarter
adjoining Miss Nannie's. A daughter of B. B. Carscallen, one of Walworth
county's earliest settlers, Miss Carrie was born in Ohio, June 22, 1871. A
very popular young woman, Miss Carrie had taught her home school for
several terms. On October 18, 1893, she and John were married. A lovely
wedding at the Carscallen home with guests from the whole country was
followed by a wedding dance given in their honor by the Kennedys. Mr. and
Mrs. John Lowry spent their honeymoon at the Worlds Fair in Chicago.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHN LOWRY

Never an enthusiastic farmer, John Lowry always contended that Dakota was a
stock grower's dream come true before the settlers plowed up the land and
made fences, but no farming country. Laying in a goodly stock of groceries,
dry goods, etc., he established a small store at Brisco--the early Walworth
County Records are full of his ads. In spite of the bad years of the 1890's
the small store prospered, and in 1900 John Lowry was appointed postmaster
at Brisco and the town of Glenham was platted on Mrs. Lowry's claim, the
railroad company paying her $2,500.00 for the land, an amazing price for a
quarter in those days. Four children were born to the Lowrys in Walworth
county; Mertice, Ernest, Jessie and Frank.

In 1902 the Lowrys with their young family moved to North Dakota and
shortly afterward to Idaho where they settled in Sand Point. There John
Lowry worked for a lumber company until his death, December 16, 1916. Two
children, Edith Ana Irvin, were born in Sand Point. Mrs. Lowry remained in
Sand Point until she passed away on March 22, 1944.

MR. AND MRS. WILLIAM H. MASTELLER

Friends and neighbors of Mr. and Mrs. William H. Masteller will always
think of them as good neighbors, and willing workers of the community in
which they have lived for 38 years. They were always ready to share in any
pleasure or help in any sorrow which came to their community.

William and Rozetta Masteller came to Selby in 1911, and settled on a farm
southwest of there. Previous to this date they had lived in Jasper county,
Iowa, where they were both born in 1869 and 1868, respectively. They were
married there in 1897. They had always lived on rented farms in Iowa and
hearing of the cheap land in Dakota, decided to come and look at it. In
1910 Mr. Masteller and four friends came out together to see if they could
rent or buy some land. He said he liked the level prairie country at first
sight and borrowing $500 to make a down payment, he purchased a small
two-room house and a small barn before bringing his wife and two children
here. He went back to Iowa, had a sale and loaded up the cars ready to go,
when his son, Merl, became ill the day before they were to leave. The family
doctor was called and he said, "Just go ahead, Willie, the little devil's
got scarlet fever." So they went. Note: not a single child or adult got the
scarlet fever from him. Five other neighbors (some of whom had gone with him
before) had packed their cars also and the five other men had gone ahead
with the loaded cars. This left poor Mr. Masteller behind to take care of
all the women and children on the passenger train. He said, "Babies cried,
women fussed, it rained and every neighbor left behind had sent a big
basket of food for me to carry." When they arrived, they found seven new
neighbors had come and met the carloads of stock and furniture and had
taken all the supplies to the new homes. Is it any wonder they have always
loved that community, with such good neighbors.

The first year they lived here, they broke up 200 acres of land and planted
flax seed which did not come up until the 4th of July, and which froze
before it ripened. They had to buy grain for their stock that winter. In
1912 it was not a great deal better and they had only a short crop. The
five families who had come with them to Selby all grew discouraged and
moved back to Iowa. The Mastellers, hating to admit defeat, stuck it out,
and have never regretted their decision. They have slowly increased their
acreage and now own an improved 64-acre farm. During the dry years of the
1930's they suffered many hardships along with their neighbors, but so far
have always come out on top.

        MR. AND MRS. WILLIAM H. MASTELLER

They have enjoyed trips to California, Oregon, Ohio, and their old home
state during their married life and had the happy privilege of celebrating
their golden Wedding in March, 1947. Mrs. Masteller passed away on April
27, 1949, leaving her family and a host of friends to mourn her loss. She
was one of the original members of the Jolly club; both were members of the
Order of the Eastern Star and she helped in the Methodist Ladies' aid work
for many years. Mr. Masteller has been a member of the Masonic lodge since
1900. He was one of the organizers of the Selby Equity union, serving as
president of the board of directors for 20 years. He was on the
registration board of the first World War, and served on the draft board of
the second World War, besides serving on bond committees, helping with Red
Cross work and being active on many other committees in his community.

They raised two children: Merl of Selby, and Mrs. Pearl Buddenhagen of
Glendale, California. Two children preceded their mother in death. They
have six grandchildren. Mr. Masteller still resides on his farm with his
son; Merl and family, and although nearly 80 years of age is very active
both in work at home and in the welfare of his community.

LEWIS W. MAXWELL

Lewis W. Maxwell was born on a farm near Auburn Maine, December 8, 1852. He
received his education in a rural school near his home, after which he
worked the farm with his father. He married his first wife in 1883 and
having heard of land open for filing came to South Dakota. He selected and
filed on a homestead. 29-123-76, and a tree claim, 27-123-76.

They built a sod house and barn and started farming operations in the
spring of 1884. These buildings were northeast of the new town of Bangor.

        IDA A. MAXWELL

Money being a very minus item, they farmed in season and his wife taught
school and Mr. Maxwell worked at the Skinner farm during the fall and
winters. In 1886 his wife became ill and they returned to Maine where she
died. He came back to the claim and continued his farming, boarding at the
G. J. Schellinger hotel in Bangor. There he met Mrs. Ida Krueger Breitting,
mother of one son, Elmer, age four years. On December 24, 1889, they were
married at Bowdle and went to the farm home to live. On December 6, 1890,
twin babies joined the group, a son who died at birth and a daughter,
Lillian.

In 1893 they moved into Bangor and opened a small boarding house. In 1895
they built the Auburn Hotel which was moved to Selby in 1900 and an
addition built which is the present Auburn Hotel.

Mr. and Mrs. Maxwell retired from the hotel business in 1936.

Mr. Maxwell died November 2, 1942. at home at the age of 89 years, 11
months and 28 days.

Mrs. Ida Maxwell resides in a small home in the east part of Selby.

MR. PERCY E. SEVRENS

Percy Sevrens was born on a farm in Wisconsin on September 27, 1874. In
April, 1881, his father came out to Brown county, South Dakota, and filed
on a homestead near Groton. When he had a house ready for them to live in,
the mother with four children came to Bristol which was as far as the
trains ran at that time on the new railroad, and was met there by the
father, riding out to the "claim" home in a lumber wagon. The pioneer home
was established and Percy and the older children went to Groton to school.
In the year 1886, on the night before Thanksgiving, the father died of
heart trouble. Percy being the oldest child, was obliged to share the
mother's burden in caring for the family and farming the land. In 1888 the
widow sold the land at Groton and bought the SW 1/4 of 27-123-78 in
Walworth county from H. B. Foster for the children and bought the
relinquishment on the SE 1/4 of the same section, filing on it as a
homestead. Later she was married to James W. Davidson who had filed on a
homestead in 1883, the year the range was opened for settlement. The latter
was a Scotchman who came out from Chicago and knew nothing about farming
and seemed not to care to learn. It is recalled that he always wore a white
shirt even while working the fields. He had been a bookkeeper and his
experience was in office work. He was elected county commissioner in 1890
and rendered service in helping collect seed loans made by the county to
the farmers.

Mr. Sevrens recalls that in 1891 he worked for George M. Mickelson for
$18.00 a month and spent $17.45 during the season, saving the balance. He
recalls he walked to Bangor to celebrate the Fourth of July that year but
did not mind it as farmers of that day walked behind all of their
machinery. He recalls he seeded 170 acres of grain that spring for Mr.
Mickelson with a 7-foot seeder pulled by an old horse and a mule. The same
team was used on a walking plow and a walking corn cultivator. In the
winter of 1892 Mr. Davidson left for parts unknown, deserting the family.
Percy recalls taking him to Bowdle and he has never been heard of or from
since. Presumably he went to Brazil. After he left, it was learned that he
had mortgaged property that did not belong to him in order to get money.
The following spring, Percy bought four oxen and with his younger brother,
Ernest, took over the farming operations. They put in 60 acres of wheat, 15
acres of flax and broke 56 acres of sod, threshing 1040 bushels of wheat
and 140 bushels of flax. This grain was hauled to Bowdle with oxen, one
team being led behind the first load, thus transporting about 100 bushels a
trip. Grain was all handled in sacks. They would leave the place at 3 a.m.
and get to Bowdle about 4 p.m., unload and stay over night and drive home
next day. Two trips a week were all the oxen could stand. Most of the farm
work and hauling was done with oxen in those days.

The late E. G. Powell was the Sevrens' nearest neighbor and he was doing
all of his farm work with oxen. Water was scarce and they had to haul it
for the stock. A shallow well on the place furnished water for the house.
Mr. Sevrens paid $165.00 for the four oxen, used them two years and sold
them for $150.00. By that time he had five horses. Powell acquired four
head about the same time.

In 1894 Mr. Powell was elected clerk of courts and spent most of his time
in Bangor, so the Sevrens rented his land with farm machinery and horses
and farmed it with their own. In the meantime, on December 8, 1895, Mr.
Sevrens was united in marriage with Cora M. Jenison and kept right on
living on his mother's place and farming both farms. A few years later he
filed on land in section 35-123-78, where they have resided ever since,
getting a total of 180 acres of land in addition to the homestead and
engaging in the raising of livestock and farming with well-drilling as a
sideline. Mr. Sevrens bored and drilled wells over a wide territory for 51
years.

During the ten years of combined depression, grasshopper infestation and
drouth he lost his land. In 1934 he sold most of his 70 head of whitefaced
cattle to the government and saw them slaughtered and buried in a ditch.
However, as times changed and crops became better, he was able to buy back
most of the land, has it paid for and he and Mrs. Sevrens spent the winter
of 1947-48 in California, Oregon and Washington visiting relatives and
friends, and had a wonderful time, but saw nothing that looked any better
than home in South Dakota. They have two sons, Fred B. of Santa Rosa,
California, and Earl L., who resides on the homestead of Mrs. Sevrens'
parents, Mr. and Mrs. J. E. Jenison. They have 7 grandchildren and 8
great-grandchildren Mr. Sevrens is 74 and she is 71 years young. They
celebrated their golden wedding in December, 1945.

Mrs. Cora Sevrens was born near Fillmore, Minnesota, January 5, 1878, and
resided there with her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Joseph E. Jenison until 1890
when the family came to Walworth county. She attended the Powell school, 4
miles away, for four terms and later attended what was known as the
Hanrahan (River) school and then the Byrne school which was 5 miles away.
Being the oldest in the family she helped a good deal with the outside work
on the farm and in the field, becoming used to handling horses and
machinery. In 1893 she carried mail for 3 months during summer between
LeBeau and the post office at Briscoe, near the present site of Lake
Molstad and the Skinner's ranch, which property is now owned by the
Carters', about a dozen miles north of Glenham, near the Missouri river.
She changed horses at the Carscallen place, 1-1/2, miles southeast of
Glenham. The trip was about 35 miles and took a day each way. At Skinner's
ranch she met another mail carrier, also a lady, who brought mail that far
from the north, both staying with Mr. and Mrs. Tom McKeever who had the
post office. At LeBeau, Mrs. Sevrens stayed with Mr. and Mrs. August
Siebrecht, who had the hotel there.

Mr. and Mrs. Sevrens are still very active members of the community and are
among the best boosters for Selby and for the Golden Jubilee.

In a reminiscent mood Mr. Sevrens observes: "When my widowed mother and her
family, including me, moved here from Brown county we were pretty well
fixed compared with many of the settlers. We had two cars of immigrant
goods consisting of household goods, six horses and one cow. Bowdle was the
end of the railroad until 1900 and we unloaded there. Arrangements were
made for building a house and storing some of the goods until the house was
built. I came with the emigrant cars, accompanied by Matt Hanrahan, the
allowance being one person for or with each car. The Hanrahans were our
neighbors in Brown county. My mother and the other children did not come
until later. She left all of the arrangements to her intended husband (J.
W. Davidson) and me, a lad of 11 years. I made the first trip to the new
home with a load of lumber, the stock, some bedding and two carpenters with
their tool chests. There was a pretty good log house on the place so we had
a place to stay. This trip was made on election day of 1888, the day Grover
Cleveland was first elected President. The house, 16x21 with ten foot
posts, was soon built. Matt and I helped as much as we could, did other
work around the place, hauling water for the stock and "batching it" taking
turns at the cooking. We had a cistern built, hauling the sand and a
homesteader by the name of Joe Young doing the mason work as well as
lathing and plastering the house.

        MR. AND MRS. PERCY SEVRENS

"My youngest brother, Gene, age 7, came out when we had the house up and he
and I spent the winter alone on the claim. We hauled water from Hanrahans a
couple of miles south, storing a supply in the cistern. There was quite a
group of young folks there and we went down quite often. We wintered the
stock on straw and native grazing. Luckily the winter was mild, with no
snow until March.

"The Indians over on the reservation were quite restless that winter and on
clear still days we could see smoke signals from the Fox Ridge country to
the southwest to the points of high land northwest along the Grand river,
which were said to be near Sitting Bull's camps. We noted this often until
the Indian scare of 1890.

"I remember that in November of 1890 the word was passed that the Indians
were coming and most people left, and we went with them, staying at Bowdle
three days, returning when nothing happened. After the death of Sitting
Bull it quieted down some. But for safety the Government sent out a lot of
old 50-70 Springfield rifles that had been used some but were accurate
shooters and would carry a long distance. A company was formed that used to
meet at Hanrahans for practice and drill but never got a chance at an
Indian and after a while the rifles were returned.

"The first schoolhouse in the district was built on the northeast corner
of mother's land and was known as the Powell school.

"For fuel we hauled wood from the island when water was low so we could
cross,--the channel was on the west side then. People came for miles for it
and by the time the railroad came and Evarts was started, the island was
pretty well cleared of timber. The timber that is there now has grown since
then."

GEORGE AND E. F. SEBERT

I, E.F. Sebert, was born November 25, 1892, in Spring Lake township,
Walworth county, South Dakota.

My parents, Mr. and Mrs. George Sebert, came to Dakota territory from Dane
county, Wisconsin, arriving in 1883 and "squatting" on a homestead north of
Ipswich, until the railroad built west to Bowdle in 1886.

Water being hard to find in the Ipswich vicinity, my father together with
Joe Stangl, Wm. H. Payne, and the Erbe brothers decided to move to a
location west of Bowdle in the Spring lake vicinity. There he filed on a
homestead and established the home in which I was born. In 1889 he returned
to Wisconsin and was married to Katherine Hessman on February 27, 1889. She
was raised in Mazomance, Wisconsin, not far from where father was born.
Mother's parents came to America from Austria, after a woman frying out
lard in a large iron kettle started a fire that burned their home,--so they
decided to come to America and settled in Wisconsin. When mother was old
enough to work out she worked in a knitting factory for several years. Then
she and a cousin went to Colorado Springs, Colorado and worked for wealthy
Eastern people, who had homes there. These people whom mother cooked for,
employed everything from a coachman to a Negro washwoman. Mother returned
to Wisconsin, got married and came to live on the Dakota homestead, in
almost a wilderness (some change).

        MR. AND MRS. E. F. SEBERT

Father's parents came from Northern Germany. Family tradition has it that
one of father's ancestors worked for Martin Luther, when he left the
Catholics and started the Lutheran Church. Father's grandfather was a
Lutheran bishop, who made plans to have all his sons become ministers of
the Lutheran faith. My grandfather never got to be a minister--he married
one of his father's servant girls. She was considered below his rank and
this kind of marriage was frowned upon. They were kicked out. She had
relatives in this country who lived in Wisconsin. So they journeyed to
Milwaukee, where they purchased a team of oxen and drove west to the Blue
Mounds not far from Madison, Wisconsin, where father was born and grew to
manhood.

There is nothing spectacular thus far about my life. I, like many others of
my age, took over where the original pioneers left off and tried to do my
small part in continuing the development of Walworth county. When I was old
enough I attended a country school located about 2-1/2 miles from home. We
walked to school whether the weather was fair or stormy. Rural schools in
those days usually consisted of two terms a year. Beginning in the fall and
continuing until the weather became too severe to allow attendance, then
closing until the arrival of warm spring weather and continuing until well
into June. This practice discontinued when enough schools were built. Edith
Baumgarten, a daughter of Mrs. George Baumgarten of Selby, was one of my
teachers. Shortly after completing school I taught a term of school in
Adams township and the next fall in Glenn district.

In the fall of 1914 I went to Montana and filed on a 320 acre homestead
about 20 miles southeast of Lewistown, in the foothills of the Snowy
mountains where ranching is the main industry. Up to the time we went to
Montana, the large ranchers were very much opposed to homesteaders coming
in and taking up the land in their pastures and used various means to
discourage and run them out. My homestead was in the horse pasture of one
of these ranchers. We were not bothered and after about a year I spent all
my spare time working for this rancher.

I established residence on the homestead, returned to South Dakota and
before returning the next year, I was united in marriage with Amelia
Stangl, who like myself grew up in the Spring lake neighborhood, walked a
long ways to school and had plenty of early morning duties to finish before
she could go to school.

We were married May 11, 1915 and a few days later accompanied by my cousin,
Frank Tinker, I left for Montana in an emigrant car containing four horses,
some machinery and other supplies and equipment. My wife followed a month
later. On arrival my cousin and I went to work moving our equipment out to
the homestead and getting a 14x16 house built, a barn, and some fencing
done. We had quite a time as it rained 21 days out of the first 23 days we
were there.

My brother came with another emigrant car, loaded with milk cows. After a
few days with us he and my cousin left for home and my wife and I continued
the work of building up our homestead. After a year or so I found that the
altitude was too high for me and that I couldn't live there so in 1918 we
sold out and returned to South Dakota.

In 1919 I purchased the farm on which we live, taking possession that fall
and moving here the next spring. In 1936 we started a dairy, serving the
city of Selby for 8 years. Labor and gasoline shortages caused by the war
forced us to discontinue the business and farm on a diversified basis.
Since living here I have served on a few minor boards and committees: the
County Welfare board during the depression, where old age assistance was
first set up, on the F.S.A. board, and the Farm Bureau board that appointed
the first Walworth county A.A.A. committee. I have been a member of the
Selby Equity Union board of directors for a number of years. This brings me
up to date.

        MR. AND MRS. GEORGE SEBERT

Father started turning over the virgin sod with two horses and an ox
hitched to his plow. He was also proud that his homestead and tree claim
are two of the few tracts of land in the county that never were mortgaged
or tax delinquent. Mr. and Mrs. George Sebert moved into Selby in I929.
Father died on Good Friday, 1942. Mother still lives in Selby as this is
written.

I would like to mention a few things I remember about pioneer days.

One fall Dad couldn't get his grain threshed before winter set in. He had
no money with which to buy coal until he had some wheat to sell. My folks
like many others had to depend upon a straw burner to heat their home. Dad
didn't want to burn his wheat. I remember Mother, my brother, and I with
our coats, mittens and overshoes on huddled around a little four-lid cook
stove, my brother sitting in the oven, while dad gathered dry manure to try
and keep us warm and cook our meals. They had to burn some grain before
they finally got the grain threshed.

There was a continuous stream of horse-drawn traffic on the Bangor road,
now U. S. Highway 12, before the railroad built west from Bowdle. The
traffic was mostly people hauling their products to Bowdle.

Grain was all hauled in sacks, unloaded onto a small scale by hand and then
wheeled on a hand truck to the far end of the flat house where the grain
was bought and stored. The farmer had to unload and dump his own grain
which became real labor as the house filled up and he had to push the hand
truck up a plank runway to the top of the pile of grain before he could
empty his sacks. If I remember right, a man named Strobel rigged up the
first elevating device in his flat house. He used a horse for power. The
old flat houses were soon thereafter torn down and replaced with elevators
similar to the ones we now have.

Small railroad engines pulled the trains to Bowdle, and on arrival the
engineer would run the engine on the turn table, blow the whistle for help,
then all hands would push on the sweeps and turn the engine around.

I can remember the Standard Oil wagon tank drawn by four mules taking
kerosene and greases to Bangor.

Outside of apples, fruit wasn't plentiful in those days, and when harvest
was over the neighbors would set a day to make a fruit gathering trip to
the Missouri river flats and gulches and gather a supply of wild plums,
grapes, and buffalo berries, from which my mother used to make up a years
supply of jell and jam.

I remember the great number of prairie chickens and grouse the dogs used to
find on the way to and from the river.

The outline of the race track which the Bangor race horse fans built, can
still be seen in a field near the old townsite.

Here is a story my father told about the night of the great Indian scare
that sent hundreds of people to Bowdle. The wife of a homesteader named
Alne was holding down a claim on the north end of Spring lake, near the
Bangor road, during the absence of her husband. She heard team after team
passing along the road all night, and became quite excited but no one
thought to let her know about the Indians. When she found out the next day
that all the neighbors were gone, and had left her there alone, she packed
their belongings and left, never again to return. This land later became Joe
Stangl's as he placed a preemption on the land.

Father also told of the wives of two neighbors digging a well 40 feet deep
by hand while their men were away working near Aberdeen.

During the time of the great blizzard of January 12, 1888, my father was
batching on his homestead. He had a barrel of stock salt standing near the
house, as he would look out of the house from time to time he could see the
entire barrel,--the next time he looked it was entirely buried in snow. The
storm hit early in the morning, and people were still home and there were no
casualties.

I remember my father telling of one time he and a friend thought they would
like a job as teamsters on the wagon train that hauled supplies from Pierre
to Dead. wood in about 1884. They walked from Ipswich to Pierre and applied
to the agent for a job. He quizzed them as to their qualifications and
being satisfied told them to stick around until the wagon train arrived in
a few days and he would have a job for them, as someone was always quitting
his job. Several days later they heard a great racket, shooting, and
yelling. Approaching town was the wagon train. When they got a good look at
the outfit their spirits fell. Those boys were a tough looking, dirty,
unshaved, gun-packing crew that weren't backing up for anything. Dad and
his partner, deciding they didn't care to work on the wagon train, bought
themselves a few provisions and started out on foot for Bismarck. They ran
out of water and might have died had they not found a low place with a
little water still in it. That changed their minds and they returned to
Ipswich.

I remember a great celebration staged at Evarts. The railroad ran an
excursion train out from Chicago, giving people all the way along the line
a chance to see the greatest primary cattle shipping point in the United
States. The promoters advertised bronc riding, roping, racing, and war
dancing by the Indians. The Indians were given a few beeves to butcher so
the easterners could see how it was done Indian style. The excursion train
unloaded a great crowd and Evarts was swamped with people. We kids all had
a great time.

I remember the old Bangor band when they played at celebrations and picnics
and hearing my folks talk about the group of men that left Bangor to take
part in the Spanish American war; the sinking of the battle ship Maine and
of Admiral Dewey and others; the first crude gasoline engine and
automobiles; the Wright brothers and the first plane that would fly and the
many things that came later to help make our country what it is today.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN K. SCHAUER

John K. Schauer was born at Neudorf, Russia, on October 1, 1889, the son of
Carl Schauer and his wife, Carolina Helm. He left Liverpool, England, on
March 13, 1909, on the English commercial liner, Laxonia, and arrived at
Boston on March 18, 1909. One brother. Jacob Schauer, preceded him to the
United States and made homestead entry near Hettinger, North Dakota. This
was young John's destination upon arrival in this country. Schauer's
parents were very poor but his father had managed to save enough money with
which to purchase John's passage to this country and that was about all.
