When John arrived at his brother's farm, he had only $2.50 with which he
purchased a pair of shoes.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHN K. SCHAUER

Schauer spent his first summer at his brother's farm and then went to
Ashley, North Dakota, to live with his uncle, Jacob Schauer. He remained
there until the summer of 1910 and then again returned to Hettinger where
he farmed with his brother until the winter of 1912. During this time he
made several trips to the Java vicinity to visit his uncles, Fred Helm,
Ludwig Helm and Christ Helm. During these visits he became acquainted with
Christine Wagner, the daughter of Johan Wagner, another Selby pioneer, and
they were married at Selby oh February 12, 1912. Mrs. Schauer was born at
Borodino, Bessarabia, in South Russia, on July 31, 1890, and came to the
United States in 1894 with her parents. The family first lived near Bowdle
and later acquired a farm two miles north of Selby.

Mr. and Mrs. Schauer spent the first year of their married life farming
near Hettinger, and then sold their holdings and moved to the Selby
vicinity and continued farming. They lived on the Gottfried Wagner farm,
now occupied by Emil Wagner, for six years and then lived on the Johann
Dupper farm for two years, before purchasing their present farm home from
Emanuel Baer in 1920. In 1946, the Schauers purchased the two quarter
sections formerly owned by Johann Dupper and in 1948 they purchased the old
Johan Wagner farm, consisting of two quarter sections, from Adolf Stangl.
The Schauers now own five quarters of land as one farming unit.

The Schauers have three children: Gerhardt Schauer, born in September,
1914, who now lives at Aberdeen, South Dakota, and is prominent in Boy
Scout work, and is employed by the Nelson Auto Electric company; Milton
Schauer, born in March, 1919, who lives at home and farms with his parents;
and Irma Steder, born in January, 1922, who lives with her husband on the
old Johann Wagner farm purchased by the Schauers in 1948.

The life itinerary of the Schauer family is typical of other families who
settled in the Selby vicinity during 1912, or that approximate date. Some
years, crops and prices were good and some years crops were good and prices
were low. Some years crops were poor and prices were low. Those were the
worst years. Schauer recalls 1921, 1933 and 1934 as being the worst years
of his farming operations. The years during and immediately after World War
I and World War II were the best years.

John Schauer's parents both died in Russia during the early thirties. One
brother, Fred Schauer, came to the United States in 1914. He was killed in
France during World War I and the American Legion post at Selby is named in
his honor. Two sisters also came to the United States but four sisters
remained in Russia.

John Schauer and his family are happy in their farm life. They continue to
be active on the farm and enjoy their children and grandchildren. Selby is
proud of this typical farm family.

MR. JOHN J. SCHANZENBACH SR.

John J. Schanzenbach Sr., was born in Gluecksthal, South Russia, on May 31,
1868, to Katharine (nee Kaul) Schanzenbach and Johan Schanzenbach.

It was not possible for Mr. Schanzenbach to go to school. At an early age
he had to help earn-the family living. The education he secured was gained
in going to Sunday school, Confirmation school and through his own efforts
to learn.

At the age of 20 he was married to Magdalene Lippert. In the old country
farms were small and there was little chance for advancement, but they
remained in Russia until 1893, when having heard repeatedly of new hopes
and promises of a free land with fortune and ad venture awaiting one, Mr.
and Mrs. John Schanzenbach, with their family of three small sons, John,
now of Mobridge; Jake, now of Selby; and Rudolph, deceased, and one other
family, by the name of Goodyear, started for America, making the journey in
seven days.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHN J. SCHANZENBACH SR.

Upon arrival they stayed a short while with a brother-in-law of Mr.
Schanzenbach, Jacob Lippert, until their claim of land was filed on their
homestead, 3-1/2 miles north of Eureka. Their story varies little from that
of hundreds of others who landed here. with nothing and battled hardships,
blizzards, Indian scares and other grave problems.

In winter it was necessary for Mr. Schanzenbach to work at odd jobs and
many times he wished he could return to his old country, but because of
lack of finances was forced to forget and work harder.

It wasn't too long until things began to look brighter and all thoughts of
ever wanting to return to their old home vanished.

Six more children were born to this now happy family: Lydia, now of Wapato,
Wash.; Christ of Leola; Katharina Schilling, deceased; Dan of Leola; and
twin boys (deceased).

The family remained on this homestead until March 10, 1905, when Mr. and
Mrs. Schanzenbach with their nine children moved to a farm 4 miles
northeast of Akaska. In April, one month later, the mother passed away.

Later he married Mrs. Katherina Ritter Oster, widow of Johann Oster, and
who had also emigrated to the United States from Gluecksthal, South Russia,
in August of 1893 and settled on a homestead near Bowdle.

In November, 1910, Mr. Schanzenbach in company with his two
brothers-in-law, John and Jacob Keim of Eureka, made a return trip to their
old homeland in South Russia, for a 3 months' visit. This time the trip took
them 9 days, and on their return they encountered stormy weather which
prolonged the voyage to 12 days. Upon returning the big question was,
"Would you like to return to Russia to live?" The answer to this was
decidedly no.

In November, 1916, the family moved from the farm to Selby where Mr. and
Mrs. Schanzenbach had a small milk route until 1936.

To this couple four sons were born: Henry of Seattle, Washington; Edward,
Emil, and Ted of Selby.

On April 24, 1945, Mr. Schanzenbach met with a serious accident. While
helping John Theis plant potatoes beside the railroad tracks, a train
passed through town, the horses became frightened and bolted, running over
Mr. Schanzenbach and severely injuring him. He never recovered to any great
extent and was confined to bed much of the time. On April 22, 1949, two
days less than four years since he suffered the misfortune, he passed away
at the age of 80 years, 10 months and 21 days.
He was laid to rest in the Selby cemetery.

MR. AND MRS. OLE OPHEIM

Ole Opheim was a native of Norway. He was born on June 23, 1860, in Aal,
Hallingdal, and spent his early life there. His was not the carefree
childhood that children of today enjoy. At an early age he had to support
himself by herding cattle, doing odd jobs, working on farms and later by
carpenter work. His education was limited to a few months of schooling each
winter which consisted mainly of reading, arithmetic and religion. These
early hardships might have been an incentive for his eventual immigration
to America, where he hoped to find an outlet for his high hopes and
ambitions.

        MR. AND MRS. OLE OPHEIM

In the spring of 1886 he married Aagot Torpe, a young girl of 18, who was
also born and raised in Aal, Hallingdal, Norway. She was the oldest of
seven children. Her parents owned a farm and she had enjoyed a fairly happy
childhood. Usually the summers were spent herding cattle. Shortly after
their marriage, they immigrated to America. Mrs. Opheim had a bachelor
uncle, Erick Rikansrud, who owned a farm in Lincoln county, South Dakota.
It was to him they went first. He was glad to have her as housekeeper while
Mr. Opheim secured work among the farmers in the neighborhood.

After two years of frugal living and saving, they decided to strike out on
their own. They came to Campbell county and bought 160 acres of land with a
one room sod house, for a small sum of money. Only three acres were under
cultivation. Good crops were realized that first year. These earnings,
supplemented by wages earned working for the neighbors, enabled them to buy
two oxen and a plow so more land could be broken. They also bought a cow
and a calf. Four hens and a brood of chicks were given them by a kind
neighbor. During his spare time, Mr. Opheim, who was handy with tools,
built the necessary furniture, such as table, chairs, and cupboards. A
spinning wheel built by him, although much used, is still in good condition
and will probably be placed in a museum some day.

As the family increased, it became necessary to move into a larger sod
house. This house burned down shortly and a four-room frame house on an
adjoining farm was purchased and moved over. This was one of the first
frame houses in the locality. Incidentally, it is still standing on its
original site and is being used for storing grain. Oxen and walking plows
were used in breaking up the land. This entailed a great deal of hard labor
and long hours of work. Grain had to be hauled by oxen or horses to Bowdle,
a distance of 45 miles, and exchanged for flour and other groceries. Like
all pioneers in a new country they had many hardships to endure.

Fourteen children were born to this union, 9 boys and 5 girls. Sickness and
death entered their home. Four boys died in infancy, one at the age of 19
and one at the age of 31. A daughter died at the age of 51.

By thrift and hard work they gradually acquired more land and livestock,
and finally became quite prosperous. In 1908 a new home was built about a
mile from their original place. Railroad towns had sprung up within 12
miles and soon tractors and automobiles came into use. Roads and fences
were built. Better schools and mail service and telephones eventually
became a reality.

Their golden wedding anniversary was observed in 1936. Mrs. Opheim is a
charter member of the Bethany Lutheran church in Walworth county and so was
Mr. Opheim while he lived.

Mr. Opheim passed away on October 4, 1944, at the age of 84. Mrs. Opheim is
enjoying fairly good health at the age of 81. She spends her summers at the
farm and her winters in the Black Hills in the homes of her children.
Surviving children are: Gena and Oscar of Mound City, Mrs. A. M. Bender
(Alma) of Sturgis, Clara and Edward of Hot Springs; Olaf of Kansas City,
Missouri; and Mrs. Ted Carter (Hilda) of Lead.

DR. MELVIN W. MYLER, D. D. S.

Dr. Myler opened an office for the practice of dentistry in Selby early in
the year 1906, in a small office on Main street in the Schaffer building,
opposite the Prann drug store. When the opera house was built he took the
office now occupied by the Selby library, later moving to the building
known now as the Vail building. In the autumn of 1913 he sold his practice
to a former classmate, Dr. G. W. Vail, and moved to Mitchell where he
practiced his profession for 10 years when he again disposed of his
business and moved to Alhambra, California, where he still practices part
time.

        DR. AND MRS. M. W. MYLER

In Selby, Dr. Myler was clerk of the school board when the first new school
house was built (the present grade school ), the other members of the board
being H. P. Gutz and Albert H. Smith. He was also a member of the City
Council, serving at the time when the first water works system was
installed.

Dr. Myler came to Selby as a young man just out of the dental school of the
University of Iowa. Being civic-minded, he immediately identified himself
with all of the local movements for the progress and betterment of the city
and is well remembered by older residents as one of those who played a most
important part in the early progress of the community. Incidentally, he
earned himself an enviable reputation in his profession of dentistry.

ALEXANDER McKINNON FAMILY

Alexander McKinnon was born in Scotland and came to America at the age of
nine, with his parents, who settled north of Toronto, Canada, where they
cleared a farm. Alexander left this home and came to the United States
during the Civil war. He remained in Buffalo a short time before locating
in Chicago, where he was engaged in the insurance business, associated with
the Etna Life Insurance company. Later, he and his brother worked in the
post office department, repairing mail sacks.

During his residence in Chicago, Mr. McKinnon met Jane Carruthers, who was
born and reared in Kingston, Canada, and after completing her education,
had come to Chicago to visit a sister. They were married at the home of her
parents in Kingston, May 24, 1869, on

Queen Victoria's birthday, and established their home in Chicago. Four
children were born to them in Chicago: Alexander M.; William D.; Arthur A.,
who died at the age of 4-1/2 years; and Jessie C.

Mr. McKinnon's health began to fail, so, in 1883, he and his family left
the crowded city and came to Dakota territory, to seek relief in the wide
open spaces. He filed on a homestead on the W 1/2 of 3-122-78 in Walworth
county, where they engaged mostly in stock-raising. It was on this
homestead that their fifth child, Margaret C., was born. Mr. McKinnon's
health continued to fail, and in February, 1894, he passed away, and was
laid to rest in the Bangor cemetery. Following his death, Mrs. McKinnon and
the children continued to live on the homestead.

William D. prepared himself for the teaching profession, and after teaching
several rural schools, held the position of principal of the Evarts school
for the year 1900-1901. In 1901 he was engaged to teach the upper grades in
the Selby school, but at the end of the first month he became ill, and in a
very few days he passed away. He was laid to rest beside his father in the
Bangor cemetery.

In 1904, Mrs. McKinnon and the family sold the stock on the homestead and
moved to Evarts, where they built a new home. She was appointed postmaster
at Evarts and held that position during the closing days of that town. The
following year Alexander M. moved to Glenham where he was engaged as
manager of the Wrigley lumber yard, which was just starting. He continued
this work for five years. During this time Evarts had broken up and the
family had moved to Glenham. Alexander was appointed postmaster at Glenham
during the time he managed the lumber yard, and was assisted in the post
office by his sister, Jessie, until he completed his work in the yard. Then
he took full charge of the post office with the telephone office in
connection. This position he held for nearly 30 years, until he was retired
by the post office department March 31, 1940.

        MR. AND MRS. ALEXANDER McKINNON

Jessie C. became one of Walworth county's teachers while living on the
homestead, and outside of the time she helped her brother in the post
office, she continued teaching in rural schools and in Evarts and Glenham,
until her mother's health began to fail, when she remained at home to care
for her. Mrs. McKinnon passed away December 18, 1935, due to infirmities of
age, leaving a host of friends who loved her for her many good deeds. She
was laid to rest in the Glenham cemetery, in accordance with a wish
expressed by her while she was alive. Mrs. McKinnon's death was a severe
shock to Jessie whose health now began to fail, and after several years of
almost helplessness, she passed away January 7, 1944. She was laid to rest
beside her mother in the Glenham cemetery.

Margaret C. chose teaching as her profession, and after graduation from
Northern State Teachers college in Aberdeen, she attended State college in
Brookings. She taught primary work in several cities in South Dakota and
later taught English and home economics in high schools of the state, with,
the exception of some years when she remained at home to help care for her
sister Jessie. She is making her home in Aberdeen at present.

On October 3, 1925, Alexander M. was married to Gertrude A. Hough, daughter
of the late James M. Hough and his wife, Tena O. She is a graduate of
Northern State Teachers college in Aberdeen and taught several years in
rural schools and in Glenham. Mr. and Mrs. Alexander M. McKinnon continue
to live in Glenham and enjoy the fellowship of a large circle of friends.

Throughout the years Mr. McKinnon has served the community in many
non-remunerative capacities for the general good of the community in which
he, resided.

MAJOR GENERAL VERNE D. MUDGE

Major General Verne D. Mudge, who was born near Bangor, South Dakota,
September 5, 1898, has won distinction for himself and the state through
his achievements in the regular army.

His father and mother, Mr. and Mrs. Richard Mudge, were early pioneers in
South Dakota and their names are well known to anyone familiar with the
early history of the west.

In 1900 the Mudge family moved from Bangor to Evarts, South Dakota, where
Mr. Mudge was engaged in cattle ranching. Subsequently the family moved to
Iowa and then to Florida where the remaining members of the family still
live.

Verne Mudge went to grammar school in Evarts and to high school in Sioux
City, Iowa. He attended the University of Florida for two years prior to
attending the United States Military Academy at West Point from which
latter institution he was graduated in 1920. Upon his graduation he was
commissioned in the cavalry and has served with that arm continuously ever
since. His peace-time service was uneventful. He attended the Cavalry
school, the Command and General Staff school, and the Army War college. At
the onset of World War II he was on duty with the Personnel Division of the
War Department General Staff. He was then transferred to become Chief of
Staff of the 1st Cavalry Division. He served with that division throughout
the war.

He was appointed Brigadier General in 1943 and assumed command of the 2nd
Cavalry Brigade. He commanded that brigade in the invasion of the
Admiralties, and participated in the assault of Manus, Hauwei and Pityliu
Island as well as several smaller islands in that archipelago. Shortly
after the close of the Admiralty campaign, General Mudge was promoted to
Major General and assumed command of the division. He was in command of the
division when it spear-headed the attack of General MacArthur's forces to
the Philippines. The division landed on Leyte, and within 46 hours had
seized the city of Tacloban, which was the first Philippine capital to be
recaptured by the United States troops. General Mudge was awarded the.
bronze star for his actions in the Admiralty Islands. He was awarded the
Legion of Merit and the Silver Star on Leyte.

In the midst of the Leyte operation the 1st Cavalry Division was withdrawn
and sent to Luzon Island, where it landed on Lingayan Gulf about three
weeks after the initial assault had been made. Thereafter began one of the
most spectacular operations in the Southwest Pacific--the movement of the
1st Cavalry Division into Manila. The division occupied Manila exactly one
week after it invaded Lingayan Gulf. About a week thereafter, General Mudge
was seriously wounded by a Japanese grenade during the fighting in the
vicinity of Antipolo. He was hospitalized as a result of this wound and at
the present date is still a patient in Walter Reed General Hospital,
Washington, D. C.

He was awarded the Distinguished Service Cross for gallantry in action in
Rizal Stadium, Manila, where he dashed across an open, fire-swept area to
rescue a wounded corporal of his command. During the Luzon operation he was
also awarded the Distinguished Service Medal, the Air Medal, and the Purple
Heart.

In 1924 he married Miss Hortense Short, daughter of Brigadier General
Walter C. Short. Their present residence is Washington, D. C., where
General Mudge is on duty in the office of the Secretary of War. They have
no children.

Before he was wounded in the service of his country, General Mudge was an
enthusiastic polo player and a splendid rider at the horse shows.

MR. AND MRS. JACOB MATHISON

Jacob Mathison was born in the southern part of Norway near Felkkefjord, on
January 18, 1869. His boyhood was spent attending school in the winter and
herding sheep in the summer.

In the spring of 1889, at the age of 20, he started for America and arrived
in Woonsocket, South Dakota, on May 1, 1889. In October of that same year
he and his cousin, Isaac went to Tacoma, Washington, and worked in the coal
mines around Issaquah. When that work slackened they went back to
Woonsocket, South Dakota, in August of 1893.

Jake worked on farms for a couple of years and then started to work on the
railroad as a section hand. The roadmaster called him to work as head
spiker on a steel gang laying steel from Bowdle to Selby in 1900. There
were no buildings in Selby at that time, but several were moved in from
Bangor and a section house and railroad station were built. Three months
later he was put in charge of a section gang working from Selby east. It is
said that one time the Russian thistles piled so high in that big cut east
of Selby that the train couldn't make it through until it pushed forward
and backward several times.

        MR. AND MRS. JACOB MATHISON

While in Woonsocket, Mr. Mathison joined the Odd Fellows lodge and later in
Selby, Dr. Gunderman persuaded him to join the United Workmen. In June of
1900 Jake's sister, Inger, and Sophie Torgerson arrived from Norway. Jake
took his sister to Bangor to file claim on a homestead northwest of Selby.
She kept house for him while he lived in Selby. Later she met and married
Jake Tisdall.

With only $45 a month as section foreman, Jake Mathison decided to look for
higher pay and went to Washington in 1903, where he worked in the harvest
for a few months before getting a job as section foreman on the OR&N, later
the Union Pacific, at $57.50 a month.

In January of 1904, Mr. Mathison married Sophie Torgerson of Walla Walla,
Washington. They moved to Starbuck where they lived for four years before
moving to Ferry county in northeast Washington. Here they homesteaded and
farmed a 320-acre place for twelve years.

At that time their oldest children were ready for high school and the
family moved to Snohomish where Mr. Mathison has had a dairy farm for many
years. The eldest son is an instrumentation engineer at Boeing's in
Seattle, one son is rural mail carrier in Snohomish and another is a
machinist in the Bremerton Navy yard. Both daughters are married, one
living in Bremerton and the other in Snohomish. Mr. and Mrs. Mathison have
been active Grange members for many years.

JEROME B. WEBB AND FAMILY

Jerome B. Webb was born at Williamston, Michigan, in 1870. When he was
fourteen he moved to Day county, South Dakota, with his parents.

In 1892 he met and married Sina Jacobson who came to Day county in 1891.
She was born near Bergen, Norway, in 1873. Immediately after their marriage
they moved to Walworth county and settled on a homestead about 2 miles
northwest of Bangor. Their only possessions when they arrived were a team
of horses and wagon and a few household goods.

During the years they lived there sickness, blizzards, hail drouth and even
fire took their toll. Their struggle for livelihood was a heartbreaking and
backbreaking one. Most of the living had to be raised as money was scarce.
However, they always managed a good living for the family they reared
there. Mr. Webb hauled wood from the river in a wagon or on a sleigh. The
trips were hard and long. He would leave home about 3:30 a.m., and if his
luck was good would return in less than 24 hours. Once it snowed so hard he
couldn't make it with the sleigh so he unhitched and dragged several logs
the balance of the way, as he knew the fuel was low.

        MR. AND MRS. J. B. WEBB

Seven children were born to Mr. and Mrs. Webb: William (known as Bill) in
1893; Golda in 1895; Ed in 1897; Joseph in 1900, Dora in 1903; Elinore in
1909; and Kenneth in 1912.

In 1897, when Ed was 2 weeks old, their home burned to the ground. They
saved only a few articles of clothing and household goods. They moved their
family into a shack owned by Frank Erickson while they built a 3-room sod
house. The children attended the Tisdall school and the Blue Blanket
school. They joined the Methodist church as Mr. Webb did not speak
Norwegian, although Mrs. Webb had been raised as a Norwegian Lutheran. The
family took part in other neighborhood affairs as well as church. Both Mr.
and Mrs. Webb helped care for the sick and often sat up with the dead. As
did all pioneers they lent a helping hand whenever it was needed.

They farmed the homestead until the spring of 1904 when a 5-day rain came.
The roof of their sod house literally opened up and let the rain in on
them. Mrs. Webb had to take the oil cloth from the table to cover the baby,
Dora, and she was the only one who kept dry. They had already purchased the
Howell farm so moved there as soon as the rain permitted. Here they lived in
the house where the former Blue Blanket post office was located.

One year their barn and 40 tons of hay burned. That afternoon Mr. Webb went
to Selby and purchased lumber. The next day the neighbors formed a building
bee and made a good start on a new barn.

Another winter during a severe blizzard Mr. Webb went to the Blue Blanket
school and brought all the children and the teacher home and kept them
until the weather cleared so he could get them to their homes.

Many of the incidents of their lives, while tragic at the time, are
laughable in retrospect. Once while Bill and Golda, about 8 and 7 years old
at the time, were in school 2 miles away a hard wind came up. Mrs. Webb was
afraid to let them come home alone and afraid to leave the younger children
alone at home. Fear for the two alone on the road prevailed so she put out
the fire in the cook stove, drove stakes into the ground, threw ropes over
the storm shed and tied it down securely. Taking a pitchfork to brace
herself she went to meet the children. They hung onto her, one on each
side. Bill was carrying a lunch basket on his arm. An extra strong gust of
wind came and lifted a heavy cup from the basket and whirled it through the
air in circles.

During the winter of 1912 and 1913 Bill and Golda taught school in Campbell
county.

In the spring of 1913 the family moved to Townsend, Montana, where Golda
taught school and Mr. and Mrs. Webb farmed and later operated a restaurant
in Townsend. In 1919 the family moved to Spokane, Washington, where Mr.
Webb passed away in 1931 following a long illness. Mrs. Webb still resides
in Spokane. She is now 76 years of age, takes an active part in Lutheran
church affairs and is a members of the Sons of Norway lodge. She has her
own home at West 2014 College avenue.

All 7 children are living. Bill is married and has 4 children, all married
and living in Washington state. Bill lives at Clarkston, Washington. Though
badly disabled by a back injury received in the shipyards during the war,
he takes an active part in civic, political and lodge affairs.

Golda is married and lives in Spokane and has 6 living children. Two sons
are in the U. S. Army, one in Japan and the other in Georgia. The other 4
live in Washington and Idaho.

Ed is married, has no children and lives in Aberdeen, Washington. He owns
and operates a restaurant there.

Joe is married and has 2 sons. He lives in Seattle, Washington, where he is
engaged in the salvage business.

Dora is married and widowed. She has a daughter and now operates a boarding
house in Spokane.

Elinore is married and has 2 daughters. She lives at Moyie Springs, Idaho.

Kenneth is married and resides in Seattle, Washington, where he is employed
by General Mills.

MR. LOAN J. WALTER

Loan Walter was born November 24, 1860, at Clarkston, Michigan. He was the
youngest in a family of seven children.

He arrived in Walworth county in April in 1882, at the age of 22 years. He
came with the intention of making a permanent home and filed on a
pre-emption and a tree claim. After proving up his land he sold out and
went back east to complete his education, later returning to Dakota.

Loan Walter was a graduate of Michigan Normal college. He taught country
and high schools at Royal Oak and Ortonville, Michigan, and was
superintendent of schools at Brookings, South Dakota. Later he came back to
Selby where he taught school for several years.

He married Jenny Whipple of Royal Oak, Michigan, when he was 26 years of
age. They have seven children, four girls and three boys. Two of his
children married while living here. His son, Clark, married Constance
Paulson and Florence married Will Mickelson (they now live in Detroit).

On his return to Dakota, Loan Walter filed on a homestead and bought the
land which is now known as the Secker farm. Here he carried on his farming
and ranching activities. He later sold the farm and went to Canada, where
he lived about ten years, then he went back to Michigan.

Loan Walter is a member of the Methodist Episcopal church and of the
Masonic Lodge. Mrs. Walter passed away several years ago. Mr. Walter is now
89 years old. In recent years he has been spending his summers in
Peekskill, New York, and flies to Miami, Florida, to spend the winter.

MR. AND MRS. IRA B. NILES

Ira B. Niles was born at Chester, Michigan, on April 2, 1874, and at the
age of twelve, came with his parents to Walworth county, where they settled
on a claim in Brown township. Shortly afterward he left home, going to
Webster, South Dakota, where he spent his early man hood, and in June,
1895, was united in marriage with Elizabeth Kraft. Mrs. Niles was born on
June 20, 1876, in Strasburg, Russia, and as a small child her parents
brought her to the vicinity of Loyalton, South Dakota, where they endured
many hardships during the severe winters of those days. During her early
womanhood, she spent some time with the Senator Pickler family at Faulkton,
South Dakota, and later went to Webster, where she met Ira B. Niles and
where they were married.

        MR. IRA B. NILES

Shortly after their marriage, the Niles family moved to Walworth county and
on the Wilson land northwest of LeBeau, with the intention of doing cattle
ranching. However, when the railroad came as far as Selby, the building
boom brought Mr. Niles there to work at his trade, that of a carpenter and
inside finisher. The family moved to Selby on May 6, 1904, and in the years
that followed, Mr. Niles built many of the homes and other buildings in the
Selby and McLaughlin areas, including the Selby Episcopal church (now the
Congregational church), and did the finishing work on the Walworth county
court house and assisted in the erection of buildings for the government on
the Standing Rock Indian reservation. He passed away after a lingering
illness in 1939 at his home in Selby and is laid to rest in the Selby Union
cemetery.

Upon the arrival of the family in Selby, Mrs. Niles became an active member
of the Methodist church and the ladies aid society. In this association she
spent many pleasant hours and became well known in the community for the
many beautiful quilts she made or assisted in making. After the death of
her husband, she remained in Selby for a number of years but in 1946
disposed of her property and has since lived with her children, all of whom
grew up in Selby and received their education there. During her many years
in Selby, Mrs. Niles humbly served her church and community and is loved
and respected by her many friends still there.

The children of Ira B., and Elizabeth Niles are: Harold, now living in San
Jose, Calif.; Clarence, of Fargo, N. D., where he operates a farm implement
store; Harvey, of Watertown, S. D., where he manages a branch office of the
International Harvester company; Ira, now of Milwaukee, Wisconsin, who is
employed by the Allis Chalmers company as an electrical worker; Mrs. Beryl
Bacon of Faulkton, S. D.; and Mrs. Frances Drayton of Ronan, Montana. There
are also seven grandchildren and two great grandchildren.

MR. AND MRS. AUGUST VOY

Caroline Voy was born in Germany July 17, 1845 and died October 29, 1935 at
her farm home northwest of Akaska. Several children were born to Mr. and
Mrs. Voy but all died in infancy except one daughter, Flora (Mrs. H. B.
Thornton) who died May 25, 1935.

With her husband she ran a tailor shop in Milwaukee Wisconsin but was lured
to the west by the promises of a homestead. They came to Walworth county in
the fall of 1883, while the surveyors were still at work, and filed on the
land where they resided until they died. When they came they were
inexperienced farmers with no farm equipment not even a team. Old LeBeau was
their nearest town and they frequently carried their flour, groceries, and
their mail from there on their backs, a distance of about 15 miles. They
lived through all the real hardships of pioneering--sickness, drouth, hail,
fire, and long hard winters with snowbound roads, but they possessed those
qualities that made them persevere. Although often dismayed they never gave
up.

Mrs. Voy's life was an unusually busy and useful one. The great work she
will be remembered most by was her willing service in times of sickness.
For many miles around there were but few families who did not call for
"Grandma Voy" and she always went. Through summer's heat or winter's cold
even in blizzards, she went when called, ministering to all alike to the
best of her ability.

Mr. Voy passed away several years before his wife.

DR. GLENN W. VAIL

Dr. Glenn W. Vail was born in Arthur, Kansas, on April 18, 1877, his mother
passing away shortly after his birth. His childhood was spent with his
father who continued to care for him with the help of relatives.

His grade education he received in Kansas and Nebraska, going through high
school at Rock Rapids, Iowa, graduating in 1896. For the next four years he
worked as a clerk in one of the stores in Rock Rapids.

In 1900 Dr. Vail decided to go into the dental profession and enrolled at
the University of Iowa, at Iowa City, Iowa, where he graduated with the
degree of DDS in 1905. During his time at the university he took various
odd jobs to defray his expenses and was still among the top few
scholastically, upon graduating.

In the summer of 1905, Dr. Vail was united in marriage with Lena R. Wood of
Mankato, Minnesota, and a home was set up at Panora, Iowa, where Dr. Vail
opened a dental office.

        DR. GLENN W. VAIL

In the summer of 1906, Dr. Vail moved to Lyle, Minnesota, opening a dental
office there.

In the fall of 1906, Dr. Vail had the misfortune of losing his wife. She
passed away on November 2, 1906, leaving an infant son. He continued his
dental practice in Lyle, and in January of 1910, he was married to Dena L.
Hedemark of Lyle.

It was in the summer of 1910 that Dr. Vail decided to come to South Dakota,
he being in poor health and feeling that the outdoor life would be
beneficial to him. He filed on a homestead about 10 miles northeast of
Morristown, South Dakota, on the Cannonball river. He also opened a dental
office in Morristown, where he would spend a few days a week in his
profession and the rest of the time on the homestead.

After proving up on the homestead the family moved into Morristown in 1912,
where they resided until 1913.

In October of 1913, Dr. Vail purchased the dental practice of Dr. M. W.
Myler of Selby. The family moved to Selby in November of 1913, where they
have since resided. Dr. Vail continued his dental practice in Selby until
his death on July 27, 1923.

From the time of his coming to Selby until his death, Dr. Vail was active
in civic affairs. During World War I, he served as a dental examiner for
the government without remuneration. He also served on the state dental
board for some time, and was a member of the Selby school board at the time
the present high school building was built in 1920. He was a member of the
Selby Masonic bodies and was active in the affairs of the organization. He
and his family were affiliated with the Methodist church.

Mrs. Vail passed away on June 18, 1938.

There are surviving, four children: Dana F. Vail married and residing in
Selby; Glenn W. Vail, married, Grace I. (now Mrs. K. B. Nilsen), and Ruth
H. Vail, all residing in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

MR. AND MRS. JOHANN WAGNER

Mr. and Mrs. Johann Wagner, having raised a family of 11, found that
chances for expanding their operations in the homeland were far too limited
for the size of the family, which caused them to decide to go to America
where land could be had just for living on it and tilling it. Johann Wagner
was born in the village of Borodeno in Besserabia in South Russia on
January 1, 1839. In 1860 he was married to Katherina Heier who was born
October 20, 1839. To this union 11 children were born: Katherina, John I.,
Peter, Elizabeth, Michael, Christine, Gottfried, George, Hanna, Julius and
one son who died very young.

Before coming to America the following children married and established
homes of their own: Katherina (Mrs. Martin Kubier); John I. Wagner was
married to Christine Riley; Elizabeth to Gottfried Heine; Peter and
Michael also were married previous to coming to America. In the spring of
1894 Johann Wagner and his family, together with some of his married
children and their families, started for America. Only two daughters and
their families stayed behind, Katherina (Mrs. Martin Kubier) and Christine
(Mrs. Loeffelbein). The Kubier family came to America a few years later,
but Christina never came.

The families were headed for Bowdle, South Dakota where a distant relative
lived who had encouraged Johann Wagner to come. The family became somewhat
discouraged when they came through Chicago a few days after the violent
Pullman strike, but when the sons got further west and saw the fine lands
they were satisfied there was no mistake. The family arrived in Bowdle
about the 3rd or 4th of May, 1894, and were brought to the Adam Wagner farm
northwest of Bowdle, where the women and children stayed a few days while
the men located land to file upon, and to build a temporary home.

Johann Wagner and two sons, John I. and Gottfried, located land two miles
north of Selby, Mr. Wagner buying a relinquishment as did his son, John I.
Gottfried filed on a tree claim. The families built a 12 room sod house,
and a sod barn as temporary housing on the NE 1/4 of 28-124-76. Peter and
Mike went further north to locate, Peter to Eureka, and Mike to Ashley,
North Dakota. Peter did not like the northern climate so went to Oklahoma
where he permanently located. Mike located on land northeast of Ashley. One
daughter, Elizabeth and her husband were encouraged by friends to join them
in going to Salem, North Dakota where they located homesteads. When proper
details were arranged the family started to put in a crop. There were a few
acres broken on Johann's and John's quarters, and beside that they were
able to rent 60 acres from a neighbor. The father and sons had conducted a
large work shop in their homeland so were able to build some of their
implements, but they bought two plows and wagons and one team of horses,
one team of oxen and three cows. While bringing the oxen and cows from
Bowdle, Gottfried became lost so when he finally saw a farm he stopped to
inquire where he was, and found he had taken the wrong fork in the road and
had wandered too far north.

Their first crop was no bumper crop but was fair and the proceeds were
sufficient to buy a few more necessities. Wheat sold for about 60 to 80
cents a bushel.

In the spring of 1895 Johann Wagner started to make adobe brick for a house
to be built on his quarter, the southeast of 21-124-76. The bricks were
made by mixing clay and straw to a consistency that it stuck. The mud was
pressed into forms and stacked in the sun for drying and aging before
building. The family was fortunate in their brick making and put out enough
to also build a barn. Lumber for the roof was bought in Bowdle. The roof of
the barn was made from timbers from the Missouri river, and covered with
sod until finances were sufficient to put a wooden roof on in 1897.

Mr. Wagner also built a house on his NW 1/4 of 28-124-76 and moved his
family over and set up farming, also to build up a very nice farm.

Gottfried, George, Hanna and Julius lived with their parents several years.
The sod house that was hurriedly built served as a small shanty for
Gottfried, and when he built an adobe brick house and barn in 1897 on his
NE 1/4 of 28-124-76, the sod house served as a temporary residence for many
immigrants. The Kubier family were the first to use the sod house as a
temporary home and were followed by the Wells family and Gottfried Heier
family, brothers of Mrs. Johann Wagner, and several others. The Gottfried
Heier family and the Kubier family located homesteads in the Akaska area.

In 1898 the crops were good but an early winter set in which made choring a
very difficult problem at times. Haystacks were completely covered and had
to be shoveled out of the snow. The supplies had to be hauled from Bowdle
which was a big day's journey. Snow along sleigh roads was 4 to 5 feet
high, and only room for one sled. You could not pass another only in
certain places. Gottfried tells of one instance when he was bringing home
some coal. He met a sleigh loaded with grain sacks. The two men did not
know what to do for a minute but it was agreed to unload the wheat sacks
and tip the sled off the road and let the load of coal pass, and then
reload the wheat. Both went their way again not to meet for many years,
neither having inquired as to the others name, but in 1916 they met on the
street in Selby and recognized each other and took time to get acquainted.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHANN WAGNER

In 1899 when the railroad was being extended west, the Wagner boys got work
on the grading gangs with their horses which enabled them to earn a little
extra money. When Selby started in 1900 the Wagner's would walk two miles
to work in Selby, helping folks who had moved homes from Bangor to get
settled.

Gottfried was married to Elizabeth Himrich on October 31, 1901. To this
union two children were born, Emil and Olga Wagner.

George Wagner started to work out as a hired hand before he became of age,
and started to work as helper in a lumber yard in Bowdle and Eureka and
Selby. He was also employed by Gross of Bowdle for a time. He was married
to Elizabeth Ketterling of Bowdle, to which union three sons were born.
George is now living in Oshkosh, Wisconsin.

Julius Wagner, who came to America as a lad, enjoyed attending the
neighboring country school a mile and a half east of his father's farm. He
in turn would teach Gottfried, who took care of the farm. When Julius
became of age he wanted a homestead and found land southwest of Akaska as
did his sister Hanna, Julius locating half a mile east of the Kubier farm.
They homesteaded in about 1903. In 1908 Julius was married to Lydia
Himrich, and to this union four children were born: Esther, Reinhold, Clara
and Susie who all attended the Selby schools at one time. Julius moved a
house in to Selby and carried mail on a rural route for a number of years,
often going out in quite stormy weather to get the mail through. He took
quite sick in the flu epidemic which caused the collapse of a lung and
therefore could not do hard work any more. He took on a Ward company
medical route in Edmunds county. He was instantly killed while crossing the
railroad tracks in Selby when his car was hit by a fast train. Mrs. Lydia
Wagner lives in Selby.

Johann Wagner died in 1906 and was laid to rest in a community cemetery two
miles east of his home. Mrs. Wagner and her daughter carried on farming a
year, renting out some land. Hanna was married in 1907 to Matt Ellwein of
Roscoe, South Dakota, after which Mrs. Johann Wagner sold the personal
property and went to live with her sons. She spent most of the time with
Gottfried across the road from her home. She stayed with Gottfried until
his health forced him to discontinue farming. Gottfried purchased a small
home in Selby but agreed to again take his mother when his new home was
finished which would have modern conveniences and living quarters for her.
She died on January 2, 1912, and was laid to rest beside her husband.

In settling the Johann Wagner estate, Gottfried purchased his father's
homestead to go with his farm across the road, which he still owns.
Although living a retired life in Selby, he still likes to spend many days
on the farm.

John I. Wagner continued to live on his farm until 1926 when he decided to
retire, and moved a house into Java where he and his wife died and were
buried in the Java cemetery, leaving four children: Emma (Mrs. Alex Huber)
of Selby; Christine (Mrs. John Schauer) of Selby; Mary (Mrs. Ed Schock) of
Aberdeen, and Richard of Selby.

Of the Wagner boys who came to this country with their father in 1894. only
Michael of Ellendale, North Dakota, Gottfried of Selby; and George of
Oshkosh, Wisconsin, and one daughter, Hanna (Mrs. Ellwein) are still
living. They have all endured pioneer hardships but have also enjoyed the
blessings of good crops and prosperity, and good clean living. The Wagners'
have often expressed gratitude to their father and mother for bringing them
to this country, and letting them enjoy the freedom of a good government.

MR. AND MRS. PETER J. THORSTENSON

To Mr. and Mrs. P. J. Thorstenson goes the distinction of being the first
couple on record to be married in Walworth county. Their wedding took place
April 5, 1887 with Tobias Risdall officiating as justice of the peace as
there were no pastors in this vicinity at that time. They were married in
the house on her homestead.

It was in the early part of 1884, long before there was a Selby, that Mr.
Thorstenson, then a young man in his early twenties, first set foot on
Walworth county soil. The area had only recently been opened to homesteading
and few families had ventured in ahead of him to set up small shanties
across the rolling and unbroken plains.

Peter Thorstenson had immigrated to America two years earlier from his
native Norway, just in time to avoid serving a 3-year hitch in the
Norwegian army. Immediately upon arrival in New York he boarded a train for
Canton, South Dakota, where he knew a family who had once lived with his
aunt in Norway. It was here that he met Sophia Birkeland who was later to
become his wife. She came from Norway in 1885 to Inwood, Iowa as she had a
brother there. She worked in the home of Mrs. Helgerson for $1.50 a month.

At Canton he soon found work on a small cattle ranch taking care of 160
head of cattle at a salary of $8.00 per month plus room and board. That to
Peter was real prosperity after the hard struggle in Norway to keep food on
the family table. During his last seven years in Norway, as the oldest son
of a motherless family of 7, he had been forced to shoulder much of the
financial responsibility of the household. It was then that Peter learned
the true meaning of the word, "thrift", and he really put thrift to
practice on the South Dakota ranch. In less than a year he had saved enough
money to help his brother Rasmus buy a steamship ticket to America. The
fare at that time was about $75.00.

        MR. AND MRS. PETER J. THORSTENSON

After Rasmus' arrival the two boys worked on ranches near Canton until the
spring of 1884, when they decided to venture to new territory and try
homesteading a place of their own. Their choice was Walworth county. The
young men traveled in an immigrant car as far as Ipswich, which was then
the end of the Milwaukee road to the west, and from there continued on
their way with four head of oxen, two cows and a used wagon to the site of
their new home, northwest of what is now Selby. Having only $20.00 between
them upon arrival at Ipswich, they were unable to file on a homestead, but
they managed to spare the $2.00 which was required to take out a preemption
on the 160 acres which they had chosen for their new home. Mr.
Molstertiegen, who lived in the neighborhood, suggested that they homestead
a few miles farther to the southwest as the land was better there. After
living for a short time in a shelter consisting of a few rough boards
beside a wagon box on a hillside they moved southwest onto the land that
became their homestead. Here they built their first dugout sod house and
barn. Mrs. Thorstenson later filed on the land adjoining this. Having no
farm equipment or seed, they were unable to do much farming of their own
that first year, so Peter hired out for 25 cents a day, some days, to other
squatters of the territory. The first money he earned in Walworth county
was from gathering buffalo bones and delivering them to Ipswich for $2.00 a
load.

The latter part of the year 1886 was the most depressing period they were
forced to endure. Having yet harvested no crop, they frequently found
themselves broke, with no food on the place and few clothes on their backs,
There was many a day they had to shoot a duck or rabbit before they could
prepare a meal, and sometimes the meat was about all they had. The
situation grew so desperate at one time that Mr. Thorstenson was forced to
borrow $2.00 from a friend, George Ross, to purchase a sack of flour, a
pair of pants, and enough rope to picket the milk cow as there were no
fences and the cow would travel several miles between milkings.

The following summer they built a three room sod house. Only one room had a
board floor. A flax-straw burner heated the house during the winter. It was
built like a fireplace and was kept filled with twisted flax straw or hay.

In the winter of 1888 Mr. and Mrs. Lars Larson came to live with them
temporarily. Mrs. Larson was the only sister of Mr. Thorstenson. So it was
that Martin Larson Sr., came to be born here attended only by Mrs.
Thorstenson as Mr. Thorstenson had gone to get Mrs. Martha Tisdall, mother
of Jake Tisdall, the only midwife in the vicinity. Peter had become lost in
a snow storm while bringing her back with him on his snowshoes, and it
wasn't until dawn that he realized he was southwest of his home. There were
no landmarks such as fences, railroads or even trees in those days.

Breaking small tracts of land the first years was done with oxen. Mrs.
Thorstenson led the oxen while he guided the plow with their baby, Henry,
tied to his back. Wells in the early days were very scarce and Peter had to
haul water from Hiddenwood creek for drinking and watering the oxen. Those
days all of their wood was hauled from the river.

In October of 1893 Thomas Ekrem came to spend the winter months in Walworth
county with his brothers Peter and Rasmus Thorstenson, and his sister, Mrs.
Lars Larson. Mr. Ekrem, who had been doing masonry in Denver since his
arrival from Norway in 1885, brought his wife and 8-months old son with him.

Early in the year of 1894 plans were being made to construct a vault for
the safe-keeping of the county records at Bangor and bids were called for.
Tom Ekrem submitted the lowest bid. The nearest known sand was 11 miles
away, but Tom luckily found a good deposit much closer, and with the use of
Peter's oxen and sled be was able to haul six yards of sand per day. This
kept him from going in the red on the job. He began construction of the
vault April 1, 1894 and completed the work three months later clearing
about $500.00. A short time later Mr. Ekrem and family returned to Denver
where he still lives today.

In 1894 Mr. Thorstenson built the present dwelling for $196.00; the frame
part was added later on. The house was made of mud brick consisting of
earth and straw mixed with water and packed by cattle walking on it.

This consistency was packed in forms and dried. This was a long and slow
process, but it saved much lumber and expense. There was also the
ever-present transportation problem which was a major difficulty in pioneer
days. While the west end of the railroad was at Bowdle, pioneers living
east of the Missouri river would stop at the Thorstensen home overnight, on
their two-day trip to Bowdle. They would sleep side by side on the floor as
many as 14 a single night. Mrs. Thorstenson recalls that she slept more
often in the rocking chair than in the bed during those times. Of the
household furnishings available in those days she was most pleased with
mosquito netting which was used for curtains and came in different colors.

Mr. and Mrs. Thorstenson had the first milk route in Selby. The delivered
price for milk at that time was 5 cents a quart or 21 quarts for a dollar.

On the 17th of May, 1925, just 40 years to the day, from the time Sophie
left for America the first time, they went back to their beloved homeland
Norway, for a few months visit. Mr. Thorstenson had previously made a trip
to Norway in 1906. Their Golden Wedding anniversary was observed at Bethany
church on April 9, 1937.

Grandpa Thorstenson was active about the farm until a few days before his
death in 1944. Grandma Thorstenson is living with her daughter, Mary
Pederson of Firesteel, at present. They have always been active in church
and community affairs.

Ten children were born to this couple, seven of whom are living. They are:
Henry, of near Timber Lake; Mary Pederson, living north of Firesteel; Ruth
Olson, of Ralph; Meniva Siewert, of Hettinger, North Dakota; August,
Adolph, and Melvin Thorstenson, living west of Selby. August built up on
the homestead of Peter A. Johnson and Adolph that of Mons S. Flattre.
Melvin is on the home place.

In closing may we use these lines from the pen of N. N. Ronning, a good
friend of Mr. and Mrs. Thorstenson:

"Histories have been written and more will be written of Norwegians in
America, but no man can tell adequately of the tearing asunder of tender
ties, the hardships and dangers crossing the deep, the work and worry, the
hopes and fears, the laughter and tears, of the men and women who with bare
hands carved out of a wilderness, a new kingdom."

MR. AND MRS. FRED TEWS

Fred Tews was born in Pomerania, Germany, on July 21, 1866. He came to
America when 17 years old and went to Early, Iowa, where an older brother
was living, and hired out when wages were from $18.00 to $22.00 a month.
After a few years he left for near Fort Atkinson, Wisconsin, where he
remained for a few years working for another brother. He then went to the
vicinity of Emerson and Wakefield, Nebraska, where he started farming for
himself. Here he met Elizabeth Gradert, whom he married October 10, 1895.
Mrs. Tews was born in Holstein, Germany, on January 10, 1878, and at the
age of four years came to Glenwood, Iowa, with her parents and family. Mr.
and Mrs. Tews farmed in Nebraska for several years, and in 1903 emigrated
to Java,

South Dakota with four children, two boys and two girls. They lived two
miles west of Java for a couple of years, when they purchased a half
section of land just southeast of Selby, where they built and established
their home. Four girls were born to them in South Dakota. One girl, Lydia,
passed away at the age of 2-1/2 years.

They maintained their home on this farm until 1931 when they moved to
Selby, where they now are located. Mr. Tews acquired his education in
Germany, and Mrs. Tews acquired her education in a common school in
Nebraska.

When Mr. and Mrs. Tews were married the farming prospects were not too good
in Nebraska, and they decided to move to South Dakota, which they felt might
hold a greater future. At the time they moved into Walworth county the town
of Selby was just two years old, and Java was just started. Crop conditions
were not too promising the first few years, and in 1911 there was a severe
drouth. From then until the drouth and depression of the 1930's crop
conditions were very good some years and not so good other years.

        MR. AND MRS. FRED TEWS

At first, their farming was done with horses, and when the boys became old
enough, they did tractor farming and operated a couple of threshing rigs
for a number of years. They had quite a number of horses and raised some
colts, raised many hogs, and always milked from 15 to 20 cows. Mrs. Tews
churned by hand from 60 to 70 pounds of butter a week at 14 cents a pound
and delivered to about 25 Selby customers each week until the opening of
the Equity when cream was sold there. Turkey raising also contributed to
their livelihood, as well as other poultry raising.

They had a near tragic experience on the 2nd day of May, 1914, when the two
sons, Edward and Fred were struck by lightning. They were sitting on a
manger before an open barn window, watching it rain. Lightning struck the
barn, ran down a rafter in the hayloft, down the side of the barn and hit
the boys. Fred had a deep hole burned above one knee, but the lightning ran
down one side of Edward, burned his hair at the temple, ripped his trouser
leg, and tore off his shoe. It also left its mark on the watch in his
pocket. It was thought that Edward would not live for he suffered agonies,
but after much doctoring and the services of a trained nurse for many
weeks, he finally was able to be up and around, although it left its
effects upon him. It was a very grim and harrowing experience for the
entire family and they always felt that it was a miracle that the boys
escaped death.

The names and addresses of their children are: Mrs. John Coan (Ella),
Emerson, Nebraska; Edward Tews, Moore, Montana; Mrs. John Unkrur (Edna),
Selby; Fred Tews, Miller; Mrs. Albert Aman (Alice), Java; Bertha Tews,
Pierre; Mrs. Dick Richards (Ann), Portland, Oregon.

A rather peculiar coincidence is that at this writing they have 11
granddaughters, 11 grandsons, and 11 great grandchildren.

MR. AND MRS. HENRY A. TAYLOR

Henry A. Taylor was born at Pittsfield, Maine, October 12, 1863. He
attended school there and graduated from college at Pittsfield.

He came west and worked in Minneapolis for a few years, driving horses on
the horse car street railway. Later he worked in the lumber mills in
Minnesota.

He came to Walworth county in South Dakota in 1887 and filed on a claim in
Adams township, northeast of Java. He built a sod house there and taught
school during the winter. He also taught school after he was married for
a number of years.

He was married to Ella Adams on September 16, 1894. Ella Adams was born at
West Haven, Vermont, December 18, 1877. She was the daughter of Emma and B.
P. Adams. B. P. Adams brought his family to South Dakota in 1886. He took
up land in Walworth county and Adams township was named for him. Ipswich
was then the end of the railroad. The house they built at that time was of
lumber but had no floor. Mrs. Adams had it covered with rag rugs. The Adams
family raised cattle and Ella and her brother, Elnathan spent their time
herding the cattle.

        MR. AND MRS. HENRY A. TAYLOR

Many stories are told of early blizzards. The houses were heated with straw
burners. The people had to live off the land.

Ella and Henry Taylor were married at a home wedding. There were 40 guests.
The minister came from Bowdle on a bicycle, 9 miles away. Among the gifts
were a cow and heifer calf.

He was elected county auditor in 1897 and they moved to Bangor, then county
seat of Walworth county. When his term expired they moved back to the farm
and built a small frame house.

Henry Taylor helped build the railroad that went through Java, Selby and on
to Mobridge. He worked there all summer and also had a team of horses that
worked, too. The family built the first hotel in Java. They lived in Java a
short time and bought a farm, 9 miles northeast of Java.

He was again elected county auditor in 1911, and they moved to Selby.
During World War I he was clerk of the Selective Draft board and was county
justice of the peace for 20 years. He was a charter member of the Masonic
Lodge at Java. He passed away at Selby on February 6, 1939.

Ella Taylor still lives at Selby. She is a member of the Eastern Star and a
past matron of that order. She is a member of the Methodist church and
served as president of the ladies aid for 8 years. She also belongs to the
Royal Neighbors. Ella Taylor was president of the Selby unit of the Red
Cross for 25 years.

Two children were born to them: Frank living in Los Angeles, California and
Nellie Anderson living at Idaho Falls, Idaho.

THE MUDGE FAMILY

In the early days of statehood of Minnesota among the early settlers were
Aaron and Lydia Mudge who with one small son, Charles, had come from Ohio
to establish a home in the new west. To these hardy pioneers five more sons
and two daughters were born. The eldest of them, William Henry Mudge, was
born at Blue Earth on February 28, 1858, the second white boy to be born in
Faribault county.

In these early days life was strenuous and the support of a large family
was difficult. For this reason it was necessary for the older children in
the family to leave the home at an early age to become independent.

William H. Mudge and his brother, Eben, left home to earn their own
livelihood. For several years they worked among friends and neighbors in
Minnesota. This employment took them into the. Pine Island territory where
they met the girls, Salome Bickford and Armida Jewell, who later became
their wives.

Eben and Armida Mudge were the parents of Major General Verne D. Mudge, who
was born in Walworth county, and who was the officer who led the first
American troops into Manila in World War II.

In 1886, William H. Mudge, having won the confidence of past employers, was
persuaded to leave Minnesota and assist a grain buyer at Houghton, South
Dakota. Here he worked until after the blizzard of 1888.

In search of a permanent location away from such blizzards he then went to
California where he was employed as an engineer. In spite of many
attractions of the west he decided to return to South Dakota and in 1889
joined his brother, Eben, in Walworth county and here filed on a claim.

He returned to Pine Island in the fall of that year and on December 23 he
married Salome Bickford, the only child of William and Frances Bickford.

Frances Salome Bickford was born June 15, 1872, at Zumbrota, Minnesota. At
the age of three her parents moved to Pine Island. She received her
education in the Pine Island schools graduating from high school with the
second class at the age of 16. Her father was charter member of La Grange
Royal Arch Chapter No. 4 of Red Wing, Minnesota, and later was instrumental
in establishing the A. F. & A. M. at Zumbrota, naming it Herman in honor of
his lodge in Maine. He was the first worshipful master and served for six
years.

After their marriage Mr. Mudge shipped his goods to Bowdle, which was the.
end of the railroad, from where he completed the trip to Bangor, hauling
goods by lumber wagon. On April 4, 1890, he was joined by his wife. The
young couple located on land near their claim. It was an early spring and
all land then broke on his claim was already seeded to grain.

He spent that summer breaking more land on his claim and for Dan Collins.
Mr. Collins, who had been a former employer in Minnesota, later purchased
extensive acreage in Walworth county and also became an early settler
here. They owned and managed a store at Bangor.

On the claim, which was located 1-1/2 miles north of Bangor, Mr. Mudge
built a house, a barn and dug a well that same year. In the years that
followed additional land was bought, improvements made and it became the
home of W. H. and Salome Mudge for many years. The farm now consists of 400
acres of land. When the town of Bangor was abandoned, Selby became the new
post office address of the Mudge family. The Mudge farm is located 4-1/2
miles southwest of Selby.

        MR. AND MRS. W. H. MUDGE

W. H. and Salome Mudge had four sons and one daughter, William, Floyd,
Kenneth, Salome and Charles. The older children were born on the farm and
Charles was born in Selby. All of the children attended the Selby schools
and Salome was a student at the University of Vermillion one year. One son,
Floyd, served with the Armed Forces in World War I. Two of the sons passed
away, the other children married and have established homes of their own.

There are 16 grandchildren, nine girls and seven boys, and one
great-grandchild. Three of these grandchildren, sons of William and Effie
Mudge, served with the Armed Forces in World War II.

After the purchase of a home in Selby, Mr. Mudge was succeeded by his sons
in the operation of the farm.

Throughout the life of Mr. Mudge he was active in all projects for the
improvement and advancement of the people of Walworth county. He served in
the following capacities during the years: Road supervisor, clerk of school
board, including Bangor, East Bangor and Selby schools, for many years and
county commissioner from 1906 to 1915.

He was an active member of I.O.O.F. at Pine Island for several years.
Because there was no lodge in Walworth county at the time he moved here he
requested a demit. He was a member of Selby Lodge No. 133 A. F. & A. M. and
the Royal Arch, advancing through the office to become Worshipful Master
and High Priest. He was also a member of the Eastern Star and Yeoman
lodges. Mrs. Mudge has been an active member of Hope Chapter No. 73 for the
past forty-two years, serving as worthy matron in the years 1918-1919. She
was also a member of W.R.C. and B.A.Y. until these orders disbanded. She
was elected president of W.R.C. and was correspondent of the B.A.Y. from
September 20, 1920, until it was disbanded. She taught in the Episcopal
Sunday school at Pine Island for several years and in the M. E. Sunday
school at Selby a short time.

The entire family of Wm. H. and Salome Mudge are confirmed members of the
Episcopal church.

Mr. Mudge passed away in 1938. Mrs. Mudge still owns and lives in her own
home in Selby.

MR. ABRAHAM S. TAYLOR

Abraham S. Taylor was known to his many friends as "Abe". He was born
August 11, 1846, at Schora, New York. When a young man, his father moved to
Sheboygan, Wisconsin, conducting a bank in which Abe worked till the time
of his enlistment in the Civil War. He was mustered into service January
22, 1864, in Company A 17th Illinois Cavalry at Camp Kane, Ill. He saw
service throughout the war, some time of which was spent in an army
hospital.

After his discharge he returned to Elgin, Illinois, where he assisted his
father on a farm which he had acquired. Here he met Clara T. Bradley to
whom he was married on September 20, 1869, at Chicago. With his bride he
returned to the farm at Elgin where he resided until it was necessary for
him to go to the mountains in Wyoming in an effort to regain his health
which had been affected as a result of his army experiences.

This accomplished, he returned to Elgin, but in 1876 it became necessary to
move to Sauk Rapids, Minnesota, because of his health and after a residence
at this place for eight years he came to Walworth county, South Dakota, and
filed on a claim near Bangor. He purchased some horses, drove to Aberdeen
and got lumber for his farm buildings. The house was very nice for pioneer
days. It had two bedrooms, dining room, front room, a kitchen, and a large
pantry. He also dug a well and so had plenty of water. This was a very rare
thing for South Dakota pioneers, as water was scarce on most homesteads. He
planted five acres of trees. This home was located about a mile and a half
from Bangor. In 1885 he moved his family to the new home. They came by
train to the end of the railroad which was Ipswich, about 50 miles from
Bangor. This last 50 miles they rode in a covered wagon. At that time the
stage came to Bangor three times a week with mail.

Mr. Taylor hauled his grain to Ipswich, the trip taking three to four days.
He served as county register of deeds at Bangor. Later he moved from the
farm to Selby where he operated a meat market. He built a home in Selby
which is the present Ed Schanzenbach residence and was formerly known as
the "August Schmidt home".

Mr. and Mrs. Taylor had a family of five children: Evelyn, Cora, Lysle,
Charley, and Blanche.

Evelyn was badly burned while visiting at her father's home and as a result
of this accident passed away; Cora, Mrs. McGlenn, lives at Phoenix,
Arizona; Lysle lives at Grand Rapids, Michigan; Charley resides in
Minneapolis, Minnesota; Blanche, Mrs. Frink, lives at Long Beach,
California.

Mr. Taylor and his family lived for about 15 years in Walworth county. Then
the family moved to Glenburn, North Dakota, where he and his son, Charley,
conducted a lumberyard for several years. From there they moved to Sheldon,
North Dakota, in 1912. Here he engaged in the hardware business for a
number of years and for five or six years conducted the Corner Grocery
store. Then because of ill health he disposed of his business interests.
Three years later in July, 1922, he passed away in Sheldon. In November,
1925, his wife passed away.

Mr. Taylor was a good reader and student. He always kept abreast of the
times, and was considered to be one of the best posted men on current
events. He was a ready conversationalist. Politically he was a life long
democrat.

W. B. MYLER FAMILY

The W. B. Myler family originated in Illinois, and moved into Iowa,
Crawford county, in 1883. Ten years later they moved to Ida county, Iowa,
near Battle Creek, and moved from there into Woodbury county near
Correctionville. In 1904, W. B. Myler and wife moved to Walworth county and
settled at Selby, where he engaged in the real estate and insurance
business for a time with the late R. W. Reynolds. Later on, he formed a
partnership with H. P. Gutz in real estate and for a number of years
operated the Gutz and Myler farm, southwest of Selby, selling the same in
the spring of 1920.

Several members of the Myler family located in Selby, and in Walworth and
Potter counties.

J. W. Myler, the father, located at Lebanon where he and his family resided
for a number of years. Dr. M. W. Myler came to Selby in 1907 and practiced
dentistry for a number of years and, during that time, filed on a homestead
in the Swan creek vicinity near the present town of Akaska. He later moved
to Mitchell, where he practiced his profession for a number of years, then
moved to Alhambra, California, where he practiced his profession and is now
living at La Harba, California.

J. E. Myler filed on a homestead near Akaska and proved up his claim, later
moving to Lebanon, and from there to Gettysburg where he has lived for the
past 25 years, during which time he has been engaged in the livestock and
auction business, he being a well-known auctioneer throughout this section
for many years.

        MR. AND MRS. W. B. MYLER

Two sisters, Marie Myler and Mrs. Winnie Ashcraft also homesteaded in the
early days near the town of Akaska. Both of these sisters have since passed
away as has J. W. Myler and his wife, father and mother of the family.

The only living sister, Mrs. Jessie Burke, resides at 220 Redondo, Long
Beach, California.

W. B. Myler was mayor of the town of Selby for a few years and later moved
to Mobridge, where he engaged in real estate and auction business and was
mayor of the town for a few years. moving from there to Hot Springs,
Montana, in 1925 where he was engaged in the lumber business. During his
residence in Selby, he took an active part in the erection of what is known
as the Selby opera house. He was also active in the promotion of the
building of four miles of highway which was then known as the Yellowstone
Trail, which has now become a part of Highway 12, passing through Selby but
on a somewhat different route than the original Yellowstone Trail. He was
also active in the promotion of the Walworth county fair, the Fair Building
association and the livestock pavilion and was one of the early subscribers
and contributors to the building of the farmers' telephone line originating
in Selby and throughout the vicinity of Selby.

Since moving to Montana, his wife, Frances Myler passed away in 1937. She
will be well remembered in Selby as being very active in all community
affairs, especially occasions where music and singing were featured
attractions. She, with Mrs. H. P. Gutz, Tillie Baumgarten, and Rose Smith,
formed a ladies' quartette and were called upon innumerable times to
render their musical selections. In 1940 he was remarried to Myrtle De Mers
of Hot Springs and, in March 1950, he passed away.

MR. AND MRS. HENRY STULKEN

I, Henry Stulken, was born in Akron, Iowa, on April 1, 1882. I had one
sister, Christina, now Mrs. Joe Lively, and two brothers, George and John.
My parents moved to a homestead near Plankinton, South Dakota. A few years
later another brother, Ben, was born. We broke the land with a walking
plow, herded cattle, and had many experiences during those years at home.

My wife, Anna Marie Huber, was born in Louisville. Nebraska. She had a
half-brother, Eugene Messenger, two brothers, George and Charles, and a
sister, Minnie, now Mrs. John Handke. Her father died when she was 12 years
old and, being the eldest at home, she worked to help make ends meet.
Sometimes she would go to the Miller home near Plankinton to work, and it
was on one of these trips that I met my wife.

We were married January 17, 1906, and lived at Louisville, Nebraska. In
1907 and 1909, Herbert and Russell were born. One experience during those
years that I will never forget was the tornado of May 12, 1909. I was
cultivating corn (with horses) a number of miles from home and saw the
storm approaching, but, before I left the field, a rider on horse-back
came, shouting like mad, "All the folks at your home and the clay pit are
dead." I unharnessed the team and headed for home. The clay pit, in
operation at the time, was less than a quarter mile from home. When I got
to the clay pit, it surely looked like everyone had been killed. The shacks
were splinters. But, at home, the house was still standing and my family
were alright. Our house was turned into a hospital for days. Our sheets and
tablecloths were torn into bandages. I helped carry in the wounded and
helped find the dead.

In 1910, we decided to take a try at homesteading and I headed for Alberta,
Canada. I filed my claim, nailed up a two-room house, and sent for my
family. We had good neighbors from all parts of the world and all different
trades. In 1911 Elsie was born. We had good crops, wonderful neighbors, and
all, but the 30 miles to market (which took at least two days), with my
family alone at home, and the distance to a doctor (and perhaps a
homesickness for the states) made us decide to find a better place to live.
We sold out and my wife and children went to Nebraska to her mother. Her
brother, George, and I and the Model T started looking for a good place to
live. We followed a two-track road over some of the Rockies and went
through Walworth county, South Dakota. There we saw crops like never
before, and such tomatoes--we decided that was the place.

We lived in Selby 7 months, rented the farm known as the Howell farm, and
moved there. The story from there is not new nor really pioneering,
although, some of the days I spent taking children many miles to school in
wagon or a fancy, green, fiberboard cab on runners in blizzards or dust
storms.

In 1918 and 1920 Charles and Melvin were born. Marie and Hubert followed in
1922 and 1924. The death of our oldest son in 1930 of infantile paralysis
was a dreadful blow and the depression years followed. We tried to send our
children to school as much as they desired and money allowed. Herbert,
Elsie, Charles and Marie attended N. S. T. C. and the rest went to high
school.

My wife passed away on September 7, 1948, after a long illness. Her comfort
then as well as mine now is our family. Russell married Thelma Stensby in
1934. Their children are: Marion, Marilyn, Gerald, Sherwood, Sharyn, Mavis,
and Tamra. They live on a farm northeast of Selby. Elsie married Lawrence
Duerr in 1934. They have three children: Marie Anne, Marlene, and Gail.
They live southwest of Louisville, Nebraska. Charles was married in 1941 to
Vivian Gould. They live on a farm west of Selby and have two boys, David
and Terry. Melvin lives in Selby and operates the Minneapolis-Moline shop.
He married Betty Steiger in 1941. Their children are Danny, Dennis, and
Sandra. Marie was married in 1942 to Harold Stensby. They live on a farm
northwest of Selby. They have three girls: Linda, Maryann, and Harriet.
Hubert and his wife, formerly Virginia Haakenson, live with me on the home
place. They were married in 1948, about a year after Hubert returned from
the Navy.

Ours has been a good life and we are thankful for the blessings God has
given us.

MR. ARNE STRAND

I was born February 6, 1857, in the community of Stod, North Enkered,
Norway. When I was a few weeks old I had to be baptized and given a name
and they called me Arne. As time went on I had to have a surname, and
according to custom that name was taken from the estate where you were
raised. Being raised on an estate called Strand, I was labeled Arne Strand.

My boyhood days were spent on the estate until I finished the common
school. I was then 16 years old. I left home and went to sea, being out one
year. I came home for a visit and found my mother very ill. Complying with
her wishes I gave up the sea and started to learn the blacksmith trade.
After learning the rudiments of the trade I hired out to the government to
do blacksmithing for a road construction gang where I worked for several
years. But during that time, I was called into the army for military
training where I spent part of 1880 and 1881. During 1881 I sought and got
permission to leave Norway. In August I said goodbye to the "Land of the
Midnight Sun"--my destination was Fergus Falls, Minnesota, where I arrived
in September. I spent the next two years in northern Minnesota.

In the late fall of '83 I went to Lanesboro, southern Minnesota, to meet a
lady (who was no stranger to me) who had come from Norway the year before
and was then staying with her uncle. Her name was Mathilda Elden, born
March 5, 1862, in the community of Namdalsied, North Enkered, Norway. In
January of 1884, Miss Elden and I were married at Preston, Minnesota.

The West was calling, so in the spring I struck out for Dakota territory
and landed in Walworth county where I filed on a homestead on the SW 1/4 of
30-123-75.

Scranton was then the county seat of Walworth county. I was then 28 years
of age.

I had small capital so had to find a job which I found at Starbuck,
Minnesota. In the fall I went back to my claim, built a shack, made a
fire-break, and in that fall election I cast my first ballot as an American
citizen. In that election Bangor was chosen county seat. After the election
I went back to Minnesota and wintered with my wife's uncle. I found it fine
to have relatives, if only a wife's relation. Our oldest boy was born that
fall at Lanesboro, Minnesota.

In the spring of 1885 I went out to the claim, after a few days there I
went back to the Jim River country and got a job for the summer. I made
several trips between the Jim and my claim that summer. During the summer
my wife and baby came out to join me at the Jim, where we stayed until the
spring of 1886.

During the winter I bought a pair of oxen, a cow, a wagon, and a breaking
plow. Thus equipped, in early spring of 1886 we started for our future home
to-be. Our first year was a blank. What the drought did not take, the hail
did. The cow kept us. But things got better and we went into stock raising
as fast as we could, and we succeeded very well. The early pioneers days in
South Dakota were some of the happiest years of my life. In years to come
we acquired a half section of land which added to our homestead, made it a
moderate-sized farm for that part of the country.

        MR. AND MRS. ARNE STRAND

Our family increased, we reared a family of 9 children, 7 boys and 2 girls.
Four of the boys were in military service during World War I.

Dakota was very good to us. From Dakota we got all we ever had. I was not
