slighted on public trust. I served one term as county commissioner. I was
representative from Walworth county to the state legislature in 1915 and
1917, also in 1933 and 1935. I was a member of the local school board for
over 20 years.

In 1927 my life's companion was taken away and I became a roamer. That will
soon come to an end.

My family of children are as follows: Martin L., who passed away in 1947 at
Strool, South Dakota; Olaf G., of Ekalaka, Montana; Carl I., of Illinois;
Ralph A., in Walla Walla, Washington Veteran's hospital from an illness
contracted during World War I; Alma, Mrs. Virgil Rice, of Shelton,
Washington; Norman A., farming our homestead near Selby, South Dakota;
Oscar F., who passed away in 1943 in Kirkland, Washington; Helen, Mrs.
Vester Rice of Shelton, Washington; and Harold of Idaho Falls, Idaho. I
have 15 grandchildren and several great-grandchildren.

In 1937 I had a sale at my farm near Selby, South Dakota, and since that
time have been living with my children. At the present time I am living
with my daughter, Alma, in Shelton, Washington.

MR. AND MRS. FREMONT STEWART

Among the early settlers of Walworth county were Mr. and Mrs. Fremont
Stewart. In 1885, at the age of 25, Fremont Stewart came from Albia, Iowa,
to file on a homestead about 10 miles southwest of the present City of
Selby. After he had filed his claim, he returned to Albia, in 1886 and
married Mary Melvina Schooley, a former school teacher of that locality.

In April 1886 they loaded their property in a freight car which consisted
of a few household goods and a team of horses and a wagon and arrived in
Ipswich, the closest railroad.

        MR. AND MRS. FREMONT STEWART

On their homestead, they experienced the privations of pioneer life and
together built up a fine farm home and reared a family of six children.
Merle is now chief accountant for the Unemployment Compensation commission
of Helena, Montana; Effie Mudge is living in Igloo, South Dakota; Harold is
in business in Morristown, South Dakota: Roxie is manager of a garage in
San Diego, California, Paul and Robert are farming near Selby, and Robert
is now the owner of the old homestead.

When the buildings were moved from Bangor to the present site of Selby,
Fremont used the same team of horses that came from Iowa to assist in the
moving.

He was always active in politics, being a staunch democrat and was elected
to the state legislature in the early days, serving with credit to himself
and satisfaction to his constituents. Later he was a member of the State
Coal commission and was a delegate to the state and county conventions many
times. He was president of the Walworth County Fair association for many
years and was active in the conduct of such fairs. He also served as an
active member of the executive board of the Selby Equity Union Exchange.

In May, 1907, he was initiated into the Masonic lodge at Selby and advanced
in order through the Blue Lodge, Chapter, Consistory and Shrine, and was a
member of Hope chapter, Order of the Eastern Star. He loved Masonry and
endeavored to live up to its teachings.

Mrs. Stewart was a charter member of the "Mothers' Club" which later was
organized into the present "Jolly Club". In the early days when doctors
were hard to locate, Mrs. Stewart was often called upon either day or night
to aid in caring for the sick.

After Mrs. Stewart's death in 1916, Fremont made his home in Selby. He died
July 14, 1938, at the age of 78 years at the home of his daughter, Mrs.
Effie Mudge at Wakpala, South Dakota.

MR. ROBERT FRANK STEWART

Frank Stewart was born July 16, 1863, at Albia, Iowa. His mother died when
he was 3 years old and his father died when he was 9 years old, after which
he went to live with his brother, Joe.

On March 24, 1886, Frank Stewart married Eva Nancy Taylor at Albia, Iowa.
The young couple, in true pioneer spirit, came at once to make their home
in the Dakota territory. They traveled by train to Ipswich (at that time
Ipswich was the end of the railroad). Here they unloaded household goods,
machinery and their team of horses and finished their journey by team and
wagon. They spent the first few months at the home of his brother, Fremont,
while building a two-room house and the typical pioneer sod barn on their
own homestead, 2 miles to the north.

Frank Stewart filed on two quarters of land about 10 miles west of Bangor.
He farmed this and adjoining land throughout the 24 years he remained in
Dakota. This is now the Paul Stewart farm occupied by Darrel Zabel.

Four daughters were born and raised in this pioneer home: Pearl Johnson
(who passed away in 1935); Stella Brown of Springfield, Oregon; Ruby Walter
of Selby; and Madge Brown of Eugene, Oregon.

When the alarm was given during the Indian Scare in the late fall of 1890,
the Stewarts all went to Bowdle as did many of the pioneers. The men went
back to their homesteads the next day but Eva Stewart with her two little
girls, Pearl and Stella, and Mrs. Fremont Stewart and Merle and Harold
returned to Albia, Iowa for a few weeks until the scare had ended.

Eva Stewart died December 9, 1894, leaving her four little girls to be
raised by their father.

Wheat was the main crop raised in this area. The grain was put into sacks
and piled high on a triple-box wagon which was drawn by a 4-horse team and
was taken to Bowdle, 30 miles to the east. A trip to market started about 4
o'clock in the morning; immediately upon reaching Bowdle the grain was
unloaded, the horses fed and the supplies loaded and he started for home at
once, reaching home late at night. This was the only means of marketing
grain until early 1900, when the Chicago, Milwaukee railroad was extended
farther west and the town of Selby was built.

        MR. AND MRS. FRANK STEWART

Mr. Stewart served on the school board 9 years in succession. In summer of
1894, Mr. Stewart built an addition to the house, making it a fine home for
those early days. In the late nineties he replaced the sod barn with a
large stock barn.

In 1910 he sold the farm and moved to Frederick, Oklahoma where he
prospered in all his business activities. He made frequent trips back to
visit his daughters and friends. On July 7, 1931, at the age of 68, Frank
Stewart was tragically killed when he was struck by an automobile.

He had been a member of the Methodist church of Frederick, Oklahoma, a
member of the Masonic Lodge at Selby and later transferred to Frederick
where he took all the higher work in Masonry.

Mr. Stewart was a progressive citizen and a good business man. He took part
in all of the forward-looking movements of the early days in Walworth
county, often accepting leaderships. The members of his family were like
him and they with their husbands set up homes in which the highest ideals
of life were nurtured and maintained, and they too took their full part in
upholding a high standard in community life.

MR. OLIVER TISDALL

Oliver O. Tisdall was born in Polk county, Iowa, February 28, 1873. His
childhood was spent in Polk and Cass counties. As a young boy he came to
Blue Blanket where he worked for the first spring and summer planting sod
corn, (i.e. corn planted on breaking). While haying for John Erbe during
the summer of '85 John's brother, Henry came to the hay field, on Spring
lake and announced he had shot a buffalo and needed help to skin and
quarter it. This was young Oliver's first sight of a buffalo and
incidentally that was the last buffalo skinned in this county.

During the following winter '85-'86 Oliver worked as ranch caretaker for
Parker Bros., on one of their ranches, which entailed the care of six milk
cows and two yokes of "bulls." With the "bulls" he hauled wood from the
river to supply the fuel for the ranch.

By the standards of the present day this would be an unheard of experience
for a 13 year old boy, but it will be remembered that boy, of that age
entered the army during the Civil War. It is a known fact that G. E. Lemmon
and his brother, Harvey served as Indian scouts for the U. P. Railroad at
the respective ages of 9 and 12 years. Boys grew to manhood quickly in the
pioneer days. In the spring of '86 his father, mother, brother and sister
came to Blue Blanket where his father, Johannes Tisdall filed on a
soldier's claim which Oliver helped him work until he was 21.

Farming was a gamble in those days; farming methods for this area had not
been studied. Drouth and hot winds ruined two crops out of three farmed in
the manner of the eastern sections of the country.

The Tisdalls' hauled their grain to Bowdle, the nearest railroad, a day's
travel each way.

At the age of 21, Oliver filed on his own land, and built a good frame
house which he subsequently moved to the town of Glenham. In 1901 he sold
his land and moved to North Dakota and in 1916 to Idaho where he worked in
the lumber mills and logging camps. In 1942 he moved to Bremerton,
Washington where he worked in the Navy ship yards. He is now retired and
lives in Bremerton.

JEREMIAH BROWN FAMILY

Jeremiah Brown known from the earliest days in this part of the country as
"Jerry Brown" was born in New York City on November 12, 1849, and died at
the Selby hospital September 18, 1929 at the age of 80 years. The end came
following an attack of stomach trouble, thought to have been aggravated by
the eating of wild fruit. He had been ill for only a few days, though he
had suffered more or less and had been retired from active labor for a
number of years. Advanced age and the effects which hardships of early life
must have left on his constitution are more remote, but probably more
potent causes of death.

The life story of men like Mr. Brown might well cover half the history of
the nation. Born ten years before the Civil War and left an orphan at the
age of seven years, when their parents were taken from them in a small pox
epidemic, he and his one younger brother, Marvin were adopted into another
family. That same year they moved with their foster parents to Fort Wayne,
Indiana where his boyhood was spent. On August 22, 1870, at the age of 21,
he enlisted in Company K, 17th Regiment of Infantry, U.S. Army, at Fort
Wayne, Indiana for a period of five years. He served as a scout, scouting
from different forts under the command of Captain Green. He was a skilled
rifleman, and later was promoted to the rank of corporal. His regiment was
one of those sent into the Indian country of the then far west, which
included the "Dakota Territory," and as a soldier traversed the region from
the mouth of the Missouri river to Fort Benton, Montana. He became well
acquainted at all the forts in the territory including Fort Benton, Fort
Yates, Fort Sully, Fort Pierre, Fort Rice, Fort Rica, and Fort Custer. He
mastered the Sioux language and often served as an interpreter. He was held
in very high regard by the Indians, and was known throughout the Indian
territory as "Long Soldier." He received his discharge August 22, 1875. His
discharge paper is at present one of the valued possessions of his son,
Pearl A. Brown of Selby.

        MR. AND MRS. JEREMIAH BROWN

He was known as a skilled hunter and crack shot. He carried mail from Fort
Yates, North Dakota to Fort Pierre, South Dakota, a distance of well over a
hundred miles. These trips were made on foot and took two to three
days--as, although he was a rapid walker, he had to be ever on the alert
because Indians were still hostile and it was necessary to follow the banks
of the Missouri river to avoid being sighted by them. The only protection
he had to defend himself and the mail pouch he carried, were his wits and a
Winchester rifle he carried.

He related in later years how when he made camp for the night he would have
to camouflage himself from the red men. This was done by wrapping in his
blankets and then covering himself with brush, vines, leaves, etc., to
avoid detection by any passing Sioux. Many and thrilling are the stories he
could relate concerning this part of his life, as his was one that touched
the actual facts of pioneer frontier living, and about which the majority
of us must be content to listen or read.

Later he worked at the carpenter trade on government buildings at different
forts, including the Indian Mission at Wakpala, South Dakota. In the late
'80's he was employed in and around Old LeBeau. On September 9, 1896 patent
for NE 1/4 Section 19-124-78, was issued to Jeremiah Brown, and patent to
the SE 1/4 of Section 19-124-78 was issued to him on September 28, 1904.
This land is located two miles northwest of the present site of Glenham. He
continued residing on his farm until his death in 1929.

On April 9, 1890 he was married to Miss Ellen Viola Watson of Boscobel,
Wisconsin. Mr. and Mrs. Brown operated their farm and raised their family
as many other pioneer couples did. They endured the blizzards, droughts,
prairie fires and plagues, as well as the good years which came to them.
Much of the time after his marriage was spent doing carpenter work in the
neighborhood during the summer, and chopping cord wood and fence posts at
the river in the winter. It is said he used to get a dollar and a half a
cord. In later years he devoted himself to his farm work. He, with his wife
and family, planted very large gardens. While the rail road bridge was
being built across the Missouri river near Mobridge they supplied the camp
with much of the fresh vegetables, cream, butter, eggs, and chickens.

Mr. Brown was a member of the Odd Fellows and the Muscovite lodges.
Politically he was a staunch democrat and represented his district for more
than two terms on the board of county commissioners. He was a member of
this board when the county court house was built. In fraternal orders, in
politics, and in the everyday walks of life he was honest, upright, and
friendly. It has been said of him that no man was his enemy and that every
one who knew him called him friend.

Mrs. Brown was a very good seamstress and did much sewing for neighbors as
well as for many others. Her sewing included many wedding gowns. She was
very handy with sick folks and did a great deal of practical nursing
including delivering a number of babies unassisted by a doctor. She
assisted Dr. George of Selby, many times in the early days to deliver
babies in homes.

Mrs. Brown and her sister, Mrs. Mabel Rinehart of Mobridge, have often told
the story of the Indian trouble at the home of another sister, Mrs. Ed
Moss. It seems that while Mr. and Mrs. Ed Moss and their daughter, Jessie,
were on an island in the river cutting wood for the government, Indians
approached and circled their house and burned it to the ground. The family
dared make no resistance for fear their lives would also be taken. Later
the government paid them for their loss. When folks east of the Missouri
heard of this Indian uprising they became frightened. Many of them turned
their stock loose, took what belongings they could pack in a hurry and
started in their wagons, or whatever means of transportation they had and
started for Bowdle where they felt they would find protection. At this time
it is said men across the river were hired to watch and try to keep the
Indians quieted.

Mr. and Mrs. Brown had a family of twelve children:

Pernie; Pearl; Bert; the twins, Dorothy and Doris; Miron; and Nathan; three
daughters passed away in infancy. Two sons, George and Lloyd have also
passed away. Mrs. Brown passed away in 1947.

Pernie served in World War I, being overseas for seven months in France,
England, and Italy. He had the honor of being guard for President Wilson
when he inspected the A.E.F. in France. He returned to America in April,
1920. He married Mildred Johnson of Mound City. They have seven children:
Jim, Viann, Jerry, Billy Phyllis, and the twins, Donna and Donald, all at
home. Mrs. Brown is a registered nurse and since her marriage she has often
"specialed" in the Mobridge hospital. Mr. Brown has been manager of the
Equity Elevator in Mobridge since 1944. They make their home in Mobridge.

Pearl A. Brown is a World War I veteran. He served overseas twenty-one
months in England, France and Germany (Army of Occupation). He served with
Red Diamond 5th Division A.E.F. and returned to the United States in
August, 1919. The following year he took the Civil Service examination for
rural mail carrier at Selby. He received his appointment from President
Wilson on November 6, 1921, which position he is still holding. Pearl is a
member of the Frederick Schauer Post 100 American Legion. He was recently
elected chief of the Selby Fire department. In 1925 he was married to Miss
Ida May Lund of Mound City, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Andrew Lund, Campbell
county pioneers. Their two sons, Raymond Dean and Harlyn Francis, are at
home. Raymond is employed by the State Highway Commission and Harlyn is
employed in the Berens Hotel. Mrs. Brown, previous to her marriage, worked
as a clerk in several of the general merchandise stores in Glenham, and in
the Lund and Dahl general merchandise store in McLaughlin. At the time of
her marriage she was employed in the Glenham State Bank.

Albert LeRoy, "Bert", resides at Glenham and is employed as a rural mail
carrier there. In 1924 he married Miss Agnes Lund of Mound City, a sister
of Mrs. Pearl Brown. They have four children: Bernice, Mrs. Ted Schweigert
of McLaughlin; Lyman, Charles, and Laurel Jean at home. They also have a
little grandson, Douglas Lee Schweigert. Bert is a "crack shot" and loves
to hunt and fish as do his two sons.

Dorothy, Mrs. Clay Hollenbeck, lives at Trail City where her husband
operates a ranch. Mrs. Hollenbeck taught school several years previous to
her marriage. They have seven children: Edith, Mrs. Ben Sutfin of Wichita,
Kansas; Henry, Victor, Laurence, Robert, Dale, and Gordon at home. They
have two grandchildren, Terry and Linda Ann Sutfin. For a bit of the Wild
West one needs only to visit the Hollenbeck ranch where you will find the
three older boys and their neighborhood friends breaking wild horses and
steers to ride. Henry, "Bud" as he is called, and Victor are skilled riders
and have taken part in public rodeos.

Doris, Mrs. George Loebs, lives at Faulkton and her husband is employed in
a general store. They have one son, Richard.

Miron lives in Woodland, California. He is employed as an automotive
mechanic. He is married and has two children: Jerry and Charlotte, a
step-daughter.

Nathan lives in Mobridge. He is employed as a conductor on the CMStP&P
railroad. He is a veteran of World War II, enlisting in service at
Marinette, Wisconsin, October 15, 1940; left the United States April 22,
1942, and arrived in the Pacific Theatre May 14, 1942. He went through the
New Guinea campaign and was separated from service on December 2, 1944. He
is married to Netta Thomas of Adelaide, Australia, and they have two
children, Caroline and Bruce.

With the passing of "Jerry" Brown and his wife, we realize that another of
the dwindling number of men and women who link the present with the
earliest days in the history of the country is gone.

The story of their achievements and what their sacrifices have meant in the
making of a great state out of a wilderness inhabited only by aborigines
can never be half told. Conditions are so different now that it could not
be appreciated or understood were it told ever so well.

THE SPIRY FAMILY

The ancestry of the Spiry family originated in the Province of Alsace
Lorraine, France. The great-grandfather was an army officer, and was
accused of being partly responsible for Napoleon's defeat. He was charged
with treason and convicted to be executed, but with the assistance of his
friends, he escaped prison and fled to Germany. He was a surveyor by trade
and was later employed by the Russian Government to assist in surveying
the Crown land which had been granted by Czar Alexander I of Russia, to his
wife Czarina Catherine II, a former German Princess.

        MR. AND MRS. PHILIP SPIRY

The land was granted for German colonization, with the privileges of
religious freedom, tax exemptions for ten years, exemption from military
service, and each family was allotted a portion of the Crown land in tracts
of about 100 acres.

The grandfather, Friederich Spiry, was the only son of the family and was
born in 1826 at Kassel, a German colony in the Ukraine of South Russia, and
was united in marriage to Louisa Jesser, a native of Wuertenberg, Germany.
Five children were born to this union, namely: Karl, Philip, Fred and
Karolina, who homesteaded and resided in Walworth county; their oldest
sister, Barbara, resided at Portland, Oregon.

The grandparents arrived in the United States in 1888 and had experienced
much difficulty on their journey as they had been swindled by a passport
salesman and their transportation ticket ended at the port of Bremen,
Germany, whereas it should have included the steamship fare to New York
City. They did not have sufficient funds to continue their trip and were
stranded at Bremen for several months until Philip and Fred Spiry had
earned enough money to pay for their steamship fare to New York. There
again they were stalled for a few months until more money was available
from the boys in South Dakota. I was told that it took nearly two years
until the grandparents had arrived at their destination at Scotland, South
Dakota.

I, Philip H. Spiry, the oldest son of Philip Spiry, Sr., was born on my
father's homestead, 3-1/2 miles north of Java, South Dakota, on August 28,
1891. My father was among the early settlers of Walworth county, a former
resident of Selby and always active in public affairs.

In the spring of 1885, my father, then a lad of 20, and his brother, Fred,
age 17, immigrated to the United States, and finally arrived at Scotland,
South Dakota, in a penniless and half-starved condition, having had their
last meal at New York City 3-1/2 days prior to their arrival at Scotland. A
kind-hearted merchant by the name of Henry Sieler noticed the half-starved
lads in front of his store and finally questioned them. After hearing of
their circumstances, he invited them into a restaurant and of course, this
was their first meal in South Dakota. After their meal, they were invited
into his store, and before the end of that day, both of the boys had landed
their first jobs on farms.

They were employed as farm laborers in the vicinity of Menno and Scotland
until they learned that free government land was available to be
homesteaded in Walworth county. In March of 1888, my father, his brother
Fred, and two other families arrived at Ipswich, South Dakota, in an
emigrant car, Ipswich then being the end of the railroad.

Father brought with him one ox, one horse, a farm wagon and a breaking
plow, while Fred had two ponies. From Ipswich they proceeded in a westerly
direction and finally arrived on Hiddenwood creek, then followed the creek
looking for water weeds, which would indicate shallow water, as they knew
that well drilling equipment was not available within miles. Then they
proceeded to dig a well with a spade and found plenty of water at 6 to 8
feet deep. They started to break sod to be used for the building of their
first house, and within a few weeks the house was completed at a cost of
$24.00.

My parents were married in the year 1889 and raised a family of 11
children, named as follows: Mrs. Magdalina Aman of Spokane, Washington;
Philip H. Spiry of Selby; C. F. Spiry of Java, who died in April, 1940;
John E. Spiry of Selby, who died in August, 1941; Rose Hochstetter, Samuel
E. Spiry and Alvin Spiry, residing at Java; Dr. Arthur W. Spiry and
Theodore Spiry, residing at Mobridge; Mrs. Bertha Hay of Aberdeen; and Mrs.
Annette Heezen of Buchanan, Michigan.

In the year 1896, my father was elected as county assessor, serving for two
terms. In 1900 he entered the farm implement business at Java in
partnership with his brother, Fred. In 1902 he was elected as county
treasurer and served to the end of 1906. In the spring of 1903 the Spiry
family moved to Bangor, then the county seat of Walworth county.

I am reminded of the first moving of the county seat to Selby. The incident
occurred on a cold January afternoon of 1905, when a caravan of wagon teams
appeared in front of the court house and proceeded to move the furniture.
My father, then being the county treasurer, protested and stated that he
would not permit the moving of his records unless proper credentials were
produced that would authorize such an act. However, a short time later, the
sheriff arrived and produced an instrument purported to be a court order
signed by a judge who had temporarily taken over during the absence of Judge
McCafferty, who then was the circuit judge of this district. The county
furniture and records were loaded into lumber wagons and the old courthouse
immediately torn to the ground. The county furniture and records were moved
to Selby and piled in a building then known as the Woodman Hall. This
building I believe is now located on the fair grounds and is used by Doctor
Byron as a barn. Much confusion was experienced by the county officers
until the records were found and placed in their proper order, and of
course, it became necessary for the county officers to make their daily
trips to Selby by team, which was not so pleasant in the cold winter.

In the spring of 1905, my parents moved their residence to Selby in what is
now known as the Coleman Wagner home. A short time later, litigations arose
and the court ordered the county seat to be returned to Bangor. A new frame
building was erected and the county records returned and, of course, it
again became necessary for father to make his daily trips back to Bangor
until the end of his term. In the fall of 1906, the Spiry home was sold to
E. C. Wilson, and in March of 1907 the family moved to Java, where my
father entered the banking business. My father, Philip Spiry Sr., died in
January, 1936, while mother followed him in death during December of the
same year.

MR. WILLIAM SIECK

William Sieck was born November 9, 1868, at Maldorf, Germany. At the age of
19 he and a young friend came to America, landing at St. Louis, Mo., and
staying with an uncle there. Later he went to Davenport, Iowa, where he
worked in a saw mill and then on to Walcott, Iowa, where he met and married
Bertha Beckman. Mrs. Sieck was born January 28, 1878, at Bellemar, Germany,
and at the age of 16 came to America alone, landing at Hoboken, New Jersey.
She was met by a sister, age 17, and together the two young ladies worked
and saved enough money to send for their father, mother, and a family of 9
smaller children to come to America from their home in Germany. It was a
difficult task for these young ladies to earn a living in a new land, and
save money for the passage fare of the family, but by patience, industry,
and thrift the family managed to be together.

Mr. and Mrs. Sieck lived in Walcott, Iowa, where he did mason work. As the
family grew larger, they moved to the farm where they lived for 15 years.
In 1915 they moved to a farm near Marshall, Minnesota, staying there for 6
years. In March of 1921 they came to Walworth county through the efforts of
N. H. (Toot) Kingman, and bought the former Charley Olson farm, 4 miles
west of Selby. There were many years of hard times with drought, hail, and
poor crops, but the family managed to stay together and prosper.

Mr. and Mrs. Sieck raised a family of 9 children: Anna (Mrs. Albert
Meinzer) lives at Amiret, Minn.; Arthur, and wife (Martha Tisdall) live on
a farm near Selby; Herbert and family live in Lucan, Minn.; Lillian (Mrs.
Edward Kiel) lives in Austin, Minn.; William Jr., lives in Selby; Herman
and wife (Elsie Birkholt) and family on the old home place; Viola (Mrs.
Charley Birkholt) and family live in Selby; Elmer, who served in World War
II for 4 years, all this time being spent overseas now lives on a farm
southwest of Selby; Lloyd passed away on April 29, 1945, after serving with
the Armed Forces in World War II for 4-1/2 years, and died of injuries
received on Luzon Island in the Pacific area.

In 1928 Mr. Sieck passed away after an illness of pneumonia. Mrs. Sieck, in
1942, moved into Selby where she now lives.

MR. AND MRS. GUDMUND OLSON

Gudmund Olson was born on the 27th of September, 1841, at or near Bergen,
Norway. He emigrated to America in 1872 and settled near Canton, South
Dakota.

Bertha Hagen was born the 26th of September, 1856, in Stamnos, Norway. She
came to America in 1884. In her diary she said she lived with her parents
until she was ten years old when she went out to earn her own living among
strangers. Of this time in her life, she says, "The persons who have to go
out among strangers to earn their living at such an early age, have a lot
of trials." Upon arriving in this country, she was employed in different
homes in and around Canton and Sioux City, Iowa.

On the 16th of November, 1885, dad and mother were married at the home of
John Moen, of Canton, South Dakota. A Rev. Olson performed the ceremony and
used as his text Psalm 124, 8th verse. She says he admonished them about
how necessary it is to begin their wedded life with God, what a blessing it
brings and what happiness and contentment results. This admonition they
faithfully obeyed, as daily devotions were a rules in our household and the
first spiritual reaction I can recall was Sunday mornings when father read
the text for the day from the "Hus Postille". He read rather slowly and the
text was long and sometimes it rather irked us children to sit still for so
long a time, but how thankful I have been in later life to have those
blessed memories to dwell upon.

In the latter part of May, 1886, they came to Campbell county, settling on
a homestead near Mound City.

Bertha Olson Fadness was born August 18, 1886, and baptized September 24 at
the home of Grandpa and Grandma Lappegard by a traveling pastor.

Inga Olson Larson was born the 29th of January, 1888, and baptized the 4th
of March by Rev. Kirkebak, who had come to serve as pastor in the newly
formed congregation. She died the 18th of June, 1949, and is buried at
Mobridge.

Our brother, Olaf, was born the 31st of March, 1889, and baptized the 28th
of April. He was nine years and seven months when he passed away following
after effects of diphtheria, which he contracted in school the 15th of
September, 1898.

How well I can remember the siege we went through then. They kept him
completely isolated in one room with mother taking care of him. The rest of
us children took care of ourselves, more or less, with the help of Dad and
Severt Byre who stayed with us through it all. The doctor administered
antitoxin to all of us and no one else came down with it. Olaf died the
26th of October and was buried the 28th, with Rev. Skartvedt preaching the
sermon in our house. It being a contagious disease, we could not have a
public funeral.

        MR. AND MRS. GUDMUND OLSON

Clara, the baby of the family, was born the 16th of April, 1894. She was
married to Oscar Olson, of Ellingson, in August, 1917.

I should like to relate some of the experiences of my parents during those
early years. When we went to church, we children were piled into the back
of the wagon box on quilts with hay underneath so as to make a softer place
to sit on and, too, to keep us warmer in cold weather.

Then, there was the ladies' aid,--that really was a gala day in the lives
of us children. We usually walked (about three, four, or five miles) and
went before dinner. How well I remember one time when we were all ready to
go; in fact, we had started, when it began to rain and we had to turn
around and come back home. What disappointed children! Another time we were
more fortunate, however. That day the rain held off until we had started
home so we had to turn back to the place where we had aid, which I believe
was Ole Opheim's. There we had to stay overnight, much to our joy and
happiness. In the morning, dad came after us with the team and wagon. The
aid meetings were conducted very differently from now. The ladies worked at
making shirts for men, knitting and I believe they even spun yarn
sometimes. If the minister was there, he read for them while they worked.
Then they sold these articles to whomever wanted them and the money always
went to missions.

Then there was a terrible prairie fire about the year 1897 or thereabouts.
My mother and dad were helping Holstad's with their threshing when we saw
it several miles south of our place, with a strong south wind bringing it
nearer every minute. We drove home as fast as we could and that afternoon
was a nightmare for us children and it must have been worse than that for
our parents. We children stayed in the house (which was of sod) and I can
still see the flames as they came roaring over the hills less than half a
mile from our house. I believe mother and dad had burned a back fire up to
our fire guard near the house so it went around the guard and our house and
barn were saved. Strange as it may seem, I don't think any homes were lost
or lives either.

About 1890 there was an Indian scare, which did not turn out to be as bad
as pictured. It was during the "Messiah" war and right after the murder of
Sitting Bull and the Indians were indignant and restless. One morning my
father started for Mound City, about 15 miles away. When he got to Rev.
Skartvedt's place a large crowd of people had gathered and they reported
the Indians really were on the move and intending to cross the river. He
came right home again and we loaded up what belongings we especially needed
and all the food we had in the house, and started for Bowdle. There were
quite a few families gathered at our place by that time and we all went
together by team and wagon. Bowdle was a distance of 35 miles so it was
quite late before we arrived there. I can't say how long we stayed,
probably a day or two, but as we didn't hear any more bad news concerning
Indians, we went back and I never heard of them having made any trouble
whatever.

My father passed away at our home about six miles northwest of Selby on
August 16, 1909. He was buried in Bethany cemetery.

In the fall of 1909, my mother went to near Hettinger, North Dakota, and
bought relinquishment on a quarter of land adjoining our homestead. She
sold her belongings near Selby and moved out here in the spring of 1910.
She lived here until the fall of 1923 when she sold most of her stock and
decided to spend the winter visiting. She was with Sister Inga out at
Firesteel until about Christmas when she returned to Mobridge. While there
she was taken sick with an acute attack of Brights disease and pneumonia
and she passed away at the Mobridge hospital January 15, 1924. She is
buried at Bethany cemetery.

Blessed be their memory to we, their children, their relatives and friends.

Written by Bertha Olson Fadness, their daughter.

MR. AND MRS. OTTO J. STEINHOFF

Otto J. Steinhoff came to Selby on March 17, 1905, from Wisconsin where he
was born on December 7, 1881. He worked in and near Selby until March 1,
1909, when he purchased the Selby dray line from Jay Ervans.

On January 26, 1910, he married Ruth Johnson, a daughter of Mr. and Mrs. E.
Gust Johnson, who had come to Walworth county from Nebraska and located on
the old Bassett farm, 5 miles southwest of Selby.

        MR. OTTO J. STEINHOFF

They set up housekeeping in Selby where they lived until September, 1913,
at which time he sold the dray line to Clarence Clark and moved to Java to
be manager of the Selby Implement company located there. After living a
year in Java, he bought back the dray line in Selby and continued to run it
until November of 1938. when the dray line was purchased by the Selby Equity
Union exchange.

Having disposed of his interests in Selby, the Steinhoffs moved to Ipswich
where they still live and where Mr. Steinhoff is a distributor of the
Watkins products. While living at Selby, Mr. Steinhoff served on the board
of county commissioners for eight years and was fire chief for 15 of the 30
years he was a member of the Selby volunteer fire department.

Both Mr. and Mrs. Steinhoff were members of St. Anthony's church and of the
Yeoman Lodge. Mrs. Steinhoff was an active member of the Royal Neighbors and
of the Women's Relief Corps and Mr. Steinhoff a member of the Woodman Lodge.

There are five Steinhoff children: Verne and Lyle, living at Ipswich;
Vincent at Mobridge; Cecelia Schlepp, who resides at Stockton, California;
and Dorothy Morrison, now located at Frankfort, Germany, where her husband
is a member of the Armed Forces.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN B. SMITH

John B. Smith was born on November 6, 1849, at Pembrook, New York, of
sturdy pioneer parents of that territory and was one of six children. When
he was 15 years of age, his father died and he, being the oldest boy at
home, felt responsible for the care of his mother and other members of the
family. On March 7, 1883, he and Julia Rachel Colby were married at
Alexander, New York, and the following year the couple, accompanied by his
mother, sister, Emma, and two brothers, Charles and Isaac, began their
westward trip, seeking new lands and an easier method of livelihood. They
arrived in Aberdeen, South Dakota (then the end of the railroad), during
March of 1884, and proceeded west in a covered wagon until they arrived at
what is now a part of the present site of Selby, and located upon the lands
where they lived the remainder of their lives, being one-half mile west of
Selby. The creek winding through the land, upon which they later filed
homestead rights, made the site attractive to the homeseekers, who very
much desired to plant trees and shrubs about their home. By patient
perseverance and much labor, they succeeded in building the present modern
farm home where they lived until their death.

Both Mr. Smith and his faithful wife were devoted Christians and spent much
of their time and efforts in the building of the Methodist church and
Sunday school in old Bangor, and later in Selby. They both taught in Sunday
school and for many years Mr. Smith was the Sunday school superintendent
and an officer of the church. Mrs. Smith, until her last illness, had
charge of the primary department of the Sunday school. Their home was ever
open for any social activities connected with the church and the fine grove
of trees near the farm buildings was the scene of many enjoyable Sunday
school picnics and other community gatherings. This Christian couple gave
to their children and the community every influence possible to the
building of good characters and upright citizens.

        MR. AND MRS. J. B. SMITH

Four children were born to John B. and Julia B. Smith, the oldest of which
is Newel B., who passed away Newell B., standing, and Walter C. in March,
1950; Walter, who passed away on June 30, 1938; George, who passed away on
December 10, 1948; and Vina (Mrs. Arnold Manke) of Selby.

John B. Smith passed away on June 3, 1936, at his home west of Selby, at
the age of 87 years, having lived for 52 years on his homestead. Julia B.
Smith preceded him in death, having died on March 30, 1925.

OLUFSON FAMILY

My father, Peter Harbo Olufson was born at Nordfjord, Norway, March 30,
1850. He was baptized and confirmed in the Davik parish. At school he
finished the course for Norwegian parochial school teacher.

In about 1885 he came to America and taught in different places in
Minnesota and Dakota. In 1888 he came to Walworth county, South Dakota and
took land about 3 miles from the present town of Selby and built a
sodhouse. Mother (Nellie Aardahl) was born February 18, 1860 also at
Nordfjord and baptized and confirmed in the Davik parish. At the early age
of 12 she started working out at dairy work and caring for cattle in the
mountains (saeterjente). In winter when she had less to do outside she
learned to card, spin, weave, knit, and sew, and became a tailor
(skraedder). She worked several years to earn her spinning wheel and hand
sewing machine, and when she came to Walworth county in 1888 she brought
these with her. The family still treasure the possession of these as well
as a chest made and given to her in Norway.

At Bangor, South Dakota, she went to work for the Kingman and Stablein
families during which time she learned to speak some English.

On December 28, 1888 she was married to Mr. Olufson at Bangor, a small
village 8 miles from their farm. Bowdle was the nearest railroad town and
it was 25 miles away.

Like all the early settlers their home had a humble beginning. It was not
easy to make a start but they were not lacking in courage. After some years
a five-roomed frame house replaced the sodhouse, a fair sized lumber barn
was built, horses replaced the oxen for work and improved machinery came in
place of the old walking plow, and other implements.

Six children were born to them: Caroline, Ottman and Mina (twins), Minnie,
Bertha, Stanley. Mina died when she was one year old.

Father and mother were both much concerned about the Christian welfare of
their family. At an early age we were taught the stories of the Bible and
table and bed-time prayers; and later the Catechism and Explanation. We
attended parochial school held at the homes or at the school. Father was
often the teacher. Rev. P. Skartvedt was our pastor in early years.
Services were held at the homes or in the schoolhouse, the present Tisdall
schoolhouse. Father also loved to sing and was the hymn leader (klokker) at
the services. His collection of books steadily grew and he loved to read
and study well.

He took an active part in the work for temperance and sent many written
contributions on that subject to the paper called "The Temperance Swallow."

He served as treasurer on the school board of the Blue Blanket school
district in 1898-99 and 1900.

Several women in the neighborhood got together and organized a ladies aid.
Mother was much interested in this work and was president for some years.

Although small of stature, mother was blessed with strong health and was a
hard worker out on the farm as well as in the house. During winter time
when father was away in other districts teaching school, she had all the
barn chores to do as well as the house work and care of the family. We had
many good neighbors, who were all kind and willing to help when it was
needed. The Tisdalls' who lived nearest were especially helpful.

The railroad came through the neighborhood and Selby, only 3 miles distant,
became our nearest town. This was a wonderful help.

At about the turn of the century, drought conditions prevailed year after
year, and things looked discouraging. At this time one heard much about
Canada, where good new land could be bought at a low price, and immigrants
from many lands were arriving there in large numbers.

        MR. AND MRS. O. H. OLUFSON

A few of the Selby farmers also then got the so-called "Canada fever."
Early in 1902, father with a few of the neighbors went to Alberta on an
investigating trip. They went to Wetaskiwin by train and from there by team
and sleigh east 45 to 50 miles and found the John Hanson and Jonas Anderson
families, who had moved there the year before. Father was well pleased with
the land and filed on a homestead. Upon their return we began making plans
to move.

In the spring father sold our farm in South Dakota. It was one half section
with improvements, we were to leave for Alberta in April. Horses, cattle,
machinery and furniture was to be shipped in cars. We (the children) looked
forward to what was to be our first ride on a train. However, it was not
easy, especially for our parents, to say farewell to the many good
neighbors we were leaving behind and the home that had been built during
the testing days of pioneer life.

We boarded the train at Herreid as did also the Stener Hilde family who
accompanied us throughout the entire trip. We traveled across vast plains
of prairie in North Dakota. We crossed the border line at Portal where we
had to stay two days. When we reached Moose Jaw it was raining and as we
traveled westward the rains increased. At Calgary we learned the railroad
track going north had washed out and that we were to stay in the Immigrant
House till it was repaired. We stayed there for over a week. Once the track
was repaired we were on our way again. The further north we went the more
trees we saw and they were beautiful to us who had hardly seen any trees in
South Dakota. Finally we reached our destination, Wetaskiwin. The train
ride was over but there was still 45 miles of wagon trail to drive with
team and wagon before the homestead would be reached and now we found the
trail was impassable due to deep water and mud.

Father, who had for sometime in Dakota corresponded with Rev. C. Nodtvedt,
a United Lutheran pastor at Silverton, Oregon, and knew he was moving to
Alberta, found he had already arrived, and he offered to share his house
with us. They made us very welcome. During this time in Wetaskiwin, father
bought more land and 400 acres were added to the homestead. The horses and
cattle were turned out to graze near town, a welcome change to being shut
in the cars. Two heifer calves had been born, one at Calgary, the other at
Wetaskiwin and we took pride in naming them Calgary and Alberta.

Finally Mr. Hanson, Andrew Anderson and Mr. Sand came to Wetaskiwin with
the news we could get through and they would help and next morning we
started. Some rode horseback chasing the cattle, others drove in wagons
going eastward over a winding wagon trail which some times took us right
across sloughs deep enough to let water into the box. The many mud holes
encountered were not easy to cross and 17 times on that trip the best team
had to be added to the one stuck and in that way made it through. The men
all got their share of wading in mud and water too. It took 2 days to reach
Mr. Sand's home where arrangements were made for us to stay until the log
house was built on our land.

In a comparatively short time the log house 16x18 was erected but not
finished. With only one side of the roof shingled, no door and no floor, we
moved in. However the shingling was soon finished and later the door and
floor put in. Humble as it was we were happy to be in a home of our own
again. We really felt good in this new land and the climate seemed so
invigorating. We had good appetites and slept good as the nights were cool.

The rich soil gave heavy growth and there were groves of trees, brush
thickets, berry bushes intermingled with stretches of grassland and sloughs
and a profusion of flowers of which the rosebush seemed predominating. Thus
our district was named Rosebush. At that time there were many trees large
enough for building material. The diamond willow made good fence posts but
the roots were hard to budge when clearing land.

Father broke 5 acres on the homestead the first year. It was hard work to
clear land: brushing, grubbing and then breaking. Slow as it was, little by
little, the fields grew larger each year.

Country stores with post offices came into being in several nearby places,
a big help to all the settlers. Hans Ellefson, also from Selby, South
Dakota, had such a store at Meeting Creek, 5 miles from our home.

Father died October 3, 1920 and mother died December 18, 1932.

Three of the children still live here in the same neighborhood on their
farms: Ottman farms the old home place as well as his own land. Mr. and
Mrs. Alfred Lien (Bertha) have a nice built-up farm and do considerable
farming each year. Mr. and Mrs. W. E. Hall (Caroline) live on a smaller
farm. Mrs. Hall was a parochial and public school teacher for a number of
years. Mr. and Mrs. Elias Olson (Minnie) were farmers also in this
neighborhood until two years ago when they retired to live in the city of
Calgary. Mrs. Olson was also a parochial teacher and taught some music.
Stanley, who finished the commercial course at Camrose Lutheran College,
went to the Gregg business school in Chicago when he became a teacher in
business. He taught the commercial course at several Lutheran colleges and
was engaged in that work for 20 years. During the past six years he has
been employed by the International Harvester Co., at Park River, North
Dakota.

MR. AND MRS. SEVERT OPHEIM

Severt Opheim was born June 11, 1868 and his wife, Gunhild Holo, April 25,
1864 in Aal, Hallingdal, Norway. They attended the common school of Norway
and were instructed and confirmed in the Lutheran faith.

They were married in Oslo, Norway and came directly to America in the
spring of 1890, living with his brother, Ole, who had arrived here a few
years earlier, until he could establish a home of his own.

They went through the usual hardships of pioneer life, starting farming
with a yoke of oxen and very little money. He worked in the harvest fields
to earn extra money and later did carpenter work and blacksmithing for
himself and his neighbors.

He filed on a preemption in Walworth county and three years later bought a
relinquishment on a quarter across the line in Campbell county. On this
land they built their home of sod, later moving a frame house onto this
land and further improving it by the planting of trees which are still
standing.

By the time Mr. Opheim retired from active farm work, their farm consisted
of four quarters and a set of farm buildings.

In 1930 he sold his farm interests to his two youngest sons, Alton, on the
home place and Lars establishing a home on the land in Walworth county. Mr.
and Mrs. Opheim moved to an apartment in the home of their daughter, Mrs.
Christ Norby, where they lived until three years ago when they moved to
Selby, their daughter, Mrs. Gena Thorstenson living with them.

Their community service centered around church work, first donating an acre
of land for Bethany Church and later contributing much time and money for
the building of the church. Mr. Opheim served many years as trustee and
caretaker. Mrs. Opheim was active in Ladies' Aid work and was one of the
early presidents of the organization.

They were the parents of 8 children, one dying in infancy. Four live on
farms in the Selby community, and are: Alton, Lars, Sankey, and Mary, (Mrs.
Christ Norby); Gena (Mrs. Gena Thorstenson) living in Selby; Emma (Mrs. H.
J. Kohler) 362 Sherburne ave., St. Paul, Minn., and Oley of Cottage Grove,
Ore. All are married and have families, there being 20 grandchildren and 6
great grandchildren at the present time.

COL. THOS. G. ORR

In 1883, Colonel "Tom" Orr, then a resident of Viroqua, Wisconsin, enthused
over the offer of free government homesteads and tree claims, made a trip
of inspection of Walworth county, Dakota territory, lands and filed on 320
acres in the Blue Blanket valley, at Aberdeen, South Dakota, then the
terminus of the Milwaukee railroad. The land selected was located 11 miles
east of the present city of Mobridge, and about 5 miles north of the
present town of Glenham.

In the spring of 1884, he shipped out by emigrant car, horses, needed  farm
machinery and equipment and household furniture, with lumber and tar paper
for a small homesteader's shack. Ed A. Newell, a brother-in-law,
accompanied him. All this was hauled over prairie trails about 100 miles to
the homestead site. It was a wet spring and every depression of the land
was level full. With no culverts or roads, the heavily laden wagons were
stuck in the mud many times. On the return trips, buffalo bones were picked
up and hauled to Aberdeen, where a triple box load of bones were sold for
about seven to eight dollars. There was an immense pile of white bones
which looked as big as a court house. The proceeds were used to buy
groceries needed for the trip.

At that time the only town of any size was LeBeau, located about 30 miles
south of the present city of Mobridge, on the east bank of the Missouri
river. It was a real old time western town, boomed by a group of Chicago
real estate dealers who had staked in preliminary surveys of seven western
railroads and platted and sold lots as far as seven miles out from the
center, as far east as New York. They claimed 4,000 population in 1884 and
advertised it as the "Western Chicago." There were only two good sized
buildings--the hotel and the school house. The balance of the buildings
were very small and crude structures and with many people living in tents
or frames covered largely by canvas. A daily horse-drawn stage from
Aberdeen, South Dakota, brought in mail and passengers over the 100-mile
prairie trail. Four cantankerous broncos were the motive power, and kept in
a steady lope for about 15 miles, where a new relay of horses was ready for
a quick change. They had to average about 10 miles per hour to make the
trip on schedule. The stage was of the light buckboard type, much favored
by the ranchers. A longer body permitted the use of two spring wagon seats
with room behind for luggage and mail. Passengers had to hang on over the
rough trail to prevent being bounced out, and had little protection from
cold weather.

In the summer of 1884 a movement was started to organize the county and
locate the county seat. Col. Tom Orr was always interested in government
and politics and was one of the active leaders. A landowner who was from
the state of Maine and had more money than the average homesteader, and
whose land was very centrally located in the proposed county, offered to
donate a block of land and a two-story frame courthouse if the county seat
was located on his land. An election was held with the majority voting to
organize Walworth county and to locate the county seat at Bangor townsite,
mentioned above. County officers were appointed by the Governor, including
Col. Tom Orr as combined auditor and register of deeds, as provided under
territorial law, to which of office he was twice re elected, serving a total
of six years.

Many homesteaders came to reside on their land without any horses or
machinery or stock and with not sufficient funds to maintain themselves.
The county was compelled to provide for the maintenance of some of these
found destitute, and had no poor house, so they "farmed them out" to
homesteaders who could provide the necessities of life for a consideration
paid by the county funds. One such applicant at a meeting of the county
commissioners was a typical aged Irishman, not long from the "auld
country." The commissioners told him of several homesteaders who had
offered to take indigents and asked him if he had any preference. He
answered, "It makes no dif, Me Lords, just so I have me three good meals a
day."

Many incidents happened during the early homesteaders experience, some
tragic and some comic, but there was a goodfellowship and comradeship and
willingness to help neighbors when in need that was typical of the great
west.

On the Orr homestead and tree claim the site for the buildings was selected
half way down the east line of one mile. After the shack was erected, a
well was dug by hand, down 72 feet, and dry as a bone. Water was hauled in
barrels from a creek waterhole 3 miles away, and later from a well on the
Howell homestead 3 miles east, one of the nearest neighbors. Later in
testing for water on the homestead with a post-hole digger and shank
extensions, sufficient water was found less than half a miles from the
buildings at a depth of 14 feet.

Col. Tom Orr's wife, Emma Newell Orr, with her son Frank and daughter
Angie, came by train from Wisconsin to the rail terminus at Aberdeen, and
on the day before Christmas, 1884, came by the daily bus previously
described, to Bangor and to the Capt. N. H. Kingman farm home where
arrangements had been made for board and room for the family until spring.
This home was about a mile east of the court house in Bangor, where at that
time no suitable living accommodations could be had. The snow came later
and was very deep, making it difficult to get around. But the neighbors
formed a literary society which met weekly at the Kingman home and helped
to pass the time.

An incident which might well have been tragic occurred on one of the trips
for water from the Howell well. Frank Orr, then about 11 years of age, was
staying with Ed Newell on the homestead. Horses brought from Wisconsin had
been traded in for oxen because there was no oats or feed for horses, while
oxen could be turned out on the prairie to get their feed. The Howell well
had been dug about 4 feet square, was 35 feet deep, with a water level of
about 14 feet and stoned up that high to prevent caving in. Planks had been
laid across the top and were tipped back when it was desired to haul up
water in a bucket. On arrival, the Howells had asked that Ed accompany the
men to help move a homesteaders shack over for an addition to the Howell
home. Charley Howell, a boy of about 14 years, was left to help Frank haul
up the water to fill the barrels. One barrel was placed on the ground, two
planks in the middle tipped back, and the two boys were able to haul up
pails of water, when they took turns stepping over the plank opening and
emptying the pail of water in the barrel from which it was later
transferred to the barrels in the wagon. Some water was naturally spilled
on the planks in handling, and Charley in carrying a pail of water across
slipped and fell, hitting the plank on the opposite side and he and the
pail fell pellmell into the well,--and he could not swim. The rope had been
coiled as the pail was pulled up. Frank had enough presence of mind to grab
the rope and let down the pail and hollered to Charley to grab the rope and
straddle the pail, which he did. Frank braced himself and held Charley's
head above water, and hollered for help. Several women came running out,
took hold of the rope and with everybody helping were able to pull Charley
up out of the well. When he tried to stand, he discovered he could
not,--that one thigh bone had been broken when he fell against the plank.
He was helped into the house and to bed. The men were summoned and Ed
Newell volunteered to go for the doctor, 22 miles away across country.

They arrived about 11 p.m., that night, but found two patients instead of
one. Frank had taken over Charley's regular job of herding the Howell herd
of cattle, with the oxen he had used hauling the water wagon. It drizzled
rain all day and Frank felt miserable. About five o'clock he brought the
cattle within sight of the buildings and rode in and told Mrs. Howell that
he felt bad and would like to lie down; that if she would call him he would
bring in the cattle to the corral for the night. When she woke him she
said, "Why Frank Orr, your face is all broken out in blotches," and sent
one of the girls to bring in the cattle. The doctor pronounced it measles
on arrival, and Frank was there six weeks recovering. The day out in the
rain just at the time of measles breaking out had bad results. At last
report, Charley Howell was a resident of McLaughlin, South Dakota, also his
sister Nellie, who married Bill Nesbit, who had been raised on a ranch on
the banks of the Missouri river, several miles north of the present site of
Mobridge, and was prominent in McLaughlin as postmaster and had other
official duties.

The homestead residence requirement was 5 years, less certain credit for
having served in the Civil War, which cut our requirement down to 14
months, because Col. Tom Orr had served 4-1/2 years, in the Civil War. The
required residence was made from the spring of 1885 to the fall of 1886,
when the family moved into a residence which had been built in Bangor,
across the corner from the new school house.

There was a very heavy snowfall during the winter we were on the homestead,
with some bad blizzards which prevented reaching the stock at the sidehill
barn about a quarter of a mile from the house, for as many as three days in
some instances. The barn was a half dug-out from a hill, the frame made of
logs from the Missouri river bottoms, covered by mesh wire and heavy straw.
The stock was warm, nibbled at the straw and got water from eating some
snow which drifted in, and seemed none the worse for the lack of feed and
water. The children were able to take their sleds to the peak of the
dwelling roof and slide down and off the roof of the shed addition on to
the snow drifts about the house. Many lives were lost during the eighties
in blizzards in the Dakotas, including a considerable number of school
children and teachers.

In the fall of 1889, the Sitting Bull Indian scare caused many settlers to
flee, some not stopping until they reached the Twin Cities. The Indians had
been having "Ghost Dances" all summer in some sort of a religious craze,
and some were aggrieved because by treaty they had been moved off the lands
east of the Missouri river a few years previous. The word came that Chief
Sitting Bull had started with a band of young Indians from the Fort Yates
reservation and planned to join other Indians from farther south in a
massacre of whites east of the river. It was learned later that one or more
cowboys took advantage of the nervousness of the settlers to put over what
they thought was a practical joke. The system was to rush up to the
settlers shack after they were in bed, pound on the door with the heavy end
of their riding quirt, and shout, "Run for your lives, the Indians are
coming." To heighten the effect, they set fire to a number of straw stacks
which to the settlers looked like burning farm homes. The result was a
general exodus eastward, with many comic happenings and some very serious,
and tragic. Col. Tom Orr was then a collector for the Walter A. Wood
Machine company, and happened to be at Gettysburg when he got the word. He
started for Bangor at once. The trail was so full of fleeing homesteaders
that he had to travel out on the prairie most of the time. He was entreated
to turn around and go back because of the danger of approaching Indian
bands on the warpath. One old lady homesteader had put her featherbed on
an ox, and she was astride that, and pleaded with tears in her eyes for the
Colonel to turn around and save himself. Frank, then about 15, had put the
harness on a team and had the spring wagon all ready to go, and dug up his
father's Civil War revolver, rim fire, as the only weapon on the place, but
awaited results until morning at least. Nobody undressed or went to bed
because of the uncertainty.

Bangor men dug up all possible firearms, put out pickets and planned to
await developments. It was a long, strenuous night, especially after the
moon went down and dawn was approaching, when it was thought an attack
would come, if at all. But it proved to be a pretty realistic hoax.

In 1891, Frank Orr, then 17 years old, moved with his mother and sister on
to a rented farm about 3 miles north of Bangor and farmed with three oxen,
getting into crop about 70 acres of wheat, oats and barley, and breaking
about 12 acres of new land in time to put in flax. It was a pretty good
crop yield, and the grain was hauled to Bowdle, then the railroad
terminus, taking three days for the round trip with oxen, and sleeping
under the wagon. Coal and winter supplies were brought back on the return
trips, the oxen finding their feed on the prairie. Wheat sold for about 40c
and flax about 70c a bushel, but the net returns for the summer's work was
around $500.

With this fund, Frank, his mother and sister moved to Brookings, South
Dakota, where Frank and Angie matriculated in the State college. After
completing a prelaw course and studying in a law office about a year, Frank
was offered the secretaryship of the college, accepted, and served about
six years when he resigned to enter the business world. He was assistant
manager of The Dakota Farmer for a time and later foreign news editor of
the Aberdeen Daily News, which position he resigned to accept the assistant
cashiership of a new bank at Russell, Bottineau county, North Dakota, at
the end of 1905. He sold his interests in the bank in 1909 and moved to
Mott, Hettinger county, North Dakota, where he opened the First State Bank
of Mott. He sold out on a consolidation of banks in 1918, and served during
the first World War as supervisor of county agents in twelve counties, and
later as representative for the First National Bank of Minneapolis and the
War Finance Corporation. In 1932 Frank and family moved to Bismarck, North
Dakota, where he resides in 1949 as this is written.

Col. Tom Orr was appointed by the Governor of South Dakota as a colonel of
militia at the time of the Sitting Bull Indian scare in 1889, and organized
a company of cavalry composed largely of cowboys and stockmen, distributed
arms and drilled them. The idea was to be prepared if an Indian uprising
should actually occur, and to instill confidence in the minds of the
homesteaders that they were being protected. Since that time he had
commonly been called Colonel.

At the time the Milwaukee railroad was extended to the Missouri river at
Evarts, opposite an island in the Missouri river where the railroad
installed a pontoon bridge to enable them to get the business of shipping in
cattle in the spring and out in the fall for the big government pasture
established for the Indians on the west side, 80 miles square. Col. Tom Orr
moved to Evarts and erected an office with living room behind, and
conducted a real estate, insurance and notary public business.

At the time the Milwaukee railroad decided to extend their line west of the
river, Col. Orr aided the officials in determining the route and was the
clerk of the lot sale for the new town of Mobridge.

He had served as a delegate to the constitutional convention at Sioux
Falls, in 1889, when the two Dakotas were admitted to statehood. He served
as secretary of the state Republican central committee in two presidential
campaigns. He thus became personally acquainted with Theodore Roosevelt and
was a strong supporter of his cause. He served as enrolling and engrossing
clerk in the house in the last two legislative sessions before statehood.
He was a member of the Blue lodge, Chapter and Commandery of the Masonic
order. He was appointed commander and Mrs. Orr as matron of the State
Soldiers Home at Hot Springs and managed this institution for seven years
when age and infirmity compelled him to retire from active life.

Mr. and Mrs. Col. Orr moved back to Brookings, South Dakota in June, 1920,
where Mrs. Orr died soon after arrival and Col. Orr followed about four
months later.

MR. AND MRS. PHILIP PFAFF

Mr. and Mrs. Philip Pfaff were both born in South Russia and were married
there in 1881. In 1885 they came to America settling at Lesterville, South
Dakota. In October of 1889 they came to Walworth county, filing on the SW
1/4 of Section 26, formerly a part of the Christman farm, and the NE 1/4 of
Section 27, land now owned by Edward Himrich. In the spring of 1904 they
purchased a total of 480 acres of land in Campbell county, 7 miles
southwest of Mound City where the family lived until the fall of 1911 when
they sold out and went to Idaho. Selling there in 1917, they returned to
Selby where they purchased the house now owned by Ed Delzer. They
celebrated their golden wedding in 1931 and, at that time, they had 25
grandchildren and 12 great grandchildren. Mrs. Pfaff passed away in
January, 1940, and Mr. Pfaff passed away last year, 1949.

Like the young people of so many of the pioneer families, the Pfaff
children and grandchildren are widely scattered, residing in many states,
the only one remaining in this section being Mrs. John J. Schanzenbach of
Mobridge. Doubtless, however, they all look back with pride to the lives
and works of their parents, wrought so well in the new land of America and
for the pioneer home in Dakota.

MR. AND MRS. FRED C. PERMAN

Fred C. and Rose Perman were both born in New Gluecksthal, South Russia,
which is near the Black Sea city of Odessa and were united in marriage
there on January 16, 1894. Their people were farmers. Almost immediately
after the wedding they embarked for America, coming to Freeman, South
Dakota, and from there to Bowdle, where he filed on a homestead in the
southern part of McPherson county and north of Bowdle. In 1900, he bought
land in Glenn township, 11 miles north of Hoven, where the family grew up
and prospered. They retired from the farm in 1928 moving to Java where they
built a new house and developed one of the fine properties of that city. In
March of 1946, they sold their Java home and purchased what is known as the
Les Herring house in Selby from their son, Ed, and moved there.

        MR. AND MRS. FRED C. PERMAN

Mr. Perman served the county as commissioner for two terms and served the
county and community in many other respects through the years. He was
always rated as one of the high class and progressive farmers of the county
and lent his influence at all times to progressive movement. He was one of
the early converts to power farming and purchased one of the first internal
combustion tractors to come into the country, one of the old two cylinder,
kerosene-burning Hart Parr outfits, which made a noise like a half dozen
freight trains and would pull anything that was loose.

MR. CHARLES O. PETERSON

Charles O. Peterson was born in Sweden, April 6, 1845, arid came with his
parents to the United States when six years of age, landing at Newport in
the month of June. Eventually, they established a home in Laporte, Indiana,
where he lived until the Civil War started. At that time, he enlisted as
private in the infantry. Later he was transferred to Company "E", 9th Ohio
cavalry. He served all through the war and received an honorable discharge
July 20, 1865, at Lexington, North Carolina. After the war he joined the
United States regulars. Among some of the medals he received while in the
service was one for standing guard on January 1, 1863 at a reservoir for 36
hours with the temperature at -60 during which time a terrific snow storm
was raging. He was a member of the G.A.R.

He was married to Christina A. Nelson on October 8, 1873. They made their
home in LaPorte, Indiana. Four children were born to them, namely Robert,
Ollie, Chester and Clifford. Mr. Peterson came to South Dakota in 1883,
filing on a homestead, where he built a home. Four years later his
courageous wife with four small children followed her adventurous husband
into a vast land of wilderness, where they endured all the hardships and
privations of pioneer life. Here they lived to see the colorful panorama of
the frontier being made into a safe and prosperous country in which to
live. As the years went on, three more children were born to them: Walter,
Thomas and Gertrude.

Mr. Peterson served as the first rural mail carrier out of Selby. Being the
possessor of a brilliant mind, much of his spare time was spent in reading
and studying astronomy.

In 1911, they moved to Centuria, Wisconsin, where he died July 8, 1922. He
was buried near Centuria with full military honors.

Christina A. Nelson was born in Stockholm, Sweden, on September 25, 1851 of
Royal lineage. When still a small child, she came to the United States with
her parents. She was a talented singer and had many fine qualities which
endeared her to all who knew her. She passed away February 14, 1930, at the
home of her only daughter. The remains were laid to rest beside those of
her husband.

Robert was born July 16, 1876. He married Dora Miller in 1899. He was a
violinist and he and his wife furnished the music for many neighborhood
parties. They lived in Walworth county until 1907, when they moved to
Alberta, Canada, moving from there to British Columbia. It was in British
Columbia that they built a nice home and reared their family. He passed away
August 16, 1936.

Ollie was born January 19, 1877. He married Bessie Hendrickson in 1906.
They made their home in LeBeau where he served as town marshal for a number
of years. Later he was employed by the Minneapolis and St. Louis railroad.
He was ever faithful to employer and friend. He passed away in 1935.

Chester was born August 2, 1879. In early life he was a cowboy and fancy
roper. Later he took up the barbering trade and worked in LeBeau, Evarts,
Selby and a number of other towns in South Dakota. He was married to Clara
Siebrecht. He passed away on October 19, 1918, of flu during the terrible
epidemic.

Clifford was born in 1881. At the age of 19 he was drowned in the little
Missouri river near Paoli, North Dakota, while working for a rancher there.

Walter was born at Bangor, April 30, 1888. He served as railway mail clerk
for a number of years and later became postmaster at Centuria, Wisconsin.
He was a talented sign painter and a skillful penman. He married Edna Farr
in 1922. He passed away May 8, 1942.

Thomas resides in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where he is employed. He has a fine
family.

Gertrude Peterson Cheskey lives on a farm southwest of Selby. She is the
wife of Charles Cheskey.

MR. AUGUST C. SCHMIDT

August C. Schmidt was born near Hamburg, Germany on May 12, 1856 and Ida
Ebert near Berlin, Germany on August 16, 1857. The couple were married in
Germany in 1871 and nine children were born to them.

In 1881 they came to America and located near Milbank, South Dakota, where
they made their home for a short time. Mr. Schmidt, having learned the
butcher business in Germany, followed this trade for a short time in
Minneapolis, Minnesota, later moving back to South Dakota and filing on a
claim.

        MRS. AUGUST C. SCHMIDT

A few years later, the family moved to Ortonville, Minnesota, where Mr.
Schmidt built a meat market and enjoyed a fine business for a number of
years. In 1900, they moved to Eureka, South Dakota, where Mr. Schmidt
entered the meat business in partnership with Emil Dierenfeldt, an old time
friend from Germany. In 1903 he moved to Selby and purchased the meat
market from Abe Taylor and continued in business for a number of years.
When he retired, he sold the business to his son, Albert, who continued to
operate it until 1945 when he sold the establishment to the Simons
brothers, Lester and Francis, of Selby.

It was often said by men of the trade that August Schmidt was one of the
best butchers in the United States as he knew his business from every
angle,--the buying of the livestock, the butchering of the animals and being
a meat curer and sausage-maker unsurpassed by anyone.

Mr. Schmidt was very active in civic and public life. He was a member of
both bodies of the Masonic orders located in Selby and gave much time and
study in the exemplication of the work. He was mayor of Selby for several
years. The surviving children are: Miss Rose Schmidt, Albert H. Schmidt and
Mrs. Leo Buchanan of Selby; Mrs. L. C. Fix of Ipswich, and Mrs. Lloyd
Button, Mrs. A. C. deMalignon and Arthur Schmidt, all of Aberdeen. Mr.
Schmidt died in Selby on January 19, 1922 and Mrs. Schmidt passed away on
September 28, 1941. Interment was made in the Selby cemetery.

MR. AND MRS. CHARLES D. SMITH

Charles D. Smith was born near Albany, New York on March 11, 1834. When
very young he moved with his parents to Three Rivers, Michigan where he
grew to manhood. Here he was married to Elizabeth Ann Baum of Three Rivers
who was born January 5, 1840.

Mr. and Mrs. Smith remained in Three Rivers until the close of the Civil
War when they moved to Waterloo, Iowa. They remained here until 1882 when
they moved to Fairview, South Dakota. In the spring of 1885 they came to
Walworth county, South Dakota. The family now consisted of 9 children;
three boys and six girls. The two oldest girls, Emma, 23 and Clara, 21 were
married and remained in Fairview.

Mr. Smith accompanied by Hiram, 18, Nellie, 16, Bert, 13, Joseph, 10, and
Lottie, 5, made the trip from Fairview to Walworth county in a covered
wagon, driving a small bunch of stock with them and camping by the wayside.

Mrs. Smith with Alice, 8, and Nettie, 1-1/2 years, came later by train to
Ipswich which was then the end of the railroad. Mr. Smith met them and they
made the remainder of the trip in the wagon.

The object of the move to Walworth county was the great land opportunity
offered by the government of a homestead, a pre-emption and a timber claim
to build up a permanent home.

The homestead was taken in Brown township. It took all of their finances
and more to get established on the farm and ready for operation. Their
first house was about 12 by 28 feet, low with a car roof and built of one
thickness of lumber. It was tarpapered and sodded up on the outside. The
inside was divided into two rooms; the kitchen having a dirt floor, and the
sleeping room having a board floor.

Mr. and Mrs. Smith belonged to the Presbyterian faith and had an average
education of that time. Mr. Smith was on the school board of the Brown
school district for several years, serving in that capacity at the time of
his death.

        MR. AND MRS. CHARLES D. SMITH

The going was hard those first years, with so many obstacles to overcome:
debts, drouths, blizzards (especially the terrible one of
January 12, 1888), the Indian Scare, and prairie fires. One of the prairie
fires burned over the homestead in the spring of 1888 on April 1st. It
burned the barns and outbuildings, four pail fed calves, several hogs, all
but one hen, all the seed grain, hay, and the summer supply of fuel (wood
hauled from the river during the winter and sawed and split). After the fire
had spent itself the sod house, the cave cellar, and sod barn walls were
all that was left standing. The family's ill-fortune was deepened by the
death of Mr. Smith, the father, by cancer in 1889. Yet by careful management
and hard work the mother and children came through those terrible years and
became prosperous, wresting their livelihood from Dakota.

The family can recall that in early days a neighbor, Mr. Frank Hurdy and
his wife who lived east of the present site of Akaska, lost one of their
two oxen. After that either Mr. Hurdy or his wife would walk beside the
remaining oxen and hold up the neckyoke of the wagon. Mrs. Hurdy made most
of the trips to the town of Bangor, a distance of eight or nine miles from
their home, walking beside the ox, helping the animal hold the neck yoke
and sometimes to help pull the load.

Another incident clear in their memory is that one year, Judge Burns of
Bangor, built a row boat and put it down on the lake southwest of Bangor
(southwest also of the present site of the old Bangor cemetery). This boat
was enjoyed by the children and young people for miles around.

The members of the family relate how oxen were broken and used for the
heavier farm work. One oxen in particular they never forgot was afraid of a
fur coat for no particular reason. Whether he was yoked up or not if he saw
anyone wearing a fur coat he would attempt to run away, and he usually
succeeded.

At the present time the following members have passed away: Mr. Smith near
Bangor in 1889; Mrs. Smith at Sand Point, Idaho in 1927; Mrs. Emma Noonan
at Fairview, South Dakota; Mrs. Clara Sparling at Ashton, South Dakota;
Hiram at Portland, Oregon; Mrs. Nellie Birkholt at Selby, Bert at Selby;
and Joe at Lewiston, Idaho.

The remaining living members of the family are: Mrs. Alice Kirkhoven at
Sand Point, Idaho; Lottie Glerup at Burns, Oregon; and Nettie B. Anderson
at Lowry, South Dakota. Surviving are also many grandchildren, several of
whom live in and around Selby: Dexter Glerup, son of Lottie; Charlie
Birkholt and Mrs. Elsie Sieck, son and daughter of Nellie; Mrs. Myrtle
Baumann and Clarence Anderson, daughter and son of Nettie. There are also
many great grandchildren of this early pioneer couple who came to South
Dakota to make their future home.

THE A. H. SMITH FAMILY

Albert H. ("Bert") Smith was one of Selby's earliest lawyers, having begun
