his practice in 1902 and continuing it until his death on October 9, 1933.

His boyhood was typical of those times, his parents having come to Dakota
from New York and Michigan via Iowa. Bert was born near Waterloo, Iowa, on
April 22, 1872,

The Smith family came to Dakota in 1882, and in 1885 homesteaded 11 miles
southwest of Selby. The mother, Elizabeth Ann Baum Smith, loved flowers so
much that she built a stone-walled garden in a low spot near her home and
grew flowers so beautiful that people came for many miles to see them.

Bert's boyhood would have been a hard one for his grandsons today. He did
farm work around the claim during the summers and went to school when he
could during the winters. As a boy of 15 he found his way home from school
in the blizzard of '88 and reluctantly gave up his plan to return to the
school with food for the others, all of whom came through unscathed.

He watched helplessly as a malignancy killed his father, Charles Demetrius
Smith. Then he helped his mother on the farm until younger brothers and
sisters had completed their schooling and could take over. Of the 9 Smith
children, the only one still living in Walworth county is Nettie Smith
Anderson of Lowry.

When he attained his majority Bert took a claim, and for the next few years
successfully combined homesteading, going to college, and teaching school.
In 1901 he graduated with a law degree from Highland Park college, Des
Moines, Iowa.

        MR. ALBERT H. SMITH

The infant town of Selby was fortunate to have Bert Smith for one of its
early citizens. He worked very hard in his modest and unassuming way to
build a good community. His thinking was years ahead of his
time--especially in education. He believed that every child had a right to
a good education, and for that reason he promoted district consolidation
long before most western localities had ever heard of it. He rode the
buses, shoveled snow, and worried until each child was accounted for at
night. He served as president of the Selby school board from 1910 until a
few months before his death. If the sound Selby schools and outstanding
graduates are a monument to his industry and foresight, nothing could
please him more.

Bert's law business prospered, and he usually had a partner. Among these
were A. A. Brown, Marcus Dubel, and Fred Shandorf. His last partner was
George Mickelson. Bert served several terms as states attorney for Walworth
county, and for years he was Selby city attorney. The duty which probably
weighed most heavily upon him was as head of the draft board for Walworth
county during World War I.

On December 2, 1905, he married Ida Rieke. She was a native of Blairstown,
Benton county, Iowa, and had been educated to be a teacher. In 1902 she
resigned her position at Tipton, Iowa, to take a claim in Walworth county.
In 1903 she came to Selby and taught in the frame schoolhouse located west
of the site of the present courthouse. This schoolhouse later burned to the
ground in a spectacular blaze.

Mrs. Smith also believed in doing one's civic duty. She was a church
worker, especially active during the time the present Methodist church was
being built and paid for, and for years she served as head of the primary
department in its Sunday school. She was also an active member of the Selby
Womans club, and helped promote and care for the rest room it originated.
These things she did in addition to her main occupations: bringing up five
children and caring for a large house. Her daughters cannot understand how
she accomplished so much, especially as she was always ready to help when
help was needed. Many a snowbound youngster stayed at her house, and many a
child besides her own got from her a firm foundation in algebra and Latin.

When Bert's death ended his part in educating the children, his wife
continued alone. No sacrifice was too great for her, and even in the depths
of the depression she did not rest until all five of her children had
finished college.

Mrs. Smith called Selby her home until 1946 when she surrendered to her
family's anxiety about her being alone and sold her Selby properties. It
was hard for her to leave friends of so many years, and she is always eager
for Selby news. Her home now is in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, and she makes
occasional visits from there to the four children in different states. She
had the misfortune to be enroute from Morton's home in Colorado to Alice's
in Wyoming on January 2, 1949, when the worst blizzard in history descended
without warning upon the Rocky mountains. Her bus was stalled and she was
marooned for three days with several hundred other people in a tavern at
Rockport, Colorado. She wonders how her blizzard of 1949 compared with
Bert's of 1888.

None of the five Smith children live in Selby, but they remember with
affection the town that was home to them all. They wish Selby a happy
birthday and many happy returns.

In order of seniority, the Smith children are:

Alice, the wife of John Robley Lane. He is a railway mail clerk, running
between Ogden, Utah, and Cheyenne. They are permanently located at 2101
Cheyenne Place, Cheyenne, Wyoming. They have two sons, Dick and Jack.

Florence, the wife of Paul S. Heide. He is a member of the Washington high
school faculty in Sioux Falls and is also well-known for his C.P.A. work
throughout the state. They are presently living at 1905 S. Walts, Sioux
Falls. They have one son, John Paul Heide.

Helen, the wife of Howard Wayne Trimm. He is a talented artist and
ornithologist, and has recently accepted a position with the Kansas state
department of Wild Life conservation. Helen and her husband are
collaborating on writing and illustrating stories with a natural history
slant. They are presently living at 1421 LeGore Drive, Manhattan, Kansas.
They are the parents of one son, Stevie.

Millard, a Commander in the United States Navy. Millard is an honor
graduate of the U. S. Naval Academy, class of '36, and has an outstanding
war record in the Pacific theatre. He married Harriet Olsen of Long Beach,
California, and Valley City, North Dakota. They have two sons, Wayne and
Harlan. Millard has recently been transferred from skipper of the Destroyer
deHaven to the post graduate faculty at Annapolis, Maryland.

Morton, a member of the metallurgical faculty at Colorado State School of
Mines, Golden, Colorado. He tried life in Alaska and research metallurgy
with an industrial firm (where he worked on phases related to the atomic
bomb), before settling down in Colorado. He married Lois Huffmon, of
Flowree, Montana, a former home economics demonstrator. They have one
daughter, Sandra.

MR. AND MRS. TOBIAS J. RISDALL

Among some of the more colorful characters of Walworth county were former
justice of the peace, Tobias Risdall and his wife, Anna.

Both Mr. and Mrs. Risdall were born and educated in Norway, but met and
were married in Renville county, Minnesota, where they lived on a farm for
several years.

        MR. AND MRS. TOBIAS J. RISDALL

During that time the grasshoppers became such a plague and constant threat
to crops, that the Risdalls decided to move. Their first move was to the
southeastern section of Iowa, where they lived until the spring of 1886,
when they again moved, this time to Walworth county, South Dakota, and
settled on the SE 1/4 of 18-124-76. They built a two-room sod house which
served as a home for themselves and their ten children until 1892. At that
time, the nearest railroad point was Bowdle, the county seat was Bangor and
post office was Blue Blanket.

Crops in those days were very uncertain and their meager possessions
consisted of four head of horses, two cows, a plow, a wagon and some pieces
of old furniture. Wood was the only fuel available at that time, and most
of the settlers, Mr. Risdall included, hauled all their wood from the
Missouri river bottoms, near the site of the present city of Mobridge. Mr.
Risdall made his first trip to the river accompanied by his neighbor, John
Franks, on a barn door drawn by horses, in order to procure poles to make a
sled or what was referred to at that time as a "stone boat".

It was not until 1888 that the area was blessed with a good crop. The
Risdalls did not have a granary and the wheat was stored in the bedroom of
the sod house; beds were made for the whole family on top of the wheat.
During severe winter months and accompanying heavy snows, the Risdall
family was often snowed in until some good neighbor came along and dug them
out or some member of the family, who was away, came home to find no trace
of house or barn. A shovel was always kept on the roof of the house for
just such an emergency.

Tobias and Anna Risdall and their family knew many reverses, but in 1892
were finally financially able to begin the building of the long dreamed
about new home--a 5-room frame house, which was never fully completed until
1900. With financial returns from grain crops so very uncertain, Tobias
Risdall decided to try his hand at raising cattle and soon had a herd of 60
to 75 head. This became about the only source of income at that time,--many
of their neighbors had proved up and left, leaving a lot of free range and
the cattle flourished. With a large family and many hands to lend
assistance, they saw the stress of near poverty removed and the family
fared well from that time on.

Tobias Risdall was elected a justice of the peace and in his official
capacity was called to the Olson home to perform the wedding ceremony for
John Olson and his bride-to-be, Miss Eli Saettemsli, but while he was
enroute, a raging blizzard overtook him and he was forced to seek shelter.
He finally arrived at the Jake Tisdall home where he remained for several
days while the anxious bride and bridegroom waited patiently for the sun to
shine and the day to arrive when Mr. Risdall could pronounce them "Mr. and
Mrs".

In 1902 the family moved to Roberts county, South Dakota, and settled on a
farm near Veblen. In 1917. Tobias and Anna retired and moved to Veblen,
where they resided until their death.

The Risdalls lived to celebrate their Golden Wedding anniversary in 1923.

Tobias J. Risdall died in 1935, at the age of 88 years and 8 months and his
wife Anna lived until 1941, passing away at the age of 91 years and 5
months.

They are survived by all of their ten children, the eldest being 76 years
and the youngest being now 58 years of age.

MR. AND MRS. J. O. MOLSTERTIEGEN

Mr. and Mrs. J. O. Molstertiegen were born in Voss, Norway. After their
marriage in 1861, they lived for 9 years on the Molstertiegen home farm
which he bought from his father in 1860. Glowing accounts from a brother
located in Cokato, Minnesota, fired the young couple with enthusiasm for
the new land, so in 1870, with their three young children, Ole, Rachel and
Julia, they set out for America, reaching Cokato, where he bought 80 acres
of his brother's land and built a home. In 1872 a forest fire left them
homeless. Immediately following this misfortune he bought another 80 acres
of heavily wooded land a mile distant, and with his wife and his brother s
help, cleared enough land to build a cabin. Scarcely was this completed
when another fire reduced it to ashes. Undaunted, Mr. Molstertiegen built
another home, cleared the land and lived there 14 years. In 1884, he moved
to Fargo, where he built two houses. He was a master carpenter and might
have built up a good business in Fargo. However, in 1886, he felt that
there was more opportunity on land in Walworth county, so with his family,
he came to Blue Blanket valley where they filed on a homestead. There his
family grew up,--the son in early manhood leaving to settle in Montana. One
daughter, Rachel, taught the home school in the district for 10 years. An
able musician, she also taught music to the daughters of the settlers
around them and was a valuable member of the glee clubs and literary clubs
of the time. Julia, who was endowed with a great deal of the same musical
ability as her sister, married Charles Ottman in 1891.

Mr. Molstertiegen lived in Blue Blanket valley until the death of his wife
in 1895 when he moved back to Fargo where he lived for 20 years. He died in
1916 and sleeps beside his wife and his daughter, Rachel, in Bethlehem
cemetery near Selby.

MR. JACOB MOOS

Jacob Moos was born near Odessa, Russia, December 29, 1861. In the fall of
1872 he came with his parents to the United States locating at Lesterville,
South Dakota. On January 20, 1885, he was united in marriage to Margaret
Berreth of Menno, South Dakota. The Reverend Hoffer of Lesterville
performed the wedding ceremony in the home of the groom's parents. Mrs.
Moos was born June 27, 1864, at South Russia and came to the United States
with her parents, one sister, and three brothers, locating at Menno, South
Dakota.

That spring after helping put the crop in for his folks at Lesterville,
Jacob Moos and his wife together with a number of other families decided to
move further up into South Dakota. They located around Eureka. They
returned to Lesterville that summer in time to help with the harvest. After
the fall work was over they went back to Eureka where they lived for
several years. Their home here was a stone house which they put up
themselves. Drought, crop failures, and the subsequent hard times caused
them to mortgage their home and in 1894 they decided to sell out and go
back to Lesterville where they rented a farm.

In 1902 they decided to try to get another homestead. They loaded their
horses and other belongings on a train and came to Walworth county. The
first year they rented the Coleman Wagner farm south of Selby. The second
year they rented the Studybaker farm and then filed on a homestead near the
town of Akaska. On the first summer spent in this new home they lived in a
tent. The baking and cooking was done on a cook stove set up in the yard.
As quickly as possible a house was built. This was made of sod and had one
large room and a kitchen. The windows were very small. Mrs. Moos loved
plants and even in this little sod house had flowers blooming nearly all
year around.

        MR. AND MRS. JACOB MOOS

In 1915 they left this home and went to Miles City, Montana, where Mr. Moos
with two of his sons, Albert and Ted, were employed by the Milwaukee
railroad. After four years of this work Mr. and Mrs. Moos returned to Selby
where they lived on a farm with their son, Henry, for a time. Later they
came to town and lived with George Hoffman, their daughter in-law's father,
who was in ill health. Mr. Moos was janitor of the court house in Selby for
several years, until ill health forced him to give up the work.

On January 20, 1935, the Lutheran church in Selby helped them celebrate
their Golden Wedding anniversary.

On September 5, 1935, Mr. Moos was taken sick. He went to bed, and although
he lingered for a year, never recovered from his ailment. During this time
he needed constant care and attention, which he received from his loving
wife and his son, Albert. He passed away in 1936.

Five children were born to this couple, four of whom are still living.
Martha was born December 30, 1885, and was married January 2, 1906, to Dave
Jones of Selby. They reside in Canada and have two children in Vancouver,
British Columbia: Violet Regan and Alvin; and five children in Fawcett,
Alberta, Canada: Earl, Harvey, Edwin, Goldie, and Marion.

A daughter was born in October, 1886, who passed away at the age of 17 days.

Henry was born October 19, 1888. On February 22, 1911, he married Mable
Hoffman of Selby. They have five living children: Mrs. Alva Carlson of
Mobridge; Alferd, Leroy, and Mrs. Sarah Stahlecker of Selby; and Donald of
Stockton, California.

Albert was born June 11, 1896. On June 23, 1937, he was united in marriage
to Luella Bucklin of Selby. To this couple have been born five children:
Tyrone, Wanda, Goldie, Myra, and Myron. Albert served 18 months in France
during World War I.

On June 28, 1898, their youngest son, Ted, was born. He was married to Fern
Borninkoff on April 12, 1943. They have one son, Wayne. Ted and his family
reside at Belle Fourche, South Dakota.

When South Dakota celebrated its Golden anniversary jubilee in 1939, Mrs.
Jacob Moos received a certificate from the state showing her fifty-year
residence here.

Mrs. Moos has always been a very active woman. She spent many years taking
in washing, ironing, doing housework and even baby sitting. She is an
active member of the Lutheran church, Ladies' aid, and American Legion
Auxiliary. At her present age of 84, she is still very active. She is still
able to crochet many lovely things, attends church regularly, and does many
other things to keep her busy. She is now making her home in the Marywall
hotel in Selby where she boards with Mr. and Mrs. Wallace Young, the
proprietors.

During his manhood Mr. Moos did a great deal of mason work and brick
laying. Even while farming he did much of this kind of work all through the
county. Many of the cement cisterns, basements, sidewalks, and buildings
show evidence of his art in this line of work.

MR. AND MRS. FRANK WALL

        MR. AND MRS. FRANK WALL

Mr. Wall, a well-known resident of Selby for many years, postmaster, city
and county justice and highly respected citizen, was born at Sheridan,
Indiana, December 20, 1853. His people came from Wales and settled in
Culpepper county, Virginia, in 1770. In 1790 they moved to Kentucky and by
1822 it had become too crowded there and they joined the westward movement
into new lands to Indiana. In the year 1865 they moved westward again
settling near Syracuse, Nebraska. They made the move in covered wagons
which was the means of transportation across country in that day and he well
remembered and was able to describe the bier of the martyred President
Abraham Lincoln since they passed through Springfield, Illinois, on the day
of Lincoln's funeral. They took up homesteads at Palmyra and went through
the adverse seasons and grasshopper days, the boys leaving home frequently
to work out and earn money to help out with the family living costs.

Mrs. Wall was born at Jefferson City, Missouri, January 29, 1861, and went
with her brother to Syracuse, Nebraska, in 1873. Her father was a slave
owner but a staunch believer in the Constitution and in the Union and, when
the Civil war broke out, freed his slaves and enlisted in the Union Army
giving up his life as the result of wounds sustained in the battle of Lone
Jack, said to be one of the bloodiest battles of the war, and in which no
quarter was given and practically all of the men engaged on either side
were killed or wounded. He gave his life for the great principles in which
he believed and three of his sons joined him in enlisting in the Union
Army, which was a popular thing to do in the border state of Missouri.

Mr. and Mrs. Wall were married December 9, 1876, and started housekeeping
on an 80 acre farm near Palmyra which he purchased. Later they sold this
land and went back to her home community in Missouri to settle up the
estate, came back to Nebraska and bought another 80 acres, which they also
sold and went to Oregon to engage in wheat farming but could not stand that
climate. The trip to Oregon was made by way of San Francisco as there was
no railroad across the Rockies to the north. From San Francisco they took a
ship to Portland. Returning to Nebraska they bought land again near Douglas
and resided on it until they came to Walworth county in 1911. Seeking
greater opportunity took him to the Rosebud reservation in Dakota which
land he did not like. He then joined a homeseeker's excursion to Ipswich
where he bought a quarter section of land. Later he came to Walworth county
where he purchased the N 1/2 of 1-122-77 and the half section which is now
the home place of Johnnie J. Brockel. This land was prairie and in the
spring of 1911 the family group, consisting of Mr. and Mrs. Wall, Mr. and
Mrs. Joe Wall and family and Mr. and Mrs. Glen Powell and family, came to
Walworth county and the Selby vicinity, their purpose being to break and
farm the new land, improve it and establish homes on it. Mr. Wall purchased
the Bowlus house, now belonging to the Baumgarten family, and buildings
were constructed on the farm northwest of Selby. The house next north of
the Legion Hall, now owned by Mrs. Louisa Wahl, was built in 1918 and the
Bowlus house was sold to G. L. Baumgarten. Later the larger home, now owned
by Wm. Dahlquist, was built and occupied, the other house being rented as
income property. The larger building site at the new house was utilized as
a garden and the premises of both houses were planted with trees, including
very beautiful evergreens, and were always among the best-kept homes in
town.

Mr. Wall ran the Victoria elevator for two years, was active in the
promotion of the Equity elevator, and served as janitor at the school for a
time. When President Wilson was elected, Mr. Wall received his appointment
as postmaster at Selby, retaining the position for 8 years. He served as
city and county justice of the peace for many years and was always
prominent in democratic party and civic affairs.

Mrs. Wall was active in many charitable organizations of the town and an
active member of the Methodist church, singing in the choir and helping in
all of the activities of the church to the extent of her ability and
strength. She passed away April 1, 1938, and he died February 15, 1940.
They rest side by side in the Selby cemetery, the deeds of their lives
appreciated and their memories revered by all who knew them.

MR. AND MRS. GLEN POWELL

Mr. and Mrs. Glen Powell came to Walworth county from the vicinity of
Douglas, Nebraska, in the spring of 1911 with the Frank Wall family group,
consisting of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Wall and Mr. and Mrs. Joe Wall. They had
been farming on rented lands in Nebraska where rents were high and where
farm land was so high that there seemed little chance to get a place of
their own, and welcomed a chance to come to the Blue Blanket valley in
Walworth county where the opportunities seemed to be much greater. They
moved on the Wall farm northwest of town, now the home place of Johnnie J.
Brockel, helping put up the buildings and during the 9 years that they
lived on it, making it into a fine farm. They then moved on the De Velde
place just across the line in Campbell county north of Selby where they
lived for 3 years, moving from there to what was known in the early days as
the Boyland farm in Spring Valley town ship, now owned and occupied by Fred
Diedtrich, where they lived for 15 years. They then farmed the Hoefs' farm
south of Selby for 6 years, holding an auction sale of their livestock and
equipment in the fall of 1944 and moving to Selby where they have since
resided. They purchased the former Adam Himrich house on the east side of
town.

        MR. AND MRS. GLENN POWELL

Mr. Powell's ancestors were English Quakers who came to Roanoke, Virginia,
in the year 1774, later moving to North Carolina and shortly after the
Civil War to southern Indiana. They came to Nebraska in 1880 and farmed
near Friend. He was united in marriage with Kate Wall at Auburn, Nebraska,
in September, 1907. She was a daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Wall whose
biography appears elsewhere in this book. They have five sons and two
daughters. Joe and Terry live at Salt Lake City where both are attending
college; Robert at Lehigh, Utah; Calvin at Santa Paula, California; and
Jack in Aberdeen, South Dakota. During World War II, Joe served his country
in the Marines and went through the hells of Guadalcanal and Tinian, being
wounded in the latter campaign and being awarded the Purple Heart for
meritorious service. Jack and Terry were in the Navy. Josie taught school
for a time, married Howard Morris and they now live at Elberfeld, Indiana.
Margaret is at home and is bookkeeper for the Perman Implement company. All
of the Powell young people graduated from Selby high school where they took
active part in all school activities, often with distinction. Mr. and Mrs.
Powell have fifteen grandchildren.

Mr. Powell was always a progressive farmer, ready to support and try out
the newer things in grain and stock raising. The family all took an active
part in community affairs, and every neighborhood profited from their
living in it.

MR. AND MRS. JOE WALL

Mr. and Mrs. Joe Wall came from the vicinity of Douglas, Nebraska, in the
spring of 1911 with the Wall family group consisting of Mr. and Mrs. Frank
Wall and the Glen Powell family. They located on the B. B. Potter farm in
Surrey township, now owned and occupied by Mr. and Mrs. Alex Bruckner,
where they lived for a year, moving from there to the farm now occupied by
the Ralph Burnette family where they lived for two years. They then sold
out and started a restaurant in the location now known as the Dettman
building in Selby which they operated for a period of four years. A fire
ruined their stock and fixtures and they sold what was salvaged and
discontinued the business.

Mr. Wall had a wide reputation as a ball player in eastern Nebraska before
coming to Walworth county playing for a time on the Omaha Western League
team in center field. He continued to play with the Selby team while he
lived here and became well known in baseball and athletic circles over this
section of South Dakota. He left here many years ago and now resides at
Centerville, Iowa.

MR. AND MRS. JACOB TISDALL

Definitely speaking one of the oldest citizens of this area is Jacob (Jake)
Tisdall, who has lived on the farm, 5-1/2 miles northwest of Selby in Blue
Blanket community continuously for 63 years. This homestead originally was
filed on by his father, Johannes Tisdall who came from Iowa in the fall of
1885 and visited through that winter with his stepson, Oliver Johnson and
his son, Oliver Tisdall, who had previously arrived. When spring came
Johannas Tisdall sent for his family. Jake was then 11 years old. He was
born March 1, 1875, in Polk county, Iowa, coming from there to Dakota. He
and his sister, Martha, accompanied the mother with the immigrant party
train to Ipswich, South Dakota, which was then the terminal of the
railroad. They arrived there April 10, 1886, and were met by Oliver
Johnson, Sam Sampson and Sam Hanson, the latter two being cousins of the
family. These men had three teams with wagons which together with another
wagon and team which came on the train, accommodated the transportation for
the family and their household goods, machinery, and other be longings
including pigs, chickens, and 150 bushels of Iowa corn. The 7 head of
cattle were driven behind the wagons.

        MR. AND MRS. JACOB TISDALL

Upon arrival at the new homestead, the residence of which was a stone
dug-out, the relatives assisted in building up the place. By the hardest
kind of labor, privation, and sacrifice they developed the land and built a
new home. Until the new home was built however, the little dug-out was a
safeguard against storm and wind and a protection against winter weather.
When spring arrived, the heavy snows melted and filled the place with water,
forcing the family out. One night was spent standing on a hill. This
stonebasement dwelling still stands intact, but the roof has been destroyed
by the elements of weather all through the years.

Jake's parents were born in Norway and immigrated to Wisconsin. Johannas
Tisdall enlisted as supervisory nurse in Field Hospital work with Co. E
15th Wisconsin Infantry on October 28, 1861. He received an honorable
discharge January 2, 1865. During his life as a soldier he endured plenty
of action in battles of Chattanooga, Vicksburg, Gettysburg, and also with
Sherman's famous army marching "From Atlanta to the Sea".

Mr. and Mrs. Johannas Tisdall, as early pioneers, helped to blaze the way
for those of later years in this Blue Blanket community. At that time
doctors and nurses were scarce and Mrs. Tisdall gave aid and comfort to the
sick, even walking for miles in the cold winter weather to give her kindly
assistance and solace to those in need.

Johannas Tisdall passed away in 1905 at the age of 95 years. Mrs. Tisdall
died in 1914 at the age of 81. Martha Tisdall, sister of Jake, passed away
in the year 1886 at the age of 18 years. She was the first person buried
in the Bethlehem cemetery located on U. S. highway 12, northwest of Selby.
The parents are also buried there.

Mr. and Mrs. Jake Tisdall were married February 21, 1903. Mrs. Tisdall was
born in Flekkefjord, Norway, and came to America in 1900. Mr. and Mrs.
Tisdall have spent all these years as energetic community workers, and in
an open house manner for the social life of both young and old of the
neighborhood. The famous Tisdall lake was noted for skating parties.

Jake was a popular auctioneer in the early days. He served as Blue Blanket
school treasurer for many years. He was an Equity Union board member for
years. He was chairman of the Liberty Loan drive in Blue Blanket during
World War I. He also served on the board of election many times, and was a
member of the board of directors for the Farm Loan association for years.

Reminiscing on his early years in Blue Blanket, Mr. Tisdall thinks that one
of the greatest changes has been in the mode of harvesting. Gone for the
most part, and almost forgotten are the once familiar and picturesque
fields of shocked grain. Today we see the huge combines that cut and thresh
grain in one operation. Jake was one of the first farmers in Blue Blanket
to own a combine.

Mr. and Mrs. Tisdall's family consist of two daughters and three sons. The
Tisdalls' aim was to educate their family, and attending school was
accepted as a "must" by the youngsters.

John, the oldest, is a resident of Mobridge. He is employed by the
C.M.St.P.&P.RR. Co. He has also been affiliated with county office work and
with the Farm Loan association. He is married to Nettie Himrich.

Mathilda, Mrs. Max Van Orman, is a graduate of Northern State Teachers
college at Aberdeen and taught in both rural and town communities for 11
years. They live on a farm west of Selby.

Martha, Mrs. Art Sieck, was a registered nurse. She lives with her husband
and their family south of Selby.

Theodore (Ted), married to Ardelle Baker, and Henry (Sy), married to Viola
Greene, are farmers. Ted lives west of Selby and "Sy" lives in Selby and
farms near there.

Mr. and Mrs. Tisdall can boast of the fact that all their children live
within a radius of 20 miles from the old homestead of their birth and
childhood. Each year at Christmas time the annual Christmas party is held at
their home. They have open house for all the family including children,
grandchildren and in-laws. This occasion has such a propensity in every way
that it makes Christmas Eve a time of family joy and happiness. The 1948
Christmas was something special for Jake because his brother, Oliver
Tisdall and wife from Bremerton, Wash., were here to help celebrate. At the
time of this writing, Jake, his sister, Sophia Lane, and his brother,
Oliver, are planning a reunion sometime in August, 1949. They all also plan
to take in the celebration in Selby in 1950. Sophia's last visit here was
in 1934,--she lives in California. His sister, Millie and brother, Henry,
have both passed on.

Mr. and Mrs. Tisdall have 4 granddaughters and 13 grandsons. The oldest
granddaughter is attending school at Vermillion at the present time.

Jake has traveled into Canada and to the west coast and back several
times. He was always glad to get back to the "Old Hill" as he refers to his
home. The longest trip he has taken in his opinion was one he made to
Ipswich with a yoke of oxen,--gone exactly one week, and walked most of the
way barefoot. Mr. and Mrs. Jake Tisdall have always lived by faith from the
first turning of the furrow until the harvest. We of the depression and
drought years of the '30s could always get encouragement from
Jake,--following every drought and dust storm he would say: "It's gonna
rain"--and it did!

MR. AND MRS. JOHN H. FRANKS

John H. Franks was born September 6, 1861, near Chicago, Illinois, where he
received a common school education and grew to young manhood. In 1886 with
other land seekers he came to the Blue Blanket district in Dakota territory
to file on land, settling on the northeast quarter of Section 17, Township
124, Range 76. Here Mr. Franks settled down to farming, gradually acquiring
more land and becoming one of the most successful farmers of the community.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHN H. FRANKS

On April 7, 1894, he was united in marriage to Miss Inga Holstad, who was
born near Aalsund, Norway, April 13, 1876. She came to Dakota territory in
1888, a child of 12. She received a common school education in the schools
of that district. However, Inga Holstad was an outstanding student,
acquiring very rapidly a command of the English language. that made her in
great demand as an interpreter for the Norwegian settlers, and started her
teaching career at the age of 17. For four years following her marriage to
Mr. Franks she taught in the Blue Blanket, Hiddenwood and Highland
townships, resigning in 1898 to care for the needs of her own growing
family.

To Mr. and Mrs. Franks were born nine children, seven of whom are still
living. Each of these children has received outstanding recognition in
their chosen field. Each received an excellent education. Rufus as a civil
engineer; Bertha as school teacher; Otto and Clifton, farmers on the home
place; Dora, nursing and stenographer; Eugene, tool and dye worker; Ione,
teacher and talented artist. The Franks had the sorrow of losing two
daughters: Etta, a graduate nurse, and Muriel, aged seven.

Mrs. Franks outstanding ability as a teacher was no doubt an aid to her
children in carving out their own careers. The Franks' family story is a
success story. Mr. Franks came to Blue Blanket, in his own words, with
"practically nothing". The same farm has remained in the family from 1886
to the present time. Mr. Franks, with all the discouragements of farming in
South Dakota during so many seasons, still acquired ownership of four
quarters of land, a home in Selby, as well as a place of business. He has
served his community well in civic affairs and as a member of the school
board. The Franks' are members of the Lutheran church. Mr. Franks is a
member of the A.O.U.W.

Mrs. Franks cites as an outstanding experience of her life, her first
electrical storm during the first summer of her residence in Dakota. She
had never seen lightning strike down to the earth before. In her own words
it was "tremendous, terrifying, majestic!"

MR. ADAM HIMRICH

I was born in southern Russia, not far from the city of Odessa, on October
13, 1873. My father, mother, three sisters, and two brothers immigrated to
the United States when I was twelve years of age.

We rented a farm near the present site of Lesterville in Bon Homme county,
South Dakota, in 1884 and lived there ten years. During this time, my
father, who was a carpenter by trade, was seldom home. This left the farm
work to my mother, brother John and myself. We had good farm land and had a
number of very good crops. After a period of bad years my father decided to
move to Walworth county where land was being opened up to settlers who
would come in and prove up a claim.

We settled on what is at present the Edward Himrich farm home. There my
brothers and sisters grew to manhood and womanhood. Each one in turn
married and made a home for himself not far from the home place.

In the fall of 1897 I returned to Tyndall, South Dakota, and there on
November 22 I married the girl of my choice, Miss Elizabeth Heil. My bride
and I settled on my claim in a little sod house which was located about a
half mile north of the present site of Selby.

In 1900 we decided to move our home a mile south and east because of a
better water supply at that location. This is now the Emanuel Himrich farm.
At this location I built a good frame house and a fair set of farm
buildings. The house, at present, is completely modern and still in good
condition.

About this time the city of Selby located one half mile west of my farm on
123-76. There was no water supply in Selby, so, for quite a number of
years, I hauled water with a tank and team of horses to Selby and filled
cisterns for the Selby citizens. The water at that time was sold for the
sum of $1 per tank. The city well is still located on land which was at
that time a part of my farm.

While I lived on this farm, I operated a threshing machine for several
years. Threshing at that time was a long and tiresome job, and usually snow
came before the work was finished. My father and I also owned quite a
number of good horses and raised quite a few horses each year. At that time
good horses were in demand.

        MR. AND MRS. ADAM HIMRICH

In 1908 we decided to leave the farm and move to Selby. We bought a small
four-room house located in the east part of town. This was our home for
many years and here my three daughters grew to womanhood. My daughters are:
Elizabeth, Mrs. Wm. J. Sawinsky, Selby; Bertha, Mrs. Herman Greene,
Detroit, Michigan; Nettie, Mrs. John Tisdall, Mobridge.

During this time the home which we purchased in town was enlarged and
modernized. I have lived practically a lifetime in and around Selby.

The picture is one of my wife and myself taken on our wedding day, November
22, 1897.

                        Note

Taken from Bangor Reporter in an issue in May, 1900, and headed "A New Town
Located". "Site chosen is straight north of Bangor, on NW 1/4, Section 4,
123-76. H. L. Hunter and a member of the St. Paul Land company came out and
located the new town. They bought the Adam Himrich quarter and some
adjoining tracts for the town site which will be platted in a short time.
There is no better location for a town in Walworth county and an unlimited
supply of water can be secured near the surface."

CORNELIUS HOVLAND

Cornelius Hovland was born August 27, 1866, and grew to young manhood in
Goodhue county in southern Minnesota. In the spring of 1889 he and C.W.
Darkwell, a young neighbor, became interested in shipping horses and cattle
into Dakota. They brought a carload to Scranton, in Walworth county, and
worked during the summer selling these animals to the farmers and ranchers.
In the fall of that year Mr. Hovland filed a preemption on a quarter of
land northeast of the Blue Blanket postoffice, and during the two following
winters he was employed by Frank Boehmer of Scranton. In the spring of 1890
he began to improve his land, and built a small frame house. With two yoke
of oxen which he now owned, he broke the sod for grain crops. Mr. Hovland
recalls that the native grass of the prairie provided abundant "ox-power"
for the arduous task of opening the tough sod. In 1891, after he had proven
the title to his original quarter, he took a homestead claim on an adjacent
quarter; this property is identified today as the farmstead where Carl
Moser resides.

Early in the spring of 1892 Mr. Hovland made the trip from his home in
Minnesota, bringing with him his own horses and farming equipment with
which to put in a crop on his new land. The same spring in June he was
married to Rachel Molsterteigen, a daughter of Ole Molsterteigen, who had
brought his family from Voss, Norway (where Rachel was born in 1865) to
Minnesota and thence to Walworth county.

The home of this young couple was blessed with four children: Tomas,
Bertha, Clifton and Ragnar. Their farming endeavors prospered as their
horses and cattle increased from year to year. The grain crops, although
never large, were of excellent quality and reflected the wisdom and
patience of a thoughtful farmer. The family were members of the Bethlehem
Lutheran congregation of which the Rev. Peter Skartvedt was pastor at the
time. They were recognized in the community as leaders and supporters of
religion and education. Mrs. Hovland had taught school for ten years prior
to her marriage. In March of 1901 the young wife and mother was taken from
her family by death. She was tenderly laid to rest in the little Bethlehem
cemetery where her father and mother are also buried.

Mr. Hovland, faced with the problems of raising his four small children,
moved back to Zumbrota, Minnesota, where his sister helped him in the
rearing of his family. That the children were all well educated in both the
school and church testifies to the care and integrity of their parents.

Clifton, the only remaining child, holds degrees from St. Olaf college at
Northfield, Minnesota, and from the University of Minnesota, and has filled
several positions as an analytical chemist. At present he is farm training
director of the Zumbrota High school and is interested with his father in
the operation of several farms which they own in that vicinity. Mr. Hovland
is still active and keenly interested in the affairs of the world and his
community. The respected position he holds in the memory and affections of
the people of the Selby neighborhood is a result of the contributions to
its development and security which were made by him and his family.

AUGUST SIEBRECHT

August Siebrecht, one of the earliest settlers of Walworth county, was born
in Germany. He came to the United States in his boyhood and settled in
Illinois.

February 14, 1865 at the age of 19, he enlisted in the army during the
Civil War and served in Co. G 62 Illinois Infantry. He was discharged one
year later. He had a good education and served as clerk in the Army, seeing
no actual fighting but serving very worthily nevertheless. Later, while
serving in the Army, Mr. Siebrecht was stationed at Fort Randall, located
at the mouth of Scalp creek, near the present site of Wheeler, South
Dakota. He was married to an Indian woman who died a few years later
leaving one daughter who became well educated.

Mr. Siebrecht's second wife was born December 18, 1853, in Saxony, Germany.
She was brought to America by her parents when she was 4 years old. They
settled in Illinois and later moved to Minnesota. Later the daughter
decided to visit her sister and her husband, who was a Major in the Army,
stationed at Fort Randall. In the spring of 1872 she made the trip to Fort
Randall by ox-team to Sioux City, then by rail to Yankton and by river boat
to Fort Randall. Here she met her life mate, Mr. Siebrecht, who was a
soldier serving in the commissary department. In 1873 they were married and
lived at Fort Randall and later at Fort Bennett until 1880.

In 1880 the family moved to LeBeau to operate a hotel. The only white man
to precede Mr. Siebrecht in permanent residence at LeBeau was Anton LeBeau,
for whom the town was named. Anton LeBeau operated a trading post at or
near the mouth of Swan creek for the purpose of dealing with the Indians,
accommodating the crews of the steamboats, the fur traders, and other
adventurers who used the great river as a highway.

Two other important functions performed by the first settlers were the
supplying of wood for fuel for the steamboats and engines and the care of
the government telegraph office and telephone line, which was built along
the river on the east bank, connecting the south forts with those of the
north.

Mr. Siebrecht was also postmaster, justice of the peace, and county
commissioner. Records show that he was the first to prove up land in
Walworth county. This land was the east half of the SW 1/4 and the west
half of the SE 1/4 of Section 8-121-78. The date was February 25, 1883.
This was a preemption.

The Siebrechts saw the first LeBeau, Old Scranton and the second LeBeau,
all near the mouth of Swan creek and practically on the site of their first
home, begin to prosper and decay. They were among those who named the big
bluff, to the north of the creek valley and overlooking the site of the old
town, "Capitol Hill" and dreamed of a day when a stately edifice would grace
its height and the government of the territory, that was cut in twain, be
conducted from the prospective Capitol city which they had found as grazing
ground for the lordly bison and which then became cow pasture.

They were the last to leave LeBeau. After leaving LeBeau they lived south
of Java for a few years and then moved to Aberdeen where they resided until
failing health forced them to go to Hot Springs, South Dakota to the
Soldiers home. Here Mr. Siebrecht passed away on March 19, 1929, at the age
of 83 years. After Mr. Siebrecht's passing, Mrs. Siebrecht went to her
daughter in Des Moines, Iowa, where she passed away June 12, 1929. She was
confirmed in the German Lutheran church in her childhood and was faithful
to Lord and Master to the end. Many stories are told of these pioneers by
those who knew of their good qualities and hospitality.

To this union 7 children were born. four daughters and three sons. The two
oldest children were born at Fort Randall, Emma now of Alameda, California,
and Augusta "Cookie", who passed away a few years ago. The other children
were born at LeBeau: Lou of Aberdeen, South Dakota; Clara of Des Moines,
Iowa; Millie, residing in Washington; one son, Ben, who lost his life in a
Mobridge livery barn fire some years ago; and Albert Swan, the first white
child born at Old LeBeau north of the present site of LeBeau.

The Indians, learning of the birth of the new white child, came to see him
and gave him the name "Swan" and that was the name he was always known by.
Swan spent most of his younger days between LeBeau and Bangor. He was liked
by everyone who knew him. In later years he went to Hoven and worked for an
insurance company. He passed away in a Pierre hospital in 1921 at the age
of 41 years. He was laid to rest in the Selby Union cemetery.

MR. AND MRS. JACOB OLSON

Jacob Olson, a young Norwegian immigrant, came to America in the summer of
1886,--not to brave the battle of life single-handed for long, for in the
month of October of the same year, Gunhild Ellefson also arrived in
Walworth county. Like Jacob, she left her homeland of Norway behind her, to
materialize dreams of a happy home with the man of her choice here in this
"Promised Land of America".

The following December, Jacob Olson and Gunhild Ellefson were united in
marriage. There were born to them in all, six children. Their two oldest
girls died in early infancy. Those living today are in ages as follows:
Olaf, Edward, Anna and Inga.

Jacob Olson was a young man of noble ambitions and dauntless courage. He
dared ventures with big strides, a homestead, preemption and tree claim
were not too much for him to tackle.

        MRS. JACOB OLSON

To walk to Bowdle from his homestead, 7 miles northwest of the present site
of Selby and back again with a load of groceries, was only one of his feats
for he was also known to walk down to the Missouri river bottom on Sundays,
some 20 miles, to conduct religious meetings with friends there.

Why a young man of such splendid influence and worthy purpose for life
should be called so early in life by his Creator to his eternal home is
sometimes hard for mortals to understand. Yet this we know, that God makes
no mistakes, and at the early age of 42 years stricken by an incurable
disease, the summons to answer the eternal call came to this worthy young
pioneer.

It was now left to Gunhild (as her friends will remember her by her given
name) to carry on with the young children and the sole management of the
farm. This, her friends know, she did ably and cheerfully.

Life could never be dull for long at the Olson home for friendliness and
hospitality were a dominant characteristic in this home, and many neighbors
and acquaintances found enjoyment in visiting there.

Then there were community activities such as the Aid Society of her church
in which Mrs. Olson was always an interesting and helpful member.

When Mrs. Jacob Olson's children had grown up and left home to make homes
of their own, she was obliged to leave the farm and move to town.

She bought a home in Mobridge, South Dakota where she lived until her
death, which came on the 15th of November, 1930.

MR. RASMUS THORSTENSON

Rasmus Thorstenson had five names, but often "R. Thorstenson" was all that
was needed to identify him. The town name "Bangor" appears on the legal
documents that refer to the land that he acquired when first he chose to
settle in a particular spot in Dakota territory. Rasmus was born on October
3, 1862, in Norway on a farm of Ekrem,--this farm name accounts for the fact
that some of his brothers had a different last name! One of his most
frightening experiences as a boy was watching a hurricane come in from the
ocean to destroy many of the buildings of his home place. Later one of his
uncles took three of his sons and two neighbor men out fishing, and another
hurricane foundered their boat, and all were lost. The constantly losing
struggle against the vast ocean made Rasmus decide he did not want to earn
his living from a crude little boat. He loved the mountains and the fjords,
but there was no land which he could purchase for farming. His brother,
Peter, who immigrated to United States, wrote back that there was room for
all over there, but it took a great deal to convince Rasmus that he should
leave the land of his fathers. The immigrant steamer accommodations which
he finally secured were almost unbearable. Even that trip included a
violent storm which lasted three days. They landed in Portland, Maine, and
the trip to Dakota territory was more pleasant. The brothers, Rasmus and
Peter, had the usual language difficulties, but the pioneers were helpful
to one another. The brothers worked in Iowa and near Canton until they had
a little stake with which to buy some old farm machinery and some oxen.
Their destination was Walworth county, and they shipped their things to the
nearest railroad point, Ipswich. That first summer was so dry that two
bushels of potatoes planted for seed yielded one gallon of potatoes about
the size of nuts. In order to earn something on which to live during the
winter the brothers drove back to Ipswich and hired out, oxen and all, for
the harvesting and threshing season.

        MR. AND MRS. R. THORSTENSON AND FAMILY
        Standing, left to right--Mrs. R. Thorstenson; Marie (Mrs. Oscar
        Olson); Herman Thorstenson. Seated--R. Thorstenson; Antonia
        (Mrs. Harry Peterson).

The young man knew that to be successful in this new, untried country a man
needed a helpmate. He wrote back to Norway to Severina, a girl born and
reared on the neighboring farm of Saetre, also in the district of Sundmore.
Her birthday was April 4, 1862, and by this time her mother was 60 years
old. Severina knew she would probably never see her mother again, but she
answered the request from America in the affirmative. She landed in New
York, and spent some time visiting a girlhood friend before the long train
ride which ended at Ipswich. She and the other Norse girls who arrived with
her stayed there until their men came with the oxen teams and drove them
out to their little sod shack, their new homes.

Rasmus and Severina were 28 years of age when they married, so their plans
and efforts were not merely the impulsiveness of youth. After a few years
on the "preemption" they moved to the farm, 3-1/2 miles southwest of Selby,
which is now operated by their grandson, Ralph Thorstenson.

Their first son, Herman Theodore, was born July 22, 1891, and their first
daughter, Marie Elizabeth, was born May 20, 1893. Anton, born in 1898, died
as an infant. Their last child, Anthonia, born October 9, 1903, is now Mrs.
Harry O. Peterson and lives at Yakima, Washington. The others have passed
away.

Mr. and Mrs. Thorstenson were among those who helped to start Bethany
Lutheran church, and a grandson is among the members today. Struggles
seemed to be the order of the day in getting anything accomplished those
many years ago, but people became good friends by sharing their efforts.
Severina was one of those women who could find beauty in little things,
like colored ribbons to tie back the starched cheese cloth curtains in the
deepset sod house windows, or the blossom on the plant grown from a slip
given by a helpful neighbor. It is these little things as well as the
rolling quarter-sections of land that we should remember about our
homesteading ancestors.

Rasmus Andrew Benjamin Thorstenson Ekrem (d) Mar. 14, 1943.
Severina Jacobina Hansdatter Saetre (d) May 24, 1926.
  Herman Theodore Thorstenson (d) May 20, 1939.
  Gena Opheim Thorstenson, Selby, South Dakota.
    Shirley--Mrs. O. T. Stenberg, Seattle, Washington (nurse).
    Bette Thorstenson, Seattle, Washington.
    Herman G. Thorstenson, Zion, Illinois (D.C.) (1 child).
    Ralph Thorstenson, Selby, South Dakota (home farm) (3 children).
  Oscar A. Olson, Northwood, Iowa.
  Marie Elizabeth Thorstenson Olson (d) Nov. 2, 1945.
    Elaine S. Olson, Everett, Washington.
    Ruth--Mrs. D. W. Backstrom, Jr., Northwood, Iowa (2 children).
  John Anton (d).
  Harry O. Peterson, Yakima, Washington.

    Robert John Peterson, student, U. of Washington, Seattle.

JOSEPH McINTOSH

Joseph McIntosh and his wife Susan came to Dakota territory in the early
'80's and filed on a homestead and tree claim located on the NW 1/4 of
Section 18 and the SW 1/4 of Section 7, Township 121, Range 74. Here they
established their home and here they went through the struggles and
hardships of the early pioneer days. But always through it all Joseph
McIntosh had an abiding faith in South Dakota. He, like many others, had
great hopes for the town of Theodore, a mile to the west of his homestead,
and he was one of the two bondsmen for the first postmaster of Theodore,
Dr. William Edwards.

These two sturdy pioneers, Mr. and Mrs. McIntosh were always ready with a
helping hand to neighbors. Mrs. McIntosh was sometimes called upon to
assist the younger generation into the world. On April 8, 1899, Mrs.
McIntosh passed away and ten years later, September 1, 1909, Mr. McIntosh
passed on.

Joseph McIntosh was born July 27, 1830 in Paisley, Scotland. He was the
second son of James McIntosh and Ann Burns McIntosh. He came to America
with his parents in 1841 and settled in Poughkeepsie, New York. They
crossed the ocean on a sailing vessel and were on the way three months.

The McIntosh family were weavers in Paisley, Scotland, the father a
designer of patterns. They followed this trade in America until 1850 when
they came west to Winfield, Wisconsin, clearing their land and enduring the
hardships of pioneer life. They made the trip from New York to Wisconsin by
boat, down the Great Lakes to Milwaukee, and overland by ox-team to
Winfield.

Susan Amy McIntosh, the wife and mother was born in Lawrence, Massachusetts
June 15, 1849. She was the eldest daughter of George and Susan Lawson who
came from England in 1848 and settled at Lawrence, Massachusetts staying
there about two years. He was a shoemaker by trade. He had come to America
in 1832 and enlisted in the United States Army, serving under Colonel
Zachary Taylor in the Seminole Indian War, suffering a leg injury which
crippled him for life. After his discharge from the army he returned to
England, married and brought his wife to America. Hearing about the wonders
of the west they moved to Wisconsin to take advantage of the grant of land
that was made to all soldiers. They too made the journey down the Great
Lakes to Milwaukee, hence by ox-team and wagon to Winfield, Wisconsin. It
so happened that the two families made the trip at the same time, and on
the same boat. They became very friendly on the long journey and settled on
adjoining farms in Winfield. There on May 4, 1873 Joseph McIntosh and Susan
Amy Lawson were united in marriage. Here they had a comfortable home and a
fine farm--and left it all--to again pioneer in South Dakota in the early
'80's.

They had two children, a son, Fred, and a daughter, Rose. Fred with his
wife, Bertha lives on the old homestead and they have a family of three
children: Dr. George McIntosh of Eureka, South Dakota. Alma McIntosh, nurse
and Supt. of the hospital in Eureka, and Clarence at home on the farm.

The daughter, Rose has been in the millinery, ready-to-wear and shoe
business in Selby for several years, and still continues in this work. She
is a member of the Order of the Eastern Star, and is the present Secretary.
She is a Past Matron of Hope Chapter, being Matron in 1933; a member of the
Methodist Church and the Ladies Aid Society of that church.

MR. GEORGE A. CLARK

George A. Clark was born at Galena, Illinois, June 23 1856. He was the only
son of George B. and Cynthia Maria Clark, who had come to Illinois from
Massachusetts to seek adventure and fortune in the west. His early boyhood
was spent at Galena in the stirring days of the Civil War and he had a
vivid recollection of General Ulysses S. Grant riding his horse through the
community. His father fought with an Illinois regiment and was with General
Sherman on his famous march to the sea.

George grew to manhood and was united in marriage with Isabelle Robinson,
who was also born at Galena of Scotch parents who had just arrived in
America seeking a new life for themselves.

The Clarks lived on a farm near Hanover, Illinois, a short distance from
Galena for several years where three children were born to them: Eva,
Clarence and Frank.

They then moved to Page county, Iowa, where they resided until 1885. Two
sons. Berte and Glenn were born there. In the summer of 1885, Mr. Clark
came to South Dakota and filed on a homestead and pre-emption in Section
18, township 124, Range 77, known as the Blue Blanket valley. The grass
stood knee high and waived in the wind like a field of grain which made the
country look like a stockman's paradise.


He built a frame house consisting of one large room downstairs and a low
upstairs which was used for sleeping quarters. He then returned to Iowa for
the winter and in the early spring of 1886, he and his son, Clarence, came
back with two carloads of livestock and household goods, and Mrs. Clark and
the other children followed shortly thereafter. Two children, Mabelle and
Homer, were born on the homestead.

There were no schools in the Blue Blanket township for the children and for
a few months during the year, they went to school in an old sod shack,
using boxes and sacks of potatoes for seats. Mr. Clark then began a
movement to have a schoolhouse built. With a great deal of effort, a frame
building was erected and used and he served on the school board while he
lived in the district.

        MR. AND MRS. GEORGE CLARK

On account of poor crops, the family was forced to leave the homestead and
moved to Bangor in the fall of 1890. Here Mr. Clark contracted to operate
the stage line from Bangor to Bowdle and from Bangor to Old LeBeau and each
of the older children took their turn at carrying the mail whenever it was
necessary for them to do so. In the summer months, Eva carried the mail
most of the time on the LeBeau route. The youngest child, Bessie, was born
to the Clarks during the time they resided at Bangor.

When the exodus from Bangor started in 1900, the Clark family joined those
who moved to Selby on the railroad where they operated a livery barn until
the auto mobile replaced the horse and the livery business folded.

Three sons started in business for themselves in Selby, Clarence operating
a dray line for a few years, then selling to O. J. Steinhoff, after which
he moved to a ranch near Lowry and finally to a farm in Blue Blanket
township where he passed away in 1929, leaving a wife, two sons and a
daughter surviving him.

Berte operated a blacksmith shop in Selby over a ten year period and then
he and Eva moved back to the old homestead where they have since resided.
Eva had carried the mail between Bangor and Selby until the time that the
Bangor postoffice was discontinued.

Frank operated a meat market in the building now being used as a cream
station by William Knecht, but was forced to give it up on account of poor
health and he passed away in 1903.

In 1916 Glenn and Homer, with the pioneering spirit went to Montana and
filed on land. There Homer married Pauline Kortum and to them were born two
daughters, Florence now of San Francisco, and Audrey (Mrs. W. W. Wolff) who
lives in Selby. Homer passed away in April, 1919, and in September of that
year, his wife and children came to Selby to live. Pauline Clark has been a
secretary in the local law office since 1924. Glenn passed away in Montana
in 1929.

Mabelle and Bessie both received their early education in the Selby schools
and taught school in the territory. Bessie married George Cleveland, Jr.,
and they have one son, Richard, who served as a machine gunner in World War
II and is now attending the University of Montana. The Clevelands have
continuously resided on a ranch near Ekalaka, Montana. Since giving up
teaching, Mabelle has been employed in the county treasurer's office in
Selby.

The family suffered the hardships of all the early pioneers and experienced
the blizzard of 1888 and the Indian scare. An incident of the pioneer days
occurred while the family lived in Bangor. Mr. Clark had rented a ranch
near the Missouri river known as the McKinley Ranch and stocked it with
cattle, sheep, hogs and chickens. The family had just moved to the ranch at
the end of a nice June day when a rain storm came up and the rain came down
in torrents. The ranch house was located on a flat, surrounded by creeks
and hills. The water came down so fast the creeks overflowed and the water
came into the house as high as the window sills. The sheep, chickens and
pigs floated around the yard and finally were washed down the creek and on
down to the river. During the flash flood, Mrs. Clark stood by the door
with the broom in hand trying to sweep out water and as the pigs went
floating by, she reached out with her broom and swept two into the house.
John Lowry had seen the storm coming and had stopped to seek shelter and he
told them that he didn't think the house would be washed away as he had
been there once before during a flood and the house stood. However, Mr.
Clark had a team hitched to a lumber wagon to take the family to safety
should it become necessary. When the storm was over, the flat was a sea of
mud, the garden and all other vegetation was washed away. A few chickens
had roosted on the rafters in the barn and were saved. Two sheep, the
cattle and the two pigs were all of the livestock remaining. The ranch was
in such a devastated condition that the family moved back to Bangor
immediately.

George A. Clark passed away at his home in Selby in November, 1934, and
Mrs. Clark passed away thirteen years later at her home in Selby at the age
of ninety-five years. A biography of this family would not be complete
without mention of the kindhearted readiness of Mr. and Mrs. Clark to lend
a helping hand to anyone in need and the rare gift of "helping without
hurting" which they possessed.

MR. AND MRS. JACOB DEN OTTER

Jacob and Gertie DenOtter came to Selby in March 1909 from Iowa.

They had paid $500 on a quarter of land situated five miles west of Selby,
along the Milwaukee railroad. They brought with them all their worldly
possessions which included four horses, four cows, two calves, and some
chickens. The family, consisting of the mother, father, seven daughters and
Mr. DenOtter's two brothers, lived in the two-room house on this farm for
three years.

The first year's crops were good, the second year there was half a crop and
the third year there was no crop at all, so they were forced to give up the
land.

        MR. AND MRS. JACOB DEN OTTER AND FAMILY
        Standing, left to right--Mrs. Bertha Potter, Mrs. Mary Maaskant,
        Mrs. Annie Maaskant, Mrs. Artha Hein, Mrs. Sadie Todd, Mrs. Martha
        Sargent. Seated--Mrs. Gertrude Mecklenburg, Jacob DenOtter, Mrs.
        Jacob DenOtter, Mrs. Margaret Masteller.

One day in the spring of 1910, Mr. DenOtter went to Selby with the wagon
and four horses to buy wheat for seeding. While he was gone the family saw
a prairie fire approaching the farm. The mother closed the house tightly
and hurried with her children to the pond in the pasture. After the fire
had passed around them, the mother sent one of the girls back to see how
things were at the farm. She returned with the word that the house might be
saved. So a bucket brigade was started and the house was saved but all
other buildings were burned as were the chickens and calves. That fall the
family rented the Riley farm two miles southeast of Selby. Then came two
more poor years, 1912 and 1913. In 1915 heavy rust ruined what might have
been a wonderful crop. Some of the wheat threshed weighed only 40 pounds.
The cattle would not eat the straw except when it was fresh.

The Jacob DenOtter family had one very good crop,--a crop of girls. In 1913
another baby girl came to join her seven sisters.

The family worked hard,--the mother always raised a large garden and the
girls and their mother helped with the field work and the milking.

One year, Mr. DenOtter broke up 24 acres of sod, planted it to flax and
cleared $1,000.00.

In 1917 480 acres of land five miles southwest of Selby was purchased and a
new farm home was built up. There was a good pasture for stock cattle, and
Mr. DenOtter broke up many an acre of sod with the walking plow. He never
owned a tractor.

The years brought good luck and bad, rust, hail, drouth, grasshoppers, dust
storms,--but these people were uncomplaining. They must have known there was
a Greater Providence that ruled.

On July 6, 1940, the couple observed their 50th wedding anniversary with
all their children present, including Mrs. Martha Sargent, Camino, Calif.;
Mrs. Bertha Potter, Ann Arbor, Mich.; Mrs. Artha Hein, Eugene, Oregon; Mrs.
Annie Maaskant, Torrance, California; Mrs. Mary Maaskant, Compton,
California; Mrs. Sadie Todd, Groton, New York, Mrs. Gertrude Mecklenburg
and Mrs. Pearl Masteller, Selby.

In the fall of 1940, with their children all married, Mr. and Mrs. DenOtter
purchased a home in Selby where they lived until the death of Mrs. DenOtter
in 1948. Mr. DenOtter passed away February 13, 1950 at the age of 81 years.

LEE W. SUNDERLAND

Lee W. Sunderland, descendant of the Earl of Sunderland, England, was born
October 14, 1855, in Plattsburg, New York. His family moved to Indiana and
it was there that Lee received his education. He attended Valparaiso
college for his higher education.

Lee came to Walworth county, South Dakota, in the spring of 1892, with four
of his brothers. They all engaged in farming but Lee found time to hold the
office of county superintendent of schools in Walworth county. He taught
several terms of school throughout the county and was considered one of the
better carpenters in this area. His hobby was wood-working and several
pieces of his work remain in the family today. A table with an inlaid top
of several hundred pieces is still in use at the Masonic temple in Selby.
Mr. Sunderland was an active member in the Masonic lodge and all worthwhile
civic projects in LeBeau and Bangor. He was awarded an emblem for being a
member of the Masonic lodge for fifty years.

He endured many experiences and hardships as did most early settlers. Crop
failure and other difficulties did not weaken his determination to make a
home for his family, with the help of his wife, Viola (nee Simon), whom he
married in Bremen, Indiana, before coming to South Dakota. She attended
school in Ohio and did typesetting in Bremen before she and Lee were
married. All of her neighbors knew her to be a kind and gracious person,
never too busy to give a helping hand in time of sickness or trouble.

Mr. and Mrs. Lee Sunderland reared a family of ten children, all of whom
are still living although both parents passed away several years ago.

Lawrence W. Sunderland, living in Neuvitas, Cuba, is manager of the Florida
Molasses Pumping plant and does ship repair work. He left South Dakota in
1909, is married and has a family of three daughters living.  His three sons
were killed in a boiler explosion while doing repair work on a ship.

Arthur Sunderland of East Rochester, New York, is married to Myrtle Drown,
has six children and is employed as an expert weaver in a woolen mill in
East Rochester.

Frank E. Sunderland of Armington, Montana, is married and operates a
poultry ranch.

        MR. AND MRS. LEE W. SUNDERLAND

Robert N. Sunderland of Sacramento, California, is married to Della Drewel
and has a family of three children. He owns and operates an auto repair
shop in Sacramento.

Ermetta (Mrs. Harry Johnson) taught several terms of school in Walworth
county before her marriage. They have a family of five.

Odessa (Mrs. William Russell) of Selby, taught school in Walworth county
before her marriage. More about Odessa appears under the Russell biography.

Viola attended school in Walworth county and NSTC in Aberdeen. She taught
several terms in Walworth county, one year in Montana, three years in Cuba,
and is now instructing at Timber Lake, South Dakota.

Floyd Sunderland did construction work in Montana and Washington, was in
the service and is now working on a farm in Walworth county.

Howard Sunderland farmed several years in Walworth county, worked in marble
quarries in Vermont and is now field man for the Farmers Union, covering
the western part of the state.

Russell Sunderland farmed a few years after graduating from Selby High
school, is married and has four children. They reside in Selby where he is
employed as a mechanic for Perman Implement company.

ANTHONY E. BIRKHOLT

A.E. Birkholt was born in Berlin, Wisconsin on March 25, 1864.

He came to South Dakota April 1, 1884, with his brothers, Andrew and
Julius, when they shipped their farm equipment to Clark county, where they
made permanent homes.

For the next two years he worked from early spring until late fall near
Castleton, North Dakota. The winter of 1885 he spent with his brothers at
Clark, but having visited Walworth county in the spring of '86 he returned
here in the fall. For two and one half years he worked for Captain Kingman.
It was customary for the settlers near Bangor to get their firewood from
the Missouri river, and during the famous winter of '88 he made the trip
with a team and wagon or sled nearly every other day. The skies were
usually sunny in the morning, but before the return journey had been
completed the winds had risen and the drifting snow covered the road and
blotted out familiar landscape. Given their heads the horses would find
their way safely home.

He worked for Abe Taylor for eight months; during this time he helped move
a house from LeBeau to the claim of his brother, Theodore. In the spring of
'89 he began farming his claim located southeast of Bangor. The present
site of the William Sawinsky home is not far from the location of the
original claim buildings.

During the summer of 1889 Mr. Birkholt bought one of the first headers
brought into this part of Walworth county, and had harvested 1200 acres of
crop in the community by the middle of October.

On the 17th day of September, 1889, he was united in marriage to Nellie
Smith. Nellie, daughter of Charles D., and Elizabeth Ann Smith, was born on
the family farm near Waterloo, Iowa, October 17, 1869. She moved with her
family to Fairview, in Lincoln county, in 1882. In 1885 the family came to
Walworth county by covered wagon, bringing with them their household goods
and driving their cattle. The family settled about 1-1/2 miles southwest of
the place known as Brown's Corners. Here the family grew to manhood and
womanhood.

        MR. AND MRS. ANTHONY E. BIRKHOLT

After their marriage Mr. and Mrs. Birkholt lived on the claim. Three
daughters were born to them here, one of whom died in infancy. The other
two were small children when the house burned, and the family moved to the
Theodore Birkholt farm. That winter, 1896-97, Sam Glerup and George Starkey
wintered 100 head of cattle there. Feed was thrown to the cattle daily, but
much of it was covered by drifting snow, as the snow on top melted in the
spring and lower layers were protected by the feed that was mixed with it,
and on the Fourth of July the family found enough ice to use in freezing
ice cream. In the spring the family purchased and moved to the farm now
owned by Albert Manke. It was while living here that Olive, age 6, and
Julia, age 4, died of scarlet fever within three days of each other. Here,
too, Lena and Charles were born.

In the fall of 1898 A. E. Birkholt was elected sheriff of Walworth county,
an office he held for two terms.

The town of Selby was founded in 1900. A year later Mr. Birkholt built a
house in the east part of town and moved the family into it. Here another
daughter, Elsie, was born. Lena passed away in 1914. Mrs. Birkholt passed
away April 11, 1928.

From the time he helped move his brother's house from LeBeau he became more
and more interested in moving buildings. His first independent job was to
move the Charles Cheskey house in 1889. By the time his second term as
sheriff had expired, his services were so much in demand that he gave up
his other interests and devoted all his time to this business. His work
took him into Potter, Edmunds, McPherson, Campbell, Dewey, Corson, and
Walworth counties. It was not unusual to see "Tony" (as everyone calls him)
driving his team along a remote road, or angling across a school section,
on his way to or from a job. He nearly always had candy tucked away in his
valise for the children wherever he stayed.

He continued with his chosen work until the fall of 1944, when he sold his
entire moving outfit and retired. He now resides in Selby where he raises a
large and bountiful garden.

The son Charles Birkholt, his wife, (formerly Viola Sieck) and three sons
live in Selby. The daughter, Elsie, her husband (Herman Sieck), two sons
and one daughter live on a farm west of Selby.

MR. ALBERT F. MILES

Albert F. Miles was born at Durand, Wisconsin, July 6, 1862 and moved to
South Dakota in 1885 at the age of 22. He helped to haul the lumber which
built the claim shanties for settlers of those days. He came out to where
Mound City now stands and established a claim in March 1885. Only a dugout,
stable and stack of hay marked the site. All his worldly possessions at the
time were represented by a fine team of horses, 60 bushels of oats and $20.

Putting his team of horses to work, Mr. Miles for a time hauled freight
between Mound City and Ipswich. The first crop he harvested in Dakota
consisted of buffalo bones. The plains were white with them. He could load
up a double wagon box in half a day. He hauled them to Ipswich, where he
sold them for $14.00 a ton.

In July 1885, Mr. Miles and W. S. Fossett, who later became his
brother-in-law, drove into Ipswich to look for work. On arriving in town
they separated, Mr. Miles going to work for Finley & Day, large scale
farmers operating 15 miles eastward.

During the winter of 1887-1888 Miles and four companions were batching in
a little dugout eight miles from Mina. Along came a terrific blizzard,
which trapped them for days. Great quantities of snow fell and the wind
blew fiercely. Provisions dwindled down to oatmeal and syrup, cooked over a
stove fed with twisted hay. Eventually, things became uncomfortable and Mr.
Miles offered to attempt the trip to Mina for food, providing someone would
go with him. Mel Day, one of his bosses, volunteered. They selected four of
the best horses and started out at daybreak. The horses appeared to be
swimming, so deep was the snow.

        MR. ALBERT F. MILES

All morning they fought the blizzard. It was not until shortly after noon
that they arrived at Mina, after covering eight miles. Trading some sacks
of wheat for groceries, they again set out into the storm, arriving back at
camp around 7:00 p.m. With the tobacco and food, they lived like princes
until the storm abated.

In the spring of 1888, Miles joined Fossett again and together they planned
to get back to Mound City and their claims. Fossett, who had been working
at Hecla, had obtained an ox which he wanted to get out to the claim. They
lead the ox 60 miles across country and covered the distance in two days
and a half. There were no roads and they got their bearings by looking for
the stone markers on the section corners.

In November of 1888 he was married at Aberdeen, South Dakota to Ida Fossett
of Winona, Minnesota, who had been waiting for him to build a home for her
in South Dakota. A two-room frame home was built on their claim where he
farmed, and served as deputy sheriff of Campbell county. He served under
Sheriff Hi Sager, who had served ten years with the Seventh cavalry of the
United States army.

In the fall of 1889 there occurred the well known "Sitting Bull Scare"
which terrified settlers in this vicinity for weeks. Mr. Miles was away
from home in his capacity as deputy sheriff when neighbors drove past the
claim and urged Mrs. Miles to go with them to Eureka, saying everybody was
leaving the country because the Indians were on the warpath and headed that
way. Unwilling to leave because her husband was not there, she stayed with
her small baby at her home, and was no doubt the only person in the whole
country that night. Mr. Miles arrived home around midnight and knew the
rumors were false, but she had known many hours of terror.

In 1895 he moved into Mound City from his claim and started a harness and
saddle business. At that time he averaged 100 sets of harness and 24
saddles in one year,--made entirely by hand.

His three children were born in Mound City. They were Rollin, who died in
1918 and is survived by a son, Raymond, who now operates the undertaking
business which Mr. Miles established in Mobridge and conducted until the
time of his death; Louise, now Mrs. Grover Hand of Mobridge, and A.D.
Miles, also of Mobridge.

In 1900 he moved his family to Selby where he first operated a harness and
saddle shop, later closing out that stock and opening a furniture and
undertaking business. He was licensed to the profession of embalming in
1904.

He served on the Selby board of aldermen from 1900 to 1912 and was active
in getting the county seat moved from Bangor to Selby in 1908. It took
eight years and three elections to get the county seat moved to Selby. The
fight developed into a long drawn-out affair, and they were always running
out of funds to keep the campaign going. Finally three men, Attorney A.A.
Brown, Editor Fred Griffin and Mr. Miles hatched the idea of getting each
of the two saloons to install slot machines and after the machines paid for
themselves, all of the money was turned over to this committee for the
county seat fund. In two years the machines netted $2000 and no one else
knew where it came from.

Expenses for the final election, at which bonds for the construction of the
courthouse building were voted, were paid out of the pockets of Messrs.
Miles, Brown and Griffin. The town of Bangor fell apart soon after the
courthouse was moved and is now farming territory.

In 1912 Mr. Miles moved with his family to Mobridge and opened an
undertaking business.

He served two terms as state senator, in 1928 and 1929, and served as
coroner of Walworth county intermittently for eight terms. He also served
many years as justice of the peace in Mobridge.

He was a charter member of the Masonic Lodge in Selby and Mrs. Miles was a
charter member of the Eastern Star there. Mrs. Miles preceded him in death
in 1934 and Mr. Miles passed away at his home in Mobridge, December 17,
1945.

MR. AND MRS. D. W. WELTON

Like so many Iowa families Mr. and Mrs. Welton had looked upon South Dakota
as a fine place to found a home. This dream began to shape up when on March
