1, 1906, they arrived in Selby on an accommodation train. A real Dakota
blizzard was raging and after hearing tales of such storms there were some
fears mixed with the realization of their anticipations.

David West Welton was born at Burlington, Iowa in 1876 and Gertrude French
Welton at Denison, Iowa in 1873. Mr. Welton's early life was spent on a
farm. Later he prepared at Moody Bible Institute at Chicago for special
Christian work. Miss French, a town girl, finished high school at Denison
and after normal training taught for 9 years in the Denison schools.

These two young people met when Mr. Welton, as a missionary for the
American Sunday School Union, contacted Miss French as to the best method
of procedure with the work near Denison. They were married in 1902. A son,
who died in infancy, was born to them in 1905.

        MR. D. W. WELTON

A short time later Mr. Welton found it physically impossible to continue
the intensive study and constant traveling of a Sunday School missionary so
he took up the carpenter trade. It was as a carpenter that he came to
Selby, having secured the contract to erect the buildings on the R. W.
Reynolds property. This place later became the home of the H. P. Gutz
family.

Six months after coming to Selby, Mr. Welton and a gang of Iowa carpenters
and N. V. Johnson of Selby went to the townsite of Cresbard, South Dakota.
Piles of lumber and identification stakes were the only markings for the
future business houses. During the stay there of 3 years the town grew to a
population of 300. It was while the Weltons resided in Cresbard that a son,
Walter, came to take his place in the home.

Upon returning to Selby in 1910, farming at the Gutz and Myler ranch was
the new venture of this family. While still on this farm a daughter, Irene,
now Mrs. Raymond Carman, joined the family circle, making a well rounded
household.

In 1919, Mr. Welton purchased the furniture store from H. R. deMalignon and
continued in that business until his death in 1929. The undertaking work
and supervision of the care of the cemetery were side lines of the
furniture business.

During all these years, weather, war and depression had their share in
developing character and making worthwhile the struggle for what measure of
success was attained. During the residence in Selby, the county fair,
chautauqua, city council and all other civic work claimed their share of
interest; but the church and Sunday School work in the city and county were
given supreme thought and attention by Mr. Welton. At the same time the work
of the Woman's club, the W. R. C. and church and Sunday school and store
work were the outside interests of Mrs. Welton.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN F. HIMRICH

John F. Himrich was born in South Russia, November 30, 1875. He came to the
United States at the age of nine years with his parents and family,
settling at Yankton where they lived for ten years before coming to
Walworth county in 1894. His father homesteaded the land now occupied by
the Edward Himrich family which became the family home. In 1897 John
homesteaded the quarter section west of the quarter on which Lake
Hiddenwood is situated, and put on a small house and other buildings on the
corner opposite where the Russell Stulken home is now. In 1899 he was
united in marriage with Margaretha Helm and they set up housekeeping on the
claim.

Mrs. Himrich was born in South Russia and came to America with her parents,
Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Helm and family, locating a few miles northeast of
the Himrich home.

In 1910 Mr. Himrich purchased land a mile east of Selby and moved the
buildings off his claim to it and built others until they had a modern set
of farm buildings and a fine home, residing on it for 35 years until his
death in 1945. Since his passing Mrs. Himrich has continued to live on the
farm with her son, Robert in charge of the farming operations.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHN F. HIMRICH

Three children were born to the couple: John Jr., is the eldest and married
Bertha Maier. They have five children and own what has long been known as
the Riley section of land, two miles southeast of Selby, which they have
made into one of the fine farms of the community. Robert was associated
with his father in farming operations before his death and has continued to
operate on a larger scale since. He is one of the substantial larger
operators in this section, diversifying his farming operations and has made
a fine success. Arthur married Freda Kast of Java, and resides at Mobridge
where he is mayor of the city. They have one daughter.

Truly the son and grandsons have carried on the traditions of honest work,
frugality and outlook for the future of the pioneers who left the old
country for a better America.

MR. HENRY MECKLENBURG

Henry Mecklenburg was born March 6, 1869, and came to the United States
from Holstein, Germany, at the age of 17, in order to avoid going into
military service in his country. He received his education in Germany. He
went to Iowa where he worked on farms for a number of years.

Dora Blunk came to the United States at the age of 7 and settled in Iowa to
be near relatives. She became the bride of Henry Mecklenburg on September
13, 1899 and the couple started farming near Shelby, Iowa.

In March 1907, lured by stories of cheap rent and land the family with four
children, Minnie, Herman, Harry and Alma decided to journey to new land.
They had sold some of their property. The remainder was loaded in an
emigrant car and was accompanied to Selby by Chris Blunk and Bill Koch.

The family came by train, arriving at Aberdeen in a blizzard. While Mr.
Mecklenburg was helping to feed the cattle in the emigrant car he met
Adolph Marxen, who was also coming to South Dakota with his family. The
families soon became acquainted and found they were to be neighbors. In
spite of the blizzard the train slowly made its way to Selby, where they
were forced to remain in a hotel for a few days.

The family were met in Selby by Charlie Meink, who took them to their new
home by bobsled. This new country seemed to be a bare expanse of white with
only a few tops of fenceposts showing above the snow.

The new home, a quarter of land with few buildings 8-1/2 miles southwest of
Selby, had been purchased from Hans Engebretson.

The years brought good times and bad. During the years of crop failures Mr.
Mecklenburg sought other work and part of the time worked on a threshing
machine. He also sold many of his horses to tide the family over some of
the hard times.

The two eldest children entered school, unable to speak the English
language, but they soon learned and all the children in the family attended
the Engebretson school during their entire grade school education. For many
years Mr. Mecklenburg was clerk of the Hilde School district. The
Mecklenburg home was known for its fine hospitality and Mrs. Mecklenburg
was a fine cook; taking many prizes at the county fairs with her baking.

In 1929 Mr. Mecklenburg suffered a stroke and was a semi-invalid until his
death in 1941. The children, Harry, Art, John, Edna, and Charlie at home,
took over the farm and in 1936 moved to Marshall, Minnesota, where they
felt a better living could be made.

Mrs. Mecklenburg was stricken with sleeping sickness and passed away in
July of 1941. Just two weeks later, Mr. Mecklenburg also passed away.

Mr. and Mrs. Mecklenburg were the parents of nine children: Minnie, Mrs.
Frank Zabel, Selby; Herman of Selby; Harry of Marshall, Minn., Alma, Mrs.
Leo Todd of Groton, New York; Tena, Mrs. Dwight Riddle of Peoria, Ill.;
Arthur of Passaic, N. J.; Edna of Marshall, Minn.; John of Los Angeles,
Calif.; and Charles of Marshall. Minn.

THE SAWINSKY FAMILY

John P. Sawinsky was born on Big Island near Berlin, Wisconsin, June 27,
1861. He drifted west as a young man to find work and also to file on land
in Walworth county, which was opened to homesteaders.

He, August Miller and Tony and Theodore Birkholt first arrived at Raymond,
South Dakota in Clark county in the spring of 1884 and from here they went
to Aberdeen, South Dakota and filed on the quarter of land in Surrey
township, south of Selby, which remained his home until his death February
22, 1936. He did not stay here permanently, as he sought work in the harvest
fields near Casselton, North Dakota at different times, until in the spring
of 1887 when he brought back his bride, Amelia Ewald of Berlin, Wisconsin.
Mrs. Sawinsky was born near Berlin, Germany February 17, 1863, coming to
this country at the age of five to Berlin, Wisconsin. To this union six
children were born: four sons, Albert, a veteran of World War I, now
deceased; William, Ralph and Carl; two daughters, Alma, now Mrs. Ernest
Beaman; and Mabel, now Mrs. A. L. Bruckner. Mrs. Sawinsky passed away
October 22, 1932. Carl lives on the original homestead. The other children
all live near by.

Henry Sawinsky came to Walworth county in 1885, coming from Berlin,
Wisconsin where he was born on Big Island on September 10, 1859. He filed
on land southeast of where Selby is now located, later selling this and
buying the quarter south of Selby in Surrey township from a Mr. Price,
which became his home until his death June 30, 1932. He was united in
marriage on February 4, 1892 to Rosa Wicks of Princeton, Wisconsin. To them
one daughter, Elizabeth, was born. At this writing Mrs. Sawinsky and
daughter still reside in the same home southeast of Selby.

Albert L. Sawinsky was born on Big Island, near Berlin, Wisconsin on June
24, 1868. He came to Walworth county in 1891 and worked for other settlers
here when he first came, then filed on the quarter of land, which was his
home until his death, February 27, 1934.

In 1896 he married Etna Jaynes who was born in Sedalia, Illinois. Their
family consists of two sons, John W. of Friday Harbor, Washington, Lloyd of
Onida, South Dakota; and one daughter, Genevieve, now Mrs. W. C. Libor of
Minneapolis, Minnesota. Mrs. Sawinsky still lives in Selby.

Mrs. Augusta Sawinsky, the mother of the Sawinsky brothers came here in
1902 from Berlin, Wisconsin with the two youngest children of the family,
Frank and Laura. John Vincent Sawinsky, the father passed away in Wisconsin
in 1891 at the age of 62. He was born March 5, 1829. He was a Civil War
veteran and made the March with Sherman to the Sea.

        THE SAWINSKY FAMILY
        Upper right picture Mr. and Mrs. A. L. Sawinsky, Mrs. Laura
        Brockman on left. Lower left picture--Mr. and Mrs. Henry Sawinsky.
        Picture on right--Mr. and Mrs. John Sawinsky.

The mother rented a farm here at first. Her health seemed improved so she
bought a farm in Surrey township near her sons' farms. They later moved to
Selby where Frank died and Laura married Henry Brockman. Their family
consists of a daughter, Florence at home and Claire, a veteran of World War
II, now deceased. Mrs. Augusta Sawinsky spent her last years at her
daughter's home in Redfield. She died in the fall of 1911.

Many interesting incidents in the lives of the Sawinsky families might be
related if space permitted. They battled on undaunted by drouth, prairie
fires, Indian scares, blizzards, long hard trips for supplies to Ipswich,
South Dakota, later to Bowdle as the railroad came closer and manifold
other hardships that were the common lot of pioneers in the early eighties.

From a start of little or nothing the early years were ones of hardships
and privations. By endurance and careful saving the wild prairies became
fine farm land the homestead shacks became modern homes and the meagre
shelter of the oxen became up-to-date farm barns.

Thus the final chapter is written of the lives of Mrs. Augusta, Frank,
Henry, Albert, John and Amelia Sawinsky who now lie beneath the sod of
Walworth county in the Selby Union cemetery.

MR. AND MRS. OLE SAVOLD

Ole Savold came to Dakota territory in 1884 from Ossian, Iowa, and filed on
a claim five miles due west of Bangor, the former county seat of Walworth
county, and the land being known now as the Hadley place owned by Calvin
Zabel.

The following year he brought his wife, nee Nellie Skartvedt, also of
Ossian, to this place where they lived until the summer of 1901, when they
moved to Oakes, North Dakota, for several years and later to Ossian, Iowa,
and to Wisconsin. Their final years were spent In St. Paul, Minnesota.

        MR. AND MRS. OLE SAVOLD

There were three children: Arthur, Ethel, and Otto, all of whom were
married at Oakes; Arthur to Mollie King of Aberdeen, South Dakota; Ethel to
Irving H. Van Horn of Cleveland, Ohio; and Otto to Mabel Smith of Oakes,
North Dakota. Arthur passed away in November 1940, in Minneapolis,
Minnesota where he resided. Ethel and Irving live in Cleveland, Ohio and
Otto and Mabel in the Canal Zone in Panama.

The second generation number four, all in the Van Horn family: Reva,
married to Glenn R. Brockway; Millie to H. J. Sheffield, Jr.; Irving Jr. to
Virginia Reeves; and Peggy to Walter S. Glover.

There are five in the third generation: Sally and Tommy Brockway, Rachel
and Eric Van Horn and Billy Sheffield.

MR. CHARLES OTTMAN

Charles Ottman was born August 30, 1860 in Wisconsin. In 1862 his family
removed to Genoa, Minnesota where he received his formal education. Like
many young men, the opening of homestead land on the prairies of Dakota
encouraged him to try his fortune in the western country. In 1884 he came
to Blue Blanket district in Walworth county and filed on a homestead in the
northwest corner of Blue Blanket township. Charles was interested in trying
out new methods of farming and new crops. In 1887-88 he raised the first
sorghum cane to be grown in Walworth county,--a wonderful stand. Encouraged
by the growth and hardiness of this crop, he planned the further step of
pressing the juice from the chopped cane for syrup, obtaining the necessary
equipment. Unfortunately, the two years following were drouth years, and
the crop was a failure. In 1891 he married Julia Molstertiegen, a young
teacher whose homestead adjoined his own. The same year they moved to a
farm near Bangor and lived there for seventeen years.

To Mr. and Mrs. Ottman were born three children: Arthur, Sadie and Joyce.
In 1908 the Ottmans sold their interest in Walworth county and followed the
railroad west where they located on a section of land east of Shade Hill
district, near Lemmon. There they engaged in ranching and farming for many
years. Their children were educated in the Lemmon schools. Arthur assisted
his father in ranching and farming, taking over the home place upon Mr.
Ottman's retirement. They have two sections of land in that excellent stock
country.

        MR. AND MRS. CHARLES OTTMAN

Mr. and Mrs. Ottman celebrated their golden wedding anniversary on March
31, 1941. They were affiliated with the Congregational church and had four
grandchildren. Mr. Ottman died at Lemmon in 1946 and Mrs. Ottman now makes
her home with her daughter, Joyce, Mrs. W. B. Cain, near Lemmon. She is 87
years of age.

MR. AND MRS. JOHANNES TISDALL

Mr. Tisdall was born in 1814 near Stavenger, Norway, and came to America in
his youth. He settled in Wisconsin, and enlisted in the 15th Wisconsin for
the Civil war.

Mrs. Martha Tisdall was born near Bergen, Norway in 1833 and with her
mother and three brothers came to America in 1858. They came by sailboat
and after three weeks landed in Quebec, Canada. They settled in Wisconsin
and some years later went to Polk county, Iowa, and later on went to Cass
county, Iowa.

Mrs. Tisdall was first married to Mr. Johnson, to which union was born one
son, Oliver Johnson, who also came to Dakota. Her first husband fought in
the Civil war and was listed among the missing.

Mr. Tisdall also was married before, and had six children from that
marriage and six children from the last marriage.

Mr. and Mrs. Tisdall and family came to Walworth county, South Dakota in
1886, and engaged in farming. Mr. Tisdall died in 1905.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHANNES TISDALL

There were no doctors here when the country was first being settled and
Mrs. Tisdall went around nursing the sick, caring for the dying and
ushering the new lives into this world, while at the same time she cared
for her own family. There were times when doing these things were, not only
inconvenient and difficult, but dangerous as the following incident shows:
At about 10:00 o'clock p.m., February 13, 1888, P.J. Thorstenson, then
living a couple of miles south and a little east of the Tisdall place, came
for help for his sister who was sick at his place. It was very stormy and
the snow extremely deep and he came on skis as that was the only thing he
had at that time. Few people had oxen at that time, fewer still had horses,
so practically all traveling was done on foot. Getting there was doubtful
and she advised waiting until day light. Thorstenson, later in the night,
came again and they hitched a team of horses, which Tisdall had brought
with him from Iowa, and all the menfolks went along to help shovel snow.
There were Thorstenson, Tisdall Sr., Henry, Oliver and Jake, and they got
as far as down on the flat a little past the Olufson place where the snow
was several feet deep. The wagon tipped over and the horses were
floundering in the snow. The men righted the wagon and horses and realized
they could get no farther that particular way, and so Mrs. Tisdall got on
the skis and with Thorstenson walking along by her side and helping her,
after a hard struggle they reached the place. They had scarcely more than
closed the door when the storm really did break loose. She took charge and
brought matters to a successful ending.

When these circumstances are considered, together with the fact that Mrs.
Tisdall had a congenital defective hip, causing her to be lame, we must
marvel at, and admire her, for her fearlessness, perseverance,
great-heartedness and heroism.

In another instance a young man, who had filed on a nearby piece of land,
needed help and care, for he had consumption. Mr. and Mrs. Tisdall took him
in and cared for him. For a long time he made a steady recovery and
evidently considered himself cured, and then he overlifted and that
eventually caused his death.

The Tisdalls', by their unselfishness, proved themselves to be helpers of
the weak and unfortunate and by their lives reflected the light of Him who
is the Light of the world.

MR. JOHN FRIEDRICH HIMRICH

We, the descendants of Mr. and Mrs. John Friedrich Himrich, are proud of
the fact that they rate as pioneers of South Dakota. Their grandparents had
migrated from Germany to Russia, at the invitation of Catherine II in 1763.
The Russian Empress, wishing to introduce a higher type of culture, looked
to the German farmers, who by their progress and advanced methods were to
inspire the Russian peasants. The privileges, as recorded, were very
enticing to the ambitious Germans. By 1768 Germany managed to stop this
emigration, but in the early part of the 19th century Catherine's
successor, Alexander I, issued a second invitation and many more Germans
were drawn by his inducements,--most of them settling in Southern Russia,
along the Black Sea. The ruler's terms were modified in later years and
finally withdrawn, but originally they allowed:

1. Full religious liberty, except that they were for bidden to propagate
   their Faith among the native Russians.

2. Exemption from military service.

3. Grants of thirty "dessatine" of land to each family (approximately 65
   acres).

4. Complete control over their own churches and schools.

5. Free transportation from Germany to Russia.

6. Tax exemption for the first ten years.

7. Interest-free loans of 500 rubles.

8. Almost complete autonomy in local government.

There, in a village called Freudenthal (Joyous Valley), Johan Friedrich
Himrich was born on April 24, 1852. He had two sisters, Mrs. Ricka
Bechtoldt, and Mrs. Barbara Wacker, both of whom were older than their only
brother. In the course of time he was married to Susanna Neumiller, who was
born November 13, 1853. Six children blessed this home while it was on
Russian soil. Renounced privileges and new incentives revealed to this
family during the late summer of 1884, caused them to immigrate to the
United States. They came directly to the southern part of the Dakota
territory. No permanent home was established, as the father worked as a
carpenter and rented small grain farms to provide for his family. Ambition
to own land and a permanent home, caused the Himrich family to come to the
northern part of the State in 1894. They proceeded westward from Bowdle.
John F. Himrich selected his homestead on section 27, township 124, range
76, located two and one half miles northeast of Selby.

At that time Bangor was the nearest postoffice, and all their farm products
had to be hauled to Bowdle. The Himrich family then consisted of eight
children, four being added since they had moved to the states. Two were
called by death: William, a lad of twelve years, and Emil, an infant and
both were buried in Bon Homme county.

Their first home in Walworth county was a sod-house, but their barn was a
frame building proudly erected by Mr. Himrich and sons. By means of hard
labor by the entire family, a neat clay-brick five-room home was built in
1895. Another baby came to bless this home,--a son, Edward, who has called
this same house his home ever since. The happy homelife of this family was
disrupted in 1905, when the mother died at the age of 52.

Sometime later, Mr. Himrich took a trip to his childhood home. He brought
with him, on his return, a new helpmate, who brought her youngest son,
Robert Abel, who has been a Selby resident ever since. Later an older son,
William Abel, followed his mother to the United States.

        THE JOHN FRED HIMRICH SR., FAMILY
        Standing, back row--Susie (Mrs. Christ Hirning, deceased) Adam
        Himrich; John F. Himrich, deceased; Elizabeth (Mrs. Gottfried
        Wagner). Second row--Mrs. Lydia Wagner; Christine (Mrs. Robert
        Abel); Katie (Mrs. C. Hirning). Front row--John F. Himrich Sr.,
        Emmanuel; Mrs. John F. Himrich Sr., with son Ed. on lap.

The Himrich family continued living on their farm home, taking an active
part in civic and religious life. In 1913. Mr. and Mrs. Himrich made
another visit to Europe to see her only daughter still living in Russia.
This daughter and her children's families were later obliterated by the
Revolution which took place in Russia after World War I. A grandson of this
daughter miraculously escaped from Siberia and came to America as a
displaced person. He was very happy to meet his great-uncles, and also to
avail himself of the wonderful privileges of our grand country.

Upon their return to the United States, the Himrichs made provisions to
build one of the first all modern homes in Selby. They occupied this home
in the fall of 1914, leaving the farming operations to their sons. Mr.
Himrich lived to enjoy this nice home only four years. He passed away May
19, 1918, and was laid to rest beside his first wife, Susan, in a country
churchyard, two miles east of his farm home.

His widow, Wilhelmina, continued to live in Selby by herself until 1926,
when her children, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Abel moved into this home with her.
In a few years she left to visit her older son, William, in Seattle, and
decided to remain for a few years. After this she again returned to Selby
to live with the Robert Abel family. The last years of her life. she was
cared for by William and his wife in Seattle. She passed away March 6, 1945
past 90 years of age, and was buried in Seattle.

The descendants of this venerable couple now residing in this part of the
state are:

1. Adam, oldest son, widower, living in Selby. Three married daughters, one
of whom resides in Michigan.

2. Susan, Mrs. Christ Hirning, passed away in 1944 leaving her husband and
three married daughters, one of whom passed away in 1945 leaving her
husband and three children. (Emelia Rutschke).

3. John F., passed away in 1945, leaving his wife nee Margaret Helm and
three sons.

4. Elizabeth, Mrs. Gottfried Wagner, living in Selby with her husband and
daughter. They also have one married son.

5. Katherina, widow of George Wolf, now married to Christ Hirning. She is
the mother of two sons and two daughters, all of whom are married. Death
has claimed a son, George and a daughter, Dora.

6. Lydia, widow of Julius Wagner, living in Selby. She has three daughters
and one son, all are married. Her son lives in Washington.

7. Christine, Mrs. Robert Abel, living with her husband in Selby. They have
three married sons, living in Fargo, North Dakota, Brookings, South Dakota,
and Dallas, Texas. They have a married daughter living in Brookings.

8. Emanuel and wife (nee Lillie Kellar) live in Selby. They have three
sons, two of whom are married, and a married daughter.

9. Edward and wife (nee Emily Sattler), the youngest son, totally
disabled, living on the aforementioned farm with wife and seven children.
One married daughter lives in Minnesota, and a son, Leo, died in 1947,
leaving a wife and two small children.

CAPTAIN NEWTON H. KINGMAN

In the history of every community, there are certain individuals who can be
designated as unique characters, and in the growth and development of Selby
and territory tributary thereto, the story of Captain Newton H. Kingman
definitely falls within this category. Newton Hawes Kingman was born on May
20, 1837, near Chester Center, Geauga county, Ohio, the second son of Edmund
and Hannah Kingman, nee Hawes, in a family consisting of seven sons and
three daughters. His ancestry can be traced to Henry Kingman, an English
emigrant who settled at Weymouth, Massachusetts, in 1633.

Kingman's parents moved to Walworth county, Wisconsin, in 1849, and it was
there that future Captain Kingman received his grammar school education,
later pursuing a course of study at Albion academy in Dane county,
Wisconsin. He taught rural schools in that vicinity for several terms until
the beginning of the war between the states, when answering Governor
Randall's first call for volunteers, he enlisted for a term of three months
in the First Regiment of the Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry, on April 17,
1861. At the end of his enlistment, he returned to Wisconsin and soon
afterward, at the request of Governor Randall, he recruited a company of
volunteers for a three year enlistment, and was given the rank of
lieutenant. This group was then assigned as Company "I" to the 13th
Regiment, Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry, and detailed to the "Far
Southwestern Front" at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Some action was there seen
in quelling rebellious Indians, and the company was then assigned to care
for army supplies at Columbus, Kentucky. It was while serving here, that
Kingman was promoted to captain on June 8, 1862, which rank he retained
until his honorary discharge late in the year 1865. Captain Kingman and his
company of volunteers served and fought with distinction during the entire
war; the latter portion of said war fighting as a part of the Army of the
Cumberland under Generals Rosencrans, Thomas and others.

Returning to civilian life, Kingman enrolled in Eastmans business college
at Chicago, and completed his course in the spring of 1866. While attending
school, he met his future wife, Mary E. Davis, and the young couple were
married at Chicago on November 26, 1866. They spent the next two years on
the Kingman farm in Wisconsin, after which Kingman secured a job as a
traveling salesman for two publishing concerns in a territory consisting
largely of Illinois and Indiana. He remained so engaged until 1873 when he
secured a more remunerative position in compiling and publishing county
histories, principally in Ohio. He remained in this work until 1876 when,
with a younger brother, he set up a similar business of his own at Kokomo,
Indiana. In 1877 the business was moved to Logansport, Indiana. Kingman was
not content with the life of a publisher and through correspondence learned
of pioneer opportunities in the new territory of Dakota, so he resolved to
investigate and, in company with two Civil War comrades and the son of a
comrade, arrived at Aberdeen, South Dakota, in September, 1883. He first
looked over the counties of Edmunds, northern Faulk and Potter, which were
accessible by railroad, and then entered Walworth county and, as he termed
it, her "charming Blue Blanket valley." He was immediately impressed with
its breadth, landscape and deep fertile soil and decided that this was the
place for him. He had also been advised that the Milwaukee railroad was
proposing to extend its line to the Missouri river, and therefore was
interested in selecting a homestead location as closely to the center of
the county as possible, with the expectation that the county seat, then at
Scranton, would be moved to a more central part of the county. He
immediately selected a homestead and tree-claim for himself and his wife's
father, and "squatted," because the land was not yet open for filing.
Kingman selected as his own homestead the south half of the southeast
quarter of section 28, and the north half of the northeast quarter of
section 23, in township 123 north of range 76, and was issued a patent to
this land by President Grover Cleveland, on February 11, 1888. The Kingmans
retained this property until 1921, when it was sold to Fred Theilen, father
of Inez Theilen, present county superintendent of schools of Walworth
county. The Theilen family sold the property in 1945 to William J.
Sawinsky, who still retains ownership. The buildings, constructed on this
property in 1884 by the Kingmans with lumber hauled from LeBeau and
Aberdeen, were sold and removed from the property in 1946.

Ever an avid booster of his adopted county, Kingman broadcast the
possibilities of Walworth county far and wide, and in a matter of a few
months following the fall of 1883 practically all of the land near his
future home was taken up by homesteaders. The Kingman home was completed
during the winter and spring of 1884 and the Captain returned to
Logansport, Indiana, for his family.

The Kingman family arrived at Ipswich on May 16, 1884, with two freight
cars laden with household wares, two young Jersey cows, six heifers, a
large cage of Plymouth Rock fowls and a corresponding crate of baby chicks;
also a large crate of sprouted black walnut seedlings and six evergreen
shrubs. Immediately, the Captain went to work breaking the soil, planting a
garden and thirty acres of corn. A terrific hail storm struck the Kingman
premises on July 21, 1884, and the thirty acres of corn, garden vegetables,
walnut seedlings and evergreens were all destroyed.

Early in 1884, the Kingman farm served as a local postoffice for several
months with the Captain as postmaster until the Bangor postoffice could be
completed. The farm also served as a change-over stop for horses on the
stage line from LeBeau to Ipswich. It was the social and religious center
during the early days; church services were often held in the Kingman home
by itinerant ministers and what is believed to have been the first marriage
in Walworth county was performed there in the summer of 1884, when Tom
Trinder, a neighbor who had settled two miles northwest of the Kingman
homestead, took unto himself a "blushing bride."

        CAPTAIN AND MRS. NEWTON H. KINGMAN

In the early days of development, politics was an ever vital factor and on
July 19, 1884, a meeting was held at the Kingman farm to organize a
committee to agitate removing the county seat from Scranton to the new town
of Bangor. The committee held a mass meeting of all settlements in the
county on September 6, 1884, and were successful in placing the question of
Bangor becoming the official county seat on the November 1884 election
ballot. The committee decided to assist its campaign by publishing a
newspaper, and the first edition of "The Blue Blanket" newspaper, a
predecessor of the present "Selby Record," was published in a wing of the
Kingman home under date of September 11, 1884. The publishers were Winn and
Fulcomer. At the November 1884 election, Bangor was selected as the county
seat by a majority vote of forty-nine. Along with the Bangor county seat
victory, the whole slate of Kingman-sponsored candidates for county office
were elected.

The next years were spent largely in acquiring more land and breaking more
soil. As a whole, the Kingman family prospered through hard work. Prairie
fires, hail and drouth at times intervened but the good years always made
up for the bad ones. Kingman was a firm believer in diversified farming and
in addition to extensive small grain farming, always maintained a large
herd of dairy and feeder cattle, some hogs, and a large number of horses.
During this time, his family was growing up and was giving him more and
more assistance on the farm. The eldest son, Arthur Judson Kingman, born
September 13, 1869, started farming and ranching on his own in 1890 and
took up a homestead in section 35, township 122, range 76, in Walworth
county. The daughter, May Louise, born January 11, 1868, was married to
Otto K. Stablein in the summer of 1886, who at that time was a young
merchant at Bangor and later moved to Selby. The second son, Newton Hawes
Kingman Jr., usually called "Tute," was born March 17, 1871, learned
telegraphy at Bowdle, South Dakota, during the winter of 1891, and nine
years later, in 1900, became the depot agent at Selby when the Chicago,
Milwaukee and St. Paul railroad was extended to that place. Newton Jr.,
served as depot agent at Selby from 1900 to 1916. The youngest son, Edmund
B. Kingman, born December 2 1881, remained on the farm until he joined his
father's real estate and abstract business at Selby shortly after the year
1900.

Captain Kingman was a life-long republican. He always claimed that he was a
"charter member" of the republican party, having cast his first
presidential vote for Abraham Lincoln in 1860. In 1894, under the gentle
persuasion of George H. Hoffman, a neighbor and comrade of Civil War days,
and long prominent in political circles in South Dakota, having served as
lieutenant governor, Kingman was "seduced" into running for county register
of deeds. He was elected and assumed office in January, 1895. In 1896 he
ran for re-election and despite a schism within the republican party,
Kingman was one of two candidates elected to county office, the remaining
county officers being from the opposition wing within the party. While a
county official, he became interested in making abstracts, selling real
estate and serving as a loan broker, and upon completion of his second term
as register of deeds, decided to stay out of politics and devote his full
time to his abstract and real estate business.

While at Bangor, Mr. Kingman had erected a building for his business which
he sold to L. W. Moody of Pomeroy, Iowa, in 1899, for the purpose of
establishing a bank. The bank was started under the name of the Walworth
County State Bank and in 1900 was moved from Bangor to Selby, and continued
to operate under that name at Selby until 1930, although under various
ownerships. After the sale of his business building to Moody, Kingman built
another building for his own business which was moved to Selby in 1900,
along with a general movement of people and property from Bangor to Selby
because of the completion of the railroad. This building was located upon
Lot 4, Block 7, Selby, and served as the business establishment of the
Kingman Investment company and Abstract office for the next fourteen years.
The original Kingman building no longer exists and has been replaced by a
brick and tile structure presently occupied by the Selby Dry Cleaners,
owned and operated by Eugene B. Brenneise. The Kingman residence at Selby
is now owned by Mrs. Mary Baer and is located on Lots 11 and 12, Block 10,
in Selby.

The Kingman Investment company did a large and prosperous business during
the early days of Selby and Walworth county and its activities extended
into Montana and other states. The company consisted of the elder Kingman
and his two sons, Arthur and Edmund, both of whom later left Selby and
entered into other business on the west coast.

The biography of Captain Kingman would not be complete without mentioning
the very prominent part he played in the Grand Army of the Republic, an
organization of Civil War veterans. While living at Logansport, Indiana, he
was a member of the post at that place, and when removing to South Dakota
took his transfer and was Charter Member No. 1 of the John Mangan Post No.
150, Department of South Dakota, G.A.R., at Bangor and later at Selby. He
was elected department commander of South Dakota in 1910 and later
appointed by the Governor to serve as chairman of a committee in South
Dakota to assist in the celebration of the semi-centennial anniversary of
the Battle of Gettysburg on July 1 to 4, 1913. It was the work of Kingman
and his committee to contact all surviving veterans of the battle still
living in South Dakota, and arrange for their round trip to that famous
battlefield. Ninety-nine of these survivors were found in South Dakota and
Captain Kingman and his committee accompanied them to the battlefield at
Gettysburg in a special train of pullman cars furnished without charge by
the C.M.&St.P. railroad.

Mrs. Kingman was a charter member of the Women's Relief Corps, G.A.R.
ladies auxiliary, both at Bangor and later at Selby.

In 1918, Mr. and Mrs. Kingman went to Portland, Oregon, for the national
encampment of the G.A.R. and to visit with their sons who resided in
Oregon. While there, Mrs. Kingman became seriously ill and never returned
to Selby. The Kingmans disposed of all of their South Dakota holdings
within the next few years and in 1920 began making their home with their
son, Edmund, who lived at Eugene, Oregon. Mrs. Kingman died on December 29,
1924, at Eugene, Oregon. After her death, Captain Kingman continued to live
with his children, until his death on February 3, 1937, lacking but 106
days of attaining his one hundredth birthday.

All of the Kingman children, except Newton H. Kingman Jr., are still
living. Mrs. O. K. Stablein lives at Seattle, Washington, and Arthur J.
Kingman and Edmund B. Kingman reside at Eugene, Oregon.

MR. AND MRS. S. J. BYRE

Sever J. Byre, son of Johannes Byre, was born at Lom, Guldbrandsdalen,
Norway, February 1, 1859, and passed away at his home after a brief illness
on Sunday morning, August 29, 1948, at the age of 89 years, 6 months and 28
days.

He was baptized and confirmed in the Lutheran faith in Norway. In 1880 he
immigrated to America, living first in Wisconsin, then Lincoln county,
South Dakota, several years before coming to Campbell county in 1887 where
he filed on a homestead. In 1900 they moved to their present home in
Walworth county.

One daughter and six sons were born to this union. One son preceded him in
death. Surviving are his wife; one daughter, Anna, Mrs. Tom Holder, and 5
sons, Joseph, Oscar, Sidney, and Raymond, all of Selby; and Elmer of
Yakima, Washington; 13 grandchildren; one brother, Ole Byre of Kennebec,
South Dakota; several nieces and nephews.

Inga S. Odland was born April 13, 1880, in Stavanger, Norway. A short time
later her mother passed away leaving her as a tiny baby and a brother, Tom
Odland, age 2 years, 2 months.

Sometime later her father, Ole T. Odland sailed for America in search of a
better living. He worked in Brown county on the railroad as section man
until 1886 at which time he came back to Norway and married Engebore
Freland. Father, stepmother, son and daughter sailed for America together,
landing in the year 1886, at which time Inga was 6 years old. They came to
Brown county and her father worked at odd jobs for a year, then moving
to Walworth county in 1887, making their home on the quarter a half mile
west of the Bethany Lutheran church, living in a dugout.

        MR. AND MRS. SEVER J. BYRE
        Children. Left to right, Elmer, Anna (Mrs. Tom Holder) and Joe.

When they came to Walworth county in 1887 all they had was three oxen, two
cows, a 2-year-old heifer, two pigs, one dog and one chicken. Her father
bought one ox and then he got word that it was mortgaged and they wanted it
back, so he walked back to Brown county leading the ox. This was a several
days trip. He had a little property left in Brown county. He sold it and
bought four broncos which he brought back to Walworth county. He used oxen
to do some land breaking until he got the broncos broke. Nearest town was
Bowdle, which was the end of the railroad.

They lived on this quarter until 1893 at which time they moved to the
northeast quarter of 17-124-77 living here until 1900 when Inga married
Sever J. Byre. Then they moved to his homestead at southeast quarter of
32-125-77. They made their home there in Campbell county until 1910, then
moving to the northeast quarter of 17-124-77 in Walworth county where she
is now living.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN J. HOVEN

John J. Hoven was born in Wisconsin in 1863 and was about 20 years of age
when his parents moved to the Hoven territory in about 1883 where they
homesteaded. The townsite of Hoven was given its name due to the gift of a
piece of land by Mr. Hoven's father to the Catholic parish for a
church-site.

Mr. Hoven's teen-age days were spent near Hoven where he worked as a hired
man on farms and helped his father with the farm work.

Eva Keiser was born in Germany and came with her parents to the Hoven
territory in about 1883. She spent most of her teen-age days in that
vicinity.

Mr. Hoven and Eva Keiser were married at Hoven on August 22, 1887, where
they resided on a farm near there until 1890 when they moved to Bangor,
South Dakota, which was the county seat of Walworth county and was located
five miles south of the present site of Selby. Mr. Hoven operated a
mercantile store at Bangor in partnership with W. B. Burr and B. B. Potter.
In 1900, after it was found that the C.M.&St.P. railroad would miss the
town of Bangor and would go through Selby, the store was moved to Selby and
the Hoven family moved with it. At that time there were eight children in
the family: Ben. Joe, Pete. Ed, Mike and Jake, who were twins, and William
and Albert, all having been born at Bangor except Ben, Joe and Pete, who
had been born at Hoven.

The store owned and operated by Burr, Potter and Hoven was moved from
Bangor and placed on the present site of the new Berens Hotel. In 1902 Mr.
Hoven sold his interests in the store and became interested in politics. He
was elected sheriff on the democratic ticket and also was part owner of a
mercantile store with Case Coyne in the new town of Evarts which was
located about twenty miles southwest of Selby close to the Missouri river
which was at that time the end of the C.M.&St.P. railroad line. Anna, the
only girl in the family, was born at Selby in 1903.

The Hoven family moved to Evarts in 1904 at which town the youngest son,
John, was born in 1905.

In 1906 it was found that the railroad would cross the river at the new
town of Mobridge so Evarts began to break up and the Hoven family moved
back to Selby where they owned a home. Mr. Hoven remained in politics
serving for several years as sheriff or deputy sheriff and also began to
buy livestock to ship to terminal markets. He remained in the livestock
game until the time of his death in 1929.

Mr. and Mrs. Hoven were of the Catholic faith and always ardent workers for
the betterment of church life and better citizenship. They were public
spirited folks and gave their children the best education possible at that
time. Six of the children graduated from the Selby high school and had
always taken active part in school affairs.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHN J. HOVEN AND FAMILY
        Standing, upper, Ben, Joe J., Pete J., Ed J.; center, standing,
        Will M., Jacob M., Mike J. and Albert M.; standing front, John  W.,
        and Anna May.

While Mr. Hoven was sheriff of Walworth county, his work was done mostly by
team and buggy which entailed many long and cold trips while on duty. A
good many trips required long drives across to the other side of the
Missouri river where Indians or cowboys, after having broken the laws
within the county, skipped back across the river.

The most interesting criminal case that Mr. Hoven had probably was the
killing of Dode McKenzie by Bud Stevens at the town of LeBeau which was
located along the river about twenty-five miles southwest of Selby. Dode
McKenzie was the son of a rich cattleman and owner of large cattle
interests west of the river. It seems that he had threatened to kill Bud
Stevens, a bartender, at LeBeau. As McKenzie entered the saloon Bud thought
he had better start shooting first so killed McKenzie in cold blood.
Stevens was kept in the jail at Selby and was acquitted of murder by trial
at Selby. Pat Morrison, a young attorney of Mobridge, defended Stevens and
won one of his first criminal cases.

Mrs. Hoven passed away in June, 1919. The family lived as a unit until the
time of Mr. Hoven's death in September, 1929.

Nine of the ten children now living are: Joe of Lewistown, Montana; Peter
of Hobson, Montana; Edward of Selby; Jacob of Alhambra, California; Mike of
Mitchell, South Dakota; William of Chicago, Illinois; Albert of Selby; Ann
Burkey of Mitchell, South Dakota; and John of Selby. Ben, who was the
oldest child, passed away at Selby in 1945.

MR. AND MRS. MODESTE MARIN

Modeste Marin was born at St. Lin, Canada, on August 31, 1856, of
French-Canadian parents, and was the eldest of a large family. At the age
of seventeen years, he went to Wisconsin to work on the river with the log
drives and gradually worked his way down the river and into Lake Michigan,
finally going to Grand Rapids, Michigan, where he worked in a sawmill. He
worked four years at the camp in Grand Rapids and on October 5, 1881, he
was united in marriage to Delilah Ann Warner. Following his desire to go
west and establish his home, he and his grandfather Thursten came to
Aberdeen, South Dakota, during the month of March in 1883, Aberdeen then
being the end of the railroad. There, they blind filed on their claims,
bought two yoke of oxen, an old wagon, a few supplies and equipment, and
started their trip to their claims, a distance of about one hundred miles.
The trip took many days as a prairie fire had burned over a part of the
distance and feed and water were scarce. They came by way of King's Ranch,
now believed to be in the vicinity of the present site of Hoven, past Swan
lake and on to LeBeau. From there they moved north up the Missouri river
and along the valley of one of the creeks that led to a flat and there they
located the land they had filed on, it being a part of section 7-122 77 (he
later acquired the whole of said section) which later became the fine farm
and home of the Modeste Marin family. It is believed that he turned the
first sod in Walworth county. He held the first tax receipt issued and paid
the first taxes in the county, which tax receipt the family still has in
their possession. After spending the summer of that year in building sod
houses and arranging for the future, Modeste went back to Grand Rapids,
Michigan, to join his family and remained there for the winter. In the
spring of 1884, he returned to his claim in Walworth county, built a small
frame house and in September of that year, Mrs. Marin and their one child
joined him. Those first years were very lonely for the young Mrs. Marin and
she was often frightened when Mr. Marin had to be away from the house. The
hardships and disappointments of the pioneer years were indeed severe. It
was ever a struggle for maintenance and progress but through the years,
their goal was reached and they attained independence. Their perseverance,
confidence and labors had been rewarded. Mr. Marin was always friendly with
the Indians and often during the severe winters, they would come to the
homestead in groups of two and three and seek food and shelter for a night.
They were never refused this aid and Mr. Marin often traded items of
clothing, trinkets and food to them. In one instance in negotiating a trade
with the Indians, he was crossing the Missouri river ice with his horse and
cart when the ice broke and Mr. Marin lost his horse and cart and almost
lost his life. He attributed his safety to the fact that he was wearing a
tightly woven overcoat buttoned tight about the neck and he believed that
the air under his coat held him afloat until he could reach the edge of the
ice. The current was very swift under the ice at that particular point and
he never saw his horse and cart again.

Any biography including the pioneer life of the settlers of Walworth county
would not be complete without a story of the "Indian Scare" of November,
1891, when Sitting Bull, the noted Sioux Chief, and his warriors were
reported to have left their hiding place since the Custer massacre, in the
Cypress Hills of Canada, and were moving south into the states to make
their raids on the settlements. The government, in anticipation of such
raids, had supplied many of the settlers with guns and ammunition. At night
the settlers would congregate in one of the homes and some of the men were
constantly on guard. After many anxious days and nights, a huge red glow
was seen in the sky which was later learned to be the fire accompanying the
war dance of the Sioux and the settlers learned that Sitting Bull had been
killed. During this time many of the settlers left their new homes and some
returned to the eastern states and others stopped in Bowdle and Ipswich.
The Marin family were among those who stayed on their land but were always
prepared to flee with their families and a few of their belongings should
it become necessary. Little did the settlers know then of how futile their
efforts to flee would be, had they been in the path of the hostile Sioux.

The Marins had eleven children, four of whom died in infancy; the living
children of the couple are: Myrtle A. Maxwell, born in October, 1883, and
now of Calgary, Alberta, Canada; Cloyd L. Marin, born in May, 1889, now of
Gladmar, Saskatchewan, Canada; Eva P. Nutter, born in May of 1885, and Edna
M. Phillips, born in July of 1886, who both reside at Mobridge, South
Dakota; Earl W. Marin, born in May, 1896, of Selby, who still resides upon
the claim land upon which his father filed homestead rights in March of
1883; and Ellery W., born November of 1898, and Dwight L., born in June of
1900, who both now reside at Puyallup, Washington. There are also living at
the present time twenty-five grandchildren and thirty-two
great-grandchildren of this couple, most of whom reside in the vicinity of
Selby and Mobridge.

        Upper, Dwight, Earl, Eva (Mrs. Nutter), Ellery, Edna (Mrs.
        Phillips), Mr. and Mrs. Modeste Marin, Myrtle (Mrs. Maxwell).

On October 6, 1906, Mr. and Mrs. Marin celebrated their silver wedding
anniversary when their family, friends and neighbors came to help them
enjoy the occasion. The Marin home was ever a hospitable one and was the
scene of many community gatherings for business and pleasure. During the
year 1927, the Marins left their farm home to the operation of their son,
Earl, and retired to Mobridge to spend their last years in comfort. After a
lingering illness, Modeste Marin "crossed the bar" on February 2, 1939, and
two years later, and on December 21, 1941, Mrs. Marin passed away at their
home in Mobridge.

Modeste Marin had had no schooling but did have a natural mathematical mind
and through his wit, foresight and labor accumulated a large estate of
approximately a hundred thousand dollars. He was one of the organizers of
the First National Bank of Selby and retained his interest therein until
the time of his death. His rare judgment and foresight in matters of
finance were an aid to the success of the venture.

During the period of development of Walworth county, real estate agents
often brought their prospective purchasers, as many as a dozen or fifteen
at a time, to the Marin farm, as an example of what could be done with the
fertile soil and climate of Walworth county. Mr. Marin encouraged these
visits as he was very interested in the development of the community and
the enhancement of values, with his usual foresight. Progress was ever his
goal and he owned original corporate stock in the Walworth County Telephone
company, the Walworth County Fair association and the Selby Equity Union
Exchange.

MR. JOHN FREDERICK WILLIAM KOCH

John Frederick William Koch, known as "William" or "Bill" Koch, was born on
the Island of Fehmarn, Province of Schleswig, Holstein, Germany, on May 8,
1888. He is the son of Frederick and Charlotte Koch. Here in Germany his
early boyhood was spent. Here also he received the first five years of his
schooling.

In 1898, when he was ten years old, William came to America with his
mother. His father had passed away in Germany. They settled in Bancroft,
Nebraska, where he attended an Indian school on the Omaha Indian
reservation. He also attended the country school near Jackson, Minnesota.

In 1906 he came to Walworth county, South Dakota, and has resided in and
around Evarts and Selby ever since. The first few summers in South Dakota
he worked on a ranch for Wm. Benoist on the Cheyenne Indian reservation.

He worked, studied, and familiarized himself with steam, gas, engineering,
and plumbing. He also broke prairie and threshed with steam and gas engines
throughout the country. He was employed for some time by Wm. Schwartz in
the hardware store in Selby. He also worked in the implement shop in Selby
for Otto Lincke, and operated the Selby Mill engine for awhile. In 1916 Wm.
Koch was appointed city marshal, superintendent of the water works, and
street commissioner by Mayor August Schmidt. He resigned this position the
following year to enlist in the Navy. He passed the examination as
L.M.M.N.A. (Landmans Machinist Mate Navy Aviation), but was rejected for
defective vision at Great Lakes Naval Training station, classified A-1 in
draft. He was placed in special service. Two calls to run the donkey
locomotives in the Spruce Division in the state of Washington were
canceled.

Later he returned to Selby. In 1920 he was reappointed as city marshal,
superintendent of the water works, and street commissioner by Mayor Eugene
Overholser. He served in this capacity for a total of twenty-six years. He
was deputy sheriff of Walworth county twenty-four years, and was a member
of the Selby fire department.

On June 28, 1923, he was united in marriage to Miss Frieda Lutz. daughter
of John Lutz Sr., and Rosina Lutz of near Java. Their married life was less
than three years, as his wife passed away May 21, 1926, at the age of
twenty-four years.

        MARSHAL WM. KOCH WITH ARLIS AND FRANCES MANKE

Wm. Koch played in the Selby concert band and directed the same for nine
years. He also played in the Yelduz Temple Shrine band of Aberdeen for
eighteen years, and in the Elks Band of Aberdeen. He belongs to the Masonic
and Eastern Star lodges of Selby, and was a member of the Woodman lodge
here. He is an honorary citizen of Father Flanagan's Boys Town. He was
baptized and confirmed in the Evangelical Lutheran Faith.

During his forty-four years spent in Walworth county, Mr. Koch has
encountered good times and bad along with all the other early residents of
this section.

Many and colorful are the stories he could relate, would space permit
regarding his experiences in everyday life, and while in the capacity of
law enforcement officer. However. in every phase of his work Mr. Koch showed
good judgment, enthusiasm, and interest. Whether it be music, enforcing the
law, or repairing water troubles, one felt when "Bill Koch" was called, the
best would be done.

Mr. Koch is at present residing in Selby, and still keeps himself busy with
various duties.

MR. AND MRS. THOMAS J. COFFEY

Thomas J. Coffey was born in Mumfordsville, Kentucky, during the Civil War.
His earliest recollections were of soldiers and carpetbaggers.

Most of his young manhood was spent in and about Dakota territory. He
freighted from Fort Pierre to Deadwood in the manner of those days, with
mule teams. He was in Bismarck, North Dakota, when it was the terminal of
the Northern Pacific railroad and at that time there were only two houses
there. He also freighted from Bismarck and boasted that he was one of the
best twenty mule team drivers in the country.

Later he drove a stagecoach from Billings, Montana, to Yellowstone National
Park driving "the finest looking four greys he ever saw". Among his
passengers were many notables, one of whom was General Ulysses S. Grant.

In 1892 he went to Alaska to prospect for gold, arriving there before the
Klondike strike. One of the high lights of his life in Alaska was traveling
600 miles by dogteam to Nome to have dental work done. He also told of
crossing the Bering Strait to Siberia by dogteam. After 22 years of
prospecting he made his "home stake" on a creek in Ruby district. This
creek bears his name since he was the discoverer of gold there. He sold out
to the Guggenheim company in 1914 and returned to the States. The
Guggenheim company is still operating on Coffey creek.

In 1922 he acquired the Hanrahan ranch, southwest of Selby, which is now
known as the Coffey ranch. He operated this ranch until his death on March
9, 1938.

Clara Marie Steffen was born in Stettin, Wisconsin, was confirmed in the
Lutheran church there and received her education in Stettin and Wausau,
Wisconsin. Her vocation prior to becoming a housewife was of a secretarial
nature in the business world. She was employed for several years in
Minneapolis and later in Boise, Idaho and San Francisco.

One of the most interesting events of her life was being chosen a delegate
from the State of Idaho to the first convention of the League of Women
Voters which was held in San Francisco in July, 1915, and there she
hobnobbed with many notables including Mrs. Nellie Tayloe Ross, Governor of
Wyoming. The guest speaker was William Jennings Bryan who was then
Secretary of State. The League of Women Voters is at present a national and
international organization. The first chapter was organized in 1913 in
Boise, Idaho. Miss Steffen was a charter member of this chapter and held
the office of treasurer. This was six years before Congress passed the
Nineteenth or Suffrage Amendment. Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and Idaho had
been equal-suffrage states for more than a quarter of a century. Washington
and Oregon adopted equal suffrage in 1912 so the convention in 1915 was
made up of delegates from only six states and Miss Steffen was among the
leaders of the great procession of women voters.

In 1918 she was united in marriage with Thomas J. Coffey and the family
lived in San Jose, California, until 1929 at which time they moved to South
Dakota to reside on the Coffey ranch. After Mr. Coffey's death in 1938 Mrs.
Coffey continued to operate the ranch and was there when the tide turned to
participate in an era of prosperity continuing until 1945 when she retired
and moved to Selby, renting out the land.

THEODORE BOHLE

Theodore Bohle was born in Odessa, Russia, October 30, 1893, of German
parents, Henry and Dorothy Bohle. He came to the United States from South
Russia with his parents in 1910. He was at that time sixteen years old.
They came directly to Eureka, South Dakota, arriving there July 2. Soon
after that Theodore hired out as a farm laborer to John Bickel who lived
five miles northeast of Herreid. His salary was twenty dollars a month
during harvest.

        MR. AND MRS. THEODORE BOHLE AND FAMILY
        Elsie (Mrs. Hill), Adeline (Mrs. Kramlich), Leah (Mrs.
        Battifarano), Calvin, Mr. and Mrs. Theodore Bohle, Albert.

In comparing the wages and prices of clothing of today with that of that
time as taken from a diary he kept, we find in 1911 he hired out to
Gottlieb Beck for $150 a year. In 1912 wages were better and he got $200
for nine months. Clothing prices were high compared to wages: work shoes
were about $2.98, overshoes $1.98, felt hats $2.50, and dress shirts about
$1.25.

In September, 1917, he was inducted into the army, being one of the first
nineteen men called from Campbell county. He spent nine months in Camp
Funsten, Kansas, before being sent overseas. He spent twelve months in
Europe, most of that time being in France and Belgium.

Mrs. Bohle is the former Lydia George. She was born in Lehr, North Dakota,
December 1, 1899.

In October, 1928, he bought 320 acres 3 miles north of Selby. This was
known as the June Franks farm and was then owned by Harry Juster. Since
that time he has bought adjoining land so his farm now totals 720 acres.
After he purchased the farm he moved his family here from Campbell county
and they have made this their home ever since.

Theodore was confirmed in the Lutheran church in Russia but in 1929 he
joined the Congregational church in Selby. He was a member of the board of
education of the Selby Independent Consolidated school district No. 2 for
ten years.

Mr. and Mrs. Bohle have a family of five children, three daughters and two
sons: Lea (Mrs. Joe Battifarana) of Turlock, California; Elsie (Mrs. G. D.
Hill) of Montevideo, Minnesota; Adeline (Mrs. Gordon Kramlich, Glenham),
formerly a nurse in the Lowe hospital in Mobridge, and Albert and Calvin at
home.

In talking about his experiences through the years Mr. Bohle says they had
to struggle hard sometimes to hold on to what they had, as during the
drought years of the '30's many times the going seemed impossible. But they
hung on and managed to come through. He considers 1942 the best crop year
he ever had. That was the year he managed to pay off the last of the debts
and he has been getting along well ever since. They have managed to educate
their children, own machinery to lighten their farm work, and are located
in the REA section and now have many of the conveniences of home which they
never dreamed would be theirs.

MR. DENSLAY L. CARMAN

Denslay L. Carman was born in Floyd county, Iowa, June 9, 1872. He came
with his parents and family to South Dakota in 1886, settling on the farm
on the county line, NW 1/4 of section 6-124-77, now owned by Mrs. Charles
R. Carman. When he became of age in 1893, he homesteaded on the SE 1/4 of
6-124-77. In the year 1905 he was united in marriage with Jessie E.
Hoffman, who was also a member of one of the pioneer families of the
county, and they began housekeeping in a sod house which he had built on
the claim. In 1906, a small frame house was built, where they lived and
raised their three children, Raymond, Edwin and Lucille. In 1929 a new
modern house was built. The original homestead was gradually added to until
it now consists of 720 acres. Mr. Carman passed away suddenly on August 24,
1934. In 1928, the oldest son, Raymond, was married to Irene Welton of
Selby, and they occupied the small house from 1929 until 1937 when they
moved to another place and Edwin took over the operation of the home farm.
Raymond later bought the Hans Engebretson farm and still later purchased
land in Section 5, Township 122, Range 76, where he has built up a modern
farmstead. The house was sold off the Engebretson place and moved to Selby
and is now the property of L. James Moell and occupied by the Milo Swift
family. The other buildings were either torn down or moved to the new place
and in 1945, one of the fine new modern farm homes of the county was built.

        MR. AND MRS. DENSLAY L. CARMAN AND FAMILY
        Standing, left to right, Raymond, Selby, S. D.; Edwin, Glenham, S.
        D.; Mrs. Carman. Seated, Mr. Carman, Lucille Stowell, Mobridge.

Lucille has taught rural and city schools in Walworth and Campbell counties
and is now married to Harry Stowell and resides in Mobridge.

Edwin and his mother operate the home farm.

Denslay L. Carman was a skillful farmer and stock raiser. In the days
before the drought it was well worth a trip out there to see his crops, his
garden and the wonderful fruit and his trees. His sons, too, are high class
farmers, following in the footsteps of their pioneer parents and
grandparents in doing their full part in continuing the development of the
land on which the family long ago pitched its tent and which all came to
love so well. The two Carman farms are among the many very good ones in
Walworth county.

MR. AND MRS. ALBERT MANKE

Albert Manke was born December 23, 1880, near Atlantic, Iowa, where he
received his education in a rural school. He was baptized in the Lutheran
church in Atlantic where he also attended German school and was confirmed.
He grew to young manhood there and was one of a family of twelve children.

On December 17, 1902, he was married to Dora J. Kruse at Walnut, Iowa. She
was born in Germany January 6, 1884, and was baptized there in the Lutheran
church. In March, 1887, at the age of three years she came with her
parents, one brother and one sister to the United States settling at
Walnut, Iowa. Here she attended grade school and high school, German
school, sewing school, Methodist Sunday school and church.

        MR. AND MRS. ALBERT MANKE

After Mr. and Mrs. Manke were married they farmed near Walnut, Iowa, for
three years. Land and rent were getting too high so they decided to come to
South Dakota where land was cheaper.

In March, 1906, they came to Selby having rented the old Kingman place near
Bangor the summer before. They ate their first dinner at Mrs. Maxwell's
hotel. They came with their two children, Arnold and Nellie, in company
with a neighbor family, Mr. and Mrs. Karl Kindt and three children and his
brother, Otto Kindt. The Karl Kindt family only stayed a few years and then
moved to Winner, South Dakota. Otto Kindt is still here, residing in the
Glenham vicinity.

Soon after the Mankes came in 1906 they purchased their first quarter
section of land from Mrs. Nellie Birkholt and built a small house and a few
outbuildings that summer. In the spring of 1907 they moved to their own
home where they resided and farmed until the fall of 1945 when they retired
and moved to Selby. From time to time they added to their farm until they
had acquired 640 acres.

They raised a large family of thirteen children, two of whom passed away in
infancy. Eleven are married and live in homes of their own. One resides in
Washington, six in California, three in Selby and one on the home farm.
They have eighteen grandchildren.

Mr. and Mrs. Manke had bad luck along with the good but are not sorry that
they came to South Dakota.

Mrs. Manke is a member of the American Legion auxiliary and of the W.S.C.S.
of the Methodist church.

MR. GEORGE J. SCHELLENGER

George J. Schellenger, pioneer educator of South Dakota, and in particular
of Walworth county and Selby community, was born on a farm near Mineral
Point, Wisconsin, on November 19, 1847. His early education was obtained in
the rural schools of his home community, supplemented by intensive self
instruction while not in school. At an early age, he secured employment as a
teacher in rural Wisconsin and saved enough money to continue his higher
education at the Platteville Normal school, Platteville, Wisconsin, from
which he graduated in 1872. Upon his graduation, he became principal of one
of the ward schools at Platteville and held this position for four years
and then held a similar position at LaCrosse, Wisconsin, for seven years.

Schellenger had a strong pioneer spirit in him and the call of the west
lured him to Dakota territory, which was then a wilderness awaiting
broad-minded, energetic and farsighted men of the type exemplified by Mr.
Schellenger. He and his family, then consisting of his wife the former Mary
E. Henderson, whom he married in 1874, and two sons and a daughter, arrived
at LeBeau, Walworth county, Dakota territory, in the spring of 1883. At
that early period of the county's existence, there was but little call for
teachers, so Schellenger established himself in a general store at LeBeau.
In the November 1884 election, the new town of Bangor was voted in as the
future county seat, and soon afterwards, Mr. Schellenger and his family
moved to Bangor where he operated a hotel and restaurant for several years.
In 1886, he was elected county superintendent of schools and assumed office
on January 1, 1887. He held this office for the next four years. As a
county superintendent he was prominent in educational councils of the state
and was known as a man of eminently good judgment and clear, hard-headed
common sense. He placed great emphasis upon the practical phases of
education and felt that if in a rural community, the pupil and student
mastered the essentials of reading, writing, spelling and arithmetic, he
could develop himself from these basic essentials. Much credit is due Prof.
Schellenger in setting up the present system of rural schools in Walworth
county.

        MR. AND MRS. GEORGE J. SCHELLENGER

From 1891 to 1899 Schellenger taught in schools at Bowdle and Carthage,
South Dakota, and in 1899, he was appointed deputy superintendent of public
instruction of the State of South Dakota by State Superintendent Collins.
He held this position for four years. He carried into the State Department
of Education the same earnest, conscientious devotion that characterized
his work as a county superintendent and teacher and during that period did
much to shape the educational policies of the state. After his term as
deputy superintendent, he returned to Walworth county and taught in the
city schools at Mobridge and then Selby, until 1907, when he was again
elected superintendent of schools of Walworth county. He was re elected and
held office until January, 1911. During these last four years, his health
began to fail but he again returned to teaching until the fall of 1913,
when he was appointed superintendent of schools of Walworth county to fill
a vacancy in that office. Shortly after this appointment, he died suddenly
on October 10, 1913. Prof. Schellenger is buried in the Selby Union
cemetery.

Mrs. Schellenger died in 1930, and the only daughter, Lulu (Mrs. Benjamin
Hoffman), died in 1939. The surviving members of the family are a son, Guy
Schellenger and a grandson, Bernard Schellenger, both of whom live at
Eugene, Oregon; a grandson, Ben Schellenger, who lives at Riverdale, North
Dakota; and two grandsons, Dr. Harold Hoffman at LaMoure, North Dakota, and
Rev. Ralph Hoffman of Watertown, Wisconsin, children of Benjamin Hoffman
and Lulu Schellenger Hoffman.

MR. LADISLAUS BERTHA SR.

Ladislaus Bertha was born near Budapest, Hungary, on June 15, 1846, to
Theresa nee Smith Bertha and Steve Bertha. Ladislaus' boyhood and youth was
spent in Hungary. He received a good Hungarian education. At the age of
twenty four, he was married to Theresa Zarka. They remained in their native
land until 1884 when they decided to journey to America with a friend and
his family, John Ritter.

Mr. and Mrs. Bertha packed their belongings into a homemade trunk and with
three sons, Ladislaus, 12 years old; Steven, 9, and Anton, a few years
younger, started for the new land, locating at Hazelton, Pennsylvania. Here
Mr. Bertha found work in a hard coal mine, at which he worked for about two
months. Then, deciding to go on farther west, they took the train to
Watertown, South Dakota. Here the father worked on a farm for a year, 1884
1885. Hearing of people filing on land still farther west Mr. Bertha and
John Ritter and son thought they would prove up land for themselves.
Leaving his family at Watertown the three came farther northwest and each
filed on adjoining land in what is now called Spring Valley, Mr. Bertha
homesteading five miles south and five miles east of Selby.

Mr. Bertha, then returning to Watertown, worked in a brick yard until his
land dealings were completely finished, this taking approximately six
months plus costs of 200 dollars. In March, 1886, he moved his family and
worldly possessions including one cow and small calf, by train from
Watertown to the end of the railroad line, Ipswich. Here he hired a team
and buggy to carry his family to their new home. Mr. Bertha and Ladislaus
Jr., remained behind to drive the cow and calf on foot to his homestead,
this taking three days as they found it necessary to carry the small calf
much of the way.

The Berthas' lived in a sod house for eight years, using the homemade trunk
they had brought from Hungary as a table as well as storage space. It was
here the homemade Christmas gifts were hid unbeknown to the children. Coal
was a very hard to get item in this part of the country, so their home was
heated by a strawburner. Two more children were born to this family Mrs.
Andrew Raba, (with whom Ladislaus Jr., 77 is making his home) in Spring
Valley township near Selby, and Mrs. John Raba, living in Selby.

Though in early days means of travel were slow, this Catholic family never
neglected their faith, loving religion. On Sunday morning Mr. Bertha was up
at 3 a.m., to get his chores finished in time to walk to Hoven, twenty
miles away, to attend church. Every two weeks he would drive his oxen to
Hoven so as to take his family to church.

When the time came to build the Selby Catholic church Mr. Bertha and sons
were among the most eager helpers. Upon its completion Mr. Bertha bought
and donated two altars which are still being used in the church.

Mr. and Mrs. Ladislaus Bertha were very generous people, always thinking of
others. They kept a very large garden, much larger than they needed for
their family, but they were thinking of the new settlers and wished to help
them as much as possible upon their arrival. There was never a stranger
turned away from their door,--they welcomed all and gave them food and
shelter. One fall he worked on a threshing machine near Hoven, walking
eighteen miles to work, working all day for 75c and returning to his family
each night.

Mr. Bertha and John Ritter Sr., worked together in their spare time digging
wells by hand.

Many of the trees in Spring Valley district were and are a part of Mr.
Bertha's work.

Ladislaus Bertha Sr., died in 1919 and is buried in the Selby cemetery.

MR. AND MRS. JOHN A. CHILLQUIST

Mr. and Mrs. John A. Chillquist were both born in Holland, Sweden, he in
1862 and she in 1874. They came to America when they were around 20 years
old.

After he had finished his schooling in Sweden he went to Denmark and
studied the dairying and butter business. After he had been in America for
a few years he married and started a creamery of his own in Illinois. Later
in 1903, his creamery caught fire and burned to the ground. It was then he
decided to come west as he thought there were greater opportunities for a
man with a family, out here in South Dakota, as there was still some land
to be homesteaded at that time. He came and bought the land from Mr.
Ingalls and then he went back to Illinois to get the family. They left
their home in Newark, Illinois, the first part of March 1905. They loaded
two emigrant cars with four horses, a cow, the furniture and what machinery
he could take and started out for Selby.

Clark Brown and Severt Austin came with the emigrant cars. The family came
by train,--Mr. and Mrs. Chillquist and six children, Anna, (Mrs. Clark
Brown) of Selby; Judith, (Mrs. George Cash) of Little Falls, Minnesota; and
four boys, Ray, Carl, Oscar, and Joe; also Mrs. Chillquist's father and
mother, Mr. and Mrs. J. B. Johanson. She (Mrs. Johanson) used to spin yarn
and knit socks and sweaters in the winter time.

They landed in Selby about a week before the cars came, and all stayed at
the Buchanan hotel. When the cars came they were all ready to go out to the
farm, about 6 miles west of Selby, which is now owned by Ted Tisdall. Mr.
Chillquist needed his horses and wagon to haul out the furniture, so he got
George Clark, who was livery man in Selby at that time, to take the family
out with his team and buggy.

The children were all excited about their new home. When they got there
they found it rather a bare looking place, no trees at all like they had
been used to and very poor buildings. The barns were just a shelter with a
straw roof to keep the snow and wind off the cattle and horses. The house
was a frame structure and very small, so the mother was rather worried as
to how they would all get along; but after they got their furniture moved in
and got the house cleaned up, papered and painted, it began to seem more
like home every day.

The older children had to start school which was a mile away. It was the
old Tisdall school, which used to stand on the north side of the trail. The
children thought it was an awful school as they had been accustomed to a
big school in Illinois and lots of children. But they finally got used to
it.

Then, the father started to look around for more cattle and farm machinery
and horses. He bought his first 20 or 30 head of cows from Bill Chesky in
the spring of 1905. As the spring went on, he seeded the grain fields and
the crops were very good that first year. He thought that everything was
going to work out satisfactorily.

He thought the farmers should have a creamery in Selby, so he started up a
creamery east of the Equity elevator and Clark Brown operated the farm for
him.

Everything seemed to improve as time went on. They built better roads and
put up telephone lines. They put up the lines along the trail and the
workers boarded with Mrs. Gunill Olson. They used to haul the dinner out to
the men as it took too much of their time to come home with the horses. The
post holes were all dug by hand. A person can surely see a lot of
improvement when you think back.

In 1905 nearly all the neighbors lived in sod houses. These homes were very
comfortable and warm to live in, but, as the crops got better everybody
built new houses, and barns for the cattle. In those days there were no
tractors, trucks, or automobiles. The writer can still remember when Dr.
George got his first car, a white Buick. The kids could see it coming a
long way off and would try to get to the road in time to see it go by.
Everyone thought it was so funny that it would go without horses.

For entertainment they used to have programs in the school houses. They had
what was called a Literary Society. They would chose up a debating team and
have a program about every two weeks, and had lots of fun getting together.
They also played all kinds of games. On Sunday they would have church in
the school houses. There usually was a full house. The ladies had their aid
society and went to the different homes and had the meetings. Then, as time
went on and they could afford it, they built a church which is the Bethany
church to day. The Norway church was built before that. Rev. Ole Stensby
and Rev. Kirkeback were the ministers at the time. People seemed to get
together more those days with the horse and buggy than they do today.

It was bad in those days if a prairie fire got started. It was almost
impossible to get it stopped if there was any wind at all. The writer can
remember,--it must have been along in 1905 or 1906,--a fire had started
down towards Glenham and it burned out the whole Blue Blanket lake. The
folks were all up there with their horses and plows trying to plow fire
guards to stop it. But with the high wind it was hard to stop. It burned
all the hay stacks and grain that was in its path.

In the fall the grain was cut with headers or binders if the grain was tall
enough. It is a big change when you see the combines of today going over
the fields and you are through harvesting and threshing in such a short
time. Then in the fall when the stacks of grain were ready to thresh, they
