would get the old steam threshing machine out. Oliver Johnson and his sons
used to do the threshing in this neighborhood. They would get up at 4 or 5
o'clock in the morning to get the steam up so they could run. They would
burn straw and some coal. The farmers would all exchange work at threshing
time. It was a busy time for the women, too, to cook for all the men. The
grain was hauled to the granaries and to Selby with horses and wagons. Most
people would haul in a load of wheat and exchange it for flour, as when
winter set in it was often hard to get to town, so they usually put in a
supply.

Mrs. Clark Brown relates the following experience: "One day the children
were all in school and a blizzard came up. It was a very nice bright
morning but there was a cloud hanging in the northwest but no one realized
what that meant. People that had lived here longer than we had knew what
was coming, so they came and got their children. Along about 9:30 the wind
and snow came. In a short time we couldn't see our hand in front of us. Dad
tried to come and get us but the horses turned in a circle so they came
back to where he started from. Dad started out again and the same thing
happened so he thought he had better follow the fence and get home before
he would freeze to death. The children had to stay in the school house all
night. It was rather a long cold night and we didn't have any lamps or food.
Our teacher, George Elling, read to us by the light of the fire from the
stove. Then we lay down on our desks and rested some. Early the next
morning the storm let up and father came to see if we were still in the
school house. They had been worried for fear that we had started out."

One can see a lot of improvement here in Walworth county. In 1905 the roads
were only small trails wherever it was easiest to get through. Now the
roads are all mostly graveled or black topped.

Today, nearly all the farmers have nice modern homes, electric lights, and
good heating equipment, while in 1905 they had to haul wood from the river
and had little coal to burn to keep warm.

Mrs. Chillquist is still living with her daughter in Little Falls,
Minnesota. Mr. Chillquist passed away April 26, 1933. The rest of the
children are scattered. Four children: Jenny, Ray, Joel, Elmer, are in
Milwaukee, Wisconsin; Oscar is at Seaside, Oregon; Emily at Plano,
Illinois; Augusta, Lenard, Judith and Iver are in Little Falls, Minnesota,
and Anna, (Mrs. Clark Brown) lives in Selby.

MR. AND MRS. GEORGE AND CLARA KIRK AND
ALPHONSO AND MARY BUCHANAN AND FAMILY

Alphonso Buchanan, better known as Fonse, came to Walworth county from
Sparta, Wisconsin in October, 1887, and filed on a homestead, the southwest
quarter of Section 3-122-77. He sold his claim and went into the hotel
business in Bangor with Bert and Belle Niles.

Later his mother, Clara Kirk and his step-father, George Kirk, came from
Sparta and purchased the Niles share of the hotel, then known as the Bangor
House.

In 1892 Fonse Buchanan married Mary Arbach, oldest child of John and
Katharine Arbach of the Hoven vicinity, who had pioneered in 1885 from
Austin, Minnesota. Three children were born to the Buchanans', all in
Bangor--Leo, Clara, and Delphia.

        MR. AND MRS. A. BUCHANAN (standing)
        Clara (deceased), Delphia Johnson, Selby, S. D.; Leo E., Selby.

When it was decided that the railroad was to go through Selby, four miles
north of Bangor, this family decided they would move their hotel there.
Lots were purchased in 1900 and there was a race to see whether the Bangor
House or the Auburn Hotel would reach Selby first. Due to breakdowns and
weather conditions, the Bangor House did not arrive in Selby until December
20, 1900, after being on the road four months and four days. The Auburn
Hotel was the first building to make it to Selby. The Bangor House did a
thriving business all through the moving, regardless of all handicaps.

George and Clara Kirk continued in this business until their deaths. Mrs.
Kirk died in Selby in February 1901. George Kirk was a colorful figure in
Selby for many years, standing in front of the hotel--a tall, slender,
curly white haired man--ringing a big dinner bell at meal times. He died in
1916.

The Buchanans' continued to operate the hotel, named the Selby Hotel, until
1926, and just two weeks after they rented the hotel, Mr. Buchanan died.

Mrs. Buchanan from then on either rented or operated the hotel herself
until 1937, when she married Arnold L. Artz of Aberdeen, South Dakota, and
moved to that city, where she still makes her home.

During the early days in Selby, Mr. Buchanan was an active member of the
Woodman Lodge and Mrs. Buchanan of the Yeoman lodge. Mrs. Buchanan is a
charter member of the American Legion Auxiliary of Legion Post No. 100 of
Selby and was president of that organization for two years. Both Mr. and
Mrs. Buchanan were members of the Catholic church. Mrs. Mary Buchanan Artz
was recorded as the second oldest settler in Walworth county present at the
Old Settlers' Picnic in Selby in 1947.

Regarding the children of the Buchanan family, Leo, the oldest child, after
completing high school in Selby took pharmaceutical training at the College
of Pharmacy, State University of Iowa. In 1917 he married Elsie A. Schmidt,
daughter of Mr. and Mrs. August Schmidt of Selby. The following year, he
entered the army during World War I, serving until June, 1919, spending
almost the complete time overseas. On his return from France he purchased
the W. E. Prann drug store in Selby, as he had received most of his
apprenticeship in this business place. He still owns and operates this same
store and his business is one of the two oldest established business places
still under the same management in Selby today.

During Leo E. Buchanan's years in business in Selby, he has served his
community in various ways. He served two terms on the Board of Education
and the City Council and acted as president of the Commercial club one
year. When the American Legion was organized in Selby in the fall of 1919.
he was elected their first commander and is still an active member. He has
also served as Legion Finance Officer of the local post for many years.

While still in high school, he joined the first Volunteer Fire department
of Selby and from 1938 to the present date has acted as fire chief of that
organization.

Mr. Buchanan has always been a booster of the local baseball team, acting
as business manager for several years, was president of the Yellowstone
Trail Baseball league for four years and in January, 1948 was appointed a
member of the State Amateur Baseball Association and still acts in that
capacity.

Clara, oldest daughter of the Buchanans', died in 1912 at the age of
sixteen years during her sophomore year in the Selby high school.

Delphia Buchanan. youngest daughter, completed high school in Selby. took a
business course in Aberdeen, after which she began a term of many years of
work at the county court house in Selby. In 1925 she married Severin M.
Johnson and they still reside in Selby.

Leo and Elsie Buchanan have three children. Leo James. Dean and Maurine.
James followed the profession of his father, graduating from the South
Dakota State college in 1940 and now operates his own drug store in
Hartington, Nebraska.

Dean Buchanan will gradate in 1950 with a degree in education from Northern
State Teachers College of Aberdeen. Dean served three years in the Navy
during World War II, spending two years in the southwest Pacific with the
Seabees.

Maurine, the daughter, will graduate in 1950 from Central high school in
Aberdeen, South Dakota.

The Buchanan family have been of the sturdy pioneer stock that weathered
the poor times along with the good and have had enough faith in this part
of the country to stay, and believe it is one of the best places on earth to
live.

MR. JOSEPH TREANOR

Joseph Treanor came to South Dakota about 1880 and to Selby the year of its
beginning, 20 years later. He traveled by covered wagon from Dubuque, Iowa,
to Dead wood, Dakota territory. His brother, James, who left Dubuque with
him, was killed by the Indians on that trip. Soon after Mr. Treanor and
family became settled in Deadwood his wife died, leaving him with two young
sons, Hugh and Eugene. Late in life Hugh married and lived in Winfield,
Kansas, where he died a few years ago. Eugene never married; he is now
living in northern Minnesota.

While living at Deadwood, Joseph Treanor drove a stagecoach from the Black
Hills to Bismarck, North Dakota, for the Wells-Fargo line. On these trips
he decided to locate along the Missouri river, at the mouth of Spring creek
in Campbell county. In 1883 the government surveyed and established the
town-site of LaGrace at this point. He and his two sons moved there where
Mr. Treanor operated the government telegraph line that ran from LaGrace to
Bismarck.

Steamboats on the Missouri river were used extensively for traveling and
transportation during those days. That was how Philena Tingley. who later
married Joseph Treanor, came to LaGrace from her home in Pennsylvania,--by
train to Pierre and then up the river on the steamboat. Joseph and Philena
Treanor conducted an Indian trading post in LaGrace for several years. They
had one daughter, Louise.

Mr. Treanor envisioned the possibility of the railroad being extended from
Eureka to Mound City, South Dakota, so he and his family moved to Mound
City where they established a mercantile business. Later when it became
evident that the railroad was going to Selby he purchased a lot on main
street in Selby at the sale of lots conducted in Bangor by the Milwaukee
Land company. Immediately, he started the construction of a building on
that lot, on the corner opposite west of the Auburn hotel.

During the summer of 1900 Mr. Treanor and his family moved to Selby. They
operated a drug store and lived in the new building. He lived only a few
months after this, passing away on May 2 190l. His wife and daughter and
son. Eugene continued to live in the building, where Mrs. Treanor and
Louise conducted a millinery store.

Louise was married to Henry P. Gutz in 1904. Mrs. Treanor closed the store
and lived with them until she died in April 1914. Both Mr. and Mrs. Treanor
are buried in the Selby cemetery.

MR. AND MRS. HENRY P. GUTZ

One of the most prominent families, and who added much to the cultural and
civic development and progress of the Selby community are Henry P. Gutz and
his wife, Louise J. Gutz. Both Mr. and Mrs. Gutz were early pioneers of
Selby, Mr. Gutz having arrived in 1901 from Sioux City, Iowa, and Mrs. Gutz
having been born at LaGrace in Campbell county.

Henry P. Gutz was born on a farm near Pomeroy, Iowa, where he received his
early education and later completed a business course at Valparaiso
university in Indiana. He was first employed by a bank in Sioux City and
came to Selby to work as a bookkeeper in the Walworth County State bank. In
1906, he organized the Farmers State bank and served as its president until
1919 when it was converted to The First National bank of Selby. He was an
active officer of that bank for 35 years and remained a principal
stockholder until 1946. He was a member of the city council for 20 years,
being its chairman during most of those years. While he served as alderman,
the city's water and sewer system was first constructed and he did much to
promote this project and to the end that Selby was the first community in
the county to have such a system. The first electricity was installed in
Selby during the time that Mr. Gutz was chairman of the board of aldermen.
He also gave much assistance and aid to the board of education of the Selby
schools during the period of the consolidation of the district and the
construction of new buildings. He also served 10 years as a member of the
board of county commissioners and as chairman of said board during most of
that time.

        MR. AND MRS. HENRY P. GUTZ

Henry Gutz was instrumental in the organization of many enterprises in the
interest of Selby's progress. He was a member of the Selby Development
company with the result that the Selby Opera House was built and the people
of the community were furnished with a common meeting place large enough to
accommodate everyone. To that company credit can also be given for the
construction of some of the other buildings still standing and being used
in Selby. The primary organization of the Lake Hiddenwood association was
under the leadership of Mr. Gutz and, in fact, he and A. C. Dobson were the
ones who conceived the idea of constructing an artificial lake on
Hiddenwood creek and worked hard for the development of the grounds
surrounding the lake and the building of the dam and spent many strenuous
hours with others in trying to save the dam when spring thaws and rains
threatened to wash it away. Mr. Gutz was appointed a member of the South
Dakota Cement Commission by Governor Gunderson in 1925 and he served on
that Commission until 1936.

Louise J. Gutz is a native of South Dakota and her father, Joseph Treanor
purchased a lot in Selby at the first sale of lots held in Bangor by the
Milwaukee Land company. He built a mercantile building on that lot and
moved his family to Selby late in the year 1900. In Tune of 1904 Mr. and
Mrs. Gutz were married in the Methodist church of Selby. They raised a
family of eight children: Max, Raymond, Carroll, Josephine, Eileen,
Kathleen, John and Marilyn, all of whom, except Marilyn, have families of
their own and there are 19 grandchildren.

Louise Gutz will always be remembered for her beautiful soprano voice.
Every public program included her as a soloist and she freely gave her
talent for weddings, funerals and similar affairs and in the Episcopal
church choir of the early days of Selby and later in the Methodist church
choir. Never to be forgotten are the musical plays produced and performed
by the people of Selby under the auspices of the Selby Woman's club during
the 1920's, and in which plays Mrs. Gutz carried the leading feminine
singing role. The plays were entitled "The Wishing Well," "Belle of
Barcellona," "A Night in Venice, or Pickles" and "Don Alonzo's Treasure"
and all were musical plays. Mrs. Gutz was a charter member and the first
president of the Selby Womans club. She was worthy matron of Hope chapter
of the Order of Eastern Star in 1932 and during all of the years she lived
in Selby, she was active in church and community affairs and gave
diligently of her time and efforts in the work of the Methodist ladies' aid
society.

The home in which this prominent family spent the greater number of their
years in Selby was a landmark of the town. It was a large house with a yard
and garden comprising one-half of a city block. Mr. and Mrs. Gutz and their
children strived hard to make their home a place of beauty and comfort. It
was a severe loss to the family and community when, on a very cold, wintry
day in 1932, while a strong gale was blowing from the northwest, the house
and practically all of its contents were destroyed by fire. The townfolk
tried valiantly to save this home but to no avail as they could not combat
the wind and freezing temperature. In a recent letter to the editor, Mr.
and Mrs. Gutz wrote, "We shall always be grateful to our many friends who
so kindly helped us through that misfortune."

In the year 1934, Mr. and Mrs. Gutz moved to Rapid City, South Dakota, and
two years later they moved to Casper, Wyoming, where they reside at the
present time. Only one member of the family, Max Gutz, together with his
family, now resides at Selby.

MR. AND MRS. WM. RUSSELL

William Russell, son of A. Russell and Mary F. Simms Russell, was born
February 15, 1897, in Nebraska City, Nebraska. William was 11 years old
when his father died. He moved with the rest of the family to his
grandfather's home in Iowa. In 1912 they moved to Osakis, Minnesota, a five
hundred mile trip made with wagons, which took a month. After two years in
Osakis, his grandfather died and it was necessary for William to leave
school to help support his mother.

After spending a season working in North Dakota, he came to Selby and was
employed by Fred Koppin, for War I. In 1921, Bill started farming for
himself.

In 1922, he married Odessa Sunderland, a daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Lawrence
Sunderland. After completing her education, she taught ten terms of school
in Pennington and Walworth counties. Along with teaching public school,
Odessa was Sunday School superintendent and teacher at LeBeau and the Hay
School. She is a past president of the Legion Auxiliary and Jolly Club.

For 22 years, Mr. and Mrs. Russell rented from the Overholser Bros., and in
1944 they bought their present home.

Mr. and Mrs. Russell have six living children:

Helen, (Mrs. Harold Wertz), now living in Los Angeles, California, attended
the Hay school and Selby High school. She was employed as a stenographer
with the four years and then spent a year in the service of World Bell
Telephone company in Aberdeen, South Dakota, before her marriage to Mr.
Wertz.

        WM. RUSSELL FAMILY
        Left to right, standing, Billy West, Leola, Everett, Juanita.
        Sitting, Mrs. Russell, Viola May, Wm. Russell, Helen (not shown).

Everett attended the Hay school and is now helping his father manage the
farm. He has always been active in 4-H club work and has won several awards
on different projects. He is the leader of the Rough Rangers club at
present.

Leola (Mrs. Ervin Hettich) attended Hay school and Selby High school and
completed two terms at NSTC in Aberdeen. She was active in 4-H club work
and received many honors, among them first place in the Home Life judging
at the State Fair. She taught one term of school and now lives in Pierre,
South Dakota, working for the Campbell Insurance company.

Juanita will graduate from Selby High school in 1950. She is active in
community affairs and 4-H club work. She placed first in Home Life judging
and went to the State Fair in Huron.

Billy West is a Junior in Selby High school and is president of the Rough
Rangers 4 H club.

Viola Mary is in the sixth grade at the Hay school and has been a member of
the Happy Hustlers club for two years.

Two sons, Raymond and Robert, have passed away.

MR. SILVESTER S. STUDEBAKER

Silvester S. Studebaker, brother of Mrs. Edward C. Hoffman, and early
pioneer of Selby and Bangor, was born near South Whitley, Indiana, on
August 23, 1863. He was educated in the rural and normal schools of his
native state, and spent the early years of his life teaching and farming
near South Whitley. In 1896, he made a trip to Bangor vicinity and was
favorably impressed with the country, so in the spring of 1897, he and his
wife and family of two children arrived at Bangor and promptly purchased a
half section of land about three miles southwest of Bangor. Mr. Studebaker,
in addition to extensive livestock and grain farming, supplemented his
earnings with work as a carpenter, at which he was very adept, and also by
teaching in the Bangor schools. Many of the early buildings at Bangor and
later at Selby were built by Mr. Studebaker, including the Taylor, Foster,
Cheskey and Elfrink homes. With the help of Art Kingman, he also built the
first sidewalk from the depot to the Burr store, now the site of the Berens
hotel at Selby.

In 1902, Studebaker sold his South Dakota holdings and returned to Indiana,
where he farmed until 1910. In that year, he purchased a section of land
near Broadview, Montana, which was then being colonized by the real estate
firm of Kingman Brothers of Selby (Art and E. B.), and moved to this farm
where he remained until 1930, being engaged in extensive raising and
breeding of sheep, horses and cattle. The farm was rented in 1930 and the
family moved to Billings, Montana, where Mr. and Mrs. Studebaker now
reside. Their two daughters also reside at Billings and their son is a
carpenter at Dishman, Washington. The Studebakers are spending a
comfortable old age at Billings and each year enjoy taking trips to other
sections of the United States.

THE LENNAN STORY
        There chanced to be, in years gone by the event of two
        births; a man child and a woman child were born and
        grew into maturity. In time the twain met, they married,
        and began life together in Bowdle, Edmunds county
        South Dakota. These are they of whom I write. Names:
        Charles Edwin Lennan--Hortense Bailey Kennedy.

The Lennans were of Scotch-Irish ancestry. Charles Lennan was a native of
the State of Maine. He was a delicate child and the beginnings of his
education were with private tutors. He later developed into a strong and
active man.

His father, Ansel Lennan, had a flare for politics, and, as a rock-ribbed
democrat, active in the party which was long in power, was privileged with
appointive positions, among others being that of Collector of the Port of
Bangor--retaining it through three presidential administrations. During the
last term son, Charles, was favored for West Point. However, the next
national election brought in the republican regime and the lad lost out.
And yet, Charles approached the arena of politics in the G.O.P. manner. Be
it said, the decision held, even though it was a sorrow to the democratic
parent that his only son should be thus minded.

Instead of a political trend Charles' inclinations were for business.
Living all his lifetime as he did along the ocean front and the Penobscot
river among sea faring men, ocean craft, lumbering, fishing, and allied
industries, he became familiar with ocean shipping and opened a ship
brokers office. This was a strenuous undertaking. His youthful persistency
was a pleasantry with his friends, one of whom said to me long afterwards,
"Charlie was just a kid, his office sign had to be: C. E. Lennan and
Father". Charles' correction was: "It was A. Lennan and Son".

Young and venturesome, the west appealed to him, that realm beyond the
Adirondacks so mysterious to New Englanders of that day. Entering upon the
way he decided on going to Texas where a favorite uncle was connected with
the Southern Pacific railway then building west. He liked Texas more than a
little and took employment with the company to have charge of a commissary
and supply depot where also he was made paymaster for a division under
construction.

Matters needing attention took him to Chicago, although with the thought of
early return to Texas. At Chicago a strong immigration movement was on for
taking up land in the Dakotas. Footloose as he was, and meaning no more
than a quick glance for adventure's sake, then on to Texas, he stepped
aboard the north bound train and was on his way to unplanned history.
Stranger to all of it he learned, by listening that the fun was to get to
the end of the rails, and the Milwaukee's "Tracks End" was Bowdle. Reasons
for going there were influenced by an extension building southwest heading
for a Missouri river crossing to continue farther west. Seeming such a sure
thing, people were taking hold around there. A town, Scranton, was a
settled fact. Minnesota promoters had a rival town, LeBeau, three miles
north. Claims were filed hither and yon, homesteads, pre-emptions, tree
claims, but with scant heed to details. The fever spread even to the
down-easter who was strange in those parts. His manner of speech was
different, some of his words lacked the "R", as in horse, he said it
"hoss". He added to the excitement by getting a white "hoss" and sallying
forth to learn the lay of the land. Coming in from out there he made a few
entries in a notebook saying nothing. He was ever a silent man and nothing
queer about this, but it was noticed and soon an alarm was sounded that he
was a government man sent to investigate land entries. Like Waterloo "there
was mounting in hot haste" and claims had their backs stroked as never
before. That was the complexion of affairs when the bubble burst, the road
was at a halt. As told by Judge Burns of Bangor, county seat of Walworth
county, the president of the Milwaukee road died, and some of the bonds
were owned in England, thus changing its financial policy and delaying
further advancement.

Those claims? That government man? Many times I have been told the story by
the older settlers of "Lennan and his white hoss"--that was as a legend
that lived in laughter from early days through times and times. Sometimes
the guilty flee when no man pursues!

The backwash of this flood of events made slight impress in the general
scheme of things. A determined pioneering spirit was abroad in the land
that offset passing frenzies such as the railroad extension proved to be.

However, there was consternation of a kind that put wheels under buildings,
principally those that housed business projects and shelters that served as
homes. Others of less substantial ideas were also on the hoof, and prairie
transportation was soon active to speed the trek to Bowdle where ventures
begun might continue.

This sketch of early boom days is given to place the time and the
circumstance that changed the current of my husband's career. The Texas
vastness, both of area and endeavor, impressed him vividly. But he was,
primarily, a northern man,--the state of Maine is up north and its very air
was in his blood stream. So it is that "as one door closes another opens".
He warmly identified himself with South Dakota--here was vastness equal to
any. He would say, "Glad to get back to God's country" whenever he had been
away.

        MR. CHARLES E. LENNAN

Meanwhile Bowdle was shifting westward, somewhat in the manner of going out
front with the welcome mat to greet those coming from Walworth county and
beyond for to buy and to sell. The county line was an obscure fantasy in
everyday thinking because of over-lapping interests at the rail's end.
Among business buildings to move was one for the post office, and that
which was vacated became the Lennan land office wherein he devoted himself
to land law. The era of title contests had begun that eventuated in a
forward reaching stability. Happily now, was Bowdle settled to hold people
within its borders and was an attractive center for congenial frontier
living.

Up to this time I have told the tale as 'twas told to me, although with
many a gap, pause, and omission. Following along, after a lapse of time,
there runs a thread connecting my life with the contexture that weaves it
into the recital of this narration. Illinois was my birth place. From there
stemmed my Dakota experience, through visits with relatives, that led to
marriage. After that event my life in the north began with different
environs, methods, and business interests. Snowbound was the country that
first winter of my home life in Bowdle.

The great day was when the snowplow cleared the railroad and joined us once
more with the outside world. Springtime came on and did us a like favor
with the country roads. Soon afterwards a matter of business came up for
attention at the Bangor courthouse. The very pleasant invitation I had to
go along won me to it. I went. Unaware of what was happening I found myself
launched into a life of greater variety than I had known before. Opening my
eyes somewhat to the situation was a verging dribble of inquiry for land
that was emphasized when loan companies asked for information. Since Charles
was immigration agent for the Milwaukee railway company he was available to
the real estate and loans fraternities for light to go by. He became active
in supplying requested data, linking their interests with his own while
investigating the widely scattered tracts. For himself a set of plat books
was in the making. This was carefully done in both legal descriptions and
resources of the locality. We, together charted a considerable part of the
Aberdeen Land district. I learned that early surveyors were careless in
marking corners, those stones with gashes cut on two sides for east and
south were many times reversed in placing, and again, were somewhere else.
Sometimes when marks were missing we would find two correct corners and
drive the line between them with a bandanna tied to a spoke and counted
the revolutions of the wheel,--then measure the wanted line from that kind
of reckoning. Often the mark was found with little trouble, then again, had
to hunt around.

The wanderlust in both our natures found much to enjoy in the wide range of
our activities for gaining first hand knowledge of the district where we
lived. Close to nature as we were, we had ample scope for holding
"communion with her visible forms" to which we added some frills of our own
with tents and camp-fires. Our camping outfit was a sure go-long. It was
not always used, hotels and homes sheltered us when not too far afield.
Numbers of times the tent was a most welcome shelter. I recall a day when
we had spent so much time on the road that night was near and a storm at
hand. There was hardly time to stake the tent and tether the horses when
the storm struck with such force it seemed that the wind would take all,
including ourselves. Morning showed that we were on the rim of a tornado
that damaged property and killed livestock. In direct contrast with this
storm detail are the few times that weather and locale blended in ideal
tranquility, when, with no wind nor impending storm, the sky was our tent.
Camping under the stars gives a night view of the heavens that, from the
prone angle, is beyond compare.

Ripening plans were bringing a quickened pulse beat to Walworth county
reviving dormant hopes for improved conditions in the business of living.
The prevalent idea in the rail zone had been: "the road is going on next
year and I am going along with it". The day for action was nearing. Not
until the government and the First Citizens came to agreement on grazing
lands west of the Missouri river did the road "come to"; and the power
behind the push was the cattle industry. It was a wake up for the county
when, with a railroad across its middle and along its river front it had a
"track's end" of its own where a pontoon bridge was constructed at Evarts
for river crossings, and things began to hum with countless trains, spring
and fall, loaded with living freight. We were driving through one day when
some one hailed us to say: "Better stay awhile; herd of cattle coming to
cross over--worth seeing". And it was. The cattle loomed upon the western
crest of the cliff and dropped down the steep pitch like an avalanche to
the river's edge to be corralled for squadding. Since future generations
will not be seated close enough to witness the show it may fit into the
picture to describe the procedure of getting them to the other side without
loss. It seems the first trials started them in a bunch, but crowding
forced some of them overboard to drown. What we saw was: One horseman rode
out on the bridge alone, a few cattle followed; another horseman and more
cattle till all were over.

Evarts held its place in the cattle shipping world until ambition seized
upon the organization and our busy branch line merged into the great
Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul and Pacific railway that bridged the Missouri
river and fulfilled the design of pioneer builders for spreading an empire
to the Pacific Coast.

The rush of rails into Walworth county had a larger meaning than appears on
the surface at first glance. The glamour of far-flung interests centered
outside of county and state impressing the worth of their activities upon
us, soon settled the home front to a realization of new opportunities right
at hand, extending beyond the immediate time of alien gains, which was the
railroad's first objective. So it was that each and every mile of rails out
from Bowdle was hailed with enthusiasm. This new thing among us touched a
popular chord of personal concern; everybody was alert to it and small
incidents on the construction line were news, unrecorded volumes of
chitchat enjoyed among the communities after the long years of waiting for
the move ahead. To illustrate the concern of public thought let us step
ahead a ways to just one small instance of the re survey for the main line.
It was on the Link Hughes farm near Java. A new house had been built and
north of it a new barn. The survey was made between the two buildings and
ran into opposition from the countryside; they would not take it. The line
was changed to north of that barn.

Java was platted at the highest point of land on the extension line. It
developed quickly into a useful and welcome addition to the life of the
county. Improvements were made on a permanent basis so that when the new
survey for the main line strung its stakes a mile or more to the north and
the powers that be waved an inviting hand for them to "c'mon over", there
was no response. The citizenry of the burgh being of the moral fiber that
wins wars and maintains kingdoms, did just that. The railroad's
graciousness in defeat was evidenced in laying a special spur track to the
determined citadel. Java's home place is like a crown upon the hill top.
Viewed from all around it is a pleasing picture for friends and strangers
alike.

Bowing ourselves away from Java for a look ahead we see a downhill grade
that is even worse the other way in the up-hill pull. In the puzzle to
overcome this incline someone must have glanced at the new moon--that slim
sickle of light above us--and saw in its lines the right contour for rail
construction to make possible more ease of transportation. The practical
application of this fantasy of mine took a sharp swing to the south
rounding north and west to find placement on level ground, easy to start,
easy to stop, a happy landing after encountering that steep slope. Nature
could not have spread a more desirable terrain for the purposes that came
into being with establishing there this second town of the rails. My first
contact with this particular spot in the broad prairies was when it was a
part of the raw, open country with few homes of settlers as yet existing.
Our tent was there one night and the day following, while certain section
lines and quarter corners were being verified and charted, I had the
diversion of a new camera, and not much "know-how", with which I succeeded
in getting pictures of wild flowers blooming out of that prairie sod
(sorry, I do not have them now)--the same prairie sod whereupon important
things were to bloom in active living as the history of the county moved
along.

The designated area for the hoped-for capital was given the name of Selby;
and as SELBY it has carried on to the Golden Age of Fifty Years--the year
of Jubilee. When its legal status as a town was perfected, contemplated
plans for its career were considered, the main one being to move on Bangor
and absorb the official power plant--the county seat of Walworth county. The
contention that a town with rail connection was the proper place for the
legal center of a commonwealth had enough advocates to get action, although
against a good deal of opposition. They of the farthest places in those
horse and buggy and farm wagon days felt it was grief enough to be getting
back and forth in all kinds of weather and road conditions such as they had
to tackle without stretching the weary way. Of course the railroad was
blamed for all of it. The peeve against that Juggernaut was expressed in
personal interests. One ranch woman said it when she told me: "Git'n one o'
them things erroun' 'll spoil our business!"

Opposition added up in various ways but the weight of the argument was on
the other side, pressed down, no doubt by the influence of visiting
attorneys during court sessions grouching over the job of that twenty mile
ride between Bowdle and Bangor in Clark's stage with its wild bronchos and
same brand of pacemaker--none knowing if all four wheels were ever on the
ground at the same time. Yarns spun out of those stage trips by legal
lights waiting in the Lennan office for train or stage would be racy
reading for the future-ites had this Jubilee Volume been foreseen.

Before my time in the Dakotas, Bangor had its beginnings in the expectation
that the railroad then starting out from Aberdeen would build through that
part of Walworth county to the river and beyond making its location
unquestionably secure for its official life.

Events of time and the county seat spasm passed into history when the
courthouse burned to the ground with all records. Rumor had it that all
records were destroyed. Of this I never knew. It was a catastrophe to those
who could sense no remedy for the loss. A woman told her story. She said:
"Our marriage papers were on record there--what will happen now"? Her
distress was for division of a property and succession to another. This is a
sample of the all around worry bulging out of the ashes of that fire.

With Selby already settled into its existence the sprouting capital soon
began taking form. Bangor's alert response to the idea of change was like
the fulfillment of a dream and was entered upon with the zeal of the spirit
of the times. The old town blending with the new and placing its useful
buildings on Selby soil hastened immediate development of the county's
capital city. Selby, with its evident advantages, could flourish without the
seat of government; but the human mind can do with a bit of prestige, and
this satisfaction found a place in the consciousness of the people and adds
to the luster of the Golden Jubilee.

"The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the
desert shall rejoice and blossom like the rose." (Isa. 35:1)

We are not through visiting yet. We must go and see our young neighbor
along west a little ways. Here it was that the railroad company pricked up
its ears for a dash across the mountains and parted with its first love at a
point where it swerved south for the cattle drive. Where this parting of
the ways occurred was stationed the third rail town of the county with the
smoothly flowing name of Glenham. The town had its big day while being the
material headquarters for the road work west; but this slight flash of
prominence neither helped nor hindered establishing its solid position as
center of a frontier region that had dealt with and overdone the hazards of
"the long, long trail a-winding"--the one north to Eureka, the one south to
Bowdle, while developing a territory of decided value to its people, to the
county and to the state. There was a certain pleasure in "going to town",
and also the burden of the long hauls which were shortened with the advent
of Glenham. Thinking of early marketing days I recall a time after the steam
threshing outfits had come on, that a man in Mound City hooked up a long
string of loaded wagons to his threshing engine and hauled to Eureka--not
once, but several times. It was front page news.

During the earliest years of my life in the Dakotas I shared several long
drives in the ranching country along the Missouri north and south of
Glenham. It fascinated me, being the reverse of what I had known and lived.
At times I wanted a ranch, and to live there, but could not get the ear of
my other half. It is a vivid life in far-off places, with a sturdy charm.

Water was a problem out on the edges. It surely was a long time between
drinks but for the jug in the buggy. One day the dog was thirsty, and a
rubber blanket was spread on the ground and curled to hold water poured
from the jug. Dog knew all about it. I did not. He drank his fill, then
rolled on the wet blanket. The man, wanting a drink when the jug was empty,
stopped at a spring or the river or some decently wet spot, and dipped water
in his hat brim and drank as though from porcelain. I began to get over
amazements. Then the jug went dry. We stopped at a ranch house up off from
the river bottom and asked and were told "Yes, you can have water". The
house supply was a barrel filled from the river and hauled up hill on a
stone boat with a chunk of wood floating a-top so it would not splash over.
The folks said they settled it with one teaspoonful of alum to a barrel.
The water on top of the mud was good. I am still wondering how much mud was
in the bottom.

Turning back through the years in retrospect is like viewing a panorama, a
constantly changing scene, an unfoldment that only years can accomplish.
Many phases of experience from those who contribute to its pages, and many
things forgotten will live again and place the seal of "Golden" on the
Jubilee Volume.

Walworth county advantageously exists on the map for more than ordinary
achievement. The unfoldment of its worth has been gradual but none the less
sure and satisfying. Its physical outlines are distinctive. The river's
circuitous flow forms a western bulge on part of its area line giving rise
to an imaginative Paul Bunyan doorstep inviting important developments
harmonizing with pleasing dwelling places. This mythical doorstep gives
place to an uptilt eastward where the higher level unrolls scenes of wide
splendor like the billows of the sea. Imagination roves through green,
growing, summers to winter's wrath of blizzards that sweep the land. In one
such storm my husband was wrapped as with a blanket and but for changing
winds could not have survived its cold suffocation. The calm serenity that
often follows these blasts is something more to be remembered.

During our years in Bowdle where we had a home built for us, we, at the
same time, with our much going and coming, lived a goodly portion in
Walworth county where personal interests and of clients claimed attention;
and the resultant acquaintances made it a natural homeland and friendships
thus formed brightened our lives. This acquaintanceship reached farther
than to ourselves, for, as immigration agent, Charles was on call by the
railroad company because of his familiarity with the country and
acquaintance with the people. This was why an order was sent to him to
secure a strong bobsleigh and a husky pair of horses, a driver speaking
both English and German, and a notary public for use in buying the right of
way for the Evarts extension. This sort of conveyance was a must, for the
snow was a couple of feet on the level. Fred Merkle was employed to man the
outfit, Harry Hunter was buyer for the company, and the notary was from the
Lennan office. He was recently from Boston and having had no experience
with outdoor activity he thought this a great joy ride and asked to go.
They were seated in the bottom of the wagon box that topped the runners
with whatever was needed for their comfort. The first time they were out
three weeks. It was a serious thing, for the weather was remarkable,--cold,
with no wind or clouds and the sun on the snow was like a scald. The notary
came back with water blisters hanging from his cheeks and whiskers piercing
through.

When the main line was moving along there was another order--this time for
Charles to go horseback, strictly on the quiet, and buy land for a townsite
at the river. This was done and the company got what it asked for. These
are instances of some. of the ways wherewith he lent a hand to the
transitional changes of the age. The Lennan land office was quite
railroad-y for a while--many men coming with questions including those who
sold for the right of way.

I never drove the car very much. I had learned and could do it but a
timidity in my nature prevented. The only times I undertook to shine was in
the hunting season when I took the car along at slow speed. I came north
with no knowledge of hunting technique. I learned some of it the first day
out. Fall came and we went a few miles from Bowdle, the dog got up a covey
and one bird was dropped and left laying in the grass, which I thought
queer. Man and dog went on looking for more; I waited a short time and they
not coming I slapped 'em with the reins and the horses started. Charles saw
me and came to ask why I drove along. Said I thought he wanted the buggy.
Then he told me he wanted me to stay where he left me so he could find the
chicken...Period.

The bag limit then was 25 birds a day. In a couple of years or more it was
15, and so down to near zero. Let us hope that our beautiful birds will not
vanish as did the pigeons whose flight darkened the skies. We have been on
the Missouri bottoms in Walworth county in choke cherry time when the trees
were fairly alive with prairie chickens filling their crops with cherries,
and they were so tame they did not fly till we were nearly close enough to
touch them, and many merely flew to higher branches. A rich field for
snipers. One winter there was bad business at the river. Reports kept
coming that snipers were shipping to market by barrels. The warden did not
or could not take action unless there were complaints. There was rank
backwardness in that. It was talked that the warden had friends that
protected him and the shippers. Sour grumblings back away from the river
seemed to have the works for reports ceased coming.

Now and then a pinch of spice sifted along the breeze. Like this: A lady
whose friendship I valued and who often called at our home, came to me in a
troubled state of mind. She at once opened the subject of concern by
saying: "I have come to advise you for your own good. I want you to give up
your long drives with Mr. Lennan,--they are too hard for you and you will
lose your complexion. The wind and sun and the cold will make your skin
coarse and your face will get red, which will not be pleasing to your
husband. Be advised by me and take warning in time". No words welled up to
skid me across such thin ice and she soon left me to think it over. I went
to the Man and laid the dire prospect before him. And I asked him--"Are you
going to love me when my face gets red? Answer: "Try it and see." There
being no other hurdles I kept on going along--going along. True, my face
did get sun burned all but to the bone, but Mother Nature is a kindly dame
and helped me out of it, so-o, when the hosses pulled up at the door I was
there, too. Human interest lives in all times and places. It has been my
privilege through the years to share interests and sympathies with many
people,--some who were friends and some who became friends through joining
experiences. Sometimes a very intimate touch has oozed into words--such as
the time where we stopped for a few hours. Our hostess had always been a
pleasant friend, but this day she almost literally took me by the ears in
behalf of my children,--"Why, and WHY, etc." was asked. Upon my saying that
I had no children or I would not be there--I would be at home taking care
of them,--she became as one of a few other angels of light that had hovered
over me, after probing down to realities.

Eventually we owned a home in Walworth county after practically living
within its confines for many moons while attending to business details.
Glancing mentally backwards, the thought that a home should be on the spot
where we had bivouacked with tent, campfire, gun, dog, with nobody
around,--no one in sight, was like something out of a book. To me, it was
for a long while like a screen picture or a mirage that would be gone next
time I looked. But time and enterprise had effected a change of scene with
the establishment here of a growing city with the individual, the
distinctive, name Mobridge, a name alone in a sea of names and here we
undertook to find ourselves in a new world. After a time some of the
business men asked Charles to take part in city affairs which he did in
accordance with opportunity and his ability for what he was asked to do.
Enlarged ideas for State welfare emerged in the Doane Robinson plan for
damming the Missouri river, and this appealed strongly to his sense for
better things ahead. When the Ashley Island dam was proposed with surveys
coupled with efforts to interest the public for its accomplishment, he gave
of himself freely to the movement, and was a disappointed member of the
legislative session that voted it down. All of this time his own affairs
were seriously distressed. Connection with public matters completed, his
efforts were then engaged to surmount rising difficulties.

Joys, sorrows, hopes and defeats, gain and loss,--these came to us. To
undertake any part of a recital of these events and results is beyond me.
The lighter side of human experiences have, therefore, been set forth in
this, my contribution to the Selby Golden Jubilee Volume.

To the question of the committee, "Why did you come"? the answer is plain.
Numbers of years before we met, my husband came on a wave of opportunity and
enterprise. Myself? I came that we might live our lives together. And this
we did more fully than many others until--his last journey.
                        Hortense B. Lennan.
                        August, 1949.

MR. AND MRS. WILLIAM ROSIN

As so many of the pioneers who came to this country from Europe, William
Rosin came to America to seek escape from the compulsory military service
imposed on every able bodied man. After having served for four years in the
Russian army and in the Russo-Japanese war, he was anxious to find a place
where a man could live in peace.

William Rosin was born February 21, 1880, in Hoffnungstahl, South Russia.
His wife, Dorothea Stoecker, was born in the same village on March 13,
1882, and they were married in the same place in October, 1906. In 1910,
they came with their two children, Tillie and John, to America and settled
near Java, in Walworth county, making their home the first summer with his
brother, Fred. They had very little money when they arrived so things were
not easy at first. In the fall of 1910, they rented a farm near Java (now
the Fred C. Wolff farm) and resided there for 4 years after which they
moved to a farm north of Selby, which is their homestead, and which they
bought after renting it for five years. Conditions were good and they
continued to prosper until the depression of the '30's when it was hard
going again for a time. They have five children, all farming in the Java
and Selby vicinity. They have been living in Walworth county ever since
they came to this country and like it here. In 1943, Mr. and Mrs. Rosin
moved to Selby to live a retired life, their son, John, remaining to farm
the home place.

        MR. AND MRS. WILLIAM ROSIN

Their children are: Tillie (Mrs. Wm. Sauer) of Java; John, of near Selby;
William Jr., who farms 3 miles northeast of Selby; Clara (Mrs. Harold
Fiedler), of north of Java; and Fred, who farms east of Java. They have 16
grandchildren.

DR. HERMAN R. GUNDERMAN

Dr. Gunderman was born in Gotha, Germany, his father being postmaster in
the city which was a much more lucrative and dignified position over there
than in America. Herman was one of four sons and received a fine education
including training in the French, English and Greek languages. He came to
America at the age of 17 to avoid service in the German army which took two
years out of every able bodied man's life and gave him nothing in return
except a liability to be called at any time for more service if the
warlords considered it necessary. He had a cousin in Baltimore, Maryland,
and went there but did not stay long and traveled on to St. Louis where he
landed almost penniless. He made up his mind to study medicine and become a
doctor and went to work, earning his way by any available means such as
waiting tables or taking any other work that he could get. After graduation
he set up to practice at Wilbur, Nebraska, and there met and married Mrs.
Gunderman who was teaching in the city schools.

Lured by the opportunity to homestead good land in Walworth county they
came to Bangor and filed on the land southwest of the present site of Selby
and now the home of Mr. and Mrs. Reynold Idler, in the year 1889. He
practiced medicine from the home on the farm and later when a real need
developed for a drug store at Bangor, they started one, Mrs. Gundermann
being in charge as the doctor was out much of the time on country calls. It
was later converted into a general store and Ed Mudge was taken in as a
partner. The business flourished at Bangor until Selby was started and then
was moved, building and all, to the new city in 1900. However, the business
was soon sold out and the buildings are now a part of the Pressler hardware
store.

Dr. Gunderman continued his practice in Selby until 1915 when he made a new
start at Monango, North Dakota where there was a wide territory without a
physician. In failing health, he spent the winter of 1933 in Long Beach,
California where he met with the accident which probably shortened his
life. As he crossed a street, a car hit him dragging him many feet. While
recovering from the shock and bruises in the hospital, the earth quake of
1933 shook the city and he arose from his bed, only partially recovered, to
help with the care of the scores of injured people who were brought into
the hospital. In the spring he returned to Monango, apparently well, but in
August he was stricken suddenly and the attending physicians believed that
the California accident was the basic cause of his death.

Three children were born to Dr. and Mrs. Gunderman while they lived on the
farm southwest of Selby, namely, Erma, Genevieve and Stewart, and all
became teachers. Genevieve is still teaching in Spokane, Washington, and
Stewart at Houston, Texas. Erma resides at Long Beach, California and she
taught in South Dakota schools 13 years before going to the sunny
southwest. Mrs. Gunderman taught in Omaha until she was past 70 and passed
away recently at Long Beach at the age of 81.

This pioneer physician and his wife filled an important place in the
communities of Bangor and Selby because of their special training,--the
physician's ministrations undoubtedly saved many lives and contributed to
the better health and consequently, happiness of others. In this day of
specialists, nurses and hospitals, people can hardly realize what it must
have meant to be stricken with a disease far out on the prairies with not
even neighbors near, nor can the task of the physician in getting to them
be fully appreciated.

MR. OSCAR OLSON

Oscar Olson came to the Blue Blanket vicinity in Walworth county from Brown
county in the spring of 1887, and settled on a quarter just west of the
Bethany church. He and his wife became widely known over this area as they
ran a country store for a number of years. His father, Gonerus Olson had
charge of the Blue Blanket postoffice which had been moved from the Major
Howell residence.

        MR. AND MRS. OSCAR OLSON

Mr. Olson owned a large number of horses and cattle and pioneers who
remember the days when he lived here, state that he loved every animal on
his place. It was said that he would walk right up to the wild mustangs
with a confidence born of intuition and experience and seemed to know just
how to handle them. The bright destiny which farsighted men saw in the
future, could be fulfilled only through the endurance and faithfulness
of horses and their obedience and service to their owners,
struggling to wrest a living from a new land.

Other members of the Olson family who settled here were Hegbert, who
settled on the homestead; Ole, Benedict and Peter, and Anna, all children
of Mr. and Mrs. Gonerus Olson. Severt Opheim now owns the land where the
Olsons once lived.

MR. AND MRS. CHARLIE REISTAD

The year 1884 found Mr. and Mrs. Charlie Reistad getting started in farming
in Walworth county. They came to Dakota territory from Vernon, Wisconsin.

        MR. AND MRS. MARTIN REISTAD AND GRANDSONS

Although farming was difficult in those days, with poor crops and poor
prices, the energetic young Reistads worked hard and managed to the best of
their ability to make a living during those trying years.

The Reistads could boast that they owned two sod houses, one on each claim,
instead of the usual one. When it was time to build the frame house, Mr.
Reistad hauled lumber from Ipswich. They lived on what is known as the
Dobson farm.

The fact that Charlie Reistad served on the school board for several years
and was county commissioner a number of years proves that even though he
was constantly striving to improve his economic situation, he never
overlooked or neglected his duties as a good citizen.

Mrs. Reistad was active in various community groups and she and her family
often attended church services in the different homes conducted by Rev.
Skartvedt, who was a brother of Mrs. Ole Savold, one of their neighbors.

Martin Reistad, one of their sons, served on the Blue Blanket school board
for a number of years. At present, Martin works on a big ranch 90 miles
from Bozeman, Montana. He lived at Deer Lodge for a number of years. His
daughter, Mrs. H. G. Kallestad, also lives at Bozeman.

Charlie Reistad's daughter, Amanda, Mrs. M. Wagner, lives at Fargo, North
Dakota. She relates that there were no doctors available when they were
kids and thanks to some higher power, no one in their family became ill
with measles, whooping cough, colds, bronchitis and other inevitable
illnesses that were so common in large pioneer families.

One daughter married Ray Hilde, an uncle of the well known Tillie Hilde of
Bismarck.

Other children are: Oscar, of Townsend, Montana;
Johnny, Joe and Charley Jr., all deceased.

MR. AND MRS. HEINRICH NUSZ SR.

Heinrich Nusz Sr., was born in South Russia, near Odessa in the year 1854.
His wife, Wilhelmina, was born in the same locality two years later. They
were married in the old country and in 1875 sought greater opportunity by
migrating to America, arriving at Yankton, Dakota Territory, in July of
that year. Land was free and there was plenty of it in Dakota at that time
and Mr. Nusz took a homestead and tree claim north of Yankton in Hutchinson
county. Being industrious and venturesome he operated on a large scale for
those times and soon had a fine start.

After 25 successful years in southeastern South Dakota, a large family
having been born to them, Mr. and Mrs. Nusz sought more room, especially
for the children, and the beautiful Blue Blanket valley of Walworth and
Campbell counties enticed them. In 1901 they came to Walworth county, being
much better off and bringing far more with them than most of the people who
came here. They loaded five emigrant cars with livestock, farm machinery,
household goods and seed grain on the Milwaukee at Freeman and came to the
new town of Selby, having purchased 11 quarter sections of land in
Hiddenwood township northeast of Selby, the tract with the buildings on it
being what was known in the early days as the Meagher place now owned by
Edmund Mauch.

With this equipment and land and his large family of helpers Mr. Nusz
immediately became one of the largest operators in farming and livestock in
the county. At one time he had 1700 head of sheep, 100 head of horses and a
herd of cattle, numbered in the hundreds, grazing his stock over a wide
area, and also put a lot of land in crops. His stock, particularly his
horses, were well known for their high quality and took many ribbons at
various shows and fairs. His other stock was noted on the markets for high
quality. His crops of grain were equally good.

        MR. AND MRS. HENRICH NUSZ AND FAMILY
        On the left, Mr. and Mrs. Heinrich Nusz Sr. and youngest daughter
        Martha. Upper right, the daughters of Mr. and Mrs. Henry Nusz Sr.
        Left to right, Martha, Jennie, Lydia and Katie. Lower right, left
        to right, top row, Robert, Edward and Christ; lower row, Barney,
        John and Henry.

In the new town and the community around it, Mr. Nusz soon assumed
positions of leadership in community affairs and in various enterprises
destined to boost the new community, to which the scope of his operations
and his personal qualifications entitled him. He and his family were
charter members of the American Lutheran church congregation then made up
of Selby, Lowry and Akaska. He entered with zest into the famous county seat
fight and gave time and spent money in the campaign to bring the county
seat to Selby. He helped organize the First National bank of Selby and held
stock in it for 35 years; promoted and at one time owned the Selby Roller
mill and elevator and was active in the many other enterprises of the new
town, giving his time, his talents and his money.

The family grew up on the big farm, married and went into homes and
businesses of their own and they, too, held important places in the
business, religious and social life of Selby and community.

In the year 1918 Mr. and Mrs. Nusz moved to Lodi, California, and both have
passed to their eternal reward. Most of the members of the family have left
the community, but the records and results of their activities are
here for all time.

MR. JOHN BERENS

John Berens, son of Margaret and John Berens was born in Luxemburg,
Germany, on July 4, 1875. He, along with his three brothers, received most
of his education in Luxemburg before the family immigrated to the United
States. The trip across water took approximately one week. They landed at
New York and settled in Jackson county, Iowa, near Galvie.

At a young age, John started working out on farms. While working for Mike
Georgen, he met the lady of his choice and later married Mary Georgen,
daughter of Mary and Mike Georgen. She was born in Luxemburg
and had migrated to the United States with her parents,
who also settled on a farm near Galvie, Iowa.

        MR. AND MRS. JOHN BERENS

Mr. and Mrs. John Berens moved from Iowa to Woonsocket, South Dakota, where
they purchased a farm two miles east of town. In March, 1903, John bought
the Carl Milde saloon and residence in Selby, moved his family here and
took possession on April 1, 1903. From this time on Mr. and Mrs. Berens
were ardent boosters for the betterment of the town.

In February, 1905, John Berens bought the Treanor building located in Block
14, Lot 12, and after remodeling, moved his saloon to said property in
August of the same year. John Berens also owned a building south of the
post office, which he moved in September, 1905, to his Lot 9, Block 14,
where he converted it to a pool and billiard parlor.

In 1910, Mr. Berens built a two story cement block structure which was
completed in July. The lower part housed his garage, while living quarters
were maintained on the second floor. In August, 1914, Mrs. Berens opened a
restaurant next to the garage. In 1920, Mr. Berens started excavating a
basement between the garage and pool hall on Lot 11, Block 14, preparatory
to the construction of a $15,000 hotel. This project resulted in a cave-in
of the north side of the basement, which caused the south and east sides of
his cement block garage to collapse, weakening the building to the extent
that it had to be taken down. This delayed the construction of the hotel.
In January, 1923, the Hill garage burned. Mr. Berens had a great deal of
the material for his new hotel stored in that building. As a result, the
idea of building the hotel was abandoned. The elder Mr. Berens' dream of
building a fine hotel in Selby was realized in the $250,000 hotel built in
1949 and completed in 1950 by Mr. and Mrs. Berens' youngest son, Joe.

Mr. and Mrs. Berens were very active in civic affairs and in their faith
loving Catholic religion. They no doubt endured their share of sorrow,
drouth and blizzards. Hardships were not particularly felt in those days by
Mr. and Mrs. Berens, as they possessed the ability to adjust themselves
readily to the prevailing conditions, looking at the brightest side of
things in most cases.

To this couple five children were born: Margaret Berens Biffle, who passed
away September 6, 1937, and is buried in Mobridge, South Dakota, beside her
mother and father; Kathryn Berens Fleming of Detroit, Michigan; Mary Berens
Lewey of Detroit, Michigan; Johnnie of Mobridge, South Dakota; and Joe of
Selby.

MR. AND MRS. ROBERT NUSZ

Robert Nusz was born at Freeman, South Dakota, in 1884, the son of Mr. and
Mrs. Heinrich Nusz Sr., who had immigrated to America from South Russia in
1875. He came to Walworth county in 1901 at the age of 17 with the family
and grew to manhood on the big farm northeast of Selby. He was united in
marriage with Minnie Fiedler and to them seven children were born, all of
them graduating from Selby high school. In the year 1942 Mr. and Mrs. Nusz
moved to Woodland, California, where they bought a home and she resides.
All of the children have also left the community of their nativity, most of
them going to California. Mr. Nusz passed away in March 1950.

        MR. AND MRS. ROBERT NUSZ AND FAMILY
        Left to right, upper row, Elnora, Olga, Arthur, Wilma, Viola
        second row, Dolores, Mrs. Nusz, Mr. Nusz, Clarine.

Robert Nusz was connected as a stockholder and employee with the W. S.
Schwartz hardware company in Selby and when that business was sold to the
Overholser-Leach hardware company he went into the real estate and
insurance business, being associated for a number of years with Stewart
Cook. He continued in this business until he left Selby. He served for many
years as clerk of the Selby school district and held many other positions
in the city. He and his family were members of the American Lutheran church
and had prominent parts in all of its activities, also in all school
activities and in most of the other community affairs in the city.

Like many others who have left Selby, this family left behind them a record
for doing their full part in all of the religious and philanthropic
activities of the community and helping to make it a good place for those
of us who have remained here to live.

MR. AND MRS. GEORGE B. WALTER

George Byron Walter was born in Clarkston, Michigan, August 18, 1853. He
grew to manhood in that community and was united in marriage with Eva Starr
of Royal Oak, a nearby town, in the year 1883. One son, Sydney Almon, was
born to them. Mrs. Walter passed away four years after their marriage
leaving her husband with the infant son who was cared for by his
grandparents until he was nine years old.

In 1889 he was married to Tillie Hersbach, also of Royal Oak, and the same
year they left the land of their nativity and came to South Dakota,
generally considered "back east" as the lands of the Indian and the real
"wild west". In a way it was "wild west" as the Sioux and Cheyennes lived
just across the Missouri river and often visited the early Walworth county
towns, and in the year after their arrival, 1890, the settlement experienced
a real Indian scare, and the Walters, like other pioneers of that time knew
not what the hostile Indians might do on a marauding expedition.

        MR. AND MRS. GEORGE B. WALTER

They settled on the land known since that day as the Walter farm in Hilde
township and set about the task of building a farmstead, breaking the sod
and building up a good home for themselves and their children. Having grown
up in the fruit growing section of Michigan, Mr. Walter was much interested
in fruit trees and amateur forestry and set out at once to emulate the
farmers of Michigan by growing a shelter belt and setting out fruit trees.
He was especially fond of cedars.

In 1906 Mr. Walter built a new house and barn on the farm, quite
pretentious buildings for those times and the place became quite well known
because of his tree plantings and the new buildings. They resided on the
farm until the year 1935 when they retired and moved to Selby where Mrs.
Walter passed away in 1938 at the age of 68 and Mr. Walter in 1943 at the
age of 90 years.

Seven children were born to them: Mrs. Nellie Zabel, John, Mrs. Eva Kins,
Mrs. Elizabeth Ellefson, Mrs. Bertha Stevenson, and Ethel and George, both
deceased. Mrs. Zabel resides in the old home neighborhood and she and her
husband, Art, purchased the home place some years ago and added it to their
fine farm. John is at Whitetail, Montana, Eva and Elizabeth at Great Falls,
Montana, and Bertha lives in the state of Washington.

Sydney resided in Selby until his sudden death on March 1, 1950.

Through the years Mr. Walter served on the Hilde district school board, two
terms as county commissioner from his district and held many offices of
lesser note. He was a member of the county board when the new court house
was built and supervised the planting of the beautiful cedar trees on the
grounds and watched over them carefully as long as he lived. He planted the
cedars at the Selby cemetery and also saw to it that they were well
nurtured as long as he was able. Mr. and Mrs. Walter were both members and
enthusiastic devotees of the Jolly club and of the Methodist church in
Selby. Mrs. Walter was also a member of the Mother's club and was often
called in time of sickness in the neighborhood.

The young people of the family took their places in the community as they
grew up. Each had an opportunity for a good education and the daughters
taught school in the home community after finishing their own schooling
and before they went to homes of their own. The family has scattered as
most families do but for many years to come the people who knew them will
always think of them when they note the handiwork of the father.

FRANK ZABEL SR.

Frank Zabel Sr., was born at Dulitz, Pomerania, Germany, on January 24,
1869, and received the equivalent of an 8th grade education in the schools
of Germany. In 1882 he came to America with his parents and four sisters,
the family settling at Monroe, Wisconsin, on timbered land which it was
necessary to clear before crops could be raised. Like most people who came
to the new land of America from across the ocean, they sought greater
opportunity and a better way of life and expected to do their full part in
clearing and making the new country. At the age of 21 he started out for
himself and went to work for a neighboring farmer, and there he met
Katharina Kubauch, who was also employed on the farm and on September 24,
1890, they were married. She was born in Gomaringen, Wurtemburg, Germany,
and her family, too, had come to America and settled at Monroe.

Their first home was a small three-room house equipped only with the bare
necessities which in that day consisted of a dresser, bed with straw
mattress, table, chairs, stove, kitchen utensils, and a few dishes. There
were no comforts or luxuries. People had no time or use for luxuries
anyway, their time and energy all being expended in reclaiming the land and
providing food and clothing. They lived several years on rented farms and
acquired a farm of their own in time.

In 1906 the family moved to Walworth county, purchasing the farm now owned
by Gottlieb Schuh in Spring Valley. It was a combination of the tree claim
of the late J. E. Hoefs, and the homesteads of John Ritter and daughter,
Rose. The few buildings on the farm were situated on the east side of the
land and there was little water so Mr. Zabel moved them to the present site
and built a new house and other buildings to make a very good farmstead.
The place had been acquired by O. D. Buchecker, from whom Mr. Zabel
purchased it through W. B. Myler and Frank Riley.

He sold this farm to James Barclay in 1908 and the family spent the year
1910 living in Selby, in the house now occupied by the Simons family. He
then purchased the west half of Section 3 in Brown township, the south
quarter of which had been Alphonso Buchanan's homestead. A new and modern
set of farm buildings were erected on this land which was mostly prairie
and the Zabel family began a farming career in that community which
illustrates the statement often made that truth is stranger than fiction.
In 40 years time the real estate holdings of the family group have grown
from this unimproved half section to a total of 36 quarter sections of land
with 6 sets of fine farm buildings all accumulated by raising crops and
selling them. In 1931 Mr. and Mrs. Zabel moved to Selby to make their home
with their daughter, Mrs. Lottie Sawinsky. Mrs. Zabel passed away in 1938
after suffering for many years with arthritis, spending 12 years in a wheel
chair and two years in bed before her death. She was tenderly cared for
always and bore her affliction cheerfully being an inspiration to all who
knew her because of her fortitude and kindliness.

Ten children were born to Mr. and Mrs. Zabel, seven of whom reside in the
Selby community. Arthur resides southwest of Selby, Mrs. Elsie Hoefs in
Selby, Mrs. Lydia Pratton in Douglas, Arizona, Mrs. Lottie Sawinsky in
Selby, Mrs. Rose Brewer in Aberdeen, Frank Jr., Mrs. Minnie Lemburg, Edward
and John in the old home neighborhood southwest of Selby and Ralph at
Bloomington, Illinois.

Mr. Zabel makes his home with his daughter in Selby and was active in
helping out with carpenter work and other things that needed to be done in
town during the war period when help was needed so badly, and until his
health failed him.

Few families have contributed more to the upbuilding of the Selby community
than the Zabels.

"TONKA COLA" The Honorable Peter Couchman

On that day in 1880 the August sun lay warm on the river boat landing at
LeBeau, Indian trading post and port of call midway between Ft. Pierre and
Bismarck on the Missouri river in Dakota territory. Keeping a practiced eye
on sand bar and channel Capt. Horn slowly warped the Last Chance in toward
the bank while with shrieking protest from the pulley wheels the apron
descended to make a gang plank for the landing on the muddy sand.

Willing hands among the half dozen white settlers from the trading post and
the adjoining frontier village of LeBeau made the boat fast. Among them
probably Antoine LeBeau, for whom the landing and subsequently the town was
named, Tom Carter, August Siebrecht and W. D. Ryan.

A few Indians crouched in the scraggly shade of the willows that fringed
the shore, wrapped, despite the August heat, in the black barred Hudson Bay
blankets of the first issue of the Indian department.

From a stout kitchen chair placed on deck the lone passenger for LeBeau
arose, gathered a couple of carpet bags and prepared to accompany Capt.
Horn, carrying the precious sack of mail, ashore.

An unusual stir of surprise ran down the line of blanketed Indians together
with the whispered word "tonka" which in the Indian tongue means "big". Not
without reason for the newcomer stood six inches over six feet, 300 and
more pounds of solid bone and muscle, "Not a military man", decided the
white men, in spite of his erect carriage and confident air, this man of
perhaps 45 years wore blue broadcloth coat, fawn trousers and a
wide-brimmed black slouch hat, "Perhaps a government official?"

With a good-natured twinkle, as if not entirely unconscious of the small
sensation created by his bulk, the stranger waited courteously for Capt.
Horn's introduction. So Peter Couchman came to LeBeau in Dakota territory,
came with the idea of a transient stay and remained for 20 odd years.

Born in New York state in the 1830's, educated and forming his friendships
and political affiliations during that uncertain period preceding the Civil
war, Peter Couchman was closely associated with two young men also seeking
their future in the city of New York: D. H. Hill, who became a warm and
life long friend, and who was in a few years to be elected governor of New
York and another young man reading law in the same office and interested,
like Peter, in the political future of the democratic party. His name was
Grover Cleveland.

Following the Civil war, Peter Couchman was elected and served as
assemblyman for his district on the democratic ticket. Subsequently he was
appointed to a commission in the south. There he disagreed so heartily with
governmental policies as to lose his job. Abandoning entirely the practice
of law he turned his attention to real estate and for several years moved
from town to town up the Mississippi. To the west through Texas, Oklahoma,
Kansas and Nebraska herds of trail-driven cattle were moving north and west
to the vast grass lands of Dakota territory. With rumors of a land boom and
land for homesteaders, especially for Civil war veterans, came Peter
Couchman to investigate the possibilities of this newly opened territory.

The first winter of his stay in LeBeau was that winter of '80-81 when
storms came howling down from the north in September and remained until
May. Not one dramatic storm, quickly past, no matter how disastrous, but
long weary months of sub-zero weather and icy biting winds. The first snow
froze over the prairie grass in a hard crust and then came storm after
snowstorm. River settlers formed rescue squads. In that winter Peter proved
his worth with unquenchable good humor, the undeniable charm of his
personality, his resourceful rigging of crude snow shoes and his ability to
outlast even the hardy settlers in endurance. The river settlers were more
fortunate in a source of fuel from the timber and a supply of wild game
whose refuge was the river timber and the sheltering draws. Relays of men
wearing Peter's make shift snow shoes hauled wood and meat to the prairie
where several families would gather in one home to conserve fuel and food.
Hay was often the only fuel available.

In the spring Peter Couchman was established in the minds and hearts of the
early settlers as one of them. The starving Indians who came into the
trading post al most instinctively turned to him and he espoused their
cause whole-heartedly. His first act in the spring was to procure a team
and buggy and he drove miles over the prairie alone or accompanied by
prospective homesteaders. A strange sight, Peter Couchman and the aver.
age man occupying a spring buggy seat, for Peter's side sagged disastrously
and it was said that Peter Couch man wore out more buggy springs than any
man in Dakota territory.

When the young state of South Dakota became a reality, Peter Couchman was
one of the signers of the constitutional amendment at Sioux Falls. When
Walworth became a county, Peter Couchman was appointed the first sheriff
for men learned that the good-natured twinkle in his eyes could turn, upon
occasion, to a slate-grey and chilling steeliness.

Twice he ran for state office, once for lieutenant governor and once for
governor of the state, piling up a surprising minority in the face of
insurmountable odds, for South Dakota at the time, was as indisputably
republican as Georgia was democratic.

During the second term of Grover Cleveland, Peter Couchman asked for and
expected the appointment of U. S. marshal. Instead he received the
appointment of superintendent of Indian Affairs at Cheyenne Agency--a great
personal disappointment. However his understanding of the Indians was
phenomenal and his grasp of their problems well known. The Indians liked
and trusted him at a time when white men in general were viewed with
suspicion by the whole Sioux nation. His friendship for Martin Charger, Mad
Bear, Pretty Bear, Four Bears, One Rib and Swift Bird, his tireless efforts
to bring recognition of the tremendous debt of the territorial whites to
these heroes of the "Crazy Band," together with his quick action in
protecting their ancient burial grounds his buying of an exemption to save
their sacred Medicine Tree (at the site of the town of Evarts) and his
ability to make and keep friends among them no doubt influenced his
appointment as superintendent.

Peter Couchman numbered his friends among young and old, red man and white.
He was affectionately known as "Uncle Peter" throughout the country and his
personal characteristics were widely known. He neither smoked nor drank and
his favorite food was thickened sour milk called "clabber" which he ate
with sugar, and burned cookies. No mail order house or frontier store could
supply the outsize clothing that he wore. It was ordered from a specialty
