company in New York, his boots being sent separately one to a package,
parcel post of the time not being adequate to handle a package to
accommodate a pair.

During the troubled year of 1890 Peter Couchman sat in on many an Indian
gathering. There is no doubt that his influence with the Indians averted
serious trouble,-relayed from Mad Bear's camp came messages from all over
the reservation. Couchman passed on this information as well as difficult
transportation made possible. Had he not been absent at the time, there
might well never have been the 1890 "Indian Scare".

From his years in the Indian service amusing stories are told. Few white
men have reached such a warm understanding of the Indian customs. He
visited their homes and respected their friendship. On the occasion of a
meeting of the chiefs early in the 1890's Peter Couchman attended as an
honored guest. For some time the peace pipe had been absent from the Indian
councils-at this meeting it was restored. Gravely it was passed to Peter
and as gravely accepted,--he knew that to refuse the pipe would constitute
an insult to his hosts. Unused to tobacco in any form, that council Peter
long remembered !

As Indian agent he was called upon to settle many a dispute, arbitrate in
many a domestic crisis. As on the day that Martin Standing Bear and Molly,
his wife, appeared in the agency office. Through the interpreter in a long
and flowery speech, Martin presented his case: "For long the 'Great White
Father in Washington' had restricted the Indian to a single wife, the
Christian missionaries also frowned on plural wives, and as a consequence
the Indians had forgone their ancient tradition of many wives and many
children, and their hearts were bad, but, (the countenance of Martin
Standing Bear shone with naive and innocent happiness)," 'The Great White
Father' in his beneficent goodness had granted them a way out of their
difficulties. This thing called 'divorce', would 'Tonka Cola' give one to
him and to Molly White Dog, (indicating a meek, shawled figure behind him)
because he, Martin Standing Bear, would then be free to espouse Ellen White
Cloud whose father, for the small consideration of eight ponies, was
disposed to part with this jewel among women. Aged also only 16 summers and
sure to bring to the teepee of Martin Standing Bear great felicity and many
children!". Martin ceased talking and waited expectantly while Peter
Couchman silently pleated his lip. Useless to try to explain the
intricacies of the law. The need of lawyer, judge and court procedure. To
Martin he was the Law and the Judge. Finally, "It is true", he said slowly,
"that the great white Father has granted to all in the State of South
Dakota, Indians and white alike, the right to put aside, for reason, his
wife or her husband. So", turning to the silent woman, "have you also a
choice, Molly, do you", ... Martin committed one of the cardinal Indian
sins, "Molly," he interrupted rudely, "will stay in my teepee to care for
her children, to cook and tend the fire". Suavely "Tonka Cola" also
interrupted, "Oh no, the divorce is for the wife as well as the husband.
The mother also takes the children", he added. The interview was ended!
With a rough push Martin made plain to his lawfully wedded wife, Molly,
that she was still such, and stalked after her, wrapped to his chin in
blanketed dignity, and Molly went, but not without a flash of gratitude
from liquid black eyes to "Tonka Cola"! Peter Couchman chuckled and then
sighed, "Might not be as easy next time!"

Peter Couchman hated the cold. As a protection he bought from the firm in
New York that furnished all his very much out sized clothing, the heaviest
and warmest of winter garments available. Among these were some knitted
suits of scarlet wool underwear, the color itself being regarded as having
a certain efficacy. Peter had carefully guarded these objects of art, which
were in truth of a size to create undesirable comment from his more
facetious friends, and he himself had superintended their washing by the
dusky maiden who presided over his personal laundry, stressing perhaps too
much their importance, to save them from the steaming maw of the wash
boiler that received the average wash in its entirety.

In early December a group of Indians craved audience with him. A group
headed by Red Feather, and among them an elderly Indian, a stranger of
sober and dignified mien. This, said Red Feather, was "Circling Hawk",
mighty warrior of the Sioux. He had brought a gift to the superintendent,
an heirloom in his family which had fathered many mighty warriors. Couchman
nodded in appreciation of the gift, although a trifle uneasily, knowing
the Indian law of a gift for a gift. However, "It was known", said Red
Feather, "that the 'Tonka Cola' was a mighty chieftain, and from the
Standing Rock, Circling Hawk had come to do him honor!" "But lately",
continued Red Feather, "it had come to be known how really great a medicine
man was the 'Tonka Cola', how in his modesty he wore his chieftain's
regalia under his outer clothing at all times". At this, agonized
realization came upon the superintendent of Indian affairs and the slow
purple of embarrassment crept from his collar to his white beard and hair.
The issue clerk and chief carpenter, present in the office, pricked up
their ears in interest. Red Feather went on remorselessly, his daughter,
Nancy Red Feather, "who plunged into water the clothing of 'Tonka Cola' ",
(Red Feather passed by in kindly tolerance that idiosyncracy) "had reported
that so great a chieftain was their honored friend, that he possessed not
one, but two, of these signal marks of valor, and so Circling Hawk had come
begging a boone in return for the gift from his fathers, one of these
scarlet suits to wear on feast days and other occasions"! Circling Hawk most
certainly got the suit! In 1920 at Bullhead he wore it at a 4th of July
celebration, faded at that time to a lurid pink and embellished with a tail
fan of turkey feathers. Also most certainly Peter Couchman's friends
refused to let him forget that interview very soon.

The years crept on. Too soon Peter Couchman felt the drag of his increasing
bulk and the ever slowing reaction of his muscles. Not an old man in years
but broken in health, his mind and heart turned nostalgically to his native
New York. Finally he resigned from the Indian service and went home. One
trip back to South Dakota he made in 1900 when the town of Evarts was
platted on the exemption he had bought to protect the Indian medicine tree.
To his satisfaction the townspeople of Evarts erected a stout iron fence
around the tree and the rocks from which it sprang. During his last visit in
Walworth county many friends came to do him honor, Indians and white alike,
for he had grown too heavy to drive over the prairie as in the past. With
great pride, at the first Old Settlers Picnic, at Bangor, June 26, 1900, he
presented his Indian friends, Chief Martin Charger, Four Bears, Pretty Bear
and Makes Fire as honored guests of the occasion. Walter Swift Bird was
also present, acting for his father, Swift Bird, and assisted as
interpreter. Peter Couchman made every effort to interest the public in the
survivors of this small band of Indians, survivors of the so-called "Fool
Soldiers" or "Crazy Band". In 1903 Doane Robinson wrote an article for
McClures about them and in January, 1904, Congressman Eben Martin presented
a bill in Congress proposing a medal for each survivor or their nearest
relatives in the case of those deceased. Also an annuity for the survivors.
Peter Couchman, however, did not live to see the results of the bill. In
March came news of his death at the home of his daughter in Gilboa, New
York.

His many friends in Walworth county and South Dakota sincerely mourned his
loss. A great company of Indians mourned his passing with a traditional
funeral feast held only for highly honored chieftains. This solemn
celebration at Mad Bear's camp was one of the very few ever held in honor
of a white man. In addition the women asked for and received permission to
sound the death wail for "Tonka Cola",--a rite usually reserved for close
relatives.

Said Martin Charger, "Far toward the rising sun our friend sleeps the last
sleep, may his reward be great in the hunting grounds of his Fathers. May
we remember his deeds as long as the green grass springs every year on the
buffalo trails, and may he live in our hearts forever. 'Tonka Cola, Big
Friend!'"

THE COLMAN WAGNER FAMILY

Colman Wagner was born in Austria-Hungary, January 18, 1868. He came to
America with his parents, Michael and Theresa Wagner, and settled on a farm
in Walworth county, 4 miles southwest of Selby, in 1888.

Christine Baer was born in Crimea, South Russia, September 2, 1871. She
came to America with her parents, Bernhart and Katherine Baer, and settled
on a farm in Walworth county, 22 miles southeast of Selby, in 1889.

Colman Wagner and Christine Baer were married February 1, 1893, and started
farming on his homestead one mile south of his father's homestead. Here on
this homestead their five children, Colman, Ernestine, Gazella, Wilhelmina
and Arnold, were born.

The Baer church which was located about ten miles north of Hoven was
started and built by Mrs. Wagner's parents and uncles.

In 1897 Colman Wagner entered into partnership with H. C. Baer in the
implement and grain business in Bowdle. He went to Bowdle and back to the
farm by bicycle until 1899 when he moved the family to Bowdle and back
to the farm again in the same year. The Baer and Wagner partnership started
an implement and grain business in Selby which Mr. Wagner managed along
with his farming operations. In 1902 he moved with his family to Selby to
continue in the business activities. The Baer and Wagner partnership
continued in the implement and grain business until 1909 when the implement
business was sold to Charles Schott and the Baer and Wagner partnership
dissolved. Colman Wagner retained the grain elevator which business he
continued until the elevator was set on fire by a train and burned down in
1923.

        THE COLMAN WAGNER FAMILY
        Mrs. Wagner, Mr. Wagner, Colman, Ernestine, Gazella, Arnold
        (on lap). Wilhelmina.

Mr. Wagner was elected to the Selby city council in 1911 and served as
councilman for 28 years until he died November 18, 1939.

Mr. Wagner loved music and learned to play the violin and cornet without an
instructor. He played with the Bangor and Selby bands for 46 years and
always took an active part and interest in all band activities. He was
considered as one of the best cornetists in this part of the country.

During the early years on the farm when Mr. Wagner was in business Mrs.
Wagner often did most of the farm work, sometimes with hired men but more
often alone. She did the chores, mowed and raked hay and took care of her
small children.

Mrs. Wagner is the only one of the family still living at Selby at this
time. The family still own the homestead farm and their home in Selby and
Mrs. Wagner would rather live there than any other place.

The children, all living, are: Colman H. Wagner, county agent, Clark, South
Dakota; Ernestine Miller and Gazella McIntyre of Idaho Falls, Idaho;
Wilhelmina Allerdings of Los Angeles, California; and Dr. J. Arnold
Wagner, a dentist at Seattle, Washington.

MR. AND MRS. GEORGE M. MICKELSON

While still a young boy, George M. Mickelson, born August 27, 1856, in
Norway, came to America with his parents and two sisters. The family lived
in Wisconsin a short time, then moved farther west to Illinois, Iowa, and
finally to Brown county, South Dakota.

George filed on a pre-emption near Groton and it was here that he married
Emma L. Craig, born in Wisconsin, June 17, 1868. Their first child, Harry,
was born June 9, 1884.

In the fall of '84, George, his wife and infant son started for Walworth
county with a few pieces of furniture, one yoke of oxen and a total of $48
in cash, to file on a homestead and tree claim.

The family located on the east half of section 7-123-77 and remained here
until 1909. During this time George and Emma were blessed with four more
sons, William Arthur, George and Clarence, and five girls, Mary, Ella,
Lilah, Lulu and Anna, all of whom are still living with the exception of
Arthur who passed away in the month of July, 1902, at the age of nine
months. The farm consisted of a small lumber house, sod barn and a log cow
barn. Cottonwood trees were plentiful near the Missouri river so were put
to many uses other than houses, such as hay racks, bob-sleighs and
workshops.

George broke the first hundred acres with one yoke of oxen but the oxen
couldn't stand the afternoon heat so George and wife would plant trees and
dig rocks from their land. To prove a tree claim, each claimant would have
to plant twenty acres of trees.

Prairie fires were a very menacing and usual occurrence, raging for miles
on the open plains. Occasionally the Sioux Indians would go on the warpath
and try to cross the river, so life was far from dull for the early
settlers.

        MR. AND MRS. GEORGE M. MICKELSON AND FAMILY
        Standing, left to right, Mary Seeley, Portland, Ore.; Ella Stewart,
        Olympia, Wash.; Harry, Compton, Calif.; William, Detroit, Mich.;
        Lilah Eivans, Mitchell, S. D.; Lulu Seeley, Olympia, Wash., Mr.
        Mickelson; Anna Brown, Sioux Falls, S. D.; Mrs. Mickelson;
        George, Pierre, S. D.; Clarence (on lap), Sioux City, Iowa.

George's family were regular members of the Norwegian Lutheran church and
he was also a member of the I.O.O.F.

Wheat farming was the big industry with George at this time as it was too
far to market to take time to raise hogs, and cattle were much too
expensive to raise for anything but the family's food. Grain was hauled to
Bowdle, a long trip of approximately thirty miles, a very tiring and rough
journey for horses. It was with much excitement and happiness that the
railroad was greeted in 1900 near the town of Bangor. Shortly, the towns of
Java, Selby, Glenham and Evarts sprung up.

Although George M. Mickelson had only a "country school education" he was
very determined that his children and others would receive better
educations, and did his utmost to promote better schools as well as better
highways. He served on the board of education for several years and was
county commissioner for two terms. Later, he became vice-president of the
First National Bank of Selby.

In 1909, George retired from farming, rented his farm to the eldest son,
Harry, and moved his family to the fast growing town of Selby. Here he
built the large "Mickelson Home" on the east side of town, now owned by
George T., present Governor of the state of South Dakota. After moving to
Selby, George dealt some in real estate until his death on August 17, 1913,
at the age of 57 years. His wife, Emma and children continued to live in
this house until her death, November 17, 1918, at the age of fifty years.

MR. DANIEL B. SHAW

This pioneer, whose American lineage has been traced back to Revolutionary
days, moved with his family consisting of wife, two sons and two daughters
to Walworth county in the spring of 1884, from Bremen, Indiana, and settled
on a homestead 21/2 miles east of the site of old Bangor. They built a
small one-room frame shack and a sod barn, broke up a strip of land, put up
some hay and then returned to Aberdeen to work until fall. In August a
prairie fire swept across the country and destroyed the hay.

The first winter on the "claim" was a severe one with many blizzards. The
nearest neighbor was a mile away and no one was really prepared to go
through a hard winter. There was no doctor west of Bowdle and when Mrs.
Shaw fell from a big snow bank and broke her arm at the wrist she set it
herself and put on splints, then went about her work. The nearest
postoffice at first was Bowdle, later they got their mail at LeBeau. The
only social life was when three or four families would meet at some home
and play cards and visit. If there was room the young people would play
games or dance.

The settlers organized and voted to build a schoolhouse. There were six
pupils in the first school and the teacher was 16 years old. Later a
Lutheran minister came to the community and held services in the
schoolhouse, the settlers of all religious denominations turning out to
welcome him and hear his message.

The Matz family at Glenham have a copy of the first newspaper printed on
the prairie, the Blue Blanket, printed in Kingman's cabin, just west of
where they lived.

When Bangor was started, people were happy for they were near town and
could get mail regularly and supplies at any time.

The three day blizzard of January 12, 1888, kept the settlers indoors. They
were not able to even get to the barns to care for stock. The snow covered
the Shaw barn, and the mail carrier from Bangor, driving to and from
Bowdle, drove over the corner of the barn without knowing it. The Shaws
heard his distress calls and went out and brought him into their cabin,
thus saving his life.

When Bangor began to boom the Shaws sold their land and went into the
mercantile business in that city, establishing the firm of D. B. Shaw and
Son, general merchandise. Mr. Shaw was appointed postmaster and served 8
years, the young people helping out in store and postoffice.

When Selby started and Bangor began to move away, the Shaws decided to move
to Glenham instead, and took their building and stock there. Again he was
appointed postmaster and served until ill health forced him to retire. The
daughters exercised their homestead right by taking land near Glenham.

The last members of this family to remain in the county were the son, Fred,
who was a painter and decorator and resided in Glenham until his health
failed. He spent his last days in the Odd Fellows Home at Dell Rapids, and
the daughter, Mrs. W. F. Matz, who with her husband, still calls Glenham
her home.

MR. W. E. PRANN

W. E. Prann and Bird V. Hazeldine grew up, attended school and were united
in marriage at Cresco, Iowa. Both graduated from Cresco high school and he
took his training in pharmacy at the college of pharmacy at Ada, Ohio. In
the year 1903 they came to Selby for the purpose of establishing a drug
store in the new and promising city. They opened their business in the
building now occupied by the Buchanan drug store after purchasing the drug
stock of Dr. H. R. Gunderman, the patent medicine stock of the Schwartz
hardware company and the stationery and school supply stock of Fred
Griffin, then publisher of the Walworth County Record. It was agreed that
the new plan would give the new town a good drug store and at the same time
relieve these other businesses of burdensome sidelines they had carried
only to accommodate the trade. Previous to the move to Selby Mr. Prann had
been employed as a clerk and pharmacist.

When the Selby telephone exchange was installed Mr. Prann took over the
central office and ran it for many years. In 1912 the drug store was sold
to C. D. Durfey, and the Pranns moved to Timber Lake buying it back and
returning the next year and operating it until the Leo Buchanan returned
from the army at the close of World War I. They sold out to him and removed
to Timber Lake and remained in the drug business there until Mr. Prann
passed away in 1940. The Timber Lake drug store was taken over by W. E.
Prann Jr., and is still operated by him. Leo Buchanan still runs the Selby
store.

Three children came to the Prann home, all born in Selby. The son resides
in the old home in Timber Lake, Mrs. Lucille Craven resides in Portland,
Oregon, and Mrs. De Maris Davidson at Denver, Colorado.

During the years that the Pranns lived in Selby Mr. Prann served as city
clerk and held many other offices in the town. He was active in all of the
affairs of the young and growing city. Mrs. Prann likewise took part in the
many local activities.

THE COUNTY SEAT FIGHT

At a meeting of the county commissioners June 21, 1883, Scranton or South
LeBeau became the first county seat of Walworth county. The trading post of
LeBeau with the post office called Scranton was at the time the only
permanent settlement in the county. The commissioners were Frank Kennedy of
the Kennedy Bros. cattle ranch, Charles Abbot Wilkins, whose land lay half
in Walworth, half in Campbell county, and Oliver Shannon Sr., all appointed
for the new county by the territorial governor.

About a year later discussion started over the location of the county seat
in the southwest corner of the county, and on September 6, 1884, a mass
meeting was called at the home of Capt. N. H. Kingman, located on SE 1/4
28-123-76 called to order by W.B. Burr with Col. N.G. Potter as chairman
and L.D. Dickerson as secretary. Plans were formulated to appoint a
committee to find a location for the county seat nearer the geographical
center of the county.

The Blue Blanket, Volume I, No. 1, dated September 11, 1884, gives full
details of the meeting. This publication printed on blue paper by Winn and
Fulcomer, proprietors, gave its location as the "Center of Walworth county,
P. O. LeBeau!" and devoted the front page to arguments concerning the
removal of the county seat from LeBeau or Scranton. On October 29, 1884,
the town of Bangor was platted by Geo. A. Fessenden on land owned by H. B.
Foster. Immediately this was presented to the voters of Walworth county as
the logical site for the county seat. In the one issue of the "Blue
Blanket" great stress was-placed on the proposition that the commissioners
appointed by the territorial governor had not looked to the best interests
of the county in placing the location at LeBeau. "In fact the commissioners
themselves were, with the exception of Frank Kennedy, foreigners to
Walworth county." That must have come as a surprise to Mr. Wilkins! The
town of Bangor due to the campaign of the "Blue Blanket" and the influence
of the committee received a majority in the election of 1884 and became the
county seat. The court house square donated by H. B. Foster with the
promise of a building was deeded to the county. A building 20 x 40, two
stories with a hip roof was built by Mr. Foster and in this the county
built a fireproof vault.

        Bangor Courthouse after it had been ruined by Selby people during
        the "Courthouse fight".

Bangor became a thriving little town. "The Rustler," a weekly published by
N. G. Parker and J. H. McVean, established in 1885, published glowing
accounts of the vigor and prosperity of the town and surrounding country.
Prominently displayed in the ads were Isaac Perman, attorney; Wagner Bros.
livery; Shaw and Sunderland, painters & glaziers; C.L. Pinkham, notary;
Miss Kate Foster, music teacher; Parmalee & Stablein, pioneer store; H.B.
Foster, Bangor lumber yard; T.G. Orr, attorney; W.B. Burr, county
attorney; B.F. Elliot, real estate; Ernest Tilley, builder; C.P. Lindholm,
grocery. Several railroads, it was announced, were merely marking time
before making Bangor a division with lines east, west, and north and south.

In the 1890's Fred Griffin consolidated The Rustler and The Central
Dakotan, established in 1887, and published under the name of The Walworth
County Record at Bangor.

For sixteen years Bangor held the county seat without dispute. In fact,
located in almost the exact geographical center of the county, the Bangor
people certainly as well as most of the rest of the county, expected it to
remain permanently the county seat.

When in 1899 there was talk of an extension of the Milwaukee railroad west
from Bowdle to the Missouri river, and of a town to be located there to
serve as a shipping point for the huge west river cattle interests, Bangor
confidently anticipated the line running through the town. Early in 1900
when the survey became a reality and the first line was run through the
Spring lake hills four miles north of the town the people were puzzled but
not alarmed. "Merely a preliminary survey" announced Editor Griffin in the
Walworth County Record, "the second and third surveys will run through
Bangor."

A week later, March 3, "The Milwaukee survey is four miles north and headed
straight west, apparently making for Midnight Bench via Blue Blanket
creek". Anxiety and uneasiness arose in Bangor. Groups of men drove out to
watch the survey and question the surveyors who had very little information
to offer. During that week an old time settler in the county reports that
very little business was done in Bangor, most of the population of the town
making daily trips to the survey. Says Editor Griffin, "The party (survey)
seems to be unduly hurried and nervous from some source or another, and we
understand remarks have been dropped indicating that the approach of
surveyors from another road are expected in the near future" --(A suspicion
occurs that the haste and nervousness of the surveying party could have
been due to remarks dropped by the local boys!) Mr. Griffin continues, "The
Record adheres to the belief that the Milwaukee people were forced to the
present move by the plans of some other company and that another road north
and south will be close on the heels of the Milwaukee and take advantage of
any mistake in route that is made. Should the Milwaukee build away from
Bangor, a road north and south could take in a row of county seats and
corral the legitimate business and at the same time cut in on the cattle
trade which seems to be the thing most sought for by the Milwaukee people".

For weeks hope and despair alternated in Bangor, Mr. Griffin's editorials
stoutly insisted that eventually the survey would be changed to include
Bangor, deriding the suggestion that intelligent engineers would consent to
build a road so obviously out of line, enumerating the expense attendant
upon such a course. Supplies for the road and equipment were unloaded at
Bowdle--one hundred and eighty tons of rails, girders, ties, etc.--"A
forehanded move on the part of the railroad", praised Mr. Griffin, "to
expedite matters when the final survey is made".

It was rumored that there would be four towns between Bowdle and the
river--Mr. Griffin as well as the citizenry pooh poohed this extravagant
idea. Nevertheless the survey went on, lots for the Evarts townsite were
sold, township plats were made on the McDowell and Himrich claims and upon
Mrs. John Lowry's homestead, the Evarts plat on the Peter Couchman
property. Rapidly the work progressed and the shining ribbon of steel
lengthened, four miles north of Bangor!

The Rev. S. F. Brown in a series of letters printed in the Record took up
the battle in defense of Bangor-"Bangor Won't Move" was his initial
article--and a new note crept into Editor Griffin's editorials. In the July
21st issue of the Record "Selby the new town 'on the railroad' is platted
and lots are on sale" also. "Petitions are being circulated ... concerning
the removal of the county seat from Bangor to Selby".

In the Record of July 28th Mr. Griffin made his stand plain--"All hope of a
railroad into Bangor is gone". Mr. Griffin proposed moving his paper to
Selby, the new town--advised others to do the same and recommended the new
town as the logical place for the county seat. "Turn Coat!" cried the Rev.
Mr. Brown in his next letter--"Mr. Griffin's personal interest may be best
served by removal to the railroad, but not the county seat". "I am not
fighting Selby" declared Mr. Brown, "What I am working for is to keep
enough interests here (Bangor) to have at least a store, post office,
school, blacksmith shop and church in the county seat--a clean orderly
country village without saloons, gamblers or tramps! The proprietors of
Selby seem to want the world and the-church--! !" Mr. Brown's enthusiasm
for a quiet country village was not accepted so whole-heartedly by ambitious
young business and professional men of Bangor and the exodus to Selby and
other railroad towns began. At the principal sale of Selby town lots at
Bangor August 4, many lots both business and residence, were sold to
Bangorites.

The first record of moving August 4th seems to have been J. J. Hoven's
machine shed, closely followed by his large store building which created
quite a problem for the movers--sixty-four horses being finally required to
finish the job. In the same issue of the paper was the announcement "about
600 signatures were affixed to the petition for the submission of the
question of the removal of the county seat this fall!" The fat was indeed
in the fire! Walworth county was split by a struggle that lasted for eight
years, the fight for possession of the county seat. Selby with its larger
population seemed to be the favorite, but the eastern part of Walworth-with
its new town of Java had a voice, too.

In the elections of November 1900 the county seat remained at Bangor.
"Skullduggery!" cried the Selby faction, "the election was crooked!
Two-thirds of the voters signed the petition." Selby had some foundation
for her protests. In a pledge from Selby to the county that no expense
would be incurred to the county from the county seat removal were such
solid names as: Fred Griffin, S.D. Balch, B.C. Smith, B.A. Amy, J.J.
Elfrink, A.A. Melgaard, H.F. Hoffman & Co., A.F. Miles, F.L. Drake, D.
Kirkhoven, Don Campbell, Gross Bros., B.B. Potter, B.B. Carscallen, R.W.
Reynolds, A.J. Kingman, J.J. Hoven, A.F. Stuck, J.E. Hoefs, S.F.
Hoffman, E.A. Jones, Joseph Treanor, L.W. Maxwell, Lewis & Wilson, W.
Vail & Co., Dr. Beil, W.B. Burr, many of them formerly of Bangor.
Furthermore these men with the further assent of A.S. Taylor, Philip
Lewis, I.F. Smith, J.G. Brady, H.R. Gunderman, M.D., signed a bond of
$5,000 dollars guaranteeing the safe removal of the courthouse, vault,
etc., to Selby without loss to the county in event of removal to Selby of
the county seat.

Without a doubt there was some underlying reason for the election returns
keeping Bangor as county seat despite the fact that Selby had the names of
a majority of the voters of the county on its petition. No proof, how ever,
of any illegal act was forthcoming--the county seat remained in Bangor for
the following four years. During that period there was a great deal of
grumbling and outspoken criticism in the press of the county. In January
1904 Selby again circulated a petition for the removal of the county
seat--so did Java. At the hearing before the county commissioners the list
read 558 for Selby, 336 for Java, out of 994 legal voters in the
county--Selby won by majority. All through the spring, summer and fall of
1904 the county seat struggle took precedence over any other issue in the
county. A final survey made by the Selby faction just preceding election
virtually "cinched" the election for Selby. The towns. people of Selby
prepared a big celebration, there was great rejoicing in the northern half
of the county. The day following the election there was a sudden sober and
stunned reaction. Apparently the voters had retained the county seat at
inland Bangor! Immediately there was an investigation; accusations flew
thick and fast--"The people who had signed the petition had not voted" cried
some--others blamed the press of the county for a too outspoken campaign
which reaped the reward of antagonism. It was found that the votes of one
precinct were nullified because of improper registration--other instances
of intimidation of whole blocks of voters were aired. While these facts
were common knowledge- tangible proof was lacking. In a series of meetings,
more or less played down, an injunction was instigated, acted upon by the
temporarily presiding judge, and served, designating "Selby by due process
of legal contest action as the county seat." On December 17 the contest
evidence was served on the county officials. On December 26, no action
having been taken by said officials, "the county records were moved to
Selby." The quotes are from the Walworth County Record--as a matter of
fact, on the 26th of December at two o'clock in the afternoon, twenty
wagons and teams and some forty husky lads from Walworth county descended
upon the county seat at Bangor--Records and contents of the vault were
loaded and taken to Selby and the courthouse at Bangor literally torn down.
While no doubt this action was neither instigated nor approved by the solid
citizenry of the Selby faction, the fact remains that the crowd of
enthusiastic young men used homemade battering rams of timbers battering
down the walls of the old court house, used spades to clear the shingles
from the roof and in the time between the 26th of December at 2 p.m., and
December 27th at 3 a.m., scattered the timber of the building over the
prairie until nothing remained of the old court house that had stood in the
little town of Bangor for twenty years.

All of these actions left the existing county officials in a
quandry--especially the sheriff and newly elected states attorney. The
sheriff was forced to serve injunctions on both sides, the states attorney
in worse plight was hard pressed by both factions--urged by the Selby
contingent to investigate the legality of the election without tangible
proof, and faced by the actual vandalism in the destruction of the court
house. From a disinterested observation and with the prospective of
forty-five odd years--there seems to be a great deal to be said for both
sides of the burning issue of the time. There is no doubt that Selby was
the logical site for the county seat. On the other hand there seemed to be
a little over-enthusiasm in the method of obtaining it. Litigation followed
litigation--the injunction removing the records to Selby seemed to be in
legal doubt. Carried to the supreme court the verdict was finally against
Selby and after more than a year the records were again returned to Bangor
for the balance of the year of 1906 and 1907 and 1908--but not without one
final try by the Selby people. In early 1906 the town board of Selby moved
to incorporate into Selby a strip of land approximately a city street wide
and four miles long running into the town of Bangor including the court
house square donated by Mr. Foster in 1894 for court house purposes.

Mr. Foster and other landholders fought this move and it came to nothing,
but not before the Aberdeen News the Chicago Herald and New York Times
printed the feature story of "Selby, the little town with a Main street
four miles long." A great deal of bitterness was generated by this county
seat fight. Neighbor took sides against neighbor. No town in the county
preserved a neutral stand. At the time the small town of Evarts was
probably the only one who did not covet the title of county seat.

The new town of Mobridge in 1907, Java, and a flareup of the hopes of
LeBeau enjoying a third era of growth --all sought the court house.

Bangor, reduced to 19 citizens and a half dozen buildings and faced by a
petition for the removal to the rail road of the county seat, signed by
virtually every voter in the county made only a token resistance.
Noncelebration marked the event, no rejoicing even in the Walworth County
Record by Mr. Griffin. Quietly in 1908 the voters of the county chose Selby
as the county seat. Long fought and hard won, there the court house has
remained for 42 years and bids fair to remain for all time.

THE INDIAN SCARE

It was a beautiful late fall day and as the sun sank in the west everything
seemed quiet and peaceful. We had spent a busy day outside in preparation
of the long winter ahead and, being tired, had gone to bed and rest. The
day was Monday, November 20, 1890. There was no snow, the moon was clear
and bright, the whole world seemed at ease when suddenly we heard the hoof
beats of an approaching rider. He came quickly to a stop near the house and
called Will to come outside. Quietly I raised the window and listened,
intently, only to hear the voice of my husband's brother, Eb, who had come
to tell us that the Indians were on the warpath, had crossed the river and
were coming to burn our homes and massacre the people.

Fear struck my heart, not for Will or myself but for my father and mother
who had come to this country to make their home with us and for whom I felt
deeply responsible.

Soon Will came back in and was preparing to go to bed again, when I asked
him what he was going to do and he said "Go to bed," not knowing of my
"eavesdropping" he thought best not to tell us about the Indians until
morning, but I told him, "No, you don't" and then revealed that womanlike I
knew all that had been said outside my window.

Will was not inclined to take the danger of Indians to heart as much as
many others as he had experienced the Indian Scare in Minnesota and knew
that rumors were not always true.

He decided not to go to Bowdle with the family that night as the horses had
worked all day and it would be a long trip, about 20 miles, for a tired
team and hitched to a wagon.

He told Eb to take his family and go but that he would stay and protect his
property, knowing that the Indians could not ravage all the homes and
hoping they would miss ours and we stayed. I tried to think but thoughts
failed to come. Suddenly I burst into tears--then realizing that we must do
something quickly and that we must wake my father and mother and tell them
of our danger.

Mother got up and dressed but father went back to sleep. We called again
and insisted that he get up and help decide what to do. He dressed quietly,
filled and lighted his pipe and sat down in the chair, seeming to feel no
fear at all and said he was content to stay with us,--come what may.

Eb and his wife came over to stay with us and as we had windows on all
sides of the house we began an all night's vigil, watching especially west
and north as that was the direction from which the Indians were to come. We
listened but only the shrill call of the coyotes broke the stillness of the
night. As morning approached the moon grew dim. In the distance we heard
the dogs barking and thought that the Indians were approaching, but it was
only the rattle of a neighbor's (Bassett) wagon in which he had loaded his
wife and new baby.

Morning came at last. We drove to Bangor to find a great many settlers had
come there to make a "fort" and defend themselves as best they could. Among
those were: Schellengers, Cheskys, Elfrinks, Hoefs, Shaws, and many others.
The Marin and Hilde families having found Bangor full had come back to the
old sod shack of the Hollands, as sod could not be seen in the darkness and
was almost fire and bullet proof.

Our friends, the Collins, were there, greatly upset because they believed
we had gone to Bowdle without them. After talking it over we all felt
better as we began to realize that the alarm was probably false and that we
were not in as much danger as we first thought.

Pathos, humor, and tragedy were so closely woven into the lives of the
settlers that night that only after months were we able to smile at the
many stories recounted as we gathered together in our homes and public
places to relieve the strain of the Indian Scare.--By Mrs. Salome Mudge.

A SATCHEL IN HER HAND

Martha Habersdatter was born in Bergen, Norway January 20, 1833, one of a
large family of brothers and sisters. She developed early in life the
aptitude for the care of the sick that was to carry this young Norwegian
girl from her native Norway, first to Iowa and eventually to Dakota
territory. Trained in the old and honorable Scandinavian profession of
midwifery she fulfilled the tradition of generations of the women in her
family. With her little black satchel, the hallmark of her profession as
midwife, and still a young girl she came to Iowa just prior to the Civil
War. There she married Johannes Tisdall and with him came to the Blue
Blanket territory in 1886. To the young Norwegian wives and mothers of this
community Mrs. Tisdall came as a gift from heaven. Many of these homesick
girls with their first babies, could speak no word of English. This small
woman with her kind hands and indomitable courage brought the memory of
their homes in Norway, with the firm ministrations of the trained midwives
of that land.

        Mrs. Johannes Tisdall

Gradually her fame spread from her own community to those adjoining. Many
years ahead of her generation in the firm conviction that cleanliness was
the first requisite in the care of any illness, Martha Tisdall went on
calmly combating age old superstitions on the one hand and the rather sour
disapproval of the medical profession on the other. With quiet insistence
she substituted clean hot water for warm chicken blood or weasel skins, for
treatment of infections, boiled water and boiled milk in typhoid cases,
clean linen and rigid sanitation for obstetrics. The physicians of her day
gave her first grudging acceptance and finally whole hearted admiration and
respect. Digressing for a moment, let it be said that there were no
hospital-trained nurses in these communities at that time and the average
so-called midwife entirely untrained, justified the physician's darkest
suspicions. They were well meaning enough, but too often the doctor's best
efforts were frustrated and his work undone through sheer ignorance.

Mrs. Tisdall delivered countless babies alone, often under the most trying
circumstances. No one ever asked for her help in vain. Night or day, in the
bitter cold of winter, the mud of early spring and fall, the prostrating
heat of Dakota summer she traveled to aid the sick, minister to the newborn
or the dying, rejoice with the happy relief of convalescence or comfort the
bereft. Her stature was small, she was a tiny woman, but she was mighty in
spirit. Though not entirely understanding, her patients and friends learned
to respect her principles and it became a standing joke to say--"Martha is
coming, put the kettles on!" Many times a weary doctor, worn out with the
battle for life on a difficult case, drew a deep breath of relief at the
advent of this small, calm, smiling woman, knowing that in her capable
hands his work would be safe. One early day physician, receiving tearful
and heartfelt thanks for a life saved, paid her deserving tribute "Rather
thank Mrs. Tisdall," he said, "The doctor is the Big Gun but Martha is the
man behind the gun! "

Men and women, grandparents in their turn, recite the legend of Martha
Tisdall. The stories of her exploits are many and varied. One elderly lady
tells of the birth of her first child during the dreadful winter of '88.
Seven times on ski and snow shoe, Martha Tisdall made the perilous distance
over deep snow and ice and through a raging blizzard before that young man
made his reluctant appearance. Another time during the breaking of the ice
in the Missouri river she crossed the river in a row boat. One large Indian
rowed the boat, another fended off the swirling chunks of ice that
threatened to smash the frail craft to kindling. One small woman sat in the
middle of the boat,--no doubt she prayed. She was needed on that farther
bank and she went.

Many were the anxious eyes, during those years that watched for her tiny
figure, carrying her little black satchel--a little black satchel of magic
properties, for out of it came all sorts of comforts and necessities, and
such an amazing supply of peppermint drops for "good children."

In her later years she became Grandma Tisdall, not alone to her own
grandchildren, but to the whole community. She died in 1914 at the age of
81. Of her living children one son, Jake lives near Selby, Oliver in
Bremerton, Washington, and a daughter, Sophia, in California.

Across half of the world from Bergen, Norway to a pioneer community on the
South Dakota prairie, Martha Tisdall born Martha Habersdatter, carried her
gift of service in her heart. A Florence Nightingale of the Prairie with a
little black satchel in her hand.

HISTORY OF SELBY WATERWORKS

When the first residents of Selby arrived in sufficient number to make it
worth while for someone to make a business of it water was hauled into town
in a big tank from a 4 x 4 foot flowing well situated about 50 yards south
of the present well site on the Emanuel Himrich farm east of town. This
area along the north and west banks of the dry water way, known as "the
creek", was wet and springy and sufficient water flowed out of the ground
to supply the small population of the town. It has long been believed in
Selby that quite an extensive shallow, artesian basin lies east and south
of town following the course of the creek and fed by seep water in the
valley. The fact that the water level falls in dry season and rises when it
rains indicates that the basin is dependent on surface seep for refill. Dr.
Rothrock, in an examination of the area in November of 1949 at the request
of the City Council of Selby came to the conclusion that the artesian basin
was much smaller than has generally been supposed, but that it was
sufficient to furnish a water supply for a city many times the size of
Selby. Back in the drouth period serious consideration was given to the
proposition of putting in a dam across the valley south of the railroad
tracks, and impounding a lake of many acres, the same to serve as a
permanent and inexhaustible water supply and recreation ground.
Difficulties in making arrangements with the Milwaukee railroad, then in
the hands of Receivers, prevented such action, but this can be done any
time if the need should ever arise.

Two artesian wells were also drilled in the town of Selby; one on lot 2 of
block 13 and the other on lot 17, block 3. These wells were approximately
1960 feet deep but the water was not considered good for house hold
purposes. The one on block 13 seeped for several years and was eventually
piped into the city sewer and will probably never be opened. The one on
block 3 was pumped for many years and the water used for washing purposes.
The owners found it profitable to vend the water around town, filling
cisterns from a tank on wheels for a long time, but the installation of
water softeners and hot water heaters-in the homes has practically replaced
the use of the soft artesian waters, and probably at some not far distant
date this well will also be abandoned. It has never flowed, being on
somewhat higher ground than the other one.

In the year 1910 the City of Selby voted bonds for water works and a
pneumatic pressure system was installed. A city building was erected and
two 15 h. p. Fairbanks Morse gas engines with combination pumps were
installed each with a capacity of 300 gallons per minute. A steel reservoir
of 32,000 gallon capacity was installed. Main and service lines were laid
throughout the city. Out at the water source a large well was put down and
pipes laid via the pumps in town to the pressure tank. The supply soon
proved insufficient and another well, 10 feet in diameter, was dug adjacent
to the other and a small engine was installed to pump the water. Fifteen
fire hydrants were installed in town.

In 1921 a 4 inch pipe line was laid into the city and a heavy duty pump
driven by an electric motor was installed. Three more fire hydrants were
added at this time and the water lines extended to the schoolhouse and
elsewhere about town where needed, including a line to the west section of
town and the Fair Grounds. An underground concrete tank reservoir of 40,000
gallons capacity was added. A centrifugal pump, motor driven with a
capacity of 80 gallons per minute at 60 pounds pressure was installed in
the city building known by now as the "Power House." The system was
improved in 1938 by the addition of another concrete reservoir and was
further extended, both jobs being WPA projects.

The Selby water supply was the seventh system in the state to be approved
by the State Board of Health for purity. It has never failed of approval;
the water though very hard due to the presence of minerals, is very good
from the standpoint of human consumption and its purity has been closely
and carefully guarded.

Thirty-seven years is a long time in the history of any system and for some
time before action was taken in 1947, it was apparent to the city council
and interested citizens that the Selby water system had about served out
its time. The mains were giving way occasionally, pipes were clogging and
in most homes the pressure was low. Those who connected directly to the
mains and who had their lead-in pipes cleaned or renewed had water pressure
while others did not.

The Staven Engineering Company of Rapid City was employed by the city to
make. a survey of the situation and make recommendations to the City
Council. Their report set out the true state of affairs and steps were
taken at once to modernize the system. In accordance with the law petitions
were circulated and signed by practically 100% of the citizens. The council
acted as speedily as possible, finding it necessary to float a bond issue
of $70,000 to cover the costs.

It was intended at first to use the old supply tanks and pressure tank, but
the representatives of the insurance companies announced that this system
did not afford the fire protection that would justify the present insurance
rates and that unless an elevated tank which would guarantee the
maintenance of pressure in the mains, was installed the insurance rates
would go up. The contract provided for this tank, standardizing of the
mains throughout the city, and the bringing of water service within easy
reach of every home in town. The job was completed in 1948.

Today Selby has one of the best water systems in the state, according to
competent engineers. The rate structure is set so that the money will be
ready to retire the bonds when they fall due. The water supply is ample to
meet the needs of the city even though it grew beyond the hopes of those
most enthusiastic.

HISTORY OF LAKE HIDDENWOOD

        LAKE HIDDENWOOD PICNIC GROUNDS

Nestling among the rolling hills surrounding the ancient bed of Hiddenwood
creek, flanked on the north and east by haughty bluffs of verdant beauty,
and on the south by gentle slopes that form a natural bathing beach, lies
the scenic beauty spot of Walworth county,--Lake Hiddenwood. The lake is
located about four miles northeast of Selby, and the name aptly describes
it, as it is hidden from view by the hills which surround and form a
natural basin for it, and one cannot see it until one practically there.

In 1925, the lake was but a vague dream conceived by a group of farsighted
men. Early in 1926, the matter was discussed at a meeting of the Selby
commercial club, and a committee made up of H. P. Gutz, E. A. Walter and A.
H. Schmidt, was appointed to investigate the feasibility of an artificial
lake project at this site and to enlist the aid of state officials. Through
their efforts the interest of Gov. Carl Gunderson, Secretary of Agriculture
B. F. Myers and Oscar Johnson, director of the State Game and Fish
commission, was aroused and they arranged for the state to pay for the land
actually flooded and for the construction of the dam, through Fish and Game
department funds. The game commission also agreed to stock the lake with
fish when the proper time came. The local committee agreed to purchase and
pay for the land adjacent to the proposed lake and to dedicate it for
public use forever. Enthusiastic support was received from the surrounding
communities and from the county and a tentative purchase was made of the NE
1/4 of section 23-124-76, for $25.00 an acre, a down payment being made to
the owner, Barney Nusz, for an option on the land.

In April 1926, state engineers investigated the practicability of
developing this natural resource and as a result of their recommendation,
the lake was located on this quarter of land which formed a natural lake
bed, the widest and deepest part of Hiddenwood creek running through a
deep, wide valley extending east and west and narrowing at the west end
where the hills formed a natural part of the proposed dam. By the middle of
May the work of moving earth and starting the construction of an earthen
dam was underway. County Highway Supt. F. E. Gehrki was in charge of the
dirt moving, and County Commissioners H. P. Gutz, Selby, and Jacob Helm,
Java, devoted much time helping and advising. Dirt for the dam was secured
by excavating from the valley, thereby deepening the potential lake bed.
This lake was one of the first artificial lakes to be built by use of an
earthen dam, and the experiment was watched with interest throughout the
state. Its ultimate success paved the way for an extensive program of the
game and fish department in which many similar lakes were built all over
the state.

At a meeting in Selby in April 1926, the Lake Hiddenwood association had
been organized with H. P. Gutz as president, A. C. Dobson as secretary, and
A. R. Scott, Glenham, W. F. Mailand, Mobridge, and Jacob Helm, Java, as
vice presidents, the five forming a board of directors. Plans were made for
financing the project by a sale of lots along the shores of the lake.

Early on the morning of Friday, May 28, 1926 when work on the dam was
nearing completion, a very heavy rain of several inches fell in the
vicinity of the lake area, and the next morning Lake Hiddenwood was a
beautiful reality, the bed being full and a small trickle going over the
concrete spillway at one end of the dam.

The following Sunday, people came from miles around to see the new "lake."
There had been considerable doubt on the part of some that a lake would
form there, but now the success of the project was assured.

        Picnic Shelterhouse at Lake Hiddenwood.

About 12,000 cubic yards of dirt were needed to form the dam. The lake
averages about 40 or 50 acres in extent and during years of normal rainfall
attains a depth of 20 to 30 feet in places.

On June 19, 1926 a big Opening Day and Lot Sale was held at the lake with
Agricultural Secretary Myers of Pierre, as the main speaker. The sale of
the lots was conducted by Auctioneer J. E. Myler of Gettysburg, who sold
the first lot to L. R. Stacy of Mobridge, for $100. Robert Nusz, Selby,
paid the highest price for any one lot and received a prize of $25, offered
to the highest bidder. When the sale ended, a total of $3,150 had been
raised for the coffers of the association. Although this was not enough to
pay off the obligations, more money kept coming in as time went on, and
before long, the association was on its feet financially. After the sale, a
program of sports was held, Earl Erbe, of near Java, gave free tides on his
motor boat, and many people sought relief from the record high temperature
of the day in the coolness of the lake waters.

When the lake was formed, many of the natural trees and shrubs which had
bordered the creek bed, were flooded with the result that many of them
died. A number of attempts were made by lot owners and other groups to
plant trees but in the dry years which followed, most of them perished. The
drought also lowered the lake level to the extent that many fish died, the
water became stagnant and unfit for swimming and for a number of years,
interest in the lake lagged.

In the fall of 1937, the county commissioners decided to sponsor the
development and improvement of the lake as a WPA project. Work commenced
that fall on building terraces on the sloping hills on the south side of the
lake, which were naturally adaptable to this form of landscaping. The work
was done under the direction of extension foresters from state college, who
now consider Lake Hiddenwood as one of the finest models of this kind of
landscaping in the state. During the winter, whenever weather permitted,
holes were dug on the terraces for the trees to be planted the next spring.
A total of 3,000 trees were planted in April 1938 and many thousands more
have been planted in successive plantings since then. During the next two
years the lake site was further improved and developed with the use of NYA
and WPA labor. The dam was riprapped to reinforce it, the beach was
graveled, a picnic shelterhouse was built of native stone at the picnic
grounds beside the creek at the east end of the lake, bath houses were
constructed at the beach, and outdoor grills and furnaces were built on the
picnic grounds, among other conveniences.

The ground around the shelterhouse was landscaped with shrubs and trees, and
it was surrounded by a low rock wall. Pathways were built and graveled to
make accessible the numerous natural picnic spots on both sides of the
creek, which were cleared of underbrush and provided with benches and
tables built from native wood. Roads leading to all parts of the lake were
also improved and graveled. The lake had been stocked with fish in August
1926 and the following January, another planting was made. In June 1927,
the lake was opened for fishing to boys and girls under 16 only. Since that
time, many plantings of fish have been made until today, it is one of the
popular fishing spots in this part of the state.

On several occasions, the lake was endangered when heavy rains resulted in
such a heavy runoff that the spillways and parts of the dam were washed
away several times and it was only by hard work on the part of local men
who sandbagged the dam, that the lake was saved from complete destruction.
This danger was remedied several years ago when a new bridge and spillway
were constructed, the dam was widened and raised and the face riprapped
with stone, the project costing approximately $30,000. About this time, the
newly reorganized State, Game and Fish department was taking over many of
the artificial lakes in the state as a part of a state park system. The
local association deemed it advisable to have Lake Hiddenwood designated as
a state park, as thereby it would be under the supervision Terracing on the
South Side of Lake Hiddenwood. of a state park supervisor, and would also
be maintained by the state department. Since the lake became a state park,
considerable improvement work has been carried on. More picnic space has
been provided, a new footbridge was built over the creek at the picnic
grounds. Trees were pruned and cared for, dead trees were replaced with new
plantings and the grounds otherwise improved and beautified. The lake has
also been designated as a wildlife reserve.

An interesting story in connection with the Hiddenwood site was told by the
late W. E. Hoffman, pioneer of Bangor and Selby. He stated that he and his
father, G. H. Hoffman and brother, Sig Hoffman visited the lake area in
1883, and found the body of an Indian suspended on a raised platform on the
north side of the creek in the timbered gulley where Hidden Beauty Park is
now situated. He also related that there was a crossing a few rods to the
south of the mouth of this gulley, which showed signs of being used
frequently, presumably by Indians traversing the area, and probably by
government freighters traveling north and south. The presence of Indians in
the Hiddenwood area in considerable numbers at one time, has also been
verified by the finding of caches of flint arrowheads in land worked near
the lake. The earliest white resident of Hiddenwood valley was W. P.
Winkley, who established a home on what has since become the Lutz place.
Mr. Winkley grazed his cattle in the area west of the lake site and watered
them in the water holes which never went dry in the creek east of the
present lake site.

Today, the lake is one of the most popular recreation spots in this part of
the state. Residents of Walworth as well as many of the surrounding
counties spend many days every summer enjoying picnicking, fishing,
swimming and boating at the lake and there is hardly a day when the lake is
not visited by someone. Ideal growing conditions in recent years have
developed the young trees and made the lake a true beauty spot, which has
repaid and will continue to repay in pleasure and enjoyment, many times the
initial cost of the project as well as its maintenance through the years.
