HISTORY OF SELBY SCHOOLS

        SELBY CONSOLIDATED SCHOOLS

A history of the Selby schools should start with a story of the Bangor and
Hiddenwood schools, which are today a part of the Selby school system. The
Bangor history would contribute more to the early story of the Selby
school, which was in reality a continuation of the Bangor school. The
Bangor school system consisted of two rural schools and a school in the
town of Bangor, with the school in town offering courses up to and
including the 9th grade. Hiddenwood district was also made up of three
rural schools, with one school board supervising the three institutions.

The start of Selby, which came with the extension of the railroad westward,
also marked the end of Bangor, and made it necessary to set up a school in
the newly born town. It is known that the old Woodman hall served for a
time as a school until the new school building could be built. One of the
prominent educators of Selby's early day schools was Prof. G. J.
Schellenger. A wooden structure was completed about 1904 on the lots now
occupied by the homes of Mrs. Lottie Sawinsky and A. H. Schmidt. The board
of education, consisting of J. E. Hoefs, chairman; Wm. H. Mudge, clerk, and
Evan Jones, treasurer, moved into Selby right along with the rest of Bangor
continuing as the school board of Bangor district No. 6. In 1907, records
show that the 11th grade was introduced in the Selby schools, so it can be
taken with assurance, that the 10th grade was offered in Selby up to that
year. This was an important step as it paved the way for the first
graduating class in 1908, when with Mr. Otho Kenyon as principal, the 12th
grade was included along with the courses generally taught in high schools
of South Dakota at that time. In the spring of 1909 on June 5, four seniors
were graduated and led the way for the hundreds to follow. They were: Erma
Gunderman, Ida Schmidt, Bessie Clark and May E. Hoefs. These first
graduation exercises were held at the opera house with Dr. Warren of
Yankton college, as the commencement speaker. His theme was timely and
appropriate with the title, "Work." What an achievement for a new town, to
be on its way educationally, in such a short while and one can see the
determination of the people, who in the space of a few years, had succeeded
in establishing a complete high school course. Today, the graduates of
Selby high school have traveled over the world and made their mark.

In the fall of 1910 it was apparent that the school building was inadequate
to accommodate all the pupils satisfactorily and the board of education
purchased the old Bangor courthouse and arranged for A. E. Birkholt to move
it to Selby. It is said that upon the arrival of the buildings at the city
limits, there was a bit of political sparring between the board of
education and a local citizen The latter swore that he would secure an
injunction to forbid the placing of the old courthouse on the school
grounds, which was countered by the reply that an injunction would be
secured forbidding the using of the grounds at all. The latter argument
being deemed the most forbidding, the hostilities ended. It is presumed the
little tiff stemmed from the courthouse Light. While the Bangor courthouse
was being moved into Selby, it was found necessary to place a rural school
building on the corner north of where Walter Seyer now lives, to
accommodate children in that part of the town ship.

        First school building in Selby. This structure burned down in 1913.

In 1911, the assessed valuation of the Bangor district was set at $370,236,
which at that time was an imposing figure. Then came woe! On the morning of
January 14, 1913, the Selby school house burned to the ground, together
with all contents. At a special meeting of the school board that afternoon,
action was taken to secure quarters so that school could be continued. The
Gunderman building was leased (this is the present site of the Pressler
hardware) and also rooms above the harness shop (the present Rose McIntosh
store building) and were used as classrooms. On February 26, 1913, with a
vote of 98-12 the district approved a bond issue for $11,000 for a new
brick structure to replace the destroyed school. On March 25, Architect
George Issenhuth of Huron, was secured to design the new building and on
April 29, a contract was let to John Schilt of Redfield, for the new
building which was to be located on land north of Main street, purchased by
the board so that the school would stand at the head of the town. An
interesting item states that G. C. Clark was hired to move a hay stack from
the spot where the building was to be placed. Another significant note was
that the new location was in Hiddenwood township, which was soon to be
consolidated with Bangor township.

By November 25, the new building was completed and the heating plant was
installed so that on December 1, 1913, the pupils were able to enter the
new structure,--back again in a building of their own. It was no longer
necessary to use the old Bangor courthouse and it was sold. A few years
later, it too, was destroyed by fire.

In 1917, the board decided to introduce domestic science and agriculture
into the curriculum. When no agriculture teacher could be obtained, manual
training was substituted. At this time electric wiring for lights and
stoves was also completed. This same year, the 3rd and 4th grades were so
crowded in one room, that it was necessary to separate them and Mrs. Leo
Buchanan was secured to teach the 3rd grade for the remainder of the year.

About this time a rumor about the consolidation of Bangor district No. 6
and Hiddenwood No. 5 was appearing like a glow on the horizon. It grew into
a movement and arguments were aired, pro and con, and according to reports
were not always cool nor suitable for parlor discussion. The school board
investigated the matter of consolidation thoroughly, visiting McLaughlin,
the nearest consolidated district school. Legal opinions were also sought.
This was in 1917 to 1919 and was a forward-looking movement which is still
continuing in this year of 1950, when there is a growing tendency toward
combining small districts into larger units throughout the state. On May
14, 1919, the order for the consolidation of the two districts was given by
the county superintendent of schools of Walworth county and there arose the
problems of a new building program and the transportation for students from
the rural areas. On May 28, 1919, the first meeting was held of the board
of education of Selby Independent Consolidated school district No. 2, which
replaced Bangor No. 6 and Hiddenwood No. 5. A. H. Smith, who served for
many years as chairman of Bangor district, was elected chairman of the new
board of education. G. C. Pierce, G. W. Vail, E. H. Noteboom and Paul
Elfrink were the other members. R. George Smith, superintendent, was
elected clerk, as was the custom at that time.

Weekly meetings were held to complete arrangements for the new system. The
old rural schoolhouses from Bangor and Hiddenwood districts were moved to
the schoolground in town to accommodate the increased number of students.
More ground east of the town school was secured for the site of the new
building, if and when it was built. Teachers' cottages were discussed but
no action was ever taken. After some discussion, five International truck
chassis were purchased from the Overholser-Leach Hardware Co., which also
furnished the bodies for the busses. These were not numbered as of today,
but carried the names of the old individual school districts like schooners
across a prairie sea. The next item was a garage for the busses, and plans
were drawn up by Charles Johnson, a contract was let and the garage built.
Drivers were then selected, Chas. Birkholt being one of the first, and R.
L. Swift was employed as head mechanic.

During this same time, a bond issue for $100,000 for a new schoolhouse was
turned down by the voters of the district. The sum was then cut in half and
on October 4, 1919, it was approved 130 to 111 to bond for $50,000 for a
building program. A building was designed by G. F. Fossum and bids were
called for but when they were opened on April 8, 1920, the amounts were too
high and an additional bond issue of $35,000 was submitted to the voters
for approval. The vote on May 8, 1920, was 97 for and 158 against. It was a
troubled district. Not even a night school, started in November, 1920,
could help, as it folded up in a couple of months for lack of enthusiasm.
While pondering the difficulty of insufficient funds for a building
program, the board received a lengthy petition from a considerable group of
patrons asking that the matter of building a new schoolhouse be dropped, in
fact, asking that the whole consolidation idea be abandoned. The board
replied that they did not have the power to abandon this matter and
furthermore felt that to do so would thwart a progressive community. Bids
were once more called for and this time a more suitable bid was received
and accepted. Overholser & Leach were awarded the contract for plumbing,
heating and ventilation and the entire amount came to about $60,000. The
voters were asked to approve additional bonds in the amount of $11,000
which they did on June 21, 1921, with a vote of 211-135. The building began
to materialize and on December 1, 1921, the teachers and pupils moved into
the new high school rooms. But all was still not roses. On December 17 of
that year, the board had to secure legal aid to fight proponents of
dissolving the consolidation.

        How many can you recognize? This picture of the students and
        teachers of the Selby school was taken November 3, 1912, about 2
        months before the structure was destroyed by fire.

                SELBY 1950 BOARD OF EDUCATION

        Walter Hieb, Vice President
        Max Gutz, President
        Walter C. Seyer, Member
        Wilson W. Wolff, Member
        Theodore Schanzenbach, Treasurer
        Robert Mickelson, Clerk
        Wm. Rosin, Member

The first superintendent of the new school was H. S. Freese. After the
building program was settled, the quarrel over consolidation died down, and
new problems of transportation faced the board. Drivers were secured with
difficulty. They were not satisfied with the pay allotted,--$1.25 per trip
or $2.50 per day. Roads made winter driving impossible and teams and sleds
had to be used.

The school waxed strong under the capable leadership of Samuel Smith, who
was elected in 1923 and served for 8 years. The Selby Womans club made a
substantial donations to the grade and high school libraries. It was ruled
that children entering school were required to be 6 years of age before
September 1, a ruling later changed to January 1, and then in 1946 to
November 1. In 1932 the transportation problem reached an acute stage. and
the board sought bids to have a private individual take on the job. Only
one bid was received and was considered too high so the school continued to
carry on. Because of the current depression, there was also a financial
crisis and the board was presented with a petition asking them to cut costs
25%, to discontinue using the busses for basketball trips, and have the
superintendent discontinue as clerk, the latter practice being held
unlawful. The petition also asked that domestic science and manual training
be discontinued as an economy measure. The courses were dropped and have
never been put back into the curriculum to date. Robert Nusz was named as
the new clerk. Teachers' wages were cut as were those of bus drivers, who
now received only 50 cents a trip ($1.00 a day) and in those hard times,
they welcomed the $1.00.

In 1933, a ban was placed on lady teachers, revoking their contract if they
married during the year. A revision came later which banned local as well
as married lady teachers. These rules were all scrapped during the
emergency of the last war, when every available qualified teacher was
welcomed. In 1934, plans for a dormitory were set up, which was operated in
the Auburn hotel. In this year, a gallery was also built in the gymnasium
to accommodate a larger number of spectators.

Several events set 1939 apart as one of the big years in the history of the
Selby schools. This year, George T. Mickelson became a member of the board
of education. He was a graduate of Selby high school and at one time drove
one of the school busses. Events that took place soon after he took his
oath of office were of singular importance. The school district was in the
red,--not because of excessive spending but because of non-collection of
taxes due the district. To make matters worse, the district had several
bonds coming due, and had no funds to pay them. The board immediately set
up the machinery for refunding the bonds, thereby effecting an interest
saving of 1-1/2%. An order was issued to the county sheriff to collect back
taxes. This, with aid from the state, provided the money to keep the school
going. The bonds had been set up so they could be paid off in 1944 and on
November 1 of that year, the last of the bonds were retired and the
district had weathered its long financial storm.

In the past few weeks, with the cooperation of the school and the city, the
athletic field was improved and enlarged. In athletics, the Selby teams,
named the Lions, have demonstrated that they have just that sort of heart.
They have represented Selby twice in the state basketball tournament, and
on other occasions have won district titles. They have also had some
outstanding teams in football and track.

Since its beginning, Selby high school has always been interested in the
extracurricular fields. Back in the early history of the high school, Mrs.
W. A. George directed the school plays, and what masterful productions they
were! Much fine work was done through the years in debate, declamation and
other speech work. In 1946, David Hoven and Mavis Himrich won state titles
in dramatic prose and poetry reading, respectively, Selby being the only
high school in the state to have two state winners in a single year. This
coupled with the election of Selby's favorite son as the Governor of South
Dakota, was a significant triumph for speech development. Selby high has
also been prominent in the music field in this part of the state. Girls and
boys glee clubs have been outstanding in many years of the school's
history. Records show that the glee clubs have been sent to Sioux Falls,
Yankton and Aberdeen to participate in state music meets. Mixed choruses,
ensembles and soloists have helped to round out a well balanced music
department. The band, functioning sporadically, has gained laurels and
contributes to many outstanding local events.

Time and space does not permit us to mention all who have served on the
Board of Education but there are a few who deserve special mention. Perhaps
the outstanding member was A. H. Smith, who began his service in the early
days and continued through the turbulent times of the consolidation. At the
time when the new high school building was erected, A. H. Smith, G. W. Vail,
P. R. Elfrink, Edward Himrich and Robert Abel were the members. During the
financial crisis of 1939, Theodore Bohle, Fred Schell, Wm. Lemburg and
Lloyd Sawinsky served with George Mickelson. The present board, consisting
of Max Gutz, president; Walter Hieb, Wilson Wolff, Walter Seyer and William
Rosin, have back of them, the time and sweat of men who struggled mightily
for the welfare of the Selby schools. They, too, have a problem in trying
to match the present school to the highgeared living conditions of today.
Of the district treasurers, Evan Jones was the first. Others who gave years
of faithful service were H. P. Gutz and Wm. G. Chesky. The present
treasurer is Theodore Schanzenbach. W. H. Mudge was the first clerk but
after that the school superintendents held the office until 1932 when Robert
Nusz was elected. He served until 1942 when he moved away and Frank Gehrki
took his place, the latter moving away, and the present clerk is Robert
Mickelson.

The history of the Selby schools is not closed. It will go on for years to
come. Many of the men and women who have passed through its portals, have
gone on to secure a higher education, others made their future at home with
the training received in the Selby school. It is encouraging to find that
many have returned to occupy positions of importance in the community and
their own children are today attending the same school. Others have gone
out into the world and made a place for themselves which reflects with
credit upon the training they received in the Selby schools.

HISTORY OF SELBY CHURCHES

        THE FREUDENTHAL CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH (1909-1949)

The history of the Selby Freudenthal Congregational church begins in
conjunction with the conducting of services at Selby, Lowry and Akaska.
These three fields were organized in 1897 by Rev. Heinrich Vogler. These
three fields were known by the inclusive name of "Glueckstal" or Valley of
Luck. This name was later adopted by the present Congregational church at
Akaska.

According to the church records a small group of devout and courageous men
and women gathered in the cold of winter on the 4th of January, 1909, to
formally organize themselves into a church. They called it the "Freudenthal
Congregational Church" of Selby. The charter members of this church were:
John Himrich and his wife, Wilhelmina; Edward Waker and his wife, Pauline,
together with their children, John, George and Elizabeth; Jacob and
Christina Christman; Peter Sieler and his wife, Emma; and George and
Katherine Wolf.

After the Rev. Heinrich Vogler the parish was served by the Rev. Konrad
Wagner from 1904-1908. The next man was the Rev. Heinrich Baumann, who
served the churches while living on his farm near Lowry. He served for
1-1/2 years or until 1910. In that year the Rev. Herman Reuteman came and
remained until 1912. It was during his time of service that a parsonage was
built in Akaska. The Rev. Jacob Weiszenburger came in 1912 and served until
1915. It was during his pastorate that the present St. Peters
Congregational church of Glenham was organized on the 7th of December, 1913.

As the little city of Selby grew the church grew with it. Thus during the
pastorate of the Rev. Henry Uhl from 1915-1917 the parsonage was moved from
Akaska to Selby. Ever after this the parish was called the "Selby Parish".

The Selby Congregational church exerted a wholesome influence on town and
community during the years from 1918-1921 under the able leadership of the
Rev. Adam Franke. Those were the years of the great flu epidemic and the
religious consolation of the men of God was greatly appreciated. The year
1922 brought the Rev. Theo. Pfennig to the Selby parish. The ground work
for the future was laid during the years of his service. Meetings of
worship had been conducted in the homes, later in the school house and
still later in the vacated Episcopal church. Under this man's progressive
leadership the Episcopal church was purchased from the Selby American
Legion on the 18th of April, 1922, for the sum of $2500.00. On May 21,
1922, the first church service was conducted in the evening by the Rev.
Pfennig. It was incorporated and formally dedicated on September 24, 1922.
In the last year of service for the Rev. Pfennig, the parish of Selby,
Lowry, Akaska and Glenham was divided, thereby offering the opportunity for
better services. The Selby and Glenham churches became one parish and Lowry
and Akaska the other.

The next pastor was a young, zestful and ambitious leader, Rev. Theo.
Radach. Under his faithful guidance the parish made great strides in growth
and spiritual influence. The year 1928 saw the present parsonage built at a
cost of $5200.00. In the year 1929 the Sutley Congregational church, north
of Java, became a part of the Selby parish. These three congregations
constitute the parish at the present time.

During the drouth years the church was served by the Rev. Chris Maedche,
1934-38, and the Rev. Philip Reich from 1939-41. As the drought years
passed and conditions improved the need for improvements in the Selby
church were also felt. Under the spirited and able leadership of the Rev.
Elmer Bettenhausen, 1941-45 the church edifice was completely remodeled
with a full basement and beautified interior and was rededicated in the year
of 1944. The Rev. Jacob Nein served a short time from 1945-46. The present
pastor, Rev. Ernest H. Sprenger, began his duties in the parish on July 1,
1947.

Parish records from 1917-49 show the following statistics for the churches
in the parish: There were 256 baptisms, 188 marriages performed, 21
confirmation classes with a total of 314 confirmants and 84 deaths.

        ST. JOHN'S AMERICAN LUTHERAN CHURCH

Lutheran believers in this area started to have church services in 1900,
being served by neighboring mission pastors. A congregation was not
organized until 1903, when the St. John's Lutheran church was established
with seven charter members: Henry Nusz Sr., Johannes Wagner, John Nusz,
Karl Milde, William Simon, John I. Wagner and Gottfried Wagner, who is the
only living charter member.

As the town of Selby grew and the community became more densely settled the
congregation also grew. Services were mostly held in the court room of the
Walworth county court house until January 23, 1910, when it was decided to
purchase the Methodist church for the sum of $1500 from which time the
congregation continued to grow and progress. About this time a parish was
organized with Lowry and Akaska which lasted until 1917 when the Selby
congregation felt they were large enough to support a pastor alone. In
order to have a parsonage the congregation decided to purchase the Lincke
home across the street from the church, the Rev. Gieken being the first
pastor.

In 1919 the congregation from McLaughlin and Wakpala asked that the pastor
from Selby be allowed to hold services in their congregation every fourth
Sunday. The result of this arrangement was that a parish was organized with
the pastor residing in Selby.

The Selby congregation purchased an altar and a new organ in the next few
years.

In 1929 the parish decided to build a new parsonage and sell the old one,
the new house to cost $5000, which was nearly all paid by voluntary
subscriptions.

The congregation proceeded to grow as did the congregations from McLaughlin
and Wakpala until 1932 when these congregations decided they wanted and
could support a pastor of their own.

Since Lowry and Akaska did not have a pastor, an arrangement was approved
whereby the Selby pastor would hold services in Selby every other Sunday,
and Lowry and Akaska on alternate Sundays.

The Selby congregation has grown to such an extent that the church has
proven too small in many instances and another church had to be rented. In
the last few years work has been done towards building a new church. A
building committee was named, who were to collect money and accept pledges
for a new church. The building committee collected a nice sum of money and
a considerable amount was pledged but with the high cost of-material and
labor it was not sufficient and therefore the building of a new church has
been postponed until conditions are more satisfactory.

The present officers of the church are: beacons, William Rosin, Walter
Hieb, Arthur Bauder, Robert Himrich, treasurer, Andrew Sulzle; secretary,
Emil Wagner; trustees, William Bauder, Christ Weiszhaar, and Fred Seyer;
sexton, Henry Scherer.

        THE METHODIST CHURCH

The beginning of the Methodist church in Selby dates back to the year 1884,
when the Rev. Samuel F. Brown filed on land here and preached in the homes
of the settlers. For the first two years, Mr. Brown preached whenever he
came out to make residence on his claim. In the meantime, any minister who
came, regardless of denomination or creed, carried on the work begun by Mr.
Brown.

In 1886, the Rev. Mr. Brown brought his family to Walworth county, and
established his home. The Board of Home Missions of the Methodist church
paid a small salary. This, with the collections at the church services,
comprised the remuneration for his pastoral services in the newly settled
community. He preached also at La Grace, Mound City, Bowdle, and other
points. He continued to serve the church whenever there was need, until
about the year 1900, although other pastors, a Mr. Perry, A. D. Smith, J.
B. Dibble, W. O. Gram, a Mr. Hitch, and P. T. Ingersoll, were appointed at
several intervals, up to this time.

The Rev. Mr. Brown, after his pastorate, continued as a faithful and useful
member of the church and church board, until the year of his death in 1908,
at the age of 83 years. His memory is perpetuated by a beautiful memorial
art window in the north wall of the present edifice.

The new court house at Bangor was completed in 1884. Its upper room became
a school room, as well as Sunday school and church room for the Methodists,
until their own church structure was erected in 1898. The lumber for this
building was hauled from Gettysburg. The hauling and most of the building
was volunteer work.

In the year 1902, during the pastorate of the Rev. P. T. Ingersoll, this
structure was moved to Selby, and placed upon the present site. In March,
1910, it was sold to the St. John's Lutheran congregation.

P. T. Ingersoll was closely succeeded in the pastorate here, by the
Reverends Johnson, Hastings, and Albert Hartl. It was under the inspiration
and supervision of the Rev. Albert Hartl, who served from 1909 to 1911.
that the present structure was erected. The cost of building was $12,500,
and for several years there was a debt on it. It was dedicated on March 4,
1911.

The three pastors who succeeded Mr. Hartl, were J. A. Willey, H. S.
Williamson and Henry D. Gough. During the latter's pastorate, 1915-1919,
the debt was paid, and there was a joyous mortgage burning.

Those who closely succeeded Mr. Gough are L. L. Lane, Arthur Edwards, and
C. C. Boslaugh. Under the pastorate of the Rev. C. C. Boslaugh, 1925 to
1931, the present parsonage was erected, which marked another epoch in
Walworth county Methodism. To the Rev. Boslaugh belongs much credit for the
erection of this building, for there were many times when he and his family
were the only workers on the job.

The ladies aid shared $1000 of the cost of this building, and later by
paying $500, saved it from foreclosure proceedings.

Since the pastorate of C. C. Boslaugh, those who have served the church
are: J. W. Terry, M. A. Chase, L. L. Goodwin, P. E. Boomer, Ernest H.
Currier, John Whalley, B. S. Locher, and Earl F. Kurtz.

L. L. Goodwin and P. E. Boomer were suppliers who served while the Rev. M.
A. Chase was on leave of absence for the purpose of attending school.

To the Rev. Ernest H. Currier belongs the honor of serving the longest
pastorate next to that of the first pastor, the Rev. Mr. Brown. Mr. Currier
served from 1935 to 1942.

Succeeding him was John Whalley, who stayed but a very short time. For a
period of three years following this, the church was without a pastor, and
the parsonage was rented.

Then the district superintendent, Dr. B. A. Davis, appointed Mr. B. S.
Locher, who had formerly preached in North Dakota but who had resided in
California for several years, and who had temporarily given up the
ministry. After a pastorate of three years, during which time a great deal
of improvement was made on the church property, Mr. Locher with his family
was appointed to Burke, South Dakota.

The present pastor, the Rev. Earl F. Kurtz was transferred here from
Redfield, South Dakota, where he served for nearly eight years. In a six
months interim prior to coming to Selby, Mr. Kurtz served in the Temperance
League of Illinois.

The Methodist church in Selby is one unit of a denomination which serves 49
nations, and uses 125 languages. It is one of 6400 churches, with 9 million
members. It supports 360 schools and colleges, 129 medical centers and 126
social service institutions.

The Selby unit is the only one of its denomination in Walworth county. It
serves a wide territory, and has a far reaching influence. May its
influence ever be felt,

and the principles for which it stands ever increase in this community, and
in the generations to come.

CHRIST EPISCOPAL CHURCH

Through the fine work and efforts of Mr. and Mrs. R. W. Reynolds the
Episcopal church was organized in Se}by during the early years of the town.

Prior to the organization of the Church, Baptismal services were held in
the Masonic Hall and the following were baptized:

Mrs. R. W. Reynolds, Mrs. Louise Gutz, children of Mr. and Mrs. Fred
Griffin, three children of Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Mudge and the Rhodes children
of Bowdle. Reverend Traggitt of Milbank, South Dakota, was in charge of
this service and Reverend Ashley of Aberdeen was present. After the
organization of the church, services were held in the Masonic Hall and the
above mentioned families together with the H. R. de Malignon, Dr. H. R.
Gunderman and B. B. Potter families carried on the work of the church and
Sunday school.

Reverend George McKay of Redfield was the first Rector of the church and he
assisted a great deal in making plans to build a church, hauling much of the
stone himself for the foundation. The exact date of the dedication of the
church is not known but Dr. Ashley had charge of this service. Later
Reverend George Dow came and served for a number of years, followed by
Reverend George. Due to the small membership it was thought best that
services be discontinued, and the building was sold to the American Legion
in 1921.

ST. ANTHONY'S CATHOLIC PARISH AT SELBY

St. Anthony's Catholic parish with its imposing church and beautiful
rectory located south of the courthouse of Walworth county, is as old as
the town of Selby. When the town of Bangor was moved to the present
location of

Selby in 1900, a small Catholic church was also brought here from that town
and Father Nicholas Dahlmann, stationed at Hillsview, visited the new
Catholic Mission at Selby once a month from 1900 to 1902. The congregation
was small; made up mostly of Hungarians who had come to this country from
Hungary in 1884 and to this neighborhood in 1886. They were joined by
Germans from Hoven and Germany and by some Dutch, Irish and Polish families.

Under Father Joseph Schell, who served St. Anthony's Mission from Herreid
twice a month from 1902 to 1910 the present church was built in 1905 and
enlarged in 1910. Father Willibald Kraus, who bought the first priest's
house at Selby, a small two-room building, and took care of the parish from
1910 to 1916, was succeeded by Father John Kettler from 1916 to 1917; Father
Michael J. Lennon, pastor of Mobridge, who made his regular visits to Selby
from 1917 to 1923; and Father P. J. Cafferky, who also attended Selby from
Mobridge from 1923 to 1924.

In 1924 Father Vincent Frech, O. S. B., pastor of Wakpala, took charge of
St. Anthony's parish, visiting it twice a month. After the fire, which
destroyed the inside of the small two-room priest's house in 1932, Fr.
Vincent built the present rectory, one of the finest and most comfortable
homes in town.

Since the time of Father Martin Stolberg, O. S. B., who resided here from
1935 to 1939, St. Anthony's parish has always had a resident pastor and
regular services every Sunday. Father Martin Stolberg, O. S. B. was
succeeded by Father Vincent Frech, O. S. B. from 1939 to 1940; Father Henry
Luig from 1940 to 1941, Father Claude Barton, O. S. B. from 1941 to 1943,
and Father George Walsh for a few months during 1942.

Father Boniface Simmen, O. S. B., who was in charge of St. Anthony's parish
from 1943 to 1946, greatly improved the church property, painted the
outside of church and rectory, built a spacious garage, remodeled and
redecorated the interior of the church with wall-board, laid a rubber tile
floor, installed a new pulpit and new Communion railing, so that St.
Anthony's church with its beautiful altars and new artistic improvements is
one of the finest and most devotional church buildings in this part of the
country.

Father Boniface Simmen, O. S. B., was succeeded by Father Hilary Hill, O.
S. B., a former army chaplain, who resided here three months in 1946 and
the present pastor, Father Othmar Buerkler, O. S. B., a former Indian
Missionary, who has been here since September, 1946. Many new improvements
have been made in recent years: a new front sidewalk has been built, a new
fuel oil heating system installed in the church, new vestments bought for
the divine services, over a hundred trees and shrubs have been planted, and
the garden and yard beautified.

There is regular religious instruction for children in the grades and in
high school during the entire school year and every summer a two weeks'
vacation school taught by some Sisters. The parish has now about two
hundred members and the prospects for the future are bright.

BETHANY LUTHERAN CHURCH

The history of the Bethany Lutheran church originates with the Scandinavia
Evangelical Lutheran and the Bethlehem Lutheran congregations which later
consolidated to form the Bethany congregation. In 1886, Rev. K. E. Kjelaas,
a member of the conference of the Norwegian church in America, visited this
part of Dakota territory to preach the gospel and perform baptisms. His work
aroused interest in the organization of a congregation and on August 7,
1886, a group of Scandinavians met at the home of Halvor Pederson in
Campbell county, to form a congregation. Tobias Risdall was elected
chairman and it was decided to name it the Scandinavia Evangelical Lutheran
congregation of Campbell and Walworth counties. The organizers included:
Halvor Pederson and family, Helge Engebretson and family, Knut Haugstad,
Chris and Andrew Tronson, Jens Jenson and family, Tobias Risdall and
family, and Sam Samson and family. At a meeting on April 20, 1887, Rev.
Kjelaas served as chairman and Tobias Risdall as secretary, and on July 19
of that year, Candidate O. H. Kirkebak, who had just finished school, was
called and he served the congregation continuously until 1905. This
congregation had a Sunday school from the very beginning, and later a month
of Bible school was held every year. A ladies aid was also organized in
1887.

The Bethlehem congregation was also organized in 1886, through the efforts
of Pastors L. L. Nervig of Revillo, and L. E. Kjelaas from Webster, who had
visited the pioneers early in 1885. Charter members of this congregation
were the families of Olaus Olson, Johannes Olson, P. H. Olafson, H. Hanson,
Guttorm Braaten, Hans Ellefson and Soren Peterson. In 1887, Rev. Peter
Skartvedt was called to serve the congregation, remaining until 1896 when
he was succeeded by Rev. J. S. Holland, who served for 3 years. In 1899,
Rev. O. L. Stensby was called and served until 1905. This congregation also
had an active Sunday school, parochial school and ladies aid society.

In the late nineties, times were hard in Dakota and a great many of the
Norwegian settlers became discouraged and sought their fortunes elsewhere.
About 20 families, most of them members of the above named congregations,
left shortly after the turn of the century, and as a result, the remaining
members of the Scandinavia and Bethlehem congregations held a joint meeting
in December, 1905, disbanded and organized a new congregation to be known
as the Bethany congregation.

The first meeting of the new congregation was held January 3, 1906. Church
officers were elected and Rev. O. L. Stensby was called as the pastor. The
matter of whether to continue using the schoolhouse for meetings or to
build a church was discussed and a committee of four was named to try to
secure subscriptions for a new building. Charter members of the new
congregation were the families of Ole Lee, Severt Opheim, Olaf Byre, John
Ellefson, Ole Opheim, Lars Larson and Helge Engebretson. At a meeting on
February 3, 1906, held in the Blue Blanket school house, it was reported
that $845 had been subscribed and more had been promised. A building
committee composed of Helge Engebretson, Severt Opheim and John Ellefson
was appointed. Severt Opheim donated two acres of land for the church and
cemetery. Others hauled stone, and built the foundation and framework. The
completion of the project was let on contract to L. Orbick and it was
completed in the spring of 1907.

The first wedding in the church was that of Hannah Thompson and William
Johnson on October 15, 1908. First class to be confirmed included: Andrew
Odland Even and Ole Opheim, Selma Byre, Richard Larson, Kari Lee, Martin
Olson, Marie Larson, Herman and Marie Thorstenson, Helmer and Hanna
Thompson. First children to be baptized in Bethany were: Jesse Johnson,
Jennie Chillquist, Alma Josephine Pederson, Oluf Karl Opheim. Oscar
Theodore Byre and Sigurd Veien in 1907 and 1908. First person buried in the
church cemetery was Bert Johnson, son of Oliver Johnson. Total cost of the
church, not including the new basement, was between $2400 and $2500, the
final payment being made in 1914. In the fall of 1931 a new basement was
built under the church, the young men donating most of the labor, so the
actual cash expenditure was about $780.

On October 1, 1936, the church observed its Golden Jubilee, with former
pastors of the church, Skartvedt, Stensby and Peterson present. In 1937,
the congregation bought a piano and in 1943, the ladies aid cleaned and
redecorated the church and purchased a beautiful rug and runner for it. In
1944 a service flag was put up with 11 stars, one of which was later
replaced with a gold star for Pfc. Gunnar W. Johnson, who sacrificed his
life on October 18, 1944. A Luther League was organized in April, 1945.
Three couples of the church have observed their golden wedding
anniversaries: Mr. and Mrs. P. J. Thorstenson, Mr. and Mrs. Ole Opheim and
Mr. and Mrs. Severt Opheim.

At a special meeting on April 27, 1947, it was decided to divide the parish
so that Mobridge could have its own resident pastor and the Pollock, Norway
and Bethany churches would be served by their own pastor. Pastors who have
served the Bethany church include: Rev. O. L. Stensby, 1906 to 1913; Rev.
K. J. Arne, 1913-1916; Rev. O. L. Stensby, 1916-1925; Rev. H. J. Peterson,
1925-1931; Rev. O. C. Hellekson, 1931-1937. John Watne, missionary, held
services in the church from January to July, 1937, when Rev. O. B. Nilsen
took up the work, serving until 1947, when Rev. Wm. J. Madson, the present
pastor, was called.

                SELBY ORGANIZATIONS

HISTORY OF CAM-WAL ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC.

Cam-Wal Electric Cooperative, Inc., had its birth June 20, 1945. On this
date a group of farmers and businessmen from Walworth and Campbell counties
met in the Opera House at Selby, S. D. They selected board members and
elected officers for the year. Those elected were: W. J. Sawinsky, Selby,
chairman; A. K. Tronson, Glenham, vice chairman; Emil Wagner, Selby,
secretary; D. C. Wittmeier, Pollock, treasurer; D. F. Boehmer, Akaska; Sam
A. Merkel, Glenham; Ted F. Biel, Java; George M. Seiler, Artas, and Ben H.
Stiegelmeier, Java, directors. Howard Fredrickson, REA representative of
Washington, D. C., was there to help them organize.

        CAM-WAL DIRECTORS AND OFFICIALS
        Standing, left to right: Earl Duncan, P. J. Rausch, A. K. Tronson,
        J. K. Wiest, S. A. Merkel, Ted F. Biel; seated, W. M. Potts, Emil
        Wagner, W. J. Sawinsky, D. F. Boehmer, Fred Harer.

The board selected W. M. Potts as project attorney and Banister Engineering
Company of Saint Paul as engineer for the project.

The first three letters in the name of each county were used to give the
organization its name--Cam-Wal Electric Cooperative, Inc.

Potter county asked and became a member of the Cooperative on January 24,
1946. Dewey and Corson counties also asked to join the organization on the
same day and were accepted as members by the board. Later these two
counties asked to be released so they could form their own Cooperative
known as the Moreau-Grand Electric. They were granted their release.

Cam-Wal Electric Cooperative, Inc., received its first loan from Washington
on June 21, 1946, for $500,000.00. This loan was known as the "A" loan and
was to build 376 miles of line which included the town of Lowry.

W. J. Sawinsky was put in charge as coordinator of the project on December
2, 1946.

Virginia Molstad was the first bookkeeper and began working November 1,
1947.

The first Annual Membership Meeting, consisting of the board members only,
was held January 28, 1947, in the courthouse, and the following members
were elected: D. F. Boehmer, Akaska, chairman; Fred Harer, Hoven, vice
chairman; Emil Wagner, Selby, secretary-treasurer; Sam A. Merkel, Glenham;
Peter J. Rausch, Gettysburg; Earl K. Duncan, Tolstoy; A. K. Tronson,
Glenham; Ted F. Biel, Java, and George M. Seiler, Artas, directors.

Robert William Bauder began work on January 1, 1948, as wiring inspector.

W. J. Sawinsky became manager of the Cooperative on March 1, 1948.

Zontelli Construction Company of Ironton, Minnesota, was the low bidder on
March 18, 1948, on a labor-only contract which continued in force until 800
miles of line were built.

The second loan of $500,000.00 was approved February 28, 1948. It was known
as the "B" loan and was used to build additional lines.

George M. Seiler resigned from the board May 3 1948, and John K. Wiest of
Herreid, was chosen to fill the vacancy.

Roy Lutz began working October 4, 1948, as work order and material clerk.

Marshall Lund began work on November 1, 1949, as head lineman.

Selby celebrated REA day November 12, 1948. This was the first day
electricity was turned into the lines running out in the country and the
town of Lowry. The W. J. Sawinsky farm was the first farm to receive
electricity which was on November 13, 1948.

Elmer Jett of Selby began working as easement man December 1, 1948.

The first large Annual Membership Meeting with all members invited was held
February 7, 1949. All members of the board were re-elected and the
organization of members remained the same.

Leo Kuehl began working as assistant lineman March 15. 1949.

The "C" Allotment in the amount of $1,515,000.00, was received March 30,
1949. Zontelli was again low bidder on 700 miles of line for labor and
material. This completed construction and gave area coverage in the three
counties--a total of 1500 miles of line and 1500 consumers.

The contract with Montana-Dakota Utilities for energy came to an end on May
25, 1949. A new contract began this day with the Bureau of Reclamation who
get their energy from Fort Peck and offer a slightly lower rate.

Herbert Bjella consented to be the head bookkeeper and started working June
6, 1949.

On June 18, 1949, Hilbert Jurief began work as assistant lineman.

Mary Mudge began work July 20, 1949, in charge of memberships and as a
stenographer.

Ernest Zimmerman and Richard Himrich were employed in December, 1949, as
groundmen.

On January 6, 1950, the board approved purchase of a two-way radio set.

The first office of the Cam-Wal Electric Cooperative, Inc., was a small
room off the AAA office in the courthouse. As construction got underway,
more office space was needed and on April 1, 1949, it was moved in the two
jury rooms in the courthouse until February 1, 1950. At this time the new
office space in the basement of the Beren's Hotel was complete, and the
Cam-Wal Electric moved into its permanent quarters.

The Annual Meeting and Opening Day for the new office was held February 6,
1950, with over 1200 members and their families present. At this meeting
the same board members were re-elected and the organization of members
remained the same.

THE COUNTY NURSE

The Public Health Nursing program was inaugurated in Walworth county under
the Federal Public Health and Social Security Act in 1934. Mary R. Cook,
R.N., was appointed Walworth county public health nurse and the office was
established in Selby, the county seat. The work continued under the federal
program until 1936, at which time the county was asked to participate;
contributing funds on a matching basis with the state and federal
government.

        MARY R. COOK

The program is educational in nature. Services are rendered schools through
rapid and annual inspections of school children, and in the control of
communicable diseases. Antepartum, post partum, infant welfare, and
pre-school services are rendered. Immunization an d vaccination clinics and
morbidity clinics are conducted by local physicians cooperating with the
nursing pro gram. Crippled children clinics are held regularly each year,
conducted by orthopedic and pediatric physicians under the State Public
Health program for crippled children. Children showing defects of
orthopedic nature are admitted to the Lutheran hospital at Hot Springs and
Sioux Valley hospital at Sioux Falls for corrective surgery or medical
care. Braces, shoes and other corrective appliances are supplied for
children through the South Dakota Crippled Children's program. Field visits
are made to homes of these children upon return from the hospitals. To
assist in the home care of the children, dental clinics have been conducted
in the county by local dentists from time to time throughout these years.
The Public Health topical Fluoride demonstration team of the United States
Public Health department visited an area of the county and children from
grade one through six were treated for prevention of dental decay. The
Mobile X-ray Unit visited the county in June, 1949, and adults and children
14 years of age and over were X-rayed. All cases showing pathology were
advised to report to their physicians for consultation and advice and for
follow-up X-rays if necessary. Assistance was given in organizing the
Walking Blood bank under Walworth county chapter of American Red Cross.
Correction of defects of school children have been a major part of the
program. The various organizations and the health committees and board of
county commissioners have given their support to the program, making it
possible to continue. these services uninterrupted.

Walworth county is one of the few counties of the state that has employed a
county nurse without interruption over a period of 16 years or ever since
the federal program was inaugurated. Mrs. Mary Cook has been in charge of
the work continuously during this time, leaving only for short periods to
attend schools and conferences. Walworth county is also one of the few
counties in the state of which it may be said that every handicapped person
has been given an opportunity for treatment and rehabilitation.

HISTORY OF PARENT-TEACHER ASSOCIATION

The Selby unit of the Parent-Teacher Association was organized December 6,
1935, in the high school auditorium by a group of parents and teachers. The
purpose of this association is educational and is devoted to child welfare.
It endeavors to create a better understanding between parents and public
schools.

The first meeting was called to order by Superintendent Jorgenson. He
explained the purpose of the meeting and discussed the work of the
Parent-Teacher Association. The following officers were elected:
Superintendent E. Jorgenson, president; Rev. E. H. Currier, vice president;
Mrs. E. H. Noteboom, secretary; and Mrs. Walter Smith, treasurer. The third
Wednesday of each month was selected as the night for P. T. A. to meet. The
first regular meeting was held January 15, 1936, in the high school
auditorium at 8:15 p. m. Sixty-three persons became members and a P. T. A.
Chorus was organized.

During the past years many fine programs have been presented by students,
teachers, parents, and out-of-town people. An Easter cantata was presented
by the Mixed Chorus one year.

A recreational program was sponsored during the summer of 1941.

On March 21, 1942, a broadcast was given at Aberdeen.

In October, 1942, the unit disbanded, but was reorganized again January 16,
1946. The time of meeting was changed to the third Monday.

The first Parent-Teacher Association convention for District 11 was held in
the Methodist church basement in Selby on October 6, 1948. Officers elected
for two years were the following: Mrs. Grace Crawford of Mobridge,
president; Mrs. Bertha Holzworth of Lowry, vice president; Mrs. Edith Gutz
of Selby, secretary-treasurer.

During the past year two one-act plays were presented by Parent-Teacher
Association members to raise money to purchase playground equipment.

An annual affair by the Parent-Teacher Association is the Graduation Tea,
this is given on Commencement Night for the graduates, their parents, and
the speakers.

The officers elected for the coming year 1949-1950 were: Elmer Jett,
president; Mrs. Clara Drown, vice president; Mrs. Walter Hieb, secretary,
E. B. Brenneise,

THE WALWORTH COUNTY FARM BUREAU

The Walworth County Farm Bureau was organized in the fall of the year 1918
under a special act of Congress providing for the setting up of Emergency
Farm Bureaus through the United States Department of Agriculture and the
Extension divisions of the State Agricultural colleges for the purpose of
increasing farm production during the period of World War I. Most of the
cost was paid by Federal funds appropriated for that purpose. Local
membership was set up. The organization was to employ a county agent and
conduct a campaign for better farming and increased production. The first
county in South Dakota to organize under this Act was Minnehaha and
Walworth was second.

The first Board consisted of Arne Strand, chairman; E. H. Noteboom,
secretary; O. S. Crawford, H. P. Gutz and Gerritt Noble. Messrs. Gutz and
Noteboom had done the organization work, assisting Ralph Patty and Harry
Boyts, who were sent out from State College.

The first county agent employed was Coleman H. Wagner, a Selby boy, the son
of Mr. and Mrs. Coleman Wagner, who had just graduated from State College at
Brookings. He went to work with energy and zeal and the Farm Bureau and
extension work got such a fine start that it became a fixture and Walworth
county is one of the very few counties in the state that have maintained
the extension work and employed a county agent without intermission for
more than thirty years.

Mr. Wagner was succeeded by Omer Mills of Wall, who left to go on a ranch,
and he in turn by L. C. Lippert. Then Mr. Lippert went into the Indian
Service and "Ham" Mateer came to Walworth county, he being succeeded by
James S. Hopkins. "Ham" went into the Soil Conservation Service and "Hop"
into the implement business in Selby. Hopkins' successor and our present
county agent is Robert Fahlberg of Beresford, who in a comparatively short
time has made good.

During Mr. Mateer's period of service the AAA came into the picture and for
a considerable length of time the county agents worked in and with it and
the Farm Bureau as the sponsoring agency in Walworth county was neglected
and has not functioned for many years now, but the old Farm Bureau spirit
exists among the farmers and business men of Selby and community with other
agencies doing the same work.

From the beginning the business men of Selby have supported all movements
for the betterment of agriculture and were 100% behind the Farm Bureau and
in like manner supported all extension work, the county agent, the AAA, and
livestock and farm practice improvement.

MISSOURI RIVER NATIONAL FARM LOAN ASSOCIATION

In 1917 the United States created 12 Federal Land Banks, located at
strategic points over the country. In order to set up this farm credit
agency, the government loaned each of the 12 banks, $750,000. This was each
bank's "cash on hand". Then National Farm Loan associations sprang up all
over the country, the idea being that as each NFLA made a loan, they would
endorse the mortgage note and the Federal Land bank would provide the money
for the loan. As each NFLA loan was made, the farmer had to have 5% of his
total loan invested in association capital stock and in turn the NFLA had
to have an equal amount invested in capital stock in the Federal Land bank.
As time progressed, the Federal Land banks repaid the government for their
initial capitalization loan of $750,000. Amortized loans were practically
unheard of prior to the creation of the land banks, as was a nominal rate
of interest. The old plan was for a farmer to borrow say, $5,000 and pay
his interest each year, but at the end of the 5-year period he still owed
the $5,000. The Federal Land bank plan was a 34-1/2-year loan with a
certain percentage of the principal, plus the interest, due each
year,--consequently at the end of the long term, the borrowed would find
his farm debt free.

To E. A. Walter, then president of the Walworth County State bank of Selby,
must go the credit for giving Walworth county its first National Farm Loan
association, which was organized in 1921 with George W. Turner, then
farming southwest of Selby, as its first president and E. A. Walter as
secretary-treasurer. Other charter members were: Chas. E. Cheskey, Henry
Stulken, F. M. Brown, E. L. Brown, August Thorstenson, Anton Reis, Abe
Switzer, G. C. Clark, Otto Fischer, Paul Elfrink and J. A. Lawrence. The
association made loans in Walworth and Campbell counties.

In 1931, Mr. Walter moved out of the community, and N. D. MacArthur,
formerly of Mellette, who had been serving as cashier of the Walworth
County State bank in Selby, was elected secretary-treasurer. In 1936, the
counties of Corson, Dewey, Ziebach and Armstrong were added to the
association and the office moved to Mobridge for the purpose of more
central location. In 1943, Potter county was added.

MacArthur, who came to Walworth county in 1919, is now serving his 19th
year as secretary-treasurer of this vast farm-ranch loan organization. The
association continues to be owned and operated as it was when it started,
by farmer-rancher stockholders residing in the above named counties. Dean
F. Boehmer, of near Akaska, the largest individual owner of Walworth county
land, is and has been president of the association since 1946. Another
Walworth county resident, Earl Olson, of near Selby, is a director.

WALWORTH COUNTY CROP IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION

The Walworth County Crop Improvement association, whose purpose it is to
sponsor an educational program on crops and soils, organize variety test
plot demonstration projects, keep abreast of new crop developments, sponsor
increase of new varieties, and promote the production of pure seed
production, was organized in February, 1943, starting with a nucleus of 20
members, later expanding to 27 members. No general meeting was held the
first year so no officers were elected. Charter members in 1943 were as
follows: Carl Sawinsky, Jake Rabenberg, Elmer Spindler, Mike Arbach, Fred
Permann, Henry Thuente, Ralph Sawinsky, Merl Masteller, Heinrich Mueller,
Ferdinand Walz, Glen Powell, Emanuel Schlepp, Clarence Schumacher, Tom
Engebretson, Fred Seyer, Earl Marin, C. C. Vogele, Ben Lemler, Raymond
Carman, Paui Stewart, Fred Buechler, James Kane, John Kaiser, Theodore
Molstad, Sam Merkel, Ed. Oxner, and W. P. Jones.

Three new varieties of oats, Vikota, Vicland, and Brunker, were introduced
by the association the first year. Fifteen bushels of Vikota oats were
given to the county for joining the state association. Of the three
varieties which were introduced, Vicland has become very popular and today
we find a large acreage of the oats sown in the county given over to
Vicland. Farmers who grew Vicland the first years noted a 5-15 bushels
increase.

The association held its first annual meeting in Selby on March 24, 1944,
when the following officers were elected: Carl Sawinsky, president; Glen
Powell, vice president; James Hopkins, secretary-treasurer. At the first
meeting of the association, they decided to sponsor a crops hazard school,
sponsor test plots and conduct a crops tour in July, and plans were also
made to distribute new oat varieties which had been increased the preceding
year.

Kota flax and Rancher sorghum were introduced by the association in 1944.
Earl Erbe and Fred Permann were selected to increase the Kota flax seed
which has become so popular in recent years. Raymond Carman was the first
man in the county to grow Rancher sorghum. During the same year, about 1000
bushels of Mida wheat was brought into the county.

In 1947 the Walworth County Crop Improvement association decided to go on
record in favor of a large scale organized weed control program. Acting on
this suggestion, County Agent Hopkins conducted meetings to organize a Weed
Board to head a program which was to gain in momentum in the years ahead.
Feebar barley, a new feed barley released by the South Dakota experiment
station, was released this same year. Sheyanne flax was also introduced.

Highlighting the 1948 program was a Recognition banquet given in honor of
Tom Engebretson, a veteran corn breeder in this community. Present at the
banquet were about 125 admirers including members of the Crop Improvement
association. Mr. Engebretson is to be highly praised for his interest in
crop improvement work for the benefit of himself and for the benefit of the
many farmers in this area who have profited so greatly from his work.

Forty bushels of plains barley were released to the association in 1948.
Although this variety did not produce well the first year it is expected to
become one of the popular varieties should we go back to seasons favoring
quick-maturing crops. In 1949 Rushmore wheat and Norghum sorghum were
released for increase. So far, it is not possible to predict their worth to
farmers in this area.

Interest in crop improvement work has increased with the association having
expanded its membership to 41 paid up members. Officers in 1949 were: Ed
Oxner, president; Clarence Schumacher, vice president; Robert Fahlberg,
secretary-treasurer.

Although it is impossible to predict the economic worth of this
organization to the grain farmers in this area it is conservative to say
that it does have a tremendous bearing in introducing and promoting adapted
grain varieties which are so important in a small grain producing region.

HISTORY OF SELBY PUBLIC LIBRARY

The idea of providing proper books for Selby's reading dates back to the
early days of the Selby Woman's club. In 1916, the Traveling Library from
Pierre was procured and circulated by the club. Later it was decided to
drop the Traveling Library project as the expense was heavy and the
readers few.

The beginning of the present circulating library was the purchase of books,
by the Woman's club, at the Otto Doherr sale. Mrs. Weiland donated a large
number of books and the exchange of the Pierre Traveling Library was
arranged.

These books were taken to the Welton furniture store by Mrs. Otto
Steinhoff, president of the Woman's club, and a real circulation commenced.

From 1931 to 1932 the books were at Mrs. Gertrude Ketterling's store and at
Mrs. Pearl Drown's studio. In 1935 the library was moved to a room in the
city auditorium and was a WPA project until July 1, 1938.

In 1938 a city library was organized.

To the Woman's club belongs the credit for the library as it is today.
Selby can justly be proud of its library.

New books are purchased every year, and many books and periodicals are
donated. The late Mr. and Mrs. Gene Overholser donated all their books to
the library.

There are 3,092 books on the shelves at present.

The following members: Mrs. Amanda Noteboom, president; Mrs. Delphia
Johnson, treasurer; Lois Manke, secretary; Mrs. Ruth Hopkins and Fred
Homeyer, are now serving on the Library board. Gov. G. T. Mickelson was a
member of the Library board until he moved to Pierre. Mrs. Anna Ingalls and
Allen George, both deceased, were board members for many years. Mrs. Eva
Swift is serving as librarian at the present time.

The American Legion Auxiliary donates annually to the library.

The dream of the Library board is a Public Library building of their own.

THE FARMERS HOME ADMINISTRATION

In accepting the request of the Historical Committee of the Selby Golden
Jubilee to write a short story of the Farmers Home Administration, we
believe that this Jubilee will have a meaning of much greater importance
than being the occasion for parades, beauty queen contests, celebrating,
and such. Fascinating, interesting and colorful as these may be to the
human eye, they are not enough. Primarily, the meaning of this Jubilee will
be thinking about the past, the present, and the future of Selby and
community. It will mean gathering up past records of life and all the
activities connected with the normal growth of this community. It will mean
the preserving of these records, studying these records to try and seek
ways and means of making these past records serve the people of today, and
also of tomorrow. The story of Selby and community reaches far into the
past, much farther than the fifty years being observed by this Jubilee. It
goes back to the first inception of life in this locality. The beginning of
a community may be simple, but as it grows it soon becomes more complex,
being affected by diverse forces, new ideas, and many times changed by
circumstances not of its own choosing. A community is a sort of pattern
into which many designs are woven.

As far back as 1918, under the Woodrow Wilson administration, the United
States government authorized the making of seed loans, and at that time
established what was known as the Farmers Seed Loan corporation. That
set-up functioned more or less erratically through a loaning procedure in
1922, and was revitalized in the late summer or fall of 1931 for the
purpose of making livestock feed loans, and in the spring of 1932, when seed
loans were again made through what was subsequently to be known as the
Emergency Crop and Feed Loan Section. From that time on, without missing
a single year, until its culmination in the fall of 1946, the ECFL section
rendered a service to the farmers through loans for feed and seed.

Along in 1935, conditions had developed to a point where a new order of
things was being injected into the picture. At that time the South Dakota
Rural Rehabilitation corporation was beginning to be woven into the life
pattern of the community. In order to view the forerunner agencies of the
FHA in proper perspective to the community at this time, it will be
necessary to review briefly the conditions as they were for a time preceding
the establishment of these agencies.

After a period of depression, it was realized that an acute farm problem
existed, and it was imperative for the nation as a whole that this problem
be met and solved. Our national stage, up to 1935 was set with the crisis of
1929, shrinking incomes for farmers, deflated farm values, country bank
failures, general business decline. From 1929 to 1932 national income
dropped from 81 billions to 38 billions. Nearly 350,000 American families,
at least a million men, women and children, were wandering from state to
state desperately seeking a living as migrant farm laborers. There were
8,000,000 families that had an average yearly income of less than $750.
Eleven million families had an income of from $750 to $1500. In 1933 one
million families were on relief. By 1935 two and one-half million rural
families, comprising more than 10,000,000 people, depended on some form of
relief for their survival.

The Emergency Crop and Feed Loan Section had not been established in a
manner to permit extensive loaning operations, and had no authority to make
grants of either money or food to farm families. The amount which could be
loaned was limited, and the loans were secured by mortgages on either
livestock or crops. To cope with the situation as it existed and to provide
funds unavailable through the ECFL, there was at first established local
agencies to take care of the emergency by giving grants of money or food to
needy farm families. But these agencies soon found all their resources
exhausted and could not cope with the situation.

The Federal government then launched the Civil Works administration which
took over the work of the local agency in helping the needy through grants
and subsidies. Various bills were proposed and passed with the intent of
helping farmers generally. All measures so far passed, seemed to affect, in
the words of the Secretary of Agriculture, "the top third of the farmers".
Little had yet been done to help the poor tenants, sharecroppers, field
laborers, or migratory workers other than the relief already offered. A few
states, by this time, began to realize that a dole to farmers would tide
them over with food and other immediate needs, but would not solve their
problem. What they needed was assistance to acquire tools, livestock, seed,
etc., for the next year's crop. Out of this experience several states began
to advance loans to farmers, along with grants, in an attempt to help low
income families become self-sustaining. This idea attracted national
attention.

When the Civil Works administration merged into the Federal Emergency
Relief administration, these localized measures from the different states
were scrutinized and studied. On March 22, 1934, the administrator of the
FERA, having noted that some states were moving toward "rehabilitating"
farmers as a method of reducing relief rolls, directed a letter to all
state emergency relief administrations, that: "Civil works and direct
relief pro. grams as at present conducted in rural areas which are designed
as open country and towns having less than 5,000 population will be
replaced as of April 1, 1934, by a program of Rural Rehabilitation. The
objective of this program is to make it possible for destitute persons
eligible for relief in such areas to sustain themselves through their own
efforts". The following June, 1935, there appeared a document entitled
"Objectives and Suggestive Procedure for Rural Rehabilitation" based upon a
study of state loans to low income farmers. The FERA in that year set up a
Rural Rehabilitation division to carry out recommendations made in that
study. Although this program was financed by Federal funds, it was set up
on a state basis. Each state participating established state corporations
to handle the new program, that of making loans for seed, livestock and
supplies.

It wasn't long, however, until these state corporations were faced with
problems which they as individual units were unable to solve. It became
apparent that a well integrated plan had to be evolved to cope with such
problems as retiring submarginal land and resettling people taken off poor
land on better land. Other problems arose, such as debt adjustment. It was
soon discovered that it was not just one problem seeking solution, but a
complexity of problems.

In 1935, President Roosevelt established the Resettlement administration
into which was gathered all state rural rehabilitation corporations, the
FERA, the Debt Adjustment, and several other projects. The RA then
functioned as an individual agency through three divisions: First, Land
Utilization; second, Resettlement division; and third, the Rehabilitation
program.

On December 31, 1936, the RA ceased to be an individual agency, having been
transferred to the Department of Agriculture. On September 1, 1937, the
Secretary of Agriculture announced the creation of the Farm Security
administration.

It must be borne in mind that during all of these years the ECFL Section
continued to exist as a separate unit, carrying on its loaning program from
year to year without any variations either as to name or purpose.

On November 1, 1946, the FSA and the ECFL ceased to exist as government
agencies. At that time the FHA was established by Public Law 731, 79th
Congress, October, 1946. The operations of these old organizations, and
much of their personnel were transferred to the new organization.

The FHA as now set up is charged with administering the program as
established by Congressional action, which includes:

FIRST: Making and servicing Operating Loans.

SECOND: Making and servicing Farm Ownership Loans. There are no Farm
Ownership loans in Walworth or Campbell counties. However, a number of farms
were purchased under the old purchase contract set-up, which is now no
longer in operation. The Farm Ownership program only makes loans to
purchase family-size farms, and in this connection it is interesting to note
that according to the United States Census of Agriculture of 1940 in
Walworth county there were 643 farms, and in 1945 there were 613 farms. In
1940 the average size farm in Walworth county was 654.2 acres, and in 1945
the average size farm was 730.6 acres. There is a tendency, therefore,
toward larger farms.

THIRD: Water Facilities Loans.

The funds which make it possible for the FHA to operate are appropriated
annually by Congress. During the last three or four years, loans have been
made to the limit of funds available. War veterans with agricultural
experience who wish to become farmers now have preference under the law for
all loans.

The local FHA office is in the courthouse at Selby. The personnel of this
office consists of Rudolph L. Sinkie, the county supervisor; and Mrs. Mavis
Kuehl, clerk-typist. This force serves both Walworth and Campbell counties.
A county advisory committee confers with the county supervisor on all loan
matters. The county committee for Walworth county consists of Leonard
Noble, Othiol Turner and Clifford Tucker, and the committee for Campbell
county consists of George Grad, Neil E. Nelson and Albert Conway.

This, then, is briefly the story of the FHA. With the cooperation of the
public, the business men, the county officials, other public agencies, and
the generous cooperation of the local newspapers which have given of their
time and space in their papers to publish such material as we believe to be
of interest to the public, this agency has woven in the years of its
existence a small design in the life pattern of this community.

What, then, is the true significance of this Golden Jubilee? It will not be
just recording the history of an agency, a business concern, or an
organization. It will be the bringing of all these and all else that has
entered into the life of this community into a composite which will aid
toward developing a wider and deeper understanding of the future. With the
experience of the past, and the knowledge of the present, and the faith in
the future, Selby and its surrounding community will continue to be the
kind of community which makes a nation great.

HISTORY OF HOPE CHAPTER NO. 73, ORDER OF
THE EASTERN STAR, SELBY, SOUTH DAKOTA

In the early fall of 1903, a petition requesting the privilege of
organizing a Chapter of the Order of the Eastern Star was circulated at
Selby, South Dakota, signed by the required number eligible to do so, and
forwarded to the Worthy Grand Patron.

A dispensation to organize a Chapter was granted by Jos. B. Vaughn, Worthy
Grand Patron, on November 27, 1903. A called meeting was held to discuss
matters of importance, name temporary officers, etc. Meetings were to be
held the first and third Tuesdays of each month at the Masonic hall. This
practice is still being continued at the present time.

        MRS. LIZZIE BURR
        First Worthy Matron of Hope Chapter No. 73

On January 5, 1904, Simon Ring, deputy of the Worthy Grand Patron, with the
assistance of Bowdle chapter No. 43 instituted Hope chapter under
dispensation, and the officers chosen to serve were installed as follows:

Worthy Matron, Lizzie N. Burr; Worthy Patron, Benjamin B. Potter; Associate
Matron, Olive Overholser; Secretary, Walter B. Burr; Treasurer, Albert F.
Miles; Conductress, Anna S. Gunderman; Associate Conductress, Mary Starkey;
Adah, Ida Miles; Ruth, Flora E. Powell; Esther, Lula B. Potter; Martha,
Bertha Burr; Electa, Emma Vick; Warder, George Starkey; Sentinel, George P.
Vick; Organist, H. R. Gunderman.

At the meeting of the Grand Chapter at Yankton on June 15, 1904, Lizzie N.
Burr was installed as Worthy Matron of Hope chapter No. 73, and was
presented with the Charter by Jos. B. Vaughn, Worthy Grand Patron. The
charter members were as follows: Lizzie N. Burr, Flora E. Powell, Lulu B.
Potter, Olive Overholser, Anna S. Gunderman, Ida Miles, Jennie Finch, Mary
Starkey, Emma Vick, Bertha Burr, Benjamin B. Potter, Walter B. Burr, Albert
F. Miles, Dr. Herman R. Gunderman.

On July 25, 1904, Simon C. A. Ring, deputy Worthy Grand Patron, constituted
Hope chapter No. 73, and installed the officers who had served under
dispensation. Four new members, namely Chauncey N. Burr, Emma B. Griffin,
Ida E. Griffin and Winifred Kingman were added to the roll, and at the
close of the fiscal year a membership of twenty-one was recorded.

This earnest conscientious group of pioneer members laid a solid and
substantial foundation for those following upon which to build a lasting
monument for years to come.

For 1905 the same corps of officers were re-elected. In 1911 Hope chapter
instituted Ionic chapter No. 103 of Mobridge, South Dakota.

At the instituting of Java chapter No. 123 on May 4, 1916, the Worthy Grand
Patron was assisted by Otto Doherr as Grand Secretary, Marie Biel as Grand
Marshal, and Flora E. Powell as Grand Chaplain. The work was conducted by
the officers of Hope chapter with Rose Schmidt as Worthy Matron.

In the Worthy Grand Patron's report to Grand Chapter he stated, "It was
exceptionally well done and was a great inspiration to the new chapter".
Java chapter later consolidated with Hope chapter on December 6, 1938.

In 1924 with Eda Overholser as Worthy Matron, Hope chapter won recognition
as one of seventeen chapters who were perfect in their work. Much credit
belonged to Julia George for her earnest efforts in helping to perfect the
work, and in her aid and assistance in the programs, plays, and social
activities of the chapter.

On February 5, 1924, the chapter celebrated its twentieth anniversary. On
this occasion a delicious turkey dinner was served to the Stars and guests
by the Masonic Brothers before the meeting of the chapter. After the
meeting a program was given. A feature of the evening's entertainment was
the high school orchestra, composed of sons of Star members, with Salome
Mudge Jr., as pianist and assisted by Elmer Schmid. This group discoursed
music during the dinner and later throughout the evening. Three charter
members were present: B. B. Potter, Olive Overholser, and Flora E. Powell.

On February 5, 1934, the chapter with Amanda Noteboom as Worthy Matron
celebrated its 30th anniversary with a birthday party--a large birthday
cake was the center of attraction. Two charter members were present: Olive
Overholser and Flora E. Powell.

A party was held honoring Mr. and Mrs. Eugene Overholser on their Golden
Wedding anniversary in 1942.

In December, 1946, when Gertrude Chesky was Worthy Matron, a party for Gov.
and Mrs. George Mickelson was held, when they were leaving to assume their
duties at the State House, as Governor and First Lady of South Dakota.

During the forty-six years since its organization, thirty seven Worthy
Matrons and sixteen Worthy Patrons have served; eleven secretaries have
served their chapter well. Olive Overholser, served as secretary for 18
years.

Hope chapter received Grand Chapter recognition when George T. Mickelson
was elected Worthy Grand Patron in 1944. George also served as Associate
Grand Patron and Grand Sentinel of the Grand Chapter. Other Grand Officers
through the years include: Winifred Kingman as Associate Grand Conductress;
Eda Overholser as Grand Adah, Clara Potter as Grand Warder; Madge Mickelson
as Grand Martha; two Grand Pages, Madge Mickelson and Ruth Hopkins.

Grand Representatives were: Ruth Hopkins, Edith Gutz, Ella Taylor, Amanda
Noteboom, Anna Gunderman, Winifred Kingman, Letta Johnson, and Lizzie N.
Burr.

One charter member remains on the roster, Flora E. Powell, who lives with
her daughter in Mountain Lakes, New Jersey.

Hope chapter has a very active Past Matrons Circle of twenty-one resident
members.

A public card party, sponsored by the Stars and Masons, has become an
annual affair for the benefit of the Children's Home at Sioux Falls.

In reviewing the minutes of the chapter through the past years we find many
good deeds recorded and also many social times enjoyed by the Sisters and
Brothers of the chapter.

Donations have been made to the O. E. S. Home at Redfield, South Dakota.
Through the years many charitable donations have been made.

The present officers of 1950 are as follows:

Ardell Tisdall, Worthy Matron; Amelia Sebert, Associate Matron; Rose
McIntosh, Secretary; Maxine Cheskey, Conductress; Gertrude M. Chesky,
Marshal; Katharine Paul, Organist; Dorothy Jett, Ruth; Marie Kramlich,
Martha; Viola Birkholt, Warder; Everett Sebert, Worthy Patron; Edward
Kramlich, Associate Patron; Belle Nickolson, Treasurer; Clara Drown,
Associate Conductress; Lois Manke, Chaplain; Gloria Delzer, Adah; Alvera
Kost, Esther; Viola Tisdall, Electa; Wayne Cheskey, Sentinel.

The present membership is now 125 members.

PAST MATRONS CIRCLE OF HOPE CHAPTER NO. 73 O. E. S.

In December 1922 Past Matrons and Patrons of the chapter were called to
meet and make plans for a Past Matrons and Past Patrons organization with
Mrs. Marie S. Beil, chairman, and Mrs. Olive Overholser,
secretary-treasurer. It was decided by vote that this organization be
perfected but no definite plans were made. An incentive to this had been an
invitation from Worthy Matron Ethelind Campbell, to attend Past Matrons and
Past Patrons night, and to assist in the work of the chapter on January 2,
1923. Later, on April 13, 1924, the organization was completed, the by laws
were written up; Olive Overholser was named secretary-treasurer and the
president to be next in line each year.

The name selected was "The Past Matrons and Past Patrons Circle of Hope
Chapter", this name being favored by Mrs. Julia George, who was
instrumental and helpful in perfecting the association. Later on the Circle
became inactive. On May 29, 1935, the Past Matrons met at the home of Mrs.
Amanda Noteboom to reorganize the Circle, with Mrs. Stella Brown as
president and Mrs. Olive Overholser as secretary-treasurer.

The name was changed to "The Past Matrons Circle". The by-laws were revised
to meet the present needs of the circle by the following committee: Olive
Elfrink, Ethelind Campbell and Bertha Schendel. The revision of the by-laws
was accepted.

The Circle has been very active since the reorganization and meets the
second Wednesday of each month except June, July and August.

The object of the Circle: To assist the Worthy Matron at the time of the
official visit of the Grand Officers; to keep up a continued interest in
the welfare and growth of the Chapter and the Eastern Star work wherever it
may be found; and to assist in any project worthy of the organization.

The first Past Matrons and Past Patrons night held January 2, 1923, was a
happy and pleasing event.

There has been a Past Matrons and Past Patrons night each year in Hope
chapter since 1923, and it has always been an evening of pleasure and
enjoyment.

Looking back through the records one finds many happy, pleasant meetings
held, many kindly deeds done and worthwhile work performed. The present
officers are: Gertrude M. Chesky, president; Kittie Lakeman, vice
president; and Ruth Hopkins, secretary-treasurer.

SELBY HOMESTEAD NO. 862 BROTHERHOOD OF AMERICAN YEOMAN

The B. A. Y., a social and insurance organization, was formed May 2, 1902,
in the Masonic hall under Special Deputy A. W. Shriver, and had the
following charter members:
