Taylor, A. F. Stuck, L. G. Eberhart, J. J. Elfrink, Caroline Elfrink, L. W.
Maxwell, Ida A. Maxwell, A. Beil, Marie S. Beil, U. E. Brown, Kate E.
Brown, G. A. Clark, Isabelle Clark, C. A. Taylor, P. E. Greenman, C. T.

The Homestead was one of the most active social organizations in Selby for
a long period of years, and the membership varied from fifty-five to
seventy five members. The monthly meetings were held the first Friday of
the month at the Woodman hall. After the Woodman hall was moved to the
Selby fair grounds, the meetings were held in the homes of the members, and
in various other places, the Red Cross room at the courthouse, H. R. de
Malignon furniture store and the rooms over the Holter harness shop. Worthy
of mention is the fine service rendered the organization by Mrs. Minnie de
Malignon and Mrs. Salome Mudge as correspondents, Mrs. Mudge serving until
the B. A. Y. disbanded. Mrs. Ida Maxwell, Mrs. Emily Baumgarten and Mrs.
Mudge are the three charter members who still reside in Selby.

MODERN WOODMEN OF AMERICA

Bangor camp No. 3028 Modern Woodmen of America was organized June 20, 1895,
by A. T. Bruiker. Place of meeting was downstairs in the Collins building
in Bangor, South Dakota. Members from the Bowdle camp assisted in the
ceremonies. The charter members were: George A. Clark, H. R. de Malignon,
H. R. Gunderman, M.D., Fred Griffin, John J. Hoven, J. P. Foster, J. A.
Koch, R. E. Mudge, C. S. Reistad, J. W. Lowry.

Election of officers resulted as follows: Venerable Consul, R. E. Mudge;
Worthy Advisor, George A. Clark; Esteemed Banker, H. R. Gunderman; Clerk,
H. R. de Malignon; Escort, J. P. Foster; Watchman, J. A. Koch; Sentry, C.
S. Reistad; Physician, H. R. Gunderman.

In November of the same year a building association was formed and a hall
was built.

The first new member initiated was A. E. (Tony) Birkholt.

In the summer of 1900 the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul railroad extended
their line through the county and the town of Selby was started four miles
north of Bangor and all business places in Bangor began moving to Selby. It
was decided at a meeting held by the camp to move the hall and camp to
Selby, but to retain the name of Bangor camp. This was accordingly done on
Sunday, September 16, 1900, when the hall was loaded and moved to Selby.

On November 20, 1901, the Bangor camp No. 3028 and the Mound City camp No.
6380 were consolidated and became Selby camp No. 3028.

On February 20, 1907, the Woodman hall was sold to the Selby Improvement
company and the camp paid rent to the company after that.

In April, 1920, the camp entered into a contract leasing the opera house
from the City of Selby and ran picture shows and dances and also used the
place as a Lodge hall. This contract ran for about three years and was
disposed of to the Mascot theatre of Mobridge. The camp then rented the
downstairs in the post office building and after that the old Potter and
Burr building, and from there it moved to the Legion hall.

The camp still is in existence with a membership of 24.  No meetings have
been held for several years.

SELBY COUNTRY CLUB

A meeting of the ladies of the Selby Country club was held at the C. A.
Potter home on March 10, 1928, and the following officers were elected for
the ensuing year: Mrs. E. R. Schmid, president; Mrs. C. A. Potter, vice
president; Mrs. F. H. Weiland, secretary-treasurer. The following
committees were appointed: Tournament, Mrs. S. M. Johnson, Mrs. R. L.
Overholser and Mrs. C. A. Potter; Entertainment, Mrs. H. P. Gutz, Miss
Shirley Potter, Miss Marcella Doherr and Mrs. R. J. Gruett; Grounds, Mrs.
Robert Abel, Mrs. Otto Lincke and Miss Rose Schmidt. The ladies of the club
numbered 24 and looked forward to an interesting and beneficial year of
golf.

The members of the Woman's Golf club of Selby assembled at the Country club
Saturday evening, June 30, 1928, for a round of golf. Twenty-seven were in
attendance. Low scores were reported for Miss Marcella Doherr and for Mrs.
Otto Lincke. A fine picnic supper followed the play, after which the
members grouped around the bonfire, spent a pleasant hour in songs,
storytelling and stunts; incidentally, enjoying the awe-inspiring panorama
of well-kept fairways, green hills, many birds and many trees,--sights on
the Country Club golf course.

"Anytime is golf time" was the slogan and the members urged everyone to
take advantage of the excellent condition of the course and to play often.

The lady members of the Selby Country club also enjoyed many breakfasts
there. They donated to the club a table and benches and helped defray
expenses of upkeep of the course. They took part in local tournaments as
well as district tournaments and brought home the trophies for victories.
Later many of the members moved away and the membership dwindled until it
was decided to disband and the lease of the course was given up.

THE JOLLY CLUB

The Jolly club was primarily a rural neighborhood club, organized on July 21
1921, at the home of Mrs. John Ekberg, nine miles southwest of Selby. Mrs.
Ione Greene was elected as the first president at this meeting and served
as such for two years. Eighteen members enrolled, and at the end of six
months, the member ship totaled thirty-eight. Later the membership was
limited to forty members and no town ladies were eligible to join. The
purpose of the club was of a social and educational nature. Meetings were
to be held every two weeks in the various homes of the members with
afternoon meetings in the summer with lunch served, and all day meetings
during the winter months with men invited and a potluck dinner served. A
small membership fee is charged which goes into a general fund.
"Penny-March" money takes care of the cost of flowers in cases of both
sickness and deaths.

        MRS. C. E. GREENE
        First President of Jolly Club

This club has cooperated to help in many good causes, which aided in its
success, such as sending clothing to the needy, sewing and knitting for the
Red Cross, sewing for the sick, giving Christmas boxes to the poor,
donations to the Flood Relief, care of the Bangor cemetery, giving toward
an iron lung, Infantile Paralysis funds, the Abbot House for homeless
children, building and upkeep of the Ladies' Public Rest Room in Selby,
South Dakota Children's Home at Sioux Falls, American cancer fund and many
others, and so the community has been benefited by the activities of the
Jolly club.

Amusements consist of picnics, programs and parties, the programs being of
home talent. A very interesting program and quilt pageant was given at the
opera house in Selby at one time, which created much interest and was a
financial success as well.

In 1946, the 25th anniversary of the club was celebrated with a banquet and
program in the Methodist church basement at Selby, the ladies' aid of that
church serving, and a special program being given and all members taking
part. At the close of the program a special memorial tribute was paid to
departed members.

BETHLEHEM CEMETERY

On the open prairie northwest of Selby lies one of the early day
cemeteries. The graves are few and far between, but every spring the grass
flourishes within its fences and the Ponderosa Pines wave in the breeze.

Land for this cemetery was granted by Hans Hansen, one of the early
settlers.

The first to be laid to rest was Martha Tisdall in the fall of 1886, who
earlier that summer had helped to construct the first fence surrounding the
cemetery. Martha, daughter of Sam Peterson was the second to be buried
there. Those first years a few more graves were added namely: Inga Olson,
Sarah Franks, Bertha Tisdall, Mary Webb, Grant Tisdall, Martha
Molsterteigen, Rachel Hovland, Lars and Amanda Anderson, Johannes Olson,
Jacob Olson, Edgar Ellefson Mary and Oscar Olson, Oscar and Samuel Baker.
Two Civil War veterans, Johannes Tisdall and B. F. Lemon were also laid to
rest there.

As the years passed one by one, some of the old settlers moved to other
parts and it was through the efforts of the late P. J. Thorstenson, who
contacted relatives of the deceased far and near and who, with the help of
the donations received, erected a good fence, gate and arch surrounding the
cemetery. Through his efforts in helping to clean and beautify the
cemetery, those small pines planted many years ago are now large and
beautiful,--a tribute to Peter Thorstenson and his three small children who
rest in peace beneath the pines.

SELBY UNION CEMETERY

On September 15, 1920, it was decided at a meeting of the Selby Woman's
club that they take up the work of assisting in the upkeep of the cemetery
and a committee was appointed to confer with Mr. D. W. Welton and others
interested and take charge of a fund subscribed for this purpose. The
committee appointed was Mrs. Louise Gutz, Miss Ann Ward and Mrs. Victoria
Smith.

Mrs. Gutz, chairman of the committee, recommended members of the committee
to consult with the city council regarding cemetery affairs and to go ahead
with the work of repairing the fence and the building of a tool house. The
council decided to appropriate funds and give the committee authority to
use the money subscribed for this purpose. A total of $170.00 was turned
over to the treasurer, Miss Ward. Mrs. Gutz reported that the city would
build the tool house and repair the fence and the money in the fund could
be used toward beautifying the grounds.

At the April 27, 1921, meeting Mrs. Gutz reported 100 trees were bought and
set out at the cemetery. These trees were native cedars and were set out
and carefully watched and cared for by the late G. B. Walters, Mrs. Eda
Overholser was appointed on the cemetery committee, replacing Mrs. Victoria
Smith.

November 14, 1922, the Woman's club donated $75.22 to the Cemetery fund.

On March 13, 1923, Mrs. Delphia Johnson was appointed treasurer of the
committee, replacing Ann Ward.

At the September 11, 1924, meeting the cemetery committee reported the
purchase of a watering tank, graveling of the driveways and planting of a
bed of geraniums, lilacs and other shrubbery.

On February 8, 1927, Mrs. Louise Gutz, Mrs. Eda Overholser and Mrs. Delphia
Johnson reported that the committee had met with the city council regarding
future upkeep of the cemetery. Mr. D. W. Welton of the city council
suggested that the club appoint three of their members to meet with the
city council to perfect a constitution for the cemetery association.

On March 8, 1927, the cemetery committee met with Mr. Welton and Mr. A. C.
Dobson and a constitution for the Selby Union Cemetery association was
drawn up and was submitted to the city council and met with their approval.
The following names were nominated to the city council as trustees
for the Selby Union Cemetery association: D. W. Welton, A. C. Dobson, Dr.
Weiland, C. A. Potter, Louise Gutz, Royce Overholser, Delphia Johnson,
Agnes Gehrki and Ruth Steinhoff; the members to act three years. On April
6, 1927, the association met in session. This was merely a meeting of the
board of trustees to elect their officers for the ensuing year, who were as
follows: A. C. Dobson, president; Mrs. Louise Gutz, vice president; Mrs.
Delphia Johnson, secretary-treasurer; and D. W. Welton, superintendent. Mr.
Welton was keenly interested in the upkeep of the cemetery and during his
years of service the cemetery was greatly improved.

At a meeting held April 12, 1928, the purchasing of a power mower was
discussed, also the planting of trees. At a meeting held June 28, 1928, it
was decided to purchase "Perpetual Care Markers", these markers to be
placed at graves where parties had purchased an endowment bond and the
caretaker was instructed to give those graves special care.

At the May 20, 1929, meeting George Head was appointed to take Mr. Welton's
place as superintendent. On May 14, 1930, Mrs. Pauline Clark was elected
secretary-treasurer. On May 26, 1932, Mrs. Dorothea Smith was appointed to
take the place left vacant on the board by Mrs. Viola Walters, who moved
out of town. On January 11, 1933, A. C. Dobson, a member of the city
council, was appointed superintendent of the cemetery, and to have charge
of the plats. On February 28, 1945, members of the board of trustees met.
Members present were: Max Gutz, Art Zabel, Lillian Hoven, May Hoefs Magers
and Inez Theilen. The following officers were elected: Mrs. Lillian Hoven,
president; Art Zabel, vice president; Inez Theilen, secretary-treasurer;
and Mrs. May Magers, superintendent. The meeting called on February 28,
1945, and the reorganization of the board was due to the efforts of the
Selby Woman's club, under the capable leadership of Mrs. Ruth Hopkins, who
at that time was president of the club.

During the years that have gone by, flowers, trees and other shrubbery have
been purchased and planted in the cemetery.

In 1945 funds were raised by contributions from the lot holders and other
interested people and in 1948 a small power sickle mower and a cub tractor
with mower attachments were purchased. Plans are now being made to have a
well dug in the cemetery so that the cemetery may be adequately watered.

The effort put forth to make the Selby Union cemetery a beauty spot is
largely due to the Selby Woman's club and the cemetery boards. Each, in
turn, have cheerfully taken up the task of working toward one goal, a well
kept cemetery.

OLD SETTLERS ASSOCIATION

As early as May 17, 1894, attempts were made to organize an Old Settlers
association, but it was not until July 4, 1899, that the Pioneer
Association of Walworth county was officially organized. However, in the
meantime, the annual Fourth of July celebration in Bangor was in charge of
a committee of Old Settlers for several years.

        Old Settlers Picnic About 1910

The preamble and constitution of the Pioneer group stated that it was
organized for the purpose of "transmitting to future generations, a correct
history of the early settlement and organization of Walworth county, South
Dakota; to record all incidents of importance connected with such early
settlement, and to cultivate that kindly feeling of friendship which can
only come to those who alike have endured hardships and privations in an
earnest endeavor to transform a wilderness into productive fields and
comfortable homes; to build up local and state government; to aid in the
maintenance of good morals, as well as good schools for our children; and
to foster a spirit of loyalty to country, to home and to mankind in
general."

The following officers were elected: G. H. Hoffman, president; Wm. Winkley,
vice president; N. H. Kingman, secretary; B. B. Potter, treasurer. The
organization was to meet annually in June and anyone who became a resident
of Walworth county prior to January 1, 1890, was eligible to become a
member.

This constitution was adopted on the 4th day of July, 1899, at Bangor. The
first organized reunion of the Old Settlers of Walworth county was
especially interesting and colorful. Headed by the Bangor brass band, a
grand parade was the main feature, and marching in it were the school
children bearing flags, members of the Modern Woodman and Maccabee lodges,
Mrs. Siebrecht and her son, Swan, first white child born in Walworth county,
the Old Settlers wearing ribbon badges imprinted with the date of their
coming to the county, and members of the G.A.R., resplendent in uniforms
and medals. Also appearing in the parade were survivors of the so-called
"Fool Soldiers", heroic Indian rescue band, a group of Indians who rescued
many captive whites from other Indians.

After the parade, the program was held at the bowery, some of the features
being the presentation of the Indians by the Hon. Peter Couchman; short
talk by Chief Charger, one of the Indians, interpreted by Pete Frazier,
assisted by Walter Swiftbird; a talk by the president, G. H. Hoffman, and
short remarks by other Old Settlers. After a bountiful dinner, there was a
baseball game between Bowdle and Bangor, with Bangor winning. In the huge
bowery erected in the courthouse square, a dance was held in the evening.

For many years, the committee met each year to make plans for the date,
place and program for the annual meeting, which was held at various places
including Bangor, LeBeau, Evarts, Swan Lake, Spring Lake, Fosters grove and
Selby. These annual gatherings, usually in the form of a picnic, were
greatly enjoyed by the people of Walworth county. Funds to defray expenses
were secured in various ways. Usually a free will offering was taken up
during the ball game. Ribbon badges were sold at prices varying from 10
cents to a dollar. The program for the day usually included a parade, if
the gathering was held in a town; formal exercises including an address by
some important speaker; a picnic dinner, baseball game, followed by all
kinds of races and street sports, and a bowery dance in the evening.

A complete record of the officers who served on the committees through the
years is not available but among them were: G. H. Hoffman, Wm. Winkley, N.
H. Kingman, B. B. Potter, H. G. Boyland, George Jurgerson, J. R. Howell, B.
J. Olson, Peter Couchman, August Brehmer, George W. Ryan, T. B. Bowlus, W.
B. Burr, G. J. Schellenger, Fred Griffin, Capt. Kingman, H. R. deMalignon,
F. E. Gehrki, B. P. Adams, I. C. Pratton, H. L. Hughes, H. A. Taylor, W. S.
Schwartz.

The association was discontinued about the time of World War I.

AMERICAN LEGION

The organizational meeting of Frederick Schauer Post No. 100, Selby,
Department of South Dakota, was held at the court house at Selby on
December 5, 1919, and Clifford Griffin acted as temporary chairman. There
were present from the Selby and Java communities thirty seven veterans of
World War I. The first officers elected were: Leo E. Buchanan, commander:
Roy Schwartz, vice-commander; Wm. Hoven, adjutant; S. M. Johnson, finance
officer; Clifford Griffin, post historian; John Barclay, John Sawinsky,
Robert Gruett, and Wilbur Reeves, executive committeemen.

        Back row, left to right: Robert Mickelson, Robert Fahlberg, Arnold
        Diedtrich, John Flemmer, Herbert Baer, Gust Knecht, Harold Hettich,
        Joe Zarka, Leo Buchanan, Richard Miller, Fred Homeyer. Second row:
        Steve Johnson, Richard Schnaible, Ted Bohle, Elmer Jett, Fred
        Diedtrich, John Miller, George Schaffer, Phil Hughes, Clarence
        Bucklin, Dana Vail, Pearl Brown, Christ Flemmer, Albert Moos,
        Wilson Wolff. Front row: Ted Schanzenbach, Emanuel Pressler, Ernest
        Himrich, Milo Schanzenbach, Darrel Zabel, Hartson White, Elmer
        Miller, Henry Weiszhaar Robert Unkrur, Herbert Bjella.

After considerable discussion, the post was named after Frederick Schauer,
a Selby serviceman, who was killed in action in the Argonne in France on
September 29, 1918, by German machine gun fire while on liaison patrol.
Other names under consideration were Harry Sandy and Adolph Wolff, both of
Java, who were killed in the service.

The Selby Post acquired its first home in 1921 by purchasing the
Episcopalian church for $1800.00. This property was sold to the German
Congregational church at Selby in 1922 for $2500.00, and is now serving as
the Congregational church at Selby. The present Legion home was constructed
during the summer and fall of 1923, and the dedication services were held
on December 17, 1923. The building cost about $4000.00 and all but $1500.00
was paid upon completion. The balance was financed by a loan from a local
bank and final payment was made in 1928, at which time a grand old "mortgage
burning ceremony" was staged by the Legionaires. During the years since
1923, the Legion Hall has served as a community meeting place, and is used
several times weekly for gatherings of community, social, and political
groups.

In May 1922, the Legion cooperated with the Selby schools in staging the
first County Play Day. This has been an annual affair since that time, with
the Legion continuing its cooperation. The Legion awards a loving cup each
year to the winning relay team and permanent possession of the cup is
retained by the relay team from the school winning the cup for the third
time.

The Post has always been interested in the youth of the community, and for
years supplied the community with an ice skating rink. In 1926, it
sponsored its first American Legion junior baseball team, and since that
time has annually had a team. The Legion has always been interested in
basketball and has sponsored many basketball teams, the first team being
sponsored in 1920.

In 1923, the Legion had its first wild duck feed, and since that time it
has become an annual event. with the Chinese pheasant being substituted for
wild duck during the last years.

Since 1921, the Legion has held patriotic programs on Armistice Day of each
year, usually followed by a dance in the evening. The Legion has assisted
with Memorial Day services since 1924, and in later years have been in sole
charge of such programs, following the death of B. B. Potter, the last
Selby survivor of the G. A. R., who for many years almost alone arranged
for the observance of that day.

Among other Legion activities during the years have been assistance in
beautifying the Selby Union cemetery, building Hiddenwood lake into an
outstanding recreational center, sponsoring Selby high school students to
the Legion Boy's State at Aberdeen, conducting school essay contests, and
assisting in holiday and county fair celebrations. In 1927, the Selby post
received the state award as the post contributing most in community service.

During the first years of the Selby post, its membership included veterans
from Herreid, Mound City, Glenham, Bowdle, Java, and other neighboring
towns. Gradually, these communities established their own posts and members
transferred to such posts. The Java community organized its own post in
1947, and since that time, the membership of the Selby post has been
confined largely to veterans residing in Selby and the adjoining rural
community. With the end of World War II, the membership increased
tremendously with veterans of that war gradually assuming active control of
Legion affairs. The present membership of the post is 99:

The Selby Post has always taken an active interest in assisting veterans
and their dependents in asserting rights to which they are entitled under
the state and national laws, as well as sponsoring worthwhile legislation.

Past Commanders of the Post and the years during which they served are as
follows: Leo E. Buchanan, 1919-1920; Roy Schwartz, 1921; Arthur Griffen,
1922; R. J. Gruett, 1923; L. C. Lippert, 1924-1925; W. A. Goodwin, 1926;
August F. Hagen, 1927; Fred C. Seyer, 1928; Oscar Strand, 1929; A. M.
Hoven, 1930; Leslie Herring, 1931; Pearl Brown, 1932-1933; Wm. Hoven. 1934;
A. D. Miles, 1935; A. M. Hoven, 1936; Floyd Mudge, 1937; E. Jorgenson,
1938; G. W. Hicks, 1939 A. D. Miles, 1940; August Thorstenson, 1941; Mike
Schmidt, 1942-1943; Emil Spiry, 1944; George Sebert, 1945; John Miller,
1946, Theo. Schanzenbach, 1947 Hartson White, 1948; Robert Mickelson, 1949.

Present officers of the Selby Post are: Robert Mickelson, commander; Darrel
Zabel, first vice-commander Gust Allerdings, second vice-commander; Richard
Miller, adjutant; Theo. Schanzenbach, finance officer; Robert Fahlberg,
service officer; Herbert Baer, sergeant-at-arms; Elmer Jett, chaplain;
executive committeemen, John Miller, Theo. Schanzenbach and Hartson White.

AMERICAN LEGION AUXILIARY

The American Legion Auxiliary Unit of Frederick Schauer Post No. 100 was
organized November 3, 1920, with fifteen charter members. They were Bertha
Schwartz, Elsie Buchanan, Ernestine Miller. Clara Barclay, Mary Buchanan,
Sadie Koch, Delilah Marin, Edna Fenslar, Julia Smith, Ella Christopherson.
Grace Hyde, Rose Schmidt, Delphia Buchanan, Vina Smith and Marie Barclay.
The first officers were. Elsie Buchanan, president; Ella Christopherson,
vice president, Ernestine Miller, adjutant; Anne Ward, historian; Bertha
Schwartz, finance officer. The meetings at this time were held in the homes
of the members.

The women eligible to the American Legion Auxiliary are the wives, mothers.
sisters and daughters of members of the American Legion. The purpose of the
auxiliary is to help care for the disabled veterans who are in hospitals
and also to help needy families.

Poppies are made by the disabled veterans who are in hospitals and every
year the auxiliary sponsors a poppy drive. The first year the drive netted
$60.37 and in 1948 twelve hundred poppies were sold and the net proceeds
were $141.36. Proceeds of the poppy drive are used to send gifts and money
to Battle Mountain sanitorium at Hot Springs, gifts to children's
hospitals, gifts to an adopted buddy and to all monthly showers called for
by the state department. They also make donations to the city library.

        Standing, left to right: Mabel Bucklin, Elva Aman, Bertha Stowell
        Adelaide Allerdings, Marv 13aer. Seated, Margaret Powell, Norma
        Hettich, Hilda Baer.

The Auxiliary helped the Legion build the new Legion Hall in 1923 and also
bought dishes, silver, electric plate, curtains and shades. In 1924 they
purchased a piano.

Their meetings are held every second Thursday in the Legion Hall.

The Junior Cradle Roll was organized in 1930 with Mrs. E. Noteboom as
chairman.

In 1927 the district meeting of the Legion and Auxiliary was held in Selby.
It was held again in Selby in 1938.

The Auxiliary has always helped the Legion with the Memorial Day and
Armistice programs. Every year on Memorial Day the graves of all deceased
members of the Legion and Auxiliary and all soldiers graves are decorated
with flags and flowers. For the past several years the Auxiliary has served
6 o'clock supper on Armistice Day and also a dance supper. This year the net
proceeds were $192.45. Other means of raising funds to carry on their work
have been: baked food sales, sponsoring of movies, candy sales, and in 1926
cook books were printed and sold. These were a great success.

The Auxiliary and Legion sponsored a boy to Boys' State for several years
and for the last three years the Auxiliary has sent a girl to Girls' State.

They have sent delegates to the district meetings and to the state
convention every year. Mrs. Madeline Lippert, one of their members, was
president of District 11. Later on the unit was transferred-to District 14.
At the district convention held at Eureka in April 1948, one of their
members, Mrs. Bertha Stowell, was elected president of District 14.

There are now 73 Auxiliary members of which there are: one Gold Star Mother
of World War I, three Gold Star Mothers of World War II, one Gold Star
sister, and one Junior Member.

Past presidents have been: Elsie Buchanan, 1920-21; Christie Zimmer, 1922;
Lola Schmid, 1923; Mary Buchanan, 1924; Madeline Lippert, 1925: Veronica
Hagen. 1926; Minnie Schwartz, 1927; Ella Christopherson, 1928, Gertrude
Gruett, 1929; Amanda Noteboom, 1930; Delphia Johnson, 1931; Eva Swift,
1932; Dorothea Smith, 1933; Florence Hoven, 1934; Ida Brown, 1935; Johann
Hoven, 1936; Lottie Sawinsky, 1937, Christine Abel. 1938; Bertha Stowell,
1939-40; Vina Manke, 1941; Ruby Schmidt, 1942; Odessa Russell, 1943; Ida
Thorstenson, 1944; Ardell Tisdall, 1945; Clara Sinkie, 1946; Hilda Baer,
1947; Norma Hettich, 1948.

historian.

GAME, FISH AND PARKS

Walworth county is one of the best game-producing counties in the entire
state. In the early days, prairie chicken and grouse were very plentiful in
all of the localities near Selby, especially in the Masteller, Mickelson
and Swan creek areas to the southwest and in the Stulken, Lee and Blue Blanket
lake areas to the northwest. Large numbers were also to be found along
Hiddenwood creek to the northeast. The cultivation of the land spelled the
doom of the prairie chicken and very few have been seen in Walworth county in
the past four years.

The Chinese ringneck pheasant was first introduced by the South Dakota
Game, Fish and Parks department on the Arne Strand farm southeast of Selby
in 1918 and many subsequent plantings were made in later years. They
thrived after a slow start and the first open season was declared in 1929
with a daily bag limit of three cock birds per day. The pheasant population
reached its peak in 1946 but it has been on the decline ever since that
time. Walworth county is still one of the best pheasant-hunting counties in
the entire state.

        Trapping pheasants on the Chas. Cheskey and Ed Hoffman farms the
        winter of 1947. Left to right, Chief Warden Dalton Logue, Warden Al
        Schmidt, Game Technician Ruel Jansen, Warden Lewis Smith.

When it comes to duck hunting this county has produced some of the finest
shooting there was to be had anywhere in the United States. Swan lake is
still considered one of the best duck lakes in the state and together with
Spring lake furnishes this outdoor sport to a great many hunters. Goose
shooting has been above average and the vicinity adjoining the Missouri
river still produces some very good hunting.

Hiddenwood lake, 6 miles northeast of Selby, was the first artificial lake
built in the state by the Game and Fish department together with the
cooperation of local citizens from Java, Selby and the county officials.
Since that time, Molstad and Evarts lakes were built in the western part of
the county with W.P.A. funds and financial help from the Game, Fish and
Parks department. All were stocked with fish and have produced some very
good fishing. In 1947 Molstad and Hiddenwood lakes were taken over by the
department as park areas and have been vastly improved. Evarts lake was
washed out in 1942 when a flood took out the spillway and was not re-built
as the Missouri river development is expected to flood this area and would
render it useless.

Hungarian partridges were introduced in the county in 1935 with only fair
success. They were on the increase for a few years but, at the present
time, coveys of them are seen only on rare occasions but are welcome guests
of any farmer who is fortunate enough to have them on his land as they are
such a friendly bird.

Albert H. Schmidt, Selby, serves as Game Warden for the State Game and Fish
department in the counties of Walworth and Campbell.

THE WALWORTH COUNTY SOCIETY FOR CRIPPLED CHILDREN AND ADULTS

        Standing, left to right: A. L. Stoddard, Margaret Masteller, E. H.
        Noteboom, Gertrude McKinnon. Seated, Minnie Schuh, Matilda Van
        Orman, Mary Cook.

This organization had its beginnings late in the year 1940 when George
Kienholz, president of the South Dakota Society for Crippled Children and
Adults, organized during the year, came to Walworth county and Selby
seeking some person who would head off an Easter seal sale for the 1941
Easter season. E. H. Noteboom then editor of the Walworth County Record,
accepted the job. A short time later Chester Solomonson of Mound City, who
had been named as chairman of District 11, made up of Campbell, Walworth
and Potter counties entered his country's military services and Mr.
Noteboom accepted that additional responsibility and has continued as county
and district chairman since that time. He is now trustee for South Dakota
for the National Society for Crippled Children and Adults.

The first Easter seal sale was held in the pre-Easter season of 1941 and
netted $75.00 in Walworth and Potter counties. No sale was held in Campbell
county. This money was divided evenly between the counties, $37.50 being
credited to each. The letters were mailed from Mr. Kienholz's office at
Pierre from mailing lists made up there, the returns coming to the district
chairman. In 1942 a similar plan was followed and Campbell county was
included. Walworth county sold $90.75 in seals. Potter $37.50 and Campbell
$18.55. By 1943 the plan was changed and the mailing lists were made up
within the counties by county committees and the returns came to each
county chairman. After county organizations were perfected and the public
became better acquainted with the objectives of the Societies, receipts
increased steadily. Walworth county sales reached a peak of $1107.45 in
1949, and the sales for the years 1941 to 1949 inclusive totaled $4712.87,
part of which has been used in helping the handicapped within the county in
various ways, the balance being held to the county's credit by the state
society. Walworth county has always ranked above the state average in total
sales, sales per person and sales in proportion to resources.

The Crippled Children's Society has always worked in close cooperation with
the county nurse's office, the physicians of the county, the Christmas seal
group, the Red Cross, the Polio group, the State Board of Health and the
State Division of Rehabilitation. The result of the combined efforts is
that few counties in the nation can boast of any nearer 100% care for the
handicapped and needy within their borders than Walworth. Truly every such
person has either been cared for or has been given a fair opportunity for
care and treatment.

The publication of the South Dakota Society for Crippled Children and
Adults, the four page magazine entitled "Helping the Crippled", is printed
in the Record print shop at Selby and is edited by Mr. Noteboom. It
circulates generally in every county in the state and goes to officials of
crippled children's societies in all states of the nation and to quite a
foreign list.

It is a matter of interest that a former Walworth county resident and
teacher, Miss Charlotte Noteboom, for two decades an instructor at the
State University at Vermillion, purchased the first Easter seals ever sold
in South Dakota. She sent a dollar to National headquarters then at Elyria,
Ohio and received a sheet of Easter seals in February of 1941.

WALWORTH COUNTY CANCER SOCIETY

This organization has just made a start in Walworth county, the year 1949
being the first in which any organized effort was made to raise funds for
use in specifically fighting this dread disease. Previously contributions
were mailed direct to state headquarters or to the national society.

        MRS. ERVIN RISHEL

Early in 1949, Mrs. Lucille Dory, Commander for South Dakota, made a visit
to Walworth county to interview interested persons in the communities and
was able to set up an organization which collected and remitted $453.33 to
state headquarters at Watertown. Mrs. Ervin Rishel served as commander for
the county and those who worked under her were Mesdames Max Van Orman, R.
O. Drown of Selby, Martin Schamber and Mrs. Wilbur Turner of Mobridge, Mrs.
Henry H. Wolff of Java, Mrs. Alex Weiszhaar of Bowdle, Mrs. Hugh Crawford
of Lowry, and others.

Early in 1950, Mrs. Rishel tendered her resignation as county commander and
Martin Schamber of Mobridge, accepted the responsibility and is organizing
a program which will bring to Walworth county residents the benefits of
county, state and national cancer societies and give everyone an
opportunity to help by contributing money and time.

AGRICULTURAL EXTENSION WORK, 4-H CLUBS AND
HOME EXTENSION CLUBS IN WALWORTH COUNTY

Agricultural extension work is a division of the U. S. Department of
Agriculture, and was provided for by Congressional passage of the Smith
Lever Bill on May 3, 1914. This law forms the foundation of cooperative
work in agriculture and home economics.

The South Dakota legislature passed an enabling act in 1915, providing for
the appointment of a director of extension work, appropriations, and
organization. The law specifically authorized the county commissioners to
appropriate money to carry on extension work. This law was amended in 1917
so as to make the Farm Bureau the sponsoring organization in the county.

        Test plots have long been conducted by Extension Service in
        cooperation with Crop Improvement Association.

The purpose of county extension work is education in applying the findings
of agricultural research and solving problems through group action. By
working through 4-H clubs, rural boys and girls have engaged in organized
group activities and have carried on projects related to the farm.

Walworth county was one of the first counties in the state to have
extension work, and even before passage of the Smith Lever Bill, according
to E. H. Noteboom, corn clubs were functioning in the county. The intense
interest shown by the people of Walworth county attracted the attention of
the extension service at State college and in September, 1917, R. I. Patty
of State college, and W. M. Cook of the United States Department of
Agriculture were sent to the county to organize the Walworth County Farm
Bureau. The executive committee working with these men consisted of A.
Strand, O. S. Crawford, H. P. Gutz, A. C. Dobson, and E. H. Notehoom. The
community committeemen were George Sebert, J. J. Wolff, Wilbur Rumsey, John
Klein, Henry Elling, Fred Schell, Frank Brown, James Barclay, W. A.
Godding, W. H. Masteller, and Wm. G. Chesky.

In December 1917, Colman Wagner was hired as the first county agent. Arne
Strand, H. P. Gutz, and O. S. Crawford were members of the first county
extension board. 4-H club work was started under County Agent Wagner. Early
activity was largely centered in Boy's clubs, the sow litter club being the
most popular. Charles Barclay was the first 4-H Club member to enter an
exhibit at the State Fair in 1919, and he won a third place award with a
fat barrow.  In the fall of 1919, under the patronage of local cattlemen
interested in purebred livestock, namely, Seeley, Chesky, and Flanagan, and
assisted by bankers H. P. Gutz and E. A. Walter, thirty purebred Hereford
and Shorthorn cattle were distributed among thirty boys and girls who were
4-H Club members.

Omer Mills served as county agent for a few months during the fall of 1919,
and then L. C. Lippert became county agent in 1920, and remained at that
position for approximately ten years. During Lippert's term of service,
extension work developed into a large program of crop and livestock
improvement in the county. Lippert was responsible for putting 4-H work on
a sound basis and many of the people today residing in Walworth county were
at one time members of his 4-H clubs. In 1922, Leonard Noble, Chas. Wilhus
and Ed Kunz entered competition at the fair at Sioux City, Iowa, as a potato
judging team.

The first home extension clubs in the county were organized at a meeting
held at the Legion hall at Selby on February 12, 1924. At that time, eleven
clubs were organized with 145 members participating. Mrs. Sada Hoffman was
the first county chairman. Home extension work is still being carried on in
the county under the chairmanship of Mrs. Jake Rabenberg, and there
presently are eight active clubs.

Home extension work and girl's 4-H Club work received added impetus in 1928
when Sylvia Newell became the first county home demonstration agent. She
was followed by M. Louise Franks, Leona Curtis, and Artaxa Denniston. Since
1941, Walworth county has had no regular home extension agent, except for
the period from September 11, 1944. to September 15, 1945, when May Freden
served.

County Agent Lippert was instrumental in encouraging and developing a large
acreage of alfalfa and sweet clover in the county during the latter part of
the 1920's. At that time, there were large numbers of hogs raised in the
county which were pastured on these legumes. The County Fair was carried on
through very successful years of showing livestock and crops. The Northern
Corn Show was also organized during Lippert's time, where many corn growers
in this section of the state exhibited their corn every fall. A large
number of trees were planted on farms during this period. Lippert left the
county in 1930.

H. A. Mateer succeeded Lippert as county agent and remained in this
position until February 1939.  During Mateer's term of service, this
section of the state was unfortunate in having a very limited amount of
rainfall low prices, and severe grasshopper infestation, all of which
curtailed the improvement and development of livestock and crops. However,
great progress was made in T. B. eradication, and at the present time the
county is practically free of T. B. in cattle. The first farm program was
started in 1933 with the assistance of Mateer, grass hopper poison bait was
distributed, and the reforestation projects at Lake Hiddenwood. Lake Evarts
and Molstad Dam were started.

The discontinuance of the county fair during the 1930 depression years was
a severe blow to extension work. but during the last few years, the
Northern Show of Progress at Mobridge, 4-H Club Achievement Day, and
similar activities have done much to replace the function of the county
fair.

J. S. Hopkins became county agent in 1939 following Mateer's resignation.
Hopkins was very instrumental in organizing the Walworth County Crop
Improvement association, which has been active in promoting new disease
resistant varieties of wheat and oats in the county. During the war years,
he was active in directing one of the finest farm labor programs in the
state, which was very essential, because of bountiful crops and a scarcity
of farm labor due to war service. Hopkins was one of the early promoters of
REA in this section, and helped organized the Cam-Wal REA, which has now
become a reality, serving virtually all farms in Campbell, Walworth and
Potter counties. Under Hopkins, a county wide weed eradication program was
instituted, as well as a program of livestock spraying. 4-H club work
likewise continued to advance under the direction of Hopkins.

Hopkins resigned in 1947, and Harold Borchard was appointed as temporary
county agent for a few months, when he was replaced by Robert Fahlberg, who
is now serving in this capacity. Fahlberg has continued the program of
livestock spraying, and the weed eradication program is now operating in
all sections of the county. 4-H club work and home extension programs which
were curtailed because of gasoline rationing, and other difficulties
resulting from the war, has been revitalized. There are now thirteen active
4-H clubs in the county. Constant crop improvement is being stressed and
new and more adaptable grain varieties are being continually introduced in
the county.

During its thirty-three years of operation, extension work in Walworth
county has had its joys and disappointments, in general coinciding with
good crops and crop failures. Many farmers left the county during the
period of drought and grasshoppers, but those who stayed have been
bountifully rewarded, and the average farmer in the county today enjoys a
good and sound farm prosperity.

The county extension service takes this opportunity of expressing its deep
gratitude to the following who have been particularly active in promoting
its activities: W. H. Masteller, W. J. Sawinsky, Dean F. Boehmer, Walter C.
Smith, O. S. Crawford, Fred Bieber, H. P. Gutz, Ralph Sawinsky, A. Rye,
Herman Fiedler, E. H. Noteboom, Ed Oxner, Elmer Spindler, Mike Arbach, Fred
Buechler, and Christ Voegele. There are many others, and to all of you, we
express our sincere appreciation.

WORKS PROGRESS ADMINISTRATION (W.P.A.)

Due to the national depression of 1929, followed by the worst drouth the
Middle West has ever had, Walworth county, Selby and vicinity became a
victim of great distress. The most urgent need was relief for the suffering.

In 1933 direct relief was allowed through the state by the government to
the investigated needy.

The drouth continued, the wind blew and the grasshoppers came, forcing more
people out of work and crops to fail.

In 1934 the Civil Works Administration was set up as a work project
program, the county or city furnishing materials and the government paying
for the labor.

        ELLA CHRISTOPHERSON RAETHER

On account of the market slump, the government bought surplus foods,
yardage, cotton, coal and hay that was shipped in and distributed. Cattle
and pigs were shipped in and distributed. Cattle and pigs were bought in
this vicinity and disposed of. In August, the Works Progress Administration
(W.P.A.I went into effect. All kinds of new jobs were created. Selby and
vicinity had the following projects approved, to furnish labor for those
out of work:

Grasshopper poison bait was shipped in, farmers and gardeners spreading it
and hoping to save what little crop they had.

Lake Hiddenwood was allowed labor.

Farm-to-market roads were built

The Selby Opera House was repaired.

One of the city reservoirs was built.

A sewer line was put in on the west side of Selby.

The Selby library was furnished a librarian, old books were rebound by
trained bookbinders.

The Selby Consolidated School district rented the Auburn Hotel and it was
converted into a dormitory for the children attending high school from the
rural district. Deans, cooks and surplus foods were furnished by W.P A Hot
luncheon were prepared and served to the children at the school house.

Seed potatoes were shipped in by the government and a large garden was put
in southeast of town; a little of everything was planted but green beans
was the best crop.

A canning center was set up in the Woman's building at the fairgrounds.
Everything that could be canned was put up and later was given out as
surplus food.

Selby had a recreation center in what was known as the Welton Furniture
store. Children played games and learned handicraft under a recreation
leader. A big event was a puppet show.

The sewing center was located in what is known as the B. B. Potter office.
All kinds of garments were made from the surplus yardage from baby things
to men's overalls, as well as many quilts from the surplus cotton. One of
the happy moments was when one of the shirts made by the Selby unit was
sent to the state for the state exhibit and from there to Washington. D.
C., for the national exhibit. On March 25, 1936, Selby had an exhibit of
things made, such as garments, quilts, toys, handicraft and painting.

Under the direction of the county agent, the National Youth Administration
boys planted cedar trees west and northwest of the court house.

In 1938 the grasshoppers took most of the crops but in 1939 rains began to
come and need for W.P.A. gradually faded away.

On January 4, 1933, Ella Christopherson was appointed by the state as
director of woman's work for Walworth county and continued as director
until 1935. In 1935 she was appointed as W.P.A. Project Supervisor for
Walworth county. In 1939 Campbell county was added to her supervision. On
December 1, 1940, she resigned to be married to Charles Raether but
continued as supervisor until January 3, 1941.

LADIES REST ROOM

On March 8, 1927, at a regular meeting of the Selby Woman's club, at the
home of Mrs. Ella Christopherson the subject of a ladies rest room for
Selby was brought up by Mrs. Minnie Schwartz. The president, Mrs. Kate
Stewart instructed the investigating and civic improvement committee to
investigate and report to the club.

The committee, Eda Overholser, Minnie Schwartz, and Margaret Smith met with
the city council, presented the matter to them and they agreed to erect the
building, but all fixtures, plumbing, wiring, furnishings, and such were to
be paid by outside contributions.

The lot west of the First National Bank was offered as a site by that
institution, the room to be heated from the bank. Organizations, business
houses, and individuals were solicited for funds by the civic committee and
the amount of $426.18 was realized.

The proposed plan called for a room 16x12. The building was started the
first part of May 1927 and was completed June 30, 1927.

This attractive building was constructed for the accommodation of Selby
visitors. It is well equipped with all modern conveniences; its setting and
furnishings make it very attractive.

The First National Bank donated the use of the lot. The Walworth County
Record donated all printing in connection with the rest room. The sign on
the outside of the building was made and donated by Mr. Peterson. All
furnishings were donated by club members.

It was the wish of the city council that the Selby Woman's club be
responsible for the upkeep of the room and grounds. The members of the club
were assigned in turn to care for the room. Two members for each week. For
many years now a caretaker has had charge of the building.

The club still makes donations to this project and is responsible for the
upkeep of the building and grounds in cooperation with the City of Selby,
which bears most of the maintenance expense at this time.

On Saturday April 28, 1928 a fence was placed from the northwest corner of
the rest room to the alley. The work was in charge of Rev. Boslaugh. Those
assisting in work on fence and grounds were: H. P. Gutz, Mr. McCracken, C.
A. Potter, L. C. Lippert, Joe Maloney and Mr. Kirkpatrick. All work was
donated. Mr. Lippert, the county agent, was responsible for the landscaping:
all plants were donated; Mr. Gutz planted the lawn.

SELBY WOMAN'S CLUB

The Selby Woman's Club, a civic and study club was organized thirty-six
years ago on August 14, 1913, with a membership of twenty and with Mrs. H.
P. Gutz as the first president; Mrs. A. H. Smith, vice president, Mrs. N.
R. Ingalls, secretary; and Mrs. C. A. Potter, treasurer. Other members of
the original club included: Mrs. C. N. Burr, Mrs. Otto Doherr, Mrs. A. A.
Brown, Mrs. I. Dudley, Mrs. W. A. George, Mrs. G. C. Pierce, Mrs. F. J.
Nimtz, Mrs. F. E. Gehrki, Miss Ida Schmidt, Miss Marie Holter, Mrs. J. C.
Allerdings, Miss Bertha Lawrence, Mrs. John Bibelheimer, Mrs. N. Shockey,
Mrs. G. W. Vail and Mrs. O. J. Steinhoff.

Two years later, in 1915, the organization became a federated club.
Adopting as its motto, "In Non-essentials, Liberty; in Essentials, Unity;
in all things, Charity," the club has devoted much of its time to the
promotion of civic welfare work in the community of Selby.

        Standing, left to right: Ruth Vail, Gertrude Chesky, Eda
        Overholser. Seated, Zella Homeyer, Leone Bornong, Margaret
        Vanderhoof.

Most of the members of the original club had been members of a Mothers'
club which had as its object, child welfare. During the first few years
after the Woman's club was organized much time was given to child study.
Over a period of years, the club assisted with a series of infants and
mothers clinics. Throughout its existence the club has always had the
welfare of the young people of the community at heart. The club's
recreation committee, working in cooperation with the local school, at one
time sponsored a tennis tournament. The club also sponsored the
organization of a Girl Scout troop some years ago, the scout leader being a
member of the club.

The club has confined many of its interests to civic affairs and has been
active in many projects for the betterment of the community. It has
contributed generously to many worthy causes, among these were buying books
for the school library, the purchase of a flag pole for the school, and
other projects. It has taken an active part in the upkeep of the cemetery,
and a member of the club serves regularly on the cemetery board.

One of the outstanding projects sponsored by the Selby club was the
establishment of the Ladies' Rest Room, which is one of the nicest to be
found in any town of this size in the state. The rest room building was
constructed by the city of Selby in 1927 with the aid of contributions
collected by the club from local business places, organizations and
individuals. The club still makes donations to this project and is
responsible for the upkeep of the building and grounds in cooperation with
the City of Selby, which bears most of the maintenance expense at this time

The Library of Selby had its beginning in 1916, when the Woman's club
sponsored a traveling library, which was sent out from Pierre.

In 1932 the club sponsored the establishment of a city library, which was
opened with a total of 1972 books donated by citizens of Selby and
community. Today the library has 3902 books on its shelves and present
quarters in the city auditorium, which are too small. The clubs' major
project now is to raise enough money for a new public library building. One
member of the club serves on the Library Board each year.

The club has devoted much time, expense and effort in its fund raising
activities to carry on and help with the various projects it has sponsored
or helped to establish. Among the methods used to raise money was the
presentation of musical comedies, plays, amateur nights, holding baked food
sales, magazine subscriptions and others. The club has also contributed its
part in charitable work, assisting with donations and collections whenever
there was a need. In 1918-19 it helped support a French war orphan. In 1920
it donated freely to Near East relief. For a number of years the club has
cooperated with the local Red Cross chairman in solicitation for annual Red
Cross membership drives. This year the club held a special collection among
members on the annual Fun Night, for the benefit of the Polio fund.

The club meets twice a month except during June, July, and August. The
first meeting each year is in the form of a picnic. Social meetings include
an annual Christmas party and a Fun Night.

Present membership numbers thirty-two and officers are: President, Mrs.
Ruth Vail; vice president, Mrs. Fred Homeyer; recording secretary, Miss
Leone Bornong; corresponding secretary, Miss Gertrude Chesky; treasurer,
Mrs. Margaret Vanderhoof; librarian, Mrs. Royce Overholser.

Mrs. George Mickelson, wife of the present Governor of South Dakota, is a
former member of the Selby Woman's club. Mrs. Royce Overholser and Mrs. S.
M. Johnson have been continuous members for over 25 years.

Members of the present club are: Mesdames Stewart Cook, Fritz Clement, R.
O. Drown, Edith Gutz, Tillie Hanrahan, F. J. Homeyer, James Hopkins, J. W.
Hoven, S. M. Johnson, Bernel Manke, Herman Mecklenburg, Robert Mickelson,
Belle Nickolson, R. L. Overholser, G. W. Paul, Ed. F. Perman, Harold
Pressler, Jake Rabenberg, Emil Schanzenbach, Gena Thorstenson, Dana Vail,
John Vanderhoof, Hartson White, Emanuel Pressler, and the Misses Leone
Bornong, Gertrude Chesky, Evelyn Ivanoff, Cecelia Miller, Maurine Peterson,
Rose Mcintosh, Inez Theilen, and Marcella Will.

RED CROSS SURGICAL DRESSINGS CLASS

On May 4, 1918, Mrs. Royce Overholser was sent to Mobridge by the Red Cross
Unit to be instructed in surgical dressings work. On May 8, 1918, a surgical
dressings class was organized in Selby with eleven members as follows:

Mrs. H. Gough, Mrs. H. R. deMalignon, Mrs. W. B. Myler, Mrs. H. P. Gutz,
Mrs. H. Taylor. Mrs. W. George,

        Standing, left to right: Mahelle Clark, Mrs. H. Gough, Mrs. Chas.
        Hoffman, Mrs. H. R. de Malignon, Mrs. W. B. Myler, Mrs. H. P. Gutz,
        Mr. Theo. Schwartz. Seated: May Hoefs Magers, Mrs. Ella Taylor, Mrs.
        Royce Overholser, Mrs. O. W. Schultz, Mrs. W. A. George.

Mrs. O. W. Schultz, Mrs. Charles Hoffman, Mrs. Theodore Schwartz, Miss May
Hoefs, Miss Mabelle Clark, with Mrs. Royce Overholser as instructor.

The class was examined on May 20 and all members passed a very satisfactory
examination. On July 9, Mrs. J. Barrick, superintendent of surgical
dressings for Walworth county, appointed Mrs. W. B. Myler as vice chairman
of the surgical dressings department of the Selby Red Cross Unit.

One of the rooms in the court house was donated for the period of the war
for surgical dressings work. The room was equipped with four tables, two
sewing machines, one large wardrobe for supplies, a long showcase for
finished dressings, electric iron and ironing board. The cost of furnishing
this room was $20.45. The tables were donated. A telephone was also
installed by the Dakota Central Telephone company free of charge.

On May 23, actual surgical dressings work began with two day volunteer
classes and two evening volunteer classes with one afternoon for cutting
gauze, weekly. Attendance averaged about 15.

On May 28, the first quota was sent to headquarters. With the exception of
six weeks enforced vacation for lack of gauze, the classes worked regularly
until December 7, 1918, when the rooms were closed.

The following dressings were made and sent to headquarters: 324 paperbacked
pads, 12 oakum pads, 266 absorbent pads. 11 split irrigation pads, 33
pneumonia packets, 124 scultetus bandages. 11 many-tailed bandages, 33
gauze rolls, 28 shot bags, 11 triangular bandages 11 webbing splint straps,
275 8 x 4 compresses, 336 3 x 3-1/4 compresses, 743 4 x 4 compresses. 2650 2
x 2 wipes, 100 abdominal binders, a total of 4957 dressings in all. The
cost of material was $149.12. Total expense was $169.57.

All wore white uniforms. The workers wore white veils and the supervisors
wore blue veils. The head supervisor of the county wore a red veil.

GRAND ARMY OF THE REPUBLIC

John Mangan Post No. 150, Department of South Dakota Grand Army of the
Republic, was organized in the spring of 1889 at Bangor, Dakota territory,
and moved to Selby in early May of 1901. G. H. Hoffman was the commander at
that time. The meetings were held in the office of Captain N. H. Kingman.

        MR. B. B. POTTER, MR. G. H. HOFFMAN, MR. N. H. KINGMAN

The membership consisted of the following comrades: Captain N. H. Kingman,
B. B. Potter, G. H. Hoffman, J. M. Pulis, Zeke Harris, Irvans, C. O.
Peterson, Tisdall, and August (Gus) Siebrecht.

WOMAN'S RELIEF CORPS

John Mangan Corps No. 17 was organized in Selby March 18, 1910, with Minnie
Schellenger being elected as its first president. It received its name from
the John Mangan G.A.R. post organized in Bangor in 1889.

Because of an inherent love of patriotism by its members, it soon became an
active organization and continued until after World War I when the Legion
Auxiliary was organized and the work was left to younger hearts and hands.

Memorial Day programs often given under the direction of Julia George
became almost a county event. Instilled in a never-to-be-forgotten wav was
the thought that this should be a day sacred to the memory of the dead of
all wars, in all lands, and a dedication of service lovingly rendered to
the living.

Patriotic instruction in school and to those seeking citizenship was also
given.

Much time and effort was spent in making useful gifts for those who spent
their days in the state Soldier's Home and Hospital and contributions were
sent to help in their amusement.

At the convention in Pierre in June, 1919, three members were elected state
officers, namely: Lulu B. Potter, president; Minnie Schellenger, secretary;
and Ruth Steinhoff, treasurer. Then again in 1929, Ruth Steinhoff was
elected state inspector. She, assisted by Salome Mudge, inspected Onida,
Pierre, Highmore, Miller and Faulkton. Thus honors were brought to our
small community.

THE SELBY FIRE DEPARTMENT

The Selby Fire Department was organized in January 1911. The authorized
strength of the department at that time was 45 men consisting of one engine
company, one hook and ladder company and two hose companies. The equipment
at that time was hand drawn and hand operated and therefore more firemen
were needed. With modern equipment today the authorized strength of the
fire department has been reduced to 24 men.

        Selby's First Fire Truck. At            The New Community Fire Truck
        the Wheel Is Wm. Koch, who
        Designed and Built It

The first officers of the fire department were C. N. Burr, president; C. R.
Johnson, vice president; C. A. Potter, secretary-treasurer; T. P.
Schwartz, fire chief; C. R. Johnson, 1st assistant chief and C. A. Griffin,
2nd assistant chief. The records of the department show that the first fire
put out by the firemen was on July 19, 1911 at the Marble Shop of A. F.
Miles.

        Selby Volunteer Fire Department

In December 1947 the goal of two of Selby's citizens was reached. For two
years Leo Buchanan the fire chief of the Selby Fire Department, and James
S. Hopkins, then the Walworth County Agent, had been working on a Community
Fire Truck which was to serve the farmers of the Selby community. This goal
was reached in December 1947 when a new modern equipped fire truck was
delivered to the Selby Fire Department. This truck has paid for itself
several times already in the saving of homes and property of farmers in the
Selby area.

HISTORY OF SELBY BASEBALL

The first records of organized baseball for the town of Selby seems to
start in about 1903 when a team playing under the name of Prann's Colts
played several games with towns surrounding Selby and made a name in
baseball history for the many games played and won during the season. Mr.
Prann, a local druggist, took a special interest in the team and
undoubtedly favored the players with his time, and standing the expense of
traveling and equipment for the team.

The following years Selby had always had a good baseball club and not too
much of a record was kept from 1905 until after World War I when an
interest was again taken in baseball after the boys returned from the
service.

        SELBY'S FIRST BASEBALL TEAM
        Matt Miller, leaning against window. Standing, top row: Clarence
        Potter, John A. Koch, Henry Gross. Middle row: Chauncey Burr, Pat
        Coffey, Nelson Personius, Frank Gehrki. Bottom row: T. P. Schwartz,
        Nelson, Overholse, Ed B. Kingman, W. E. Prann.

Considerable money was spent during the following years to hire
professional players to strengthen the local boys and among the outstanding
paid players was Red Ulmer, a pitcher who helped the team win the majority
of games. Other towns also had good teams and at most games a considerable
amount of money was bet on the favorite teams and intense rivalry existed
at every game. Many a game was discussed on the street corners for several
days after it had been played.

The Yellowstone League was organized in 1933, made up of eight nearby towns
and played under a set of rules set up by a board of directors. Several of
the towns hired players to strengthen their team and a high class of
baseball was played at every game.

In about 1925 the Frederick Schauer Post No. 100 of the American Legion
sponsored a Junior ball club and a Legion member acted as manager during
each season.

This sponsorship was responsible for a good many boys learning the game who
later played with the first team. In later years the majority of players in
the League teams was made up of boys who had played in the Legion sponsored
teams of previous years.

A state amateur baseball association was organized which allowed teams from
all over the state who won in their immediate district, to play in the
final state championship games. The winner of the state championship was
sent to the National Amateur tournament at Battle Creek, Michigan, to
compete with teams from all over the United States for the national
championship. The State amateur baseball association has been responsible
for increasing interest in amateur baseball through out the whole state. A
good many towns have recently installed a lighting system so that baseball
can be played in the evenings instead of the afternoons.

        SELBY 1940 STATE TOURNAMENT FINALISTS
        Standing, left to right: Leo Buchanan, Club president; Ted
        Schanzenbach, Berry, Lester Jesse, Virgil Currier, John W. Hoven,
        Henry Schlomer, Harold Pressler, Joe Mueller, Gene Sawinsky, Merle
        Thorstenson, Al Ochsner, Ora DeSart, manager. Kneeling position:
        Herb Baer, Max Hoven, Pearl Brown, Emanuel Pressler, Bachman, Dean
        Buchanan, Robert Mickelson, Dr. Vanderhoof, and Mascot Tom Unker.

Selby won the district championship six times and were privileged to enter
the state tournament in which they made a good showing each time although
never winning the state championship. In the year of 1940 they went into
the finals against Aberdeen but lost the game by a score of 8 to 0.

After 1941 and all during the World War II baseball was hard to carry on
due to most of the younger men being in service. Although teams were
organized base ball did not have the zip and support all during the war.

After the boys began to return from the armed services in the fall of 1945
and spring of 1946 a new interest was taken in the National game and more
of the towns organized teams. The Yellowstone League was re-organized and
teams played on a schedule outlined at the beginning of the season and
played under rules and regulations set up by the league. Up to date Selby
has played twelve games in the state tournaments and made a very good
showing which the hits and runs will indicate. In the. twelve tourney games
Selby scored 81 runs on 107 hits to their opponents' 63 runs on 108 hits.

For the past few years Selby has had an active baseball club and has had
the support of all local fans and have always made a good showing in their
district. The writers of this article wish to give special mention to Theo.
Schwartz, deceased, and Jacob Allerdings, who were ardent fans and
supporters of the teams of the early days, also to Steve Johnson, Leo
Buchanan and Ora DeSart, who have been ardent fans and supporters of teams
for the past thirty years. Mr. DeSart managed the local team for almost ten
years, his teams winning many games, and his splendid coaching has been
responsible for Selby's being on the map of baseball history for the past
decade.

SELBY CONGREGATIONAL LADIES AID

Under the leadership of the Rev. Phillip Reich the Selby Congregational
Ladies' aid was organized on the 2nd of February, 1940. The following
ladies were the charter members of this group which was organized to help
wherever there was Christian need, both in and outside of their circle:
Mrs. Albert Allmendinger, Mrs. Oscar Boettcher. Mrs. Edward Bossert. Mrs.
John Knecht, Mrs. Conrad Miller, Mrs. Fred Miller, Mrs. Edward Himrich,
Mrs. Louisa Maier, Mrs. Jacob Schanzenbach, Mrs. John Schanzenbach, Mrs.
Phillip Reich and Mrs. George Wahl.

Having no public meeting place the aid met in private homes at monthly
intervals. During the course of the first year the membership grew to 23
faithful workers. Results of this bonded effort were gratifying for by May,
1944, the ladies' aid provided almost all of the funds for the church
basement and the furnishing of the kitchen in the basement.

Through the years, projects of a progressive nature have been carried out
by this group of ladies. United with the Sunday school the aid helped to
purchase a set of Christian and American silk platform flags and a Service
Roll for the church. When the need for an individual Communion service set
arose, it was met by the ladies' aid. Later additional church hymnals and
offering plates were also presented to the church by the aid.

The missionary projects of the church were wholeheartedly supported by the
aid. Pleas for food and clothing from devastated Europe were
conscientiously heeded by the sending of CARE packages and individual food
and clothing packages. Since 1947 almost all of the income has been
expended to meet such needs.

During 1948 a platform and aisle woolen rug purchased by this group made a
very marked improvement in the church interior. Other projects are
contemplated for the future.

In the nine years of its existence the approximate sum of $3500 has been
raised. These funds have been raised by semi-annual food and fancy work
sales, the serving by the aid at public auctions. Conference groups, such as
the state conference, the Laymen's convention and the Sunday school and
Christian Endeavor convention were hospitably entertained at various times.

An especially memorable day was spent when the aid paid a visit to the Old
People's Home at Eureka. There some 60 old folks were personally called
upon and presented with gifts of flowers, food and religious reading
material.

All of the charter members have continued as active members except two, who
moved away and two who were called to Eternal Rest. The present membership
in the aid stands at 16 members.

BETHANY LADIES' AID

As near as memory can recall a ladies' aid was organized in this community
in 1893, known as the Bethlehem Ladies' aid. Rev. Skartvedt, having started
a congregation here in 1887, was present and assisted in organizing this
aid. P. H. Olafson and Claus Olson, who were teaching Sunday school in the
congregation were also great promoters of the ladies aid.

Mrs. P. H. Olafson was the first president and Mrs. Claus Olson was the.
first vice president. The charter members were: Mesdames Johannes Tisdall,
O. P. Lee, P. H. Olafson, Hans Lee, P. N. Johnson, Olaus Olson, Gunhild
Olson, Eli Olson, Rasmus Thorstenson, P. J. Thorstenson, Lars Larson and
Soren Pederson.

These good pioneer women would get together as early as possible in the
forenoon and work until dinner was served by the hostess. This would give
them more time in which to work as they had a lot to do. Their work was
varied; some would card the wool for those who were spinning; others would
knit or sew; then again they would make quilts. They also had their time
for devotions which consisted of prayer, Bible study, singing of hymns and
mission study.

Money was scarce in those days so donations such as ready-made garments or
goods to be made up into clothing, were given. The cloth would be cut into
aprons, dresses or other garments by the president or some other helper.
This was sewed at the meetings or given to someone who would volunteer to
sew at home.

Sales of the articles made or donated were then held; at this time a dinner
was also served, for which each one paid according to their means. The
proceeds were disposed of according to the wishes of the members of the
aid. It was usually divided between the mission and church benevolences,
such as parochial school, charity and the like.

Other members who joined in the later nineties were: Mrs. S. T. Peterson,
Mrs. Martha Ellefson, Mrs. Odland and Mrs. Marie Olson.

In 1899 several members from Scandinavia congregation, as well as
Bethlehem, moved to Canada and elsewhere. This decreased their band of
workers so much that the north and south groups decided to work together.
This union took place at the Hans Lee home.

During those years, services were held in schoolhouses but in 1906 a church
was built and was named Bethany so the aid changed their name to Bethany
Ladies Aid.

For several years thereafter they donated to the church building fund. Then
there were pews, altar, carpet, paint and things of that sort to buy
besides doing missionary work and sometimes helping with the pastor's
salary.

Members of the aid and others are especially grateful to Mrs. Marthe Ekrem
for the outstanding work in compiling historical data and pictures for our
fine history book of the ladies aid dating back to its organization in
1893. Mrs. Ekrem has been a faithful member of our aid for many years and
is a present making her home with her daughter and family, Captain and Mrs.
Norman Slater at Concord, California.

Gifts were presented to Mr. and Mrs. Ole Opheim, Mr. and Mrs. Severt Opheim
and Mr. and Mrs. P. J. Thorstenson for their golden weddings. Among those
who have observed silver weddings recently are: Mr. and Mrs. Christ Norby,
Mr. and Mrs. August Thorstenson and Mr. and Mrs. John J. Brockel.

The aid helped financially with the new basement under the church which was
completed in 1931 and as time went on has equipped the kitchen with stoves,
cupboards, tables, dishes and the like.

The Golden Jubilee was celebrated at Bethany on September 29, 1935. People
were asked to bring their lunch baskets and the aid served hot coffee.
Before this event, histories for the church and the aids were written by
members who had been in the aid for a long time.

We now have a membership of twenty-four and there are four charter members
still with us: Mrs. Severt Opheim, Mrs. Ole Opheim, Mrs. Lars Larson and
Mrs. P. J. Thorstenson.

At present our aid contributes to the many charities of the church
including the Children's and Old Peoples' Homes at Beresford, the House of
Mercy at Sioux Falls, the Pension Fund. Home and Foreign Missions and many
other departments of the church. The last few years we have been working
for a new furnace for the church. This has at last become a reality as we
now have an electrically controlled bottle gas furnace.

For several years we have enrolled baptized children of the congregation in
the Cradle Roll. Proceeds of this goes to the Alaska Missions.

Life membership certificates and pins have been presented to the charter
members and to several of our older members.

Many of our pioneer mothers have been called to their final resting place.
Others have moved from the community. So today as we look back we see a
great change has been wrought in our midst.

In pioneer days, time and distance were an important factor. Today it is
relatively insignificant. But regardless of the transformations that are
going on in our material life, let us always keep foremost in our mind the
fact that the laws of God and of nature are the same today as they were in
pioneer days.

In preparing this history we had to consult the early settlers and draw
from records. If we are in error in places we ask you to bear with us.

We sincerely hope that this history will serve in a humble way to
perpetuate the memories of our pioneer mothers and members of the ladies'
aid of the Bethany Lutheran church.

BANGOR BAND

The Bangor band, later called the Walworth county band, was organized about
1895, at Bangor, with H. R. de Malignon as band master, and was the first
band in the county.

The first instruments were brought in by individuals who had played in some
band before coming to Bangor, and by getting together soon created interest
enough to form a band. New instruments and uniforms were purchased with
money earned by giving minstrel shows, home talent plays and playing for
different celebrations and in different towns such as Hoven, LeBeau, Evarts,
Mound City, Bowdle, and others.

Some of the noted engagements were: playing in Aberdeen when President
McKinley visited the city, and later when Theo. Roosevelt spoke there. Also
for a 5-day carnival in Aberdeen and a 3-day 4th of July celebration at
Eureka, where they drove in a wagon similar to that in the picture.

THE WALWORTH COUNTY FARMERS UNION

The first meeting of the Walworth County Farmers Union was held in the
commissioners room at the courthouse in Selby, March 11, 1946 with August
Dahme of Warner, as the organizer. The first officers elected were as
follows: Carl Mueller, Java, county chairman; Clifford Tucker, Selby, vice
chairman; Max Van Orman, Selby, secretary-treasurer; James Kane, Java,
legislative committeeman.

        Standing, left to right: Mathilda Van Orman, Max Van Orman, James
        Kane. Seated: Cliff Tucker, Eddie Anderson, Herbert Fiechtner.

From this beginning the organization spread to four active Locals in the
county with an enrollment of over 200 members in 1948. In 1949, the Locals
were reduced to three, namely the Java, Selby and Akaska locals, but their
combined membership still totaled about 200. During this time, Clifford
Tucker, Selby, served for two years in 1947 and 1948 as county chairman.
Eddie Anderson, Java, present chairman, is now serving his second term.
Albert R. Aman, Java, served as vice chairman in 1947; Clifford
Schanzenbach, Selby, in 1948; and the present vice chairman is Clifford
Tucker, Selby. Herbert Fiechtner, Java, succeeded Max Van Orman as
secretary-treasurer in 1947 and is still serving in this office at present.
James Kane has served as legislative chairman ever since the organization
was started.

Ed J. Miller, Bowdle, has been influential in the educational field. Mrs.
Max Van Orman, Selby, is serving as the present educational director. An
active youth movement has been established and Mrs. Henry J. Mueller, Java,
has done very commendable work in this field.

The Walworth County Farmers Union has pledged itself to award annually a
trophy to the 4-H youngster showing his calf to the best advantage at the
annual Calf show at Mobridge.
