THE WALWORTH RED CROSS

The Walworth County Chapter of the American Red Cross was organized at
Mobridge in June and July of the year 1917, in the midst of World War I for
the purpose of meeting the needs of the war conditions. Mrs. Lillian Doud
of Mobridge was selected as the first chairman with Mrs. Mabel Conger as
secretary and Mrs. G. H. Bugbee as treasurer. Work for the soldiers was
started at once. and within a comparatively short time branches were set up
at Selby, Java, Glenham, Akaska, Lowry. LeBeau and at the Hilltop school
southwest of Selby. Everyone went to work and county quotas in all
departments of work were met. Though interest in these branches continued
for several years after the war was over, eventually they all ceased to
function and some were disbanded as the officers left the several
communities and no new ones were selected to take their places, excepting
in Mobridge, Selby, Java and Glenham. In these towns the interest waned and
before World War II the branches had all been discontinued and the
organization functioned only as a county chapter with no local units. There
arose no need for any change in this form of organization and a return to
the old plan throughout World War II.

        Back row, left to right: Robert Fahlherg, A. L. Stoddard, F.
        Clement, A. C. Schlepp, A. E. Lakeman. Second row: Mrs. A. M.
        McKinnon, Julius Skaug, George Lehnert, E. H. Noteboom, Max Gutz.
        Seated: Ella Taylor, Rose Schmidt, Verna Schanzenhach, Mary Cook.

Shortly after the organization of the county chapter a Junior Red Cross
organization was set up with E. H. Noteboom of Selby, then county
superintendent of schools as chairman; Mrs. Ida de Malignon of Selby,
secretary; and Miss Norma Koehne of Mobridge, as treasurer. This activity
flourished during the World War I period but practically ceased to exist
for many years in the interim but is now functioning under the auspices of
the National Red Cross and the county chapter very efficiently. Mrs. Verna
Schanzenbach is the present county chairman.

The Selby branch continued to be active and to meet the local and chapter
needs through the years under the leadership of Mrs. Ella Taylor, Miss Rose
Schmidt, Miss May Hoefs, C. A. Potter, E. H. Noteboom and others,
discontinuing and amalgamating with the county organization with the other
branches.

The present officers of the Walworth County Chapter of the Red Cross are
all in Selby: E. H. Noteboom, chairman; Mrs. Ella Taylor, vice chairman;
Mrs. J. S. Hopkins, secretary; and Rev. E. H. Sprenger, treasurer.

NATIONAL FOUNDATION FOR INFANTILE PARALYSIS

The first activities in organized money-raising effort on a local level in
Walworth county for fighting infantile paralysis took place in the year
1935 when Stewart Cook of Selby, was appointed Selby chairman for a
President's Birthday ball and charged with the duty of raising funds for
the purpose of doing what could be done in diagnosing, treating and
controlling infantile paralysis. Mr. Cook appointed Roy E. Hoefs, Wm. M.
Hoven and Mrs. Mary Cook a committee and they put on the first Birthday
ball in Selby and raised about $60.00. In the course of time a county
organization was set up and the work of raising funds extended to the other
towns and to the rural areas.

        INFANTILE PARALYSIS COMMITTEE
        Standing, left to right: George Lehnert, J. Ed Meyers, A. C.
        Schlepp. Seated: Tom Goar, Min Boschker, A. E. Lakeman.

The county organization in time became not only a fund-raising
organization, but also assisted the victims of infantile paralysis, seeing
to it that they received hospitalization and treatment, and performing all
of the various functions outlined in the charter under the national
organization.

During the recent epidemics of the dread disease everything possible has
been done to help out those afflicted and all cases have been carefully
followed up. The organization has worked in close cooperation with the
other charitable bodies in the county and through the years has raised
considerable sums of money and expended the same in the alleviation of the
suffering of the particular group in whose interests it functions.

A. E. Lakeman of Mobridge is the president of the Walworth county
organization, and Mrs. Emma Perman is the Selby member of the county
committee.

SELBY BUSINESS HISTORIES

THE PERMAN IMPLEMENT COMPANY

The Perman Implement company, one of Selby's most successful, largest and
best housed businesses, had its beginnings in Lowry 26 years ago when J. F.
Perman bought out the implement business of Philip Oxner. He had farmed for
some time and had made a trip to the west coast before deciding to go into
the business. He was successful and sought a wider field of operation so in
1925 sold out to local parties and purchased the implement business of the
Equity Exchange at Java, taking his brother, Ed, in as a partner. The
Equity people had lost the old Zeller implement building by fire and had
erected a new structure which was quite modern in that day.

In 1928, the company purchased the holdings of the Lincke Implement at
Selby and Ed F. Perman came here to manage it, the business being conducted
in the Pitcher building, now occupied by the Three-B Hardware. This place
did not meet the needs of the growing concern and in 1941 the lots now
occupied by Smith Locker plant were purchased. the buildings on them
sold,--the large garage building to Art Beckman who cut it down and moved
it to a new location where it is now occupied by the Stulken Implement
company and the smaller building to Alferd Moos.

The large building owned by the company at Java was moved here and set over
a full basement, this last improvement being fitted as a service and repair
shop. The main floor was modernized. In the meantime, Jake Perman had left
the business to go into the oil business at Moorhead, Minnesota, and Henry
F. Perman took charge of the Java end, buying it outright in 1941, when
Jake came back from Moorhead and started in the implement business at
Eureka.

In 1945, the partnership was dissolved, the Eureka business was sold, and
soon afterward Jake went to California. The next year Henry sold out at
Java to the company and construction began on the new prototype building on
north Main street, which was finished the next year. Henry later came to
Selby as shop foreman.

The lots on which the new building was located were occupied by the Equity
Service station, the building of which was sold and is now used as a farm
home on the "second bench" a couple of miles southeast of Old Evarts. The
other lots were used for various purposes through the years, as an ice
skating pond, a site for circus and chautauqua tents, playground for
children and many other uses. At one time what was considered quite a
pretentious "Picnic House" for tourists was situated on the north lot. The
only residence that ever existed on the property was a small shack which
old timers remember as being occupied by a unique character in the early
days, by the name of Johnny Bloom.

Ed F. Perman and Emma Lakeman were married September 30. 1928, at Java and
set up housekeeping in the William Koch house. Since then they have lived
in and owned a number of houses in Selby, the last being the former E. G.
Powell home where they now reside but which has been sold to Christ Reuer.
When the apartments at the new Berens hotel are ready, they expect to
occupy one of them. They have one daughter, Virginia, who is a student at
the University of South Dakota.

The Perman Implement company has always sold the International Harvester
company line of farm implements. It has ever been a policy of the company
to carry a complete line and offer the. best of service. The Plymouth and
Chrysler automobiles are also sold and serviced. As of today, the Perman
Implement company offers the Selby trade territory a complete line of farm
equipment plus every facility in servicing and repairing tractors and
automobiles that may be had anywhere. The line of special equipment for
this kind of work is complete and up to the minute. The business now
employs seven people besides the proprietors.

During their residence in Selby, Mr. and Mrs. Perman have both taken an
active part in community and church affairs. Everything worthwhile in Selby
has had their financial support and their time. Ed F. Perman has been a
member of the city council for many years.

THE CENTRAL LUMBER COMPANY

The Central Lumber company started business in Selby in 1901 when E. Hudson
made a deal purchasing the yard, including stock of lumber and coal from A.
S. Taylor, and hired P. E. Greenman as manager. This yard was located
directly north of and adjoining its present site. Mr. Greenman (known as
Phil) ran the yard until 1904 and then was transferred to Aberdeen as
manager of that yard. Selby was one of the first yards owned by the
Central, and was really the start of a company that has grown from three or
four small yards until it now owns and operates 64 yards in South Dakota,
North Dakota, and Minnesota. Emil Schmidt took charge as manager of the
Selby yard when Phil Greenman was transferred and continued as manager for
several years. Records do not show when he left or who was the next
manager, but some of the later managers were John Freyer, Hans Larson,
Walter Valentine, and at present, Jacob J. Wolff.

In 1933 during the dry years, the Central took over the Selby Lumber
company, then owned by Mr. Dobson, and moved their stock to the Selby
Lumber company plant, which is its present location. The old, original
Central plant had now been dismantled.

The first few years were probably the most interesting to the real old
timers,--the town was new, the railroad had just pushed west, and new
people were coming in and settling on the farms. The Central Lumber company
stock then consisted of lumber, millwork, lime plaster, cement, posts, barb
wire, and coal. Those were the "base burner" days when it was a real luxury
to have a hard coal base burner going in the parlor. At that time hard coal
sold for about $12.00 per ton.

The Central Lumber company is proud of its part in Selby's growth and of
the many buildings in town and on the adjacent farms for which they
furnished the building material, and although the present management will
change, they hope the company will still be here to help celebrate Selby's
100th anniversary.

DR. J. A. VANDERHOOF

The business building occupied by Dr. J. A. Vanderhoof was moved from
Bangor to Selby in the year 1901 by Dr. August Beil and Dr. H. B. Foster,
the former a physician and the latter a veterinarian. The lots, like all
others in Selby, were purchased from the Milwaukee Land company. Soon after
the building was moved, Dr. Foster sold out to Dr. Beil and the latter
maintained his office in the building until 1910 when he sold out to Dr. M.
W. Myler, who opened the first dental office in the new town.

In 1917, Dr. Myler sold out to a classmate, Dr. G. W. Vail, who came here
from Morristown where he and his family had held down a "claim" and took
over the successful practice that had been established, continuing until
the time of his death in 1923. Dr. Weiland of Mobridge, came from Mobridge
on stated days each week to serve the people of this community for a time
and then located here permanently, occupying the building until 1933 when
he closed up his office and went to Florida. Dr. J. A. Vanderhoof then took
over for a year and then moved to the rooms under the First National bank.
For four or five years the building was occupied by several tenants, Mr.
and Mrs. Vincent Steinhoff and Mr. and Mrs. Elmer Swanson making it their
homes for short periods of time, and later Esther Chesky opened a beauty
shop there and occupied it for two years.

In 1940 Dr. Vanderhoof came back from Arkansas where he had practiced for a
short time and set up business again in the building and has occupied it
since. The property is still owned by the estates of G. W. Vail and Dena H.
Vail. Dr. Vanderhoof is a graduate of the College of Dentistry of the
University of Minnesota. He was united in marriage with Margaret Gehrki of
Selby in 1938 and they have five children. Both are very much interested in
local and community affairs and he is a member of the city council and
enjoys a large dental practice, serving patients from over a wide area.

PILLEY AND SONS, CREAM STATION

The building in which this business is conducted was once a granary on a
farm near Bangor and was moved to Selby when the town started in 1900 by
Frank Clark, who opened a meat market in it in partnership with a man
named Campbell. The next year this business was discontinued and Dick
Kirkhoven rented the building and opened a pool hall. In 1905 Mrs. Theresa
Kane moved her millinery business in when she sold the building now known
as the Dettman building to the Hempfthings. In 1906 Johnny Ballensky of
Akaska bought the building and started a barber shop. Later, in 1906, A. F.
Rounds opened a jewelry store in the same building, soon moving to the
building now occupied by the Drowns, and Dudley Martin rented it for a
barber shop, staying until 1909 when he moved into the basement of the new
First National bank building.

When Mr. Martin moved out, Chet Peterson continued the barber business in
the building. Some time later a cream station was started, among the
operators being Gottfried Wagner and Henry Hammer. Jess Richardson was the
last operator before the Jederbergs took it over.

On March 1, 1921, Mr. and Mrs. Otto Jederberg took possession and bought
the building of Dave Irwin who was the owner at that time. They bought
cream and handled produce for more than 26 years for the Hanford, Borden
and Pilley people, selling out and moving out July 1, 1947.

Mr. and Mrs. Jederberg operated a business which was a credit to the city.
They made an important place for themselves in the business circles of the
city. After selling out they went west, but liked Selby so much better that
they have come back here and plan to remain here permanently, having an
apartment at the Marywall hotel. Mr. Jederberg is employed by the county
highway department.

The Pilley station is now operated by Mr. and Mrs. Wm. Knecht, both of whom
are natives of Walworth county. They are offering the people of the
community a very good local market for their cream and the business is one
that the town needs and is being very well conducted, drawing a good
patronage.

The living rooms at the rear have been occupied by the family of the tenant
of the business room.

THE SELBY RECORD

The history of the Selby Record really starts in Bangor where in 1890 on
July 17, Fred Griffin and Willis G. Brown consolidated the Rustler and the
Central Dakotan and called the new publication the Walworth County Record.
The Rustler had been established in 1885 and the Central Dakotan in 1887.
The Griffin-Brown partnership lasted only a short time, with Mr. Brown
selling his interest to Mr. Griffin. Mr. Griffin continued to publish the
paper for many years, moving the plant to Selby in 1900. In 1914 he sold
the Record to A. C. de Malignon and A. H. Schmidt who operated it as a
partnership until May 1, 1917 when de Malignon sold his interest to
Schmidt. A month later Schmidt resold the publication to Mr. Griffin who
had returned from Raton, N. M. Mr. Griffin continued as publisher until
March 1, 1925, when E. H. Noteboom purchased the equipment and operated the
paper until April, 1944, when it was suspended because of the lack of
mechanical help. For several years Patsy McNeely acted as co-publisher with
Mr. Noteboom. It was during the period that Mr. Noteboom owned the paper
that the name was changed from the Walworth County Record to the Selby
Record. The paper was published for many years in the building now owned by
the Hopkins Implement company. In April, 1945, the publication was
purchased by Fritz and Ida Clement of Java, who commenced publication of
the Record the first week in May.

The late Carl F. Clement and his wife, Kate, established the Java Herald in
September, 1903, having purchased the equipment of the Rising Sun of
Bangor. They continued the publication of the Herald until 1922 when Mr.
Clement passed away while on a pleasure trip to the west coast. Mrs.
Clement and son, Fritz, continued the publication of the Herald until 1926
when the mother retired from newspaper work and the Herald continued with
Fritz and Ida Clement as publishers. The Herald plant was consolidated with
the Record in 1946 when the Herald building was moved from Java to Selby and
set down on the corner lot once occupied by the Elfrink store building,
which had been torn down in 1944 by E. H. Noteboom.

The Clements, Ida and Fritz, are at present the editor and publisher of the
Record and the Herald, two separate newspapers, both being printed in the
Selby plant. They have one son, Bruce, now a printing and journalism
student at State college at Brookings, and a daughter, Germaine, a freshman
in Selby High school. His mother, Mrs. Kate Clement, also makes her home
with them.

The Elfrink building which stood on the Record corner for many years,
originally came from LeBeau, being first moved by J. J. Elfrink to Bangor
and later to Selby. The store was closed in 1914 and from that period until
it was torn down was occupied by several different businesses. Among them
was the post office, the Drown Studio and others. There were several
apartments in the rear and upstairs that were rented out for many years.
The Record plant was housed in a one-room building attached to the left
rear of the Elfrink building. This one-room structure is now part of the
Record-Herald plant.

The Record today is one of the better equipped small town newspapers.

THE SELBY GAS COMPANY

The building of the Selby Gas company plant began in 1946 and was completed
early in the year of 1947. Operations were begun in February of 1947 when
they hired their present manager, Robert Mickelson. Harlyn Brown was hired
on May 1, 1948, to assist in installations and as bulk truck driver. The
territory serviced by the Selby Gas company extends fifty miles in each
direction from Selby.

The cost of the Selby Gas company was $20,000.00 for equipment which
consists of an 18,000-gallon bulk storage tank, a 10 x 10 pumphouse which
houses a pump for filling cylinders and bulk trucks and a compressor for
unloading tank cars, a 10 x 20 filling house and platform for filling
cylinders and storage for appliances, one 1000-gallon bulk delivery truck
and a 1/2-ton pick-up used for appliance deliveries.

Propane gas is used in the territory for motor fuel heating, refrigerators,
cooking, water heaters, and chicken brooders.

The propane business has grown to where the company handled 200,000 gallons
in 1949.

The present stockholders and directors are: Jake Rabenberg, president; Ed
F. Perman, treasurer; and Adam Pressler, secretary.

THE RED OWL AGENCY

One of the few remaining buildings in Selby which after fifty years is
still in the possession of the original owners, is familiarly known as the
Hoefs building presently occupied by the Red Owl Agency located on the site
where it was first built.

Julius Emil Hoefs and Emma Albertina Zirbel were both born in Germany,
coming to Watertown, Wisconsin, at an early age with their parents. They
were married there in 1885 and came directly to Walworth county where Mr.
Hoefs had a claim on the land where L. J. Moell now resides. He went in
with Jake J. Elfrink in the store in Bangor. In 1900 he built his own
business in Selby. The building was erected during the summer of 1900 by
Lee Sunderland and George Zieder and its present excellent condition
testifies to the skill of the carpenters. The store was opened in the fall
carrying a complete line of groceries and general merchandise and as Mrs.
Hoefs relates, "sold everything but whiskey". They were assisted in the
operation of the store by their daughter, May (now Mrs. Harvey Magers) and
Mable Bucklin. The business continued until 1943, Mrs. Hoefs carried on
after the death of her husband in 1938, but due to age and failing health
she closed the store which had served the community for almost half a
century. The stock was later disposed of at public auction and the
building was unoccupied for several months. In August, 1945, it was leased
to Leo Walz for a Red Owl Agency which he managed until January, 1947, when
Bernel Manke purchased the stock and fixtures and is the present owner of
this completely modern food market.

Bernel is the son of Mr. and Mrs. Albert Manke of Selby, and has spent all
of his life in Walworth county except for two years on the west coast. He
was married in 1934 to Lois Ingalls. They have three daughters, Arlis and
Frances, twins, 13, and Cynthia, 3, and one son, Wally, 10. Mr. Manke has
improved the building by the installation of a new walk-in cooler for the
refrigeration of meats and perishable foods. Mr. Manke's friendly and
accommodating manner and fine stock of groceries have earned his store the
reputation of a pleasant place to shop. Mrs. Tillie Hanrahan is regularly
employed as a clerk, with Mrs. Manke and Mrs. Ted Schanzenbach as frequent
assistants.

CLASSIC BEAUTY SALON

This building was moved to Selby from Bangor in August, 1900, and housed
the Walworth County bank. On September 23, 1905, the bank moved out and
into their new building which is the present home of Mr. and Mrs. Robert
Bauder.

In 1905 after this building was vacated by the bank, James Coffey moved in
his law office. In May, 1911, Haynes and Tofflemire, real estate dealers,
came in from Akaska. The next occupant this building housed was a cream
station owned by Jake D. Schanzenbach, which remained in business at this
location until December 6, 1919, when Jake purchased the A. F. Miles
building which Rose McIntosh was renting for a millinery shop. These two
businesses exchanged locations. Later Miss McIntosh added dresses to her
shop and remained here until November of 1932. The building was vacant for
a short while for remodeling. In 1933 Gertrude Hoefs Ketterling opened a
dress shop, closing right after Christmas in 1934. Mr. and Mrs Ketterling
kept their living quarters there until 1935.

In late summer or fall of 1935 Martha Rabenberg opened a beauty shop and
then sold to Judy Swenson in 1938. Alma Baer, now Mrs. Herbert Wolff,
bought the shop from Miss Swenson and took possession September 13, 1943.
She operated the shop alone until March 28, 1947, when she secured the help
of LaVerna Baer. They worked together one year, and the shop was then sold
to LaVerna Baer who took possession April 1, 1948, and is still operating
the Classic Beauty salon at the present time (1950).

HOPKINS IMPLEMENT

One of the first essentials for the new town was a newspaper. Fred Griffin
provided this by bringing the Walworth County Record to Selby. The building
was moved up from Bangor and set on lots 15 and 16 in block 8, which were
secured from Adam Himrich. The United States post office for this thriving
community was established in the front part of the building with Fred
Griffin as postmaster and Jim D. Stewart as his assistant. The same persons
published the Walworth County Record in the print shop at the rear of the
building. The post office began service on December 17, 1900, the mail
arriving by a stage from Bowdle.

In 1907 August C. Schmidt became owner of the premises, and upon his death
the property passed to his heirs, with Albert Schmidt retaining ownership.
From 1914 until the beginning of World War I, Albert Schmidt and Robert de
Malignon published the Record in its original location when it was resold
to Mr. Griffin and moved out of the Schmidt building, to the corner north
of the Burr store on October 7, 1922.

There were several short-lived business venture housed on the main floor
during the ensuing years. Stewart Mickelson was proprietor of Tiny's Tip
Top tavern and Allen George sold fruit and vegetables for several months.
During its vacancy it was frequently used by various organizations for
chicken suppers and ice cream socials and also as a storehouse for the
Schmidt Market.

Albert Moos set up a shoe and harness repair shop in the northwest corner
of the street floor and continued until a fire in his establishment gutted
the lower floor and made further occupancy impossible.

The upper floor has always been the home of the Eastern Star and several
Masonic bodies, and in 1946 the building was purchased by the Masonic
Building association. Later Joe Berens bought the lots and building, and in
1947 they were resold to the Hopkins Implement company. After extensive
repair and renovations, James Hopkins moved his implement business into
this location in the fall of 1947.

Mr. Hopkins came to Walworth county in 1939 from Watertown, South Dakota,
and served as county agricultural agent until he purchased the Oliver farm
implement agency from Jake Rabenberg in July, 1947. He is widely known and
respected for his enthusiasm and energy in all matters pertaining to
community improvement. He has four children in the Selby schools, and is
assisted in the store by Marvin Lutz.

THE SELBY LIVESTOCK SALES COMPANY

The first livestock auction sale was held in the Walworth county fair
grounds pavilion at Selby. on Friday, July 23, 1937, by the Selby Livestock
Auction company of which E. B. Moser of Java, and J. E. Myler of
Gettysburg, were the managers. Mr. Myler and Auctioneer C. W. Leighty of
Aberdeen, were the auctioneers and Max Gutz of the First National bank of
Selby, officiated as clerk. The project had been worked up by Mr. Moser and
Mr. Myler, both of whom were handling livestock and buying and selling over
quite a wide area. Mr. Moser had been a solicitor for a livestock
commission company and had learned the livestock buying and selling business
very well and had also gained a wide acquaintance among men engaged in that
line of business. Mr. Myler had a wide experience in the stock business and
was well known as an auctioneer in this section. The two men also
interested Jacob Helm of Java in the enterprise. Mr. Helm had been in
various businesses in Java, including many years in banking and was also
interested in farming and stock raising with a wide acquaintance over the
territory from which the sale would draw patronage and he took charge of
the business and financing of the project. Mr. Myler never had any
financial interest in the business.

The livestock sales barn was built in the flush days following World War I
for the purpose of holding sales of purebred livestock and had been
remodeled on the inside to better fit it for the new use, and pens were
built on the outside. Loading and unloading chutes were also built. A good
deal of money was put into the enterprise and a lot of money was needed to
handle the actual sale. The organization was licensed and bonded in
compliance with the state laws and a licensed veterinarian, Doctor A. E.
Byron, was employed for the inspection work. The nearest sales ring to the
east was at Aberdeen and there were none established to the westward even as
far west as Montana. The enterprise was really pioneering and the reason
for locating it at Selby was the fact that highways numbered 12 and 83
crossed here and a suitable plant was available at this point.

The early sales drew patronage enough to net the owners a profit and before
long it became a really big sale, and for years, after other sales had
sprung into existence at Gettysburg, Linton, Bowdle, Mobridge and
elsewhere, the Selby sale was known as one of the best little sales in the
state.

Mr. Moser later sold his interest to Dr. A. W. Spiry of Mobridge, and John
E. Spiry of Java, and started a sale at Bowdle. Later Ed Hirsch of Java and
Earl Thorpe. of Britton, bought the Spiry interests and in 1944, Christ
Helm of Java, bought out Hirsch. After the death of Jacob Helm in 1944,
Christ Helm bought his interest from the executors and he and Earl Thorpe
have continued the business.

Jacob Helm was also interested in sales at Linton and at Gettysburg and
made quite a success of directing the three sales until his health failed.

Through the years, the Selby sale has kept pace with the times. As the
livestock auction sale business developed in the country, supplanting to
quite an extent the shipment of livestock directly to the terminal markets,
and other concentration points, new regulations were necessary and new ways
of doing business developed. The sales barn was purchased from Dr. Byron in
1945 and the floors of the pavilion and pens were concreted in accordance
with the laws of sanitation, and inspection has become more rigid. Also
selling by weight is now required and all of these matters mean more and
more investment of capital into the business.

The Selby Livestock Sale is one of the well established thriving businesses
of the city and brings a lot of people to town on sale days. Christ Helm
has become a permanent resident of Selby and has built two houses here. The
hired help required in conducting the sale brings a substantial payroll
into the city's business. This sale has been a real asset to the community.

HANK'S BAR

The building in which this business is conducted was built in the year 1906
by the Gutz interests for the Farmer's State bank of Selby and was used as
a bank building until 1909 when the new brick building on the corner, now
the First National bank was ready. The old bank property was then sold to
John Reistad who moved his saloon business into it, later selling out to
Dave Irwin who in 1912 sold to J. P. Wagner. In 1916 Wagner raised the
roof and built on the second story, thus providing living quarters upstairs
which the Wagners occupied. In 1917, when prohibition caused the closing of
all liquor businesses, the Wagners went into the restaurant business which
they sold to Mr. and Mrs. Pete Thompson in 1931. The Thompsons continued
the business until 1934 and then sold to Otto Fischer, retaining ownership
of the building and continuing to live in the upstairs apartments. In 1935
Fischer discontinued the restaurant and took out an on-sale liquor license.
In 1935 this business was sold to Sam Raich who also acquired the building.
Raich later sold the liquor business to Milo Swift who operated there two
years and then purchased the Schmidt building and moved his business into
it. Henry Weiszhaar then rented the building and opened a second on-sale
liquor store which on January 1, 1950, was changed to a soft drink and
recreation parlor.

Henry J. Weiszhaar was born at Hazelton, North Dakota, and his parents are
Christ and Lydia Weiszhaar, both born in Campbell county and now residents
of Selby. His father was in the meat business in Bowdle Linton and Ashley
and at one time the family resided on the farm southwest of Selby now
belonging to Albert Almendinger Henry graduated from Ashley high school and
served in the armed forces from June, 1944, until October, 1946, in the
navy, receiving his training at Farragut, Idaho, and being assigned to
service in the South Pacific and particularly at Okinawa. He was united in
marriage with Doris Himrich, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. John Himrich Jr., and
they have a small daughter. Mrs. Weiszhaar grew up in the Selby community.

Mr. Weiszhaar has enjoyed a good business and is endeavoring to treat his
customers in such a manner that his business will continue to be good. He
is a consistent booster for Selby and is doing his share in all promotional
affairs of the city.

HETTICH S SUPER VALU MARKET

Hettich Brothers Super Valu Market is the continuation of one of the oldest
businesses in Selby, in one of the newest buildings. The business was
started with the town in 1900 and the building was just recently completed,
having been built during the winter of 1948-1949.

Harold and Ernest Hettich came to Selby in February, 1946, and bought out
Lester and Francis Simons who were running the Super Valu store, long
known as Schmidt's Market. The Simons boys had purchased it from Albert
Schmidt who retained the ownership of the building. The Hettich Brothers
rented the building from Albert and operated the meat market, grocery
store, and the meat locker plant.

In August, 1948, the building was sold to Milo Swift, so they had to vacate
it by September 15 of that year. The boys sold out everything they could
and the remaining merchandise was stored in the basements and garages of
their homes.

Now what were they to do,--no building, but still owning fixtures and
stock. At first they thought of buying a store in some other town, but
having their homes established here, it was a little harder to leave Selby.

They decided to build a store. It was hard to get a vacant lot in a good
location. There was one vacant lot between the post office and the opera
house, but there was some trouble in getting a clear title. This was
overcome the last week in September, 1948.

Digging operations began immediately and with the help of brothers and
other relatives they poured the footings and foundation. Cement was nearly
impossible to get, but by patiently waiting and driving all over the
territory they got enough to finish the project.

Next they needed bricks and tile without delay so the same could be laid
before freezing weather. They borrowed trucks and hauled them from Aberdeen.

Bricklayers were also scarce and rather than wait until the next spring or
summer they undertook to do the work themselves. This tile and brick work
was started on November 1 and finished the 8th of December, the brothers
getting the roof on the day before the first heavy snowfall.

They next commenced with the inside work doing all the work themselves,
except plastering and wiring. The concrete for the floor was poured during
a January blizzard. The frozen sand was chopped out, hauled inside and
thawed out. A slab at a time was poured and had to be troweled at night,
sometimes as late as one o'clock. The floor was then covered with asphalt
tile.

Painting, building of shelves, and other work was done during January and
on February 18 the store was opened for business.

The store is one of the most modern Super Valu stores in South Dakota. It
has a canopy with fluorescent lighting all around the sides. The newest
type of shelving, designed to accommodate a greater amount of stock and
doing away with store room space, was also installed. The store carries a
complete line of groceries, fresh meats and vegetables.

Harold is married to Norma Huber of Selby, and they have one daughter.
Ernest is married to Frieda Himrich of Selby, and they have a son and a
daughter.

MARYWALL HOTEL

Congratulations to the City of Selby on your 50 years of progress! May you
continue to grow and prosper.

We have been asked to write the history of our hotel for the Golden Jubilee
book but, since we have not lived here so very long, there are no doubt
many interesting details we do not know.

Mr. Buchanan built this hotel a number of years ago in Bangor and it was
later moved into Selby. They rented rooms and served meals for a period of
years, when it was later leased to a Mr. and Mrs. Fisher. Mr. and Mrs.
Lakeman then took over the management and purchased it. They, too, rented
the rooms and enjoyed a fine cafe and ice cream business. They purchased a
large ice cream machine where they made large amounts of ice cream. In
1942, Mr. Lakeman passed away very suddenly. Immediately the cafe equipment
was sold and Mrs. Lakeman made several apartments which she rented along
with her other rooms. She was here several years and then sold to Mrs.
Lydia Hepper of Java. We then heard the hotel was for sale so purchased it
and took possession on April 1, 1946. Mrs. Lakeman was in charge until this
time. We have made many improvements each year and we are especially proud
of our innerspring mattresses and good bedding. The hotel inspector has
always complimented us on this and has declared our hotel to be nice and
clean and in good repair. We named our hotel The Marywall Hotel. It is a
combination of our given names,--Mrs. Young's name being Mary and mine,
Wallace. Our slogan is: YOUR HOME AWAY FROM HOME.

We came here from Hastings, Nebraska, where we both worked at the Hastings
Ammunition Depot, the largest of its kind in the world. We spent three
years there and came here in 1946. We have seen Selby grow by leaps and
bounds, have enjoyed a fine business here, and have enjoyed meeting the
people in and around Selby. We have shared in the joys and sorrows of our
many fine people who have stopped with us since being here. For the first
two years every service man or lady was never charged for their night's
lodging. It seemed to bring us good luck and we have received lovely notes
of thanks later from both service men and their folks. We are both proud to
count Selby as our home and have enjoyed a feeling of being among friends.

Again let us congratulate you, City of Selby, and may you always enjoy the
continued civic spirit and cooperation you have had in the past.

VIVIAN'S BEAUTY SHOP

This business is located in the basement of what known as the Selby
hospital, built by Dr. Beil in the early days of the city. The heating
plant for the hospital proper is located in this basement and, while the
institution was in operation, nurse's quarters and the kitchen took up most
of the space. At times the hospital cook and family lived in the rooms.
Eventually the front and rear sections were divided by a partition and a
beauty shop was started in the front part by Mrs. Vivian Chesky, then Miss
Vivian Wilde, who opened the shop under the present name in 1940. She came
to Selby the year before to work for Miss Engebretson who had the Vanity
Beauty Shop in what is now the Drown studio.

Miss Wilde was a graduate of the Christie Beauty school of Bismarck, North
Dakota, and had worked in Aberdeen before coming here. Her skill as an
operator and her friendliness as an individual soon established a fine
business which has continued to the present time.

On February 12, 1942, Miss Wilde was united in marriage with Allen George
who was taken from her in a sad hunting accident. They had two children. In
June of 1949, she was united in marriage with Jack Chesky. They are making
their home in the rooms and she is continuing to operate the beauty shop
while he works in the garage of the Chesky Auto company.

This beauty shop is one of the substantial businesses of the city and
enjoys a fine trade. It is an important asset to the town and community.

HOLTER BUILDING, LOT 8, BLOCK 9

On September 13, 1900, Henry F. Ottman and Wm. B. Flick bought from the
Milwaukee Land company, Lots 8 and 9 in Block 9 in the town of Selby and on
November 21, of the same year, Mr. Flick and wife sold their interest to H.
F. Ottman by quit claim deed. In the fall of 1900 or spring of 1901 Mr.
Ottman built what is now known as the Holter building on Lot 8 and it was
used as a saloon. Three years later he sold it to G. N. Zeider and wife
(recorded March 27, 1903.) The next transfer was from Zeider to the Sioux
Falls Brewing and Malting company, December 29, 1906. This company held it
until 1913, when it was transferred to the Sioux Falls Brewing company.

After Zeider went out of the business it was continued under the management
of Ed Shepherd and Johnny Reistad, who in turn sold to Dave Irwin, who
continued until 1910. Up to this time the business had been a saloon. When
the Methodist church was built in 1910, there were some objections to
having a saloon in the same block with the church so the saloon business
was moved to the corner building in the next block south. After this the
building on Lot 8 was vacant for a year or so. About 1913 or 1914, B. P.
Holter started a harness and shoe repair shop there and in 1917 bought the
lots. He did business there until his death in 1922. From then until the
present time it has been in the Holter estate. After Mr. Holters death,
Paul Dettman continued the business for a year or two and after his removal
it was rented to different parties. W. E. Hoffman had a cream station there
for sometime and later in 1927 Elmer and Frieda Swanson moved in, the front
part being used as a beauty parlor. The Swansons lived there for about two
years and it was again vacant until 1932 when the Rose E. McIntosh
millinery and ready-to-wear business was moved to this location and has
continued in business there since. Lot 9 was sold in 1926 by Mrs. Holter to
the Overholsers.

THE PRESENT POST OFFICE BUILDING

The building on Lot 7, Block 8, which is the present Post Office building,
was built by Albert H. Schmidt of Selby, South Dakota, in April, 1929. Mr.
Schmidt operated a Piggly Wiggly store in it from the time it was built
until November, 1929. The U. S. Government rented it from Mr. Schmidt in
the fall of 1930 to be used as a post office and it has been used for the
same purpose up to the present time.

Mr. Schmidt sold the building to John W. Hoven in 1936. In the fall of 1946
Mr. Hoven sold it to the present owner, Joe Berens.

The following have served as postmaster or postmistress since the beginning
of Selby and, as near as could be found out, the years each served:

 Mr. Fred Griffin       1900 to 19l3
 Mr. Frank Wall         1913 to 1921
 Mr. Art Griffin        1921 to 1923
 Mr. Robert Abel        1923 to 1928
 Mrs. E. K. Hill        1928 to 1934
 Mr. John W. Hoven      1934 to the present time

BUCHANAN DRUG STORE

The Buchanan drug store is the pioneer drug store in Walworth county and
was one of the early established business places in Selby. W. E. Prann, a
registered pharmacist, came to Selby from Iowa about 1903 and became the
first owner and manager of the store, known as The Prann Drug Store. Leo E.
Buchanan, the present owner of the Buchanan drug store, was employed by Mr.
Prann in 1905 and continued there until he completed high school and left
to take. his pharmaceutical training at the University of Iowa in 1912.

While he was away the business was purchased from Mr. Prann by Mr. and Mrs.
C. D. Durfey who continued as owners of the store until 1914. Mr. Prann
resumed ownership of the store in the fall of 1914 but because of other
business interests he employed Buchanan as manager of the store. Buchanan
remained in this capacity until he was called to the armed services in
World War I in May, 1918. After returning from the armed services, he
purchased the business from Mr. Prann in August 1919. The Buchanan drug
store is now one of the oldest established businesses in Selby, and has
been operated longest of any in town under the same ownership. Leo E.
Buchanan has continued as owner and active manager of the business since
1919. The store features the Nyal line of medicines, cosmetics and sundry
items. A complete file of all prescriptions filled since the origin of the
store, is maintained.

The store building was erected in the year 1900 and must have been one of
the first of the newly constructed buildings in the new town. It was built
by a man named Swanson for Kashman and Bazankos who operated a restaurant.
Mr. Prann bought it when he came to Selby in 1903. It was remodeled in 1949
to keep pace with the growth and progress of Selby and is one of the better
business buildings in the city. The rooms upstairs were the home of Pranns
while they operated the store and have been the home of the Buchanan family
since ownership by them.

Courtesy and efficiency with service has at all times been the aim of the
Buchanan drug store.

THE SELBY EQUITY UNION EXCHANGE SELBY, SOUTH DAKOTA

The first meeting of farmers of the Selby community to organize the Selby
Equity Union Exchange was held on the 13th day of July, 1912, at the court
house in Selby. At this meeting John M. Schulte was elected chairman; R. O.
Drown, secretary; and Wm. Koppin, N. F. Stewart and L. H. Koplen as
directors. The articles of incorporation were filed at Pierre on July 30,
1912, with the names of John M. Schulte, Wm. Koppin, W. H. Masteller, W. H.
Vanderflugt, Fred Koppin, A. O. Armstrong, B. O. Brown, F. M. Brown, H. P.
Gutz, Bert Wink, Alexander Coull, F. Hagedorn, A. Hagedorn, A. E. Reeves,
Jas. Barclay, R. O. Drown, N. F. Stewart, J. E. Byers, C. C. Rice and L. H.
Koplen as charter members.

Several other meetings were held to invite other members to join, and on
September 4, 1912, the directors met and leased the Colman Wagner elevator
for one year and hired J. E. Byers as manager. The organization began to
buy grain, soon after that also renting the warehouse and small office
building known as the Wm. Breidenbach buildings which were located on the
present office site of the organization.

On January 4, 1913, another stockholders meeting was held and the following
board of directors was elected: Jas. Barclay, president; Wm. Koppin, vice
president, and Wm. Chesky, secretary-treasurer; Bert Brown and A. O.
Armstrong, directors. John Bibelheimer and Stewart Cook were hired to help
the manager with the book-work.

At a meeting held March 8, 1913, the directors instructed the manager to
hire a lawyer, if necessary, to help locate a carload of wheat which had
not been heard from. This act on the part of the directors demonstrated the
fact that they were going to see that things were run right and were not
going to let anybody get away with a carload of their grain without a fight
on their hands.

On March 20, 1913, John Bibelheimer was hired as manager to replace Mr.
Byers. On May 24, 1913, at a meeting of stockholders it was decided to buy
an elevator from the Crown Elevator company, which is the present west
elevator at Selby, for $3500. They also bought the Breidenbach buildings at
that time for $540 and notes which were signed by the directors took care of
the payments. Several other members also signed the notes. The commission
company handling the Equity business at that time was Stair, Christenson &
Timmerman company of Minneapolis.

At a meeting on December 8, 1913, it was brought out that it was contrary
to cooperative laws for a director to be elected for a period longer than 3
years, so at this meeting it was decided to elect new officers. The
following were elected: John M. Schulte, president; Wm. Chesky,
secretary-treasurer; F. M. Brown, W. H. Masteller, R. O. Drown, directors.
Business increased during 1914 and minutes of meetings showed that money had
been borrowed from local banks to carry on the business. On December 12,
1914, Jacob Tisdall was elected to replace R. O. Drown whose term had
expired as he had been elected for only one year. On October 23, 1915,
Harry Campbell was hired as assistant to Manager Bibelheimer, and on
December 29, Walter Smith was hired to assist at the elevator with Mr.
Campbell assisting the manager with the book-work at the office.

At the December 11, 1915, annual meeting W. H. Masteller and F. M. Brown
were re-elected as directors; F. M. Brown was elected secretary-treasurer.
W. H. Masteller, vice president, and John M. Schulte continuing as
president. On December 9. 1916, F. M. Brown and Frank Wall were elected as
directors. It was decided at this meeting that the regular annual
stockholders meetings should be held on the last Saturday evening in July
each year. At the directors meeting held the same day W. H. Masteller was
elected president; John M. Schulte, vice president; and F. M. Brown,
secretary.

At a directors meeting held March 14, 1917, Mr. Bibelheimer resigned as
manager. Harry Campbell was hired as manager and A. M. Hoven was offered
the job as assistant manager beginning April 1, 1917. A new office building
had been built in the fall of 1916 which is the present office of the
company.

At the annual meeting in July. 1917, it was decided to buy the elevator at
Sitka from J. G. Brady of Aberdeen, and Wm. Fansler was hired to operate it
as manager.

At a board meeting held April 6, 1918, it was decided that the organization
should start shipping livestock for members and patrons. John J. Hoven was
hired to take care of this branch of service. At the annual meeting July
27, 1918, Wm. Masteller was re-elected as director, and Wm. Mickelson was
elected as a director. The directors elected Mr. Masteller to continue as
president, Wm. Mickelson as vice president, and F. M. Brown re-elected as
secretary. In the fall of 1918 A. M. Hoven resigned his position to join
the armed forces and Jess Richardson was hired to take his place. In
December, 1918 Wm. Fansler died at Sitka and was replaced at that time by
Mr. Richardson. A. M. Hoven, having returned from the armed services, was
re-hired to work at Selby.

At the board meeting May 17, 1919, it was decided to buy the Bagley
elevator which is now the east elevator and was taken over on July 1, 1919.
At the annual meeting July 28, 1919, F. M. Brown and Lee Sunderland were
named directors. The company at that time were dealing through the Tenney
Commission company of Minneapolis. Ralph Schwartz was hired to help with
the bookwork at Selby and Lloyd Engebretson was hired as manager of the
Sitka elevator. A. M. Hoven resigned in August and went to Montana to
operate a ranch with his brother.

A roller type feed grinding mill was installed in the east elevator in the
fall of 1919. Elmer Swanson had been working during the summer of 1919 and
winter of 192() and resigned his position in March, 1920. Chas. Hoffman was
hired to take his place starting April 1. Edward Swanson was hired to help
at the elevators in the summer of 1921. About the 28th day of May, 1922,
the Sitka elevator was struck by lightning and burned to the ground.
Immediate plans were made to build a new elevator to cost $11,000.00. It
was built by the T. E. Ibberson company of Minneapolis.

At the annual stockholders meeting July 29, 1922, John Fiedler and A. C.
Dobson were elected on the board, with Mr. Dobson elected as secretary. In
the spring of 1923 Ed. Swanson resigned his position and A. M. Hoven was
hired to take his place. At the annual meeting in July, l923, Steve Rishel
was elected to the board and in July, 1924, Frank Zabel Sr., was elected to
the board. The other board members at that time were W. H. Masteller, A. C.
Dobson, Steve Rishel and John Fiedler. The old style wagon dumps were
replaced in the summer of 1925 with the air dumps and other general repairs
made at all the elevators. A new cleaner had been installed in the east
elevator, also an annex built.

At the annual meeting in 1925, W. H. Masteller was re-elected as president;
M. L. Hornby. secretary; Steve Rishel, vice president; John Fiedler and
Frank Zabel Sr., directors. Walter Smith was elected as a director at the
1926 annual meeting. A. M. Hoven resigned as an employee effective January
1, 1927, as he had been elected as county register of deeds that fall.
Walter Goodwin was hired to take his place. Harry Johnson was elected
director at the July, 1928, meeting. The board was now made up of Walter
Smith, president; Frank Zabel Sr. vice president; M. L. Hornby, secretary;
W. H. Masteller and Harry Johnson, directors. Wm. Christman was hired to
help with the book-work. Manager Harry Campbell passed away September 22,
1928, after a short illness. A. M. Hoven was hired to act as manager until
his term as register of deeds expired on January 1, 1929, and then was
hired as manager. The death of Mr. Campbell was a severe loss to the
organization as he had been a faithful and loyal worker for the cooperative
movement and during his 13 years with the company had been responsible for
much progress and improvement. His friendly and honest dealing with each
member and patron had done much to increase the membership and patronage of
the company.

J. W. Hoven was hired as bookkeeper in June, 1930, which position he held
until he was appointed as postmaster at Selby. On March 1, 1930, the
organization took over the facilities of the Sterling Oil company which
included a bulk and service station and all its goods and equipment and
started to retail petroleum products. Harry Mickelson was hired as manager
of the bulk department and Ed Mickelson as manager of the service station.
Henry Schanzenbach was hired to replace Walter Goodwin who had resigned to
move away from Selby. On April 7, 1934, Lee Baer was hired to replace John
W. Hoven who was appointed postmaster. During the dry years of 1934-1935
and 1936 the Equity shipped more grain into the community than they shipped
out as there was a continual demand for feed grains and roughage. The
Equity also acted as an agent for the government agencies to distribute
feeds and grains to needy farmers.

On July 27 Nils Carlson was hired to operate the Sitka station to replace
Lloyd Engebretson, who had accepted the position as manager of the Glenham
Equity Exchange. On May 20, 1936, Herman Mecklenburg was hired to replace
Henry Schanzenbach who was leaving for the west coast. Wm. Sawinsky and
Arthur Sieck were elected directors at the July, 1936, annual meeting
replacing Wm. Masteller and Frank Zabel Sr. In the latter part of June,
1938, President Walter Smith passed away. His passing was a severe loss to
the Equity organization and community as he had alwavs been a faithful
cooperative worker and had served a good many years on the board during the
depression years. At the annual meeting of July, 1938, M. L. Hornby was
elected president; Wm. Sawinsky, vice president; and Harry Johnson
secretary; directors were Arthur Sieck and E. F. Sebert. About four months
later President M. L. Hornby passed away.

Lee Baer resigned as bookkeeper in June, 1939, and was replaced by Arthur
Jenisom At the July, 1939, annual meeting it was decided to buy the Bagley
elevator which is located on the south side of the track at Selby. At this
meeting Harry Johnson was elected president; Wm. Sawinsky, vice president;
Arthur Sieck, secretary; E. F. Sebert and Wm. Krokel, directors. The Equity
took over the city dray line in the fall of 1939 and hired Eddie Knecht to
manage this department. During the fiscal year the president, Harry Johnson
and director. Wm. Krokel passed away. At the annual meeting in July, 1940,
O. J. Kundert and Frank Zabel Jr.. were elected as directors and at the
directors meeting Wm. Sawinsky was elected president; E. F. Sebert, vice
president; Arthur Sieck, secretary. In December, 1949, O. J. Kundert passed
away and Geo. Ritter, Mound City, was appointed. They are the present
directors at the time this history is written.

In the summer of 1941 a 30,000 bushel annex was built at Sitka station and
Fred Miller was hired as manager of the Sitka station. Soon after war
started in December, 1941, Arthur Janison resigned to join the navy.
Clarence Anderson was hired to take his place. In January, 1944, the
capitalization of the company was raised from $50,000 to $100,000 which was
necessary as the membership was continually increasing. Richard Schnaible
was hired as manager of the Sitka station in August, 1944, and Fred Miller
moved to Selby to continue as an employee and be closer to schools. Richard
Schnaible joined the armed services for a couple years and Willie Ackerman
acted as manager at Sitka until Richard returned in 1946.

Present employees are as follows: Richard Schnaible at Sitka; Joe Heinen,
manager, with Clarence Bucklin and John Gab as employees in the gas and oil
department; Herman Mecklenburg, Fred Miller and John Litschewski in the
elevator department; and Ed Hoven taking care of livestock one day per
week. A. M. Hoven is general manager.

A new $15,000.00 Super Service station was built in the summer and fall of
1948 and is located on Main street one block west of the main office site.
A complete overhauling job and improvements were made on the three
elevators during the summer of 1948 and winter of 1949 at a cost of
approximately $35,000.00. The Equity now operates three grain elevators at
Selby and one at Sitka. The petroleum bulk station has a capacity of 32,000
gallons as several large tanks have been purchased since 1930 at which time
the plant was purchased. Most all farm supplies are handled in the elevator
department including seeds, feeds, twine, salt, coal, fencing and paints.
Livestock is shipped on a commission basis. The Super Service station on
main street handles a large line of auto accessories, tires and Coop
electrical appliances. The present membership is 447 members and there is
$78.550.00 of capital stock issued. The net savings for stockholders in the
37 years of operation in the elevator department amounts to $721,909.07 and
in the 19 years of operation in the petroleum department the savings have
been $136,654.50 making a total of $854,563.57 net savings since the
organization started in 1912. The company has a record of being able to
show a net saving to its members for every year while in business. Much
credit for the success of the Selby Equity is due to the commission
companies at Minneapolis who have always worked with the management by
giving honest and worthwhile advice when needed and at times large amounts
of money were loaned when needed during the peak of the grain movement. The
membership has been very loyal to the organization and the trusting
cooperation of all concerned has been also responsible for the success. The
employees of the organization have in most cases been men who were born or
reared in this locality and have been very loyal to their local-owned
institution, and much credit is due to them for the success of the company.

THE SELBY DRY CLEANERS

The history of the business known as the Selby Dry Cleaners, owned and
operated by Mr. and Mrs. E. B. Brenneise, actually began in the year 1926
when Fred Adolph bought the property, lot 4 of block 7, and established a
tailoring and dry cleaning business which he operated until his death on
December 16, 1944.

Mr. Adolph was born in Russia, coming to America with his people in his
youth, and was handicapped throughout his life by a crippled leg. He was
twice married; his first wife passing away leaving him with two children,
Fred and Ramona, one daughter preceding her father in death. His second
wife was born in Campbell county, the daughter of Philip and Christina
Brockel. Their children are George, Reinholt, Calvin, Herbert and Betty. Of
these children George is taking business accounting at St. Louis, Missouri,
and the others are attending the Selby schools.

After Mr. Adolph's death Mrs. Adolph occupied the home, renting the front
part to Mrs. Dana Vail for a time and to the Soil Conservation association.
In January, 1947, she sold the property to E. B. Brenneise, purchasing the
former Frank Gehrki house for herself and family, from Guy Miller.

The Brenneises were well received by the public, the people showing their
appreciation of again having a dry cleaning establishment in town by being
generous in their patronage in return for courteous, high class service.
The somewhat obsolete equipment was replaced by modern machinery with which
it is possible to do superior work. The business has grown and a weekly
pickup service has been established in the nearby towns of Mound City,
Herreid, Java, Bowdle, Akaska, Lowry, and Hoven. While no tailoring is done
Mr. Brenneise conducts an extensive made-to-measure business in men's
clothing, something he learned to do well in many years of experience with
it as a side line while teaching school.

Mr. Brenneise was born near Greenway in McPherson county and grew to
manhood on his parent's farm, graduating from Eureka high school in 1932.
He then took a one year Normal course at the Aberdeen Teacher's college and
taught school near Artas, Eureka, and the Schilling and River schools near
Akaska, living in that city and driving out each day. Mrs. Brenneise (Alma
Diede) was born at Lehr, North Dakota. They have three children, all boys:
Chester, Larry, and Dennis. Mr. Brenneise is community-minded and is
serving the city of Selby as justice of the peace, Red Cross disaster
chairman, member of the Executive Committee for the Boy Scouts and
treasurer of the Parent Teacher association.

The property on which the business is situated, like all other real-estate
in town, was originally owned by Adam Himrich who acquired it from the
original homesteader and turned it over to the Milwaukee Land company on a
deal which opened the way for establishment of the new town on the present
site. Early transfers are from the townsite company to N. H. Kingman, from
Kingman to George Starkey and back again. The small building in which the
early businesses were conducted and which is now a part of the much larger
building on the lot was moved to Selby by the Kingman company in the fall
of 1901. In that day it was quite a pretentious office building and the
Kingman Investment company, made up of Captain N. H. Kingman and his sons,
did lots of real estate and loan insurance business in the rapidly
developing city and county.

In 1913 the Kingman company moved to Broadview Montana, the older gentleman
retiring and the young men taking it over. The Selby property and business
was sold to the J. D. Newcomer company at Eldora, Iowa. John Bibelheimer
was the last manager for the Kingman company and the Newcomer company
brought Elmer H. Barkus here. Mr. Barkus built the house now occupied by
Mrs. Lottie Sawinsky and her father, Frank Zabel Sr. and remained with the
Newcomer company until they closed out their business here, selling the
property to E. A. Walter, and he in turn selling to Fred Adolph.

The Newcomer company engaged solely in the farm loan business, acquiring
land only when they were forced to foreclose mortgages when not able to
collect principal or interest. The founder of the company, J. D. Newcomer,
was often associated with the late C. E. Lennan in the latter's dealings,
and in later years interested his sons Carl S. and Jay S., in the business.
He passed away in 1911. Mrs. Newcomer passed away in 1943 at the age of 91
and Carl S. Newcomer died at Pasadena, California in 1938. Jay S. Newcomer
is retired and resides at Eldora Iowa. At one time the company had
extensive real estate holdings in Walworth and adjoining counties in South
Dakota and Emmons county, North Dakota. The last quarter section of this
land was sold to Fred J. Berg of Akaska two years ago.

The story of the Selby Dry Cleaners property really covers the history of
four businesses: The Kingman Investment company, the J. D. Newcomer
company, Fred Adolph, and the present occupants, E. B. Brenneise and family.

THE BASEMENT OF THE SELBY OPERA HOUSE
OWNED BY THE CITY OF SELBY

The opera house was built in the year 1910 by a share holding stock company
and in later years was sold to the City of Selby.

In 1922 the late J. F. Yost made a deal with the City of Selby for the
basement of the Selby opera house to install a recreation parlor. The
basement at that time was just a bare ground floor,--you might say just a
hole in the ground. Mr. Yost remodeled it all the way through. He put in
two bowling alleys and five pool tables and was reimbursed from the city by
taking it out in rent.

Carl Doherr worked for Mr. Yost from 1922 until the fall of 1923. George
Eichelberg worked from the fall of 1923 until the summer of 1924. Ed Hoven
worked from the summer of 1924 until the summer of 1928 and Art Flemmer
worked from the summer of 1928 to the spring of 1929.

In the spring of 1929 Ed Hoven and Jake Nehlich bought the business from
Mr. Yost. In the fall of 1931 Ed Hoven sold his interest to Jake Nehlich,
and in the summer of 1932 Jake Nehlich sold the business to George
Schwarting, who owned it until the fall of 1934 and then sold it to the
late John Simons.

While Mr. Simons was owner of the recreation center or Selby pool hall
business he sold the alleys and pool tables. It is now just a soft drink
and card room, but it always has been called the pool room or the bowling
alley.

Jake Yost passed away in the fall of 1933 and John Simons passed away
November 10, 1945. After John passed away the business was operated by Mrs.
Simons and family until January, 1950, when it was sold to Herbert Baer,
the present owner.

THE SELBY SHOE SHOP

The lot on which the Selby Shoe Shop is located, and the one adjoining it
on the north, were originally the site of the John Franks store,--at the
north end and on the west side of Main street. The two lots were purchased
by John Franks and John Dupper from the Milwaukee Land company in 1900.
They constructed a mercantile building and conducted a general merchandise
store together for a few years.

John Franks bought Mr. Dupper's share in the business and real estate, and
he and his family continued with the store until 1919. In 1920 A. C.
Tousley rented the building and used it for a restaurant. After operating
the restaurant for about a year he sold his equipment to a Mr. White who
kept on with the business until 1923, when Henry Taylor purchased the
restaurant equipment.

Mr. and Mrs. Henry Taylor operated the cafe for five years and then sold
out to Clyde Avery. However, his tenure in the business extended for not
much more than six months, and the Taylors again became the restaurant
operators. They continued as such until 1930.

For the next five years the building was used for various purposes. At one
time or another it was the Equity cream station, Cobbs cream station, Leo
Todd's barber shop, and Charley Dion's living quarters. In 1935 Earl Payne
rented the building. Mr. Payne and his family operated a Gamble store in
the front of the building, and lived in the rear part.

In 1936 Claude Drown became the occupant of the building. He used it for a
second hand store; but soon turned it over to Martin Hoefer who had it for
a short time. The building was next used as the premises for a mattress
factory for a few months. Then it was used for storing waste paper and war
materials. Mrs. John Franks, still the owner of the property, donated its
use as storage space to the Selby Troop of Boy Scouts. The Boy Scouts,
under the direction of Max Gutz, who was scoutmaster at that time, were
conducting waste paper drives in the interests of the national shortage
during World War II, and Mrs. Franks was most generous with the use of her
building in that respect.

After the war, Clifton and Alton Franks, who were sons of Mrs. Franks,
moved the building out to their farm north of Selby. It was torn down and
the lumber used in the construction of a new barn. The two lots were sold
in 1945 to Arthur Cheskv.

In 1947 Mr. Chesky had a basement built at about the middle section of the
lots, and moved upon it a house he had purchased northeast of Lowry. Art
(as he is better known) was a veteran of World War II, and after his return
from the service had opened a shoe repair shop, using a portion of his
father's Ford garage for space. He and his wife, the former Agnes Bucklin,
were industrious and ambitious. They saw the possibilities of having a
profitable shoe repair business, and became eager to expand.

Doing practically all of the work themselves, Art and Agnes constructed a
concrete-block building in 1948. This building fronts on to Main street,
and is connected in the rear to their house. They have purchased new and
modern machinery, thus being equipped to supply Selby and its territory
with fast and efficient service. Always with a desire to expand. Art and
Agnes are gradually accumulating a stock of shoes for retail. Their
building and their business are an asset to Selby.

LAW OFFICE OF MICKELSON & HOMEYER

The present law firm of Mickelson & Homeyer at Selby is the successor to
the pioneer law office of Albert H. Smith. Smith began his practice at
Selby in 1902 in the building now owned by Sam Raich on Lot 2, Block 4
Selby, which now houses the Ed Schaffer lunch room. The law office remained
at this location until 1905 when Smith purchased the C. E. Lennan property
described as Lot 1, Block 4, Selby, now occupied by the Albert E. Moos
family. The law office remained here until January, 1940, when the present
quarters below the First National bank, at Selby, Lot 12, Block 7, were
obtained.

A. H. Smith practiced alone until 1909 when he formed a partnership with A.
A. Brown, and practiced under the firm name of Brown & Smith until 1919,
when Brown moved to Missoula, Montana. Fred Shandorf became a partner of
Mr. Smith in 1920 and remained until 1923, and the firm practiced under the
name of Smith & Shandorf. M. G. Dubel joined the firm in 1924 and remained
until 1925, and the law office was operated under the name of Smith &
Dubel. George T. Mickelson became a member of the firm in 1927 upon his
graduation from the University of South Dakota, and the partnership of
Smith & Mickelson continued until the death of Mr. Smith in October, 1933.
George T. Mickelson practiced alone until November, 1945, when Fred J.
Homeyer became a partner in the firm which now practices under the name of
Mickelson & Homeyer.

George T. Mickelson was states attorney of Walworth county from 1933 to
1937. He served in the South Dakota legislatures of 1937, 1939, and 1941,
being Speaker of the House of Representatives during the year 1941.
Mickelson was Attorney-General of South Dakota from 1943 to 1947, and
Governor of South Dakota from 1947 to 1951, presently completing his second
term.

Fred J. Homeyer graduated from the University of South Dakota in 1935 and
practiced at Eureka, South Dakota, from 1935 to the spring of 1944 when he
entered World War II. He was state's attorney of McPherson county from 1941
to 1944.

Various members of the firm have at other times served as state's attorney
of Walworth county and city attorney at Selby during the firm's existence.

Pauline Clark has been the secretary of the law office since December, 1924.

THE HOME STUDIO

Most of the Selby pioneers will remember the building now occupied as the
Home Studio, situated on Lot 13 of Block 13, as the Rounds building. A. F.
Rounds owned it and conducted his jewelry business in it for a good number
of years during the forepart of Selby's history.

H. P. Hankins was the first owner of this property. It was deeded to him on
October 29, 1902. Soon after that date, according to all obtainable
information, he moved the front room, or business part of the present
building, to Selby from Bangor. Mr. Hankins is remembered as being an
undertaker and furniture repair man. The building was his place of business.

On March 23, 1907 Mr. Hankins conveyed the title to A. F. Rounds. Living
quarters had to be provided for the Rounds family. There is no record of
when it was done, but it is known that Mr. Rounds had rooms built on the
rear of the original business building. For a period of almost 20 years Mr.
and Mrs. Rounds and their family of three children lived in those rooms,
while Mr. Rounds operated his jewelry store in the front part. Then he held
an auction sale, which is well remembered by many. On May 31, 1929 Tom H.
Engebretson purchased the building from Mr. Rounds.

Soon after that date Mr. Engebretson's sister, Emma Engebretson, moved into
the building. During her occupancy she conducted various lines of business,
principally a beauty parlor. After owning the property for 14 years, Mr.
Engebretson sold it to Mr. and Mrs. R. O. Drown.

It was on the 16th day of February, 1943, when the Drowns purchased the
property. They remodeled the living rooms and Mrs. Drown set up her
photographers shop in the front business room. The Home Studio, under the
management of Mr. and Mrs. Drown, has been operating since that time.

THE ROSE E. McINTOSH STORE

The Rose E. McIntosh millinery store, established in the spring of 1917 in
the upstairs front room of what was known as the Elfrink building, was a
new and very interesting business to the ladies of Selby and the adjoining
territory. Besides the millinery business, dressmaking and altering of
men's and women's ready-to-wear were carried on.

The hearty support of the ladies of the community was very encouraging to
the new business which began to expand. Ladies ready-to-wear, coats, suits,
dresses, together with hosiery, gloves, corsets and lingerie were added.

The necessity of being on the ground floor became apparent and the business
was moved to the building now occupied by the Snack Shop. After nine months
in this location, the building was sold to Jake Schanzenbach for a cream
station and it was necessary to move to a new location in the corner
building now occupied by the Classic Beauty salon. The business continued
there until November 1, 1932 when it was moved to the Holter building and
has continued at this location since.

The years between 1919 and 1929 were the Golden years in millinery. Pattern
hats (hand made) were beautiful, they had a lot of work on them and sold
from $10.00 and $12.00 up to $20.00 and $25.00. They were lovely hats.
Other hats sold from $5.00 to $10.00 and $12.00. The first hat sold in the
business was sold to Marie Elling, and was a very pretty hat. Most of the
millinery was bought from Robinson Straus and company, a very fine business
firm in St. Paul. Besides pattern hats, it was necessary to buy untrimmed
shapes, flowers, feathers, braids, and fancy ribbons and linings. No hat
was sold from the store unless it had the Rose E. McIntosh imprint on the
lining. The pattern hats were ready to wear. All other hats and shapes had
to be trimmed by the milliner to suit the customer, hence the great demand
for flowers, ribbons, and other trimmings. Pattern hats were always on
display early. Spring hats were out before Christmas and fall hats out
before the 4th of July. Pattern hats are a thing of the past. All hats now
are factory made.

During the early years of the business, there was an excise tax on corsets
and on hats over $15.00. Now there is an excise tax on jewelry, purses, and
furs.

Ruth Crawford was the first customer for a dress which was a two-piece of
wool plaid. This and many similar styles came from the Skirt-Waist House of
Chicago, the first house to send out dresses to the new business in 1919.
In 1945 shoes and rubber footwear were added to the business.

In 1929 at the Walworth County Fair, on August 29, 30, and 31, a public
wedding was staged under the auspices of the business firms of Selby. The
wedding dress, a beautiful rose pink formal, was donated by this store.

In 1933 in a parade at a 4th of July celebration and the Walworth county
fair, the float made by this store won second prize. This float, called
Miss Prosperity, was a car covered with red, white, and blue crepe paper
and a young lady, Fern Baumgarten, rode on the float.

Again in 1947, a float put out by this store won second prize in a parade
on Old Settlers Day. This float compared the early day styles with the
styles of 1947.

During the years that this store has been in operation, two fine young
girls, Margaret Commet and Grace Vail, worked in the store. Margaret worked
for four years and Grace for ten years. Later both girls went into business
of their own. Now for the past few years the store has been operated
without much regular help.

The store now is known as Rose E. McIntosh, Millinery, Ready-to-Wear and
Shoes.

CHESKY AUTO COMPANY

The history of the present site of the Chesky Auto company, Lots 5 and 6,
Block 24 in Selby, South Dakota began August 29, 1900 when Adam Himrich
secured 160 acres comprising the southwest quarter of section 33, township
124, range 76 in Walworth county, South Dakota from the United States
government. On December 6, 1900 Mr. Himrich sold this land to the Milwaukee
Land company by warranty deed.

On June 29, 1905 the Milwaukee Land company caused a portion of that land
to be platted as the Milwaukee Land company's first addition to the town of
Selby as shown by the plat, and dedicated to the public use the avenues,
streets, and alleys as shown upon said plat which embraced blocks 21 to 25
inclusive. Each block embraced lots 1 to 12 inclusive.

On June 17, 1908 J. J. Hoven and C. V. Conyne purchased Lots 5 and 6, Block
24 and on November 5, 1909 Mr. Conyne transferred his interest in the land
to J. J. Hoven by quit claim deed.

On May 10, 1917 Mr. Hoven sold Lot 6, Block 24 to Walter A. Goodwin and
Robert J. Gruett. At the same time he sold Lot 5, Block 24 to H. A. Taylor.
That spring Goodwin and Gruett had a frame building 40 x 90 erected on
their lot which was to be used as a garage, repair shop, and filling
station. Bert Niles put up the building and John Unker put in the floor.

In June of that year they were able to advertise their business as the
Yellowstone Garage in the local paper. They also had the agency for the
Oakland and Dort automobiles. The business continued in this way until
December 1917 when Robert Gruett went into the army of World War I. Walter
Goodwin continued the business until March 5, 1918 when he too went into the
service. At that time the garage was rented to William Drewein who operated
it for a while. Then H. A. Taylor, owner of Lot 5, took over and kept the
business going until Mr. Gruett returned in the spring of 1919 when he
resumed charge. He was joined by his partner, Mr. Goodwin on the latter's
return to Selby in May, 1919. These men secured the agency for the Ford
cars, trucks, and Fordson tractors from the Ford Motor company and operated
a filling station in connection with the garage until February 19, 1926
when they sold Lot 6, Block 24 together with the building, fixtures, and
parts, and filling station to Wm. G. Chesky, a farmer from southwest of
Selby. Mr. Chesky also secured the agency from the Ford Motor company. The
name of the business was changed from The Yellowstone Garage to The Chesky
Auto company. On July 9, 1928 Mr. Chesky purchased Lot 5, Block 24 from H.
A. Taylor. At the time of entering the garage business Mr. Chesky retained
in his employ for a time the two mechanics, Charlie Birkholt and Frank
Taylor; the car salesman, Jack Anglin; and Louis Anderson, a high school
student who did the bookkeeping. Mr. Chesky took over the management of the
business. His sons helped in the shop and attended the filling station, and
his daughter, Esther took over the bookkeeping.

In 1928 Mr. Chesky had the original frame building moved to the west end of
the lot and had a 50 x 60 brick fireproof building and filling station
erected adjoining the old building on the east. George F. Fossum, architect
from Aberdeen, got the contract to draw the plans. The original frame part
was to be used for storage; the new brick structure had a shop, parts room,
oil room, show room, office, rest rooms, and basement. It was equipped with
electric lights and running water. At the time this was completed it was
one of the most modern and finest buildings in Selby.

The Mobil products were handled in the filling station for a while, also
the White Eagle products. In 1931 Mr. Chesky took over the Standard Oil
company products. He has continued doing business with the Ford Motor
company as an authorized dealer, and with the Standard Oil company ever
since.

At the present time the business is still a family affair, with Mr. Chesky
as general manager. His sons, Wm. A., and Arnold have charge of the shop
and assist him in car sales and filling station service. A daughter,
Gertrude, is bookkeeper. In 1946 Mr. Chesky received recognition from the
Ford Motor company of his 20th year as a Ford dealer.

NORTHWESTERN BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY

Early in 1899, the Western Dakota Telephone Company built a single-wire,
iron telephone line between Bowdle and Evarts, a distance of 52 miles.
About a year later a branch line was built to Bangor and, so far as known,
Selby was on this branch line.

By 1904, the company which built the Bowdle-Evarts line had become a part
of the Dakota Central Telephone Company and the latter is known to have had
an exchange in Selby m 1905, serving 49 telephones.
