In 1910, a copper telephone line was built between Bowdle and Mobridge.
Selby was on this long distance line. In 1917, the central office equipment
was replaced at Selby. It was then that a one-position magneto switchboard
was installed.

Selby's first telephone central office is reported to have been installed
in the Potter & Burr store in about 1900 and was later moved to the Prann
drug store. Prann's later became Buchanan's drug store.

The Selby exchange has been served by the Northwestern Bell Telephone
company since 1942, when the Dakota Central Telephone company was
purchased. A total of 281 telephones are served by this exchange, of which
173 are Northwestern company owned. At present the exchange is housed in
part of the opera house building owned by the city of Selby.

SELBY OIL COMPANY

This business, then named East River Oil company and handling Phillips 66
products, was started in the spring of 1935, consisting of a bulk and
service station, located on lot 6, block 23, purchased from H. P. Gutz, by
Emil Kost and Henry Orth.

In 1936 when Highway No. 12 was changed these two co-partners bought Lot
One of County Auditor's First Addition to the City of Selby, from Wm.
Weigum. In 1937 when Highway No. 12 was near completion, this business was
moved to its new and present location. A 14 x 32 addition was built to
accommodate a growing business.

In January 1938 Henry Orth sold his half interest to Emil Kost.

In 1939 another 30 x 50 addition was added for shop work and a new hoist
and new modern greasing equipment was also added.

In January 1949 Edward Schanzenbach (who had been employed here since May
of 1935) and Herbert Wolff bought this business and the name was changed to
Selby Oil Company.

E. H. NOTEBOOM (BUSINESS STORY)

The Dettman building on Lot 7, Block 8 of Selby, was purchased of the
Milwaukee Land company by John Rhodes, late of Bowdle, for $100.00 cash at
the town lot sale on September 1, 1900. In December of 1904 Mr. Rhodes sold
it to Mrs. Theresa Kane for $215.00. She in turn sold it to John
Hempfthing. The next transfer was to H. P. Gutz who bought it in 1909 and
sold it to Paul Dettman in 1923.

Mrs. Kane erected the building in the spring of 1905. Alex Heiser doing the
carpenter work. When the building was completed, Mrs. Kane moved in a
millinery stock which she had purchased of Mrs. Treanor, which she later
sold to the Hempfthings. This group consisted of a brother and two sisters,
the sisters running the store and living in the rooms above.

When the Hempfthings left, an E. Moger opened a gent's furnishings store.
In 1909 F. J. Prann put in the first soda fountain in Selby and ran a
confectionery store and ice cream parlor, later selling to R. D. Hazeldine,
who in turn sold to Mrs. Durfey. In 1913 Mr. and Mrs. Joe Wall bought the
business and ran it for two years when a bad fire ruined most of their
stock. They sold out the balance and quit. Sometime later, Steve Johnson
moved his barbershop in and occupied the building until Mr. Dettman bought
it. Mr. Dettman moved the shoe and harness-making equipment from the Holter
building on the west side of the street and operated a harness and shoe
repair business until he left, the family living in the rooms upstairs.
Since the closing of the shoe and harness shop a number of businesses have
been conducted in the building for short periods of time and Mr. Noteboom
has occupied it since early in 1946. The rooms upstairs have been occupied
by many tenants through the earlier years but the Dettman family has
occupied them almost continually now for more than 25 years.

Early residents state that in the board sidewalk days of the city one of
the tenants had a graphophone which he used to set out on the sidewalk and
the younger group would gather on nice evenings to visit, listen to the
music, and have a good time.

Mr. Noteboom came to Walworth county with his parents, Mr. and Mrs. Case
Noteboom and family, who purchased the Buchecker farm in Spring Valley
township. He had attended the rural schools of Sioux county, Iowa, Hawarden
High school and had taught one term of school at Struble, Iowa, before
coming here in the year 1909. He remained on the farm, teaching school at
LeBeau and in River and Hiddenwood districts in the winter until 1914 when
he was appointed county superintendent of schools for Walworth county and
came to Selby in June. He was elected to that office in the fall and served
until 1919. He was united in marriage with Amanda Eskelson of Rushford,
Minnesota, in 1918. He served as South Dakota's first rural school
supervisor for two years and in June of 1921 came back to the home farm on
the death of his father.

Mr. and Mrs. Noteboom came back to Selby in 1925, when he purchased the
Walworth County Record from Fred Griffin, and have resided here since. Both
have been active in city and county civic affairs. They have two daughters,
both of whom reside in Los Angeles, California, and three grandchildren.
Mr. Noteboom sold the newspaper business to Fritz Clement of Java in 1945
and has since been engaged in the real estate and insurance business. He
served Walworth, Potter, and Faulk counties in the South Dakota State
Senate during the 1945 and 1947 sessions and has held and holds many
positions of responsibility in the city.

BYRE BLACKSMITH SHOP

The blacksmithing business now conducted in Selby by Oscar Byre was started
in October of 1933 by Art Beckman who brought what tools he had in from the
farm northwest of town, purchased more equipment and started business in
the Tom Engebretson building northeast of the Equity. Wanting a place of
his own he purchased the southwest three lots of the Berens estate in block
14 and moved the structure, long known as the Schanzenbach garage building,
off Main Street in the same block to the south side of the lots facing it
on railroad street. He cut the building down a few feet and made an
acceptable shop out of it. This building is now the Stulken Implement
warehouse, office, and shop.

In 1944 Mr. Beckman sold out to Oscar Byre who operated in the same
building until 1948 when he purchased lots in Out Lot C in the northwest
corner of town, a part of what was once included in the Hagen hatchery
acreage and moved on a building for a shop. Mr. Byre also buys old iron in
connection with his blacksmithing business.

Oscar Byre was born in Campbell county, the son of the pioneers, Mr. and
Mrs. Severt Byre, who later moved to the Byre farm in Blue Blanket. He went
to school in Blue Blanket district and graduated from Glenham high school
in 1929. He did farm work, was employed as mechanic at the Chesky garage
and operated the Wolff Standard Oil station at the junction of old Highway
12 and 83 for a time. but sold out just before Pearl Harbor and went to
work in a defense plant at Brighton, Minnesota, coming back to Selby in
1944 and buying the blacksmith business.

He was united in marriage in 1939 with Lillian, daughter of Mr. and Mrs.
Gaius Falde, who was born in Perkins county and got her schooling in
Campbell county. They set up housekeeping in the house on the Wolff station
property which was later sold and moved to his farm south of town by Elmer
Swift. They have five children, two boys and three girls.

Mr. Byre has always endeavored to give his customers good service and hopes
to improve and enlarge his plant and stock and keep up with the city in
developing his business.

THE WALWORTH COUNTY ABSTRACT COMPANY
A Pioneer Institution of Walworth County

The history of the Walworth County Abstract company parallels and is almost
contemporaneous with that of Selby, and with Walworth county. The character
and nature of the functions of the abstractor is such as to be an essential
element in the development of territories into established communities ...
when the pioneer settlers arrive in a new land, or territory, seeking
homes, they usually find the abstractor already established. He is strictly
a product of the American system,--necessary to the establishment of homes
and farms in our land and to the business of the nation.

The present Walworth County Abstract company was organized on December 19,
1896 at Bangor, South Dakota, having as its principal officers, A. J.
Ellis, L. J. Ellis and E. H. Cowell. Actually, the company then organized
was the successor to the original abstract of title firm of Walworth
county, and the incorporation was merely the formal organization of a
business which had been functioning since the county was organized and
settled in territorial times.

Since it was formed, this company has been continuously operated in the
county. Persons associated with the company during its long history include
the following: A. J. Kingman, L. W. Moody, R. Jackson, George Starkey, A.
Gunderman, E. G. Powell, and at the present, Dana F. Vail and Chester E.
Solomonson. E. G. Powell perhaps, is the best known of the persons once
connected with the company. Mr. Powell, a pioneer of the county, managed
the affairs of the company for many years, commencing when the firm was
operating in Bangor, the first county seat, and continuing until his death
in 1937.

The place of business was moved from Bangor to Selby in January 1905, and
is presently located in the courthouse.

During the entire span of the history of this community, the company has
played an important part in its growth and development; has shared in, and
made its contribution to such progress.

RABENBERG IMPLEMENTS

This important business establishment in Selby is situated on Lots 5, 6, 7,
8, 9, 10, 11 and 12, in Block 4. The history of these lots is a
considerable portion of the history of Selby. Like all other lots in Selby,
they were a part of the Lafayette Brazill homestead. later sold to Adam
Himrich and traded by him to the Milwaukee Land company and deeded by that
company to the several early owners. Lots 5 and 6 were sold by the Milwaukee
Land company to S. F. Hoffman at the town lot sale in 1900. He and the late
G. H. Hoffman moved a double building up from Bangor which had been
constructed or put together by Eb Mudge, he using one side for a postoffice
and the other used by Mr. Hoffman as a barbershop. Mr. Mudge was the last
postmaster at Bangor. Sig Hoffman, Selby's first barber, operated his shop
in the north section of the building and lived in the south section. The
Hoffmans eventually went to California and the place passed into the hands
of Mrs. Maggie Pitcher, a Canadian resident, who held it until 1942 when
she sold to Ed F. Perman. Mr. Perman removed the buildings, taking the
north section down and utilizing the lumber in improving his implement
house and selling the south part to Alferd Moos, who moved it on a lot on
the east side of town and has made a very nice home of it. The lots were
later sold to Mr. Rabenberg who now uses them for display room and storage
place for farm machinery. After the departure of the Hoffmans there were a
number of tenants in the building, Steve Johnson having a barber shop there
at one time and Dr. Byron using it as office and home for many years.

Lot 7 was sold by the Milwaukee Land company to George F. Flashman in 1900.
In 1903 he sold it to John Berens. who in 1906 sold to George Raba who ran
a shoe shop for many years, this business being continued by Henry Hammer
and George Sulzle. who lived on a farm west of Selby. About the year 1915,
Miss Hilda Bergstrom, now Mrs. W. C. Miller, shipped in a stock of
millinery, opening a store temporarily in the building across the street
now the Drown store, then moving it to the Raba building. She came from St.
Paul and Clinton Minnesota and brought an expert hat trimmer with her.
After this business was sold out. the building was vacant more or less,
being occupied by tenants for periods of time. Mr. Raba eventually deeded
the property to Walworth county and Mr. Rabenberg procured it in 1944.

Lot 8 was purchased at the town lot sale by Carl Milde who sold to Arie and
Dirk Kirkhoven who in turn sold to John Berens in 1903. A Nick Stoyanoff
owned the building for a long time, it eventually falling back to Berens by
the foreclosure route. V. V. Van Osdol closed a restaurant in this building
in 1914, selling the fixtures to Mrs. Berens and she continued the business
for a number of years. Previous to the Van Osdol tenantry, it is believed
that a Palace restaurant was operated in the building by the Misses Paulson
and Christensen, starting in 1906. Then E. Moger had a clothing store which
he opened in 1907, followed by Turner and Gallon with a meat shop in 1909.
J. W. Coates opened a general merchandise store in 1910, Mrs. Heen moving
in a millinery stock with him in the store. Coates closed out in 1911 and
then Van Osdol moved in following a fire in the building across the street.
Verne Duncan had a bakery in the place after Mrs. Berens quit the
restaurant business. The building eventually burned down and was never
replaced and the lot reverted to the county and was sold to Mr. Rabenberg
in 1944. The story of the various businesses tried out on this property is
indicative of what took place in the new town of Selby. Business people
came with big ideas, only to find that they had misjudged the possibilities
of the new country and moved on, others coming in to make another trial.

Heinrich Nusz Sr., bought Lot 9 from the Milwaukee Land company in 1902 and
sold to John Berens in 1905, who moved a building on it from the south of
the then postoffice, on which the Hettich store is now located, and Matt
Arens opened a pool hall in it. In 1914 Philip Preszler bought it and
continued the pool hall. In 1920 Preszler sold to Carl Hauck and Carl
Brockel and they later sold to Jake Yost. Affairs in this pool hall led to
one of Selby's famous trials. It was alleged that intoxicating liquor was
being sold on the premises, disguised as catsup. A John Doe proceeding was
instituted and many well known citizens were haled into court to testify as
to the character of drinks which they had allegedly purchased there from
time to time. There was much discussion of the veracity of the testimony of
quite a number of citizens and one was recorded as stating that the potion
which he bought smelled like an intoxicant, tasted like one and had the
effects. but he could not swear that it was intoxicating. The building on
this lot eventually burned down and the lot fell to the county for taxes
and Mr. Rabenberg bought it from the county in 1944.

Lot 10 was purchased by Gust Peterson at the town lot sale in 1900. It
passed to a Robert W. Wisch, then to a W. R. Birder and the latter
transferred it to Heinrich Nusz Sr.. in 1903 and in 1905 the latter sold it
to John Berens. Mr. Berens erected a two-story cement block building on it
in 1910, l00 feet long and the full width of the lot. The upper story was
designed for a rooming house and the lower floor for a garage. Berens had
the Reo and Ford auto contracts and did a big automobile garage business
for many years. The general plan was to widen this building later,
extending it over the next lot south and erect a modern hotel. The execution
of the building plan was delayed until 1920 when work began in excavating a
basement for the hotel, on the lot next south. Removing the earth next to
the south wall of the big garage building so weakened the foundation that
the south wall fell out and into the cellar hole and that ended the
venture, and the ambition of the Berens family to have a modern hotel in
Selby langished until twenty-five years later when Joe Berens, a son of John
Berens, began plans for the fine new hotel that he now has erected on north
Main Street. The debris of the old garage was cleared away and the premises
were vacant until Mr. Rabenberg procured the lot in 1942.

Lot 11 has always been vacant excepting when the basement was dug on it
with the results outlined in the preceding paragraph.

Lot 12 was sold at the town lot sale to Joseph Treanor of LaGrace. Mr.
Treanor. father of Mrs. H. P. Gutz, formerly of Selby, was one of the
pioneers of what has become the ghost town of LaGrace six miles north and
west of Pollock. He built a building on this lot for a drug store which
seems to have been utilized as a millinery store by Mrs. Treanor and her
daughter. This business was sold to Mrs. Kane who moved it to what is now
the Dettman building and the location was sold to John Berens who put in a
liquor business which he operated until the country went dry in 1917. He
then opened a pool hall which he operated for some years. The building
stood idle for many years and was used for storage. The last business
venture undertaken in it was a night club with Walter Ress as owner. Mr.
Rabenberg bought the building of the Berens heirs in 1914. There is
probably as much history within the walls of this building as in any place
in Selby. It is told that in the days of the county seat fight a slot
machine in the saloon yielded the spot cash to finance the litigation in
connection with the attempts to move the seat of government from Bangor.
Lots of important affairs emanated from that corner. All of said lots are
now owned and occupied by the Rabenberg Implements and Mr. Rabenberg has
constructed thereon a large modern tile and brick structure which houses
and serves Rabenberg Implements.

SWIFT'S BAR

Records show that the lot on which the building which houses this business
was deeded June 3, 1901, the purchase price of $150 being paid by Phil
Lewis to the Milwaukee Land company. The Walworth County Record of August
25, 1901 states that the Lewis meat market was moved from Bangor to this
lot on the Main Street of Selby on Wednesday of that week and that Charlie
Wilson had gone in with Phil Lewis. Mr. Lewis was a homesteader in the
county, having filed on a quarter section of the land now owned by Fred
Seyer. south of where the Spring Valley schoolhouse now stands. He was a
neighbor to Ladislaus Bertha Sr., and the two men made quite a reputation
for themselves in the early days digging wells around the country by hand.
Lewis later established a butcher shop in Bangor and sold meat to the
farmers from a wagon, traveling from farm to farm during the hot season of
the year. He married a sister of Charlie Wilson named above, and of Will E.
and Willis E. Wilson, who operated the Wilson ranch west of Akaska for many
years.

Lewis sold the property in 1903 to A. S. Taylor, who owned it a short time
and sold it to August C. Schmidt in 1903. Taylor homesteaded the land now
occupied by Walter Seyer and was interested in the lumber business in the
early days of Selby.

August C. Schmidt owned the property and operated the business continuously
until his death, with the exception of a period of six months in the year
1912 when he sold it to Dave Irwin and then purchased it back again. After
his father's death, Albert Schmidt took over the business and property and
operated it until he sold the business to Lester and Francis Simons who
later sold to Hettich Bros. They operated it until the property was sold to
Milo Swift in September of 1948. Albert Schmidt had incorporated the
business in 1928 and added an extension of brick, modernizing the whole
structure and putting in the first locker plant in Selby. The meat shop
became a general food store and operated under several trade names, as
Piggly-Wiggly, Schmidt's One Stop Market I. G. A., and Super-Valu.
Throughout the years it always ranked as one of Selby's leading business
places. Mr. Swift renovated the building before moving in and has one of
the most attractive and best equipped liquor establishments in this section
of the country. Operating under the name of Swift's Bar, the business is
handled by the owner, Milo Swift, his father, Roy Swift, and one assistant,
Emanuel Baer being employed at the time this is being written.

The Swift family came to Walworth county in 1910, residing first on the
farm now owned by Fred Seyer in Spring Valley, and on several other farms
in that community. The parents of the Swift boys who reside in the Selby
community, Roy and Elmer, were among the pioneers of Sioux City, Iowa.
Their grandfather was a Union soldier who fought in many of the important
battles in the western campaigns of the Civil War and was with
Sherman on his "March to the Sea."

The Nies family, grandparents of Milo Swift on the maternal side, came to
Walworth county in 1907 from Wayne, Nebraska. They purchased what has always
been known as the Buchecker farm, now owned by Henry Seyer Sr., from Jay
Musson and resided on it for several years, later moving to the Gordon farm
in the same neighborhood and to other farms in that locality.

The older members of both of these families have passed to their eternal
reward and the young people are widely scattered, only the Roy and Elmer
Swift and Peter Nies families remaining in this part of the state.

Milo Swift was married to Miss Helen Nimbar of Mobridge, and they have one
son, Ronald Roy.

THE MILWAUKEE RAILROAD

The Milwaukee railroad, of course, made Selby--that is, the locating of the
right of way across Walworth county four miles north of Bangor, then the
county seat and the trading center of this section of the country, in
retrospect practically made it certain that a town would be located almost
north of Bangor and that this town would supplant the older and isolated
village and become the county seat. The spring east of Selby and the creek
through it no doubt determined the location. The spot where the city well
is now located was quite wet and springy in the early days, the site
overgrown with rushes, giving every evidence of plenty of water. The large
amount of water pumped dried up the surface water but the vein below, which
overflowed at this spot before it was pumped, is still ample for the
railroad and city needs.

The depot was the first building in town and the only one for some time,
and the stockyards were built before the town lot sale. The first shipment
of livestock from Selby was made by O. D. Buchecker, who resided on the
farm now owned by Henry Seyer, 10 miles southeast of Selby, and was made on
August 22, 1900. The next shipment was made by Fenelon Brothers of Pollock,
who shipped 11 carloads of cattle. The first trains arrived in Selby on
August 17, being a work train and a mixed train. N. H. Kingman Jr.,
remembered by the older residents as "Toot" Kingman, was the first agent
and served with occasional temporary relief until about 1917. He was
interested in blooded horses owning some fine racers. He also did a lot of
real estate business, being instrumental in bringing many families from the
east into the new country. The receipts at the depot for the first three
days of operation amounted to $2000.00. The first regular train service was
a tri-weekly mixed freight and passenger service running between Roscoe and
Evarts, and inaugurated November 1, 1900. Daily passenger service began in
1903 and has never failed since.

Other agents succeeded Mr. Kingman including Irwin Dudley, M. O. Joachim.
R. L. Vanderhoof, and the present agent, S. L. Winn.

The extension of the Milwaukee to Seattle and Tacoma and the routing of the
two longest highways in the world, viz. highways 12 and 83 through Selby
has made this an important passenger station, and the area naturally
tributary to the city has also made it an important shipping point.

Through the years, the city boosters and the company officials have had
many occasions for getting together for the common good and Selby and the
whole trade territory is appreciative of the fine service rendered by the
"Milwaukee" and feels a justifiable pride in being located on, served by,
and having an opportunity to patronize this great railroad system. Selby
citizens feel that the long Diesel-propelled freights and the new Hiawatha
streamliner are like their own and are certainly a part of what makes Selby
a fine place in which to live.

The railroad regularly employs from six to ten men here, which results in
about that many families being added to the town's population.

THE AUBURN HOTEL

The history of Selby practically begins with the "coming" of the Auburn
hotel. It is generally conceded that this building was the first place of
business to be located in the town of Selby. A great portion of Selby's
history as well as many of the stories connected therewith, cannot be told
without including the Auburn hotel. Many of Selby's actual
"town-pioneers,"--those people who came and resided within the townsite and
had much to do with the affairs of the town and its progress,--maintained
their first residence at the Auburn hotel.

Lots 7 and 8, Block 13. were sold at the lot sale of the Selby townsite
conducted by the Milwaukee Land company on August 3, 1900, in Bangor. Mr.
and Mrs. L. W. Maxwell were the buyers. They owned the Auburn hotel
building in Bangor and immediately after the sale they proceeded to move it
to their new location for "the railroad was coming."

Three days later, on August 7, the building was set down in Selby. It was a
frame. two-story structure 18x40. The Maxwells saw the need for a larger
building and began a remodeling program at once. They converted their hotel
into a 30x40 three-story building. Selby was "booming" and there was need
for a hotel, both from the residents' standpoint and from the proprietor's
position as to revenue. So business was conducted during the remodeling
program. The story prevails that at one time the kitchen and the dining
room were in separate buildings. It was no easy task to serve hot meals.
During rainy weather the waitress had to walk a plank between the two
buildings, and sometimes the coffee and gravy served was in a somewhat
diluted condition.

Like most of the pioneers who immigrated to this country, Mr. and Mrs.
Maxwell came to Walworth county seeking a comfortable livelihood. Their
monetary funds were limited. Ambition and industry were their greatest
assets. Much could be said to give proof of their use of these attributes.
They always put in and cared for a large garden. It was located on the east
side of town. Incidentally, Mrs. Maxwell retained possession of that garden
spot until 1949. Mr. Maxwell kept a team of horses for helping with the
work in their large garden. And how he drove that team--mostly by sound--it
seems. Many of our "younger pioneers"--present-day citizens of Selby, who
were born and raised here--remember the quiet spring mornings when they
could hear "Old Mac" out in his garden working with his team. He had a loud
gruff voice, and he was continually shouting commands and rebukes at his
horses. Or if it wasn't at his team, it was his hogs.

Mr. Maxwell was much interested in his farming and for many years farmed
the NE 1/4 of 27-123-76, which he homesteaded and on which he had a field
of oats one season that threshed out 125 bushels to the acre,--the largest
yield, it is believed, that was ever known in Walworth county. He also
raised a Poland China hog one season that weighed nearly 1200 pounds.

The Maxwells worked hard to keep their table well supplied for the guests
of their hotel. Besides the garden they raised and fattened hogs. What with
trying to keep a hotel attractive and comfortable for guests, and the task
of maintaining a reputable dining room, one can imagine how busy this
couple was. And in addition to those burdens. they had to put up with the
pranks of the "town sports."

Henry Gross, Frank E. Gehrki, Henry P. Gutz, Phil Greenman, and Henry
Brockman--some of the aforementioned "town pioneers" who resided at the
Auburn Hotel in the early days--were among the younger generation at that
time. They like to tell of the time they smuggled one of the Maxwell's hogs
into the hotel and up to the rear of the hallway on the second floor. "I
can still hear its squeals as it tumbled down the stairs" is a typical
phrase when the story is being told. But the Auburn hotel continued to
function. In fact, not too many years went by before it was enlarged. In
1917 a 24x34 addition was built onto the rear of the hotel.

The Maxwells must have had an abundance of industry and perseverance. They
withstood all of the economical ups and downs, and continued as owners and
operators of the hotel until 1931. In that year they leased the building
and equipment to Mrs. Bertha Ress, who operated the hotel as lessee for
three years. Mrs. Ress became the proprietor in a later year, but in 1934
Mr. and Mrs. Maxwell resumed the operation of the hotel. They did not
attempt to conduct it as a whole unit but rented a part of it as a
dormitory for out-of-town students attending the Selby high school. After
another year of toiling with the affairs of the hotel, the Maxwells found
that their age would not permit them to continue. They sold to Harry Juster
who soon afterwards transferred the title to Mrs. Ress.

On January 3, 1936. Mrs. Bertha Ress took possession of the hotel as owner
and operator. There must be something within or about the four walls of the
Auburn hotel. It seems to draw proprietors who abound in ambition and
industry. Since the day she became its manager, Mrs. Ress has worked
diligently to keep it up-to-date and a pleasant place for Selby's visitors
to reside. Her success is evidenced by the fact that all of her rooms are
practically always occupied. A large number of nonresident hunters who come
to Selby for their pheasant hunting have stayed at the Auburn hotel. They
come back each year, and perhaps they will for many more Years.

THE PRESSLER HARDWARE

The building in which this important Selby business is located was moved to
Selby in 1900 from Bangor. The north section which housed the Melgaard drug
store was moved in September and the south section was brought in, in
November. Dr. Gunderman had his office in the drug store. New fronts were
put on the buildings after arrival at Selby and Dr. Gunderman had his
office in the south section. Dr. Gunderman and Mr. Melgaard were in
partnership in the drug business, the same being dissolved in July of 1921,
Dr. Gunderman continuing the business. The office of R. W. Reynolds the
townsite agent who had taken a Mr. Balliet in as a partner, was moved into
the office section of the building about this time.

Early in 1902. the Schwartz and Spork hardware firm rented the building and
the hardware store which has been such a factor in Selby business circles
and has rendered the community such fine service, came into existence. Will
Schwartz was a skilled tinsmith and plumber who had worked in Minneapolis
and St. Louis and had come to the vicinity of Roscoe and Loyalton with his
family group. Spork was a brother-in-law of Will and Theodore Schwartz.
Improvements in the plant were started at once and a complete stock of
hardware and harness put in, also a tin and plumbing shop started. Later
Mr. Spork left the business and it became the Schwartz Hardware company.
Theodore Schwartz was interested in it at one time and also John and Henry
Nusz. B. P. Holter had charge of the harness shop for a time before going
into business for himself. A lot of Selby history was made around this
store.

In 1917 Schwartz sold out to the Overholser-Leach Hardware company owned by
Eugene and Royce Overholser and R. H. Leach. They had one hardware at
Glenham and Mr. Leach remained in charge there and the Overholsers took
charge here. In 1919 the Overholsers bought out the Leach interest and in
1924 they sold out to Adam Pressler who has operated the store for 26
years. In 1927, Mr. Pressler added a substantial addition to the south part
of the building and in 1939 extended the north side, providing room for an
increasing stock. New shelving has been added from time to time and many
changes made in the interior which have facilitated the handling of the
business and made it possible to offer customers better service and
accommodations. The plumbing service is now handled for the store by Alferd
and LeRoy Moos, who are always ready to serve both the city and the rural
areas on short notice.

In 1937, a grocery line was added to the business and in 1938 a dry goods
line was added. In 1945, the drygoods stock was moved to the Overholser
building and Pressler's Ready-to-Wear store was started. While both
businesses are a family affair, Emanuel Pressler is with his father in the
hardware store and Harry with his mother in the Ready-to-Wear.

Lot 7, used by the Pressler Hardware as a storage for heavy and bulky
stock, was acquired by Dr. Gunderman when he came to Selby and in 1905 he
erected a building 24x28 with a 15-foot ceiling and rented it to A. F. Miles
who moved his furniture and undertaking business into it. In 1910 Mr. Miles
moved his stock to Mobridge and the building was used by the Selby District
for school purposes. The local school building had burned down and this
building was used until the new building was ready for occupancy in 1913.
Henry de Malignon then moved his furniture stock in the building. In 1919
the building and stock was sold to D. W. Welton. At one time Mr. Wickland
had a jewelry shop in the furniture store. In 1929, George W. Head acquired
the Welton stock from Mrs. Welton. The building was used during WPA days as
a recreation hall and in 1940 Nils Carlson moved the bakery into it from
the Burr building, selling later to Wm. M. Hoven who discontinued the
business. Later the building was sold to Frank Gosch Jr., who tore it down
and used the lumber in rebuilding his farmstead west of town. Later Mr.
Pressler acquired the lot.

In 1945, Mr. Pressler purchased the Overholser building from R. L.
Overholser and has utilized the south store room for the ready-to-wear
store and has continued to rent the middle store room to G. W. Paul for a
drug store and the north rooms to Steve Johnson and later to Herbert Aman
for a barber shop.

Adam Pressler was born on a farm north of Freeman South Dakota where he
attended country and grade school. The family moved to Freeman in 1900 and
to Eureka in 1906 and to Hosmer in 1907. There Adam clerked in a grocery
and hardware store until 1913 when he and his father began a hardware
business for themselves. In 1924 Mr. Pressler sold out to his brother and
bought the Overholser hardware at Selby.

Mrs. Josie Pressler was born at Bowdle and received her education in the
Bowdle schools. She was united in marriage with Adam Pressler on November
5, 1914. They have two sons, Harold and Emanuel, who are associated with
them in business. Both were in their country's armed forces in World War
II. Harold married Ruth Evans of Aberdeen, who taught in the Selby schools
and they have two daughters. Emanuel married Eleanor Kent of Denver,
Colorado, and they have three boys.

The Presslers have built three fine houses since they have been in Selby,
all among the best in town. Their business has always been conducted in a
thoroughly up-to-date manner and of their lines it may truly be said: "If
you cannot get it at Presslers, you cannot buy it anywhere." Such service
has developed it into the leading hardware store in this area through the
years.

No progressive civic or religious movement in Selby or this part of
Walworth county has ever lacked the backing of the Presslers, either in
personal effort or financially since they have been in the community.

PRESSLER'S READY-TO-WEAR

This business is conducted in the south room of what has always been known
as the Overholser building built in 1926 and purchased by Adam Pressler in
1945. The south store room was first occupied by F. S. Jones and company, a
dry goods firm who opened October 9, 1926, their business being known as
the Golden Rule Store with Mr. and Mrs. H. W. Stoetzel in charge. About a
year later the J. C. Penney company acquired the business, discontinuing
the same when their new store building at Mobridge was ready for occupancy,
the stock being moved there. Immediately afterwards, a group operating as
the Selby Mercantile company moved in. Harry and Nathan Gross and Morris
Lurie were in charge of it; Mr. and Mrs. Nathan Gross and Mr. and Mrs.
Morris Lurie residing here and being in active charge of the store. They
sold out the stock and started another store in Minnesota. For a time after
they left, the store room was vacant and was utilized as Republican
headquarters and for various other short term uses.

In the fall of 1939 Robert Hepper opened a grocery and meat market in the
store but did not stay long. A Gamble store owned by Calvin Hamann was the
next occupant. In 1943 Presslers moved their Red and White grocery
department from the hardware store to this building. also putting in a line
of dry goods. By midyear of 1947 they had gone out of the grocery business
altogether and started Pressler's Ready-to-Wear, the aim being to supply
the community with an up-to-date and complete line of ready-to-wear
clothing for men, women and children and similar lines. The business has
grown steadily and is now one of the best patronized in town. supplying
needs which bring many people to Selby to do their merchandising. The store
is operated by the Pressler family and is in charge of Harry Pressler and
Mrs. Adam Pressler. Miss Luella Steiger is at present the assistant in the
store.

SMITH'S LOCKER PLANT

This business is situated on Lots 3 and 4 of Block 14. The first building
on these lots was moved in from Mound City in two parts by the late A. F.
Miles of Mobridge, one of the real pioneers of this city. The first section
arrived here on August 18. 1900 and the second on the 25th. Mr. Miles
occupied it with his harness and other lines, including undertaking, until
the new city of Mobridge seemed to offer him greater opportunity and he
sold his Selby property and moved there. The occupancy of the property from
the time Mr. Miles left until Will Schwartz moved in cannot be determined.
One section of the building was used as living quarters and was moved off
and is now the home of Mr. and Mrs. George Keiser, on the west side.

The property came into possession of W. S. Schwartz after he sold out the
hardware store in 1917 and he established a business selling automobiles
and running an auto repair shop. In 1920 John J. Schanzenbach purchased it
and moved his garage business from the Roy Hoefs building back of the
beauty shop on north Main Street and named it the Central Garage. The
business changed hands a number of times, among the owners being Ed.
Schaffer, S. P. Christy and Forrest Wonders. Later Adam Pressler rented it
and remodeled the front into a display room and the rear into an auto
repair and service, putting in a glass front and making quite a nice
business building of it. After his tenancy it stood idle for many years,
and in 1937 A. C. Beckman purchased it cut it down about 6 feet and moved
it to the southwest corner of the block where it now houses the Stulken
Implement company.

In 1941 Ed. F. Perman took title to the site and moved the Perman Implement
company building over from Java, reconstructing it into a modern implement
house. When the new Perman Implement building was ready on north Main
street this property was sold to Paul Smith who built on an addition to the
rear and made it into a locker plant with a store room in front. Ernest
Flemmer put in a Red and White store in the front and Mr. Smith operated
the locker plant. Last year, 1949, Flemmer sold out the store to Smith and
it now houses Smith's Red and White store in front and Smith's Locker plant
in the rear.

The store is modern and well equipped, in common with the Red and White
stores generally over the country. It offers fine services to its patrons
and is in charge of Mrs. Bertha Wagner. The locker plant represents a large
investment in modern slaughtering and meat handling equipment, the latest
addition being a Cry-o-vac vacuum wrapping machine by means of which food is
wrapped in packages from which all of the air has been exhausted, insuring
the keeping of foods almost indefinitely. The refrigeration department is
complete and the whole plant is large enough and so well equipped that it
easily offers the community the very best of locker service. Smith's locker
service is a much needed and appreciated convenience for all of the people
of the community. is widely patronized and helps to make Selby a popular
shopping center.

Paul Smith was born on the Smith farm west of Selby, his parents being
members of families who were among the earliest settlers in the Selby
community, the John Smith and Jacob Elfrink families coming to Walworth
county long before anyone even dreamed of Selby. Paul attended grade and
high school in Selby and had business training at Northern State Teacher's
college at Aberdeen. his higher education being interrupted by World War II
in which he served from February 1944, until June 1946. He was trained at
Camp Blanding. Florida, and saw fighting in the European theatre, serving
in western Belgium and Holland. While yet in his country's service he was
united in marriage with Stella Sorenson at Copenhagen Denmark, she being a
native of Thisted, Denmark, where she grew up and received her education.
When the war was over they came to America and established their home on
the Smith farm west of town and went into business in Selby. They have one
son, aged three years, and a daughter.

The Smiths have taken and are taking their full part in Selby's social and
business life and are making an important place for themselves in the
present history of Selby which will be written in future years.

THE C AND E STORE

The building in which this store is operating was built in 1900 by Phillip
Preszler, who opened a merchandise store which he operated until 1907 when
he sold out to Henry Wolf who came from a farm east of Selby to take it
over. In 1909 W. A. Campbell bought both the building and the business and
taking in his son, Harry as a partner they ran the business under the firm
name of Campbell and Campbell until 1917 when the Juster Brothers bought
building and stock and changed the name to the Selby Cash Store. During the
Campbell incumbency Miss Bergstrom, now Mrs. W. C. Miller, ran a millinery
store in the same building for a short time.

In 1918 Harry Juster bought out his brother, John also a second equity that
had been held by Joseph Goldstein and became the sole owner, expanding the
business and increasing the patronage and sales, drawing trade from a large
area. In 1929 Juster sold out to Sam Raich who again enlarged the stock,
remaining in the business until 1940 when he sold out to Lloyd Sawinsky who
had recently sold the Selby bakery, Raich retaining the building. Mr.
Sawinsky ran the store until November 1948 when he sold the stock to Ernest
Drown and went into the theater business at Onida.

The north part, or residence section, of this building was moved up from
old Bangor by the owners of the Selby Mill who used it as a feed store. It
had been the Catholic church building in Bangor and was moved here in 1904.
The feed store closed in 1908 and John Hagen opened a restaurant known as
the Big Onion. later selling out to V. V. Van Osdell. In 1912 a bad fire
ruined the interior and destroyed the restaurant equipment. The building
was later reconditioned and made into a residence and has since been used
as a home by the families that owned the store.

Through the years this business has been one of the outstanding stores of
Selby, most of the owners operated it with financial success, and also
served the people of the city and community well. The stock has fluctuated
from time to time but the store has often carried the largest stock in
Selby and at times has drawn trade from far beyond the regular territory of
the city. Mr. and Mrs. Drown have modernized the interior and carry a
complete stock of foods and meats and a smaller stock of staple dry goods.
Modern merchandising along with never failing courtesy and prompt service
is increasing their business and helping to extend Selby's trade territory
by bringing more and more people to town.

Ernest E. Drown was born on the Drown farm southwest of Selby in 1909, the
youngest son of Mr. and Mrs. R. O. Drown, who were among the early settlers
in Hilde township. He received his education in the rural schools of Hilde
district and Selby high school and engaged in farming on the home place.
When his brother, Claude took over the farm he went to work in the Red Owl
Store at Sheldon Iowa, later going to Cherokee, Iowa, and Dell Rapids, S.
D., in the same line of work. In 1937 he was united in marriage with Clara
Podoll of Judd, N. D.. and they moved to the Los Angeles area in California
where he worked for Safeway Stores and Royal Farms Dairy. Later he went
into the chicken business and operated an orange grove at Norwalk and then
ran a dairy at Long Beach. In 1945 the family moved back to Selby and
farmed the former DeVelde place north of town for three years and then came
to town and took over the store.

Mrs. Drown was born at Judd, N. D., and is a graduate registered nurse,
receiving her training at Hot Springs, S. D., and Mankato, Minn. She
practiced her profession at the old Lincoln hospital at Aberdeen, then
owned and operated by the Lutheran Good Samaritan Society, for three years
and took executive training. Later she became superintendent of the
Sheldon, Iowa hospital remaining for four years. While residing in
California she did private and hospital nursing in Glendale for one year.
The Drown's have three children: Audrey, Ralph and Vicki Jo.

They are interested and active in the business, social and religious life
of Selby and are doing more than their part in making Selby one of the best
of places in which to live.

PAULS REXALL DRUG STORE

In the fall of 1926 R. L. Overholser opened a newly equipped, modern drug
store in one of the three business rooms of a fine, new brick building he
had just erected on the vacant lots directly north of the First National
bank. Mr. Overholser became a registered pharmacist in 1905 and followed
his profession in the towns of Canova. Chamberlain and Andover. It was at
this latter place that he met Miss Eda Werness, a nurse, whom he later
married. After disposing of the Andover store, Mr. Overholser was for a
time traveling representative for Eli Lilly & Co., pharmaceutical
manufacturers. The Overholsers came to Selby in 1917. Immediately preceding
the opening of his new drug store here, he and his brother, Gene, owned and
operated the hardware store now known as Pressler Hardware company. Mr.
Overholser operated the drug store, which came to be known as the Rexall
Store, until January 1, 1946 when he sold the stock and fixtures to George
W. Paul of Milbank, South Dakota.

Mr. Paul took possession on the above date and his family joined him at the
end of the school year. They purchased the Gene Overholser house which is
now their home. Mr. Paul came to South Dakota in 1919, after a course in
pharmacy at the North Dakota college at Fargo, to accept a position with
the Swartz drug store at Mobridge. He was later employed as a pharmacist in
Aberdeen and in 1920 began work in a drug store in Milbank. For several
years Mr. Paul called on the retail drug trade as salesman for Parke, Davis
& Co. The Pauls were married in Milbank in 1925 and made that town their
home until coming to Selby. Mrs. Paul's parents were long time residents of
Milbank where her father was in the jewelry business for many years. The
Paul's three children are: William E., a veteran of World War II and now a
student at the university of Iowa: Robert M., who attends the state
university at Vermillion; and Susan H., a graduate in this year's class of
Selby high school. The family attends the Methodist church and has taken
part in many activities of the city. In 1948 Mr. Paul served as president
of the Selby commercial club. He is a Mason and a Shriner. Mrs. Paul served
as worthy matron of Hope chapter, O.E.S. in 1949.

THE FIRST NATIONAL BANK OF SELBY

Saturday, April 10. 1909, was the first day of business of the First
National bank of Selby, although the institution had been doing business
for three years prior to that as the Farmers State bank. The First National
bank was a conversion of the banking institution from a state bank to one
authorized to operate under the National Banking Department. so all of the
assets and liabilities of the Farmers State were transferred to the First
National. Consequently, the total deposits on the opening day of the First
National were $113,390.98.

Henry P. Gutz, who had come to Selby in 1901 to work as a bookkeeper in the
Walworth County State bank, organized the Farmers State bank among local
people. Besides Mr. Gutz, the local men who owned capital stock of this
bank were George M. Mickelson. Peter J. Thorstenson and Henry Nusz. The
first meeting of these stockholders was held on June 25, 1906 at which time
Mr. Gutz was elected cashier of the bank and Rose M. Schmidt was employed
as bookkeeper. Two years later Clarence A. Potter was added to the force as
assistant cashier.

At a meeting of the stockholders on June 2, 1908 it was voted to buy Lots
10, 11, and 12, in Block 7 and erect a modern brick building. Construction
was started soon afterwards. and the building was ready for occupancy about
nine months later. In the interim Henry Gutz had applied to the Comptroller
of the Currency, Washington, D. C. for a national bank charter. On January
6, 1909 the stockholders voted for the conversion and two new stockholders
were added, Modeste Marin and Louise J. Gutz. The officers chosen for the
new bank were: John F. Gutz, president; George M. Mickelson, vice
president; Henry P. Gutz, cashier; Clarence A. Potter. assistant cashier;
and Rose M. Schmidt, bookkeeper. There was no change in the personnel of
the bank until 1914.

Arthur A. Brown, who had recently purchased some of the bank stock was
elected a director in January of that year. He filled the vacancy caused by
the death of George M. Mickelson who passed away in October 1913. Mr.
Potter became a stockholder in 1918 and was elected a director to replace
Henry Nusz who moved to California that year. Otto Doherr entered the bank
staff as a stockholder and director in 1920 to take the place of Mr. Brown
who had joined a law firm in western Montana. George T. Mickelson, a son of
George M. Mickelson, was elected president of the bank in 1935 when Henry P.
Gutz resigned and moved to Rapid City as a member of the State Cement
Commission, to assist with the management of the cement plant. In November
1945 Clarence A. Potter suddenly passed away and Max Gutz, son of Henry
Gutz was elected to fill the vacancy of cashier. Other well known citizens
of Selby who became stockholders and served on the board of directors, were
Eugene Overholser and Royce L. Overholser in 1922, W. E. Marin in 1942, and
August Thorstenson in 1945.

The records of the bank reflect the ups and downs of the community; and the
over-all picture gives evidence of the prosperity of Selby and its
neighboring territory. In April 1919 the deposits had grown to $379,175.50
and the capital of the bank had been increased to $38,000.00. At the end of
the next ten-year period the deposits were almost one-half million. Then
followed the national economic calamity and the depression. The bank made
every effort to withstand the continual decrease of deposits, what with the
almost complete non-existence of income in its territory, which meant the
inability of borrowers to pay their loans, but finally had to close in 1932.
When the bank reopened one week later after the termination of the National
banking holiday there followed a steady and remarkable growth. Forty years
after the institution had opened as a national bank its deposits had
increased to around three million dollars, its capital structure had been
enlarged to $117,000.00, and its number of depositors had increased
four-fold.

The officers and directors now comprising the staff of the First National
bank of Selby are George T. Mickelson, who at the present time is serving
his second term as Governor of the State of South Dakota, president and
director; R. L. Overholser, vice president and director; Max Gutz, cashier
and director; August Thorstenson, director; W. E. Marin, director; Theodore
Schanzenbach, assistant cashier; Robert Glerup and Arlene Simon,
bookkeepers.

EAST RIVER OIL COMPANY

The East River Oil company was established in Selby May 2, 1934,--the year
the grass never turned green,--by Emil Kost and Henry Orth. It was first
located on the Gutz lots, one block south of the schoolhouse but moved to
the present site of the Phillips 66 station on highways 12 and 83 in 1936.
During 1937, Orth sold his interest to Kost, who continued to operate the
bulk and service station until January 1, 1949 when he sold it to Ed
Schanzenbach and Herbert Wolff. In 1946, Kost purchased the Texaco station,
just a block farther south on the double highway and in 1947 erected a fine
cement block 10-room all modern tourist cabin camp. The abstract of title
shows some interesting data on this location. Lafayette Brazill obtained
the property on September 3, 1887 and in turn it was deeded to Adam Himrich
on November 3, 1897; to the Milwaukee Land company July 9, 1900; to Joseph
P. Maloney May 18, 1927; to Ella Christopherson November 6, 1929; to A. H.
Brown on May 28, 1939, who improved it by constructing a two-bay service
station. It was leased by the Texaco company that year and sold to Emil
Kost on October 14 1946. In 1949 Mr. Kost bought up the Texaco lease and
became the distributor of Skelly Oil products. Mr. Kost also operates the
East River Oil company station at Webster, and other service stations at
Eden, Lily and Mound City, South Dakota. Emil Kost has always been very
active in Selby community affairs and is at present a member of the city
council and the city fire department. He is a member of the Congregational
church, Elks lodge and is a Mason and a Shriner. He is married to Alvera
Hanson of Scotland, and they have three sons, Ronald, Robert and Roger. The
family resides in the former Henry Pipher house which they purchased in
1936.

THREE B HARDWARE

The building now occupied by the Three B Hardware, located on lot 18, block
13, in Selby was erected in the summer of 1900 by John and Henry Gross who
operated the Selby Implement Co. In February 1904 George Flashman built a
bowling alley on the south side of this implement building. In January 1906
Ed Kingman leased the bowling alley and put Bert Clark in charge, but later
in 1906 Otto Lincke purchased the business and building which included the
bowling alley. Mr. Lincke operated the implement business, and for a winter
season or two operated the bowling alley. The growth of the implement
business caused Mr. Lincke to combine the space to enlarge his implement
business. Mr. Lincke continued in this business until 1928, when he sold the
building to Frank Pitcher and the business to Perman Implement, who
operated this business in this location until December 1941, when they
moved to their own building on the west side of main street. For several
months this building stood empty and in 1942 was purchased by Art Beckman,
who opened the Beckman Hardware. This concern occupied the location until
October 1948 when Wm. Hennig Jr., became the present owner of the property
by buying building and hardware stock.

Mr. Hennig came to Selby from Milwaukee, Wisconsin and is capably assisted
in his business by his wife, Betty. The third B is their young son, Billy,
now four years old.

Mr. Hennig has remodeled the interior of the building and it now includes
an attractive apartment for his family.

THE BERENS HOTEL

The first lot sold in the Selby town lot sale on August 3, 1900, held in
the Court House at Bangor was Lot 1, Block 7. Lot 2, of the same block was
also purchased at the sale. The first building in Selby was a small tool
and oil shed moved up by J. J. Hoven and company the day after the sale and
the fourth building was the Hoven company store which arrived after several
breakdowns, and they were located on these lots, and these with Lot 3
(which has always been vacant) are now the site of the new Berens Hotel.
The pioneer Hoven company merchandising firm was made up of B. B. Potter
and W. B. Burr along with Mr. Hoven. All had been active in business and
promotional affairs at Bangor and saw that the new town would soon replace
the old. They also had a store at Evarts. In 1903 the partnership was
dissolved, Hoven taking the Evarts property and the new firm became Potter
& Burr and continued thus until World War I when Claude Potter was called
into his country's service and Mr. Burr and his son, Chauncey took over as
Burr & Son for a time. Chauncey became sole owner sometime later. In 1925
he closed out the business entirely, holding an auction sale of the
remaining stock, J. J. Hoven serving as auctioneer.

After that time one room of the building was used as a MWA and RNA hall,
and in 1931 the Selby Bakery was moved in by the proprietor, A. M. Avery.
The ownership of that business passed to Lloyd Sawinsky, then to Nils
Carlson, the latter moving it to the Welton building in the year 1940. A
number of other businesses were conducted in the building from time to
time, generally for short periods, and the structure gradually went to
ruin. The lots went to the county for taxes and Fred Adolph purchased a tax
deed to them, later transferring to August Lutz who tore down the buildings
and used the lumber on his farm. The city bandstand stood on the lots for a
time and there was a period when the corner was a weed patch.

When Joe Berens decided to build his hotel, he selected these lots as a
good site and purchased them. Today, one of the finest hotels in the
northwest stands on the historic site. The new structure is 53x140 feet, two
stories high, with full basement. It is of brick and is fireproof
throughout and modern in every respect. One half of the basement has been
fitted as an office for the REA, the other half being utilized for
accessories and storage. The front of the first floor is divided for a bar
and cafe. The Clover Leaf Lounge as the bar has been named, has no
superiors and few equals in design, furnishings and appearance anywhere in
the northwest. The same is true of the DeLuxe Cafe. John Simons is in
charge of the bar and Mr. and Mrs. Melvin Delzer are the tenants in the
cafe. The lobby of the hotel is in the north rear and is also very finely
finished and equipped. The remainder of the building is divided into 6
apartments, 22 rooms and one office room. All are strictly modern. The
general manager is Francis Simons and at least five families will earn a
livelihood in the administration of this property.

Mr. Berens is another of the men who have shown a pioneer faith in Selby by
taking a piece of property that was almost worthless and developing it into
one of the finest business properties in this section of South Dakota. The
investment amounts to half a dozen comfortable fortunes; the taxes it will
pay will mean much to the city and county, and the patronage that it will
bring to the city will bring profit to many other businesses.

Joe Berens is the son of Mr. and Mrs. John Berens, pioneer residents of
Selby, and was born and grew up in this area. He has long been one of the
largest farm operators in Walworth county, being an exponent of the
application of tractor power to diversified farming and soil conservation.
Mrs. Berens is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Anton Allmendinger and was born
in South Russia coming to America with them while she was quite young, and
has resided most of her life in Walworth county. They were married at Selby
in 1926 and have two sons, Leo and Eddie, both at home and interested in
the farming operations, and one daughter (Anna) who is attending Selby high
school. They have resided in Walworth county practically ever since their
marriage. Their first home was on the Lemke quarter next west of the Nels
Anderson place southwest of Selby.

Starting with practically nothing, the Berens' now have one of the finest
sets of farm buildings in Walworth county and own a total of 3280 acres of
land. They went through the depression and dry years along with others. The
farm plans have always provided for soil conservation by means of crop
rotation, summer fallow and stock raising. Many new methods have been tried
out and the farm equipment has always been of the best and most up-to-date.
The Berens' farm is one of the largest, best-equipped and best-tilled in
several counties.

MANKE'S CHEVROLET GARAGE

The lots on which this business is situated were first utilized for
business purposes as a site for a livery barn in the year 1902 when Hugh
Personius bought the home and livery stable of C. E. Wilson and moved the
barn to Lots 8 and 9. Lots 6, 7, 8, and 9, Block 18, had been purchased at
the town lot sale in 1900 by Jay Irwin. Personius ran the livery stable
until 1905 when he sold out to Matt Miller who in turn sold to John Berens
and Jake Allerdings and they operated the business for many years. C. E.
Boling had a garage and implement business in it for a time, handling the M
& M line, and when it burned down in 1923, it was Hill's Garage. This fire
is known as Selby's most costly fire to that date because of the large
number of cars stored in it and, also a lot of building material belonging
to John Berens. Since the fire, these lots were vacant until recently.

The first building was erected on Lots 6 and 7 in the year 1917 when Harry
Mickelson and "Bug" Stablein put up the cement block garage which is still
in use. Harry Mickelson moved in from his farm southwest of Selby to go
into this business. Stablein having been employed elsewhere in the city.
When it was built, this garage was considered quite a pretentious building.
The Mickelson and Stablein partnership was dissolved in 1923, Mickelson
taking over. A short time afterward he sold out to Hill and Schwarting.
Arnold Manke bought it in 1926 from Wolf and Miller who had purchased from
Hill and Schwarting and operated for only a short time. Frank Taylor and
Paul Bertha were associated with Mr. Manke in the business for a time.

Mr. Manke obtained the Chevrolet contract and from time to time added new
equipment, operating a sales and service Household appliances were added
later. In 1948 he purchased the vacant lots where the livery barn, above
mentioned, had been situated and built a new brick building 40x50 with full
glass front as a show and sales room adjoining the garage. The older
building has been repaired and improved as time passed and the place is now
one of the modern attractive business structures of the city.

Arnold Manke is the son of Mr. and Mrs. Albert Manke and was born at
Atlantic, Iowa, but grew up on the Manke farm southeast of Selby. The family
came to Walworth county in 1906. He received his education in the schools
of Surrey district and his technical training at the Sweeney Auto School in
Kansas City, and in short courses in his line of work from time to time.
Mrs. Manke is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. John Smith and grew up on the
Smith farm west of town, receiving her education in the Selby school and
the Aberdeen Normal. Before her marriage she taught successfully in the
Selby school for a number of years. They have two children,--John, who is
attending the State university at Vermillion and Joyce, a student in Selby
High. They have a fine home in the west part of town and both are much
interested in civic, religious, and educational affairs in the city and can
be depended upon to boost for the good of Selby and its institutions at any
and all times. Mr. Manke has been a member of the Selby City Council for
several years.

NATIONAL INSURANCE & REALTY CO.

The building occupied by this business was once the Farmers & Merchants
bank building at Bangor, owned by Balch and Smith, and was moved to Selby
soon after the town started. This bank and the other Bangor bank building,
the Walworth County bank, took part in a friendly bank race on the day they
were moved, the Farmer & Merchants building winning the race by a matter of
seconds, the time being clocked as two hours and 15 minutes, during which
time the structure was moved the 4 miles from Bangor to Selby. On January
13, 1902, the two banks consolidated, operating thereafter as the Walworth
County bank and the Farmers & Merchants building was sold to R. W.
Reynolds, who started a real estate business. which was the basis for the
present real estate and insurance business still being conducted in this
building.

In 1907. the building and business was purchased by W. B. Myler who came to
Selby from Armour, South Dakota, and operated a real estate business in
Selby and the famous Blue Blanket valley. In 1910, Stewart Cook came to
Selby as secretary for Mr. Myler, and later purchased an interest in the
business, eventually succeeding Myler as owner of the business and
building. For a time, John Seeley rented the south room of the building for
a barber shop and housed his family upstairs. Vudley Martin also operated a
barber shop there for a number of years. For a short time, Robert Nusz was
a partner in the insurance business with Mr. Cook. In 1939 the agency was
incorporated as the National Insurance and Realty company and continues to
operate under that title. The present owner of the building is George
Schaffer.

Stewart S. Cook was born in Ferney, Brown county, South Dakota, on May 21,
1890, and received his education in the public schools and business college
at Aberdeen. Prior to coming to Selby, he was employed in a bank at
Houghton. In 1921 he was appointed city auditor by Mayor Overholser, which
office he continues to fill. On April 30, 1924, he was married to Mary C.
Reilly of Aberdeen, South Dakota. He has taken an active part in city and
community affairs, serving as secretary of the commercial club and other
organizations from time to time. Mrs. Cook is the Walworth county public
health nurse and maintains her office in the south room of the building.
They reside in the upstairs apartment over their offices.

THE MINUTE CAFE

The building in which this business is conducted was moved to Selby from
Bangor in the year 1900. In Bangor it was the home of the Walworth County
State bank, the first in the county and was built by W. R. Green, one of
the founders of the bank. Dr. A. E. Byron opened his office in this
building when he located in Selby in 1906 and Dr. M. W. Myler had his
dental office in it when he first came to Selby. August Schmidt became the
owner of the property in 1907 and in 1909 Frank Pechek of Eureka opened a
tailor shop. In 1913 Mrs. Anna Larabee opened a bakery and lunch room and
in 1919 Rose McIntosh rented it for a millinery store.

Jacob D. Schanzenbach purchased the building a short time later and moved
in his cream station and built on an addition for more space. A year or two
later he went to Isabel, selling the property to George Schaffer, who built
in living quarters and continued the cream station. Albert Moos had a cream
station and shoe shop in the building for a time. George Schaffer finally
sold the property to Sam Raich who rented it out for a mattress factory for
a time, later to various temporary tenants and then to Hettich Brothers who
put in a lunch room. During this year the lunch room was sold to Mr. and
Mrs. Edward Schaffer by the Hettichs.

Edward Schaffer was born on a farm 2 1/2 miles northwest of Eureka, his
parents having come to South Dakota from Russia and homesteaded in the
early days. He received his education in the rural schools of McPherson
county and worked as a garage mechanic for many years in Java, Mobridge and
Selby. He served the Selby school district for eight years as a mechanic
and school bus driver before his recent resignation. He also spent a number
of years in the west river country homesteading at Lightcap in Corson
county and owning several pieces of land in that area. He then traded his
land out there for the Central Garage at Selby, which he later sold.

Mrs. Schaffer was born at Medora, North Dakota, and received her education
in the schools of that state. Her parents were born in South Russia and
resided in several localities in North and South Dakota before coming to
Walworth county in 1933 when they moved northeast of Java near the Edmunds
county line. She was united in marriage with Ed Schaffer at Leola in 1940.

Mr. and Mrs. Schaffer have recently started in business in Selby and are
endeavoring to give good service and be accommodating and friendly. They
offer to the public lunches and soft drinks. They make their home in the
building and offer service at all hours.

THE SANITARY BARBER SHOP

The first barber shop in Selby was located on Lots 5 and 6, Block 14, on
the west side of Main street. These lots were purchased by Siegel F. (Sig)
and Agnes Hoffman in 1902 from the Milwaukee Land company, and they moved
their building from Bangor. It housed the shop and their living quarters. A
few years later the Hoffmans moved to California and rented the shop to a
man by the name of Dowdy. Mr. Dowdy's wife assisted in the operation of the
shop, doing the lathering for him on busy days. This was the only time a
woman was known to work in a barber shop in Selby. In 1914 Mr. Dowdy rented
the shop to Irvin Dudley who employed S. M. Johnson to work with him.

In the fall of 1915 the Dudley family left Selby and S. M. "Steve" Johnson
purchased the shop furnishings and equipment; thus beginning a long career
as Selby's barber. Johnson kept the shop at this location for two more
years; and although he had no regular help, it was during those years that
Clayton Allerdings, better known to his many friends as "Lefty" worked
there as a boy and conducted one of the biggest little businesses in Selby
as a first class shoe shiner.

The shop was moved in October, 1917, to the downstairs of the H. P. Gutz
building, known now as the Dettman building, and remained at this location
for the next nine years. During a part of this time Ray Hyde, who came from
Bingham Lake, Minnesota, was employed to operate a second barber chair in
the shop. Also, there was an interval of one year while Johnson and Hyde
served in the World War I army when the shop was operated by Ole Olson of
Herreid, South Dakota. Ray Hyde continued to work with Steve for two years
after the war and then returned to Minnesota, where he still resides.
Dudley Martin, who formerly operated his own shop in Selby, joined Steve at
this time and worked at a chair between his several terms as sheriff of
Walworth county.

Late in the year 1926 Steve moved his shop to the then newly constructed
Overholser building, where rooms suitable to a barber shop had been
completed in the north part. He equipped it with new fixtures and gave it
the name "Sanitary Barber Shop." Shortly before this move William Haux,
called "Red" by all, came to work for Steve and became a familiar figure
beside the front chair. Three years later he left and went to Mound City
where he purchased a shop. Mr. Haux is now at the Sherman Barber Shop in
Aberdeen, South Dakota. After his departure from Selby the Sanitary Barber
Shop was conducted by Mr. Johnson alone for several years.

In October, 1947, Herbert Aman came to work for Steve, and on January 2,
1949, he purchased the fixtures and equipment and became proprietor of the
shop.

Mr. Johnson retired with the distinction of being in business continuously
for the longest period of time of any business man in Selby.

Herbert Aman was born and reared on a farm near Mound City, South Dakota.
After his discharge in 1945 from the armed services following the close of
World War II, he married Elva Rossow, daughter of Alfred C. Rossow, also of
Mound City; and upon completing his barbering course in Fargo, North
Dakota, the couple came to Selby. In the winter of 1948 a daughter, Deanna
Faye, was born to the Amans. Since taking over the barber shop Mr. Aman has
worked without assistance except occasionally when Steve gave him some
relief.
